Something broke on this page : "The rest of EiN still works." An error while drawing the page; the error text is shown under it, and below that where it happened. Reload . If it keeps happening, choose Copy details and send what it copies to your administrator. An entry you expect is not in the sidebar It is for administrators, its module is not installed, or someone hid it. See the sidebar table above, Modules and Your sidebar and top bar .

Search and the finder : everything the search box and the Search page can find. The terminal : the command line behind Alt + T . Keyboard shortcuts : every key, by area. Your sidebar and top bar : rename, hide and add entries. EiN on a phone : the menu behind the mark, swiping and adding EiN to the home screen. Your profile, favourites and trash : your own pages from the account menu. Addresses in the Web UI : every page's address, for links.

EiN gives you two ways to find something: the finder in the top bar, which takes you to a page, an action or a command in a few keystrokes, and the Search page. What there is to search comes from the modules installed; this page covers what EiN itself gives, for everyone who uses EiN in a browser. With the Archive installed, Searching your pictures covers finding photos, videos, recordings and documents, and the albums, people and places they belong to.

p.h: The finder in the top bar
p.x: The box in the middle of the top bar, Search for anything , is the finder. Click it, or press Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) wherever you are, and a list opens under it. The list closes when you press Esc , click somewhere else or choose a row, and choosing a row empties the box. When something covers the box (a dialog, the viewer, or a page shown full screen), the same keys open the finder as a dialog of its own, with the prompt Search, or go to a page… . Esc , or Ctrl + K again, closes it. On a phone the box reads Search , the list takes the width of the screen, and the keyboard's search key does what Enter does. EiN on a phone covers the rest. With no module installed, the finder finds the pages in your sidebar, the actions in the top bar and EiN's commands. Each module adds its pages and actions, and the Archive adds its albums, people, locations and cameras by name.

With the box empty, the list shows two groups: Go to : every page in your sidebar, with the sidebar section it is in beside it. Do : every button in the top bar, and every row of its menus named after its menu. With the Archive and the assistant installed, these include Chat , Random album , Create: Album , Create: Import media and Account: Favourites . Use the arrow keys to light a row and Enter to open it, or click it. While nothing is typed, Enter does nothing until an arrow key has lit a row.

As you type, the list changes to these groups, in this order: Group Rows A row takes you to Search Search for "<your words>" , and with the Archive installed Pictures of "<your words>" The Search page, or the Archive's Media page, searching for the words Go to and Do The pages and actions whose names hold your words That page or action The kinds the Search page finds Their things whose names match, with the kind of each beside it. With the Archive installed the group is Albums, people, locations, cameras Its page The first row is lit, so Enter opens the Search page for your words, and so does the arrow button at the end of the box. To go straight to a page or a thing, light its row with the arrow keys or click it. With the Archive installed, in the Wrenfield demo, typing peggy offers Peggy Wrenfield, and typing christmas offers albums such as Christmas 1975, Christmas 1998 and Christmas in Wellington. While names are being looked up the list says Looking… ; when nothing fits it says Nothing matches. Note Words you take to the Search or Media page from the finder are searched exactly as you typed them. To have a sentence read into people, places and years (see Write what you are looking for ), press Enter once more in that page's own box.

Starting with > turns the finder into a search of EiN's commands. Click the box or press Ctrl + K . Type > followed by what the command should do, or part of its name, such as >person . Up to six commands appear under Commands , each with its one-line description. Choose one to open its entry in EiN's documentation ( Documentation in the sidebar). Choosing a command does not run it: you run commands in the terminal . With fewer than two letters after the > , the list says Type what the command should do. , and when nothing fits, No command matches. The line at the foot of the list, Type > to find a command , is there as a reminder. When the assistant module and the media service are installed, the finder looks for commands by what they are for, so a command can turn up even when its name and description use other words than yours. Without them, and while the media service is not answering, it matches your words against the commands' names and descriptions. The command reference lists every command.

Search , under Explore in the sidebar, searches the kinds of things the installed modules make searchable. With no module installed it has nothing to search: before you type it says Search for anything , and a search answers No results found . With the Archive installed it finds albums, people, locations and cameras; see Find albums, people, locations and cameras . Open Search in the sidebar, or choose Search for "…" in the finder. The header reads Search and Search by name, date or @mention . Type in the box, Search, or type @ to pick something by name , and press Enter . The results appear as cards, 60 at a time, with more as you scroll. A card shows the name, a cover picture and the kind. Click a card to open its page. When the modules make more than one kind searchable, narrow the results with Show : All , or one of the kinds. Order them with Sort : Relevance (the default), Name (A-Z) , Newest first or Oldest first . When nothing is found, the page says No results found . The box takes @ to pick something exactly, turns what it understood into chips you can remove one by one, and offers the Interpreted filter to show what it searched for. Which words it reads as people, places, years and kinds comes from a module: the Archive reads them, and Searching your pictures explains how. Without it, the box searches your words as they are. Every search finds only what you are allowed to see; a visitor browsing without signing in finds only what is shared with everyone ( Sharing ).

Before you type, the Search page shows Recent searches : your last eight searches on this page. Click one to run it again, its × ( Forget … ) to drop it, or Clear to drop them all. They are kept in this browser, not in your account, so another computer or phone has a list of its own. Under them come the sections the modules give the page. With the Archive installed, these are the people, locations, years and labels to start from; see Start from people, places, years and labels . With no recent search and no module to offer a section, the page says Search for anything and "Type a name, a year or a few words; @ picks something by name."

The address in your browser holds the whole search: the words, the chips, Show and Sort . So a search can be linked, and the browser's Back and Forward step through your searches. Copy the address to send a search to someone in the family, or to come back to it later. Whoever opens the link sees only what they are allowed to see. To keep a search in your sidebar, see Your sidebar and top bar .

EiN's search is one command, search , and the modules supply what it searches. A module plugs in by the names of its commands and by its manifest: What a module gives What it adds to search search-<x> commands Hits for the words of a search; search asks every one on the path and puts the hits together subject-<kind> commands What a person, location or camera picked with @ has Node types marked searchable in its manifest The kinds the Search page finds and offers under Show , and the things the finder finds by name Panels for the Search page The sections shown before you search, and what a search for one label adds A reader for the box, named by CFG_SEARCH_PARSER How a sentence is read into chips A command finder, named by CFG_COMMAND_FINDER Commands found by what they are for, in the finder With no module, search has no provider to ask and the Search page no kind to find. The Archive brings the providers for albums, people, locations, cameras, tracks, media and documents, and the reader for the box; the assistant brings the command finder. Writing a module shows how a module plugs in, and the settings are in the settings reference . In the terminal , search answers the same questions as the pages. Its options are in the command reference ; Search from the terminal gives examples over the Archive.

Home is the page EiN opens on, with three sections the installed modules fill: On this day , News and Events . The Statistics page shows how what EiN holds has grown, with sections modules add. This page is for everyone who uses EiN, and covers what EiN itself gives; with the Archive installed, Memories, news and events on Home covers what it shows there.

Choose Home at the top of the sidebar. On a computer, the EiN mark at the top left also takes you there. EiN opens on Home when you sign in, unless you were on your way to another page. The page is headed Welcome , "What is new in the archive, what is coming up, and this day in years past". Under the header: On this day runs across the top, when there is anything to show; News fills the wider column on the left; Events stands in a card on the right. On a narrow window or a phone it comes after News, so scroll down past the news to see it. Each section loads on its own, so one can appear before the others. All three show only what you may see. "Today" is the date on your own computer or phone, not the server's.

Each section gathers what every installed module has to say about it, and each entry is drawn by the module it came from. EiN itself adds no entries: Section What EiN does with the modules' entries On this day One row, newest year first, up to 8 entries; when you have more than fit, swipe the row sideways or scroll it with a trackpad. With no entry the section is not shown at all. News A timeline, newest first, up to 8 entries. Beside each is the portrait of the person whose account did it, when the account is linked to a person in the archive ( Your profile, favourites and trash ); otherwise an icon. Events A card headed Events with the number of entries beside it, in up to three groups: Today , Coming up (nearest first) and Recently (the most recent first). It looks 7 days back and 30 days ahead, and holds up to 16 entries. At the right of each Events entry it says when: "Today", "Tomorrow", "Yesterday", "in 9 days" or "3 days ago" up to 13 days away, and after that in weeks, "in 3 weeks" or "2 weeks ago". When there are more than 16 entries, the ones their module marks as milestones are kept first, then the ones nearest to today. With no module installed, Home shows the Welcome header, News says "Nothing has been added yet" and "What people add shows up here.", Events says "Nothing comes round in the next few weeks.", and On this day is not shown. A module can offer a way to begin under the empty News: the Archive offers Import media when you are signed in. With the Archive installed, On this day shows the pictures taken on today's date in earlier years, News the albums people made lately, and Events the birthdays, memorials and wedding anniversaries around today; see Memories, news and events on Home .

Choose Statistics in the sidebar, under System . Everyone can open it. The page is headed Statistics , "Archive statistics over time". It holds the sections the installed modules give it, then Nodes , which is EiN's own. With the Archive installed, the first section is Events , charts of when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall; see Life events on the Statistics page .

The Nodes section shows what has been added to EiN, year by year. Everything in EiN is a node: each file and folder, and with the Archive each photo, album, person and place, and each file EiN makes from them; see How EiN works . File storage growth runs across the full width: the size of the files added each year, counting the originals and the smaller versions EiN makes of them, with a line for "Cumulative file size by month". The total is at the top right. Then one chart for each kind of node, such as Person nodes or Album nodes , File nodes first and the others largest first: bars for the nodes created in each calendar year, a line for the "Cumulative total by month", and the total, such as "2,431 nodes". Rest the pointer on a bar to read the year's count. A node counts in the year it was created in EiN. The charts leave out the kinds that make up the system itself, such as folders, links, accounts and sessions, and they count what you may see. These charts can take a few seconds to appear on a large archive. When there is nothing to count, the section says "No node history found".

What you see Why, and what to do Home is empty No installed module fills it. Modules says which modules there are. Events is a day out Home takes today's date from your computer or phone. Check its date and time zone. A red box above the sections One section could not be loaded, and the box gives the reason. The other sections still show. Reload the page; if the box stays, tell whoever looks after EiN. Memories, news and events on Home covers what goes differently in the Archive's entries.

Home runs ordinary commands, which you can run yourself in the terminal . The Home page passes your own date to them; run in the terminal, they take today's date in UTC unless you name a day. # in EiN's terminal onthisday # what On this day shows, one line a year onthisday 12-25 -- limit 20 # another day, more years news # what News shows, with the time in UTC news -- limit 20 events # what Events shows: 7 days back, 30 days ahead events --today 2026-01-20 # around another date events --days-ahead 0 --days-past 0 # today only events -- source anniversaries # only what the Archive's events-anniversaries gives Each of the three gathers what every installed module offers, from the commands named onthisday-… , news-… and events-… ; with no module they print nothing. Writing a module shows how a module adds to them. The full options are in the reference for onthisday , news and events , and Commands by task lists more.

Memories, news and events on Home : what the Archive shows on Home and on the Statistics page. Sharing : who sees what. Modules : the modules that fill Home. Commands by task : the shell commands by what they do.

The Devices page holds the things outside EiN that report to it or can be switched from it: the sensors, plugs, switches, lights and buttons in the house, a phone that says where it is, a GPS logger, a boat. Each has a page with what it reports now, how that went over time, and the switches to turn. The members of the devices group see them all and add phones and loggers; anyone else sees the devices a member has shared with them. This page is for everyone who uses them. Devices, endpoints and drivers explains how they are kept, and Devices and their keys who may do what.

A driver finds them. With the Automation module, a sensor or a plug that announces itself on the house's MQTT broker, such as one running ESPHome or a Shelly, is on the Devices page within seconds of connecting, with everything it reads and does. Nothing is entered in EiN. One that is on the network but not yet on the broker is counted in the header, such as 2 found , and a Shelly is added from there ( Add a device found on the network ). Someone makes them. A phone or a GPS logger announces nothing, so a member of the devices group makes it by hand (see A phone or a GPS tracker ). EiN's own tracker driver then reads what it sends. So is a button, a sensor or a script that posts to an address, read by EiN's webhook driver (see A device that posts to a webhook ), and, with the Automation module, a camera ( A camera ). A device has a name, such as hall-plug , that commands and automations use, and a label, such as Hall lamp , that the pages show. Each thing it reports or takes is an endpoint with a name of its own within it: hall-plug/switch-0 is the plug's relay, hall-plug/switch-0-power the power it draws, ruby-phone/position where the phone has been.

Open Devices in the sidebar, under Browse . It has a card for every device you may see: its label, its main value, and badges for online or offline , what it is (such as plug or phone ) and how many endpoints it has. A camera's card shows its picture as it was when the page last read the devices. The main value is a temperature when the device has one, then power, humidity, light or energy, else any other reading, else a switch; a device with none shows its manufacturer and model instead. A device that only posts what it has, such as a phone or tracker sending its position or one posting to a webhook, is online while it has been heard from in the last 15 minutes; a device that says nothing of whether it is on has neither online nor offline . Choose a card to open the device. Every device you may see, with what it is and how many endpoints it has. Type in the filter box to narrow the cards by label, name, what it is, manufacturer or model. Show All devices or only those Online . Sort by Name (A-Z) or by Latest value , the device that reported most lately first. The header counts the devices and how many are online. With none yet, the page says No devices yet : "Devices appear here when a driver finds them, or when someone makes one with device-create."

The header names the device, its manufacturer and model, whether it is online, what it is, and how long ago its last value came. Under it are three tabs, and any that modules add: A tracker's Overview is its last position, with the way it came that day. Tab What it shows Overview The page opens here: a tile for each endpoint as it is now, with the switches History How each endpoint went over a day, a week, a month or a year Info What the device is, its driver, each endpoint and its key Trips With the Archive , on a device that has a track: its trips Live With the Automation module, on a camera: its picture as it comes The header's corner has Share , which decides who sees the device ( Sharing ). Members of the devices group also have Edit beside it, and Forget under ⋮ (see Rename or forget a device ); on a phone they are all under ⋮. The address is /devices/ and the device's name, such as /devices/hall-plug , and the tab is in ?tab= ( Addresses in the Web UI ). A device opened from the Nodes page opens here, and so does any of its endpoints.

A tile for each endpoint: A reading , such as a temperature: its value with its unit, how long ago it came, and a line of the last six hours. A button : its last press, such as single , and how long ago it was ("pressed 4 min ago"), or "not pressed yet". A position : a small map of the day up to its last position, and that position: its coordinates, its altitude, speed (in knots on a boat, km/h otherwise) and course when the device sent them, and when it came. The button on the map, Enlarge map , opens it large, with the choice of map; Over time opens it on the History tab. A switch or a light : a toggle that switches it. A setting that takes a number , such as a thermostat's target: a slider, set when you let go, or a box with Set when it has no range. A setting that takes one of some choices : a list to pick from. A setting that takes a word : a box with Set . A colour , such as a light's: a colour box whose picker sets it when you let go, or a colour typed as #ff8000 and set with Set . An action , such as a restart or a chime: Press , with when it was last pressed and by whom. A camera's stream : its picture now, taken again every ten seconds while the page is open, with its size and codec under it, or No picture while the camera gives none. Live plays it as it comes. A switch or a setting you change shows what you asked for at once, with "asked on, waiting for the device" under its label, until the device says it has done it; then it shows what the device reports. A switch you may not change is greyed out. What tells of the device itself rather than of the house, such as its own temperature or its Wi-Fi signal, is under About the device itself . An endpoint the device no longer announces is left out; its history stays.

Every endpoint kept over time is drawn at once, over the span picked at the right of the header's tabs: Day , Week , Month or Year (on a phone, the span's icon button). A track's map comes first, then a chart for each reading, the device's main value, the one its card shows, first among them. Over time on a position's tile puts its track at the top. An endpoint the device no longer announces is marked (retired) . A reading is charted as the average of every 15 minutes over a day, of every 2 hours over a week, of every 6 hours over a month and of every day over a year, to five significant digits. Anything on or off , a switch, a door or a motion sensor, is charted as the share of the time it was on. A button is charted as how many presses there were. A track is drawn on a map, each position of the span, up to the latest 20,000, with how many there are and how long ago the last was. A span with nothing in it says No values in this span. or No fixes in this span.

What the device is: its Name in commands and automations, Class , Driver , Manufacturer , Model , Firmware , Serial and MAC . A driver whose module's service is stopped reads (not running) , in red: the device's switches do nothing until it runs again. Web page , the device's own page, opened in a new tab, when its driver knows it: a Shelly's and an ESPHome node's from what they say of themselves, a printer's admin page and the HTTP page of anything added from the network at its address now. It is on your home network, so it opens only where that network is reached. Each endpoint, with its label and name, its type ( log , track or control ), its unit, its latest value, and whether you may write it. events marks a button's presses, diagnostic or config what tells of the device itself, not read an endpoint whose values its driver cannot read, and retired one the device no longer announces. Config , what its driver was given when the device was made: a camera's stream addresses, a web API's address and what to read of it. A secret field, such as a password, reads set and never shows its value. A member of the devices group changes it with Change while the driver runs; a secret field left empty keeps what it had. The driver takes the change at once. Device key , for a device whose driver reads what is posted to it, such as a phone: the address it posts to (see A phone or a GPS tracker ). Only those who may change the device see it.

The toggles, sliders, colour pickers and Press buttons on a device's Overview switch it. In the terminal, write the value to the control: # in EiN's terminal echo on > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 echo toggle > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 echo 21.5 > /dev/heater/target-temperature echo eco > /dev/heat-pump/mode echo '#ff8000' > /dev/desk-lamp/rgbw-0-color echo press > /dev/hall-sensor/restart A switch takes on , off or toggle ; a number setting a number within its limits; a choice one of its options; a word setting any line; a colour #rrggbb or r,g,b ; an action press . The device's Info tab and device-show say which endpoints are controls and whether you may write them. The value goes to the device at once, and the command ends when the device's driver has taken it, or fails, saying why: hall-plug/switch-0 takes on, off or toggle, not '7' : the value is not one the control takes. hall-plug's driver shelly is not running : the module that drives it has its service stopped. hall-plug/switch-0: not connected to the broker, so nothing was sent : with Automation, EiN does not hear the MQTT broker just now. Access denied for operation 'w' on node: … : the control is narrowed to others ( Devices and their keys ). Nothing is kept to be sent later: a lamp switched on an hour after it was asked would surprise. Use > to switch, never >> (see Writing to a device ). With the Assistant and the Automation module, asking the chat to "turn on the hall lamp" gives a proposal card with the echo line, which you run or decline. With Automation, automations switch things by themselves when a reading, a press or the clock says so.

# in EiN's terminal devices # every device, with its main value devices --online device-show hall-sensor # its endpoints and their values now device-history hall-sensor/temperature -n 10 # the latest 10 values device-history hall-sensor/temperature --since 7d --bucket 1h # an average an hour device-history heater-plug/switch-0-power --since 30d --bucket 1d --agg max # the highest each day device-history ruby-phone/position --since 1d # the day's positions cat /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 # every state the plug reported tail -f /dev/hall-sensor/temperature # each new reading, until Ctrl+C device-history prints a line per value, its time, a tab and the value: --since and --until take a time or a duration such as 24h or 7d , and --bucket sums the values up per interval, with --agg as avg (the default), min , max , sum , count , first or last ; on and off count as 1 and 0. Without --since it gives the latest 100, -n for another number. A track gives its positions.

p.h: A phone or a GPS tracker
p.x: A phone that reports where it is as it moves, a GPS tracker on a boat or in a car, and a logger whose files you copy in are all devices driven by EiN's tracker driver, each keeping where it was in its position track. Members of the devices group make one with Create › Device in the top bar: a name, Reports by (its position, for these), and What it is . Create opens the new device. Or in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create 'Ruby phone' --driver tracker --class phone device-create 'Sailboat' --driver tracker --class boat device-create "Jon's eTrex" --driver tracker --class foot --manufacturer Garmin --model 'eTrex 30x' device-create prints the device's path, such as /dev/ruby-phone . --class says what it is: phone , tracker , or, for something that always travels the same way, boat , car , bike or foot , which the Archive takes as how its trips travel . --manufacturer and --model say more about it, and let a GPX file that names them find it.

A phone with the free Traccar Client app adds its position to the device's track as it moves: Open the device's page at the address the phone will reach EiN at, such as https://ein.wrenfield.example , and its Info tab. Under Device key , choose Make a key . A QR code and the address appear. On the phone, install Traccar Client and scan the QR code in its settings, or with the phone's camera, which opens the app. It fills in the server URL with the key in it and, as the device identifier, the device's name. Or type the server URL in by hand shows the address to type instead. Set how often it reports, for example every 30 seconds, and switch tracking on. OsmAnd reports the same way: give its online tracking the device's address with &lat={0}&lon={1}&timestamp={2} added. So does a hardware tracker that posts the OsmAnd protocol, or GPRMC sentences, over HTTP. The phone posts to EiN from wherever it is, so EiN must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS ( Phones and trackers posting ). The address holds the device's key, and anyone who has it can add positions to the device: New key makes another (the phone stops reaching EiN until it is given the new address), and Take the key away stops it and keeps the track. In the terminal: # in EiN's terminal device-key ruby-phone --new --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example # a new key, and the address device-key ruby-phone --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example # the address, while it has one device-key ruby-phone --off

A GPS logger, a watch or a tracking app saves its routes as GPX files. Write one to the device and its positions join the track; a position with a time the track already has is not added twice, and one without a time is left out: # in EiN's terminal cat ~/tararua-walk.gpx > /dev/jon-s-etrex Over SFTP, copy the file onto the device's path, /dev/jon-s-etrex . With the Archive, a GPX file uploaded into staging finds its device by itself, and the device's Trips tab has Upload GPX ; see GPX files .

p.h: A device that posts to a webhook
p.x: Something without a driver of its own, such as a button that calls an address, a sensor that posts JSON, or a script reading a meter, posts what it reads to a device driven by EiN's webhook driver. A member of devices makes the device and gives it the device's key: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create 'Garden sensor' --driver webhook --class sensor device-key garden-sensor --new --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example # on the machine that posts curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <the key>' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --data '{"soil-moisture": 41.5, "battery": 87}' https://ein.wrenfield.example/file/dev/garden-sensor The key is the part of the address after key= . Each field becomes a reading on the endpoint of that name, made the first time it comes, here soil-moisture and battery : it shows on the device's page and is published on the bus as dev.garden-sensor.soil-moisture , where the Automation module's automations hear it, like any driver's reading. A device that only takes an address sends its values in it instead, https://ein.wrenfield.example/file/dev/garden-sensor?key=<the key>&soil-moisture=41.5 . What the driver reads, and how a button's presses are kept, is in Core's webhook driver .

A script can also write a value straight to a log it made under a device, with no driver in between: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create 'Garden sensor' --class sensor mklog /dev/garden-sensor/soil-moisture attrs -s valueField=value /dev/garden-sensor/soil-moisture device-key garden-sensor --new --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example # on the machine that runs the script curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <the key>' --data 41.5 https://ein.wrenfield.example/file/dev/garden-sensor/soil-moisture Each value is kept with the time it arrived, as {"value": 41.5} , and shows on the device's page like any reading; valueField makes the log keep a value written in the terminal the same way, echo 41.5 > /dev/garden-sensor/soil-moisture . Values written this way are not published on the bus; post them to a webhook device for that.

Members of the devices group rename a device on its page with Edit : Name , what its pages and cards call it, and under Endpoints a name for each endpoint it announces, each field headed by the endpoint's name in /dev . Save writes what changed. Forget , under ⋮, removes the device and everything it kept after asking "Forget <device> and all it has kept? A driver that finds it again makes it again." A sensor that is still on comes back when it next announces itself, without its old history. In the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-label hall-plug 'Hall lamp' # the label its page shows device-label hall-sensor/temperature 'Hall temperature' device-forget old-sensor # the device and everything it kept The name in commands and automations stays as it is. Forgetting removes the device's history with it; a device a driver still hears comes back new.

Task Command List the devices, with their main value devices , devices lamp for those whose name or label holds a word, --online for those that answer List the drivers running, and their devices devices --drivers A device's endpoints and their values now device-show <device> An endpoint's history device-history <device>/<endpoint> , --since , --bucket , --agg Switch or set a control echo <value> > /dev/<device>/<endpoint> Follow an endpoint as values come tail -f /dev/<device>/<endpoint> Make a phone, tracker or logger device-create <name> --driver tracker --class <class> Make a device that posts to a webhook device-create <name> --driver webhook , --config events=<field>,… for a button's presses Give a GPX file to a tracker cat <file>.gpx > /dev/<device> Show, renew or take away a device's key device-key <device> , --new , --off , --origin <address> Show or change what its driver was given device-config <device> [name=value …] , name= takes one away Rename a device or an endpoint device-label <device>[/<endpoint>] <label> Forget a device device-forget <device>

What you see What it means What to do Devices is not in the sidebar You are not signed in Sign in No devices yet No driver has found one, and nobody has made one With Automation, see Check that EiN hears them A switch stays "waiting for the device" The device took the command but has not said it switched: it is off, or out of reach Check its power and its network; the switch shows what it reports once it does The driver reads (not running) The service of the module that brings the driver is stopped An administrator starts it on the Status page's Services tab, or with service start toggle needs the state the device last reported, and it has reported none The control has never reported a state Write on or off instead device-create says only the devices group's members make, name and forget devices You are not in the devices group, or were added since you signed in Ask the administrator to add you, then sign in again Edit and Forget are missing The same The same device-create says 'null' is core's own in /dev, not a device's name The name is one of EiN's own in /dev Choose another name cat ride.gpx > /dev/thermometer says the device has no driver Only a device with a driver that reads raw input takes a file Write it to the tracker it was recorded on The phone reports nothing It cannot reach EiN over HTTPS from where it is, its key was renewed or taken away, or tracking is off in Traccar Client See Report from a phone and Ports, HTTPS and remote access

Devices, endpoints and drivers : how devices are kept, written to and published. Devices and their keys : who may do what, and what a device key opens. Automation : sensors, plugs and buttons over MQTT, and automations. Trips : with the Archive, the trips a device's track is cut into.

Whoever may change something in EiN decides who else sees it. This page is for everyone who shares what they keep in EiN: the Share dialog, the chip that says how visible something is, links for people without an account, keeping a few photos private in a shared album, how new albums start out, and why you may not see everything that is there. The Share dialog is EiN's own and works on any node. Most of what people share are albums, which come with the Archive , so the examples here are albums, and the parts that only albums have say so.

An album, and everything in it, can be seen by: its owner , usually whoever made it, who can always see and change it; the people and groups it is shared with , each with Can view or Can edit ; everyone with an account , when it is shared with them, as most albums are; visitors who are not signed in , only when the administrator lets visitors browse and the album is shared with them; anyone with its link , a link you send to someone without an account. On a standard installation a new album starts out seen by everyone with an account and changed only by you. How new albums start out has the details. Note The administrator sees and can change everything, private albums included. "Private" keeps an album from the rest of the family, not from the administrator. You do not need to know how this is stored. The Share dialog says it in words, and Permissions in depth has the exact rules underneath.

Share is offered only on things you may change: Anything in the tree : open Nodes , pick the node and choose the Sharing tab. Nodes is under System in an administrator's sidebar; anyone signed in can open it at /system/nodes . With the Archive installed, its pages offer Share as well: An album : Share in the album's header. On a phone the header's buttons are under ⋮ . A person, a location or a camera : Share in its header. Sharing a person shares their page, not the photos they are in. One photo, video or recording : open it in the viewer and choose Share in the cog menu of the details panel (see Viewing photos, videos and recordings ). Several photos of an album : select them and choose Share in the selection bar; see Keep some photos private in a shared album . The chip under an album's title, and the one in the viewer's details panel, both the Archive's, open the same dialog; see The visibility chip . Opened by someone who may only look, the dialog shows who has access without letting them change it, and says "Only Helen Okafor and people who can edit it can change who it is shared with." One dialog decides who sees an album and who may change it, and makes the link for someone without an account. The dialog is headed with what it shares, such as Share “Christmas at the cottage” , and has up to four parts: Who can see it , People with access , Share with a link (albums only) and With their own sharing (when some photos keep sharing of their own).

Open the album and choose Share . Under People with access , click Add people or groups and type a name. The list offers Everyone with an account first, then groups, such as Family (group) , then people, such as Jon Wrenfield (jon) . Choose one. The new row starts at Can view . To let someone change the album too, open the menu at the right of their row and choose Can edit . To take someone away, open the same menu and choose Remove access . Choose Save . Nothing changes until you choose Save . Until then the button at the left says Cancel , and closing the dialog drops your changes. Once nothing is left to save it says Close .

p.h: Who can see it, and the two presets
p.x: The top of the dialog says in a sentence who can see the album, with the visibility chip beside the heading. The sentence follows your changes before you save, so you can see what a change will do. Two buttons fill the list for you: Button What it sets Default The administrator's default sharing: its group, with what it gives the owner and the group. Nobody else is listed. Private Nobody but the owner: every person, group and visitor row is taken away. The button that matches the list is highlighted. A preset only fills the list; Save applies it. Default is the sharing your administrator chose for what is created as shared, under Settings → Permissions → Sharing ; resting the pointer on it says whom it shares with. On a standard installation that is everyone with an account, who can view it. Where the administrator also named an owner, Default gives the album to that person, and the dialog shows them as its owner before you save; you then keep only the access the default sharing gives you. It is not How widely what you create is shared on your profile, which is yours alone. Private does not touch a share link. An album with a link stays Public to anyone holding the link until you choose Delete link under Share with a link . On a photo that keeps its own sharing there is a third button, Like the album . It shares the photo as the album is, and lets the album's later changes reach it again. See Put photos back to the album's sharing .

The list starts with the owner, marked Owner (and "(you)" when it is you). Then comes everyone the album is shared with, each row with a picture, a name and a line under it: Row The line under it Who it is Everyone with an account The Users group Everyone who signs in, including accounts made later. A group, such as Family Group · 6 people The members of the group, as the administrator set it up. A person Their username That account only. When the list is empty, it says "Nobody else has access." Each row's menu sets what they may do: Level What the menu says What it allows Can view See it and download it Open the album and its pictures, and download them. Can edit Also add to it, change it and delete from it Everything above, and add pictures, change them, delete from the album, and change who it is shared with, links included. Remove access Takes the row away when you save. Give Can edit only to people you trust with the album: they can share it further or make it private. Groups are made by the administrator, under Settings → Groups (see Accounts and groups ). To share with part of the family only, ask for a group such as family , then share with the group rather than with each person. An administrator can rest the pointer on a group's row to see who is in it.

p.h: Visitors who are not signed in
p.x: Visitors who are not signed in is a row of its own, under the others. It is there when the administrator lets visitors browse EiN without an account, and then says "Anyone who opens EiN, without an account". Its menu has only Can view and No access : visitors never change anything. When visitors may not browse, the row is shown only on something already shared with them, and says "This EiN asks visitors to sign in, so they see it only once it lets them browse." To let one person without an account see an album, send them a link instead.

Save applies the list to the album and to everything in it, in one go. Two kinds of things inside are left as they are: photos that keep their own sharing (see Keep some photos private in a shared album ); what you may not change, or may not even see. The dialog says what happened under the list: "Saved.", followed by "2 items inside keep their own sharing." or "3 items inside were left as they were: you cannot change them." where that applies. Pictures uploaded into the album later get the album's sharing, its link included. A picture added to the album from another album keeps the sharing of the album it lives in: sharing this album does not change it, and someone who may see this album but not the other one cannot open it.

With the Archive installed, under an album's title, and in the viewer's details panel for a single file, a small coloured chip says how widely it is shared. Resting the pointer on it shows the sentence from the table, and clicking it opens the Share dialog. The chip answers one question at a glance: who besides you can see this. Chip When What it says Public , green, with a globe A share link opens it, or it is shared with visitors and visitors may browse. "Anyone with its link, or any visitor, can see it without signing in" No chip Everyone with an account can see it. "Everyone with an account can see it" (in the dialog) Restricted , orange, with a lock in a frame Some people or groups besides the owner can see it, but not everyone with an account. "Only some of the people with an account can see it" Private , red, with a lock Nobody but its owner. "Only its owner can see it" Most albums have no chip, because most are seen by everyone with an account. Visitors and people who opened a link never see the chip: they are not told who else can see something.

p.h: Share an album with a link
p.x: A link lets someone without an account see one album, without signing in. The dialog makes links for what a module offers them for: albums, which come with the Archive, and dashboards, whose display links show them on a screen that never signs in; see Show a dashboard on a screen . Open the album and choose Share . Under Share with a link , next to "Send a link to someone without an account", choose Create link . The link is made at once; it does not wait for Save . Click the address, your EiN's address followed by /s/ and a code, or the copy button at its right. EiN says "Link copied to clipboard". Paste the link into a message to the person. The address starts with the address you opened EiN at. Open EiN at an address the person can reach before you copy the link: one with localhost in it works only on the machine EiN runs on, and one such as http://ein.local:8080 only on your home network. Reaching EiN from outside the home is the administrator's to set up; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Under the address, the link's row says when it stops working and how often it has been opened: When it stops working. A new link works for 30 days: "Expires in 30 days, on 24 Nov". Click that text for the Works for menu: 1 day , 1 week , 30 days , 3 months , 1 year or No end date , counted from now. The change is made at once. A link without an end says "Never expires", and one in its last day "Expires within a day". How often it was opened. "Not opened yet", "Opened once, last today", "Opened 4 times, last yesterday", "Opened 9 times, last 3 days ago", or a date. The count covers everyone who has the link; it does not say who opened it. Delete link turns the link off at once, for everyone who has it. The album gets one link in the dialog, so everyone you send it to uses the same address. While the album has a link its chip says Public . The link opens the album and everything in it that you may change, except photos that keep their own sharing: then the dialog adds "The link does not open what keeps its own sharing, listed below." Pictures uploaded into the album later are opened by the link too. Someone who may only look at the album sees that it has a link, when it expires and how often it was opened, but not the address. Without a link, they see "No link opens this album."

p.h: What the person you send it to sees
p.x: The link opens a page that says "Opening what was shared with you…". Then the album's page opens, without signing in. They see that album and what is in it, and no other page of EiN: there is no sidebar and no search box, and the EiN mark at the top leads back to the album. Any other page asks them to sign in. In the viewer they see the pictures without the details panel, and can save each one with Download in the viewer's More menu . A few things to know about links: A browser holds one link at a time. Opening a link to another album leaves the first one. To go back, open the first link again. Someone signed in stays themselves. If the person has an account and is signed in, the album opens as their own account sees it. Where visitors may browse , someone who opened a link still sees only what the link opens, not what is shared with visitors. When a link has expired or been deleted, or the address is mistyped, the page says This link no longer works : "It may have expired, or the person who shared it has turned it off. Ask them to send you a new link." with a Sign in button for someone who has an account.

An expired link opens nothing. The dialog shows it marked Expired until EiN clears expired links, which it does every hour by default. While it is still listed, choose a new time in its Works for menu to make the same address work again, or choose Delete link and then Create link for a new address.

p.h: Keep some photos private in a shared album
p.x: With the Archive installed, you can keep a few photos of a shared album to yourself, or show them to fewer people, without moving them out of the album. Share in the selection bar gives the chosen photos sharing of their own, apart from the album's. In the album, select the photos: tick the round box in a picture's top-left corner, Ctrl -click ( ⌘ -click on a Mac) to add more, or Shift -click to add a range. On a phone, press and hold a picture. Albums has every way to select. Choose Share in the selection bar at the bottom. The dialog is headed Share 3 photos , with "In “Christmas at the cottage”" under it. Choose Their own sharing : "Only those you choose below. They keep this when the album's sharing changes, and the album's link does not open them." Under People with access , the photos start with nobody but their owner ("Each keeps its owner, who can always see and change it."). Leave it so to keep them to yourself, or add the people or groups who should still see them. Choose Save . EiN says "3 photos now keep their own sharing". Everyone else no longer sees those photos in the album at all, and the album's link does not open them. When the album's sharing changes later, they keep theirs. If you may change the album, a lock in the corner of a picture marks one that keeps its own sharing; resting the pointer on it says "Keeps its own sharing". A folder inside an album can carry the lock too. People who may only look at the album do not see it. Share in the selection bar is greyed out when the selection includes a picture that is only linked into this album from another album. Such a picture has the sharing of the album it lives in; change it there. Selecting only photos that already keep their own sharing opens the dialog on Their own sharing , with the first photo's people, so you can change who sees them.

p.h: Put photos back to the album's sharing
p.x: There are three ways: From the selection bar. Select the photos, choose Share , then Like the album : "Whoever can see “Christmas at the cottage” can see them. When the album's sharing changes, they change with it." Choose Save . EiN says "3 photos shared like the album". From the album's Share dialog. With their own sharing , with a count beside it, lists the photos that keep their own sharing: "These keep their own sharing: changes to the album's sharing, and its link, do not reach them." Each row shows the photo, its name and Private , Shared differently or Open to visitors . Share like the album on a row puts that photo back at once, and Share all like the album puts every one of them back, listed or not. The first five are listed; Show all 12 lists the rest. The list stops at 50, and "And 7 more." under it counts the others. From the viewer. Open the photo, choose Share in the cog menu, and the dialog says "It keeps its own sharing: changes to the album “Christmas at the cottage” do not reach it." Choose Like the album , then Save .

Albums come with the Archive. Create → Album asks only for a name and a description. The new album gets the sharing your new albums start with, which comes from two places, both EiN's own settings. The administrator's default sharing , under Settings → Permissions → Sharing , sets who may see and change anything created as shared, which group it is shared with, and, if they choose, an account that owns it instead of its creator. On a standard installation the group is users , so a new album is seen by everyone with an account and changed only by you. See Permissions in depth . Your own preference narrows or widens that. Choose your picture at the right of the top bar, then Profile , the Preferences tab, and How widely what you create is shared : Choice A new album starts out default As the administrator set it. This is the choice until you change it. private Seen by you alone, and yours even where the administrator chose another owner. Its chip says Private . shared Seen by the administrator's default group. On a standard installation that is everyone with an account; with a narrower group, such as family , only its members. everyone Seen by the default group and by everyone with an account. It never includes visitors who are not signed in. Change the choice and Save change appears under it. Your profile, favourites and trash has more on preferences. The preference applies to albums you create with Create → Album , and to new albums you make when you file pictures from your staging area. There, New private album always makes one only you can open, and pictures filed into an existing album take that album's sharing; see Sorting in staging . Anything else you create, such as a person or a location, or a picture you upload into an album, takes the sharing of where it is created. Changing the preference changes no album you already have. To change one, use its Share dialog.

EiN leaves out what you may not open. A folder, file or album that is private to someone else is not listed to you at all: not in search, not in ls or find in the terminal, and with the Archive not on Albums , in News or on the map. Here EiN differs from the files on a computer, where you see every name in a folder you can open, only not what is inside. So two people can see the same album differently, and an album can look emptier to you than to its owner. The administrator sees all of it. What is hidden is still there, and that explains some surprises: Counts are your own. The number on an album's card counts only the pictures you can see, so it can differ from person to person. Changing an album's sharing leaves what you cannot see as it is. The Share dialog says "3 items inside were left as they were: you cannot change them."; in the terminal, share-set and chmod -r say "1 child the caller may not read left unchanged". Moving or renaming an album or folder takes everything in it along , including what you cannot see. So does moving it to the trash. A folder can look empty and not be. In the terminal, rmdir answers "Directory not empty" and rm "Node not empty" for a folder whose only contents are hidden from you. A name can be taken by something you cannot see. Moving something to that name fails with "Access denied for operation 'w'". Copying a folder fails if it holds anything you cannot read , with "Access denied for operation 'r'" naming the folder, rather than making a copy that is missing it. Deleting a folder you may change with rm -r deletes everything in it , including what you cannot see, as on a computer, where deleting needs only the right to change the folder. If something behaves as though it holds more than you see, ask its owner or the administrator.

There is no Share button. You may not change the album, person or file. Ask its owner to give you Can edit , or to share it for you. Someone you shared with cannot see the album. If you shared it with a group they joined recently, they sign out and in again: group changes apply at the next sign-in. If they see the album but miss some pictures, those keep their own sharing (the lock), or live in another album that is not shared with them. Share in the selection bar is greyed out. The selection includes a picture linked in from another album. Select only pictures that live in this album, or change the other album's sharing. There is no Share with a link part. Links are made for albums only, not for a person, a location, a camera, a device or a single photo. The person you sent a link to sees "This link no longer works". The link expired or was deleted, or the address was cut short when it was pasted. Look in the album's Share dialog: create a link, or give the expired one a new time, and send it again. The link does not load for them at all. The address points somewhere they cannot reach, such as localhost or your home network. Open EiN at an address they can reach and copy the link again. The person with the link sees the album as their own account sees it. They were signed in when they opened the link, and then their own access counts. If they sign out and open the link again, it opens the album for them. EiN says "The browser would not copy the link: it is selected for you to copy." Browsers allow copying only on some pages, such as those over HTTPS. The address is selected: press Ctrl + C ( ⌘ + C on a Mac). The album still says Public after you chose Private. It has a link. Choose Delete link under Share with a link . There is no Visitors who are not signed in row. Visitors may not browse this EiN. The administrator turns that on; see Accounts and groups . To show one album to someone without an account, send a link instead. New albums start out private, or shared more widely, than you expected. Check How widely what you create is shared under Profile → Preferences , and ask the administrator what the default sharing is.

The same can be done in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal share-info '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # who has access, and through what share-link create '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # a link for 30 days share-link list # the links you made share-link remove 3f9a0c1d2e4b5a69 # turn one off, by its id album create '/archive/albums/Christmas 1998' --name 'Christmas 1998' --share private share-link create prints the end of the address, what it opens and until when; put your EiN's address in front of it: /s/q7Rk2mWx9TbN4vLc8HsJ3d opens /archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage until 2026-11-24T10:12:00.000Z The share- commands are EiN's own and work on any node; album comes with the Archive. The reference has every option: share-info , share-link , share-set and album . Permissions in depth explains chmod , chown and acl , which the dialog sets for you.

This page covers the pages that belong to your account alone: your profile, where you change your name, your preferences and your password; your favourites, which the Archive gathers on a page of their own; and your trash, where what you delete waits before it is removed for good. It is for everyone who has an account on EiN. All three open from the account menu, Favourites once the Archive is installed. Choose your picture at the right end of the top bar: Favourites, Profile and Trash are the pages of your own account. They need you to be signed in. A visitor who opens one of them is asked to sign in first, and lands on the page afterwards. Finding your way around describes the rest of the account menu.

Choose your picture, then Profile . The page's header shows your display name, your username after an @ , and the description you gave yourself. With the Archive, its picture is the cover photo of the person your account is linked to; without one it shows the first letter of your name. The profile has three tabs: Account , Preferences and Security . The tab you are on is in the page's address, so /profile?tab=preferences opens your preferences and /profile?tab=security the password form directly.

Choose your picture, then Profile . It opens on the Account tab. In Display name , "Your name as it appears to others", type your name the way you want others to see it, for example Helen Okafor . In Description , "A line about you, shown under your name", type a line about yourself, such as Peggy's daughter, in Wellington , or leave it empty. Choose Save changes . Saved appears beside the button. Save changes stays greyed out while Display name is empty: every account has a name. Your picture's tooltip and the profile's header show the new name at once. Three things about your account are not on this tab: Your username , the name after the @ . Nobody can change it once the account exists, an administrator included. Your e-mail address. Only an administrator sets it, in your account under Settings → Users ; see Accounts and groups . When your account has one, you can type it instead of your username when you sign in. The profile does not show it; user-info in the terminal does, under From the terminal . Your picture , which with the Archive comes from the person your account is linked to, below. Note Your display name, description and e-mail address are not private. Anyone who is signed in can read them, for example with user-info in the terminal.

p.h: Your picture and the person you are
p.x: EiN has no way to upload a picture for an account. With the Archive installed, your picture is the person in the archive that your account is linked to. Helen Okafor's account, for example, can be linked to her page among the People , and then: your picture in the top bar and on your profile is her cover photo; the account menu has Me above Favourites , which opens her page; News on Home shows her picture beside the albums you add; her picture is beside your name on the comments you write on a picture; an event or note you add to an album starts with her under Written by ; staging uses her homes to tell a trip from days at home when it suggests albums; see Sorting in staging . Without a link, your picture is an image of your username's first letters, which the browser fetches from the outside service ui-avatars.com . Where the browser cannot reach the internet, the first letter of your name shows instead. There is no button to link an account to a person. An administrator makes the link in the terminal: it is a softlink named person in the account's folder under /etc/users . For the account helen and the person whose page is at /people/helen-okafor : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator ln -s /archive/people/helen-okafor /etc/users/helen/person Helen sees her picture and Me the next time her page loads. rm /etc/users/helen/person takes the link away again; removing a link never removes the person it points at.

Choose your picture, then Profile , then the Preferences tab. It says: "These apply to you alone. They are stored in your home directory and follow you to the terminal as well." Your preferences belong to your account, so they follow you to every browser and device you sign in on. Preferences are grouped in categories; the badge under each says whether the value is the default or your own. The tab is laid out like the administrator's settings page: Find a setting searches names, descriptions, modules and keys, across every category. Categories , at the left, shows one category at a time. On a phone a Category list above the settings does the same. Overrides only shows only the settings you have changed; the button gives their number in brackets once there are some. A badge under each setting says where its value comes from: Default when nobody has changed it, Your setting when you have, and From deployment when the administrator gave everyone a starting value when setting up EiN. Your own value wins over the other two. A setting a module adds also carries the module's name, such as archive . To change a setting: Change the value in its control: pick from the list, type a number, or flip the switch between On and Off . Cancel and Save change appear under the control. Choose Save change ; Cancel puts the value back as it was. The badge turns to Your setting . To undo your choice later, choose Restore inherited value under a setting marked Your setting . It removes your own value, and the setting falls back to the deployment's value or to the default. If a save fails, the reason shows in a red box under the setting.

Category Setting Default What it changes Appearance Header entrance drawn How the tiles of the coloured band at the top of a page arrive when the page opens; the choices are below. A device set to reduce motion never animates it. Appearance Header entrance time 450 How many milliseconds that entrance takes, from the first tile starting to the last one in place. 0 shows the header as it is, without an entrance. Appearance Header over a cover split How the tiles meet a page's cover photo, such as an album's or a person's: split gives the left of the header to the tiles, which dissolve into the photo along a slanted edge; lines lays only their outlines over the photo. Language Date and time format empty How dates and times are written for you; see below. Empty follows the administrator's Date and time format . Playback Seconds per slide 3 How long each photo is shown in a slideshow. Playback Ken Burns effect On Slowly pan and zoom each photo during a slideshow. Sharing How widely what you create is shared default Where an album you create starts out; see below. Shell Shell history length 1000 How many commands the terminal remembers between sessions, in ~/.bash_history . Todo Todo widget Off A button floating over every page, which you can drag anywhere, counting and listing the todos about what is on screen; see The todo widget . EiN itself gives the settings under Appearance, Language, Sharing and Shell. The two under Playback come with the archive module, and only an EiN with the archive has them; the one under Todo comes with the todo module. Viewing photos, videos and recordings shows a slideshow, and the settings reference lists each with its key, such as CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS . The choices for Header entrance : Choice The tiles are drawn drawn as if by pen, and filled from the bottom up falling falling into place sliding sliding in from the right sweep swept in from left to right growing growing from the bottom edge ripple rippling out from the title puzzle snapping in like puzzle pieces wave crossed by a wave of light

Every date and time in the Web UI is written as this preference says, whatever language your browser is set to. Its value is a locale: a language and a country, such as sv-SE , and the country decides the order of the date and whether the clock has 24 hours. Value A time is written A date is written sv-SE 2026-11-09 13:26:05 9 nov. 2026 en-SE 2026-11-09, 13:26:05 9 Nov 2026 en-GB 09/11/2026, 13:26:05 9 Nov 2026 en-US 11/9/2026, 1:26:05 PM Nov 9, 2026 Left empty, it follows Date and time format under Settings → System , which an administrator sets for everyone and which is sv-SE unless changed: Swedish month and weekday names, a 24-hour clock and the date year first. en-SE keeps the Swedish order and clock with English names. A value that is not a locale is refused, for example config set: CFG_USER_TIME_LOCALE: expected a locale such as en-SE or sv-SE, got 'english' . Its key is CFG_USER_TIME_LOCALE , so a line in your ~/.config sets it too, as below: export CFG_USER_TIME_LOCALE= 'en-GB'

p.h: How widely what you create is shared
p.x: This preference decides how an album you create starts out: one made with Create → Album , with New album “…” in Add to an album , or with New album in staging. It does not change albums that exist already; to change who sees one of those, use its Share button. Albums come with the Archive; without it, nothing you create follows this preference. Choice A new album starts out default As the administrator's default sharing says, under Settings → Permissions . Unless the administrator has changed it, everyone with an account can see the album. private Seen only by you, and yours even where the administrator chose another owner. shared Seen by the members of the default group the administrator chose. Unless the administrator has changed it, that group is everyone with an account. everyone Seen by everyone with an account, even where the administrator's default group is a smaller one. None of them shows an album to visitors who are not signed in, unless you keep default and the administrator's default sharing lets everyone else view; otherwise you grant that yourself in the Share dialog. An administrator can see every album, whatever you choose. New private album in staging is always private, whatever you choose here. Sharing explains the default sharing and the Share dialog.

Setting Takes effect Appearance and Playback At once, in the browser tab where you saved it. Other open tabs, and your other devices, when their page loads again. Date and time format In the browser tab where you saved it, on the next page you open. Other open tabs, and your other devices, when their page loads again. How widely what you create is shared At once, for the next album you create. Shell history length In the next terminal you open.

EiN keeps your preferences in the file .config in your home folder, /home/<your username>/.config , which only you can read. Every shell you open reads it, in the web terminal and over SSH, so a preference is also a variable there: # in EiN's terminal echo $CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 It prints an empty line for a setting you have never changed: defaults are not written into the file. A terminal that is open when you save a change reads it before its next command; only a command that was already running keeps the old value. The config command lists and changes your preferences: # in EiN's terminal config list --scope user # your preferences, and where each value comes from config set CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 # the same as Save change config unset CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS # the same as Restore inherited value config list --scope user prints each setting and its value, followed by (user) for your own value or (environment) for the deployment's; a default has no mark: CFG_USER_HEADER_ENTRANCE drawn CFG_USER_HEADER_ENTRANCE_TIME 450 CFG_USER_HEADER_COVER split CFG_USER_TIME_LOCALE CFG_USER_KEN_BURNS true CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS 5 (user) CFG_USER_DEFAULT_SHARE default HISTSIZE 1000 config set answers CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS = 5 , and config unset answers CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS reset to 3 (default) . A value of the wrong kind is refused, for example config set: CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS: expected a number, got 'five' . The file holds one line per setting, such as export CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS='5' , and you can edit it with edit ~/.config ; nothing then checks the values you type. Configuration explains how settings work for the whole installation, and Configuration files lists the files.

Update password stays greyed out until all three fields are filled in and the two new ones match. Choose your picture, then Profile , then the Security tab. In Current password , type the password you sign in with. In New password , type the new one. In Confirm new password , type the new one again. If the two differ, the field says "Does not match the new password". Choose Update password . It can be chosen once all three fields are filled in and the two new ones match. Password updated appears beside it, and the fields empty. The eye at the right of each field shows what you typed. EiN has no rules for passwords: it takes any password that is not empty, so how strong yours is is up to you. The new password is the one you sign in with from then on, in the browser and over SSH and SFTP. A key you added for SSH keeps working; see SSH and SFTP . Changing your password does not sign out the browsers and terminals where you are signed in already. If you change it because someone else may know it, ask an administrator to choose Disable sign-in for your account and then Enable sign-in : that signs your account out everywhere. If the password is not changed, the reason shows in a red box above the fields: Message What it means What to do user passwd: authentication failed Current password is not your password. Type it again. If you have forgotten it, see the next section. user passwd: no existing password found, contact admin Your account has no password to check against. Ask an administrator for a sign-in link.

p.h: If you have forgotten your password
p.x: EiN sends no e-mail, so there is no "forgot password" button. Ask an administrator for a sign-in link: they make one in your account under Settings → Users and send it to you however they like. Open it, choose a new password, and you are signed in; Sign in with a link shows the steps. Your old password stops working once you have chosen the new one. An administrator can also set a new password for you in the same place, with Set password . Sign in with the one they give you, then change it on the Security tab to one that only you know. An account that an administrator made without a password, and an account marked as needing one ( mustResetPassword ), cannot sign in at all until a password is set, by an administrator or with a sign-in link. Accounts and groups covers this from the administrator's side.

Your favourites are the pictures you have marked with a heart, from any album, gathered on one page. Only someone signed in has favourites; visitors have none. The heart, the Favourites page and its row in the account menu come with the Archive ; in any EiN, star in the terminal marks a node as a favourite (see From the terminal ). A favourite is a link to the picture where it lives, kept in the folder stars in your home folder. Hearting a picture never copies or moves it, and taking it out of your favourites never deletes it. Links explains how one picture can be in many places.

In the viewer , press the heart in the bar under the picture, whose tooltip says Favourite (s) , or press s . The heart fills in. On a phone it is Favourite in ⋮ at the top right. In a grid , such as an album or the Media page, select pictures and choose Favourite in the selection bar. EiN says, for example, 12 files added to favourites , with Undo . A small heart on a tile marks a picture in your favourites. A picture marked as a favourite in a Google Photos export becomes one of your favourites when you import it; see Getting your photos in .

Choose your picture, then Favourites . The page, "The pictures you have hearted", shows them in day sections, the way an album shows its pictures. Click one to open it in the viewer, which then steps through your favourites; Start slideshow there shows them all. With nothing hearted yet, the page says No favourites yet , "Select pictures and choose Favourite, or press the heart in the lightbox.", with a button Open Media .

p.h: Take a picture out of your favourites
p.x: In the viewer, press the filled heart, Unfavourite (s) , or press s again. In a grid, select pictures that are all favourites already. The selection bar's button reads Unfavourite ; choose it, and EiN says, for example, 3 files taken out of favourites , with Undo .

When you delete something in the Web UI, such as with the Archive a picture, an album or a person, it goes to your trash first. You can restore it from there for 30 days, unless your administrator chose another number; the few ways of deleting that skip the trash are listed below. Only you see your trash, apart from an administrator, who can see everyone's.

Every row but the last is on the Archive's pages; trash put works in any EiN. What you do What goes Delete in the selection bar The selected pictures that live where you are; see Albums . Move to trash under ⋮ on an album, person, location or camera That album, person, location or camera, with everything that lives in it. Delete in Edit event That event or note. Discard in staging The files, kept together as one entry; see Sorting in staging . Removing copies in staging's Duplicates The copies, kept together as one entry; see Duplicates . trash put in the terminal What you name, if you may change it. Each of these in the browser says what it did in a message at the foot of the screen, with Undo . Undo is the quickest way back; the Trash page is for later. What you delete goes to your trash, also when it belongs to someone else who lets you change it. If a picture disappears from an album of yours, the person who deleted it has it in their trash. While something is in the trash, it is gone for everyone: from search, ls and every other list, and with the Archive from albums, the map and the counts of the people in it. It keeps what EiN worked out about it, such as faces and a transcript, and comes back with all of it when you restore it.

p.h: What is deleted for good at once
p.x: Warning These do not use the trash. What they delete is gone at once, with no Undo : Delete in the Nodes explorer, which runs rm ; rm in the terminal; deleting a file over SFTP, which takes its thumbnails and faces with it; see SSH and SFTP ; Delete for good and Empty trash on the Trash page. To delete something in the terminal that you may want back, use trash put instead of rm .

Choose your picture, then Trash . The list shows what you deleted, newest first. Each row is named by the place it came from, such as /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg . Things deleted together, such as a group discarded in staging, are one row with a name and a count, such as Discarded from Inbox: “Boat trip” · 86 items . Select a row. The pane beside the list, or under it on a phone, shows its name, From where it came, when it was Deleted , and a preview. Hold Ctrl ( ⌘ on a Mac) while you click to add a row to the selection, or Shift to select a range. On a phone, press and hold a row, then tap the others. Choose Restore , or Restore 3 with three rows selected. EiN says Restored to and the path, or how many it restored. A restored thing goes back where it came from, and the links to it work again: a restored picture is back in the albums it was added to, and in your favourites if it was one. If something else has taken its name there in the meantime, it comes back beside it with a number, such as IMG_0412 (2).jpg . A row that holds several things opens with Enter , or the arrow at its left. In a row of things deleted together, you can select one of them and restore it alone. Something inside a deleted album or folder cannot come back without the rest: the pane says "Inside what was deleted; restoring puts back all of it." Restore all , in the bar at the top of the page, puts back everything in the trash at once, without asking.

On the Trash page, select one or more rows. Choose Delete for good , or press Delete . The dialog Delete for good? says, for a single item: "This item and everything derived from it is removed for good. This cannot be undone." Choose Delete for good , or Cancel . Empty trash , in the bar at the top, does the same for everything in the trash, and its dialog's button reads Empty trash . "Everything derived from it" is what EiN made from a file: its thumbnails, faces, transcript and the rest. Something in the trash still takes up its space on disk, so removing it for good frees that space.

p.h: How long things stay in the trash
p.x: Things stay for the number of days set by Days in the trash , CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS : 30 unless the administrator changed it, under Settings → System , in the category Trash . An empty Trash page gives the number: The trash is empty , "What you delete waits here for 30 days, in case you want it back." The days count from when you deleted it; for things deleted together, from the last time something was added to that row. EiN clears out what is older when it starts and every 12 hours after that, so something can stay up to half a day past its time. Once it is cleared, nothing in EiN brings it back: EiN has no backup of its own; see Your data: backup, moving and removing .

The trash command works on the same trash as the page: # in EiN's terminal trash put "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg" trash list trash restore 01J9Z8Q4R7XKD3V5B2N6M0PA1C trash empty --older-than 7 trash list prints one line per row: its id, when it was deleted and where it came from. 01J9Z8Q4R7XKD3V5B2N6M0PA1C 2026-10-22T09:14:03.120Z /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg trash restore takes that id and answers Restored and the path. trash empty --older-than 7 removes for good what was deleted more than 7 days ago; trash empty with no id and no --older-than empties your whole trash, for good.

Besides config and trash above, these commands do in the terminal what this page does in the browser: Command What it does user-info <username> Shows an account's display name, numbers, e-mail address and description. user-update <username> --name=… --description=… Changes your display name and description, as Save changes does. user-passwd <username> --old-password=… Changes your password; it asks for the new one with Password: . A password typed on the command line can end up in your shell history, so the Security tab is the better way. star <path> , star -d <path> , star list Marks a node, such as a picture, as a favourite, takes the mark away, or lists your favourites. # in EiN's terminal user-info helen user-update helen --name= 'Helen Okafor' --description= "Peggy's daughter, in Wellington" star "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg" User: Helen Okafor UID: 1003 GID: 1003 E-mail: helen@example.com Description: Peggy's daughter, in Wellington User 'helen' updated Starred /archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg
