What you see Why What to do There is no Me in the account menu, and your picture is letters The Archive is not installed, or your account is not linked to a person in the archive. Ask an administrator to link it, as under Your picture and the person you are . Update password stays greyed out A field is empty, or the two new passwords differ. Fill in all three, and type the new password the same way twice. A preference you saved does not show in another tab That tab loaded your preferences before you saved. Reload the tab. echo $CFG_USER_… prints an empty line You never changed that setting: defaults are not written into the file. config list --scope user shows every value, defaults included. There is no heart in the viewer and no Favourite button You are not signed in. The viewer and the button come with the Archive. Sign in. Something you deleted is not in your trash Someone else deleted it, and it is in their trash; or it was deleted for good; or its days ran out. Ask the person who deleted it. Nothing brings back what was deleted for good. Restoring fails with a message that ends in is gone The folder or album it came from is no longer there. Restore that album or folder first, if it is in the trash, then restore the picture.

Finding your way around : the account menu, signing in and out, and admin mode. Sharing : who sees what you create, the Share dialog and share links. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the heart and slideshows in the viewer. Albums : Delete and Remove , and moving an album to the trash. Configuration : how settings work for the whole installation. Settings : every setting with its key and default. Accounts and groups : passwords, e-mail addresses and accounts, for administrators.

You can move the entries of the sidebar, the buttons of the top bar and the rows of the menu under your picture between the three, and put them in another order, by dragging them: see Arrange by dragging . That writes a short JSON file for you. Everything else — renaming and hiding entries, adding pages, buttons and menus of your own — is done by writing that file yourself. This page shows how, for yourself and, if you are an administrator, for everyone on your EiN or for one group. You need to be signed in and able to edit a few lines of JSON, usually in the terminal .

p.h: How the sidebar and top bar are put together
p.x: The sidebar and the top bar are laid together from four layers, read in this order: Layer File Written by Applies to The modules' entries /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json , one for each module; EiN's own is /etc/ui/nav.d/ui.json each module, when it is set up everyone Changes for everyone /etc/ui/nav.json an administrator everyone A group's changes /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json , in the group's home the group's members the group's members Your changes ~/.ui/nav.json , which is /home/<your username>/.ui/nav.json you you only Each layer changes only what it names, so your file holds only what you want different. Every entry has an id, such as archive.albums for Albums . A later layer works on the earlier ones by id: Same id: change fields. Naming an id that an earlier layer gives changes only the fields you write. The entry keeps all the others. Another id: add. An id that no earlier layer gives adds an entry of your own. hide : remove. The ids listed under "hide" are left out. So your file holds only what you want different, and when a module is updated, its changes still reach everything you left alone. A few things follow from this: None of /etc/ui/nav.json , /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json and ~/.ui/nav.json exists until someone writes it. What one layer hides stays hidden. There is no way to unhide, so you cannot bring back an entry your administrator hid. The files in /etc/ui/nav.d are links to the modules' own files, and an update replaces them. Leave them alone and put changes in /etc/ui/nav.json instead. EiN reads the navigation once, when a page loads. After you change a file, reload the page in your browser. Your terminal sessions come back after the reload.

Run ui-nav in the terminal. It prints the sidebar and the top bar as they are for you, with every entry's id: # in EiN's terminal ui-nav For someone signed in who is not an administrator, on an EiN with the archive, the assistant and the media service modules, it prints: (main) Home / ui.home Chat /chat assistant.chat Media /media archive.media Staging /staging archive.staging Explore Search /search ui.search Year /year archive.year Map /map archive.map Browse Albums /albums archive.albums People /people archive.people Locations /locations archive.locations Devices /devices ui.devices Cameras /cameras archive.cameras System Settings /settings ui.settings Statistics /stats ui.stats Documentation /docs ui.docs top bar Chat assistant.chat Create ui.create Import media archive.import Album archive.create-album Person archive.create-person Location archive.create-location Camera archive.create-camera Random album archive.random-album (alt+R) Account ui.account Favourites archive.favourites panels search.explore People /explore/people archive.explore-people search.explore Locations /explore/locations archive.explore-locations search.explore Years /explore/years archive.explore-years search.explore Labels /explore/labels archive.explore-labels device.tabs Trips /trips?device={path} archive.trips nodes.tools Duplicates /duplicates?path={path} archive.duplicates stats.sections Events /stats/life-events archive.life-events home.start Import media /start/upload archive.start-upload search.label Looks like /looks-like?path={path} archive.looks-like about.services Language model /about/language-model assistant.about system.overview GPU /system/gpu ems.gpu system.tabs Media service /system/media-service ems.media-service about.services Media service /about/media-service ems.about shell.float Todo widget /todo-widget todo.widget The sidebar comes first, a section at a time. Each section starts with its heading; the first section has none, so its id shows in brackets, (main) . Under it, each entry's label, its address and its id. top bar lists the buttons with their titles and ids, and a key in brackets where one is set. A dropdown's rows are indented under it: Create is the plus, and Account is the menu under your picture. panels are parts that modules draw inside other pages; see Change the panels inside pages . An administrator also gets Nodes and Status under System . The sidebar and top bar sections of Finding your way around say what each entry is. The first part of an id says where the entry comes from: ui. is EiN's own, and archive. , assistant. and ems. are the Archive 's, the assistant 's and the media service module 's, there once that module is installed. On an EiN with no modules, the sidebar holds only Home , Search , Devices for someone signed in, Settings , Statistics and Documentation , with Nodes and Status for an administrator, and there are no panels. When something in a file cannot be used, ui-nav says so after the list, on lines that start with ui-nav: ; When something goes differently explains each one. The browser's console shows the same lines. To read every field a module gives its entries, print its file, for example cat /etc/ui/nav.d/archive.json . JSON_OUTPUT=1 ui-nav gives the result as JSON, the form the Web UI reads.

Open the terminal with the Toggle Terminal (Alt+T) button in the top bar, or press Alt + T . Make the folder and open the file in the editor: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ui edit ~/.ui/nav.json When the file does not exist, the editor starts empty and creates the file when you save. Type or paste the JSON. The editor checks it as you type and marks a mistake with ✗. Press Ctrl + S to save, then Ctrl + Q to quit. If the JSON has a mistake, saving first asks Save with errors? (y/N) and shows the problem. Run ui-nav to check the result, then reload the page. The editor lists all of the editor's keys. You can do the same over SSH from your own computer, or put the file at /home/<your username>/.ui/nav.json with an SFTP client. A phone has no terminal button; use a computer for this.

p.h: In the Nodes explorer's code editor
p.x: The Nodes explorer opens an existing file in a code editor, but it cannot create a file. Make the file in the terminal first; after that you can edit it here: Open Nodes . Administrators have it under System in the sidebar; anyone signed in can open it at the address /system/nodes . The first time, it opens at your home folder. Names that start with a dot are hidden. Press Ctrl + H , or choose the eye button, Show names starting with a dot (Ctrl+H) . Double-click the .ui folder, then right-click nav.json and choose Open . Make your changes, then choose Save or press Ctrl + S . While a change is not saved, the editor shows unsaved , and Close asks Discard unsaved changes? with Keep editing and Discard . This editor does not check the JSON. Run ui-nav afterwards, or reload the page and look.

Open the menu under your picture and choose Arrange navigation . The menu stays open, and every place an entry can go is outlined with a dashed line: each section of the sidebar, the top bar beside the search box and at the right, and the menu itself. Drag an entry to where you want it. A line shows where it lands. Drop a sidebar page in the top bar and it becomes a button that opens the page; drop a button in a section and it becomes an entry there; drop either in the menu and it becomes a row of it. Choose Done . On a phone, or with the keyboard, tap or choose an entry instead: a menu moves it Earlier or Later , or to another place under Move to . Some entries cannot go everywhere. A dropdown, such as Create , and a button that runs a command, such as Random album , stay in the top bar; a dropdown does not go into the menu under your picture. Those places are not outlined while you drag them, and are greyed out under Move to . Reset puts every entry back where the modules and your administrator have it. It takes away only what arranging wrote, the places and the order, and keeps your own renames, hidden entries and pages. Each move is written to your ~/.ui/nav.json as the entry's id and where it goes, for example: { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "ui.stats" , "place" : "topbar" , "parent" : null , "order" : 15 } ] , "topbar" : [ { "id" : "ui.trash" , "place" : "sidebar" , "section" : "explore" , "parent" : null , "order" : 15 } ] } This moved Statistics from the sidebar to the top bar, between the chat button (10) and Create (20), and Trash from the menu under your picture to the Explore section. null takes away a field a module gave, here a parent ; see Move an entry between the sidebar, the top bar and a menu . When the right of the top bar has more buttons than there is room for, eight or three on a phone, the rest are under a More button at its end.

The examples on this page change entries the Archive and the assistant add, and lead to their pages, such as /albums and /people/peggy-wrenfield . The same works for any entry, EiN's own included, and for any address on your EiN. To rename Albums to Photo albums , move it up beside Home , and hide Map , write this in ~/.ui/nav.json : { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "archive.albums" , "section" : "main" , "label" : "Photo albums" , "order" : 15 } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.map" ] } Save, reload the page, and the first section reads Home , Photo albums , Chat , Media , Staging ; Explore has no Map . ui-nav shows the same: (main) Home / ui.home Photo albums /albums archive.albums Chat /chat assistant.chat Media /media archive.media Staging /staging archive.staging Explore Search /search ui.search Year /year archive.year Browse People /people archive.people ... order places an entry within its section, lowest first. The shipped entries count in tens ( Home 10, Chat 20, Media 30), so 15 lands between Home and Chat . An entry without order goes to the end of its section. section moves the entry to another section: main , explore , browse , system , or one of your own. hide takes away anything by id: an entry, a top-bar button, a panel or a whole section. A hidden section takes its entries with it. One id can name both a sidebar entry and a top-bar button: assistant.chat is the sidebar's Chat and the top bar's chat button, so hiding it removes both.

p.h: Move an entry between the sidebar, the top bar and a menu
p.x: Every entry is written in the list it was given in, sidebar or topbar , and is shown where its place and parent say: "place": "topbar" on a sidebar entry makes it a button in the top bar that opens its page, with its label as the tooltip; "place": "search" stands it beside the search box. "place": "sidebar" on a top-bar button, with a section , makes it an entry in that section. It keeps what it does: the chat button moved there still opens the chat beside the page. Only a button that opens an address can move there, not a dropdown or one that runs a command. "parent" on either makes it a row of that dropdown, wherever place says. null takes away a field an earlier layer gave, such as a row's parent . { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "archive.albums" , "parent" : "ui.account" } ] , "topbar" : [ { "id" : "ui.trash" , "parent" : null , "place" : "sidebar" , "section" : "system" , "order" : 5 } ] } This puts Albums in the menu under your picture and Trash at the top of System . Sections can be changed the same way. This gives the first section the heading Start and renames Browse : { "sections" : [ { "id" : "main" , "label" : "Start" } , { "id" : "browse" , "label" : "Collections" } ] }

p.h: Add a page of your own
p.x: An entry of your own needs an id that nothing else uses, and four fields: section , label , icon and to . This adds a section Family with two people's pages, and puts a saved search for Cornwall in Explore after Search : { "sections" : [ { "id" : "family" , "label" : "Family" , "order" : 25 } ] , "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "me.peggy" , "section" : "family" , "label" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "to" : "/people/peggy-wrenfield" } , { "id" : "me.ruby" , "section" : "family" , "label" : "Ruby" , "icon" : "user" , "to" : "/people/ruby-wrenfield" } , { "id" : "me.cornwall" , "section" : "explore" , "label" : "Cornwall" , "icon" : "beach" , "to" : "/media?q=Cornwall" , "order" : 15 } ] } With "order": 25 , Family stands between Explore (20) and Browse (30). Your entries also appear in the search box's list under Go to , like every sidebar entry. to is an address inside EiN, starting with / . The easiest way to get one is to open the page and copy what your browser's address bar shows after the host, such as /people/peggy-wrenfield . Filters you set on a page are part of its address, which is how /media?q=Cornwall opens Media already searching for Cornwall. Addresses in the Web UI lists them all. A sidebar entry cannot lead to another website. icon is the name of any icon at tabler.io/icons , written as it is there: map-pin , beach , heart . Add -filled for the filled form, heart-filled . It can also be the full path, starting with / , of an SVG file in EiN that you may read, which is drawn in the colour of the text. id can be anything no one else uses. The shipped ones are <module>.<name> ; starting yours with me. keeps them apart. The sidebar lights the entry whose address is the page's, or the start of it, so Albums is lit on an album too. When several match, the longest address wins: on /system/nodes only Nodes is lit, not Status at /system . An entry whose address has a ? in it, like the saved search above, is never lit.

p.h: Add buttons to the top bar
p.x: A top-bar button is an entry under "topbar" with an id , a title (its tooltip), an icon and an action that says what choosing it does: Action What choosing the button does { "navigate": "/albums" } Opens the address as the page. { "dialog": "/albums/new" } Opens it in a dialog over the page you are on. { "drawer": "/favourites" } Opens it in the side drawer at the right, or closes the drawer when it shows that address. The button is lit while the drawer is open, and left out on that address's own page. On a phone it opens a dialog instead. { "fullscreen": "/map" } Opens it over everything, the top bar too, until Esc or the browser's Back. { "run": "<command line>" } Runs the command line as you, as the Web UI runs its commands: with JSON_OUTPUT=1 . { "run": "album-random", "navigate": "/albums/{path}" } Runs the command, then opens an address filled in from its answer. Finding your way around shows what a dialog, the side drawer and full screen look like. This adds four buttons: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.peggy-button" , "title" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/peggy-wrenfield" } } , { "id" : "me.new-album" , "title" : "New album" , "icon" : "photo-plus" , "action" : { "dialog" : "/albums/new" } } , { "id" : "me.favourites" , "title" : "Favourites" , "icon" : "heart" , "action" : { "drawer" : "/favourites" } } , { "id" : "me.map" , "title" : "Map" , "icon" : "map" , "action" : { "fullscreen" : "/map" } } ] } They stand between Create and the terminal button, in the order you wrote them; hold the pointer over one to see its title. They also appear in the search box's list under Do . About run : The command's output is not shown anywhere. The button turns into a spinner while the command takes more than a moment. If the command fails, the page shows nothing; the browser's console has the error. With navigate as well, EiN reads the command's answer as JSON and replaces each {key} in the address with the answer's field of that name, or with nothing when there is none. The archive's Random album is made this way: album-random answers with an album's path , and the button opens /albums/{path} . Three more fields change a button: "place": "search" stands the button beside the search box, as Random album does, instead of with the others at the right. "phone": false leaves the button out on a phone. Its key, if it has one, still works. "color" colours its icon: blue , cyan , grape , green , indigo , lime , orange , pink , red , teal , violet or yellow . { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.year" , "title" : "This year" , "icon" : "calendar" , "color" : "teal" , "place" : "search" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/year" } } ] }

A top-bar entry with no action becomes a dropdown when other entries name it as their parent . Each of those is a row of the menu and needs an action of its own: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Family" , "label" : "Family pages" , "icon" : "users" , "order" : 15 } , { "id" : "me.family-peggy" , "parent" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Grandma Peggy" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/peggy-wrenfield" } } , { "id" : "me.family-ruby" , "parent" : "me.family-menu" , "title" : "Ruby" , "icon" : "user" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/people/ruby-wrenfield" } } ] } The dropdown's title is its button's tooltip, and its label is the heading at the top of the open menu. With "order": 15 the button stands between Chat (10) and Create (20). A row's title is its text, and order places it in the menu. Rows can go into the menus EiN has as well: "parent": "ui.create" adds a row to the Create New menu under the plus. The archive's rows are Import media (5), Album (10), Person (20), Location (30) and Camera (40); Recipes puts Recipe at 31, EiN its Device at 50 ( ui.create-device ), and Dashboards Dashboard at 60. "parent": "ui.account" adds a row to the menu under your picture, after Me . The archive puts Favourites there (10), and EiN its Profile (900, ui.profile ) and Trash (910, ui.trash ), which can be moved, renamed and hidden like any entry. The menu's other rows, Me , Arrange navigation , Shortcuts , About EiN and Logout , are EiN's own and cannot be changed. { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "me.new-category" , "parent" : "ui.create" , "title" : "Staging category" , "icon" : "folder-plus" , "color" : "cyan" , "order" : 50 , "action" : { "dialog" : "/staging/categories/new" } } , { "id" : "me.docs" , "parent" : "ui.account" , "title" : "Documentation" , "icon" : "book" , "action" : { "navigate" : "/docs" } } ] } A dropdown with no rows left, because they were all hidden or none were given, is not shown. A row goes where its dropdown goes: hide the dropdown, or keep it from someone, and its rows go too. In the search box's list a row reads with its menu's title, as Create: Staging category .

A sidebar entry, a top-bar button or a dropdown's row can have a key that does what choosing it does, from anywhere outside a text field, and an Alt key from a text field too, except on a Mac: { "topbar" : [ { "id" : "archive.create-album" , "shortcut" : "alt+B" } , { "id" : "me.map" , "title" : "Map" , "icon" : "map" , "shortcut" : "alt+K" , "action" : { "fullscreen" : "/map" } } , { "id" : "archive.random-album" , "shortcut" : null } ] , "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "archive.cameras" , "shortcut" : "alt+U" } ] } This gives Create › Album the key Alt + B , gives your Map button Alt + K , takes Alt + R away from Random album , and opens Cameras with Alt + U . A key is modifiers and one key, joined by + . The modifiers are alt , ctrl , shift , meta , and mod , which is Ctrl , or ⌘ on a Mac. Letter case does not matter: alt+R and Alt+r are the same key. null takes a key away, which is how you remove a module's key. The key shows in the button's tooltip, such as Map (Alt+K) , beside the row in its menu, and in the Keyboard shortcuts list that ? opens, under Anywhere ; a row is listed with its menu, as Create › Album . A sidebar entry's key shows in its icon's tooltip when the sidebar is narrowed to icons, and under Go to in the list. The finder shows every key beside its row. On a Mac, Alt shows as ⌥ . A sidebar entry's key does nothing while a dialog or the viewer is open. A dropdown itself cannot have a key; its rows can. A key is given once. When two entries ask for the same key, the sidebar's come first, in the sidebar's order, and then the top bar's: by order , lowest first, and a dropdown's rows where their dropdown stands. A button placed beside the search box counts by its order too. The shipped entries already hold Alt with H , S , I , Y , G , A , P , L , C and R ; Keyboard shortcuts says which is whose. EiN keeps its own keys: Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K ), ? , and Alt with T , N , M , W or an arrow key, which the terminal uses. An entry that asks for one of these as EiN writes it ( mod+K , shift+? , alt+T and so on) does not get it. Some pages have keys of their own while they are on screen, such as the photo viewer. Press ? on a page to see which keys it uses before you pick one; Keyboard shortcuts lists every key EiN knows.

Panels are parts that modules draw inside EiN's own pages, such as the Media service tab on the Status or the People , Locations , Years and Labels sections of the Search page. They are in the same files under "panels" , so you can reorder, rename or hide them by id like any entry. This puts Years first on the Search page and hides Labels there: { "panels" : [ { "id" : "archive.explore-years" , "order" : 5 } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.explore-labels" ] } Each panel has a slot, the place in a page where it is drawn: Slot Where it is drawn Panels the modules ship search.explore A section of the Search page before you search archive.explore-people , -locations , -years , -labels search.label Above the Search page's results when it searches for one label archive.looks-like ( Looks like , signed in only) home.start Under News on Home while there is no news archive.start-upload ( Import media , signed in only) stats.sections A section of Statistics archive.life-events ( Events ) nodes.tools A tool in the Nodes explorer's tool pane archive.duplicates ( Duplicates ) system.tabs A tab of the Status ems.media-service ( Media service ) device.tabs A tab of a device's page, after Info archive.trips ( Trips , on a device with a track) system.overview Gauges beside the computer's own on the Status 's overview ems.gpu ( GPU ) about.services A tile in About EiN assistant.about ( Language model ), ems.about ( Media service ) shell.float Floating over every page and the lightbox, under dialogs todo.widget ( Todo widget , signed in only) A panel draws a page that a module made for that place. Adding panels of your own works the same way in principle, but it is a module's work; see Writing a module .

As an administrator, signed in as admin or in admin mode , you write the same kind of file to /etc/ui/nav.json . It applies to every account and to visitors, and each person's own file is laid over it. # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator edit /etc/ui/nav.json Three fields show an entry to some people only. They work in any file, but the file for everyone is where they matter: Field The entry is shown "admin": true Only to administrators: the admin account and anyone in admin mode. In your own file, it shows the entry only while you are in admin mode. "signedIn": true Only to someone signed in, never to a visitor browsing without signing in, where Visitors may browse is on. "group": "devices" Only to the members of that group, and to administrators. EiN uses them itself: Nodes and Status are admin ; Staging , Settings , Create and the account menu are signedIn ; Device under Create is the devices group's. This file, for a family with no cameras to register and no devices, hides Cameras and Devices in the sidebar and Camera in the Create menu, keeps Statistics from visitors, and gives administrators a button that reruns failed work with pipeline-heal : { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "ui.stats" , "signedIn" : true } ] , "topbar" : [ { "id" : "site.retry" , "title" : "Retry failed work" , "icon" : "refresh" , "admin" : true , "action" : { "run" : "pipeline-heal --apply" } } ] , "hide" : [ "archive.cameras" , "ui.devices" , "archive.create-camera" ] } Everyone gets the change the next time they load a page. People can still rename and move, in their own files, what you changed, but they cannot bring back what you hid. To change the navigation for some accounts only, write a group's file . Processing and pipelines explains what pipeline-heal reruns.

p.h: Change the navigation for a group
p.x: The members of a group with a shared home can change the navigation for all of them, such as a link to a page only they use. The file is /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json in the group's home, where <group> is the group's name as group-list prints it, not its title, in the same format as the other files. Any member can write it, and so can an administrator. This gives the members of a sailors group a page of their own in the Explore section: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of sailors mkdir -p /groups/sailors/.ui edit /groups/sailors/.ui/nav.json { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "sailors.boats" , "section" : "explore" , "label" : "Boats" , "icon" : "sailboat" , "to" : "/search?q=sailboat" } ] } A group's file is laid over /etc/ui/nav.json and under each member's own file, so members can still rename and move what it gives. Someone in several groups with a file gets each of them, in the order of the groups' names. Groups are read at sign-in, so someone added to a group gets its file the next time they sign in. A group without a home has no file of its own; to keep an entry from visitors browsing without signing in, give it "signedIn": true in /etc/ui/nav.json . A group's home may also hold .ui/nav.d , with the entries of the modules kept to the group . mod setup links them there, and they count as modules' entries, under everything else, for the group's members alone and for the administrator. Warning hide , admin and signedIn decide only what the sidebar and top bar show. A page still opens by its address for anyone whose permissions allow it, and anyone can add an entry of their own that leads to it. To keep people away from something, set its permissions; see Permissions in depth .

A file is one JSON object with any of these keys: Key Holds sections A list of the sidebar's sections. sidebar A list of sidebar entries. topbar A list of top-bar buttons, dropdowns and dropdown rows. panels A list of panels. hide A list of ids to leave out, of any kind. Hidden in one layer means hidden in all after it. Every entry in the four lists needs an id . To change an entry, give its id and the fields to change; null takes a field away. An entry of your own needs every field marked required below.

Field Required Value id yes main , explore , browse , system , or one of your own. label no The heading, shown in capitals; choosing it folds the section. Without one the section has no heading and cannot fold, as main . order no The section's place, lowest first: main 10, explore 20, browse 30, system 40. Without it, 1000. A section with no entries left to show is not drawn, except while you arrange the navigation, so entries can be dropped in it.

Field Required Value id yes The entry's id: archive.albums , or one of your own such as me.peggy . section yes The id of the section it is in. label yes The text. icon yes A Tabler icon name ( map-pin , heart-filled ), or the path of an SVG file in EiN. to yes The address it opens, inside EiN, starting with / . The entry is lit on this address and those below it, unless the address has a ? . order no Its place in the section, lowest first. Without it, 1000; entries with the same number keep the order the files give them. admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor. shortcut no A key that opens the page, such as alt+U ; see Give an entry a key . null takes a key away. action no What choosing it does away from its page, instead of opening to ; see action . A button moved here keeps its own. place no "topbar" or "search" : shown as a button in the top bar, at the right or beside the search box, that opens the page. parent no The id of a top-bar dropdown it is a row of, such as ui.account .

Field Required Value id yes The entry's id. EiN's dropdowns are ui.create (the plus) and ui.account (the menu under your picture). title yes A button's tooltip, a row's text; also its name in the search box's list and the Keyboard shortcuts list. icon yes As for the sidebar. action see text What choosing it does; see action . A button and a row need one. An entry with neither an action nor rows is left out, without a warning. parent no The id of the dropdown this entry is a row of: ui.create , ui.account or one of your own. label no A dropdown's heading in the open menu, such as Create New . color no The icon's colour: blue , cyan , grape , green , indigo , lime , orange , pink , red , teal , violet or yellow . order no Its place, lowest first: among the buttons ( Chat 10, Create 20, Random album 30), or in its menu for a row. Without it, 1000. place no "search" : the button stands beside the search box instead of at the right. "sidebar" : it is an entry in section , if it opens an address. section no With "place": "sidebar" , the id of the section it is in. phone no false : the button is left out on a phone; its key still works. shortcut no A key, such as alt+R or mod+shift+K ; see Give an entry a key . null takes a key away. Not on a dropdown. admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor. The terminal button and your picture are EiN's own, always at the right end, and cannot be moved or hidden; neither can the search box.

Give one of these: Action Does { "navigate": "<address>" } Opens the address as the page. { "dialog": "<address>" } Opens it in a dialog over the page. { "drawer": "<address>" } Opens it in the side drawer, or closes the drawer when it shows it. A dialog on a phone. { "fullscreen": "<address>" } Opens it over everything until Esc or the browser's Back. { "run": "<command line>" } Runs the command line as you. Its output is not shown. { "run": "<command line>", "navigate": "<address>" } Runs it, then opens the address with each {key} replaced by that field of the command's JSON answer, URI-encoded; a missing field leaves nothing.

Field Required Value id yes The panel's id, such as archive.explore-years . slot yes Where it is drawn; see the slots in Change the panels inside pages . label yes The tab's or tool's label, or the section's heading. route yes The address drawn there. In nodes.tools , search.label and device.tabs , {path} is replaced by a path in the tree. icon no An icon, as for the sidebar, for the slots that show one. order no Its place among the panels of its slot. Without it, 1000. when no In device.tabs , { "has": "<node type>" } : shown only on a device with an endpoint of that type, such as track . admin no true : shown to administrators only. signedIn no true : never shown to a visitor.

ui-nav prints a line for each thing it could not use, and leaves that thing out. The rest of the file still applies, except when the file is not valid JSON. Line after ui-nav: What it means What to do /home/anna/.ui/nav.json: Expected ',' or '}' after property value in JSON at position 71 (line 3 column 3) The file is not valid JSON, so none of it is used. The end says where the parser stopped. Look just before that line and column: often a missing comma, or a comma after the last item of a list. <file>: not a navigation object The file is valid JSON but not one object in { } . Put everything inside one pair of braces. <file>: sidebar is not a list sidebar , sections , topbar or panels holds something other than a list. Put the entries in [ ] , even a single one. <file>: a sidebar entry without an id An entry in that list has no id . Give it one. <file>: hide is not a list hide holds a single id. Write "hide": ["archive.map"] . me.cornwall: no icon, to An entry of your own lacks the required fields named. Add them. If you meant to change a module's entry, check the id: a misspelled id makes an entry of your own. me.peggy: no section family The section does not exist. Check the spelling, or add the section under "sections" . me.random: only an entry that opens a route goes in the sidebar A dropdown, or a button that runs a command, was given "place": "sidebar" . It stays in the top bar. Move one of its rows instead, or a button that opens an address. me.family-peggy: no top-bar entry me.family-menu The parent names no top-bar entry. Check the spelling, or add the dropdown. me.map: action is none of navigate, dialog, drawer, fullscreen or run The action has none of those keys with text after it. Check the spelling and the quotes. me.map: shortcut "alt+" is not modifiers and one key joined by + The key is not written as modifiers and one key. Write it like alt+P . me.family-menu: a dropdown has no shortcut, its rows may A key was given to a dropdown. Give keys to its rows. The dropdown is still shown. me.map: shortcut alt+A is already archive.create-album's Another entry, earlier in the top bar's order, has the key. Choose another key, or take it from the other entry with "shortcut": null . me.map: shortcut alt+T is already the shell's EiN keeps that key for itself. Choose another key. ui: archive.albums is already given by archive Two modules give the same id; the first by module name keeps it. Tell the authors of the module named first. Other things that can go differently: Nothing changes. Reload the page; EiN reads the navigation only when a page loads. Then check that the file is where EiN looks, with cat ~/.ui/nav.json . A button you added is missing, and ui-nav says nothing. It has no action and no rows; or it is a dropdown whose rows are all hidden; or it has "phone": false and you are on a phone; or it opens the side drawer and you are on that address's own page. An empty space where an icon should be. The name is not one of Tabler's. ui-icons checks names: it prints the size of each icon it has and none for a name it does not know. # in EiN's terminal ui-icons beach beech beach: 807 bytes beech: none An entry of yours is never lit. Its address has a ? in it, so it cannot match the page. A key does nothing. A key without Alt , and on a Mac any key, does not work while the cursor is in a text field. Press ? to see whether the key is listed; if it is not, run ui-nav for the reason. An entry you want back was hidden by your administrator. You cannot unhide it. Ask your administrator.

Finding your way around : every part of the sidebar and the top bar. The editor : editing files in the terminal and in the Nodes explorer. Configuration files : /etc/ui/nav.json , a group's file, ~/.ui/nav.json and the other files you can edit. Writing a module : how a module gives its own entries, routes and panels.

This page covers what is different when you use EiN on a phone or a tablet: the menu behind the EiN mark, the gestures in grids and in the viewer, uploading from the phone, and putting EiN on your home screen. It is for everyone in the family who opens EiN away from a computer. The grids, the viewer and the uploads are the Archive 's, and the sections on them apply once it is installed.

Open the same address you use on a computer, for example http://ein.local:8080 , in your phone's browser, and sign in as you would on a computer (see Sign in ). It is the same EiN, with the same account, pictures and permissions; only the layout changes to fit the screen. The phone keeps a few choices of its own, separate from your computer's: whether the menu shows icons or names, whether it is shown, and how many pictures a grid puts in a row. They are kept in the phone's browser, not in your account.

p.h: What changes on a small screen
p.x: What you get depends on the width of the browser window, and on whether the screen is a touch screen. Screen Layout Narrower than 768 pixels: most phones held upright The phone layout this page describes. 768 to 991 pixels: tablets, and some large phones held sideways The computer's layout, with the sidebar beside the page and the terminal button. The chat's side drawer covers the page, and the browser's Back closes it. 992 pixels and wider The computer's layout, with the side drawer beside the page. On any touch screen, whatever its width, the Archive's viewer uses its touch layout and pressing and holding a picture selects it. So a tablet has the computer's frame with the phone's viewer. Home on a phone. The menu is out of sight until you tap the EiN mark or swipe right. In the phone layout: The top bar shows the EiN mark without the name, the search box (it reads Search ), then the buttons the modules add, such as the Archive's Random album , the assistant's Chat and the plus of the Create menu, and your picture. Its buttons are larger, to suit a finger. The Uploads button appears there while files are going up. The menu is hidden until you ask for it: see Open the menu . There is no terminal button. When the connection drops, a red crossed-out plug stands in the top bar in place of the Disconnected badge. The search box opens its list across the whole width of the screen, above the keyboard, and the keyboard's search key does what Enter does. Search and the finder covers what it finds. Dialogs fill the screen , with their buttons in a bar across the foot. Fields use larger text, so the phone does not zoom in while you type. A question that only asks you to confirm stays a small box. The phone's Back closes a dialog. The chat , with the assistant installed, opens as a dialog over the whole screen instead of in the side drawer; see Chatting with the assistant . The create and account menus are wider, with taller rows.

On a phone the tabs show only their icons, except the one you are on, and the header's actions are under ⋮. Actions such as Upload , Share and Edit fold into ⋮ at the header's top right, with the page's other actions. Tabs with icons show only their icons, and the tab you are on keeps its name. On a person's page, which the Archive adds, the icons stand for Info , Media , Faces , Heard in , Family and Homes . Choices such as Show and Sort become a button that shows the chosen option's icon; on some pages, such as Year , several fold into one button. Scrolled down , the header goes away, and the page's filter box and choices float at the foot of the screen beside Back to top . An empty filter box folds to a magnifier: tap it to type, and it takes the whole row while you type.

On a phone the EiN mark at the left of the top bar is the menu button; there is no separate menu icon. It does not go to Home, as it does on a computer: Home is the first entry in the menu. The menu has two forms: A column of icons at the left of the screen, which is what you get at first. Tap the mark to show it; the page moves over to make room. Tap an icon to go to its page; the column stays until you tap the mark again. The full list with names , under the headings Explore , Browse and System . Tap the button at the foot of the icon column ( Show labels ) to switch to it. It opens over the page, and closes when you choose a page; tap the mark to open it again. The button at its foot ( Collapse to icons ) switches back to the column of icons. You can also swipe: a one-finger swipe to the right across the page or the menu brings the menu out, and a swipe to the left puts it away. The swipe has to be mostly sideways and quick, and it does nothing: in the viewer or anything else shown full screen, where a sideways swipe moves between pictures; in a dialog, such as the chat; on something that moves sideways itself: the map, the time rail at the right of a long grid, a story, a slider, a text field, or a row that scrolls sideways. A swipe that starts at the very edge of the screen may be taken by the phone as its own Back gesture, so start a little way in. The phone remembers which form of the menu you chose, and whether the icon column is shown. Finding your way around lists what is in the menu.

p.h: Pinch, press and tap in a grid
p.x: With the Archive installed, a grid of pictures, such as an album or the Media page, works by touch like this: To Do this Open a picture in the viewer Tap it. Show fewer, larger pictures Spread two fingers apart on the grid, then lift them. Each pinch takes away one picture per row, down to 2. Show more, smaller pictures Pinch two fingers together, then lift them. Each pinch adds one picture per row, up to 5. Start selecting Press and hold a picture for a moment. It is ticked, and the phone gives a short buzz where its browser allows it. Add or take away a picture Once anything is selected, tap it. Select a whole day Tap the date in the day's heading. Move through a long grid Drag the time rail at the right edge, which appears once the grid holds more than 120 pictures. A phone's grid starts with 2 pictures in a row, and keeps the number you pinch to in this browser. Pinching works where pictures keep their own shapes, such as an album or the Media page in its Default layout. The Days and Months layouts of the Media page have square tiles, three and five across on a phone, and do not change with a pinch; see Media, Year and labels . Where the grid is 640 pixels wide or more, as on most tablets, it fills its rows by height instead, and a pinch does not change it. Moving your finger while you hold cancels the press, so scrolling a grid never selects a picture. Once something is selected, the bar at the foot of the screen shows how many, for example 3 selected , with all its buttons in one Actions menu and × to clear the selection. Albums covers selecting, and The selection bar what each action does. A video in a grid plays a short silent preview when it scrolls into view, as there is no pointer to rest on it.

With the Archive installed, its viewer takes a touch layout on any touch screen, and in any browser window narrower than 768 pixels. Swipe sideways between files, up for the details, and down to put them away or, with them closed, to close the viewer: the touch layout has no close button. On a phone or tablet covers its layout and gestures, and Watch the memories story the story that On this day plays on Home, which works by touch too.

With the Archive installed, bring the photos and videos on your phone into your staging area with Import media : Tap the plus in the top bar, then Import media . The dialog fills the screen. Under Into which category? , pick where the files go. The Inbox is chosen at first. To keep a phone's pictures together, choose New category and, under What it holds , Phone ; see The kinds of category . Tap Choose files . Your phone's own picker opens, with your photo library, the camera or your files, depending on the phone. Pick the files, then tap the button that counts them, for example Upload 24 . The category opens on its Files tab, and the Uploads ring in the top bar shows how far the upload is. Getting your photos in covers the dialog in full, and Sorting in staging what to do with the files once they are in. Upload also sits under ⋮ on an album you may change, on the Media page and on a staging category. Its picker is your phone's own, as in Import media : your photo library, the camera, so you can take a picture and upload it in one go, and your files, such as a GPX track or a GEDCOM family tree. An album's Upload puts the files straight into that album; the Media page's puts them into your Inbox. Choose a folder and Upload a folder need a browser that can pick a folder, which a phone's browser may not offer. Warning An upload runs in the open page. Keep EiN on screen until the upload has finished: a phone may pause a browser that is in the background or behind a locked screen, and closing or reloading the page stops the files not sent yet. The files already sent stay. For a whole camera roll, thousands of files, copying from a computer is steadier than uploading from the phone. The Import media dialog itself suggests copying over SFTP for more than about 10,000 files; see Copy files in over SFTP . On the Media page, Search with a picture can take a photo with the camera and find what looks like it; see Search with a picture .

p.h: Put EiN on your home screen
p.x: You can add EiN to your phone's home screen, where it looks and opens like an app: its icon is the EiN mark, named EiN under it; it opens on Home , using the whole screen, without the browser's address bar and buttons; the phone's status bar and the screen shown while it starts are in EiN's dark colour. Most browsers, Chrome on Android among them, install it as an app only over HTTPS: an address that begins with https:// . EiN on its own serves plain HTTP, on port 8080, so your administrator first has to put it behind an HTTPS proxy; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Over plain http:// , a phone may only add a bookmark that opens in the browser. To add it: iPhone or iPad, in Safari: open EiN, tap the share button, then Add to Home Screen , then Add . Android, in Chrome: open EiN, open the browser's ⋮ menu, choose Add to Home screen or Install app , and confirm. The names of these menu items differ between phones and browser versions. EiN itself has no install button and never asks to be installed. Opened from the home screen, EiN has no address bar and, on an iPhone, no Back button: use the menu to move between pages, swipe down to close the viewer, and the × to close a dialog. On an iPhone the home-screen EiN may keep a sign-in of its own, separate from Safari's, and ask you to sign in once more.

EiN has no offline mode. Nothing is kept on the phone for use without a connection: every page, picture and search comes from your EiN as you open it, so you need a connection to it, at home or wherever your administrator has made it reachable. When the connection drops while EiN is open, pages stop loading and EiN tries again every 2 seconds by itself. On a phone a red crossed-out plug in the top bar tells you, in place of the Disconnected badge; EiN picks up again by itself once the phone is back on the network.

p.h: What a phone does not have
p.x: The terminal. There is no terminal button on a phone. With a keyboard connected to it, Alt + T still opens it; see The terminal . Keyboard shortcuts , unless a keyboard is connected. Shortcuts in the account menu still lists them. Edit faces in the Archive's viewer while the phone is held upright; turn it sideways to draw face boxes. Keys and the column beside the stream in the Archive's staging Sort tab , and selecting several groups there; see Sorting in staging .

What you see Why What to do The address does not open on the phone The phone is not on the network EiN is on, or it does not understand a name ending in .local . Join the same network, or use the address with the machine's IP number that your administrator gives you. Away from home, see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . No Add to Home Screen or Install app , or EiN opens with the browser's address bar from the home screen EiN is reached over plain http:// . Ask your administrator for an https:// address. Swiping does not bring the menu out The swipe was too slow or too slanted, began at the screen's edge, or landed on the map, a slider, a field or a row that scrolls sideways. Tap the EiN mark instead. Pinching does not change the grid The grid has square tiles ( Days or Months ), or the screen is wide enough for the grid to fill its rows by itself. Choose the Default layout on the Media page. The upload stopped The phone paused the browser, or the page was closed or reloaded. If Uploads in the top bar lists failed files, choose Retry failed . After a reload the list is gone: choose the files that did not arrive and upload them again. An exact copy of a file already sent is recognised in staging; see Duplicates . You cannot find Upload , Share or Edit On a phone they are under ⋮ at the top right of the header. Tap ⋮. You cannot find the viewer's close button The touch layout has none. Swipe down on the picture, or use the phone's Back.

Finding your way around : the top bar, the menu and how pages, dialogs and full screen open and close. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer, its details and its gestures. Getting your photos in : every way files get into EiN. Albums : selecting pictures and the selection bar. Ports, HTTPS and remote access : HTTPS and reaching EiN from outside the home, for administrators.

The terminal is a command line inside EiN's Web UI: a shell that works on the same tree of nodes that the pages show, with the same commands and the same permissions. This page is for anyone who signs in and wants to use it: how to open it, work in tabs, move around with the keyboard, find earlier commands, get help, and find the command you need.

Sign in. Visitors browsing without an account have no terminal. Choose the terminal button in the top bar (tooltip Toggle Terminal (Alt+T) ), or press Alt + T wherever you are. The terminal drops down from the top of the window over the page, half the window high, with the cursor ready at the prompt. Try a first command: # in EiN's terminal ls /archive albums cameras locations people tags That is an EiN with the Archive installed, which makes every folder there but tags . Without it, /archive holds only tags , and ls / shows the rest of the tree . To hide it again, press Alt + T , choose the chevron at the right end of the tab bar ( Hide terminal (Alt+T) ), or click anywhere outside it. Hiding the terminal does not stop it: the shells keep running, a command you started goes on, and the terminal is as you left it when you open it again. On a phone-sized screen the top bar has no terminal button; Alt + T still works with a keyboard attached. From your own computer you can also reach the same shell over SSH (see Use the same shell over SSH ). Administrators have one more way in: in the Nodes explorer, right-click a folder and choose Open terminal here . EiN opens a new tab and types cd to that folder for you. The terminal works on the same tree the pages show: people, albums and photos are paths you can list, read and open.

The prompt says who you are and where you are: helen@:~$ helen is your username, in green, or in red for an administrator. Between @ and : stands the host name, which is empty unless you set one, for example with export HOSTNAME=ein in your ~/.bashrc . ~ is the folder you are in. ~ stands for your home folder, /home/helen ; elsewhere you see the path, such as /archive/albums/christmas-2019 . $ becomes # when the shell acts as an administrator. Folders and files are nodes of EiN's tree: paths start at / , .. is the folder above, and cd moves you around. The tree shows what lies where.

The tab bar runs along the foot of the terminal. Each tab is a shell of its own, with its own current folder, its own variables and whatever is running in it; switching tabs does not stop the others. Add a tab : choose + ( New session (Alt+N) ) or press Alt + N . The first tab is called Session 1 , and a new one takes the lowest number no open tab has: with Session 2 closed, the next is Session 2 again. If the terminal is hidden, Alt + N adds the tab without showing it. Know which is which : once a tab's shell has reported its folder, the tab shows that path instead of its name, such as /home/helen or /archive/albums/christmas-2019 . Switch : click a tab, or press Alt + ← and Alt + → . Close a tab : choose its × , or press Alt + W while you are typing in it. Closing a tab ends its shell and everything running in it. The last tab has no × and cannot be closed. End a shell from inside : type exit , or press Ctrl + D on an empty line. The tab goes away; if it was the only one, a fresh shell takes its place.

p.h: Make the terminal taller or shorter
p.x: The terminal starts at half the window's height. Maximize (Alt+M) , the button at the right of the tab bar, makes it fill the window. Pressed again, as Restore (Alt+M) , it returns to half the window. Alt + ↓ makes it a tenth of the window taller, Alt + ↑ a tenth shorter, between a tenth and the whole window. The browser remembers the height for the next time, on that computer and in that browser.

The ? button at the right of the tab bar ( Terminal shortcuts ) lists the keys of the terminal itself. They work whether you are typing in the terminal or not, and only with Alt alone, without Ctrl , Shift or ⌘ : Keys In the ? list What happens Alt + T Toggle terminal Shows or hides the terminal Alt + N New tab Adds a tab with a new shell Alt + W Close tab Closes the tab you are typing in; never the last one Alt + M Maximize Fills the window, or returns to half the window Alt + ← Previous tab Moves to the tab on the left, from the first to the last Alt + → Next tab Moves to the tab on the right, from the last to the first Alt + ↑ Shrink height A tenth of the window shorter Alt + ↓ Grow height A tenth of the window taller The Keyboard shortcuts dialog that ? opens anywhere in EiN lists only the first two, under Anywhere . Keyboard shortcuts has every key in EiN. Note On a Mac, ⌥ with a letter types a character of its own (⌥T types †), while the terminal looks for the letter itself, so ⌥T, ⌥N, ⌥W and ⌥M may not reach it. The top-bar button and the buttons in the tab bar do the same. ⌥ with the arrow keys is not affected.

p.h: Come back to a running shell
p.x: Reload the page, or lose the connection for a moment, and the terminal comes back as you left it: the same tabs, open or hidden as before, and in each tab the same shell, in the same folder, with up to 1000 lines of what scrolled past drawn again. A command that was running carries on while the page is away. How long EiN waits. EiN keeps a shell without a page for five minutes. The administrator sets this with Terminal reconnect grace ( CFG_TERMINAL_RECONNECT_GRACE_SEC , 300 seconds; 0 ends a shell as soon as its page goes; a change applies from the next disconnect). After that the shell ends, with whatever runs in it, and the tab starts a fresh one when you come back. To keep a long job going after you leave, see The shell language . One browser tab, one set of terminals. The tabs belong to the browser tab they were opened in. EiN in a second browser tab gets terminals of its own, starting again at Session 1 , and closing a browser tab leaves its shells to end after the five minutes. Signing out ends every terminal of that sign-in and starts the tabs over, so the next person who signs in on that browser finds none of your shells. When EiN restarts , for example for an update, every shell ends. The tabs stay, and each starts a fresh shell once EiN answers again. While the connection is down , the top bar shows a red Disconnected badge, and each tab whose shell is not connected shows a red crossed-out plug in place of its terminal icon. The terminal reconnects by itself; there is nothing to press. Your command history is kept through all of this (see Find an earlier command ).

Drag files from your computer onto the terminal and let go. EiN uploads them into the folder the tab is in, the path the tab shows. The Uploads button in the top bar follows them, as for any upload, and a file whose name is taken in that folder is stored under a numbered name beside it. Where you drop decides what happens next. With the Archive installed, go to a staging category or an album first to have it take new pictures in: # in EiN's terminal cd ~/staging/files/inbox Then drop the files. Getting your photos in explains staging, albums and what happens after an upload. You need permission to write in the folder; an upload into a folder you may only read fails and is listed under Uploads .

cat on a picture or a video draws it right in the terminal, 20 lines tall, wherever the file is in the tree. Here it draws a photo in one of the Archive's albums: # in EiN's terminal cd /archive/albums/christmas-2019 && cat 20191225_155434.jpg cat -s draws it half as tall, cat -l twice as tall. export MEDIA_LINES=30 changes the height for the rest of the session (see Environment variables ). A video plays at once, with its controls under it. A recording gets a player two lines tall and starts playing. A text file is printed with colours for its language, such as JSON, YAML, bash or Markdown. Only the terminal in the browser draws pictures. Over SSH, cat prints marker lines starting __IMG: instead. Note A picture whose path holds a space or a colon, such as one in /archive/albums/Summer 2020 , is not drawn: the terminal shows its __IMG: lines instead. Open it in the Web UI.

The line you type is edited with the keys of bash on Linux, in its default (emacs) mode. The ones used most: Keys What they do Tab Complete what you are typing (see Let Tab complete ) ↑ ↓ The previous and the next command from your history Ctrl + R Search your history as you type Home End , or Ctrl + A Ctrl + E Start and end of the line Ctrl + ← Ctrl + → A word left or right Ctrl + K / Ctrl + U Cut from the cursor to the end / to the start of the line Ctrl + Y Paste what you cut last Alt + . Insert the last word of the previous command (not with ⌥ on a Mac) Ctrl + C At the prompt: drop the line ( ^C is printed). While a command runs: stop it Ctrl + D On an empty line: end the shell and its tab. While a command runs: end its input Ctrl + L Clear the screen, as the command clear does Some keys mean something else in the browser: Alt + ← , Alt + → , Alt + ↑ and Alt + ↓ are the terminal's own keys for tabs and height; move by word with Ctrl + ← and Ctrl + → . Ctrl + R searches your history instead of reloading the page. To reload, press F5 . The browser keeps some keys for itself before the terminal sees them. In most browsers Ctrl + W closes the browser tab rather than cutting a word; use Alt + W to close a terminal tab. While a command runs, what you type goes to it, and Enter ends a line as in any Linux terminal. A command that reads the terminal takes your line when you press it: head -n1 returns the one line you type, and xargs -o gives each command it runs the terminal to read from. Ctrl + D ends the input of the command reading the terminal, so it finishes with what you typed: cat > notes.txt saves your lines, sort and wc -l print their answer, and read takes a line you did not end with Enter . The next command reads the terminal again. Ctrl + C stops the command instead. Ctrl + Z does not pause a running command. Start a long one in the background with & instead; The shell language covers jobs.

Press ↑ to step back through the commands you ran, ↓ to step forward again. To find one by a word in it, press Ctrl + R and type part of it. The prompt turns into the search and shows the newest command that matches: (reverse-i-search)`peg': person-info /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield Ctrl + R again finds the next older match. Enter runs the command found. Esc leaves it on the line for you to change first. Ctrl + G gives up and brings back what you had typed. bash's history commands work too: history lists what you ran, !! runs the last command again, !42 runs number 42 of the list, and ^old^new runs the last command with old replaced by new . What EiN keeps: Your history is the file ~/.bash_history . Every terminal tab and every SSH login of yours adds to it as each command runs, so a tab you open afterwards finds the commands typed in the others. A tab that is already open keeps the list it started with. A command typed with a space in front, or the same as the one before it, is not kept. It keeps the last 1000 commands. Change this under Profile → Preferences , Shell history length ( HISTSIZE ); a tab you open afterwards uses the new length. Your profile, favourites and trash shows where. Commands the web pages run for you, and commands sent with ssh host 'command' , are not kept.

Press Tab while you type a command name, a path, an option, a user or a group. When only one thing fits, EiN fills it in, with / after a folder and a space after anything else, and quotes it if it holds spaces. When several fit, it fills in as much as they share; press Tab again to list them all. The first two rows are on an EiN with the Archive installed: You type Tab gives cd /archive/al cd /archive/albums/ person-info /archive/people/Peg person-info /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield search --ki search --kind= , ready for the value user-info he user-info helen pipeline , a space, Tab twice the list of pipeline 's subcommands Completion reads each command's own description of its arguments and options, so it knows a command's options without being told. A command of a family, such as pipeline status , is completed as two words. Scripts of your own can take part; see The shell language .

Put --help (or -h ) straight after a command's name. The command does not run; it says how to use it instead: # in EiN's terminal onthisday -- help Usage: onthisday [OPTIONS] <day> What the archive has from a calendar day (MM-DD, default today) in earlier years, from every onthisday-* command on PATH Arguments: <day> day as MM-DD (default today, UTC) Options: --limit <number> entries returned across all providers (default 8) -h, --help Show this help message Returns: the entries of every onthisday-* provider, newest year first: the year, what, the node it is about, which provider, and the route that draws it. Examples: onthisday onthisday 06-21 --limit 20 A family of commands , such as config , docs , group , mod , pipeline , pool , service and user , lists its members with --help : service --help . Each member answers for itself: service status --help . The two words are another way of typing the member's name: service status runs service-status . bash's own commands , such as cd , export and history , are described by help : help cd . -h first always means help , even for a command whose own -h means something else: du -h shows the help of du . Put another option first, as in du -sh . There is no man and no pager. Long output scrolls past; scroll back with the mouse wheel or the scrollbar. The same descriptions are in Documentation in the sidebar, under Commands , for every command installed on your EiN, and on this site in the command reference .

When you know what you want done but not which command does it, ask by what it does. In the finder. Press Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) and type > followed by what the command should do, or part of its name. Up to six commands appear under Commands ; choosing one opens its description in Documentation . It does not run the command: you run it in the terminal. Search and the finder has the details. Starting with > in the finder searches EiN's commands rather than the archive. In the terminal. docs find lists the best commands, best first, each with a score, its name and its description: # in EiN's terminal docs find restart a service With the assistant module installed there is also assistant-commands find , which adds whether each command only reads or also changes something, and assistant-commands judge tells you which a whole command line would do: # in EiN's terminal assistant-commands find 'list running services' assistant-commands judge 'service restart pipeline-pruner' How well this works depends on what is installed: Installed How commands are found Core alone Your words are matched against the commands' names and descriptions; a word in the name counts double The assistant module The assistant answers for docs find and the finder, and still matches words The assistant module and the media service Commands are found by meaning, so one can turn up even when its description uses other words than yours The settings behind this are Command finder ( CFG_COMMAND_FINDER ) and Text embedder ( CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER ); the assistant module and the media service set them when they are installed.

p.h: Use the same shell over SSH
p.x: The terminal is one of several interfaces to the same shell. From your own computer you can log in over SSH with your EiN username and password, on port 2222 unless your administrator chose another: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local You get the same shell as in a terminal tab: the same prompt, your history, your ~/.bashrc , Tab completion and the same keys. Two things belong to the browser alone: pictures and videos drawn by cat , and dropping files to upload them. Over SSH, copy files with SFTP or scp instead. Whichever interface you use, the same commands run as you, with the same permissions. The web pages run these same commands for you, and so does the assistant, always as the person signed in. A command you may not run in the terminal is refused through every other interface too. SSH and SFTP covers keys, running one command at a time, and copying files.

Commands marked archive come with the Archive and exist only where it is installed, as do the /archive/albums and /archive/people paths in the examples. search , news , events and onthisday are EiN's own, but answer with what the installed modules provide, so without a module they find nothing. Commands by task has many more, grouped by what you want to do. Command What it does ls Lists what is in a folder; ls -l with details cd Moves into a folder; cd alone goes home, cd - back to where you were cat Prints a text file, or draws a picture edit Edits a text file in the terminal; see The editor cp Copies; cp -r for a folder and what is in it mv Moves or renames, and keeps the links to what it moves pointing at the new place rm Deletes for good; rm -r for anything that has children, a processed photo included trash trash put <path> moves into your trash, from which you can restore it mkdir Makes a folder; mkdir -p makes the folders above it too mkfile Makes an empty text file, what touch does elsewhere du Adds up sizes; du -chs * gives readable sizes and a total find Finds nodes under a path, as GNU find does: find /archive/people -maxdepth 1 -type person search Searches what the modules make searchable: search christmas --kind photo stat Shows a node's details: type, owner, times ln ln -s makes a softlink, one thing in a second place news What has been added lately, newest first events What falls on the days around today, such as birthdays and anniversaries onthisday What the modules have from this day in earlier years timeline archive : albums, life events, birthdays and tracks, newest first person-info archive : a person's details, relations, homes and events top Watches the system live; q quits ps , who What is running now, and who is connected; your own, or everyone's for an administrator health One line on how the system is doing, and the checks behind it docs docs find <words> finds a command by what it does whoami Prints your username Warning rm deletes at once and for good: it does not use the trash, and nothing brings the node back. Use trash put for anything you may want again; it then shows under Trash in your account menu (see Your profile, favourites and trash ). top fills the terminal with what EiN is doing and keeps it up to date. Press Alt + M first to give it the whole window. Health and status explains what it shows and all its keys. top shows on one screen what the Status page spreads over several tabs. Steps that belong together can be joined with && , and paths with spaces go in quotes, as in bash: # in EiN's terminal cd "/archive/albums/Summer 2020" && ls -l The shell language covers what else bash syntax can do in EiN, and how it differs from bash on Linux.

There is no terminal button. You are not signed in, or the window is phone-sized. Sign in; on a small screen press Alt + T with a keyboard, or use SSH from a computer. The terminal closed while I was clicking on the page. A click outside the terminal hides it. Its shells keep running; press Alt + T to bring it back. The top bar says Disconnected, or a tab shows a red crossed-out plug. EiN cannot be reached from the browser just now: the badge is the page's own connection, the plug that tab's shell. The terminal reconnects by itself and finds its shell again if the connection is back within five minutes. The screen was cleared and a fresh prompt waits. The shell ended: you were away longer than five minutes, EiN restarted, or you signed out. Your history is still there; ↑ and Ctrl + R find your commands. error: command 'albm' not found . No command of that name is on your path. Check the spelling with Tab , or look for it with docs find . Commands such as timeline and person-info exist only where their module is installed. service-restart: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . The command is for administrators. Through every interface it is refused the same way; ask your administrator. du -h shows help instead of sizes. -h straight after a command's name always asks for help. Write du -sh or du -ch . cat prints lines starting __IMG: instead of the picture. You are connected over SSH, or the picture's path holds a space or a colon. Open the picture in the Web UI. Dropped files landed in the wrong folder. They go into the folder the tab is in, the path on the tab. cd to where they belong and drop them again, or move them with mv . The browser tab closed when I pressed Ctrl+W. The browser keeps that key for itself. Open EiN again: you get new terminals, and the old shells end after five minutes.

The shell language : the bash syntax EiN understands, scripts, jobs and JSON_OUTPUT=1 . Commands by task : which command does what, grouped by task. The editor : edit and its keys. SSH and SFTP : the same shell from your own computer, and copying files. Commands : every command, with all its options. Keyboard shortcuts : every key in EiN.

EiN's shell speaks bash: the quoting, variables, loops, functions, pipes and redirections you know from bash on Linux work the same way on EiN's tree. This page is for anyone who writes more than one command at a time: what EiN's shell does like bash, where it differs, how to keep settings in ~/.bashrc , how to write scripts of your own, how to run long jobs in the background, and how to get answers as JSON. The terminal itself, with its tabs, keys, history and Tab completion, has a page of its own: The terminal . Commands by task tells you which command does what. The examples work on the Archive 's folders, such as /archive/albums and /archive/people , which are there once it is installed. The shell itself is the same on any EiN: try them on your home folder or /etc where the Archive is not installed.

p.h: Bash, on a tree of nodes
p.x: The shell is a bash written for EiN and tested against the test suite of GNU bash 5.2. Nearly all of the language is there: What Example Pipes and lists find /archive/people -type person | wc -l , cd /archive && ls , a || b Quoting ls "/archive/albums/Summer 2020" , echo 'no $expansion here' Variables and parameters name=${file%.jpg} , ${#name} , ${name^^} , ${dir:-/archive} Command substitution count=$(ls -1 /archive/people | wc -l) Arithmetic $(( 6 * 7 )) , (( n >= 10 )) , let n++ Brace expansion echo {2019..2023} Arrays people=(Peggy Ruby Jon) , "${people[@]}" , declare -A seen Tests [[ $name == *.jpg ]] , [[ $line =~ ^([0-9]+) ]] , [ -e "$path" ] Control flow if , for , while , until , case , for (( i = 0; i < 3; i++ )) Functions count() { ls -1 "$1" | wc -l; } Redirections > out.txt , >> log.txt , 2>/dev/null , 2>&1 , < in.txt Here-documents cat > note.txt <<'EOF' … EOF , and here-strings <<< "$line" Process substitution mapfile -t names < <(find /archive/people -type person) Jobs cmd & , jobs , fg , bg , wait , kill %1 Options and traps set -euo pipefail , shopt -s globstar , trap 'echo bye' EXIT The difference is what the words name. A path is a node of EiN's tree, not a file on a disk: / is the root of the tree, ~ is your home folder /home/<you> , and globs such as *.jpg match the names of nodes. Commands are EiN's own, not programs installed on a machine. The tree shows what lies where, and Nodes and node types what a node is. # in EiN's terminal for person in /archive/people/*_Wrenfield; do echo " ${person##*/} " done arthur-wrenfield erik-wrenfield freya-wrenfield jon-wrenfield kiri-wrenfield leo-wrenfield peggy-wrenfield ruby-wrenfield thomas-wrenfield

p.h: What happens when you press Enter
p.x: The shell reads the line you typed. When it is not finished yet, because a quote is open, an if has no fi or a here-document has no end line, the prompt changes to > and waits for the next line. Press Ctrl + C to give up on it. The first word is then looked up in this order, the first match wins: An alias, such as ll for ls -al . A function you defined. A builtin of the shell: cd , echo , read , export , source and the others in Builtins . One of EiN's own commands, such as ls , cp or search . A command found on PATH : core's other commands, then each installed module's. echo $PATH shows the folders: /usr/bin and /usr/lib/core/bin first, then /usr/modules/<module>/bin for each module. A word with a / in it, such as ./tidy.sh or ~/bin/album-sizes , runs that node instead. type <name> says which of these a name is, and command -v <name> prints only where it is found. When nothing matches, you see: error: command 'albm' not found and the status is 127 . Commands such as person-info exist only where their module is installed; mod list shows which modules are. Ctrl + C stops the command that is running. A loop stops too, rather than going on with the next round.

p.h: How EiN's shell differs from bash on Linux
p.x: Most scripts written for bash run unchanged. These are the places where EiN behaves differently, because the tree is not a disk and the commands are not Linux programs. Every node can hold others. A file can have children of its own, as a photo in the Archive has its EXIF data and the regions of its faces, so [ -d "$path" ] is true for every node that exists. Test with [ -e "$path" ] whether a node is there, and [ -f "$path" ] whether it is a file. [ -s "$path" ] is true only for a file with content. [ -t 1 ] is always false. Plain variables reach commands. A command or script started from the shell sees all of the shell's variables, not only the exported ones. JSON_OUTPUT=1 on a line of its own therefore changes every command after it until you unset JSON_OUTPUT . Put it in front of one command to change only that one. Three options start on. ** matches any depth of folders, ls /archive/**/*.jpg , as under shopt -s globstar . Aliases work in scripts too, not only where you type ( expand_aliases ). Job control is on in scripts as well, so fg works there ( set -m ). shopt -u globstar , shopt -u expand_aliases and set +m turn them off. ls in the terminal writes columns into a pipe too. In the terminal panel and an SSH login, ls lays names out in columns even when its output goes to another command. Give -1 when you count or loop over names: ls -1 /archive/albums | wc -l . find always writes one path per line. -h right after a command's name asks for help. du -h prints du 's help instead of sizes; write du -sh . A value that starts with a minus goes after an equals sign, --lng=-3.7 ; on its own -3.7 would be read as another option. There is no sh or bash command. Run a script by its path, or read it into the shell you are in with source . See Write a script . Ctrl + Z does not pause a command. Start a long one with & instead; see Run a long job in the background . Process substitution waits for the end. <(cmd) writes the command's whole output to a temporary node under /tmp before the reading command opens it, so it is not streamed. Many Unix programs are missing. tar , curl , diff , less and others have no EiN command. Commands by task lists what to use instead. Permissions are EiN's. A command you may not run is refused the same way in the shell, the Web UI and over SSH. Permissions in depth explains who may do what.

Each terminal tab, and each SSH login, is one shell that lasts until you close it. A cd , an export , an alias or a function you define stays for the next command in that tab, and survives a page reload (see Come back to a running shell ). Other tabs have shells of their own and do not see it. A command sent with ssh host 'command' from your own computer gets a fresh shell that ends with the command. Join what belongs together with && in one line: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'cd /archive/albums && ls -1 | wc -l' SSH and SFTP covers logging in from your own computer.

When a terminal tab or an SSH login opens, the shell reads, in this order: /etc/bashrc , the same for everyone. It defines the aliases ll ( ls -al ), la ( ls -A ), whoami and id , and reads the settings: the modules' own, the administrator's in /etc/config , then your own in ~/.config . /etc/bashrc.d/<group> for each of your groups that has one, in the order of their names: what the administrator gives a group, such as the commands of a module kept to the group . An administrator also gets /etc/bashrc.d/admin . ~/.bashrc , your own file, if you have one. EiN reads no ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile . A command sent with ssh host 'command' reads /etc/bashrc and your groups' files but not ~/.bashrc . To make a change that lasts: Open the file in the editor: # in EiN's terminal edit ~/.bashrc Add what you want, for example: # ~/.bashrc export HOSTNAME=ein export PATH= " $HOME /bin: $PATH " alias albums= 'cd /archive/albums && ls' people () { find /archive/people -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 - type person; } Save with Ctrl + S and leave with Ctrl + Q . The editor has its other keys. Run source ~/.bashrc to use it in the tab you are in. New tabs read it when they open. A ~/.bashrc that fails does not stop the shell from opening: you get a prompt all the same. Fix the file and source it again.
