Some things to put there: Line What it does export HOSTNAME=ein Shows a host name in the prompt, helen@ein:~$ PS1='\u:\W\$ ' Changes the prompt; see below export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" Lets your own scripts in ~/bin run by name export MEDIA_LINES=30 Draws pictures with cat 30 lines tall export HISTSIZE=5000 Keeps more history in this shell set -o ignoreeof Ctrl + D on an empty line no longer ends the shell complete -F _my_func my-script Your own Tab completion for a command PS1 understands \u (your username), \h (the host name), \w (the folder, with ~ for your home), \W (the last part of the folder), \$ ( # when the shell acts as an administrator, $ otherwise), \t and \T (the time in 24- and 12-hour form), \n (a new line) and \e for colour codes. Unset PS1 to get EiN's coloured prompt back. Settings such as the length of your history are better changed under Profile → Preferences , which writes them to ~/.config ; see Your profile, favourites and trash . Configuration explains how the administrator's settings and yours are layered.

A script is a text file of shell commands. EiN runs any text file you have execute permission on as a bash script. Make a folder for your scripts and open a new file in it: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/bin edit ~/bin/album-sizes Write the script. Start it with #!bash , so the editor colours and checks it as bash: #!bash # How much each album holds, largest first for album in /archive/albums/*; do printf '%6d %s\n' " $(ls -1 " $album " | wc -l) " " ${album##*/} " done | sort -rn Save it, and give yourself permission to run it: # in EiN's terminal chmod 755 ~/bin/album-sizes Run it by its path: # in EiN's terminal ~/bin/album-sizes With ~/bin on your PATH (see Keep your settings in ~/.bashrc ), album-sizes alone is enough. A script run like this is a process of its own: its cd , variables and functions end with it, and exit ends the script, not your shell. $1 , $2 , $@ and $# are its arguments, and $0 is its path. source ~/bin/album-sizes (or . ~/bin/album-sizes ) runs the same lines in the shell you are in instead, so what they change stays; a sourced file needs no execute permission. Pick a name that is not already a command: a name such as ls or cp always runs EiN's own command, whatever is on your PATH . type album-sizes shows what a name runs. A file whose first line is #!ts is a TypeScript command, and EiN runs those only from a module installed under /usr/modules . Writing a module covers that.

p.h: Give a script options and help with arg
p.x: The builtin arg gives a script the options, help and Tab completion that EiN's own commands have. Declare what the script takes, then arg --export reads the arguments and sets one variable for each, named in capitals: #!bash arg --desc "Count what each album holds" arg '[<under>]' path = /archive/albums "where the albums are" arg -m --min number = 0 "leave out albums holding fewer" arg --example "album-sizes --min 50" arg -- export for album in " $UNDER " /*; do n=$( ls -1 " $album " | wc -l) if (( n >= MIN )); then printf '%6d %s\n' " $n " " ${album##*/} " ; fi done album-sizes --help then prints: Usage: /home/helen/bin/album-sizes [OPTIONS] [<under>] Count what each album holds Arguments: [<under>] where the albums are [default: /archive/albums] Options: -m, --min <number> leave out albums holding fewer [default: 0] -h, --help Show this help message Examples: album-sizes --min 50 An option the script does not declare, a missing argument, or a word where a number belongs stops the script with a message such as Unknown option: --bogus and Try '/home/helen/bin/album-sizes --help' for more information. , status 1 . Line Declares arg --desc "text" What the script does, shown by --help arg '<name>' type "text" An argument that must be given; its value is in $NAME arg '[<name>]' type = value "text" An argument that may be left out, with its default arg -s --long type "text" An option that takes a value, $LONG ; = value gives it a default arg -s --long "text" An option without a value: $LONG is 1 when given, empty if not arg --rest Leaves the arguments it does not know in $@ instead of refusing arg --example "command line" An example for --help arg --returns "text" What the script answers with, in a sentence arg --effect read or write Whether running it changes anything arg --export Reads the arguments and sets the variables; put it last The types are string , number , boolean , path , user , group and command . A - in an option's name becomes _ in its variable: --max-count is $MAX_COUNT . Because the script declares what it takes, Tab completes its options and, for a path , user or group , their values, once the script is on your PATH . A script without arg completes paths.

p.h: Run a long job in the background
p.x: End a command with & and the prompt comes back at once while it runs: # in EiN's terminal ~/bin/album-sizes > ~/album-sizes.txt & [1] bg-01JBXK4T9Q2M8N5R7V3W6Y0Z1A [1] is the job's number in this shell, and the rest is its process id, which ps lists too. When the job ends, the shell says so before the next prompt, as [1]+ Done with the command. Command What it does jobs Lists this shell's jobs and whether they still run fg %1 Waits for job 1 in the foreground; Ctrl + C stops it wait Waits for all of this shell's jobs to end kill %1 Stops job 1, everything it runs included kill <pid> Stops a process by its id from ps ; your own, or anyone's for an administrator echo $! The process id of the last job you started A background job belongs to its shell. When the shell ends (you close the tab, sign out, or stay away longer than the five minutes the terminal waits), its jobs are stopped with it.

p.h: Keep a job running after you leave
p.x: To let a job go on after its shell has ended, detach it. Start it detached with nohup : # in EiN's terminal nohup album-sizes --min 50 nohup: [1] bg-01JBXM2C6D8F0G3H5J7K9L1N4P -> /var/logs/jobs/bg-01JBXM2C6D8F0G3H5J7K9L1N4P/ Or detach a job you already started with & : detach %1 , or detach alone for the latest. EiN answers detached [1] <pid> <command> . A detached job leaves the shell's jobs list and no longer writes to the terminal. Its output goes to stdout.log and stderr.log in /var/logs/jobs/<pid>/ , beside a status.json that says whether it still runs and how it ended. detach --list lists the detached jobs, newest first, one line each with the process id, the state, when it started and the command, or no detached jobs . running means it still goes, exited gives its status in brackets, and abandoned means EiN restarted while it ran. A detached job does not survive a restart of EiN. nohup runs one command with its arguments. For several steps, or a pipe, put them in a script and detach that, or nohup source ~/sweep.sh . Stop a detached job with kill <pid> . detach and nohup are in the reference.

Put JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of a command and it answers in JSON instead of text. This is how the Web UI runs every command, so the JSON holds everything the pages show. Read it with jq : # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls /archive/people | jq -r '.[]' JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums | jq '.[].name' ls alone answers with a list of names; ls -l with a record for each node. JSON_OUTPUT=1 <command> --help answers with the command's description of its arguments and options as JSON, a script's from its arg lines included. Text tools such as grep , sort , head , cut , wc and cat keep writing text, so they work in the same pipe. Set without a command in front, JSON_OUTPUT=1 holds for every command after it in that shell, until unset JSON_OUTPUT . jq is EiN's own, a lighter jq that knows filters such as .field , .field.nested , .[] , .[] | .name and startswith("x") , with -r for plain text and -c for one line per result. Environment variables lists JSON_OUTPUT with the other variables that change how commands behave, and docs env prints them in the terminal.

These are part of the shell itself, so they have no entry in the commands reference . help <name> prints a builtin's usage in the terminal. Builtins For cd , pwd , pushd , popd , dirs Moving around; cd alone goes home, cd - back echo , printf , read , mapfile , readarray Writing and reading lines export , unset , local , declare , typeset , readonly , let , shift Variables source , . , eval , exit , return , true , false , : Running and ending test , [ Tests jobs , fg , bg , wait , kill , disown Jobs set , shopt , trap , umask , ulimit Options and signals alias , unalias , type , command , builtin , hash , enable , help Names and lookup history , fc History; see Find an earlier command complete , compgen , compopt Tab completion getopts , arg , caller , times Scripts disown takes a job out of the list and lets it outlive the shell, as detach does. kill takes the signals HUP , INT , TERM , KILL , PIPE , TSTP and CONT by name, kill -TERM %1 .

The prompt shows > and nothing happens. The line is not finished: a quote or a bracket is open, or an if , for or here-document has no end. Type the rest, or press Ctrl + C to start again. error: command 'album-sizes' not found . The script's folder is not on your PATH . Run it by its path, ~/bin/album-sizes , or add export PATH="$HOME/bin:$PATH" to ~/.bashrc and source ~/.bashrc . Running a script by its path is refused. You have no execute permission on it. Run chmod 755 <script> , or read it in with source <script> . error: <name>: a #!ts command runs only from a module in /usr/modules . A #!ts file runs only from an installed module. Write the script in bash, or make it part of a module. A count from ls | wc -l is too small. ls wrote its names in columns. Use ls -1 . Every command answers in JSON. JSON_OUTPUT=1 was set on its own line, or in ~/.bashrc . Run unset JSON_OUTPUT . An alias or function from ~/.bashrc is missing. It is read when a tab opens: run source ~/.bashrc in tabs that were open before you changed it. A command sent with ssh host 'command' does not read ~/.bashrc . A background job stopped when I closed the tab. Jobs end with their shell. Start it with nohup , or detach it before you leave. nohup: <command>: nothing left to detach — it had already finished . The command ended, or failed to start, before nohup could detach it. Run it without nohup to see what it says. detach: no such job: %2 . This shell has no such job, or it has ended. jobs lists the ones there are.

The terminal : opening it, tabs, keys, history and Tab completion. Commands by task : which command does what. The editor : edit , for ~/.bashrc and scripts. SSH and SFTP : the same shell from your own computer. Commands reference : every command with all its options. Environment variables : the variables every shell has. Writing a module : commands that come with a module.

This page is for power users and administrators who know what they want to do and need the command for it. Each table row gives a task, a command line that does it, and a link to that command's full entry in the reference .

Every command runs as you, with your permissions, in the terminal or over SSH . The examples use the demo archive's invented Wrenfield family: the album /archive/albums/christmas-2019 , the person /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield , the account helen . Albums and people come with the Archive , so those paths are there once it is installed. administrators only marks a command that anyone else is refused before it starts, with <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . A member of the sudo group can type admin to act as the administrator in that terminal. Accounts and groups explains who that is. This page has core's commands. The modules' commands come with their modules , and their tasks are on Archive commands by task and Assistant commands by task ; the media service 's are on its page. Without the module, the shell answers error: command '<name>' not found . mod list shows what is installed. A command of a family can be typed as two words: mod install is mod-install , and pipeline status is pipeline-status . The families are config , docs , group , mod , pipeline , pool , service , share and user , and with the archive also person and camera . <family> --help , such as mod --help , lists its subcommands; typing mod alone answers mod: missing subcommand . An option that takes a piece of text, such as comment add 's --body or file-set-description 's --text , reads it from standard input when its value is - : cat notes.md | comment add <file> --body - . That suits text over several lines or with quotes in it, which is awkward to type on a command line. <command> --help prints a command's arguments, options and examples without running it. JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of a command makes it answer in JSON; The shell language covers that and the rest of the syntax. cd , pwd , jobs , kill and the other bash builtins have no reference entry. They are described in The shell language .

The tree works like a file system: paths start at / , .. is the parent, and cd moves you around. Any node can have children, so cd into a photo works and ls shows what EiN learnt about it, such as exif , position , thumbnails and regions . The tree says what lives where. Task Command Reference See where you are, move around pwd , cd /archive/albums , cd - bash builtins List a folder, with details ls -l /archive/albums ( ll for ls -al ) ls List one page of a large folder ls -l --limit 200 --after 20191224_141841.jpg . ls Show a text file or a log cat notes.txt , cat -t /var/logs/system (each entry's time first) cat Look at a picture in the web terminal cat /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191224_141841.jpg cat The first or last lines of a file head -n 20 notes.txt , tail -n 50 notes.txt head , tail Edit a text file, or start one edit ~/notes.md edit Make an empty text file (what touch does elsewhere) mkfile ~/todo.txt mkfile Make a folder, with its parents mkdir -p ~/drafts/2026 mkdir Copy a file or a folder cp notes.txt notes-old.txt , cp -r ~/drafts ~/drafts-copy cp Move or rename mv ~/drafts/letter.txt ~/letters/ mv Move something to your trash trash put ~/drafts/old.txt trash See your trash, restore from it trash list , trash restore <id> trash Delete for good rm ~/todo.txt , rm -r ~/drafts-copy rm Remove empty folders rmdir ~/drafts/2026 rmdir Make a softlink to a node ln -s /archive/albums/christmas-2019 ~/christmas ln A node's type, owner and times stat <path> , info <path> , props <path> stat , info , props A node's attributes attrs /archive/albums/christmas-2019 attrs The path of a node id resolve-id <id> resolve-id A file's type: stored, by name and by content mime <file> mime A file's bytes on disk, with its sha256 file-stat -f <file> file-stat How much a folder holds du -sh /archive/albums/christmas-2019 , du -chs * du Unpack a zip file unzip -d ~/unpacked ~/takeout-001.zip unzip Bookmark a node, list bookmarks star <path> , star -d <path> , star list star Label something, see labels label add <path> sailing , label remove <path> sailing , labels label , labels Comment on a node comment add <path> --body 'Taken at the cottage' , comment list <path> comment Warning rm deletes for good: it does not use the trash. Without -r it refuses any node that has children, with rm: cannot remove '<path>': Node not empty , and a processed photo has children (its metadata, thumbnails and faces). Use trash put for anything you may want back. Links explains what deleting and moving do to links.

search looks through what EiN knows about your content. It asks each installed module's search, so what it finds comes from the modules: with no module it finds nothing, and with the Archive the words, what the pictures show, the people in them, dates and places; Archive commands by task has those searches. find walks the tree by name and type, as GNU find does. Search and the finder covers searching in the Web UI. Task Command Reference Search everything by words search sailboat search Search everything below a folder search --within ~/staging/files --undated search Find nodes by name find /archive/albums -iname '*.heic' -type f find Find nodes by type find /archive/people -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -type person find Find large files find ~/staging -type f -size +10M -printf '%s %p\n' find Find what changed in the last hour find ~/staging -type f -mmin -60 find Find lines in text files grep -n -i cottage ~/notes.md grep Find a command by what it does docs find restart a service docs-find The node types find -type takes are listed in Node types .
Accounts and groups explains the built-in accounts and groups, and Permissions in depth the permission model these commands change.

Task Command Reference List the groups and their members group-list --members group-list One group's details group-info family group-info Create a group, administrators only group-create family --title 'Family' group-create Give a group a shared home, administrators only group-home family group-home Add someone to a group, administrators only group-add-member family anna group-add-member Take someone out of a group, administrators only group-remove-member family anna group-remove-member List a group's members, administrators only group-members family group-members Rename a group's title, administrators only group-update family --title 'The Wrenfields' group-update Delete a group, administrators only group-delete family --to users group-delete A change of groups applies the next time that person signs in. To let someone use ssh and scp from EiN, add them to the group ssh : see Reaching other machines .

Task Command Reference Who has access to a node, and through what share-info /archive/albums/christmas-2019 share-info Give a group access to an album and what is in it share-set -m g:family:rx /archive/albums/christmas-2019 share-set Set the mode of a node and everything below share-set --mode 0750 /archive/albums/malpas-summer share-set Keep a node's own access when its folder changes share-set --pin <path> share-set Make a link that opens an album without signing in share-link create /archive/albums/christmas-2019 share-link A link that does not expire share-link create --never /archive/albums/christmas-2019 share-link List your links, turn one off share-link list , share-link remove <id> share-link Change mode bits chmod 750 <path> , chmod -r g+rx <path> chmod Change owner or group chown helen:family <path> , chown :family <path> chown Show a node's access list acl <path> acl Add or remove an access list entry acl -m u:anna:rx <path> , acl -x u:anna <path> acl The recursive flag of chmod , chown and acl is a lower-case -r . A share link made with share-link create lasts 30 days unless you give --expires or --never . Sharing shows the Share dialog that does the same in the Web UI.

Configuration explains where a setting's value comes from, and Modules what installing a module does. Every setting and its default is in Settings , for example CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS .

The sensors, plugs, phones and loggers under /dev ; Devices shows the pages that do the same, and Devices, endpoints and drivers what writing to a device or an endpoint does. Task Command Reference Every device, with its main value devices , devices --online devices The drivers running, and how many devices each drives devices --drivers devices A device's endpoints and their values now device-show hall-plug device-show How an endpoint went, an average an hour device-history hall-sensor/temperature --since 7d --bucket 1h device-history Switch or set a control echo on > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 , echo toggle > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 Switch something Follow an endpoint as its values come tail -f /dev/hall-sensor/temperature tail Every press of a button kept, as the administrator mkqueue -k 'dev.porch-button.#' ~/presses mkqueue Share a device, as a member of devices share-set -m g:parents:rx /dev/front-door Share a device Make a phone, tracker or logger, as a member of devices device-create 'Ruby phone' --driver tracker --class phone device-create Give a GPX file to a tracker cat ~/walk.gpx > /dev/jon-s-etrex cat The address a phone posts to, with a new key device-key ruby-phone --new --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example device-key Rename a device or an endpoint, as a member of devices device-label hall-plug 'Hall lamp' device-label Forget a device and its history, as a member of devices device-forget old-sensor device-forget A write to a device's log or track appends to it, with > as with >> , and a bare value such as 21.4 is kept as {"value": 21.4} ; a control takes > .
Health and status , Processing and pipelines and Services and logs explain what these commands report and what to do about it.

In EiN a pid is a name, such as sleep- followed by a unique id, not a number. Ctrl + Z does not suspend a command; start it with & instead.

Use queue-peek to look.

There is no logs command. The system log, each service's output and the metrics series under /var/logs/metrics are log nodes, read with dmesg , tail , cat and log-read . Task Command Reference The system log dmesg -n 50 dmesg The last ten problems dmesg --level warn -n 10 dmesg Follow the system log as it grows tail -f /var/logs/system tail A service's own output tail -f /var/logs/services/metrics-sampler/stdout.log , and stderr.log beside it tail A log's entries over a time range log-read /var/logs/metrics/memory --since 24h log-read A log summed up per hour, as a chart wants it log-read /var/logs/metrics/memory --since 7d --bucket 1h --field usedBytes --agg max log-read Who changed, moved or removed what, administrators only audit --user anna --since 2026-10-01 /archive/albums audit Every change under a folder, older ones too, administrators only audit --all /archive/albums audit The system log starts empty at every start of EiN, and a service's two log files start empty at every start of that service.

ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id are for administrators and members of the group ssh . Reaching other machines covers them, with the host key prompts and ~/.ssh/config . Task Command Reference Make a key pair in ~/.ssh ssh-keygen ssh-keygen Put your public key on another machine ssh-copy-id anna@nas.local ssh-copy-id Log in to another machine, or run one command there ssh anna@nas.local , ssh nas.local 'df -h' ssh Copy files in from another machine scp -r anna@nas.local:photos/1968 /home/anna/staging/files/inbox/ scp List what is mounted mount mount Mount a folder of another machine (administrators) mount --save /mnt/nas sftp "host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos" mount Connecting to EiN from your own computer is described in SSH and SFTP .

These work on text files, logs and the output of other commands, as their GNU namesakes do. Run <command> --help for the options each has. Task Command Reference Pick fields from JSON JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums | jq -r '.[].name' jq Find lines matching a pattern grep -i -c christmas ~/notes.md grep Replace text in a stream sed 's/Wrenfeld/Wrenfield/g' ~/notes.md sed Work with columns awk -F'\t' '{ print $1 }' , cut -f1 awk , cut Sort, count and remove repeats sort , uniq -c , wc -l sort , uniq , wc Run a command for each line of input ls /archive/people | xargs -I {} info /archive/people/{} xargs Change or delete characters tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' tr Dates, numbers, waiting date -I , seq 1 10 , sleep 5 date , seq , sleep Parts of a path basename <path> , dirname <path> , abspath <path> basename , dirname , abspath The environment of your shell env , docs env env , docs-env

p.h: Unix commands EiN does not have
p.x: EiN's commands are its own, so some familiar names are missing. Use these instead. You may type Use instead touch mkfile vi , nano edit less , more , man the terminal's scrollback, <command> --help , and the reference realpath abspath which type <name> or command -v <name> passwd , useradd , usermod user-passwd , user-create , user-update ; for groups, group-add-member chgrp chown :<group> <path> sudo , su admin or user-elevate , for members of sudo ; runas for an administrator to act as someone else getfacl , setfacl acl tar , rsync , curl , wget , diff , tee none in EiN; unzip unpacks zip files, and scp copies over SSH There is also no sh or bash command: a script is run by its path, or with source . The shell language explains scripts.

p.h: When a command is refused or missing
p.x: What you see Why What to do error: command '<name>' not found No command of that name is on your PATH : a typing error, or a module that is not installed Check the name with docs find <words> ; see mod list <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it The command is for administrators Ask an administrator, or type admin if you are in the sudo group <name>: permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id need the ssh group An administrator adds you with group-add-member ssh <you> ; sign in again <name>: sign in first You are not signed in, and visitors may not browse login <username> rm: cannot remove '<path>': Node not empty The node has children rm -r <path> deletes it with them; trash put <path> keeps it recoverable edit: not a terminal edit needs a terminal, which ssh host 'command' does not give Log in with ssh first, or use the terminal panel <name>: no terminal to answer on; add --force The command would ask a question, and ssh host 'command' or a script has no one to answer Give the answer as the option it names, or run it in the terminal panel mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount Mounting is for administrators Ask an administrator For anything else, Troubleshooting goes through problems by area, and the reference has every command with all its options.

EiN has two places to change a text file: edit in the terminal, which colours the text and checks JSON, YAML and bash as you type, and the code editor on the Nodes page of the Web UI. This page is for anyone who edits a script, a note or a configuration file in EiN.

edit runs in a terminal: the terminal panel in the browser, or an SSH login from your own computer. Open the terminal with the terminal button in the top bar, or Alt + T . Type edit and the path of the file, and press Enter : # in EiN's terminal edit ~/notes.md The editor fills the terminal. Change the text, press Ctrl + S to save and Ctrl + Q to leave. The shell's screen comes back as you left it. A path is read from the directory you are in, so edit tidy.sh opens tidy.sh there. Tab completes paths after edit as it does after any command. What the editor shows, here on a nav.json with a missing comma: 1 { ✗2 "hide": ["archive.map" "archive.cameras"] 3 } ~ ~ nav.json ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element JSON ✗ L 1:1 ^S Save ^Q Quit ^F Find ^G Line ^Z Undo ^Y Redo ^K Cut ^U Paste The text , with line numbers at the left. The cursor's line number is in the text's own colour, the others grey. Rows after the end of the file show ~ . The status bar , the second row from the bottom. At the left: the file's name, [New] for a file not saved yet, [Modified] while there are unsaved changes, then a message or the syntax error described under Checks as you type . At the right: the language, a check mark or cross where the language is checked, and the cursor's position as L line:column . The bottom row lists the main keys, ^S meaning Ctrl + S . While the editor asks you something, such as Find: , the question takes this row.

Give edit a path that does not exist yet. The editor opens empty with [New] in the status bar. Nothing is created until you save; leaving without saving leaves nothing behind. The first save creates the file in the folder the path names, and decides its type: from the name's extension: notes.md becomes Markdown, nav.json JSON, tidy.sh a shell script; for a name without a known extension, from a first line starting with #! : #!bash makes a script, #!/usr/bin/env python3 a Python file; otherwise plain text. Typing a #!bash line into a new file colours and checks it as bash at once, unless its name already has one of the extensions under Colours and line wrapping . The folder must exist. To start a file in a folder that is not there yet, make the folder first: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ui && edit ~/.ui/nav.json A script you write with edit needs execute permission before it runs as a command: chmod 755 tidy.sh . The shell language covers scripts.

p.h: When edit will not open a file
p.x: edit prints one line and goes back to the prompt: Message Why What to do edit: missing file operand You gave no path. Name the file: edit notes.md . edit: not a terminal The command did not run in a terminal: one command sent with ssh … 'edit notes.md' , or a script started without one. The assistant never runs edit . Use the terminal panel, or sign in over SSH with a shell of your own ( ssh -p 2222 anna@ein.local ) and run edit there. edit: /home/anna/staging: not a file (directory) The path is a folder, or another kind of node such as an album or a person. The type is in brackets. Name a file. ls -l shows what a folder holds. edit: /home/anna/beach.jpg: not a text file (mimetype: image/jpeg) The file is a picture, a video, a PDF or another file that is not text. Nothing to edit here. With the Archive, a picture opens in its viewer. edit: /home/anna/old.txt: not UTF-8 text The file is text in another encoding, such as Latin-1, or holds bytes that are not text. Convert it to UTF-8 on your own computer and upload it again. edit: /etc/keys: Access denied … You may not read the file. Ask its owner or an administrator. Permissions in depth explains who may read what. The full entry for the command is edit in the reference.

Press Ctrl + S . The status bar says Saved and [Modified] goes away. If the text has a syntax error, the editor asks first, on the bottom row, with the first error after the question: Save with errors? (y/N) ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element Press y to save anyway. n , Enter or any other letter leaves the file as it was and the status bar says Not saved ; Esc takes the question away. To leave, press Ctrl + Q . With nothing unsaved the editor closes at once. Otherwise it asks: Save changes? (y/n, Esc cancels) y saves and leaves. If the text has an error, Save with errors? (y/N) comes first. n leaves without saving. Esc or Ctrl + C goes back to the text. Ctrl + C does not leave the editor: on its own it only shows ^Q quits . Tip If your browser or terminal program keeps Ctrl + S or Ctrl + Q for itself, Ctrl + O saves and Ctrl + X quits. Saving keeps the file's line endings: a file written with Windows line endings (CRLF) keeps them, and a file that ended without a final newline still does. A new file ends with a newline.

The status bar shows Not saved: and the reason in red, and your text stays in the editor. The usual reasons are a folder that does not exist and a file you may read but not change ( Access denied ). In the terminal panel you can put it right without losing the text: Press Alt + N for a new terminal tab. Make the folder there with mkdir -p , or ask for access to the file. Go back to the editor's tab, by clicking it or with Alt + ← , and press Ctrl + S again. Over SSH, open a second SSH login for the same purpose. edit does not notice when someone else changes the file while you have it open: saving writes your text over theirs.

Keys What they do Ctrl + S or Ctrl + O Save. With a syntax error in the text, asks first. Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + X Leave. With unsaved changes, asks first. Ctrl + F Find. The question starts with the last search; Enter goes to the next match. Ctrl + G Go to a line, or to line:column . Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Y Undo / redo. Ctrl + K Cut the cursor's line. Lines cut one after another collect into one cut. Ctrl + U Paste what was cut, at the cursor. ← → One character left or right, on to the next or previous line at a line's end. ↑ ↓ One row up or down, keeping to the column you started from. Ctrl + ← Ctrl + → , Alt + ← Alt + → , Alt + B Alt + F One word left or right. In the terminal panel Alt with an arrow switches tabs instead. Home or Ctrl + A To the first character of the line that is not a space; pressed again, to the very start. On a wrapped row, to the start of that row. End or Ctrl + E To the end of the line. On a wrapped row, to the end of that row. Ctrl + Home / Ctrl + End To the start / end of the file. PgUp / PgDn A screen up / down. Enter A new line, indented as the line it came from. Tab Indent. See Indentation . Backspace / Delete Delete the character before / after the cursor. At the start or end of a line, join it with the line before or after. Esc or Ctrl + C Cancel a question: find, go to a line, save with errors, save changes. Ctrl + C with no question open Shows ^Q quits . On a Mac, too, the keys are Ctrl , not ⌘ .

p.h: Find text and go to a line
p.x: Press Ctrl + F . The bottom row shows Find: , with your last search already typed. Type what you are looking for and press Enter . The cursor moves to the next match after it. Case does not matter. When the search runs past the end of the file it goes on from the top and the status bar says Search wrapped ; with no match at all it says Not found . To go on to the next match, press Ctrl + F and Enter again. Ctrl + G shows Go to line[:column]: . Type 40 for line 40, or 40:12 for its twelfth column, and press Enter . A number past the end goes to the last line; anything that is not a number shows Not a line number .

Ctrl + Z undoes up to 200 steps, and Ctrl + Y redoes them. A word typed in one go is one step, and so is a run of deletions or a paste; a pause of half a second starts a new step. With nothing left, the status bar says Nothing to undo or Nothing to redo . Ctrl + K and Ctrl + U use the editor's own clipboard, not your computer's: press Ctrl + K three times to cut three lines, move, and press Ctrl + U to put them back there. Text pasted from your computer goes in exactly as it is, without being indented again, and undoes in one step.

Enter starts the new line with the indent of the one before. A line left holding only spaces is emptied. Tab inserts one step of the indent the text has when you press it, so it follows what you paste or type: a tab, when the text indents mostly with tabs, and always in a Makefile; otherwise as many spaces as the smallest indent of two or more spaces the text has, at most 8; two spaces in a text with no indent yet. Shift + Tab does nothing; take an indent away with Backspace . Tabs in the text reach the next stop of four columns, and other control characters as ^ and a letter.

edit works out the language of a file in this order, and colours the text by it: the name: its extension, or the names Makefile and GNUmakefile ; the file's type, as EiN recorded it when the file came in; a first line starting with #! , when the type says no more than that the file is text. Language Files Checked as you type JSON .json Yes JSONC .jsonc : JSON in which comments are allowed Yes YAML .yaml , .yml Yes bash .sh , .bash ; a shell-script type; a #! line naming bash, sh or any other interpreter not below Yes Markdown .md , .markdown Its code blocks TypeScript .ts , .mts , .tsx ; #!ts or #!deno No JavaScript .js , .mjs , .cjs , .jsx ; #!node or #!js No Python .py ; #!python or #!python3 , also through #!/usr/bin/env No XML .xml , .html , .htm , .svg No CSS .css No Makefile Makefile , GNUmakefile , .mk No Others .scss ; .ini , .conf and .toml (as ini); .sql ; .diff , .patch ; .go ; .rs (rust); .lua No The status bar names the language at its right; a file that matches none is text . A file without an extension, such as ~/.bashrc , is plain text unless its first line starts with #! . In a Markdown file, each fenced code block is coloured in the language its fence names; a console block is a session, with the $ prompt dimmed, the command after it coloured as bash and the output left plain. A text longer than 262,144 characters (256 K) is shown without colours. Plain text and Markdown wrap at the edge of the window, at the last space that fits; a row that continues a line has no line number in front of it, and ↑ and ↓ move by rows on the screen. Code does not wrap: a long line scrolls sideways to keep the cursor in view, and Home brings the indent back into view. cat colours a text file in the terminal the same way, without opening it.

edit checks a JSON, JSONC, YAML or bash file after each change. In a Markdown file it checks every fenced code block whose fence names one of those languages: json , jsonc or json5 , yaml or yml , and bash , sh , shell or zsh , fenced with ``` or ~~~ . A console block holds output as well as commands, so it is not checked. An error in a block is shown at its line in the whole document. Hide the map for everyone: ```json { "hide": ["archive.map"] } ``` An error shows in three places: A red ✗ in front of the line number of the line it is on. The character where the parser stopped, underlined in red. When the error is at the end of the line, a red block stands after its last character. The status bar : at the left, ✗ , the line and column, and what is wrong, such as ✗ 2:26 expected ',' or ']' after array element , followed by (+2 more) when there are more. It shows the error on the cursor's line when there is one, otherwise the first. At the right, the language with ✓ when the text is correct, ✗ when it has an error, and … while a check is still to come. Fix the error and the marks go away as you type. An empty JSON file is not an error: it is one you are starting. For bash the messages are those of EiN's shell, among them unexpected token 'fi' , unexpected end of file , and here-document not closed (wanted 'EOF') for a here-document that is never ended. A check that takes longer than 50 milliseconds waits until you stop typing for half a second, and the status bar shows … meanwhile, so a long file stays quick to type in. A text longer than 1,000,000 characters is not checked. Saving always checks the text as it is at that moment. The checks say whether a file can be read, not whether it does what you mean. For the file of your sidebar, ui-nav also checks the fields in it; see Your sidebar and top bar .

p.h: Edit in the terminal panel and over SSH
p.x: In the terminal panel: Alt + M gives the terminal the full height of the window, and the editor redraws to fill it. The editor also follows any other change of size. Alt + ← and Alt + → switch between terminal tabs, and Alt + ↑ and Alt + ↓ change the panel's height, so they never reach the editor. Move by word with Ctrl + ← and Ctrl + → . Hiding the panel, with Alt + T or a click outside it, leaves the editor open in its tab, unsaved changes and all. Warning Closing the editor's terminal tab, with its × or Alt + W , ends the editor without saving and without asking. So does closing an SSH connection. Over SSH, edit needs the shell you get by signing in: ssh -p 2222 anna@ein.local , then edit notes.md . A command sent along on the ssh line, even with ssh -t , runs without a terminal and stops with edit: not a terminal . SSH and SFTP has the rest.

p.h: Edit a file in the Web UI
p.x: The Nodes page has a code editor for those who would rather stay in the browser. Nodes is under System in an administrator's sidebar. Other people do not have it in their sidebar, but anyone signed in can open it at /system/nodes (for example http://ein.local:8080/system/nodes ), and sees there what they may read. The Nodes page browses the whole tree. Right-click a text file here and choose Open to edit it. Open Nodes . It starts in your home folder, /home/<you> . Go to the folder that holds the file. Names that start with a dot, such as .bashrc , .config and .ui , are hidden: press Ctrl + H , or the eye button at the end of the address bar ("Show names starting with a dot (Ctrl+H)"), to show them. Right-click the file and choose Open . Double-clicking or Enter goes into the file instead, to the nodes it holds. The code editor opens in a dialog, titled with the file's name and with its path under it. Beside the title, badges name the language (such as JSON , SHELL or TEXT ), say READ-ONLY when you may not change the file, and UNSAVED once you have changed it. Make your change and choose Save , or press Ctrl + S ( ⌘ + S on a Mac). Save is greyed until there is something to save. Choose Close when you are done. If you close with unsaved changes, the dialog asks "Discard unsaved changes?": Keep editing takes you back, Discard closes without saving. Esc closes the dialog only when there is nothing unsaved. Raw , at the left under the editor, opens the file itself in a new browser tab. The code editor has line numbers, Ctrl + F to find, Ctrl + Z to undo and Tab to indent. It colours JSON, JavaScript, TypeScript, YAML, Markdown, HTML, CSS, XML and shell scripts, by the file's type first and then its extension. What Open does depends on the file: a text file opens in the code editor, a picture, video or recording in the viewer that the Archive adds, and any other file in a new browser tab. The Preview in the tool pane beside the list shows the first 64 KB of a text file without opening it. Where the code editor stops: What you see or want What to do "Too large to edit here (N KB). Open the raw file instead." The file is larger than 2 MB. Use the link to read it, or edit in the terminal to change it. A new file The Nodes page makes folders ( New directory ) but not files. Start the file with edit , or upload it. A check of your JSON or YAML The code editor colours but does not check. Open the file with edit to see errors as you type. A red box under the editor: "could not write …" The file was not saved: usually you may read it but not change it. Your text is still in the editor; copy it before you discard it.

edit in the terminal Code editor on the Nodes page Where Terminal panel, SSH login Browser, Nodes page New files Yes, on the first save No Checks JSON, YAML and bash Yes, as you type, and before saving No Colours By name, type or #! line By type, then name Largest file Any; no checks over 1,000,000 characters 2 MB Keys Its own , Ctrl on a Mac too A browser editor's, ⌘ on a Mac Files people often edit are ~/.bashrc ( The shell language ), ~/.ui/nav.json ( Your sidebar and top bar ) and the files listed in Configuration files . Every key in EiN is gathered in Keyboard shortcuts .

EiN runs its own SSH server, so you can reach it from your own computer: log in to the same shell as the terminal in the Web UI, run one command from a script, and copy files in and out with SFTP, scp or a graphical file manager. This page is for anyone with an EiN account who wants to work from their own machine; going the other way, from EiN out to a NAS or another server, is on Reaching other machines .

What Example Where it comes from The host ein.local The name or address of the machine EiN runs on, the same one you open in the browser. The SSH port 2222 2222 unless your administrator chose another. Your account helen Your EiN username. Your e-mail address works too, where your account has one. Your secret your password The password you sign in to the Web UI with, or a key once you have added one. SSH and SFTP share the one port. With the standard install it is set by EIN_SSH_PORT in .env on the machine EiN runs on; Ports, HTTPS and remote access explains how to change it and how to reach EiN from outside your home network. Inside its container EiN always listens on 2222 , the port EIN_SSH_PORT is passed on to. The examples below use Helen Okafor's account helen on ein.local , port 2222 . Use your own.

On your own computer, open a terminal (on Windows, PowerShell has ssh built in) and run: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local The first time, ssh shows the key EiN's server identifies itself with and asks whether to trust it: The authenticity of host '[ein.local]:2222 ([192.168.1.20]:2222)' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:… Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? Type yes . Your computer remembers the key and does not ask again. To be sure it is your EiN answering, ask your administrator to compare the fingerprint; they see it in EiN's terminal with ssh-keygen -l -f /etc/ssh_host_key.pub . Enter your EiN password. You land in your home folder, /home/helen , at the same prompt as in a terminal tab. Everything on The terminal holds here too: your history, your ~/.bashrc , Tab completion and the same keys, and every command on Commands by task . The editor works as well ( The editor ). Two things belong to the browser alone: the pictures, videos and recordings cat shows, which over SSH print lines starting __IMG: , __VID: or __AUD: instead, and dropping files to upload them. To log out, type exit . Closing the window or losing the connection ends the shell too, and stops whatever command was running in it. Tip If your username is an e-mail address, give it with -l so the two @ do not get mixed up: ssh -p 2222 -l helen@example.com ein.local .

With a key you are no longer asked for your password. If you have no key yet, make one on your own computer with ssh-keygen and accept the defaults. Give EiN the public half of your key, once: # on your own computer ssh-copy-id -s -p 2222 helen@ein.local It asks for your EiN password this one time. The -s matters: it makes ssh-copy-id copy the key over SFTP. Without it, ssh-copy-id sends a script of Unix shell commands, which EiN's shell does not run. Log in as before. ssh and sftp now use the key and do not ask for the password. The key lives in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys in your EiN home, one key per line, as on any Linux server. You can add and remove lines there yourself. EiN reads lines starting with a key type such as ssh-ed25519 , ssh-rsa or ecdsa-sha2-nistp256 , and skips empty lines and lines starting with # . A line with options in front of the key ( command="…" , from="…" , no-pty and the like) is skipped entirely. EiN trusts the file only while nobody but you can change it, since anyone who could write to it could sign in as you. Your home, ~/.ssh and authorized_keys must each be owned by you (or the administrator), writable by neither group nor others nor by anyone else through an access list, and none of them may be a link. ssh-copy-id -s sets the modes for you.

Where ssh-copy-id is missing, as on Windows, add the key from EiN's terminal. Copy the contents of your public key file ( id_ed25519.pub in the .ssh folder of your home on your own computer), then: # in EiN's terminal mkdir -p ~/.ssh chmod 700 ~/.ssh echo 'ssh-ed25519 AAAA… helen@laptop' >> ~/.ssh/authorized_keys chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys The two chmod lines are what make EiN trust the file. If key sign-in still asks for a password, check the modes with ls -la ~/.ssh : the folder should show rwx------ and the file rw------- .

p.h: Run one command at a time
p.x: Give ssh a command after the host and it runs just that one, prints the answer and exits with the command's exit status. That is what a script on your own computer wants: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'ls /archive/albums' ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls -l /archive/albums/cornwall-1968' | jq . The examples on this page use the Archive 's albums, which are there once it is installed; any folder you may read works the same way. With JSON_OUTPUT=1 commands answer in JSON instead of text (see Environment variables ). Each command gets a shell of its own, so cd does not carry over to the next ssh . Chain steps that belong together in one line: 'cd /archive/albums && ls' . The command runs without a terminal, so edit and anything else that needs one stops; log in with a shell for those. A command that would ask a question, such as a password or "Remove module?", stops instead with <name>: no terminal to answer on , followed by the option that gives the answer: mod remove --force , user-passwd --new-password , user-elevate --password . Commands sent this way are not added to your history. What you pipe in reaches the command byte for byte and ends where your input ends, so ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'cat > ~/photo.jpg' < photo.jpg copies a photo in. Errors arrive on their own stream, as with any SSH server, so 2>/dev/null on your side drops them and 2>errors.txt keeps them apart from the output. Use the exit status to tell success from failure.

Any SFTP client works: the sftp command, a graphical client such as FileZilla or Cyberduck, or your file manager's "connect to server". Give it the protocol SFTP, the host, the port and your username, with your password or key. # on your own computer sftp -P 2222 helen@ein.local Note the capital -P for the port in sftp and scp , where ssh takes a lowercase -p . You start in your home folder. Then move around and copy as on any server: sftp> cd /archive/albums/cornwall-1968 sftp> get beach.jpg sftp> put harbour.jpg sftp> bye scp works the same way, one command at a time: # on your own computer scp -P 2222 harbour.jpg helen@ein.local:/home/helen/ scp -P 2222 -r helen@ein.local:/archive/albums/cornwall-1968 . scp from OpenSSH 9.0 and later copies over SFTP, which EiN serves. An older scp uses a different protocol that EiN does not speak; with OpenSSH 8.7 or 8.8 add -s , and with anything older use sftp . What you may see and change is decided by the same permissions as in the Web UI: a folder you cannot open in the browser cannot be opened over SFTP either.

p.h: Bring in a large batch of photos
p.x: With the Archive installed, an export or a scanned box of tens of thousands of files is better copied over SFTP into your staging area than uploaded in the browser, and a photo copied into an album is taken in as an upload is. Copy files in over SFTP gives the folder to copy into and how to keep folder names for the grouping, and Zips what happens to a zip you copy in.

p.h: What the tree looks like over SFTP
p.x: EiN's tree holds more than an ordinary file system can show, so a few things look different. What belongs to a photo. A file can hold nodes of its own: with the Archive, a photo keeps its EXIF data, the faces found in it and its thumbnails. Those live in a hidden folder named after the photo with _ added: what belongs to beach.jpg is in beach.jpg_ . It is not listed, so copying an album with scp -r or get -r copies the photos without it. You can still go in by typing its name ( cd beach.jpg_ ), look around and download at any depth. Nothing in it can be changed over SFTP, and removing the photo removes it too. Modification times. A file's modification time is when its content last changed, not when EiN last added something about it. Backup tools therefore see a photo as unchanged while its faces or description are being worked out. put -p , scp -p and cp -p on a mount keep the time they set. Sizes. A file can be emptied by setting its size to 0. Any other change of size without writing the content is refused. Photos you copy in are frozen. A picture, video or recording is frozen once the whole of it has arrived, as an upload in the browser is, so writing over it is refused with Permission denied ; renaming, moving and deleting it work. A copy that stopped part-way is not frozen and can be sent again. Which types are frozen is up to your administrator, in /etc/frozen-uploads . Links. Softlinks, such as your favourites, or with the Archive an album's cover, a picture added to an album and a person tagged in a photo, appear as symbolic links, and following one takes you to what it points to. A recursive copy therefore copies the link, not what lies behind it. ln -s in sftp makes a new link, and removing a link removes only the link, never what it points to. Links explains what they are for. Warning Removing a file over SFTP deletes it for good, with everything that belongs to it. It does not go to your trash, as deleting in the Web UI does. Removing a folder works only once it is empty.

With sshfs on Linux or macOS you can mount EiN's tree as a folder on your own computer and use any program on it: # on your own computer mkdir -p ~/ein sshfs -p 2222 -o transform_symlinks helen@ein.local:/ ~/ein -o transform_symlinks matters: a link's target is a path in EiN, such as /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield , and the option makes it point inside the mount rather than to the same path on your computer. fusermount -u ~/ein (on macOS umount ~/ein ) unmounts it. With the Album folders module, the albums are also folders of real files on the machine EiN runs on, which a shared folder can offer without SSH. rsync works against such a mount. Over SSH directly, rsync helen@ein.local:… does not, because it needs an rsync program on EiN's side, and EiN's shell has none.

Every account with a password can sign in over SSH and SFTP; no group membership is needed. Being in the group ssh is about reaching other machines from EiN, not about reaching EiN (see Reaching other machines ). An account still waiting for a password, such as one imported without one, cannot sign in over SSH, with a key or with a password, nor anywhere else, until the administrator sets one for it. A disabled account cannot sign in at all, and disabling an account, or deleting it, ends the SSH and SFTP connections it already has open. Accounts and groups covers both. After five wrong passwords from one address, that address is refused for a while, starting at a second and doubling with each further failure up to 15 minutes; failures are forgotten an hour after the last one. Your ssh shows the same Permission denied as for a wrong password, so wait before trying again. EiN's SSH server offers logins, single commands and SFTP. It does not forward ports, X11 or your SSH agent.

What you see Why What to do Connection refused or a time-out Wrong port or host, or EiN is not running, or the port is not reachable from where you are. Check the port with your administrator; from outside your home network see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Permission denied (publickey,password) with the right password The account still waits for a password, is disabled, or your address is held back after failed attempts. Ask your administrator to set a password or enable the account, or wait and try again. The key is not used and you are asked for the password authorized_keys is missing, the key line has options in front, or the modes let others write. Check with ls -la ~/.ssh in EiN's terminal and fix with chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys . WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! EiN's server key is not the one your computer remembers, as after EiN was installed again from scratch. Ask your administrator whether that happened. If so, forget the old key with ssh-keygen -R "[ein.local]:2222" and connect again. ssh-copy-id fails without -s Without -s it runs Unix shell commands on EiN's side. Run it with -s . scp fails right away An scp older than OpenSSH 9.0 uses a protocol EiN does not speak. Add -s (OpenSSH 8.7 or 8.8), or use sftp . edit: not a terminal The command was sent along on the ssh line, without a shell. Log in with ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local and run it there. A copied folder lacks faces, EXIF and thumbnails What belongs to a photo is in its hidden _ folder, which recursive copies skip. Go into beach.jpg_ by name to fetch it; the photos themselves are complete. Permission denied when copying a photo over one already there The photo there is frozen . Copy it under another name, or lift the mark with attrs -d frozen <file> in EiN's terminal first. Writing in a folder is refused You may not change that folder, or it lies inside a photo's _ folder. See Permissions in depth , or copy into your home or staging area instead.

From EiN's shell you can log in to another machine, run a command there, copy files in and out, and put your key on it, with ssh , scp , ssh-copy-id and ssh-keygen . An administrator can also mount a folder of another machine into the tree over SFTP. This page is for members of the group ssh and for the administrator who lets them in. Everything here goes out from EiN to another machine. To come in to EiN from your own computer, see SSH and SFTP .

Membership of the group ssh , or the administrator account. ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id refuse everyone else: ssh: permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' ssh-keygen works for everyone, since it only touches your own ~/.ssh . An account on the other machine , and that machine running an SSH server. A network path from the machine EiN runs on. The connection starts there, not on the computer your browser runs on. A host you can reach from your laptop is not always one EiN can reach. The commands work the way OpenSSH's do, and read and write the same files, but those files live in your home folder in EiN's tree ( /home/<you>/.ssh ), not on the machine EiN runs on. You can look at them with ls -la ~/.ssh and open them with edit .

The group ssh is made when EiN starts for the first time, with the title SSH users . It is empty until the administrator adds people. Open Settings → Groups and choose SSH users . The page says what the group is for: "Its members may use ssh, scp and ssh-copy-id to reach other machines." Under Members , tick the people who may use them. Ask them to sign out and in again. As the section says, changes apply the next time each person signs in. The same from the terminal, as the administrator: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator group-add-member ssh helen Take someone out again by unticking them, or with group-remove-member ssh helen . Accounts and groups covers groups in general. Warning A member of ssh can copy anything they may read in EiN to any machine they can log in to, and run commands on those machines from the machine EiN runs on. Add only people you would give that.

# in EiN's terminal ssh anna@nas.local The first time, ssh does not know the machine and asks: The authenticity of host 'nas.local' can't be established. ED25519 key fingerprint is SHA256:Xb7k2Qy9mWv0Tz4hJc1pLr8sNe5uGa3dFo6iKq2YwBM. Are you sure you want to continue connecting (yes/no/[fingerprint])? Compare the fingerprint with the one the other machine shows for its own key (on a Linux machine, ssh-keygen -l -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub there). Type yes , or paste the fingerprint, to go on; anything else is asked again, and no stops. The key is then written to ~/.ssh/known_hosts : Warning: Permanently added 'nas.local' (ED25519) to the list of known hosts. Next, ssh offers your keys. When none is accepted it asks for the password: anna@nas.local's password: You are then in the other machine's shell, in the same terminal tab. Everything you type goes to it, Ctrl + C included, and full-screen programs such as top or an editor draw as they would anywhere. Resizing the panel resizes the remote terminal. To leave, type exit or press Ctrl + D . If the other side stops answering, type ~ and . at the start of a line (after Enter ): that cuts the connection, and ssh prints Connection to anna@nas.local closed. Who you log in as: You type Remote user ssh anna@nas.local anna ssh -l anna nas.local anna ssh nas.local a User from ~/.ssh/config , else your EiN username The port is 22 unless you give another with -p : ssh -p 2222 backup.example.com . A host followed by :port is not understood; use -p . An IPv6 address may be bracketed: ssh anna@[fe80::1] .

p.h: Run one command on another machine
p.x: Put the command after the host. Everything after the host goes to the other machine, flags included: # in EiN's terminal ssh nas.local 'df -h' ssh anna@nas.local ls -la photos The output comes back to your terminal, and ssh ends with the remote command's exit status, so it works in scripts and with && . When the connection itself fails, the status is 255 . A single command runs without a terminal on the other side. Add -t for one that needs a terminal, such as top ; -tt asks for one even when ssh itself runs without a terminal. -T never asks for one. Input is passed along, so pipes work in both directions: # in EiN's terminal cat ~/notes.md | ssh anna@nas.local 'cat > notes-from-ein.md' ssh anna@nas.local 'cat photos/list.txt' | wc -l A plain ssh nas.local without a terminal (in a script, or with input from a pipe) warns Pseudo-terminal will not be allocated because stdin is not a terminal. and runs the remote shell on your input. -q leaves out that warning and the Connection to … closed. line.

p.h: Log in with a key instead of a password
p.x: A key saves you typing the password, and is required for a mount . Make a key pair: # in EiN's terminal ssh-keygen Generating public/private ed25519 key pair. Enter passphrase (empty for no passphrase): Enter same passphrase again: Your identification has been saved in /home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519 Your public key has been saved in /home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub The key fingerprint is: SHA256:4fJq0Vw2nRb8tYc6LmZ1xKd9sPe3uHa7gTo5iNy2QwE helen@ein A passphrase protects the private key; ssh and scp then ask for it when they use the key. Leave it empty for a key that scripts and mounts can use without anyone at the keyboard. Put the public key on the other machine: # in EiN's terminal ssh-copy-id anna@nas.local ssh-copy-id: INFO: Source of key(s) to be installed: "/home/helen/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub" anna@nas.local's password: Number of key(s) added: 1 Now try logging into the machine, with: "ssh 'anna@nas.local'" and check to make sure that only the key(s) you wanted were added. It logs in once with the password, adds the key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys there (making the folder and file when they are missing), and adds nothing when the key is already in the file. Run ssh anna@nas.local . It logs in without asking for the password. When you do not name a key, ssh and scp offer every key they find of ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 , ~/.ssh/id_ecdsa and ~/.ssh/id_rsa , in that order; ssh-copy-id installs the first public key it finds of the same three. Name another with -i . Task Command An RSA key, for an old server ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -C "backup key" A key in a file of its own ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/nas -N '' Show a key's fingerprint ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub Print the public key of a private key file ssh-keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/nas Show what ssh-copy-id would add ssh-copy-id -n anna@nas.local Install a named key on another port ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/nas.pub -p 2222 anna@backup.example.com Key types are ed25519 (the default), ecdsa (256, 384 or 521 bits) and rsa (3072 bits unless you give at least 2048 with -b ). The comment is <your username>@ein unless you give one with -C . A key named with -f goes into a folder that must exist already: plain ssh-keygen , or accepting a first host key, makes ~/.ssh for you. When the file exists, ssh-keygen asks Overwrite (y/n)? ; without a terminal it stops instead. See ssh-keygen and ssh-copy-id for every option.

scp copies between EiN's tree and one other machine. A path is remote when it has host: before any / , as in OpenSSH: anna@nas.local:photos/1968 . A remote path without a leading / starts in the remote user's home folder; anna@nas.local: alone is that home folder. Copy in from another machine: # in EiN's terminal scp anna@nas.local:photos/sailboat.jpg /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ scp -r anna@nas.local:photos/1968 /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ scp "anna@nas.local:photos/*.jpg" /home/helen/staging/files/inbox/ Quote a remote pattern so EiN's shell leaves it alone; the other machine's files are matched against it ( * , ? and […] , and a name starting with a dot only by a pattern that starts with one). When nothing matches, scp says No match . A file copied in is recorded the way an upload is: its size, checksum and type are worked out, and the installed modules' pipelines take it in from there. The examples copy into a staging folder, which the Archive gives you: with it installed, that is a way to bring a machine's photos into the archive; see Sorting in staging . Copy out to another machine: # in EiN's terminal scp -r /archive/albums/christmas-2019 anna@nas.local:backup/ Copying a folder out carries its files and folders only. What EiN keeps beside a photo (its thumbnails, the metadata read from it, its links to people and places) stays behind. Option What it does -r Copy folders and everything in them. Without it a folder is refused with not a regular file . -p Keep modes and modification times. -q No progress meter. The meter shows only in a terminal. -B Never ask for a password or passphrase. -P The port (capital P, unlike ssh ). -i , -F , -o A key, a config file, an option: as for ssh . scp ends with 0 when every file was copied and 1 when any failed; each failure is printed with the path. It does not copy between two remote machines ( copying between two remote hosts is not supported; copy into EiN first ), nor between two EiN paths (use cp ). All remote sources in one command must be on the same machine. See scp .

Settings you would otherwise type every time go in ~/.ssh/config , in OpenSSH's format: # ~/.ssh/config in your EiN home Host nas HostName 192.168.1.20 User anna IdentityFile ~/.ssh/nas Host backup HostName backup.example.com Port 2222 StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new Then ssh nas , scp -r nas:photos/1968 . and ssh-copy-id nas use them. Open the file with edit ~/.ssh/config . EiN acts on these keywords, from the file or from -o Keyword=value on the command line: Keyword What it sets HostName The machine to reach, when the name you type is an alias. Port The port. User The remote user. IdentityFile The key to use. ~/ is your EiN home. StrictHostKeyChecking What to do about an unknown host key: see the next section. BatchMode yes : never ask for anything. ConnectTimeout Seconds to connect and log in (15 unless set). ServerAliveInterval Seconds between keepalives (none unless set). PasswordAuthentication no : do not fall back to a password. As in OpenSSH, the first value found for a keyword wins, so put the specific Host blocks before a Host * block. Match with all , host , originalhost , user and localuser works, and so does Include . Other keywords in the file are skipped without a word; on the command line, -o with a keyword not in the table stops with unsupported option . -F <file> reads another file instead, and -F none reads none.

~/.ssh/known_hosts holds the key of each machine you have accepted, filed under its name, or under [name]:port for a port other than 22. Each EiN account has its own. What happens with a machine whose key is not in the file is up to StrictHostKeyChecking : Value Unknown host Changed key ask (default) Asks you; refuses when there is no terminal Refuses yes Refuses Refuses accept-new Adds the key without asking Refuses no Adds the key without asking Warns, then connects In a script, -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new saves the first question while still catching a key that changes later. When a machine's key has changed, ssh stops with a warning that starts WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! , prints the new fingerprint and the line numbers of the old entry, and ends with Host key verification failed. Either someone is between you and the machine, or the machine was reinstalled and has a new key. When you know it is the second, forget the old key and connect again to accept the new one: # in EiN's terminal ssh-keygen -R nas.local ssh-keygen -R '[backup.example.com]:2222' known_hosts lines written by OpenSSH work as they are, hashed names and @revoked included. @cert-authority lines are skipped: EiN does not check host certificates.

p.h: Mount a folder of another machine
p.x: The administrator can mount a folder of another machine into the tree over SFTP. Its files then show under the mount point and stay on the other machine. As the administrator, make a key without a passphrase and put it on the other machine. A mount logs in with a key only, since it reconnects on its own when nobody is there to type a password. If ~/.ssh does not exist yet, run ssh-keygen once without -f first, or mkdir ~/.ssh : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator ssh-keygen -f ~/.ssh/nas -N '' ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/nas.pub anna@nas.local Mount the folder. A mount point that does not exist yet, such as /mnt/nas , is made as a folder, with any folders above it: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mount --save /mnt/nas sftp "host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos,key=/home/admin/.ssh/nas" mounted sftp at '/mnt/nas' (saved in /etc/fstab) The first mount from a terminal asks about an unknown host key as ssh does. --save writes the mount to /etc/fstab , so it is made again every time EiN starts. Run ls /mnt/nas to see the files, and mount alone to list every mount. Option What it is host The machine. Required. port The port; 22 unless set. user The remote user; the administrator's EiN username unless set. path The remote folder to mount. A relative one starts in the remote user's home. key The key file in EiN's tree. Without it, the default keys in ~/.ssh are tried. hostkey The host key's fingerprint ( SHA256:… ) to accept, instead of known_hosts . uid , gid The EiN user and group that own every file in the mount; the administrator's unless set. readonly Nothing in the mount can be changed from EiN. Options are key=value pairs separated by commas; values cannot hold a comma or = . How a mount behaves: Ownership comes from the mount, permissions from the other machine. Every file belongs to the mount's uid and gid , whoever owns it there; the permission bits are the other machine's. To let a group read the files, give the mount that gid and make the files group-readable there. Nothing is processed. The mount is a mirror: EiN makes no thumbnails, reads no dates and finds no faces in it. With the Archive installed, copy photos into staging to bring them into the archive. It reconnects on its own. When the other machine goes away, commands on the mount fail with the reason and the time of the next attempt ( next attempt in 8s ); the wait grows to at most a minute between attempts. At start-up it does not wait. EiN mounts the saved entries without waiting for the other machine, and connects once it answers. It asks nobody about host keys then, so a host must already be in known_hosts or be pinned with hostkey= . Pinning the fingerprint is the safer choice for a saved mount. To take a mount away, and out of /etc/fstab : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator unmount --save /mnt/nas mount -a makes every /etc/fstab entry that is not mounted yet. Only the administrator can mount and unmount; everyone can list mounts with mount . See mount and unmount .

The commands cover logging in, running commands, copying and keys. There is no port forwarding ( -L , -R , -D ), no agent and no agent forwarding, no jump hosts, and no sftp or rsync command; use scp , or a mount. ssh refuses flags it does not have with unknown option .

Message What it means and what to do permission denied, you must be a member of group 'ssh' Ask the administrator to add you to SSH users , then sign out and in. Could not resolve hostname nas.local: Name or service not known The machine EiN runs on does not know that name. Names ending in .local may not resolve where EiN runs; use the IP address, or set it as HostName in ~/.ssh/config . connect to host nas.local port 22: Connection refused Nothing listens on that port: the SSH server is off, or on another port ( -p ). connect to host nas.local port 22: Connection timed out No answer within 15 seconds: the machine is off, or a firewall is between it and EiN. anna@nas.local: Permission denied. The keys were refused and the password was wrong or not asked for. In a script there is nobody to ask, so only keys are tried: install one with ssh-copy-id . No ED25519 host key is known for nas.local … Connect once from an interactive shell to accept it. The host is unknown and there was nobody to ask (a script, BatchMode , or StrictHostKeyChecking yes ). Connect once from the terminal, or use -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new . WARNING: REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED! See Host keys . Warning: Identity file /home/helen/.ssh/nas not accessible: No such file or directory. The key named with -i or IdentityFile is not there. Check the path with ls ~/.ssh . Load key "/home/helen/.ssh/id_rsa": encrypted, and no one to ask for its passphrase A key with a passphrase and no .pub beside it, used where nobody can type it. Use a key without a passphrase for scripts and mounts. ssh-copy-id: no public key found in ~/.ssh; make one with ssh-keygen Run ssh-keygen first. ssh-copy-id: WARNING: All keys were skipped because they already exist on the remote system. Nothing to do: the key is installed. -f adds it again. mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount Mounting is for the administrator.

SSH and SFTP : reaching EiN from your own computer. The terminal : where these commands run. Commands by task : the other commands, grouped by what they do. Accounts and groups : groups and how membership works. Ports, HTTPS and remote access : the network around the machine EiN runs on. Files and storage : where file contents are kept.

This page is for whoever installs and runs EiN on a machine: every option and variable the installer takes, what its checks measure, podman and Docker, what runs where once EiN is up, and how to run it day to day. Install EiN is the short path; read it first if you have not installed EiN yet.

The install is two scripts, run one after the other: Script Where it is What it does install.sh einhq.eu/install.sh , from the einhq.github.io repository At a first install, asks how EiN is to be installed. Checks the machine. When nothing is missing, clones ein/deploy into ~/ein , or updates it there with git pull --ff-only , and runs ~/ein/setup.sh with your options. setup.sh ~/ein/setup.sh , from ein/deploy Asks nothing. Brings ~/ein up to date from ein/deploy, writes ~/ein/.env the first time, downloads the images (or, from another source, fetches the sources into ~/ein/src and builds them), starts them with compose, waits for EiN to answer and lists its modules. Run again, it updates. Both run as your own user and need no root. The installer takes the names of EiN's official modules besides the options, and makes each name the options it stands for: Name Options archive --ems --module archive assistant --llm --module assistant automation --automation --module automation album-folders --ems --module album-folders recipes --ems --module recipes todo --module todo A name given to an option, as in --module archive , stays a name. The installer keeps --home , --yes and --check to itself and passes every other option on to setup.sh , the names made options; setup.sh takes options only, not the names. It reads some of them on the way: --ems , --no-ems , --llm , --no-llm and --module to choose which checks to run, --source to fetch ein/deploy from there, and --data , --http-port , --ssh-port and --bind to answer their questions. # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- archive The installer's code runs from a function called on its last line, so a download cut short runs nothing. curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --help says where its help is: the head of the script.

The installer asks at a first install, which is a run where the folder EiN goes in has no .env , and only at a terminal. Its input is the script curl pipes to it, so it reads the answers from the terminal itself. It asks nothing: with --yes or -y , or with --check ; without a terminal, such as from a script, over ssh without -t , or in a container. It then says No terminal to ask on: installing with the defaults and the options given, as --yes does. ; where EiN is installed. At a terminal it says EiN is installed in /home/anna/ein: updating it, with the settings it has. and updates it. Before any question, it stops on anything but Linux on x86-64: EiN runs on Linux on x86-64; this is Darwin on arm64, so nothing was installed. Each question shows its default in brackets, and Enter takes it. An option answers its question, and the installer leaves that question out: Question Default Answered by What else Where EiN goes ~/ein --home Asked only while ~/ein has no .env . A folder you name that has EiN in it is updated, with no more questions. The folder for your files, the database among them data in the folder EiN goes in --data ~ and a relative folder are made whole paths, from the folder you run the installer in. The admin account's password, 8 characters or more one made for you INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD , in the environment Not shown as you type, and asked again: The same password again . A shorter one, one with ' or \ , or two that differ are refused with a line saying why, and it asks again. Enter alone leaves setup.sh to make one. EiN's official modules none a module's name, or --module A line for each, its name and what it brings, ending [y/N] : y installs it. A name given on the command line leaves out the whole question, so the modules you name are the modules you get. The web interface's port 8080 , or the next free port --http-port When something on the machine listens on 8080, the default is the next free port, and the question says so: The web interface's port [8081] (8080 is taken): . Anything but a number from 1 to 65535 is asked again. SSH and SFTP's port 2222 , or the next free port --ssh-port As for the web interface's port. Can other machines reach EiN? n keeps it to this machine, behind an HTTPS proxy of your own yes --bind Yes is --bind 0.0.0.0 , every address of the machine; n is --bind 127.0.0.1 , the machine alone. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . The answers become options for setup.sh , and a password you typed goes to it as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD , never on its command line. Then the installer shows what they add up to, and asks before it does anything: EiN is to be installed with: folder /home/anna/ein your files /home/anna/ein/data admin password the one you chose modules archive assistant, with the media service, the language model web interface port 8080, every address of this machine SSH and SFTP port 2222 Install? [Y/n] Enter or y goes on to the checks; n stops with Nothing was installed. , and nothing has been written. Without questions, the defaults hold: ~/ein , ~/ein/data , a password made for the admin, ports 8080 and 2222 on every address, and the modules the options name.

These are setup.sh 's options, and so the installer's too. ~/ein/setup.sh --help lists them. The installer has three of its own besides, which it does not pass on: Option What it does --home <folder> Installs EiN in this folder instead of ~/ein , or updates the EiN there. Later, run setup.sh from there, or the installer with the same --home . --yes , -y Asks nothing: the defaults, and what the other options say. --check Checks the machine against what the options ask for, and stops, installing nothing and asking nothing. Option What it does --ems Adds the media service, which the Archive needs: every media tool and model, in an image of about 30 GB. Sets EIN_EMS=1 in .env . See The media service . --no-ems Takes the media service out again: its container stops and is removed. Sets EIN_EMS=0 . Its data stays. --llm Adds the language model the Assistant answers with, Qwen3.5-4B in llama.cpp. Sets EIN_LLM=1 . --no-llm Takes the language model out again. Sets EIN_LLM=0 . The downloaded model stays in the data folder. --automation Adds the Automation module's sidecar: an MQTT broker, Mosquitto, which the Automation module's devices talk to, on port 1883 ( MQTT_PORT ); a listener for devices on the network; and a restreamer for cameras, go2rtc. Sets EIN_AUTOMATION=1 , and gives EiN the broker's and the restreamer's addresses and accounts. See The installer's sidecar . --no-automation Takes the sidecar out again. Sets EIN_AUTOMATION=0 .
