What it kept stays in the data folder. --module <name> Adds a module's name to EIN_MODULES in .env , such as archive or assistant . EiN installs it at its start, with the modules it needs. Give it once for each module. A name is lower case letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter. --http-port <port> The port of the machine the Web UI is reached on, 1 to 65535, instead of 8080. Sets EIN_HTTP_PORT . --ssh-port <port> The port of the machine SSH and SFTP are reached on, instead of 2222. Sets EIN_SSH_PORT . --bind <address> The address of the machine the two ports listen on: 0.0.0.0 , every address (the default), or 127.0.0.1 , the machine alone, behind an HTTPS proxy of your own. Sets EIN_BIND ; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . --data <folder> The first run only: the folder for your files, instead of data in ~/ein . A relative folder is taken from ~/ein . Sets EIN_DATA . A later run with another folder stops setup.sh ; Your data says how to move it. --engine podman|docker The first run only: the container engine, instead of podman when it is installed, else Docker. Sets EIN_ENGINE , and later runs use that engine; given later with the other one, it stops setup.sh . See Podman or Docker . --only <service> Updates one service, core , ems , db , llm or automation : downloads its newest image, or builds it from another source, and restarts it alone, leaving the others running ( db restarts EiN with it). It updates an installation, so it needs .env , and takes no other option. --source <address> Fetches the sources from this organisation instead of https://github.com/einhq , such as http://forge.example:3000/ein on a Forgejo or a Gitea. Sets EIN_SOURCE . See Where the sources come from . --db-dir <folder> Keeps the database in this folder, an absolute path, instead of db in the data folder, such as on a faster disk. Sets EIN_DB_DIR . The folder must be empty or hold a database. -h , --help Prints the help and stops. An option other than --only is kept in .env once given, so a run without it keeps it: ~/ein/setup.sh alone runs with the options you chose before. Anything else stops setup.sh with setup.sh: unknown option <option> (--help lists them) . With no module installed, EiN is core alone: the tree, the shell, accounts and the frame of the Web UI. --module only adds names; there is no option that takes one out. To stop EiN installing a module at its start, remove its name from EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env . Modules explains installing, updating and removing modules, which EiN does itself, not setup.sh .

Every setting is an option. Only the secrets come in the environment, so they stay off the command line, which others on the machine can see: Variable Read by What it does INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD both, the first time The admin account's first password, instead of the question or one made for you: 8 characters or more, without ' or \ . setup.sh writes it into .env for EiN's first start, and removes it from there once EiN has answered. EIN_SOURCE_KEY both The token that reads --source 's repositories when they are private. Kept in .env with the source; a --source on another host without one drops it. A variable goes in front of the command it is for, for the installer in front of bash , not in front of curl , which only downloads it. To keep a password out of your shell's history too, read it into the variable first: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user read -rsp 'Password: ' INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD && export INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- -- yes archive

--source names an organisation on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea, not a repository: it must hold deploy , core , db , and ems and llm when you use those options, under those names. The installer fetches ein/deploy from there, and setup.sh keeps the address in .env as EIN_SOURCE , so later runs fetch from there too. EiN's, the database's and the media service's images are downloaded ready-made only from https://github.com/einhq , which publishes them; from any other organisation setup.sh builds them on the machine from its core , db and ems , since the published images have none of its own commits, and the media service's build takes about an hour. On GitHub the modules do not come from there: EiN looks for them in the places the setting CFG_MODULE_SOURCES names, https://github.com/einhq unless you change it. On a Forgejo or a Gitea, setup.sh sets CFG_MODULE_SOURCES in .env to the same organisation, and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY to its token, so EiN installs its modules from there too.

The installer checks the machine before it touches anything. Each check prints one line: ok , low (the install goes on) or missing (nothing is installed). The thresholds depend on whether --ems is among the options, or a module that brings it, named or chosen at the questions, or EIN_EMS=1 is already in ~/ein/.env from an earlier install and --no-ems is not given; the same goes for --llm . Check ok low missing system Linux on x86-64 anything else; the installer stops at once, before its questions podman podman installed and rootless podman run as root, or podman info fails neither podman nor Docker installed docker Docker installed, when podman is not compose podman compose version or docker compose version runs; under podman, with podman-compose, or with docker-compose and podman's socket answering it does not, or docker-compose under podman finds no socket network podman's older network backend, CNI, with its dnsname plugin; the line appears only under CNI CNI without dnsname : the containers cannot find each other by name git , curl installed not installed processor 2 physical cores; with --ems , 6 with --ems , 4 or 5 fewer than 2; with --ems , fewer than 4 memory 4 GB; with --llm , 10 GB; with --ems , 30 GB with --llm , 4 to 9 GB, enough with the model on the card; with --ems , 15 to 29 GB less than 4 GB; with --ems , less than 15 GB disk 10 GB free; with --ems , 100 GB; --llm adds 6 GB for the model's file less graphics an NVIDIA card with driver 610 or newer no NVIDIA card, nvidia-smi cannot reach the driver, or an older driver card memory 15000 MB or more; the line is left out then less container GPU nvidia-container-toolkit 1.18 or newer, with its spec in /var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml no toolkit, an older one, no spec, or a spec made by hand in /etc/cdi ; podman before 5 with a spec it rejects; Docker before 28.2 archive the Archive module named, by --module archive or in .env , without the media service; the line appears only then The three before archive appear only with --ems or --llm , and none of them can stop the install: without a usable card the media service and the model run on the processor. With several cards, the line names the one with the most memory. The graphics card explains what each low line asks of you. A few details of how the checks count: Cores are physical cores, counted with lscpu across every socket, not threads. When lscpu gives nothing, the thread count stands in. Memory is the machine's total, rounded to whole GB. That is why the full threshold is 30 GB: a machine sold with 32 GB reports a little less. Disk is measured where your files go: on a later run the data folder .env names, which setup.sh keeps to, else the folder you chose or gave with --data . When that folder does not exist yet, the check measures the nearest folder above it that does, and says so: (not made yet; measured on /home/anna) . The container engine is checked podman first. With both installed, the report shows podman's lines even when you give --engine docker or .env keeps Docker: only setup.sh reads them. The images and a download's or build's scratch files live in the container engine's own storage, not in the data folder. For rootless podman that is usually ~/.local/share/containers , for Docker /var/lib/docker . When that is another disk than your data folder, it needs room too: the disk check does not measure it. To run only the checks: # on the machine that will run EiN curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --check --ems --llm

You can do what the installer does yourself, for example to read setup.sh before it runs or to put EiN in another folder. This skips the machine checks. Clone ein/deploy into the folder EiN should live in: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user git clone https://github.com/einhq/deploy.git ~/ein Run setup.sh from it with your options: # on the machine that will run EiN, as your own user ~/ein/setup.sh --data /srv/ein-data --ems --llm --module archive --module assistant setup.sh asks nothing: what the installer would ask are its options, and it makes the admin's password unless INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in its environment gives one. setup.sh changes to its own folder first, so you can run it from anywhere. Each later run brings the folder up to date itself, with git pull --ff-only from the source, and runs the new setup.sh when that changed it; the installer with --home naming the folder does the same.

EiN runs under either. At the install, setup.sh takes podman when the podman command exists, Docker when only docker does, and Docker when it is given --engine docker . It keeps the engine in .env as EIN_ENGINE , and every later run uses it, whichever else is installed. It then needs podman compose or docker compose to run, or stops with setup.sh: 'podman compose' does not run: install podman-compose (or docker-compose) for podman, or the compose plugin for Docker . The compose files are plain Compose Spec, so both read them alike. What differs: Rootless podman Docker Who runs the containers your user the Docker daemon; your user needs access to it, usually by being in the docker group, which nothing checks Who owns what EiN writes in EIN_DATA your user root, unless Docker itself runs rootless Where images and the database are ~/.local/share/containers , usually /var/lib/docker , usually The graphics card through the CDI spec; podman before 5 needs a fix first, see The graphics card through the CDI spec, from Docker Engine 28.2 After the machine restarts podman-restart.service starts the containers, once setup.sh or you have turned it on; see Start EiN when the machine boots Docker starts the containers again with its daemon, unless you stopped them A download's or build's scratch files setup.sh puts them in a tmp folder in podman's storage, as /tmp is often too small for the media service in Docker's own storage All data folders are mounted with z , which labels them for sharing between containers under SELinux and is ignored where SELinux is not on.

Each engine has its own images and containers. Install with one and keep to it: the database's folder is made for the engine that runs it. setup.sh keeps the engine it installed with in .env as EIN_ENGINE , and every later run uses it, whichever else is installed. Run with an --engine that names the other one, it stops before building anything: setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker (EIN_ENGINE in .env); under podman it would be a second, empty EiN beside it. Run ./setup.sh without --engine podman An installation whose .env has no EIN_ENGINE line yet gets one at its next run, for the engine that run picks: podman when it is installed, unless --engine docker is given. On a machine with both, run that first update of an installation made under Docker as ./setup.sh --engine docker . Otherwise it is built again under podman, and .env then keeps podman. While Docker's containers hold ports 8080 and 2222, setup.sh moves podman's EiN to the next free ports and writes them into .env ; with Docker's stopped, it takes 8080 and 2222. The database's folder in the data folder belongs to Docker's postgres user, which podman cannot use, so EiN does not come up under podman. If that has happened, remove podman's containers, put EIN_ENGINE=docker in .env , put EIN_HTTP_PORT and EIN_SSH_PORT back if setup.sh moved them, and run setup.sh again: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose down ./setup.sh If EIN_DB_DIR in .env is empty, the database is a volume of the engine instead, and podman made an empty one of its own: podman compose down keeps it. Remove it with podman volume rm ein_db once you are sure your EiN runs under Docker, as removing it under the engine your EiN actually uses deletes its database.

compose runs EiN as the project ein , from the files in ~/ein . Each service is a container of its own, and only core is reached from other machines, and with --automation the sidecar, which the devices on your network talk to and the cameras are watched through. Only EiN is reached from outside; the database, the media service and the language model answer EiN alone. Service Image Reached at Memory limit When core ghcr.io/einhq/core , ready-made with the Web UI; built from the core sources as localhost/ein-core from any other source ports 8080 (web) and 2222 (SSH and SFTP) on the machine EIN_MEMORY , 6g always db ghcr.io/einhq/db , PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB, pgvector and PostGIS, ready-made; built from the db sources as localhost/ein-db from any other source db:5432 , on the compose network only none always ems ghcr.io/einhq/ems , ready-made with every model; built from the ems sources as localhost/ein-ems from any other source ems:8181 , on the compose network only EMS_MEMORY , 16g with --ems llm llama.cpp's server, downloaded ready-made from ghcr.io llm:8190 , on the compose network only LLM_MEMORY , 10g with --llm automation ghcr.io/einhq/automation , the broker, the network listener and the restreamer, ready-made; built from module-automation's sidecar/ as localhost/ein-automation from any other source the machine's own network: port 1883 ( MQTT_PORT ) for the devices; 1984 ( STREAMS_PORT ) and 8554 ( RTSP_PORT ) for the cameras' streams 512m with --automation Every service restarts by itself if it stops on its own: compose.yaml gives each restart: unless-stopped , and under podman compose.override.yaml makes it always , the policy podman starts again at boot. EiN starts once the database answers a query, and waits up to 60 seconds to stop cleanly, as does the media service. How EiN works says what each part is for; The media service , which the Archive needs, and The language model , which the Assistant uses, cover the two optional ones.

Path What it is From setup.sh the install and update script ein/deploy compose.yaml EiN and its database: what every install runs ein/deploy compose.ems.yaml the media service ein/deploy compose.llm.yaml the language model ein/deploy compose.automation.yaml the Automation module's sidecar ein/deploy .env your options, settings and the passwords made at the install made by setup.sh compose.override.yaml the options in .env as services made by setup.sh src/ the sources: llm with its option, and core , db , ems and module-automation from any source but GitHub's einhq , which are built made by setup.sh data/ the data folder, when you kept the default made by setup.sh Leave the files from ein/deploy as they are: the installer and every run of setup.sh update the folder with git pull --ff-only , which stops when a file you changed is in its way. What you want to change goes in .env , which git ignores.

setup.sh makes these folders in EIN_DATA on every run. EiN mounts the first four; the media service mounts none of them, and reaches the files of each request through EiN ( The media service ). Folder Mounted at What it holds files /files ; read-only for the media service your originals old /old ; read-only for the media service older originals files-volatile /files-volatile thumbnails and other renditions, which EiN can make again llm /models in the language model the model, downloaded at its first start, with --llm mqtt /data/mqtt in the sidecar with --automation , the broker's two accounts, hashed, and what the devices announced modules /modules-installed in EiN the installed modules, so they stay when EiN is updated or its container made again db /home/postgres/pgdata/data in the database the database, unless --db-dir put it in another folder The database's folder is EIN_DB_DIR in .env : db in the data folder, or the folder you gave --db-dir . setup.sh gives it to the database's own user before the database starts, so under rootless podman it belongs to one of your subordinate ids, and ls shows it only through podman unshare ; under Docker it belongs to the image's postgres user. An installation whose EIN_DB_DIR is empty, from before the database moved into the data folder, keeps it in the volume ein_db in the container engine's storage. Your data explains what to back up and why the database and the data folder belong together.

setup.sh writes ~/ein/.env the first time it runs, readable by your user only. It is three things at once: compose reads it for the values in the compose files, EiN and the media service get every line of it as their environment, and setup.sh keeps your options in it. A fresh one looks like this: # ~/ein/.env, as setup.sh writes it (without the comments it writes) COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME =ein EIN_HOSTNAME =ripley EIN_ENGINE =podman EIN_EMS = 0 EIN_LLM = 0 EIN_GPU = 1 EIN_AUTOMATION = 0 MQTT_PORT = 1883 MQTT_EIN_PASSWORD = 9 d41c7e2a05b38f61e8d2c74b09a5f3e6c18d27b4a9e05c3 MQTT_DEVICE_PASSWORD = 4 e7a1c9d02b5f83e6a1d7c40 STREAMS_PORT = 1984 RTSP_PORT = 8554 STREAMS_PASSWORD = 0 b7e3d91c46a28f5e1d09c7b3a6f2e84d5c1a9073b6e2f48 EIN_MODULES = "" EIN_DATA =/home/anna/ein/data POSTGRES_PASSWORD = 5 c0d2e7a91f84b36a0e9c4d17b2f6385e1a9c07d4b2e8f13 EMS_KEY =a83f19c26d0e47b5928c1f6e3d7a04b9c5e2f18d6a3b7c90 TZ =Europe/Stockholm INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD = 5 e0c9a2f71b3d846 EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 # CFG_LLM_URL=https://api.openai.com # CFG_LLM_KEY= # CFG_LLM_PROVIDER=OpenAI # CFG_LLM_MODEL= EIN_SOURCE =https://github.com/einhq EIN_SOURCE_KEY = EIN_DB_DIR =/home/anna/ein/data/db setup.sh then sets the options you gave in their own lines: EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_AUTOMATION , EIN_MODULES , EIN_BIND , EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY and EIN_DB_DIR . With a Forgejo or a Gitea as the source it adds CFG_MODULE_SOURCES , and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY with a token. When a port is taken, it changes EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT or one of the sidecar's. Line What it is COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME ein , the compose project's name, which names its containers, network and volumes EIN_HOSTNAME this machine's name, without its domain, which EiN's container takes: EiN shows the machine as the device of that name ( The machine as a device ). Written at the next run of an installation that lacks it EIN_ENGINE podman or docker , the engine setup.sh picked at the install, or --engine named, and keeps to; see Keep to one engine EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM 1 when the media service or the language model is installed; --ems , --no-ems , --llm and --no-llm set them EIN_AUTOMATION , MQTT_PORT , STREAMS_PORT , RTSP_PORT 1 when the Automation module's sidecar is installed, which --automation and --no-automation set, and its ports: the broker's, 1883, which the devices reach, and the restreamer's API (1984) and RTSP (8554); setup.sh moves one to the next free port when something else uses it MQTT_EIN_PASSWORD , MQTT_DEVICE_PASSWORD , STREAMS_PASSWORD the passwords EiN ( ein ) and the devices ( device ) sign in to the broker with, and EiN's to the restreamer, random, made here. A change takes effect at the next ./setup.sh ; see The installer's sidecar EIN_GPU 1 when the first run found an NVIDIA card that nvidia-smi reaches, with a CDI spec in /var/run/cdi/nvidia.yaml or /etc/cdi . Set only then; see The graphics card for a card added later EIN_MODULES the modules EiN installs at its start when they are missing, separated by spaces EIN_DATA the data folder, chosen at the install with --data or at the question POSTGRES_PASSWORD the database's password, random, made here EMS_KEY the key EiN and the media service share, random, made here TZ the machine's time zone, from timedatectl , /etc/timezone or UTC INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD the admin account's first password, which EiN takes at its first start; changing it later does nothing. One made here, random, setup.sh prints at the end of every run until you delete the line, which you do once you have changed the password. One you chose at the install setup.sh removes, with the comment above it, once EiN has answered EIN_BIND the address the ports listen on: 0.0.0.0 for every address of the machine, 127.0.0.1 for the machine alone; --bind sets it EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT the ports on the machine for the Web UI and for SSH and SFTP, which --http-port and --ssh-port set; setup.sh moves one to the next free port when something else uses it while EiN is stopped CFG_LLM_… the Assistant's settings for a hosted language model instead of --llm ; see The language model EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY where the sources are cloned from, and the token that reads them when they are private; --source sets them, and one on another host empties the token unless EIN_SOURCE_KEY gives a new one EIN_DB_DIR the database's folder, db in the data folder; --db-dir sets another. Empty keeps it in the volume ein_db The database's password and the media service's key are kept nowhere else. Without them the database cannot be reached, so copy .env with every backup. Configuration files has every file EiN reads.

Every compose command reads compose.override.yaml beside compose.yaml by itself, so a plain podman compose up -d starts the same services setup.sh does. setup.sh writes it from .env and the container engine on every run; do not edit it, as the next run writes over it. Under podman, with the media service, the model and a card, it reads: # ~/ein/compose.override.yaml # Written by setup.sh from the options in .env and the container engine; edit those and run # setup.sh again. services: db: restart: always ein: environment: CFG_LLM_CARD: card restart: always ems: extends: { file: compose.ems.yaml , service: ems } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always llm: extends: { file: compose.llm.yaml , service: llm } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always Under Docker the restart: always lines are left out. CFG_LLM_CARD , the Assistant's setting, tells EiN whether the model runs on the card ( card ) or the processor ( cpu ).

To change Do this Add or remove the media service or the language model ~/ein/setup.sh --ems , --no-ems , --llm or --no-llm . This is also an update: see Updating . Add or remove the Automation module's sidecar ~/ein/setup.sh --automation or --no-automation ; see Automation . Add a module EiN installs at its start ~/ein/setup.sh --module <name> , or install it at once in Settings → Modules ; see Modules . A setting of EiN or a module ( CFG_… ) or of the media service ( EMS_… ) Add the line to ~/ein/.env , then run podman compose up -d in ~/ein . Most settings can instead be changed while EiN runs; see Configuration . The ports, or keep EiN to the machine ~/ein/setup.sh --http-port <port> , --ssh-port <port> or --bind <address> , which also updates EiN; or change EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT or EIN_BIND in .env , then podman compose up -d . See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A container's memory limit Add EIN_MEMORY=8g , EMS_MEMORY=20g or LLM_MEMORY=12g to .env , then podman compose up -d ; see Performance and sizing . The language model's model or image LLM_GGUF_REPO , LLM_GGUF_FILE , LLM_IMAGE and LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB in .env ; see The language model . The data folder EIN_DATA in .env names it, but changing the line does not move your files; see Your data . When a change does not take, podman compose up -d --force-recreate makes every container again. With Docker, write docker compose for podman compose . Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one: the media service's idle models then go to swap, and a search waits for them. ~/ein/setup.sh makes the containers again with it. Some of EiN's environment is set by compose.yaml and wins over a line in .env : POSTGRES_URL , CFG_HTTP_PORT and CFG_SSH_PORT (always 8080 and 2222 inside the container), the ems module's CFG_EMS_URL and CFG_EMS_KEY (from EMS_KEY ), and the folder paths. For the media service, EMS_PORT and EMS_KEY are set the same way. setup.sh writes the ems module's CFG_EMS_FILES_ADDRESS into compose.override.yaml unless .env names one.

Run compose from ~/ein , where it finds the project and its .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose ps # what runs, and whether db and ems are healthy podman compose logs -f core # follow EiN's log; ems, llm or db for the others podman compose restart core # restart EiN alone podman compose stop # stop everything, keeping the containers podman compose start # start them again podman compose down # stop everything and remove the containers podman compose up -d # make the containers and start them With Docker, write docker compose instead. down keeps the database and the data folder; the containers are made again by the next up -d . It does remove the log, and with it a random admin password a new EiN printed there; the first password setup.sh made stays in .env as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD . Warning podman compose down -v also deletes the volumes. With an empty EIN_DB_DIR , the volume ein_db is your database: every name, album, person, setting and account. Never add -v unless you mean to start from nothing. EiN is down while it restarts, and a restart takes longer when there is a module to install. Services and logs covers EiN's own logs and services, the ones inside the container, and Health and status what to watch.

p.h: Start EiN when the machine boots
p.x: Under Docker the containers come back with the Docker daemon, which starts with the machine on most systems, as long as you did not stop them yourself. When the daemon is not set to start at boot, setup.sh says so and lists sudo systemctl enable docker . Under podman, compose.override.yaml gives every service restart: always , the policy podman's own podman-restart.service starts at boot. Under rootless podman that is a service of your user's, which runs at boot only when your user lingers, that is, when its services run without you being signed in. At the end of every run, setup.sh turns on both where your user may, and says so: Enabled podman-restart.service, which starts EiN's containers at boot Enabled lingering for anna, so podman-restart.service runs at boot without a login EiN starts again when the machine does. What it may not do, it lists instead. Lingering often needs an administrator: EiN does not start again when the machine does until this has run: sudo loginctl enable-linger anna Until then, start it after a reboot with: cd /home/anna/ein && podman compose up -d Run what it lists once. After the next restart of the machine, podman compose ps in ~/ein shows the containers up.

Running the installer or ~/ein/setup.sh again is the update: ~/ein itself and the newest images of everything installed, downloaded and started again, every container made again from the new images, and a service you left out stopped and removed. ~/ein/setup.sh --only core (or ems , db , llm , automation ) updates one service and leaves the others running. Updating explains what it touches and what it keeps. There is no uninstall script. Your data says how to move EiN to another machine and how to remove it with its data.

The commands are written for podman; with Docker, write docker compose . Install EiN covers the messages of a first install, and Troubleshooting everything after. What you see What to do fatal: destination path '/home/anna/ein' already exists and is not an empty directory. ~/ein exists but is not a clone of ein/deploy. Move it away, or install elsewhere with --home , or by answering the first question with another folder. git pull stops with a message about local changes, and nothing is installed, or setup.sh: /home/anna/ein could not be brought up to date from …: git status there says why A file from ein/deploy in ~/ein was changed. See what with git -C ~/ein status , put back the original with git -C ~/ein checkout -- <file> , and move the change into .env . setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker (EIN_ENGINE in .env); under podman it would be a second, empty EiN beside it. … --engine was given for the other engine. Run ./setup.sh without it; see Keep to one engine . setup.sh: --data is chosen at the install, and the data folder here is /home/anna/ein/data The data folder is chosen once. Leave --data out; to put your files on another disk, see Move the data folder to another disk . setup.sh: INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD is shorter than 8 characters , or … holds a ' or a \, which .env cannot keep as they are: choose one without The password given in the environment does not do. Run again with another, or without INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD to have one made. Nothing was started. No terminal to ask on: installing with the defaults and the options given, as --yes does. To answer its questions, run it at a terminal, or with ssh -t over SSH; or give what you want as options. setup.sh: EiN here runs under docker, which is not installed The engine .env keeps is gone from the machine. Stop it, or choose other ports in .env . setup.sh moves EiN to the next free port by itself, but only while EiN is stopped. setup.sh: 'podman compose' runs docker-compose here, which needs podman's socket: … Turn on podman's socket for your user with systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket , or install podman-compose , and run setup.sh again. setup.sh: podman's networks here give no names, which EiN needs to find its database: … podman uses its older network backend, CNI, without the dnsname plugin. Install the package the message names and run setup.sh again. setup.sh: the database of an earlier install is here, in /home/anna/ein/data/db, and its password was in the .env that is gone. … .env is missing but the database is not. Put the old .env back, or, to start from nothing, remove the database with podman unshare rm -rf ~/ein/data/db (under Docker, sudo rm -rf ). setup.sh: the database of an earlier install is here, the volume ein_db, and its password was in the .env that is gone. … .env is missing but the database is not. Put the old .env back, or, to start from nothing, remove the database with podman volume rm ein_db . setup.sh: EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ in 10 minutes: podman compose logs core Read the log it names. podman compose ps shows whether db became healthy; EiN does not start before it. The Archive module needs the media service, which is not installed here: ./setup.sh --ems adds it. at the end The Archive is in EIN_MODULES but EIN_EMS is not 1 . Without the media service its photos, videos and documents are not analysed. Run ~/ein/setup.sh --ems . After an update, a module is still the old version setup.sh does not update modules, and EiN's start replaces only one it cannot run. Use Update in Settings → Modules ; see Modules .

This page is for whoever runs EiN: which ports it listens on and how to change them, how to put it behind an HTTPS proxy, and how to reach it from outside your home safely. It assumes an installation made with the installer, in ~/ein ; Installing in detail explains that folder.

EiN publishes two ports, and more with the Automation module's sidecar, on every address of the machine it runs on: Port What answers Protocol 8080 the Web UI, its files and its WebSocket plain HTTP 2222 the SSH and SFTP server SSH 1883 with --automation , the MQTT broker that the Automation module's devices talk to plain MQTT 1984 with --automation , the restreamer's API, which EiN gives the cameras to and watches them through, behind STREAMS_PASSWORD plain HTTP 8554 with --automation , the cameras' streams served again over RTSP, behind STREAMS_PASSWORD , and to this machine without one RTSP These are the ports setup.sh picks; MQTT_PORT , STREAMS_PORT and RTSP_PORT in .env are the sidecar's, which it listens on itself, on the machine's own network. When another program on the machine already listens on one, it takes the next free port instead, writes it to .env and says so ("Port 8080 is taken on this machine: EiN uses 8081 instead"). Nothing else is reachable from outside. The database, and the media service and the language model when they are installed, answer only EiN, on the containers' own network: no port of theirs is published on the machine's network, unless .env sets EIN_EMS_BIND for callers of the media service on other machines ( Callers on other machines ). Under rootless podman, EiN does not sit on that network: there a published port would reach EiN from the network's own address, and EiN would see every visitor as that one address. EiN gets a network of its own, which keeps each visitor's address, and reaches the others on the machine's loopback address, where they are published for it alone: Line Default What answers on 127.0.0.1 EIN_DB_PORT 15432 the database EIN_EMS_PORT 18181 the media service EIN_LLM_PORT 18190 the language model setup.sh moves one to the next free port when another program has it, and writes it to .env , as with EiN's own ports. Under Docker and rootful podman these lines do nothing. EiN reaches the sidecar at the machine's loopback too, on its own ports, and under Docker and rootful podman at the machine's address on the containers' network, which is why the sidecar needs EIN_BIND to be 0.0.0.0 there. EiN itself serves plain HTTP only. It has no certificate and no HTTPS port of its own. On your home network that is fine; for anything else, an HTTPS proxy goes in front of it, as described in Put EiN behind HTTPS .

p.h: Change the ports or the address
p.x: Which ports the machine publishes, and on which address, are three lines in ~/ein/.env , written at the install from your answers to the installer's questions, or from its options --http-port , --ssh-port and --bind : # in ~/ein/.env EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 Line What it decides EIN_BIND The address of the machine the two ports are published on. 0.0.0.0 is every address; 127.0.0.1 keeps them to the machine itself. EIN_HTTP_PORT The port of the machine that reaches the Web UI. EIN_SSH_PORT The port of the machine that reaches SSH and SFTP. To change one: Open ~/ein/.env in an editor and change the value. Apply it: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Running ./setup.sh applies it too, and also updates EiN. ./setup.sh --http-port 8443 , --ssh-port or --bind changes the line and applies it in one go, with an update. Open EiN at the new address, such as http://ein.local:8443/ after EIN_HTTP_PORT=8443 . Inside its container EiN always listens on 8080 and 2222; these lines only change what the machine maps to them. The ports are not settings, so nothing on the Settings page can move EiN off them. A few things to know: Ports below 1024 , such as 80 or 443, cannot be published by rootless podman unless the machine allows it (the kernel setting net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start ). Use a port above 1024, or let an HTTPS proxy take 443. EIN_BIND takes one address. With an address other than 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 , such as the machine's LAN address, EiN runs normally, but setup.sh waits for it at 127.0.0.1 , does not find it, and ends with "EiN did not answer" after ten minutes. The documentation , here and on EiN's Docs page, shows SSH commands with port 2222 whatever EIN_SSH_PORT maps. Tell your family the port you chose.

p.h: Open the ports in the firewall
p.x: When another computer on the network cannot open EiN while the machine itself can, the machine's firewall is the usual cause. Open the two ports there: # on the machine EiN runs on, with ufw (Ubuntu, Debian) sudo ufw allow 8080/tcp sudo ufw allow 2222/tcp # on the machine EiN runs on, with firewalld (Fedora, RHEL) sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp --add-port=2222/tcp sudo firewall-cmd --reload With the Automation module's broker, open 1883 too, to your home network only, such as sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 1883 proto tcp . Use your own port numbers if you changed them. Behind an HTTPS proxy on the same machine, open the proxy's port (443) instead, and not 8080. Note Docker opens the ports it publishes in the machine's packet filter itself, past rules set with ufw. A closed port in ufw does not keep EiN's ports off the network under Docker; EIN_BIND=127.0.0.1 does.

An HTTPS proxy is a web server that holds the certificate, answers browsers over HTTPS, and passes each request on to EiN over plain HTTP. You need one when: EiN is reached from outside your home, so that passwords and pictures do not cross the internet unencrypted; a phone should add EiN to its home screen as an app, which needs an address beginning with https:// (see EiN on a phone ); you want the browser's clipboard to work everywhere: over plain HTTP, copying a share link falls back to selecting the text.

p.h: What EiN needs from the proxy
p.x: Any proxy works, such as Caddy, nginx or Traefik, when it does the following: Requirement Why Serves EiN at the root of its own host name The interface asks for /file/… , /s/… and /__shell from the root. EiN cannot be served under a path such as https://example.org/ein/ . Passes WebSocket connections The whole interface talks to EiN over a WebSocket at /__shell , not only the terminal. Without it, pages do not load their contents. Sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https (or Forwarded: proto=https ) EiN then marks its sign-in cookie Secure , so the browser sends it only over HTTPS. Over plain HTTP the cookie is not marked, so the same EiN keeps working on the home network. Has no limit on the size of a request A file is uploaded in one request, whole: a long video is several gigabytes. Allows long requests and idle connections Uploads and downloads of large files take time, and the WebSocket can be quiet for minutes. When the proxy closes it, the interface reconnects after two seconds. The proxy keeps the Host header as the browser sent it; EiN uses whatever address the browser shows.

Caddy gets a certificate from Let's Encrypt by itself and does everything in the table without further settings. For a host name that points at your home, such as ein.wrenfield.example : # /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, on the machine EiN runs on ein.wrenfield.example { reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 } Then reload Caddy ( sudo systemctl reload caddy ). For the certificate, Caddy must be reachable on ports 80 and 443 from the internet under that name. For HTTPS on the home network only, such as for ein.local , Caddy can sign its own certificate with tls internal . Browsers warn about it until Caddy's root certificate is installed on each device: # /etc/caddy/Caddyfile, on the machine EiN runs on ein.local { tls internal reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:8080 }

nginx needs the WebSocket, the size limit and the timeouts set explicitly. With a certificate you have already obtained, for example with certbot: # /etc/nginx/conf.d/ein.conf, on the machine EiN runs on map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade { default upgrade; '' close; } server { listen 443 ssl; server_name ein.wrenfield.example; ssl_certificate /etc/letsencrypt/live/ein.wrenfield.example/fullchain.pem; ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/ein.wrenfield.example/privkey.pem; client_max_body_size 0; proxy_request_buffering off; proxy_buffering off; location / { proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:8080; proxy_http_version 1.1; proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade; proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade; proxy_set_header Host $host; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for; proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; proxy_read_timeout 1h; proxy_send_timeout 1h; } } Check it with sudo nginx -t and reload with sudo systemctl reload nginx .

p.h: Keep EiN's own port to the machine
p.x: With the proxy on the same machine, nothing else needs to reach port 8080. Close it to the network: In ~/ein/.env , set EIN_BIND=127.0.0.1 . Apply it with podman compose up -d (or docker compose up -d ) in ~/ein . ./setup.sh --bind 127.0.0.1 does both, with an update. At the install, n to the installer's question Can other machines reach EiN? does the same from the start. Open https://ein.wrenfield.example/ and sign in. This closes port 2222 to the network as well, since EIN_BIND applies to both, and the sidecar's ports, so the devices cannot reach the MQTT broker. To keep SSH and SFTP reachable from other machines, leave EIN_BIND=0.0.0.0 and close 8080 in the firewall instead (under Docker, see the note in Open the ports in the firewall ). To check that the proxy passes everything, sign in, open a few pages, upload a file, and open the terminal with Alt + T (see The terminal ): each of these uses a different part of the table above.

p.h: Reach EiN from outside your home
p.x: There are three ways, from the least exposed to the most: Way What you set up Who can reach EiN A VPN, such as WireGuard or Tailscale The VPN on the machine and on each device. EiN needs no change: devices open its usual address over the VPN. Only devices on the VPN. An SSH tunnel through the machine The machine's own SSH server (not EiN's), reachable from outside. On the laptop: ssh -L 8080:127.0.0.1:8080 you@your-home , then open http://localhost:8080/ . Only people with an account on the machine. A public HTTPS proxy A host name pointing at your home, ports 80 and 443 forwarded by your router to the proxy, and the proxy in front of EiN as above. Anyone on the internet can reach the sign-in page. EiN's own SSH server does not forward ports, so the tunnel goes through the machine's SSH server, not through port 2222. Only the public proxy makes share links work for people outside the family: a share link begins with the address the person who made it had open, so it reaches whoever can reach that address. Make links while EiN is open at its public address, not at http://ein.local:8080 .

A phone or a GPS tracker that reports its position to its device (see Report from a phone ) posts to EiN from wherever it is, without signing in, so it needs the public HTTPS proxy: over a VPN it reports only while the VPN is up, and an SSH tunnel does not reach it at all. It posts to /file/dev/<device> with the device's key, in the address or as Authorization: Bearer , which the proxy passes on like any other request; the key is all that lets it in, and it opens that device for writing and nothing else. A request with a wrong key is refused with Forbidden and logged as "device write refused", with the client's address. Devices and their keys says more.

p.h: Before you open EiN to the internet
p.x: Change the admin password if you have not: Install EiN shows how. Give every account a password of its own; Accounts and groups covers them. Leave visitors out. The setting Visitors may browse ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING , under Settings → System ) is off after an install. Keep it off: on, anyone who reaches EiN can browse what is shared with visitors without signing in. Publish HTTPS only. Forward only the proxy's ports, never 8080, which is plain HTTP. Keep the sidecar in. Never forward ports 1883, 1984 or 8554. The broker speaks plain MQTT without TLS, and whoever reaches it with the device password can switch the house's devices; whoever reaches the restreamer with its password watches the cameras. A phone away from home needs only the HTTPS proxy, which shows the cameras too. Decide about SSH. Port 2222 is not needed for the Web UI. Leave it closed to the internet and use SSH and SFTP over the VPN, or forward it on your router and have people sign in with keys; see SSH and SFTP .

p.h: How EiN slows down password guessing
p.x: EiN counts failed sign-ins, in the Web UI and over SSH alike, per client address and per account: After five failures from one address, that address is refused without its password being checked, with "too many failed sign-ins; try again in" and the number of seconds. The wait starts at a second and doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes. After five failures at one account, each attempt at it waits, up to 10 seconds, but the account is never locked: someone guessing a password cannot lock its owner out. A failed attempt is answered no sooner than a second after it was made. A successful sign-in is not counted: once an address's wait has passed, it may sign in with the right password as often as it likes, and its next failure waits as long as it would have without them. Failures are forgotten an hour after the last one. Repeated failures are logged as "repeated failed sign-ins", with the address or account; Services and logs shows where to read them. EiN believes X-Forwarded-For and Forwarded only from a proxy whose connections reach it from the loopback address, or from an address named in TRUSTED_PROXIES in ~/ein/.env . When the proxy's connections reach EiN from another address, as can happen with the container's network in between, EiN sees every visitor as the proxy: who in EiN's terminal then shows the proxy's address for every web connection, and failures from one visitor hold back everyone who comes through the proxy. Run who once after setting up the proxy to see which you have. If it shows the proxy's address, put that address in .env and run ~/ein/setup.sh again: # in ~/ein/.env on the machine that runs EiN; several addresses are separated by commas TRUSTED_PROXIES=192.0.2.10 Name only your proxy's address: a client that reaches EiN from an address in the list can make who , the access log and the sign-in throttle show any address it likes. Under rootless podman with a podman-compose older than 1.1, as on Ubuntu 24.04, a proxy on the same machine reaches EiN from 10.0.2.2 rather than from the loopback address; setup.sh adds 10.0.2.2 to the list there itself, so such a proxy needs no line. # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator who

p.h: SSH and SFTP from another network
p.x: SSH does not go through an HTTPS proxy. To reach EiN's SSH server from outside, forward a TCP port on your router to the machine's EIN_SSH_PORT , or connect over a VPN. Then connect with the host name and the port: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.wrenfield.example sftp -P 2222 helen@ein.wrenfield.example The server's host key is made at EiN's first start and kept in the tree as /etc/ssh_host_key , with its public half in /etc/ssh_host_key.pub , so it stays the same across updates and new containers. A client warns about a changed host key only when EiN was installed afresh. SSH and SFTP covers keys, clients and file managers.

What you see What to do EiN opens on the machine itself but not from another computer Open the ports in the machine's firewall, and check that EIN_BIND is 0.0.0.0 . Try the machine's IP address instead of a name ending in .local . compose up fails because the address or port is already in use Another program has the port. Choose another EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT , or under rootless podman EIN_DB_PORT , EIN_EMS_PORT or EIN_LLM_PORT , in .env , or stop that program. Behind the proxy, the page frame loads but stays empty, and the terminal does not connect The proxy does not pass WebSocket connections. Add the Upgrade and Connection headers (nginx) or check the proxy's WebSocket support. Uploads of large files fail behind the proxy, often with 413 The proxy limits the size of a request. In nginx, set client_max_body_size 0; . The terminal or the interface reconnects every minute behind the proxy The proxy closes idle connections. Raise its read timeout, such as proxy_read_timeout 1h; in nginx. A device on the network cannot reach the MQTT broker Open port 1883 in the machine's firewall, to your home network, and check that EIN_BIND is not 127.0.0.1 . podman compose ps in ~/ein shows whether automation runs; Automation has more. Signing in works, but the next page asks you to sign in again The browser uses plain http:// while something in front of EiN sends X-Forwarded-Proto: https , so the cookie is marked Secure and the browser does not send it back. Open the https:// address, or have the proxy send the scheme the browser used. Signing in says "too many failed sign-ins" Wait the seconds it names. When it keeps happening to everyone behind your proxy, EiN sees all of them as one address: see How EiN slows down password guessing . A share link does not open for the person you sent it to It begins with the address you had open. Open EiN at its public address and make the link again; see Sharing . setup.sh ends with "EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:… " When EIN_BIND is an address other than 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 , this is expected and EiN is running: open it at that address. Otherwise read podman compose logs core ; see Troubleshooting .

Installing in detail : the ~/ein folder, .env and setup.sh . Configuration : settings, .env and where each is kept. SSH and SFTP : signing in with keys, file managers and scp . EiN on a phone : what HTTPS gives a phone. Sharing : share links and who can open them. Environment variables : CFG_HTTP_PORT and CFG_SSH_PORT , the ports EiN listens on inside its container. Troubleshooting : when EiN does not start or answer at all.

This page is for the administrator who runs EiN: where its settings live, how to change them on the Settings page, in the terminal or in the installation's .env , which value wins when several are set, and what a change restarts. Every setting itself, with its default, is listed on Settings .

EiN has a single table of settings. Each one is an environment variable, such as CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS , with a plain name, a description, a kind of value and a default. Core declares some, and each module declares its own when it is installed, so the table grows and shrinks with the modules. Each setting belongs to one of two scopes: Scope Who changes it Where Named System An administrator, for everyone Settings → System , or config set CFG_… Personal Each person, for themselves Profile → Preferences , or config set CFG_USER_… , and HISTSIZE This page is about the system settings. Personal ones, such as Shell history length , or Seconds per slide with the Archive installed, are described in Your profile, favourites and trash . Apart from the settings, the installation has its own environment in .env , in the folder EiN was installed in ( ~/ein with the installer). It holds what is fixed before EiN starts: where your files are, which ports the machine publishes, the database password. It can also give a setting its starting value. Set a value in the deployment explains how the two meet.

p.h: Change a setting on the Settings page
p.x: Sign in as an administrator. Accounts and groups explains who that is. Choose Settings in the sidebar, under System . The page opens on the System tab. Pick a category in the Categories list on the left, or type in Find a setting to search names, descriptions, modules and keys across every category. Change the value in the setting's field. Save change and Cancel appear under it. Choose Save change . A line under the setting says what was restarted, for example "Restarted trash-purger.", or why nothing could be. Settings are browsed by category, and each says where its value comes from and what a change restarts. Each setting is saved on its own; there is no button that saves the page. The other tabs of Settings hold accounts, groups and modules: Accounts and groups covers Users , Groups and Permissions , and Modules covers Modules . The Permissions tab shows some of the same settings as System , such as the default sharing, and a change made on either shows on both. The control depends on the kind of value: a switch shows On or Off , a choice is a list, a number has arrows, a person or a group is picked by name, and a permission mode is a choice of None, View or Edit for the owner, the group and everyone else. On a narrow screen the categories are a Category list above the settings instead.

p.h: Read where a value comes from
p.x: Under each setting's description, a badge says where the value in force comes from. A second badge names the module the setting belongs to, and settings that restart a service say which, as in "Restarts trash-purger". Badge What it means Default Nobody has set it: the setting's own default is in force. From deployment The installation's environment sets it, usually .env . From module , such as From archive An installed module chose the value, such as the Archive naming its search parser. Set here An administrator saved it on this page or with config set . Not set A key to another service that nobody has given. Default , From deployment and From module can all be overridden: save a value and the badge becomes Set here . A setting that is set here shows Restore inherited value instead of Save change . Choose it to remove your value, and the setting falls back to what it would be without it: the module's choice, the deployment's value or the default, in that order. Overrides only limits the page to the settings set here, with their number on the button. It is the quickest way to see what has been changed on this installation. When nothing matches a search, Clear filters empties the search and turns Overrides only off. Some settings mean something when they are empty. For those, the description ends with what an empty value does, such as "Currently: the person who creates it.", and an empty text field says what it means, such as "Empty means no model".

p.h: Give a key to another service
p.x: A few settings are keys that EiN sends to another service: the access tokens for private module sources, and, with the modules that bring them, the media service's key and a hosted language model's key. Their names end in _KEY , and they are kept apart from every other setting: Nobody can read a key back, administrators included. The field is empty, with "Not set" or "Set — type a new one to replace it" in it, and the badge says whether the key comes from the deployment or was set here. To replace a key, type the new one and choose Save change . The field empties again once it is saved. A key is in no shell's environment, and EiN sends it only to the address set for its service. If a shell gives that address another value for one command, the request goes without the key. Warning With the ems module installed, the media service's key, CFG_EMS_KEY , must be one the media service accepts. The installer gives both sides the same key from .env . A different key saved here leaves EiN unable to reach the media service; Restore inherited value brings back the deployment's. The media service explains the keys.

A setting that names the services that read it when they start restarts them when you save it, so the change takes effect without restarting EiN. The setting's card lists those services before you save, and the line under it confirms what was restarted afterwards. A setting that names no service restarts nothing. Work already running is not lost: it is picked up again when the service is back. Only services that are running are restarted. A service you stopped stays stopped, and reads the new value when you start it. Services and logs shows how. If a restart fails, the value is still saved, and a red message says "Could not restart" with the service's name and the reason. The service keeps running on the old value until it starts again. Worker backlog rotation (ms) is read by each pipeline worker as it starts, so the services that run one must be restarted by hand. Settings that are policy, such as the default sharing or Visitors may browse , are read each time they are applied, so they take effect at once and restart nothing. Some settings that name no service are read by the commands a pipeline runs, in the environment of the service that runs them, such as the Archive's Face match threshold . Nothing restarts for them: the service's shell reads the settings again before its next command, so they take effect from the next step it runs, such as the next picture it looks for faces in. A step already running finishes with the value it started with. A terminal that is open when a setting changes reads the settings again before its next command, so echo shows the new value. A command already running keeps the value it started with.

The config command does everything the Settings page does. Everyone signed in can list and read settings, and change their own; only an administrator can change a system setting. # in EiN's terminal config list # every setting, with where its value comes from config list --scope system # the system settings only; --scope user for your own config get CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS # the value in force config set CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 config unset CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS config list prints a setting per line: its name, a tab, its value, and in brackets where the value comes from. A default has no mark. A key shows (set) in place of its value, or nothing when it is not set. On an EiN with the Archive, the Assistant and the ems module installed, it starts like this: CFG_EMS_KEY (set) (environment) CFG_COMMAND_FINDER assistant-commands (module assistant) CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL llm-chat (module assistant) CFG_SEARCH_PARSER archive-parse (module archive) CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER ems-text-embed (module ems) CFG_SESSION_REAP_INTERVAL 3600 CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 (system) The marks match the badges on the Settings page: (system) is Set here , (environment) is From deployment , (module archive) is From archive , and (user) is a person's own value. config set answers with the new value and what it restarted, and config unset with the value it falls back to and where that comes from: $ config set CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS 14 CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 14 Restarted: trash-purger $ config unset CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS reset to 30 (default) Restarted: trash-purger For a port, the answer ends with the note that it takes effect the next time the server starts. For a key, config set answers only CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY set , without the value. The command line you typed is kept in your shell history like any other; start it with a space to leave it out. A value of the wrong kind is refused before anything is written: Kind What config set accepts Refused, for example number digits, with an optional minus and decimals config set: CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS: expected a number, got 'four' on or off true or false expected 'true' or 'false', got 'yes' choice one of the setting's choices expected one of en, sv, got 'english' permission mode an octal mode such as 0750 expected an octal mode such as 0750, got 'rwxr-x---' person or group a name of letters, digits, . , _ and - 'Anna Andersson' is not a valid user name text or key anything An empty value is refused too, with value must not be empty , except for the settings where empty means something. To return a setting to its inherited value, use config unset , not an empty config set . Other refusals: config set: unknown setting 'CFG_TRASH_DAYS' : no installed part of EiN declares that name. config list shows the names there are; a module's settings exist only while the module is installed. config set: 'CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS' is a system setting and needs administrator rights : you are signed in as someone else. Accounts and groups explains how a member of the sudo group becomes the administrator in a terminal with admin . A value with spaces, such as two module sources, is best quoted: config set CFG_MODULE_SOURCES 'https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/family' . With JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front, config list , config get , config set and config unset answer in JSON: config list and config get with each setting's label, description, value and source, config set and config unset with the value and what was restarted. Core commands has the full entries.

p.h: Set a value in the deployment
p.x: .env is EiN's environment. Every CFG_… line in it reaches EiN when its container starts, and appears on the Settings page as From deployment . Use it for a value that belongs with the installation rather than with the running system, such as a hosted language model's address and key. On the machine EiN runs on, open .env in the folder EiN was installed in. Add or change the line: # ~/ein/.env, on the machine EiN runs on CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS = 14 Apply it. This makes EiN's container again with the new environment: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Under podman-compose, a container made again this way has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one; ./setup.sh makes the containers again with it. Reload the Settings page. The setting shows the value with From deployment . Running ./setup.sh applies .env too, but it also downloads the newest images: it is an update. Updating explains it. A value in .env does not always win: A value set here wins over it. If the setting shows Set here , the line in .env has no visible effect. Choose Restore inherited value , or run config unset , to let it through. A module's choice wins over it. An installed module may name commands for the Search settings: the Archive names CFG_SEARCH_PARSER , the Assistant CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL and CFG_COMMAND_FINDER , and the ems module CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER . To use another one, set it on the Settings page. Some variables are fixed by the installation's compose.yaml , which wins over .env : CFG_HTTP_PORT and CFG_SSH_PORT , the ports EiN listens on inside its container, which are not settings, and the ems module's settings CFG_EMS_URL and CFG_EMS_KEY . A line for them in .env changes nothing. The published ports are EIN_HTTP_PORT and EIN_SSH_PORT instead, and the media service's key is EMS_KEY , which goes to both sides. The Assistant's CFG_LLM_URL is read from .env and defaults to the language model the installer adds. An empty line sets nothing. CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL= in .env is the same as leaving the line out. The rest of .env is not settings but the installation's own variables: EIN_DATA , EIN_BIND , EIN_HTTP_PORT , EIN_SSH_PORT , EIN_MODULES , EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_GPU , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY , EIN_DB_DIR , EIN_ENGINE , EIN_HOSTNAME , COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME , TZ and the passwords. setup.sh 's options set most of them, such as --http-port for EIN_HTTP_PORT ; Installing in detail explains each, and Environment variables lists every variable EiN reads besides its settings. With the media service installed, its settings are EMS_… lines in the same file; The media service describes them. Note .env holds the database password and the media service's key, and nothing else keeps them. Keep a copy of it with your backups; Your data: backup, moving and removing says what else to keep.

A setting can be given a value in up to four places. The narrowest wins: Order Layer File in EiN's tree Badge 1, wins A person's own value, for personal settings ~/.config Your setting 2 The administrator's value /etc/config Set here 3 A module's choice /etc/config.d/<module> From module 4 The deployment's environment /etc/environment From deployment 5 The setting's default none Default A personal setting comes from ~/.config , the deployment or its default: neither a module nor /etc/config sets it. A system setting is never read from anyone's ~/.config . The highest layer that sets a value wins, and each scope skips the layers that are not its own. Every shell in EiN, the services' shells included, sources these files at its start, /etc/environment first and ~/.config last, so each is exported over the one before. That is why every setting is an ordinary environment variable in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal echo $CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS cat /etc/config The files are ordinary shell files in EiN's tree, kept in the database, so they survive a restart. Each line is an assignment such as export CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS='14' : /etc/environment is written again at every start, from the CFG_… variables EiN's container was started with. A value the deployment stops passing is gone from it. It never holds a key. /etc/config.d/<module> is a module's etc/config , linked there when the module is set up and gone when it is removed. /etc/config is what Save change and config set write for a system setting. Everyone can read it. /etc/keys holds the keys saved here. Only the administrator can read it, and no shell sources it. A key from the deployment stays in EiN's own process and is never written to a file. Configuration files lists these and EiN's other files.

p.h: Edit the settings file by hand
p.x: An administrator can open /etc/config in the editor, edit /etc/config , and add, change or remove export lines. Two things differ from the Settings page: Nothing checks the values. A number written as four reaches the service that reads it as it is. Nothing is restarted. Policy settings apply at once, and settings read by the commands a pipeline runs from the next step; a setting a service reads at its start applies when that service restarts, from Services and logs or the next time EiN starts. A line for a name no part of EiN declares is exported into every shell but shows nowhere. Prefer the Settings page or config set for anything listed there.

p.h: When a change does not take effect
p.x: The value in .env does not show. The setting is Set here or chosen by a module, both of which win; or it is one of the values compose.yaml fixes; or EiN's container was not made again. See Set a value in the deployment . The page says the value is saved, but the service behaves as before. Look for a red "Could not restart" message under the setting, or check the service on Services and logs . A stopped service reads the value when it starts. The terminal shows the old value. A command that was already running when you saved keeps the value it started with; the next command reads the new one. A port change did nothing. Ports take effect when EiN starts again, and with the installer's setup they are changed with ~/ein/setup.sh --http-port or --ssh-port , or in .env , not here. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A module's settings are missing. They exist only while the module is installed and working; check it on Settings → Modules , as Modules describes. Something else is wrong. Troubleshooting goes through the common problems.

Settings : every setting, with its default, kind and what it restarts. Environment variables : the variables EiN reads that are not settings. Your profile, favourites and trash : personal preferences. Accounts and groups : the Users , Groups and Permissions tabs, and the default sharing. Modules : the Modules tab, module sources and their tokens. Processing and pipelines and Performance and sizing : what the Processing settings do in practice. The media service and The language model : their addresses and keys.

Modules decide what your EiN is for: the Archive, the assistant and the client for the media service are each a module. This page is for the administrator: which modules there are and what they need, how to install, update and remove them on Settings → Modules or in the terminal, how to keep one to some groups, how to see whether each one works, and what to do when one does not.

EiN without modules is the tree, the shell, accounts and the frame of the Web UI. Every page for photos, people and places, the chat, and the work done on what you upload comes from a module. How EiN works explains what a module is made of. Each module has a section of its own in this documentation, under Modules ; skip the sections of modules you have not installed. The published modules are the repositories named module-<name> in the einhq organisation on GitHub: Module What it gives you What it needs archive The Archive: albums, media, people and the family tree, locations, cameras and the trips of devices, staging, and the search that finds things among them The ems module, installed along with it, and the media service to do its work assistant Chat : the assistant that answers questions by running EiN's commands for you A language model , either the installer's --llm or a hosted one ems EiN's side of the media service: the client the Archive reaches it through, its health and the graphics card's readings on the Status The media service A module needs only what its manifest names as dependencies; EiN installs those with it. A service that runs beside EiN, such as the media service or the language model, is no module: the installer adds it (see Installing in detail ). Installing archive without the media service gives no error, only a reminder from the installer and setup.sh when EIN_MODULES names it, but nothing you upload gets thumbnails, dates, faces or searchable text until the media service is there.

Open Settings in the sidebar and choose the Modules tab. Everyone who is signed in has this tab; for anyone but an administrator it is the only one, and it shows the modules without the buttons that change them. Each installed module, whether it works, and everything it brings, in one place. The list at the left holds every installed module with its description; above it, beside the filter box, is the administrator's Install button (see Install a module ). Anyone else has Published there instead, which lists the published modules without a way to install them. A module that works shows its version at the right; one that does not shows a badge instead and is listed first: Badge What it means Active Set up since EiN started: its commands are on the path, its services are registered and its pages are built. Setup failed EiN tried to set it up and refused or failed; the module's panel says why. Not set up Installed, but not set up since EiN started: its commands are not on the path and its services are not running. Type in the filter box to narrow the list by name or description. Show only active modules , at the foot of the list, leaves out the ones that do not work; your browser remembers the switch. Choose a module to open its panel. At the top are the module's name, its version, its state and what it is; a long description shows three lines, and More opens the rest. Under them are the buttons: Update and Remove for the administrator, on a module installed from its repository (see Update a module and Remove a module ), and Documentation , which opens the module's own page in Documentation , with its pages in this guide and every command, setting and node type it brings. When its setup failed, why is said under the buttons. Below are tabs; Overview and Dependencies are always there, the others show how many things each holds, and a tab the module has nothing for is left out: Tab What it shows Overview Its details, and beside them In the guide : its pages in this guide, or "The guide has no section on it." Dependencies The modules it needs ( It needs ) and the modules that need it ( Needs it ), with the versions accepted, the version installed and each one's state, or Not installed Services Its background services, their state now and how long they have been up. They are started and stopped on the Status 's services tab. Pages The addresses of the pages it adds; one without a parameter is a link to the page Commands Its commands; each opens to its help Settings Its settings with their values, each marked personal or system ; a row opens to the setting's description and, if you may change it, its control Node types The kinds of node it defines, with how many of each exist The details on Overview are: Detail What it says Available to Everyone , or the groups it is kept to; see Keep a module to some groups Version The version in its mod.json Core API The version of EiN's module API it is written for, such as ^0.7.0 Source The repository it was installed from, as a link, or Comes with the deployment Installed The release, branch or tag it was installed at and its commit, such as v0.1.0 · 5e1c07a42 , and when; one installed at a commit shows the commit alone Set up When EiN last set it up, or Not since EiN started Folder Where it is inside EiN, such as /usr/modules/archive A module's system settings are the same ones the System tab lists, and its personal ones are those on Profile → Preferences ; they save the same way: Configuration explains where a value comes from and what a change restarts. The About EiN dialog, in the menu under your picture, also lists the installed modules, with a setup failed badge on any that did not set up. In the terminal, mod list gives the same list: # in EiN's terminal mod list archive (0.1.0) assistant (0.1.0) ems (0.1.0) A module that does not work has [setup failed] or [not set up] after its version. mod list --long adds each one's description, the problems its setup ran into, its path, the repository and commit it was installed from, and its commands and services. mod info archive shows one module's manifest: its version, core API, the modules it requires and whether they are installed, what it exports, and the modules that use it.

You need to be an administrator: signed in as admin , or in admin mode . EiN needs to reach GitHub, or whichever forge holds the module. Open Settings → Modules . Choose Install beside the filter box. The panel at the right is headed Install a module and lists the published modules in groups: Updates , Not installed and Installed , each with how many it holds. A module under Updates or Not installed is a card with its version, its repository and what it is. Choose Install on the card of the module you want. EiN asks who the module is for. Keep Everyone , or choose Only some groups and the groups (see Keep a module to some groups ), then choose Install and the module's name. The published modules and what is installed of each; these came with the deployment, so none offers Install. EiN fetches the module, checks it, installs any module it needs that is missing, sets them all up and starts their services. Its entries in the sidebar and its pages appear without reloading the page. The install runs on its own: closing the page, or signing out, does not stop it. While it runs, the top of Settings → Modules says so to everyone who opens the tab, with who started it, how many of the module's files are in place and the last thing it did, and Install and Update wait for it, since EiN installs one thing at a time. A module of many files, such as one with map tiles, can take a long while. When it ends, the tab says what it installed, with a link to each module, or why it failed. The group a published module is in says what is installed of it: Group What it holds Updates Modules installed from this repository with a newer release out. The card says which version is installed, such as "0.1.0 installed", and its button reads Update . Not installed Modules no version of which is installed; the button reads Install . Installed The rest, a row each that opens the module's panel: installed from this repository at its newest release, or at a commit past it, or else marked Installed from elsewhere , from another repository, or The deployment's , when the deployment itself provides it (see Modules the deployment provides ) and it cannot be installed over. When nothing is to be installed or updated, the panel says "Every published module is installed, and none has a newer release this EiN can run." A module written for a different core API says "Needs core API ^0.6.0, which this EiN does not provide." (with its own range), and its button is greyed out. When only its newest release is written for another core API and an older one runs here, the module is listed at that older release, with a note such as "0.3.0 needs core API ^0.8.0, which this EiN does not provide; 0.2.4 is the newest release it can run.", and Install installs 0.2.4. Refresh asks the sources again. In the terminal, mod search lists the same, and mod install installs: # in EiN's terminal mod search archive 0.1.0 The family archive, with people, media, places and staging https://github.com/einhq/module-archive assistant 0.1.0 [installed] The chat that answers questions about the archive https://github.com/einhq/module-assistant ems 0.1.0 The client for EMS, the media service https://github.com/einhq/module-ems A module's description is the one in its mod.json at the release listed, or its repository's when that has none. Words after mod search narrow the list to modules whose name or description holds them all. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install archive Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-archive at v0.1.0 (5e1c07a42)... archive needs ems ^0.1.0, which is not installed Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-ems at v0.1.2 (b83d2f610)... Installed ems 0.1.0 from https://github.com/einhq/module-ems at b83d2f610 Installed archive 0.1.0 from https://github.com/einhq/module-archive at 5e1c07a42 Setting up module 'ems'... A line follows for each step of each setup, ending in Module 'archive' setup complete and the services it started. mod install takes several modules at once, and each can be named in three ways: You write What is installed archive module-archive from the first module source that has it, at its newest release https://github.com/einhq/module-archive That repository, at its newest release archive@v0.1.0 , …/module-archive@<commit> That branch or tag, or a commit by its id, whole or its first seven characters or more, which EiN records whole A release is a tag v and a version, such as v0.3.1 , and the newest is the highest version; a prerelease such as v0.4.0-rc.1 does not count. When the newest release is written for a core API this EiN does not provide, EiN takes the newest release that is written for it instead and says so: archive 0.3.0 needs core API ^0.8.0, and this core provides 0.7.2: taking v0.2.4 . A ref, such as archive@v0.3.0 , takes that release or none. A repository with no release is installed at its default branch, and @main installs the default branch of one that has releases, with whatever was pushed after the last one. A module that is missing and needed by the one you install comes at its newest release that the module accepts: archive needing ems ^0.1.0 gets ems 0.1.2 even when 0.2.0 is out, and the newest in that range this EiN can run. mod search lists each module at the release mod install would take, its version and the core API it needs, and names a newer release written for another core API: archive 0.2.4 (0.3.0 needs core API ^0.8.0, this is 0.7.2) . The install goes on when the terminal is closed or the connection drops; mod install only follows it, and stops following when you press Ctrl + C . mod install --background archive starts it and returns at once. mod status says how far the install running now has got, or what the last one came to, and mod status --follow follows it to its end: mod install seacharts: running for 32s, for admin Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-seacharts at v0.4.0 (3a9c0e1f2)... 12759 files of seacharts unpacked EiN installs one thing at a time. While an install runs, mod install with the same modules follows it, and with any other refuses, naming the one running. An install EiN stopped in the middle of, by restarting, leaves nothing installed of it; the next install clears away what it left. The reference lists its options.

The installer's --module option names a module for EiN to install at its start, with the modules it needs: # on the machine EiN runs on ~/ein/setup.sh --module assistant setup.sh adds the name to EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env and, as on every run, fetches the newest sources, builds and starts EiN again, which installs every module named there that is missing.
