At the end setup.sh lists the modules installed, each with its version and the release it was installed at, and below them the lines EiN's start logged about a module it could not install or run: The modules installed: archive 0.3.1 (v0.3.1) assistant 0.2.0 (v0.2.0) ems 0.1.2 (v0.1.2) If EiN cannot download a module at its start, its log says some modules could not be installed or replaced; continuing boot , and the mod install: line below the list says why. EiN starts without it; install it from Settings → Modules once EiN is up. Installing in detail has the other options.

p.h: What EiN's start does with installed modules
p.x: At every start EiN goes through the modules installed from a repository. One it can run is left as it is, at whatever version, without asking GitHub, so a restart never updates it. One installed at a release written for a module API this EiN does not provide, as after an update of EiN that changed the API, is replaced from its repository by the newest release this EiN can run, as mod install without a ref would take it, and a module it needs that this EiN cannot run either is replaced the same way. The log says so: archive 0.3.1 is installed and needs core API ^0.7.0, and this core provides 0.8.0 Fetching https://github.com/einhq/module-archive at v0.4.0 (8c2e41d07)... The release it takes can be older than the newest published: when the newest needs a newer EiN than this one, it takes the newest that runs here. When no release runs here, the module stays as it was, does not set up, and setup.sh 's list ends with the reason, such as mod install: archive: needs @ein/client ^0.7.0, this core provides 0.8.0 .

Updating EiN with setup.sh does not update its modules. Update them here instead. On Settings → Modules , choose Install beside the filter box and choose Update on a module under Updates . Or open the module's panel. A module installed from its repository has Update and Remove under its name, and its Overview says under Source and Installed which repository and commit it came from and when. Update there fetches the newest release for one installed at a release, and the newest commit of the branch for one installed from a branch. One installed at any other tag gets that tag again, and one installed at a commit stays there, and its panel offers no Update . The top of the tab says how it goes, as for an install, and when it ends what it updated, or that there was nothing newer. In the terminal, mod install archive updates an installed module. The same commit again is left alone: archive is installed at 5e1c07a42 (v0.1.0) already . An update installs what the new version needs and is missing. It is refused when an installed module depends on this one and does not accept the new version; the message names them, for example letters needs archive ^0.1.0, and this is archive 0.2.0: --force installs it all the same . mod install --force updates anyway, and also fetches again a commit that is installed already. After the update EiN sets the module up again and restarts its services; its settings take the new version's defaults and descriptions, and a setting it no longer has is gone. Every module that depends on it, directly or through another, is set up again too, and its running services restarted, so nothing keeps running the code that was replaced. The new version takes the old one's place in a single step: the module's folder always holds one whole version. An update that changes only the module's pages, the files under its ui/ folder, restarts nothing: its services run none of them, and a restart would stop the work they are in the middle of, such as the pictures and videos its workers are sending to the media service. The install says so: Nothing but the pages of archive changed: its services keep running . To keep a module at a version, install it at a commit, such as mod install archive@463a92f ; its panel then has no Update . The published modules still compare it with the newest release this EiN can run, so they may offer Update for it, which installs that release, as mod install archive without a ref does. A module installed from its default branch past the newest release is not offered the release.

p.h: Keep a module to some groups
p.x: A module is everyone's until you keep it to some groups. Then only the members of those groups, and administrators, have it: its commands, its entries in the sidebar and the top bar, its pages, its personal settings, and the module itself on Settings → Modules and on the Docs page's reference. For everyone else it is as if it were not installed. On Settings → Modules , open the module. Available to , on its Overview , says who has it. Choose Change , choose the groups in the box and choose Save ; empty the box to make it everyone's again. When you install a module there, Install asks first who it is for: Everyone , or Only some groups with the groups to choose. The modules it needs and brings along stay everyone's, and an Update asks nothing and keeps whom the module was for. In the terminal, mod groups says who a module is for and changes it, and mod install --groups installs a module for some groups from the start: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod groups assistant family mod groups assistant family # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod groups assistant --everyone mod install -- groups family,friends assistant mod groups names groups as group-list prints them, and refuses one there is not: mod groups: no group famly . Someone outside the groups who types one of the module's commands gets command not found , and one who names it by its path is refused: /usr/modules/assistant/bin/assistant-ask: permission denied: module assistant is kept to groups you are not in . The module's services and pipelines go on working for the whole archive, as they run as the administrator. Groups are read when someone signs in, so a person added to a group gets its modules the next time they sign in. A terminal open already picks up a change to who a module is for at its next command. When a module that is everyone's needs the one you keep to groups, mod groups and the panel warn that what it runs of that module fails for anyone outside them, for example mod groups: archive depends on ems and is everyone's: what it runs of ems fails for anyone outside family . Keep both to the same groups, or neither. Behind this, the groups are in /etc/modules/<module>.groups , one name per line. Setting the module up puts its commands on the path in /etc/bashrc.d/<group> for each group and for admin , instead of in /etc/bashrc , and its sidebar entries in /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.d/<module>.json , in each group's shared home , instead of in /etc/ui/nav.d . A group without a home is given one, so a module can be kept only to a group that can have one: not to admin , guest , ssh or sudo , nor to a person's own group, which mod groups refuses with mod groups: a module is kept to groups that can have a home, for its navigation, and 'sudo' is a built-in group . Removing the module forgets its groups. Configuration files lists these files.

Open Settings → Modules and choose the module. Choose Remove under its name. EiN says what goes: "Removing assistant stops its services and takes its commands, pages and files away. What it made in the archive stays." When other modules need it, it adds which ones and that they will not work without it. Choose Remove assistant to go ahead, or Cancel . In the terminal, mod remove asks first, and --force skips the question: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod remove assistant Remove module 'assistant' (0.1.0)? (y/N) y Where no one can answer, as in ssh host 'mod remove assistant' or a script, it does not ask: it stops with mod-remove: no terminal to answer on; add --force , and removes nothing. Removing stops and unregisters the module's services, takes its commands off the path, retires its pipelines, its sidebar entries and its documentation, rebuilds the pages and deletes its folder. Some things stay, so that installing it again finds them as they were: What it made in the tree: albums, people, labels and the folders under /archive that hold them. Values set for its settings. They no longer appear on the System tab, but come back with the module. The database indexes it asked for. EiN does not stop you removing a module that others need. Those modules then fail to set up at the next start, with requires module 'ems' (^0.1.0), which is not installed ; install it again to bring them back. Warning A module named in EIN_MODULES in ~/ein/.env comes back at EiN's next start, because EiN installs every module named there that is missing. To keep it removed, delete its name from that line as well.

Module sources , CFG_MODULE_SOURCES , lists where published modules are looked for: organisations on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea, as their addresses separated by spaces. It is https://github.com/einhq by default. Each repository named module-<name> in a source is a module; mod install <name> takes the first source that has it, and a module's dependencies come from its own organisation first. Change it on Settings → System , in its Modules group, or in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator config set CFG_MODULE_SOURCES "https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield" A source that is not public needs an access token. Tokens for module sources , CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY , takes one per host, as host=token separated by spaces, such as forge.example:3000=… . Like every key, nobody can read it back once set, and EiN sends each token only to its own host. The settings reference has both. A source that does not answer is named above the published modules, as " https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield did not answer" with the reason, and the other sources are still listed. A module that is in no source can still be installed from its repository's address: mod install https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield/module-recipes , or the From a repository's address box at the foot of the Install a module panel, whose Install asks who the module is for as on a published one. EiN fetches modules over plain HTTPS, so the forge must answer git's HTTP protocol and serve an archive of a commit, as GitHub, Forgejo and Gitea do. Writing a module is for making one of your own.

A module installed from its repository is kept in a folder of its own outside EiN's container, so it stays when EiN is updated or its container is made again. With the standard installation that folder is modules/ in the data folder, ~/ein/data/modules unless you chose another data folder. Inside EiN it is /var/lib/modules , and each module is linked as /usr/modules/<name> . Each module's .install.json records the repository, the branch or tag, the commit and when it was installed. At every start EiN links each module in the folder and sets them all up, in the order of their dependencies. A module whose setup fails is logged and the others carry on.

A deployment can also mount a folder of module checkouts of its own, named by DEV_MODULES_PATH (see Environment variables ). The standard installation does not; it is for running EiN from its source. A module the deployment provides runs from there: the published modules mark it The deployment's , mod install refuses it with 'archive' is one of the deployment's modules (…), which runs instead , and it has no Update or Remove in its panel. mod remove takes away only its link, which the next start puts back. It is updated with the deployment.

p.h: When a module does not work
p.x: Open Settings → Modules : a module that does not work is at the top of the list with its badge. Setup failed. Its panel shows "Its setup failed" with each problem, as mod list --long does. The usual ones: Problem What to do archive: requires module 'ems' (^0.1.0), which is not installed Install the missing module: mod install ems , or Install on the Install a module panel. archive: requires 'ems' ^0.2.0, but 0.1.0 is installed Update the module it needs. archive: needs @ein/client ^0.7.0, this core provides 0.6.0 The module is written for another version of EiN, often after EiN was updated, and EiN's start found no release of it that fits. Update the module once one is published; until then it waits. After fixing the cause, set the module up again with mod setup archive , or every module with mod setup --all , which is what EiN runs at each start. Restarting EiN does the same. Not set up. EiN has not set the module up since it started, for example because it was put in place without setup. mod setup <name> sets it up. Active, but something is missing. Check its Services tab: a service that shows failed or disabled can be started again on the Status 's services tab, and Services and logs explains how to read its log. A module installed from the terminal shows its pages in a browser tab that was already open once that page is reloaded. Install or update refused. The message says why, in words like these: Message What it means no module source has 'recipes': … None of the module sources has module-recipes , or none answered; the reasons follow. https://github.com/einhq/module-archive has no branch, tag or commit 'v9' The ref after @ does not exist. … has no mod.json at its top: not a module The repository is not a module. /usr/modules/archive is a module mod install did not put there; mod remove archive first Something else holds the name. no module sources to find 'archive' in: CFG_MODULE_SOURCES is empty; name its repository instead Module sources is empty. Troubleshooting covers problems beyond modules.

Every command here runs in EiN's terminal or over SSH. Those that change something are for administrators only. Command What it does mod list [--long] The installed modules and whether each works mod info <name> One module's manifest, what it requires and what uses it mod search [words] The published modules of the module sources, and what is installed of them mod install <module>... Install or update modules with what they need, and set them up mod groups <name> [group...] Who a module is for, or keep it to groups; --everyone makes it everyone's mod remove [--force] <name> Stop and remove a module mod setup <name> , mod setup --all Set up one module, or every module in the order of their dependencies The core commands reference has each one's options, and Updating covers updating EiN itself.

This page is for the administrator who gives people accounts in EiN and puts them in groups. It covers the Users , Groups and Permissions tabs of Settings , the built-in accounts and groups, how to let a second person administer, and the same work in the terminal. What a group may see and change is decided by the sharing of each folder, and with the Archive of each album, not here. Sharing shows how to share with a group, and Permissions in depth explains owners, groups and modes.

Choose Settings under System in the sidebar. The Users , Groups and Permissions tabs are there only while you act as the administrator; anyone else sees Modules alone. On Users and Groups , nothing opens over the page. The list is on the left; pick an entry and its panel opens beside it, where each change is made as you make it. The button beside the list's filter makes a new entry: New user on Users, New group on Groups. On a wide screen the list and the panel fill the window side by side and each scrolls on its own. On a phone or in a narrow window they take turns: the panel has All users or All groups above it, and the browser's Back button returns to the list too. The open entry is part of the address, such as /settings?tab=users&user=helen , so you can bookmark an account or send the link to another administrator.

p.h: The accounts and groups EiN starts with
p.x: EiN makes these at its first start, and none can be deleted. The two accounts are marked Administrator and Guest in their panels, and each of the groups Built in . Account Title What it is admin Administrator The administrator. It cannot be disabled or deleted. Its first password is the one you chose at the install, or one setup.sh made, kept as INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in ~/ein/.env and printed at the end of each run until you delete that line; First steps shows how to change it. guest Guest Who a visitor browses as when Visitors may browse is on. It has no password, cannot be given one, and its groups give it nothing. Group Title What it is for admin Administrators The admin account's own group, as root 's is on Linux. Being in it does not make anyone an administrator and gives no write to the system's own folders and settings. users Users Every account that signs in belongs to it, without being added, unless you take it out. Sharing with users shares with everyone who has an account. ssh SSH users Its members may use ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id to reach other machines from EiN. See Reaching other machines . sudo Administrators on request Its members may act as the administrator for one sign-in, after entering their own password again. See Let a second person administer . guest Guests The guest account's own group. What this group may see, visitors may see. EiN also makes the group devices ( Devices ) at every start when it is missing: its members make, rename and forget the devices under /dev ( Devices and their keys ). It is not built in, and starts empty. Besides these, every account made on the Users tab or with user-create gets a group of its own, named like the account: Helen Okafor's account helen has the group helen . These are its personal group.

Open Settings → Users and choose the New user button beside the filter. Type the person's Name , such as Helen Okafor. E-mail is optional. With one, the person can sign in with it instead of the username. No two accounts can have the same address, and EiN sends no e-mail to it. Check Username . It is suggested from the name ( helen ) until you type one. It is lower case, holds only letters, digits and . _ - , starts with a letter or _ , and cannot be changed later. It cannot be the name of an existing account or group. Type a Password and Repeat it, or leave both empty to set the password later. An account without a password cannot sign in. Under Groups , Users is ticked and greyed: everyone who signs in is in it. The groups set as the default for new users are ticked already (see What new accounts start with ). Tick or untick the others. Choose Create user . EiN says "Created helen." and opens the new account. The account has a home folder, /home/helen , which holds the person's own things, such as their preferences and, with the Archive installed, what they upload to staging, and a personal group helen . While something is missing, Create user says why under it: "Choose a username", "Already taken", "Repeat the password" or "The passwords do not match". If the account was made but its password could not be set, the account opens with the reason in its Password section; set the password there. Each account opens in a panel beside the list, where every change is made in place

Pick the account in the list. Its panel shows its picture, display name, username and uid, and badges for its state: Administrator , Guest , Disabled , Needs a password or Signed in now . Below are five sections, each saved on its own.

Display name , E-mail and Description , saved with Save profile . The display name is how the account is named to others; the person can change their own name and description too, on their profile (see Your profile ). Only an administrator sets the e-mail address. Empty the field and save to remove it. Save profile stays greyed out while Display name is empty: every account has a name. The account's picture is not set here: with the Archive installed, it is the cover photo of the person in the archive that the account is linked to. Your picture and the person you are shows how to make that link in the terminal.

A box per group: tick to put the person in, untick to take them out. Each box saves as you click it. Users is ticked for everyone who signs in; unticking it takes the account out of what is shared with everyone with an account, which is what an account for a screen wants (see Show a dashboard on a screen ). Some boxes are ticked and greyed, with the reason beside them: primary group , or their own group, primary : the account's primary group, which it leaves only when its primary group is changed. Other people's personal groups are listed only while this account is in one. Primary group is a group the person is always in. It does not decide the group of what they create: a new file or folder takes the group of the folder it is created in, whoever creates it. It is used where nothing else names a group, such as what they create as shared when CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP is empty. It starts as the personal group. You can pick any shared group instead. Note Group changes apply the next time the person signs in. Until then they keep the groups they signed in with, and the section says so when they are signed in now. To make a change apply at once, sign them out everywhere with Disable sign-in and then Enable sign-in .

Type a New password , Repeat it, and choose Set password . Password set appears beside it. Their current password stops working at once, in the browser and over SSH and SFTP, but browsers and terminals where they are signed in stay signed in. EiN has no rules for passwords: it takes any password that is not empty. It sends no e-mail, so it has no "forgot password" of its own, and cannot make someone choose a new password at their next sign-in. When someone has forgotten theirs, or has never had one, send them a sign-in link to choose their own. Or set one here and ask them to change it on their profile's Security tab (see Change your password ). An account marked mustResetPassword has no usable password. It shows Needs a password , and cannot sign in by any means, an SSH key included, until a password is set, here or with a sign-in link; setting it clears the mark.

A link the person opens to choose their own password. It also shows them their username, which they may not know, such as an account you made for them, or one brought over from another system. Choose Make a sign-in link . The link appears, an address on this EiN that ends in /invite/ and a long code, with when it expires: in 7 days. Click the link to copy it, and send it to the person however you like: a message, a mail of your own, a note. EiN sends nothing itself. They open it, see their username, and choose a password, which signs them in ( Sign in with a link shows their side). The link works once: choosing a password with it spends it, and the section is empty again. Until then, anyone who has the link can choose the account's password, so send it only to the person. Make a new link replaces it, and the old one stops working; Turn off takes it away. A disabled account gets no link: choose Enable sign-in first, and a link made before it was disabled works again once it is enabled, if it has not expired. In the terminal, user-invite <username> --new --days 30 makes one that works longer, up to 90 days.

Signed in now lists where the person is signed in: In the browser , Over SSH or In a terminal , each with the address it comes from and since when. Earlier sign-ins, failed ones included, are on the Status page's Activity tab . Disable sign-in signs them out everywhere at once, ends what they have running, and keeps them out of the browser, SSH and SFTP alike. Nothing they own is changed. The button then reads Enable sign-in , which lets them sign in again with their password. A disabled account is hidden from the Users list until you switch on Show disabled users at the foot of the list, which is there only while some account is disabled. The admin account has neither button: "The administrator can't be disabled or deleted." The guest account's panel shows only what it is for.

Open the account and choose Delete account… under Sign-in and removal . Read what will happen. Deleting the account removes its home folder and everything in it: the person's preferences, their staging with the Archive, and anything else they kept there. Pick who takes over everything they own elsewhere, such as folders and files, and with the Archive albums and pictures. The administrator is picked to start with. Choose Delete followed by the username, such as Delete helen . EiN ends the person's sessions, says how many items passed to whom, and returns to the list. Their personal group goes too, unless someone else is in it; then it stays, and EiN says so. Warning There is no undo, and deleted home folders do not go to the trash. If you only want to keep someone out, use Disable sign-in instead. EiN has no backup command; see Your data before you delete an account whose home folder holds anything you want to keep, such as pictures still unsorted in the Archive's staging.

A group is a set of accounts to share with. If everyone with an account is family, the built-in users group covers them and you need no other. Make a group when only some accounts should see something, such as a family group when friends also have accounts. Open Settings → Groups and choose the New group button beside the filter. Type a Name , such as family . It is how commands and settings name the group, follows the same rules as a username, and cannot be changed later. Type a Title , such as Family, and a Description if you like. The title is what people see where things are shared with the group. Tick the Members . This is optional; you can add anyone later, here or on their own page. Choose Create group . EiN says "Created family." and opens it. The Groups list shows each group's title and name, and up to four of its members' faces with a count of the rest. users reads Everyone . Personal groups are hidden until you switch on Show personal groups at the foot of the list, which is there only when there are some. In a group's panel: Profile changes its Title and Description , saved with Save profile . Members has a box per account: tick to add, untick to remove. Someone whose primary group it is stays ticked and greyed; the panel links to their page, where their primary group is changed. An account that no longer exists but is still linked shows as no longer an account , ready to untick. In users every account is ticked without being added; unticking one takes it out of what is shared with everyone with an account. Built-in groups say what they are for at the top, and "Built-in groups can't be deleted." Shared home gives the group a folder of its own; see below. Built-in groups other than users and personal groups have no such section. Built-in groups say what they are for; the Users group shows Everyone instead of faces

A group can have a shared home, /groups/<group> : a folder its members share and nobody else sees, where they keep what the group has in common and where modules keep the group's things. users has one from the start, /groups/users , so everyone with an account shares one folder. To give a group a home, open it and switch on Shared home . The switch then shows where the folder is, such as /groups/family . Everything put in it, however deep, belongs to the group: every member can read, change and remove it, and anyone who leaves the group stops seeing it. Switching Shared home off moves the folder, with everything in it, to your trash, from where Restore brings it back. users stays without one once you have switched its home off. A group a module is kept to gets a new home the next time the module is set up, since its home holds the module's sidebar entries.

Open the group and choose Delete group… under Delete . Pick the group that takes over what this one owns. Administrators is picked to start with. Choose Delete followed by the group's name, such as Delete family . A group with a shared home says so in the confirmation: its home goes to your trash. Nobody loses their account. Accounts whose primary group it was go back to their own groups, and grants that named the group on folders, or on albums with the Archive, are dropped, so its members lose what they could see only through it.

The Permissions tab has four cards. Each says in a sentence what its saved values come to, and each setting on it is saved on its own with Save change , as on the System tab. A value changed here is marked Set here , and Restore inherited value clears it again. Card Setting What it decides Default New users Groups ( CFG_DEFAULT_USER_GROUPS ) The groups ticked on the New user form, besides the account's own. Empty means none. users Visitors Visitors may browse ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING ) Whether someone who has not signed in browses as guest , seeing what is shared with visitors, instead of being asked to sign in. off Sharing Owner , Group , Permissions Who owns anything created as shared, such as a new album with the Archive, which group it is shared with, and what the owner, the group and everyone else may do with it. creator, users , 0750 Sign-in sessions Browser sign-in ( CFG_SESSION_MAX_AGE_SEC ) How long a browser stays signed in after it was last used: opening EiN or moving between its pages. A tab left unused longer asks to sign in again, then returns to its page. 1 day Sign-in sessions Idle session ( CFG_SESSION_EXPIRES_SEC ) How long a session lasts unused. A change applies to new sign-ins. 12 hours Leave Visitors may browse off for a family's own archive. With it off, someone who is not signed in can only sign in or open a share link. Sharing explains what visitors see when it is on. The Sharing card's settings are CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_OWNER , CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP and CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE . They apply to what is created after you change them; First steps suggests values for common households, and How new albums start out shows how each person can narrow them. Each card says in plain words what new accounts, visitors and new albums get

Being in the admin group does not make anyone an administrator. To let someone you trust act as the administrator, or to keep an everyday account for yourself, put that account in Administrators on request ( sudo ): Open their account in Settings → Users . Under Groups , tick Administrators on request . Ask them to reload the page. Membership of sudo counts at once, without signing in again. They then have Administer… in the account menu under their picture. It asks for their own password again: "Enter your password again to act as the administrator until you sign out or leave admin mode." After Administer , the page reloads with the administrator's tabs and pages, an orange ring and a shield on their picture, and Leave admin mode in the account menu in place of Administer… . A wrong password answers "That is not your password." In a terminal, admin does the same for that terminal alone, and admin --off ends it. user-elevate --session acts for the whole sign-in, every page and terminal of it. Taking someone out of sudo ends their admin mode at once, in every page and terminal. Such a person can also set a new password for admin if it is lost, so keep at least one account you trust in sudo .

p.h: Signing in and why it fails
p.x: People sign in with their username or their e-mail address, in the browser under Username or e-mail , and over SSH and SFTP (see SSH and SFTP ). Their groups are read at that moment. A wrong password, an unknown username and an account without a password all fail the same way, so the answer does not tell anyone which accounts exist. Only with the right password does EiN say that an account is disabled. After five failed attempts from one address, that address is held back for a while that doubles with each further failure, up to 15 minutes, and the answer says how many seconds to wait. Failed attempts at one account only slow it down; they never lock its owner out. Failures are forgotten an hour after the last one.

Every change on these tabs is a command, and the tabs run the same commands. They are for the administrator, apart from reading lists and changing your own name and password. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator user-create helen --title= 'Helen Okafor' --email=helen@example.com -- groups = users ,family user-passwd helen # asks for the new password after Password: user-invite helen --new # a sign-in link, /invite/<code>, for 7 days; --days 1 to 90 user-invite helen # show it again; --off takes it away user-update helen --name= 'Helen Okafor' --description= 'Scans the family letters' user-set-primary-group helen family user-disable helen # signs her out everywhere and keeps her out user-enable helen user-delete helen --to=peggy # what she owned passes to peggy group-create family --title=Family --home # --home: with a shared home, /groups/family group-home family # give an existing group its shared home group-home family --off # move it to your trash group-add-member family helen group-remove-member family helen group-remove-member users kitchen # out of what is shared with every account; add-member puts it back group-update family --description= 'The Wrenfield household' group-delete family --to= users # --force when it is someone's primary group, # --remove-home when it has a shared home To see who there is and who is signed in: # in EiN's terminal user-list # every account, with uid and title; --inactive for the disabled ones user-info helen user-groups helen group-list --members # every group, and who is linked into it who # who is signed in, from where, and what they run user-create without --groups uses CFG_DEFAULT_USER_GROUPS ; --groups= with nothing after it adds the account to no group but its own. user-delete and group-delete without --to hand what was owned to admin . Commands by task and the core command reference list every option.

What you see What it means What to do Needs a password on an account It has no password, or is marked mustResetPassword until it is given one. Send a Sign-in link , or set one under Password . Someone does not see a folder or album shared with a group you just put them in Group changes apply at the next sign-in. Ask them to sign out and in, or choose Disable sign-in and Enable sign-in . Create user says "Already taken" An account or a group has that name. Each account's personal group is named like it. Choose another username. "Another account has this address" under E-mail Two accounts cannot share an address. Use another address, or remove it from the other account. user create: '<name>' is the name of a built-in group The names users , ssh and sudo belong to built-in groups. Choose another username. user update: a display name cannot be empty Every account has a name. Give --name a name, or leave it out to keep the one it has. group delete: cannot delete the built-in group '<name>' Built-in groups stay. Nothing to do. user passwd: the guest account cannot have a password guest never signs in. Turn Visitors may browse on or off instead. <name>: permission denied: only an administrator may run it The command is the administrator's. Choose Administer… , or type admin in that terminal, if you are in sudo . The admin password is lost Nothing else keeps it. A member of sudo sets a new one with user-passwd admin .
