Every node in EiN has an owner, a group, mode bits and, when it needs one, an access list. This page is for administrators, and for anyone who wants to see what the Share dialog writes: how EiN decides who may read, change and pass through a node, what a new node starts with, and how to read and change it all from the terminal. The Share dialog sets all of this without numbers, and Sharing explains it for everyone in the family. Accounts and groups themselves are made on Accounts and groups . The examples use albums such as /archive/albums/Summer 1987 , which exist with the Archive installed. The commands and rules are core's, and work the same on any node, such as a folder under /home .

p.h: The four parts of a node's access
p.x: Like a file on Linux, every node carries: Part What it is Shown as Owner One account, by its uid. Usually whoever created the node. helen Group One group, by its gid. Usually the group of the folder it was created in. users Mode Read, write and execute, once for the owner, once for the group and once for everyone else. rwxr-x--- , or 0750 Access list Further users and groups, each with its own read, write and execute. Optional. group:family:rwx What the three letters allow on a node: Bit On a node On a folder, album or anything with children r read See its bytes and attributes. See what it holds; listing takes r and x . w write Change it, its attributes, its mode and its access list. Add to it and remove from it (with x ). x execute — Pass through it to what lies below. Any node can hold children here, so the folder column applies to folders and files alike, and with the Archive to albums, people and locations: a photo holds its thumbnails and metadata as children.

EiN asks, in this order, and stops at the first yes: Are you an administrator? Then yes, always. Is this a write, and are you not signed in? Then no, whatever the bits say. Are you the owner, and do the owner's bits allow it? Is the node's group one of your groups, and do the group's bits allow it? Do everyone else's bits allow it? Does an entry in the access list name you or one of your groups, and allow it? Every step can only grant. Unlike Linux, being the owner does not shut you out of what the other bits give: a node at 0074 still lets its owner read it. The access list adds people and never takes anyone away; there is no entry that denies. Note Write on a node is enough to change its mode and its access list. That is why Can edit in the Share dialog also lets someone change who a node is shared with. Changing the owner is the exception; see Change the owner and the group .

Who uid Groups What is special The administrator, admin 0 admin ( 0 ), users Passes every check. An account, such as helen its own its own group, users , and every group it is a member of — A member of sudo who chose Administer… its own as above Passes every check until the sign-in ends or they leave admin mode. The guest, guest 1001 guest ( 1001 ) Never writes. Whoever opens EiN without signing in. A share link one of its own, from 1073741824 up none Never writes; its entries stop granting when the link expires. A few rules follow from how groups are read: Every signed-in person is in users (gid 1002 ). Sharing with users , which the dialog calls Everyone with an account , shares with all of them. A member is someone with a membership link. group-add-member family jon puts a link named jon to /etc/users/jon in /etc/groups/family/users . Anything else placed there makes nobody a member. Groups are read when someone signs in. A person added to or taken out of a group keeps the groups they signed in with until they sign in again. Membership of sudo is the exception: it counts at once, and taking someone out of sudo ends their admin mode at once. Being in the admin group makes nobody an administrator. It is the administrator's own group, as root's is on Linux, and gives no write to the system's folders. To let someone act as the administrator when they need to, add them to sudo ; see Accounts and groups . To see who you are: # in EiN's terminal user-whoami user-groups helen

Open Nodes under System in the sidebar. Go to the node. The Mode , Owner and Group columns show its access; a lock in place of the arrow means you may not list what it holds. Choose Properties in the node's context menu, or press Alt + Enter . The Nodes page shows every node's mode, owner and group, and the properties dialog changes them. The properties dialog has three tabs: General shows the node's Mode as a number and as a grid of Owner , Group and Other against r , w and x , with Owner and Group pickers. Apply saves them, and stays off when you may not change the node. Attributes lists the node's attributes. Sharing is the Share dialog's own body: owner, grants, visitors and links in words.

# in EiN's terminal ls -l '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # mode, owner and group of what it holds stat '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the node itself: type, mode, owner, times acl '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # owner, group, bits and access list share-info '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the Share dialog's view, as YAML In ls -l a + after the mode, as in rwxr-x---+ , says the node has an access list. acl prints the bits and the list in the shape getfacl uses: # node: /archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage # owner: helen (1003) # group: users (1002) user::rwx group::r-x other::--- group:family:rwx user:jon:r-x link:1073741825:r-x A link: line is a share link's entry, by its uid; share-link list <path> says which link it is. share-info also lists the photos below a folder that keep their own sharing, its links, and, for an administrator, everyone who has access and through what.

chmod takes a mode as four octal digits or as symbolic clauses: # in EiN's terminal chmod 0750 '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod g+w '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod u=rwx,g=rx,o-rwx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' chmod -r o-rw /archive # the whole subtree; each node keeps its other bits Form Meaning 0750 , 750 Set all nine bits. The same mode on every node of a recursive change. u , g , o , a Owner, group, everyone else, all three. No letter means all three. + , - , = Add these bits, take them away, or set exactly these; o= clears them. r , w , x The bits. Clauses are joined with commas. A symbolic mode is worked out from each node's own mode, as coreutils' chmod -R does, so chmod -r o-rw clears only those bits and leaves every node's other bits as they were. EiN has no setuid, setgid or sticky bit and no X . -r applies the change to the whole subtree (see What a recursive change does ); -L changes a softlink itself rather than what it points to.

p.h: Change the owner and the group
p.x: # in EiN's terminal chown jon '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # owner only (administrator) chown jon:family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # owner and group (administrator) chown :family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # group only chown -r :family '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' # group of the whole subtree The owner and group are written user:group (or user.group ), by name or by number, and either half may be left out. The rules are Linux's: Only an administrator gives a node to another user. Anyone else is refused with Access denied for operation 'change uid' . Anyone else may move a node only into a group they are in , and needs write on it. Another group is refused with Access denied for operation 'change gid' . Without these rules someone could make what they wrote look like someone else's, or file it in a group they do not belong to. The owners of accounts, groups and sign-in sessions are the administrator's alone to change.

p.h: Grant more people with an access list
p.x: The mode names one group. An access list adds as many users and groups as you need, each with its own bits: # in EiN's terminal acl -m g:family:rwx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the family group may edit acl -m u:jon:rx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # Jon may view acl -x u:jon '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # take Jon's entry away acl -b '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # remove every user and group entry acl -r -m g:family:rx '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' # the whole subtree An entry is u:<user>:<bits> or g:<group>:<bits> ( user: and group: work too), by name or number. -m replaces an entry for the same user or group rather than adding a second. Can view in the Share dialog is rx and Can edit is rwx . -b leaves share links' entries in place: share-link gives and takes those. share-set --drop-links removes them too. Each node in a recursive change edits its own list, as setfacl -R does, so an entry a folder inside already has beyond the edit stays.

p.h: Set it all at once with share-set
p.x: share-set changes the mode, the owner, the group and the access list together, in one walk of the subtree, and is what the Share dialog runs when you click Save . Unlike chmod -r , it is recursive unless you say otherwise: # in EiN's terminal share-set '/archive/albums/Christmas at the cottage' --mode 0750 -b -m g:family:rwx -m u:jon:rx share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --group family --mode g+rx share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --default-owner # the configured default owner and group share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --mode 0700 -b --drop-links --pin updated 214, kept own access 3, skipped 0, failed 0 Option What it does --mode The mode, octal or symbolic. --owner The owner, by name or uid. Administrators only. --group The group, by name or gid: one you are in, unless you are an administrator. --default-owner The configured default owner and group (see The default sharing ), applied by the server to every node you may write. --reference <path> Share the node as another one is: its group, mode and access list. The owner stays. -m , -x , -b Edit the access list, as acl does. --drop-links Remove share links' entries too, so no link opens the nodes. --pin , --unpin Hold the node against changes from further up, or let them reach it again. --pinned-below Change the pinned nodes below each path named, in place of the path itself. --no-recursive Change only the node named. --strict Exit non-zero when any node below could not be changed. share-set exits 0 when only some nodes below refused, and reports them in its counts and on standard error; it fails only when every path it was given refused. Every option is in the reference .

A pinned node keeps its access when a change comes from further up. A recursive change always writes the node it was aimed at, but passes over a pinned node and everything below it. With the Archive, this is what Share in an album's selection bar does when you give chosen photos sharing of their own, and how one photo stays private in a shared album; see Keep some photos private in a shared album . # in EiN's terminal share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --pin share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987/IMG_0042.jpg' --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --unpin share-set '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --pinned-below --reference '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' --unpin The pin is written on that node only. share-info on the album lists the pinned nodes below it, and a share link made on the album does not open them. The last line shares every pinned node in the album as the album is, which is what Share all like the album in the Share dialog runs.

chmod -r , chown -r , acl -r and share-set walk the subtree the same way: It reads the whole subtree first and writes the folder you named last. A change can take away the access the walk needs to get through, so nothing is written until everything has been found, and the folder's own access, which share-info reports, is never ahead of what is below it. Pinned nodes and everything below them are passed over , and counted as "kept own access". Softlinks are changed as links , never followed to their targets, so a link in an album to a photo elsewhere does not change that photo. It stops at mount points. What another store mounts inside the subtree is left alone. A node is changed once , however many places it hangs in. A node that refuses is counted, not fatal , as chmod -R behaves over files someone else owns. What you may not read is not listed to you, so it counts against its folder without names. Ctrl + C stops between batches , with the folder you named as it was. A plain chmod of a large folder rewrites the stored reach of everything below it (see A folder governs what is under it ), so expect it to take a while on an album of thousands of photos.

p.h: What a new node starts with
p.x: When a node is created and nothing names its access: Part What it gets Owner Whoever created it. Group Its parent's group, as a setgid directory does on Linux. Mode Everything for the owner; read and pass-through for the group, plus write where the group could write the parent; for everyone else, only the read and pass-through the parent gives them. Others' write is never inherited. Access list Its parent's, as a Linux default ACL carries down. So, with the Archive, a family album's new uploads, and the thumbnails, faces and metadata processing adds under them, take the album's group and grants whoever created them: a person or group granted an album sees what is added to it later. What is made under /home/<user> stays in that user's group, and the system tree under / stays 0755 . Moving a node with mv keeps its own access, as on Linux. Copying with cp is a create in the destination: the copy takes the destination's group and keeps its source's mode, less group write where the new parent gives none and less everyone else's write.

The default sharing is an owner, a group and a mode for what is created as shared, which an administrator sets under Settings → Permissions , on the Sharing card. Default in the Share dialog and share-set --default-owner apply it to a node. With the Archive installed, a new album, made in the Web UI or with album create , and what staging publishes start with it. The Sharing card sets what every new album starts with, and says in a sentence what that comes to. Setting On the card Default CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_OWNER Owner empty: whoever creates it CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP Group users CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE Permissions : None , View or Edit for owner, group and everyone else 0750 With the defaults, a new album is therefore owned by its creator, seen by everyone with an account and changed only by its owner. Each person narrows or widens that for what they create with How widely what you create is shared on their profile ( CFG_USER_DEFAULT_SHARE ); see Your profile . With the defaults, Default in the Share dialog lets everyone with an account see a node. The same settings in the terminal, in the octal form: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator config set CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_GROUP family config set CFG_DEFAULT_SHARE_MODE 0750 Configuration explains where settings are kept.

p.h: A folder governs what is under it
p.x: Reaching a node by its path takes execute on every folder along the way, from / down. EiN applies the same rule wherever it finds a node without walking a path: search and links, and with the Archive the Media feed, the map, a person's faces and duplicates. A node shows up only when you may read it and at least one of its paths is open to you all the way down. With the Archive, this is what keeps staging private. /home/<user>/staging is 0700 , so the uploads inside it stay out of everyone else's search and map, whatever their own modes say. A node linked in two places is reachable through either. A hard link ( ln without -s ) into an open folder makes it visible there even when its other path is closed. A softlink is not a path. It points somewhere; whoever follows it still needs the access along the target's own path. What is in someone's trash is never offered by a search , to anyone, the administrator included, though counts may still include it until the trash is emptied. EiN keeps on each node who can get there, and works it out again below every node whose parents or access change, so group membership and link expiry are judged as you read and changing them rewrites nothing. If you suspect the stored answer is wrong, an administrator can check a sample of nodes against a walk of their paths: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator reach-check reach-check --sample=10000 2000 nodes judged for 9 callers: 0 disagree Any line under it names a node, a path and a uid for which the stored answer and the walk differ, and the uids or gids the stored answers name that no account, group or link holds.

p.h: The other bits are the system's
p.x: The bits for everyone else give every visitor and every account the parts of EiN they all need to run: / , /etc , the commands, the Web UI, the modules' files. Content does not use them to share: Path Owner and group Mode Why /archive admin , users 0771 Everyone may pass through; nobody but the group reads it. /archive/tags admin , users 0771 The same. /dev admin 0755 Everyone passes through; only the administrator adds to it, and members of devices make devices with device-create ( Devices and their keys ). A device is 0770 with the group devices , so only its members and whoever they share it with read it. /home/<user> the account, its own group 0751 Others may pass through to what the owner grants, and read nothing else. /home/<user>/staging the account 0700 With the Archive. Nobody else, not even through search. /etc/users/<name> admin 0755 The account itself; only the administrator changes it. /etc/users/<name>/.password admin 0600 Its user can neither read nor replace it. /etc/groups/<group>/users its creator, the group 0750 Members may see who else is in the group, not add anyone. /var/links/<id> admin 0600 A share link's record, holding its token. Content reaches every account through the users group, and visitors who are not signed in through an access-list entry for the guest group, g:guest:rx , which the Share dialog shows as Visitors who are not signed in . When you open the Share dialog on something whose everyone-else bits still read it, the dialog shows them as Everyone with an account , and Save moves them there and clears the bits. To clear what older content still gives everyone else: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator chmod -r o-rw /archive

Someone who opens EiN without signing in acts as the guest. Whether they see anything depends on Visitors may browse under Settings → Permissions ( CFG_GUEST_BROWSING , off unless set): Off : the guest gets the sign-in page and nothing else. In the terminal they may run only login , logout , user-whoami , share-link , config and config-list ; anything else answers sign in first . On : the guest sees what is granted to the guest group, and what the other bits give. The guest never writes, whatever a mode or an access list says, its own /home/guest included. A share link is a principal of its own: a uid nobody else holds, in no group. Making a link adds an entry rx for it on the node and on everything below it that its creator may change, passing over pinned nodes. Whoever opens the link reads what it opens and nothing an earlier link opened, never writes, and loses the access when the link expires. Turning a link off takes its entry off every node, wherever the node has moved since. Someone already signed in who opens a link stays themselves. Every opening is recorded, with the address it came from, on the Status page's Activity tab . How to make and send one is on Sharing .

The administrator, uid 0 , passes every check, as root does on Linux: other people's homes and private albums included. A member of the sudo group passes them too while their sign-in is elevated, which they start with Administer… in the account menu (or admin in a terminal) and end with Leave admin mode (or admin --off ). A terminal acting as the administrator ends its prompt in # . Accounts and groups covers who may do this. Commands that only an administrator may run refuse everyone else before they start: user-create: permission denied: only an administrator may run it Only an administrator creates or hard-links an account, group or session node, and nobody, the administrator included, changes an account's uid or a group's gid once it exists, since ownership and access lists name the number. When an account or group is deleted, its number is taken off every node first: what it owned goes to the account named with --to (the administrator by default), and every access-list entry naming it is dropped, so whoever is given that number later inherits nothing.

p.h: Over SSH, SFTP and the web
p.x: The same rules apply wherever you come in: the Web UI, EiN's terminal, SSH and SFTP all sign in as the same account and see only what it may. Downloading a file over the web takes read on it. See SSH and SFTP . A folder mounted from another machine with mount … sftp is different: every node in it is owned by the mount's owner and group (the administrator who mounted it, by default), and its bits are the ones the SFTP server reports.

A command says Access denied for operation 'w' on node: … . The letter is what was missing: r , w or x . The node named is the one that refused, which may be the folder above what you asked for: creating, removing or moving a node takes w and x on its folder, and moving it also takes w on the node itself. Check with acl on the node and on its folder. Someone added to a group still cannot see what is shared with it. Groups are read at sign-in. Ask them to sign out and in again. A folder's mode changed but a file inside did not. The file is pinned, or you may not write it. The counts after share-set ( kept own access , failed ) and the lines on standard error say which. share-info on the folder lists the pinned nodes; share-set <path> --unpin lets changes reach a node again. A file is open to someone but they cannot find it in search, or on the Archive's map. A folder on every path to it is closed to them. Give them pass-through on that folder, or link the file into a folder they can reach. chown says Access denied for operation 'change gid' . You are not in the group you named. An administrator can make the change, or add you to the group. share-info says sign in to see who has access . You have not signed in, or you came in through a share link. Who has access names people and groups, so it is shown only to someone signed in. A visitor sees the sign-in page instead of what was shared with visitors. Visitors may browse is off. Turn it on under Settings → Permissions , or send them a share link , which works either way.

Sharing : the Share dialog, the visibility chip and share links. Accounts and groups : making accounts and groups, membership, sudo . Configuration : where the default sharing and other settings are kept. The tree and Links : where nodes live, and hard and soft links. Core commands : every option of chmod , chown , acl , share-set , share-info and reach-check .

Devices are the devices group's to look at, switch and look after, and anyone else's once a member shares one with them, and a device's own to write to when it has a key. This page is for administrators: who may do what with the devices under /dev , how to share a device or keep a switch to some people, what a device key opens, and what reaches EiN without signing in. Devices describes the pages, and Devices, endpoints and drivers how devices are kept.

Who What they may do Members of the devices group See every device, its readings and its history; switch and set every control; share a device; make ( device-create ), rename ( device-label ), change what their driver was given ( device-config ) and forget ( device-forget ) devices Someone a device is shared with See that device and its readings, and switch it when it is shared to edit The administrator Everything: own every device, add people to devices , and bind queues and logs to the devices' routing keys Everyone else signed in Nothing of the devices: no device, reading or switch, nor what they publish A visitor who is not signed in Nothing either, whether or not visitors may browse EiN makes the group devices ( Devices , "May see, switch, share, make, name and forget every device under /dev") at every start when it is missing. Add someone to it in Settings → Groups , or in the terminal; the change applies from their next sign-in: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator group-add-member devices helen /dev stays the administrator's, with the mode 0755 , and EiN sets this again at every start: nobody else adds to it or removes from it, so EiN's own null and event routers, and the devices, stay where they are. The members of devices make, name and forget devices through the three commands, which do it for them as the administrator. device-forget also tells the device's driver to let it go, so a broker's last announcement does not make it again. Every device belongs to the administrator and the group devices , whether a driver found it or a member made it with device-create , and its endpoints take its owner and group. The machine EiN runs on is the one exception: its device belongs to the administrators' group, so only they see it ( Core's host driver ). Node Mode So The device, /dev/<device> 0770 The members read it, change it and share it A reading, a log 0660 The members read it and add to it A track 0770 The members read it and change it, and what the Archive keeps under it (its homes, its trips) A control 0660 The members read its states and switch it Nobody outside devices reads any of it until it is shared with them. That is what keeps a door or motion sensor, which says when someone came home or moved in a room, and a phone's track, which says where its owner has been, to the people who should know. Only the administrator binds a queue or a log to routing keys, so nobody else hears what a device publishes either ( Changes and pipelines ). An automation of the Automation module hears and switches as the person whose automation it is, with that person's rights.

A member shares a device on its page with Share , as anything else is shared ( Sharing ): a person or a group to view sees the device, its readings and its history; to edit they also switch its controls, write to it and share it on. Sharing a device shares every endpoint in it, and an endpoint its driver adds later is shared the same way. In the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices share-set -m u:ruby:rwx /dev/ruby-phone # Ruby's own phone: hers to see and change share-set -m g:parents:rx /dev/front-door # the parents see when the door opens share-set -x g:parents /dev/front-door # and no longer

p.h: Keep a switch to some people
p.x: Each control is a node of its own, and whoever may write it may switch it. To keep the heater to a group, such as parents , take the switch from the members and share it with the group: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator chmod 640 /dev/heater-plug/switch-0 share-set -m g:parents:rwx /dev/heater-plug/switch-0 Anyone else is then refused with Access denied for operation 'w' on node: … , on the page, in the terminal and in their automations, while the members still see its state. A driver leaves the owner, group, mode and access list of an endpoint it already has as they are, so the change holds. One endpoint can be kept from someone a device is shared with the same way, with share-set -x on the endpoint: it is left out of the device for them. Permissions in depth explains owners, groups and modes.

A device cannot sign in. A phone, a tracker or a script that posts to EiN carries the device's key instead, made with the device's Info tab or device-key : # in EiN's terminal device-key ruby-phone --new --origin https://ein.wrenfield.example https://ein.wrenfield.example/file/dev/ruby-phone?key=Zt2v… What it opens. Writes to /file/dev/<device> and /file/dev/<device>/<endpoint> of that one device, and nothing else: no other device, no reading, no other address. A GET with the key on the device is the device talking, for a tracker that sends only GET s, such as OsmAnd. A write with the key is made as the device's owner, the administrator, limited to the device's folder, and the device's driver is told it came from the device ( device:ruby-phone ). How it is sent. As Authorization: Bearer <key> , or as key= in the address for a client that takes only an address, such as Traccar Client. Who sees it. Whoever may change the device: the members of devices , someone it is shared with to edit, and the administrator. It is kept in the device's .key , mode 0600 and the administrator's, so the address can be shown again. Renewing it. --new , or New key on the Info tab, makes another; the old address stops working at once. --off , or Take the key away , removes it, and nothing writes to the device without signing in. A request with a wrong key, a key for another device, or a device whose owner's account is disabled is answered 403 Forbidden , the same for each, and logged in the system log as device write refused with the reason and the client's address: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator dmesg | grep 'device write refused' A write without a key is a signed-in person's, as every /file write is, and needs their session.

p.h: What reaches EiN without signing in
p.x: A device with its key , writing to /file/dev/<device> as above. Any other write there needs a signed-in session. Nothing else of the devices. A visitor reads no device, reading or track and switches nothing, even with Visitors may browse on ( Visitors and share links ): the devices are the devices group's. The MQTT broker , with the Automation module's, is not EiN: the devices sign in to it with their own password, and whoever reaches it with that password switches them. Keep its port in your home network ( Before you open EiN to the internet ). A phone away from home reaches EiN only when EiN is reachable from the internet over HTTPS; see Phones and trackers posting .

What you see What it means What to do only the devices group's members make, name and forget devices The person is not in devices , or was added since they signed in Add them, and have them sign in again device-key: only whoever may change <device> sees or changes its key The person may not change the device A member of devices makes the key, or shares the device to edit devices lists nothing, or Access denied on a device The person is not in devices and the device is not shared with them Share the device with them, or add them to devices A phone's posts are refused with 403 Forbidden Its key was renewed or taken away, or its owner's account was disabled Give the phone the address device-key shows now, or a new one device write refused in the system log, from an address you do not know Something tries keys, or holds an old address Renew the key with device-key <device> --new if it may have got out Access denied for operation 'w' on node: /dev/… when switching The control is narrowed to others Widen it, or leave it

Devices : the pages, switching, and a phone as a tracker. Devices, endpoints and drivers : endpoints, drivers and the routing keys. Accounts and groups : adding someone to a group. Permissions in depth : owners, modes and access lists. Ports, HTTPS and remote access : reaching EiN from a phone away from home.

This page is for the administrator who keeps EiN running: how to tell at a glance whether it is well and keeping up, what each part of the System status shows, how to ask the same questions in the terminal or from another computer, and what to do when the answer is not Healthy .

Choose Status under System in the sidebar. The sidebar shows it only to administrators; the page is at /system , and someone who is not an administrator and opens that address reads the same figures without the controls to start and stop services. The badge above the title answers the first question: is anything wrong The page, System status , has up to three badges above its title, with how long EiN has been running beside them ( up 3d 4h ), and five tabs below it, six with the ems module installed: Badge What it says Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person How things stand. Hover it for the sentence behind it, such as 1,240 jobs waiting, the slowest kind done in 25m00s . offline The browser has lost its connection to EiN and is reconnecting; the figures are from the last update. warming up The sampler that records CPU, memory and disk has not written anything yet. The charts fill in within a minute of a start. Tab What it holds Overview The checks that are not fine, the machines' CPU and memory, the work done, storage and the database Work Every pipeline and every kind of job: what is waiting, how fast it goes, when it will be done Media service With the ems module: the media service's own state; see The media service Services Which services run, with start, stop and restart for the administrator Log The last problems logged, and the system log as it is written Activity Who signed in, opened a share link or downloaded what, and who changed what The tab you choose goes into the address ( /system?tab=work ), so a link opens the same view. The pipeline figures update whenever the pipelines change; every other card asks EiN for its own figures every 10 seconds, and only while its tab is open. The badges and the alarm above the tabs are kept current on every tab. Nothing is fetched while the browser tab is hidden, and the numbers refresh as soon as you come back.

The badge is the first line of the health command. It is decided in this order: a failed check first, then whether anything is waiting, then whether the waiting work moves. Verdict When What to do Healthy No check failed and nothing is waiting. Nothing. Catching up Work is waiting, and some kind of it was done, or some pipeline instance finished, in the last hour. Wait. After an import this can last hours; it turns to Healthy when the work is done. Stuck Work is waiting, and none of it was done and no instance finished in the last hour. Look at the checks on Overview and at Where the work is on Work ; see below. Needs a person At least one check failed. Read the failed check on Overview : each one says what is wrong and, often, the command that fixes it. Warnings never change the verdict on their own. An install that has the ems module but no media service, or the Assistant but no language model, reads Healthy with a warning about each, and the same warnings show for a while after every start while the services load their models. An EiN with no modules has neither check. A busy service only makes work wait; a person is asked for only when work fails through every retry and heal, or a check fails.

On Overview , a card above the tiles lists every check that is not fine, failed ones first, each with its reason; a red edge marks a failed check, a yellow one a warning. When every check is fine the card is not there. health in the terminal lists them all, the fine ones too. These are the checks core makes about EiN's own work, with or without modules: Check State Reason, as it reads What to do intake ok 12 matched triggers waiting to start pipeline work Nothing: new work about to start. kind <name> ok 340 left, 120/h eta 2.8h , 340 waiting, the oldest for 4m10s , or 340 waiting behind other work, the oldest for 2h05m Nothing: a line of work that is being done, has just arrived, or waits while its worker does other lines. The Work tab shows which. kind <name> ok 340 waiting: EMS could not run it just now, and it is tried again on its own in 1m30s Nothing: with the Archive, the media service was busy, restarting or loading a model. The check goes back to the line above as soon as one of the jobs is done. kind <name> warn 340 waiting: EMS has not been able to run it for 42m00s. See EMS on the Services tab; the Work tab shows what it answered With the Archive: the media service has turned this work away for half an hour. Look at it on Services ; what it answered is under Where the work is on Work . See The media service . kind <name> warn 340 waiting, the oldest for 2h05m, and the workers that take it are idle: EiN is not handing it out. The Log tab may say why Work waits while the workers that take it do nothing. Read the Log tab for why; restarting EiN starts its workers anew. kind <name> fail 340 waiting, and no worker offers this kind, the oldest for 12m30s See Work that nothing will run . failed work warn 3 failed instances, run again on their own after 1 h, 6 h and 24 h Nothing yet: failed work is run again on its own. failed work fail 2 instances failed again after three more runs and need a person (pipeline-instances --status failed) List them with pipeline-instances -s failed and see Processing and pipelines . input ok 5 steps met input nothing can process, and will not be run again Nothing: a damaged or unreadable file. Running it again would give the same result. quiet steps warn 1 running step silent for 30m00s or more: media-transcode/transcode A step has written nothing and moved no progress for a long while. It keeps running; nothing stops a step for taking long. queue <name> fail 4 entries dropped after their delivery attempts (queue-dead /var/queues/archive-bridge: --retry or --drop) Look at them with queue-dead <path> , then put them back with --retry or delete them with --drop . How long a step may stay silent before it counts as quiet is the setting CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS , 30 minutes by default. Modules add checks of their own, through the services they run. Each is there only with its module installed, and asked only while its service runs: Check From What it says ems and ems … the ems module's ems-link service ( ems-status --checks ) Whether the media service answers, its model worker, each degradation and the card; the table is in The media service . Only ems gpu can fail. llm and llm model the Assistant's llm-link service ( llm-status --checks ) Whether the language model answers, whose it is and where it runs, and whether its model has been tried with the assistant. See The language model . automation bridge the Automation module's automation-bridge service ( automation-status --checks ) Whether the bridge hears the MQTT broker: fine with the devices its drivers drive and their endpoints, a warning while it cannot reach the broker, failed while its service is stopped; none while no broker is set. See Check that EiN hears them . the service's name any service whose check does not answer its check did not answer , as a warning. When a check names a hosted language model, its reason says so plainly, for example …: questions, and what the assistant reads to answer them, leave this host .

Under the checks, Overview shows the machine and the work in four parts. The machines : a card for each machine you may see, made from its device under Devices . The machine EiN runs on comes first ( Core's host driver ). With the ems module installed, Media service is the machine the media service runs on, a card of its own even when it is the same machine ( The media service's machine as a device ). A NAS or a server that EiN reads over SNMP has one too ( Automation ). A card's name opens the device's page, and its badge says whether it answers. Its tiles, each with a small chart of the last six hours: CPU : the share of all the machine's processor cores in use, with its load. On EiN's own machine it also gives EiN's own share. A machine that does not tell its CPU share has its load instead. memory used : the share of the machine's memory in use, with how much of how much. On EiN's own machine it also gives how much EiN holds. GPU and VRAM used , on a machine with a graphics card: how busy the card is, with its temperature and power draw, and the share of its memory in use. They are missing when the media service sees no card: no tile means no card, not an idle one ( The graphics card ). The hottest of the machine's temperatures, named as the machine names that sensor ( x86_pkg_temp is the processor). A share in use turns its tile amber at 75% and red at 90%. A device of class host or storage that has none of these readings, such as a NAS EiN only pings, has no card. Work : Done per hour , the pipeline instances finished in the last hour, with the count for the last 24 hours and a chart of them; the total number of instances; and Instances by state , a bar of In line , Running , Failed , Done and Cancelled . Storage : a card for each storage tier, with its path, a pie of its free space and of the used space split in two, the tier's own files and other , whatever else is on that disk; then the free space, % of … used , the size of the tier's files and of the other, how much it grows per day and, when it grows, full in ~N days , in red when that is under 14 days. Tiers that share one disk say shares and the device: their free space is the same space, counted once, and each counts the other's files as other . The size of a tier's files is the sum of the sizes EiN has recorded for them, counted every 15 minutes, so it is absent until the first count and includes a file that is only a link to bytes on another disk, such as an original imported from an older archive. Beside them, Database : its size and a pie of what takes it, its five largest tables and the rest as other . The free space on the database's own disk is not shown, since the database may run on another disk or machine; see Performance and sizing for how much it needs. Files and storage explains the tiers. The storage projection is measured over the last seven days. A tier that is not growing has no "full in" figure, and a tier filling up fast is the one thing on this tab that needs action before it becomes a problem: Your data covers moving the archive to a bigger disk.

Work shows what the pipelines are doing; Processing and pipelines explains pipelines, how to rerun, cancel and retry work, and what each one does. Where the work is shows where everything stands now; the table below says, per pipeline, how fast it goes and when it will be done Where the work is draws the work left to right as it moves: Not started (changes noticed, work not made yet, by pipeline), In line (made, waiting for a worker; each line of work under the workers that serve it, the one a worker is on now outlined), and Running in EiN (each worker, its slots and the line it is on, with how much of its turn is left). With the ems module installed, the media service's lanes and the models it holds follow. Under it, each line that is not moving says why. Processing and pipelines explains it. The pipeline table has a row for each pipeline doing something, with Workload , Not started , In line , Running , Failed , Done and Cancelled ; the idle ones fold into one row that show opens. In is the work arriving for it per hour, Out what it finished in the last hour, and Finishes in the work not started divided by Out ; no rate when nothing finished recently, — when nothing waits. When queue entries were dropped after their delivery attempts, a red N dropped stands above the table. Choose a row to see that pipeline's instances. Lines lists each line of work in the work pools that has something in it or was done lately: In line , Running , In , Out , Finishes in and Oldest in line . A red no worker badge marks a line nothing serves; with the Archive, a yellow waiting for EMS badge marks a line resting because the media service refused several of its jobs in a row, with the next try and what the media service answered in its tooltip. EMS could not run one marks a line whose last job the media service refused, with its answer in the tooltip, until one of the line's jobs is done. Ongoing lists the instances running now, with how far the running step has come, for a step that says, and how long each has run. Steps that have written nothing and moved no progress for the quiet time are listed above it in a yellow box.

When a line has jobs ready and no running worker serves it for more than five minutes, a red box, Work that nothing will run , stands above the tabs on every tab, and the kind <name> check fails. The box names the pool, how many jobs are ready and for how long, and the pipelines that queue that line. When it names pipelines, the worker that should serve the line is not running. Open Services and start the stopped one, or read the Log tab for why it stopped. When it says that no defined pipeline queues the line any more, the jobs belong to instances whose pipeline changed or is gone. If the pipeline now queues that step in another line, cancel the jobs with the command the box gives, and the engine queues them again in the new line: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pool cancel /var/pools/media --kind gpu-describe If the pipeline is no longer defined, cancelling does not last, since the engine queues the jobs again while their instances are open; pipeline prune removes the instances and their jobs once it has been gone for ten minutes. Work that nothing will run has both.

The ems module adds this tab, and it is there only while that module is installed. It shows the media service's version, its models, what it runs now and what is on the graphics card; The media service describes it. Which models the media service holds, and where: on the card, in RAM, or both

Services lists the services inside EiN, the ones that are not running first. Each row has the service's name, its own status line or description, how long it has been up, how many times it has restarted ( ×3 ), and its state: running , starting , stopping , stopped , failed or disabled . The heading counts them, 21 healthy , or in red 2 down when enabled services are not running. A service that has restarted many times, or is down while enabled, is the row to look at An administrator has Restart and Stop on a running service and Start on a stopped one. A disabled service has no buttons; enable it from the terminal first. Services and logs explains each service and the commands behind these buttons.

Log has two cards. Recent problems shows the last 10 lines logged at WARN or ERROR, newest first, each with what was logged beside its message (the step, the pool, what a service answered) under it, or Nothing logged at WARN or above . Live log follows the system log, /var/logs/system , as it is written: choose DEBUG , INFO , WARN or ERROR to show that level and above, pause it, or clear it. While you read further up, new lines do not scroll the view away. Recent problems answers whether anything went wrong while you were not watching With the Archive, a warning such as pooled step could not run yet, job waiting means the media service was not ready for a job; the job is tried again on its own, and the kind's other jobs run meanwhile. pooled step could not run yet, kind resting means it refused several in a row, so the whole kind waits. Services and logs covers the logs and dmesg .

Activity lists, newest first, who reached EiN and what they did: Shown as When signed in , signed out Someone signed in or out in the Web UI, a terminal or over SSH. An SSH sign-in says password or publickey . sign-in failed A wrong password, an account that may not sign in, or too many tries. The reason is under the row. An account that does not exist shows as unknown account : what was typed is not kept, since it is sometimes a password. became administrator , elevation failed A member of sudo chose Administer… , or got the password wrong. opened share link A share link was opened. A visitor shows as the link's number; someone signed in as themselves. downloaded A file someone put in /archive or a home was sent in full, saved or shown, in the browser or over SFTP. Thumbnails and other renditions are not counted, and the same person reading the same file again within ten minutes counts once. downloaded zip Several files were downloaded as one zip; the row names the folder that holds them and how many there were. created , changed , moved , deleted … A change to the archive, from the audit trail: the row names the kind of node and, for a change, what changed. Each row has the time, the account, where the event happened (a path), how it came ( web , terminal , ssh , sftp or http ) and from which address, and the session. Choose a name, path, address or session in a row to show only that; the session shows a sign-in together with everything that sign-in changed. Above the list you can show only Sign-ins , Failures , Downloads , Share links or Changes , and narrow by user, path, address, session and days. Show more reads further back. Changes are read from the last 14 days; at the end of the list, Show older changes reads the rest, which takes longer. Choosing days or a session reads those days or that session, however old. What pipelines derive from each file (thumbnails, faces, text) is left out of the changes unless you turn on Include what pipelines derived : there are about ninety such records for every photo. The same lists are in the terminal, for administrators only: # in EiN's terminal access-log --event sign-in-failed --since 2026-11-01 access-log /archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987 --event download --event download-archive audit --sid session-01JC4ZK3E2 --no-pipeline EiN keeps sign-ins and downloads for a year: the access-log-purger service removes older ones, after Days the access log keeps sign-ins and downloads ( CFG_ACCESS_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS , 0 keeps them for good). Changes are kept for good, as Trace a result back to its cause describes.

Every figure on the Status page comes from an ordinary command, and you can run the same commands in EiN's terminal or over SSH. health gives the verdict and every check: # in EiN's terminal health On an EiN with the Archive and the ems module, it reads like this: catching up: 1,240 jobs waiting, the slowest kind done in 2h48m warn kind transcribe 40 waiting: EMS has not been able to run it for 42m00s. See EMS on the Services tab; the Work tab shows what it answered ok ems EMS 3f2a91c answering, up 2.1h ok intake 12 matched triggers waiting to start pipeline work ok kind faces 1,188 left, 420/h eta 2.8h What you want to know Command The verdict and the checks health CPU, memory and event-loop lag, with history host-metrics Free space per tier, when it fills, the database's size df Which instance, its versions and uptime system-info Each pool and kind of job: left, rates, oldest waiting pool-stat Every pipeline's counts and rates pipeline-overview The meters services add, such as the card's memory gauges The services and their status lines service-list --detail The last problems in the log dmesg --level warn -n 10 What is running now, and who is connected ps , who host-metrics also shows the event loop's lag, lag p99 1.2 ms max 8.4 ms , which the Status page does not: how long ready work waits for EiN's process. High lag with low CPU is the case where everything feels slow and nothing looks busy; Performance and sizing covers it. Put JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of any of them for the answer as JSON. The verdict is then one of healthy , catching-up , stuck and needs-person : # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 health | jq -r .verdict

top draws on one screen what the Status page spreads over its tabs: a CPU graph and the load, memory, the event loop and the services' gauges, the disks, the verdict with every check that is not fine and the work done in the last hour, the running commands, the sessions, the services and the latest problems. It redraws every 2 seconds. # in EiN's terminal top top fits the whole Status page into one terminal, and works over SSH In the terminal panel, press Alt + M first to give it the whole window ( The terminal ). Key What it does q or Ctrl + C Quit ↑ ↓ , k j Scroll the list of commands PgUp PgDn , Home End Scroll a page, or to the top or bottom s Sort the commands: newest, oldest, by user or by command + and - Update less or more often, in steps from 0.5 to 60 seconds p Pause, so a list can be read; again to go on Space Update now top -d 5 starts at 5 seconds between updates. top -n 1 writes one frame and stops, which is what you want in a script or over ssh without a terminal.

EiN sends no e-mail and raises no alert outside itself: the Status page and health are where problems show. To look without opening the Web UI, send health over SSH: # on your own computer ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local health health always ends with exit status 0, whatever the verdict, so a script that watches EiN has to read the verdict. The first word of the text is enough, or the JSON: # on your own computer, for example from cron verdict=$(ssh -p 2222 helen@ein.local 'JSON_OUTPUT=1 health' | jq -r .verdict) [ " $verdict " = needs-person ] && echo "EiN needs a person" | mail -s "EiN" helen@example.com SSH and SFTP explains signing in with a key so a script needs no password.

The metrics-sampler service records EiN's own and the work's figures, one log per series under /var/logs/metrics , and the machine's as the readings of its device, /dev/<machine> ; the Status page, top and the commands above read them back. The charts therefore survive a reload of the page and a restart of EiN. Series What it holds How often Kept cpu Processor time used by EiN's container 15 seconds 7 days memory EiN's container's memory in use against its limit 15 seconds 7 days runtime Event-loop lag 15 seconds 7 days pools Jobs per pool, by state 15 seconds 7 days pipelines Instances completed per pipeline 1 minute 30 days disk Free and total space per storage tier 15 minutes 90 days nodes How many nodes of each type 15 minutes 365 days With the ems module installed, its ems-sampler service writes the media service machine's card, memory and CPU every 15 seconds as the readings of its device, /dev/ems , which the Overview draws as the Media service card ( The media service's machine as a device ), and adds an ems-models series, every minute, of what the media service holds. Memory and CPU are read both ways: the whole machine's, since the media service and the language model, when installed, load it from containers of their own, and EiN's container's own, from its cgroup. The machine's are its device's readings, cpu , load , memory-used and memory-total , with its disks and temperatures beside them, kept for 30 days and a year; Core's host driver lists them, and the device's page under Devices charts them. How the tree has grown over the years is not on the Status page: Statistics , under System , shows it, and anyone can open it ( Home and statistics ).

What you see Why What to do warming up stays, the tiles are empty, host-metrics says no metrics sampled yet — is metrics-sampler running? The metrics-sampler service is not running. Start it on the Services tab, or service start metrics-sampler , and read the Log tab for why it stopped. Storage says No tier data sampled yet , df says no disk sample yet — is metrics-sampler running? The disk is sampled every 15 minutes; right after a start there is no sample yet. Wait 15 minutes. If it stays, check metrics-sampler as above. offline next to the verdict The browser lost its connection to EiN, for example while EiN restarts. Wait; it reconnects by itself. If it stays, reload the page and see Troubleshooting . Stuck , with EMS has not been able to run it on a kind With the Archive: the media service is down, restarting over and over, or cannot load a model. See The media service . The work goes on by itself once it answers. Stuck , with the workers that take it are idle on a kind The work is not handed out. Read the Log tab, and restart EiN. Services and logs . Needs a person , kind <name> failed Nothing runs that kind of job. Work that nothing will run . Needs a person , ems gpu failed With the ems module: the media service is meant to have a graphics card and sees none. The graphics card . Needs a person , failed work or queue <name> failed Work failed for good, or queue entries were dropped. Follow the command in the check's reason, and see Processing and pipelines . full in ~N days in red A storage tier will be full within two weeks at its present rate. Free space, or move the archive to a bigger disk: Your data . A machine's CPU or memory tile is red for long The machine's processors or memory are 90% or more in use. Performance and sizing . Status is not in the sidebar You are not an administrator. Ask an administrator, or open /system to read the figures; health works for everyone.
