This page is for the administrator. It covers core's pipeline engine: how pipelines, steps, pools and workers run, how to watch them on the Status and in the terminal, what to do when work fails or stops moving, how to run work again on purpose, and the settings the engine has. Core brings the engine and no pipelines of its own, so an EiN without modules runs none, and the Work tab of the Status stays empty. Pipelines come with modules: of the published ones, the Archive brings them all, with the workers that run them. Processing pictures covers the Archive's pipelines, workers and settings. The examples on this page name the Archive's pipelines, such as media-faces , which exist only with the Archive installed.

A pipeline waits for one kind of change and then runs its steps, each a command, on the node that changed. Changes and pipelines explains the idea; this page is about running it. Work is done in three places: The pipeline engine (the pipeline-engine service) matches changes to pipelines, creates an instance for each pipeline and node, and runs the short steps itself. Pool workers run the long steps. A step that names a pool and a kind of job goes as a job into that pool, under /var/pools/ , in the line for its kind, and a worker takes it when it has room. A worker is a service that runs pipeline-worker , which takes from the lines it names in one pool, as many at once as its capacity allows. Core runs no workers of its own; a module that brings pipelines brings their workers. Background services of the modules turn changes into the events their pipelines wait for, and may announce work again on their own. Every pipeline runs at most once per node at a time: a file announced ten times while it waits is worked on once. Waiting work is kept in nodes, so nothing is lost when EiN restarts. pipeline-list prints every pipeline that is defined, with its trigger.

p.h: Watch the work on the Status page
p.x: Sign in as an administrator and choose Status in the sidebar, under System . Read the badge above the title System status : Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person . Health and status explains each word and the Overview tab. Choose the Work tab. Where the work is shows where everything stands now; below it, one row per pipeline says how much is left, how fast it goes, and when it will be done. At the top, Where the work is draws the work as it moves, left to right. Its first three columns count what the table below counts as Not started , In line and Running ; what failed or finished is only in the table. Column What it counts Not started Changes EiN has noticed and not made into work yet, by pipeline: a new photo that still needs its faces found In line Work that is made, with its next step waiting for a worker, or for an earlier step of its own Running in EiN Steps a worker is running this moment At the media service With the media service: the requests in its lanes On a model With the media service: the models it holds Not started names the pipelines with the most waiting. In line shows the lines : a step that takes time, such as finding faces or reading the text in a picture, stands in the line for what it does, and a worker takes from the lines it serves. Each line sits under the workers that serve it. The line a worker is on now is outlined, and a line that is not moving says why, for example that the models worker is on faces for 41 more minutes. The models worker takes one line at a time, for up to an hour, so a model stays loaded while it works. Running in EiN shows each worker with its slots, a square each, filled while in use, and the line it is on with how much of its turn is left. With the media service installed, two more columns follow: its lanes, with their slots and the requests in them, and the models it holds, the working ones first. Under the board, each line that is not moving says why. When the media service could not run its work, that line ends with what the media service answered, such as ems: media.probe: … mount failed: Permission denied (files_unavailable) . The table below has a row for every pipeline that is doing something; the idle ones fold into one row, N pipelines idle , which show opens. A total row, All pipelines , is at the foot. The bar draws the same counts as the columns. Column What it counts Not started Nodes the pipeline has matched but not yet started on: no instance yet In line Instances that are started and waiting for a worker or for an earlier step Running Instances with a step running this moment Failed Instances that failed Done Instances that finished, counting those pruned since. Taken once a minute, so it can be a minute old Cancelled Instances stopped on purpose In Jobs that arrived per hour, over the last hour Out Instances done in the last hour, the rate Finishes in divides by Finishes in When what is not started will be done at that rate; no rate when nothing finished recently Hover over the lightning sign beside a pipeline's name to see what starts it. Choose a row to open the pipeline's page. Below the table, Lines lists each line with work: In line , Running , In , Out , Finishes in and Oldest in line . This is where the slow steps are. A line may carry a badge: waiting for EMS : five jobs of this line in a row could not run yet, each for the first time, because a service they need was busy, loading a model, restarting or unreachable; for the Archive's steps that service is the media service. The jobs are not failed. The line rests for 30 seconds, then twice as long each time it rests again, up to 10 minutes; hover over the badge for the next try. A worker that turned to other work for the rest comes back to this line when the rest ends. no worker : no running worker serves this line, so its jobs will never run. Ongoing lists the instances with a step running, with the target file, how far the step has come and how long it has run. Progress is filled in for a step that says how much of its work is done, such as finding the faces in a long video, as a bar and a percentage that move about once a minute; a quick step leaves it empty. A step that has written nothing and moved no progress for 30 minutes is listed above it as quiet, with "Still running; nothing stops a step for taking long." No step is stopped for taking long; a quiet step is for you to look at, not a fault in itself. Two warnings can appear above the tabs or the table: Work that nothing will run names each line that has jobs and no worker, and the pipelines that queue it. See Work that nothing will run . N dropped , above the table, counts events that failed every delivery attempt. See Dropped events .

p.h: Watch the work in the terminal
p.x: Everything on the Work tab comes from ordinary commands, which you can run in the terminal or over SSH: # in EiN's terminal health # the verdict in one line, and each check that decides it pipeline-overview # instances by pipeline, unfinished steps, queues, completions in the last hour pool-stat # each pool and line: what is left, how fast, each worker, its slots and line pipeline-instances -s failed # the failed instances, newest first top # all of it live, with CPU, memory and services; q quits pipeline-instances lists 100 at a time and prints (more: --after …) when there are more; pass that to --after for the next page. Give it pipeline names to narrow it: pipeline-instances -s failed media-faces media-ocr .

p.h: Look at one pipeline and its instances
p.x: A pipeline's page, opened from the Work table, shows its description, its Trigger , its Steps and its Priority , and below them its Instances : Status , Target , Started and Duration . The tabs All , Running , Completed , Failed and Cancelled narrow the list, and Load more fetches the next page. Choose an instance to open it. Its page is named after the target node, with the way back above the name: System status › Work › the pipeline, as on the pipeline's own page. It shows the status and the steps: Step , Status , Depends on , Command and Duration . A step's status is one of these: Status What it means pending Waits for the steps it depends on queued Waits for a free place in the engine waiting Waits in a pool for a worker; the pool and line are shown beside it, and "retrying" if it ran before running Runs now; "last output … ago" says when it last wrote anything completed Finished failed Failed on its last attempt skipped Not run: its condition said no, or the instance was cancelled Choose a step to see its Exit code , its Attempts , its pool and its condition, for a failed step the Error it wrote, and for a completed step that wrote something the end of its Output , where a command that sums up what it did says it. In the terminal, pipeline-status prints the same: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-status media-faces/< id > An instance is named after the node it works on, so one file has the same id in every pipeline that ran on it. Give the id as <pipeline>/<id> , as pipeline-instances and the pages show it; a bare id that more than one pipeline uses is refused with the pipelines it could mean.

A failed step is tried again up to its limit of attempts, three unless the pipeline says otherwise, before the instance fails. Two kinds of failure are treated differently: A service the step needs could not do it yet. The step goes back to wait with its attempt given back, and is tried again after 30 seconds, then twice as long each time up to 10 minutes; the other jobs of its line run meanwhile. When five in a row are refused, each for the first time, the whole line rests, as waiting for EMS shows; a job refused again does not count. Nothing fails however long the service is away. The Archive's steps fail this way while the media service is busy or away, or when the graphics card has no room for the model a file needs. The file itself cannot be processed , such as bytes no decoder can open. The step fails at once, whatever attempts are left, and the file is not tried again. health counts these under input and treats them as settled. A step tells the two apart by its exit code; Changes and pipelines lists them.

p.h: Failed work is run again on its own
p.x: The pipeline-pruner service runs pipeline-heal --apply every hour ( CFG_PIPELINE_PRUNE_INTERVAL , 3600 seconds). It runs each failed instance again 1 hour after it failed, then 6 hours after the next failure, then 24 hours after that. An instance that fails all three times is marked as needing a person and left alone, and health then reads Needs a person . Instances that failed on their input, and instances of pipelines no longer defined, are never run again. pipeline-heal without --apply only says what it would do: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-heal would rerun 3, would mark 0 for a person; 12 waiting, 1 failed on their input When you know the cause has passed, for example after the media service was fixed, run them all now. --now skips the waits, and the run does not count as one of the three: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-heal --apply --now Your sidebar and top bar shows how to give administrators a button that runs pipeline-heal --apply .

List the failed instances: pipeline-instances -s failed , or the Failed tab of the pipeline's page. Open one and choose the failed step to read its Error . Fix the cause: start the service the step needs, free disk space, or replace the file. Run the instance again with Rerun on its page, or with pipeline-rerun : # in EiN's terminal pipeline-rerun media-faces/< id > To act on many at once, tick them on the pipeline's page and choose Rerun . To On the pages In the terminal Run an instance afresh from the pipeline's current steps Rerun pipeline-rerun <pipeline>/<id> … Run only the failed steps again none pipeline-restart <pipeline>/<id> Run one failed or skipped step again Retry on the step pipeline-step-restart <pipeline>/<id> <step> Stop a running step that hangs and run it again Restart on the step pipeline-step-restart <pipeline>/<id> <step> Stop a running or queued instance Cancel pipeline-cancel <pipeline>/<id> Delete instances, cancelling running ones first Remove pipeline-remove <pipeline>/<id> … Only an administrator sees these buttons, and only an administrator can run these commands. On an instance's page, Remove is under ⋮ in the header's corner.

A line with jobs and no worker never moves. Work that nothing will run on the Status and health (as a failed check kind <name> ) both say so. The usual cause is that the worker service is stopped: Open the Services tab of the Status , or run service-list , and look at the workers; with the Archive installed, they are media-worker and models . Start the one that is stopped, or read its log if it keeps stopping. Services and logs shows how. When no defined pipeline queues the line any more, the jobs belong to instances whose pipeline changed or is gone, and the warning says what to do in each case: The pipeline now queues that step in another line. Cancel the jobs, with the pool's path, such as the Archive's /var/pools/media , and the engine queues them again in the new line within a minute: # in EiN's terminal pool-cancel /var/pools/media --kind <kind> The pipeline is no longer defined. Cancelling its jobs does not last: the engine queues them again while their instances are open. pipeline-prune removes the instances and their jobs once the definition has been gone for 10 minutes, and the pipeline-pruner service does it in its next round.

An event that fails ten delivery attempts, for example because its node no longer exists, is set aside rather than tried forever. The Work table then shows N dropped , and health fails its queue … check until you deal with them. The engine's own queue is /var/queues/pipeline-engine ; a module that turns changes into events has a queue of its own, such as the Archive's /var/queues/archive-bridge : # in EiN's terminal queue-dead /var/queues/pipeline-engine # list what was set aside queue-dead --retry /var/queues/pipeline-engine # put them back in line queue-dead --drop /var/queues/pipeline-engine # delete them --id limits --retry or --drop to one entry.

When waiting for EMS stays on a line, the service its steps need is the place to look; for the Archive's steps it is the media service, and The media service shows how to check it. Once it answers again, the line tries on its own at its next try. To try at once (the steps that were refused still wait out their own pause): # in EiN's terminal pool-wake # every resting line pool-wake transcribe # one line

pipeline-start runs one pipeline on one node: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-start media-faces /archive/albums/christmas-2019/IMG_2041.jpg pipeline-start --var FORCE=-f media-transcode /archive/albums/christmas-2019/MVI_0412.mp4 It starts the run at once, in the normal lane, and skips the checks a trigger makes. --var sets a variable the pipeline declares; the second line makes the Media module's media-transcode redo a video that already has its renditions. A pipeline that reads its starting event has nothing to read when started by hand, and pipeline-start warns about it. A module may bring commands of its own for redoing its work over many files: the Media module's regenerate and renditions-scan , described in Media , and the Archive's media-scan , in Processing pictures .

An event can put the work it starts in the bulk lane, below all other work, so that what people do in the meantime is processed first. Bulk work is put behind, never stopped: it runs whenever nothing else that could run is waiting. With the Archive installed, the work on a large import runs there; Processing pictures says which. pipeline-rerun and pipeline-start always run in the normal lane; pipeline-heal keeps the lane an instance had.

These settings are in the Processing category of Settings → System , or set with config set . Saving one restarts the service that reads it, when it is read by a service, and work in progress is picked up again; CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS restarts nothing and counts from the next look. Configuration explains how. Setting Default What it decides CFG_PIPELINE_MAX_CONCURRENT 4 Steps the engine itself runs at once CFG_PIPELINE_MAX_OPEN_INSTANCES 5000 Instances open at once, those waiting in a pool included CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS 1800000 How long a running step may be silent before it is listed as quiet CFG_PIPELINE_PRUNE_INTERVAL 3600 Seconds between the pruner's rounds, which also run pipeline-heal With 5000 instances open, the engine starts new ones only for the pipelines holding less than an equal share of the 5000, up to 10000 open in all, and the rest of the new work waits in the pool /var/pools/triggers until instances finish; nothing is lost. Every minute the engine looks at each open instance again, so raise the limit only together with CFG_PIPELINE_STUCK_SWEEP_MS . The engine has more settings, for how many triggers and steps it holds; their defaults suit a machine of any size, and Settings lists them all. The Processing category also holds the settings modules bring, such as how much work the media pool's workers run at once; Media covers those. Performance and sizing says what to set on a small or a large machine.

Instances are nodes under /var/pipelines/instances/<pipeline>/ . Every hour the pipeline-pruner service deletes pool jobs that finished more than 24 hours ago, runs pipeline-heal --apply , and then keeps the 2000 most recently completed instances of each pipeline and deletes the rest. It leaves failed and running instances alone. A pipeline that is no longer defined, because its module was removed or it was renamed, loses all its instances once its definition has been gone for 10 minutes. To delete by hand, use Prune on a pipeline's page, which removes its completed and cancelled instances, or only those of the tab you are on, or pipeline-prune . Neither removes a failed instance unless you ask for failed ones, from the Failed tab or with -s failed , since pipeline-heal runs those again: # in EiN's terminal pipeline-prune # completed and cancelled instances, every pipeline pipeline-prune -s failed media-faces # the failed instances of one pipeline pipeline-prune --older-than 30d # completed more than 30 days ago, every pipeline

A module's pipelines are defined when it is set up and removed when it is removed; Modules covers both. Removing a pipeline cancels its running instances. To write a pipeline of your own, see Writing a module .

Changes and pipelines : how a change becomes finished work. Processing pictures : the Archive's pipelines, workers and settings. Health and status : the four words and the Overview tab. Performance and sizing : what to set on your machine. Services and logs : starting, stopping and reading the workers. Troubleshooting : when work does not get done. Core commands : every pipeline- and pool- command.

This page is for whoever runs EiN: the services that run inside EiN and keep it working, how to see and restart them on the Status page and in the terminal, and where EiN, its services and its containers write what they do. The containers themselves, and how to start and stop them with compose, are on Installing in detail .

Inside the core container, EiN runs a set of long-running jobs it calls services: the web server, the SSH server, the pipeline engine, small loops that tidy up on a timer, and the services modules bring, such as the Archive's workers that process your media. Each service is a shell script, start.sh , that EiN runs in a shell of its own as the administrator. A service is not a container: the database ( db ), and the media service ( ems ) and the language model ( llm ) when they are installed, are containers beside EiN. The ems module and the Assistant watch the last two through services of their own, ems-link and llm-link . Core brings ten services, the first ten below, and they are all an EiN without modules runs. Each module brings its own, listed after core's with the module they come from. With the Archive , the ems and media modules it brings along ( The media service and Media ) and the Assistant installed, there are 22: Service From What it does http-server core Serves the web UI and the WebSocket API ssh-server core Serves the EiN shell and SFTP over SSH pipeline-engine core Matches events against pipeline triggers and runs the resulting steps pipeline-pruner core Runs failed pipeline work again after a growing wait, and keeps the pipeline instances and the pools bounded relations-guard core Removes links that would dangle after a node is deleted metrics-sampler core Samples EiN's own resources, storage and workload into /var/logs/metrics , which the Status page draws, and the machine's readings into its device /dev/<machine> session-reaper core Removes expired sessions, and turns off expired share links; hourly tmp-sweeper core Removes files left in /tmp once they are older than CFG_TMP_RETENTION_HOURS ; hourly trash-purger core Removes trashed files for good once they are older than CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS ; twice a day access-log-purger core Removes access-log records once they are older than CFG_ACCESS_LOG_RETENTION_DAYS ; twice a day archive-bridge archive Turns changes in the tree into the Archive's facts that pipelines trigger on: a file dated and placed, a face found, staging, albums and locations changed media-heal archive Starts a pass of the media-heal pipeline when one is due, which closes media gaps nothing announced, such as a pipeline never run on a file or work a crash lost album-metadata archive Keeps each album's photo stacks, time span and cover current label-models archive Keeps the models behind label suggestions trained person-covers archive Gives every named person without a cover the crop of one of their own faces staging-organizer archive Runs the staging organizer when something waits for it, and matches the groups due a match ems-link ems Watches the media service and reports what it holds ems-sampler ems Drives the machine the media service runs on as a device, /dev/ems , and samples what models it holds ems-files ems Serves the media service the files of its requests in flight, its only way to them; idle while CFG_EMS_FILES_ADDRESS is empty media-bridge media Turns changes in the tree into the facts of a media file itself that pipelines trigger on: arrived, its bytes changed, read, turned, removed, its renditions made, its text and transcript, and the unread files of a folder moved in whole renditions-heal media Every hour, announces the files whose renditions are missing or were made by another rendition table, unless rendition work is waiting pictures-heal media Every hour, announces the photos and videos whose picture vectors are missing or were made by another model than the media service runs now, unless picture work is waiting fingerprints-heal media Every hour, announces the pictures, videos and recordings that were never fingerprinted to the end, unless fingerprint work is waiting text-heal media Every hour, announces the files whose text was never read, or whose reading, transcript or text vectors are not what the media service makes now, unless that work is waiting media-worker media Worker for the processor work the modules hand the media pool: the Media module's reading, renditions and fingerprints, and for the Archive, dates and places, face matching, duplicates, staging models media Worker for the model-bound work the modules hand the media pool: picture and text vectors, text in pictures, transcripts, and for the Archive, faces and voices models-second media A second worker for the same work, in the reverse order; it runs idle, doing nothing, while CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS is 0 llm-link assistant Watches the assistant's language model and reports whose it is and where it runs Every time EiN starts, it registers and enables core's services and those of every module that is set up, then starts every enabled service as the last step of its start. A module's services are added when it is installed and removed with it; see Modules .

p.h: See the services on the Status page
p.x: Open Status under System in the sidebar. The Status page is the administrator's; see Health and status for its other tabs. Choose the Services tab. One row per service, with the ones that need attention sorted to the top The card lists every service, one row each, and asks again every 10 seconds while the tab is open: The service's name, and under it its description. A service that reports on itself shows that line instead, and its description when you hover it: with their modules installed, ems-link shows what the media service holds, or not answering , and llm-link shows where the language model runs. Module : who brings it, core or a module such as archive , whose documentation explains the service. A dash is a service an administrator added by hand with service-add . How long it has been up, such as up 8h 50m . Hover it for the time it started. × and a number when EiN has restarted it since it was last started by hand. Hover it for "Restarted 2 time(s)". A badge: running , starting , stopping , stopped , failed , or disabled for a service that is switched off. The heading counts them: 21 healthy , or in red 1 down when an enabled service is not running. Rows are sorted by what needs attention: failed services first, then other enabled services that are not running, then services that have restarted, then the rest by name. Settings → Modules also shows a module's services and whether each runs, on the module's Services tab; the controls are here on the Status page.

p.h: Restart, stop and start a service
p.x: On the Services tab, as the administrator or in admin mode , each row has buttons at its right: Service is Buttons running Restart (the circling arrows) and Stop (the square) stopped or failed Start (the triangle) starting or stopping a spinner; wait for it to settle disabled a dash; its tooltip says "Disabled — enable it from the shell to run it" The row shows a spinner while the action runs and is read again as soon as it is done. If the action fails, a red line above the table names it and the reason, such as stop media-worker: … . In the terminal the same actions are commands, which only an administrator may run: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator service-restart metrics-sampler service-stop trash-purger service-start trash-purger service-start-all # every enabled service that is not running service restart metrics-sampler , with a space, is the same command. Each answers with one line, such as Restarted service 'metrics-sampler' . What happens when you stop a service: EiN sends the command the script is running a stop signal and waits for the script to end: 5 seconds by default, and up to 16 minutes for pipeline-engine , which lets the steps it runs finish. A script that has not ended by then is closed. Work the service would do waits. A worker that is stopped, such as one of the Archive's media workers, leaves its jobs in the pool, and they run when it starts again; see Processing and pipelines . A stopped service stays stopped until you start it, or until EiN itself starts again, which starts every enabled service. With their modules installed, ems-link and llm-link add the media service's and the language model's checks to health . While one is stopped, its checks are missing from the Status page's verdict rather than failing. Warning Stopping http-server takes the Web UI away, the page you stopped it from included, and stopping ssh-server closes SSH and SFTP. Start them again from the other one ( service-start http-server over SSH), or restart EiN's container: podman compose restart core in ~/ein . Restarting http-server from the Status page drops the page's connection for a moment. Saving a setting on the Settings page restarts the services that read it by itself; Configuration lists what restarts what.

p.h: When EiN restarts a service by itself
p.x: Every service that ships with EiN restarts when its script fails: when it ends with an exit code other than 0, EiN starts it again a second later, and the × count on its row goes up. A service that has been restarted three times within a minute and fails again is not started again; it stays failed until you start it. A script that ends with 0 is stopped , and is not started again. The count belongs to the run you started: Restart , or service-restart , starts it at 0 again.

p.h: Look at services in the terminal
p.x: service-list lists every service; anyone may run it. # in EiN's terminal service-list --detail On an EiN with the Archive and the ems module, it starts: NAME MODULE STATUS ENABLED RESTARTS DESCRIPTION -------------------- -------------- ----------- -------- -------- ----------- access-log-purger core running yes 0 Removes access-log records once they are older than their retention album-metadata archive running yes 0 Keeps each album's photo stacks, denormalized time span and cover current archive-bridge archive running yes 0 Turns VFS mutations into the archive's facts — a file dated and placed, a face found, staging, albums and locations changed — that pipelines trigger on ems-link ems running yes 0 Watches the media service and reports what it holds not answering … --detail asks each running service that reports on itself for its line, printed under its row; it is the line the Status page shows. Without --detail the list is quicker. The MODULE column is who brings the service, - for one added by hand. With JSON_OUTPUT=1 it is JSON, with each service's start time and its module . service-status shows one service, and where its output goes, here the ems module's ems-link : # in EiN's terminal service-status ems-link Service: ems-link Status: running Enabled: yes Description: Watches the media service and reports what it holds Started: 2026-10-25T06:12:40.512Z Restarts: 0 Output: /var/logs/services/ems-link/stdout.log Errors: /var/logs/services/ems-link/stderr.log Last exit code appears once the script has ended. top shows the running services in a panel of its own, beside the machine's figures; Health and status covers it.

EiN writes to four places. Three are logs in the tree, which you read in EiN's terminal; the fourth is the container's own log, which you read on the machine. Log What is in it How long it is kept /var/logs/system EiN's own messages: each line with a time, a level, the part of EiN that wrote it and the message Emptied each time EiN starts /var/logs/services/<name>/stdout.log What a service's script prints Emptied each time the service starts /var/logs/services/<name>/stderr.log What a service's script prints as errors Emptied each time the service starts The core container's log The same messages as /var/logs/system , with the details behind them, such as an error's stack, and what EiN prints while it starts Until the container is removed or made again, by podman compose down or by an up -d after a change A service's own output goes only to its pair of logs under /var/logs/services , never to the container's log. Two other folders hold logs of other kinds: /var/logs/metrics , the figures the Status page draws, and /var/logs/jobs/<pid> , the output of a command started with nohup or kept running with detach .

p.h: Read the system log on the Status page
p.x: Open Status under System and choose the Log tab. Recent problems answers whether anything went wrong; the live log shows what EiN is doing now Recent problems lists the last ten lines at WARN or ERROR, newest first, with the time, the part of EiN and the message, and under it what was logged beside the message as key=value , as dmesg shows it. It is read again every 10 seconds. With none, it says "Nothing logged at WARN or above". Live log shows /var/logs/system as it is written: the last 200 lines when you open it, then every new line as it arrives, up to 500 kept. It follows the newest line while you are at the bottom, and stays put when you scroll up to read. The controls at the right of Live log : Control What it does DEBUG , INFO , WARN , ERROR Shows lines at that level and above; INFO is chosen when the tab opens Pause Stops adding lines. The stream stays open and the lines that arrive meanwhile are dropped; Resume goes on Clear Empties the panel. The log itself is unchanged A yellow connecting badge means the page is reaching the stream; a blue paused badge that it is paused.

p.h: Read the logs in the terminal
p.x: dmesg prints the system log, oldest line first: # in EiN's terminal dmesg -n 50 # the last 50 lines dmesg --level warn -n 10 # the last 10 problems, as Recent problems shows them dmesg --level error # every error since EiN started 2026-10-25 21:34:13 WARN pool-worker pooled step could not run yet, kind resting 2026-10-25 21:35:02 INFO service-registry Service 'label-models' started --level filters before -n counts, so --level warn -n 10 is the last ten problems, not the problems among the last ten lines. The levels are debug , info , warn and error . Pipe it on as with any command: dmesg | grep ssh-server . For a service's output, use tail , which prints each line as the service wrote it. The examples are the ems module's ems-link and the Archive's models : # in EiN's terminal tail -n 50 /var/logs/services/ems-link/stdout.log tail -f /var/logs/services/models/stderr.log # keep following; Ctrl+C ends it tail -n 0 -f /var/logs/services/models/stderr.log # only what is written from now on ems-link: watching http://ems:8181 ems-link: down — not answering tail -f /var/logs/system follows the system log in the terminal the way the Live log does.

The container's log is on the machine EiN runs on, and compose shows it: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose logs -- tail 200 core # the last 200 lines podman compose logs -f core # follow; Ctrl+C ends it podman compose logs db # the database: ems or llm for the others, when installed With Docker, write docker compose . Each line reads [2026-10-25 21:35:02] [INFO ] [service-registry] Service 'label-models' started , followed by any details the message carries. This is the log to read when EiN does not start, since the tree's logs are not there until it has, and when a line in the system log needs its details: the system log keeps the message only. It also holds the admin password a new EiN prints once, Admin password set to: … , which is gone once the container is made again, as after podman compose down . The database, and the media service and the language model when installed, write only to their containers' logs. The media service covers reading its log.

How much EiN logs is set by two variables in ~/ein/.env , read when the container starts: Variable Default What it does LOG_LEVEL INFO The lowest level EiN logs: DEBUG , INFO , WARN or ERROR LOG_MODULES none A level for one part of EiN over LOG_LEVEL , by the name the log shows, such as ssh-server:DEBUG,pipeline-engine:WARN A line below the level is written nowhere: not to the system log, not to the container's log. The DEBUG button on the Live log shows DEBUG lines only once EiN writes them. Add the line to ~/ein/.env : # in ~/ein/.env LOG_MODULES =ssh-server:DEBUG Apply it, which restarts EiN: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d Take the line out again when you have what you need; DEBUG fills the logs quickly. Environment variables lists the other variables of the deployment.

p.h: Add a service of your own
p.x: A service is a folder in the tree with a start.sh , and optionally a config.json . EiN runs start.sh in its own shell, the same shell language as the terminal, as the administrator, with SERVICE_NAME and SERVICE_PATH set. This one writes the free space to its log every hour: Make the folder and the script: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mkdir -p /home/admin/services/disk-report edit /home/admin/services/disk-report/start.sh # /home/admin/services/disk-report/start.sh while true ; do df sleep 3600 done Give it a description, and have it started again when it fails, in /home/admin/services/disk-report/config.json : { "description" : "Writes the free space to its log every hour" , "restartPolicy" : "on-failure" } Register it, enable it and start it: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator service-add disk-report /home/admin/services/disk-report service-enable disk-report service-start disk-report It is on the Status page from then on, and EiN starts it whenever it starts. Its output is in /var/logs/services/disk-report/stdout.log . The keys config.json takes: Key Default What it does description none The line under the service's name restartPolicy never on-failure starts it again when it ends with an exit code other than 0, always whenever it ends, never not at all maxRestarts 3 Restarts allowed within restartWindow before EiN leaves it failed restartWindow 60000 That window, in milliseconds stopTimeout 5000 Milliseconds a stop waits for the script to end before closing it env none Variables set for the script, as an object of names and values workClass none background makes its database work give way to people's, as EiN's own workers do statusCommand none A command whose first line of output is shown under the service's name, in place of its description checkCommand none A command answering checks for health , as JSON gaugeCommand none A command answering gauges for top and the Status page, as JSON To take a service away, stop it, disable it and remove it: service-stop disk-report , service-disable disk-report , service-remove disk-report . Removing it removes only the registration, not the folder. A module's services are declared in the module itself; Writing a module covers them.

A service is failed, with ×3 beside it. It was restarted three times within a minute and failed again. Its stderr.log holds the output of the last attempt only, since each start empties it, so read it first: tail -n 50 /var/logs/services/<name>/stderr.log . dmesg | grep "<name>" shows EiN's lines about it, such as Service 'media-worker' exited with code 1 and Service 'media-worker' exceeded max restarts (3) within window ; the container's log has the details behind them. Start it again with Start once you have fixed the cause. service start: 'x' is not enabled . The service is switched off; the Status page shows it as disabled . Run service-enable x , then service-start x . Disabling one of core's or a module's services lasts only until EiN starts again, which enables them all. service stop: service 'x' is not running or service 'x' is already running . The service was already in that state; the Status page row may be up to 10 seconds old. service remove: 'x' is running, stop it first or 'x' is enabled, disable it first . Stop it and disable it, then remove it. service-restart: permission denied: only an administrator may run it . Sign in as admin , or use admin mode ( admin in the terminal). The Status page shows the buttons only to the administrator. A restart of pipeline-engine takes minutes. It waits for the steps it runs to finish, for up to 16 minutes, and its row shows a spinner meanwhile. ems-link says not answering . With the ems module installed, this means the media service's container is down or still starting; ems-link only reports it. The media service has what to do. The system log starts only a little while ago. It is emptied each time EiN starts. Older lines, as far back as the container's life, are in the container's log: podman compose logs core . The Live log says "Waiting for the stream" or shows connecting . The page has lost its connection to EiN, for example while http-server restarts. It reconnects by itself; reload the page if it does not. The Web UI is gone after stopping http-server . Start it over SSH with service-start http-server , or restart the container with podman compose restart core . Troubleshooting covers problems that are not a service's own.
