This page is for the administrator who runs EiN on their own machine: what each part of EiN uses of the processor, memory and disk, how big a machine to give it, how to set the containers' memory limits, and which settings decide how much processing runs at once. The graphics card has a page of its own, The graphics card . EiN without modules needs little. Most of what this page sizes and tunes comes with modules: the media service, which the Archive needs, and the language model, which the Assistant answers with, are containers of their own, and the settings that pace media processing belong to the Archive. How big a machine they need is kept here, on this page alone.

EiN runs as two containers, core and db , and up to four with the media service and the language model. Each has its own appetite, and three of them have a memory limit that compose sets from ~/ein/.env . Container What uses the machine Memory limit Processor ein The Web UI, every shell and SSH session, the pipelines that decide what to do with each file, and the modules' services EIN_MEMORY , default 6g not limited db PostgreSQL: every node, link, setting and the search index none; 1 GB of shared memory not limited ems The media service, with --ems , for the Archive: thumbnails, video encoding, fingerprints, and the models for faces, voices, transcripts, text and vectors EMS_MEMORY , default 16g not limited llm The language model, with --llm , for the Assistant: about 5.6 GB of model, on the card or in memory LLM_MEMORY , default 10g not limited Nothing limits how many cores a container uses. With the Archive, the heavy work is in the media service: most of the Archive's pipeline steps are calls into it, and EiN mostly decides what to ask for and stores the answers. A machine running EiN Core alone, without the media service, does little beyond serving the interface and the shell.

The installer checks the machine against the first two rows of these figures before it installs anything ( What the checks measure ); the language model's row is advice it does not check: What you install Processor Memory Free disk EiN Core 2 cores 4 GB 10 GB, plus your files With the media service ( --ems ), for the Archive 4 cores; 6 or more recommended 16 GB; 32 GB recommended about 100 GB, plus your files With the language model as well ( --llm ), for the Assistant as above about 5.6 GB more, unless the model is on the card about 6 GB more, for the model's file Cores are physical cores, not threads. With both installed, the default limits of the three containers that have one add up to 32 GB (6 + 16 + 10). On 16 GB the installer calls the memory enough with the language model left out or hosted, so leave it out or use a hosted one, as The language model describes. What the figures mean in practice: More cores let more of the Archive's media work run side by side, once you raise the settings in Let more work run at once . The defaults are set for a small machine and use few cores. More memory matters for the media service, which holds several models at once, and for long videos, which are decoded on the processor without a card. A graphics card changes how fast the models run, not what they find. On a card a recording's transcript takes about a minute; without one it takes about twice the length of the recording. The graphics card has the details. Disk holds your originals once, plus the thumbnails and other renditions EiN makes of each, plus the images and the database in the container engine's storage. Watch disk space shows how to see how fast it grows.

A memory limit is a ceiling, not a reservation: a container uses what it needs up to its limit, and the rest of the machine's memory stays free for the others. Change a limit in ~/ein/.env : Open ~/ein/.env in an editor and add or change the line for the container: # in ~/ein/.env EIN_MEMORY = 8 g EMS_MEMORY = 20 g LLM_MEMORY = 12 g The value is a number with a unit, g for gigabytes or m for megabytes. Leave out a line to keep its default. EMS_MEMORY and LLM_MEMORY matter only while the media service or the language model is installed. Make the containers again with the new limits: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d compose makes again the containers whose settings changed. EiN is down while it restarts. With Docker, write docker compose . Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, so it may swap as much again as its memory limit; ./setup.sh makes the containers again with the swap limit. Check the new limit. In EiN's terminal, top shows EiN's memory against its limit in its Memory panel, for example 367 MB of 6.0 GB . top shows EiN's memory against its container's limit, so you see how close it comes. How to choose the limits: Keep the limits together below the machine's memory , with a few GB to spare for the database, which has no limit, and for the system itself. A container that grows is then stopped at its own limit, and the kernel does not have to pick a process to stop somewhere else on the machine. EIN_MEMORY : EiN itself, its shells and its pipelines. Raise it from the default of 6 GB if top shows EiN close to its limit during an import. EMS_MEMORY : the media service holds the models it is using and decodes videos. A video decoded on the processor is planned within a budget of 4000 MB ( EMS_CPU_ENCODE_MAX_MB ) and split into parts when it would need more, so keep the limit well above that. Its main model process restarts itself when it passes 60% of the limit, so the rest is left for the decoding and the tools. LLM_MEMORY : the model and its working memory. The default fits the default model; The language model explains which other models the container can run.

p.h: When a container reaches its limit
p.x: When a container needs more than its limit, the kernel stops one of its processes. Each container restarts by itself if its main process stops, and the work it had in hand is picked up again: a pipeline step that was interrupted runs again, as long as it has attempts left. To see whether that happened, read the kernel's log on the machine: # on the machine EiN runs on sudo dmesg | grep -i 'out of memory' A line that names Memory cgroup out of memory is a container that reached its limit. Raise that container's limit, or lower the work that runs at once ( Let more work run at once describes the settings, which work in both directions). The media service's model processes log a warning of their own when the models alone do not fit under their ceiling, ending in "Raise CFG_MODEL_MAX_RSS if this is the real footprint." For the media service, set it as EMS_MODEL_MAX_RSS in ~/ein/.env , such as EMS_MODEL_MAX_RSS=12g , or raise EMS_MEMORY , which raises the ceiling with it.

This section and the next two apply with the Archive installed. New files go through its pipelines, and the pipelines' heavy steps go to two workers inside EiN, which decide how much runs at once. Both are services of the Media module, which the Archive brings along, and both are paced by its settings in Settings → System , category Processing . Worker Runs Paced by media-worker Unpacking zips, reading metadata, thumbnails and posters, fingerprints, duplicates, matching faces to people, staging's dating and grouping, video and audio encoding Media worker budget ( CFG_CPU_SLOTS , default 2 ) models Faces, picture vectors, text in pictures, text vectors, transcripts, voices and shots: each a request to the media service's models Model requests in flight ( CFG_MODEL_SLOTS , default 2 ) The media worker's budget is shared by cost: most jobs take 1 of it, and a video's encoding takes 2. With the default budget of 2, an encoding runs alone, while two smaller jobs can run together. Matching faces to people has a higher priority than encoding, so a queue of videos does not hold up people appearing in the interface. Media lists every setting of the two workers. The models worker takes turns between its lines of work. It stays on one line for up to Model backlog rotation (ms) ( CFG_MODEL_KIND_QUANTUM_MS , an hour) while others are waiting, so that a model stays loaded while it works, and faces, which keep coming during an import, do not hold back the transcripts. A line it left because the media service refused several of its jobs in a row ( waiting for EMS ) is taken up again as soon as that rest ends, rather than an hour later. The Work tab's Where the work is shows which line each worker is on and how much of its turn is left. The media service has its own limits on how much it runs at once, set in ~/ein/.env : Variable Default What it bounds EMS_LIMIT_MODELS 8 Model requests running at once EMS_LIMIT_TOOLS 4 Tool work at once: reading metadata, thumbnails, fingerprints EMS_LIMIT_ENCODES 2 Whole-file work at once: video encoding, storyboards, finding shots EMS_QUEUE_DEPTH 64 Requests of one system that may wait for a place; past it the media service answers that it is busy, and EiN tries again later EMS_WATCHES 4 Cameras watched for faces at once; past it a camera is not watched EMS_INTERACTIVE_RESERVE 1 Extra places for models and tools, kept for a person waiting, such as a search, so that processing never makes them wait behind it EiN's settings decide how much it asks for; the media service's decide how much it does. Asking for more than the media service runs at once only moves the wait into its queue.

p.h: Let more work run at once
p.x: With the Archive, on a machine with more cores than the minimum, raise the media worker's budget so that more thumbnails, fingerprints and encodings run side by side: Sign in as an administrator and choose Settings in the sidebar, under System . Choose the category Processing . Set Media worker budget to the number of jobs you want at once, for example 4 on a machine with 6 cores, and choose Save change . The line under it says "Restarted media-worker." If you set the budget above 4, raise Media worker jobs in flight ( CFG_CPU_WORKERS ) to the same number. It caps how many jobs can be in flight whatever the budget. Watch the result on the Status , on its Work tab, as described in Watch it keep up . Most of these jobs are work for the media service, so with a budget above 4, raise EMS_LIMIT_TOOLS in ~/ein/.env to match and run podman compose up -d . Warning Keep Media worker budget at 2 or more. A video's encoding takes 2 of the budget, and with 1 no video is ever encoded. With a graphics card that has room to spare, or many cores for the models, raise Model requests in flight the same way; it restarts the models service. Keep it at or below EMS_LIMIT_MODELS . More requests at once do not always finish sooner: the media service runs the requests for one model one after another, so the gain comes from different kinds of work overlapping. From the terminal, the same changes are: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator config set CFG_CPU_SLOTS 4 config set CFG_MODEL_SLOTS 4 config unset CFG_CPU_SLOTS # back to the default The other settings in Processing are core's and tune the pipeline engine itself: how many steps, queue entries and triggers it handles at once, and how often it cleans up. Their defaults suit any machine EiN runs on, and Processing and pipelines explains what they do. Every one is listed on Settings .

p.h: Keep the interface quick during heavy work
p.x: While the media service works through the Archive's import, people still search and browse. Several things keep their requests ahead of the processing without any setting: The media service answers searches from a model process of its own, on the processor, while the processing runs in another at a lower priority ( EMS_WORKER_NICE , default 10 ). When the card has been free of processing for 10 minutes ( EMS_CARD_QUIET_AFTER , 600 seconds), searches move to the card. The process that runs them there waits ready while the card is busy, so the move takes about as long as loading the two search models, under a minute on a slow disk; it holds about 1 GB of memory meanwhile. A search uses at most a few cores ( EMS_QUERY_WORKER_THREADS , the machine's cores less two, at most 4), so it does not wait on threads the processing holds. EMS_INTERACTIVE_RESERVE keeps a place free for a person waiting. If the interface still feels slow on a small machine during an import, lower Media worker budget back towards 2 and Model requests in flight towards 1 until the import is done. The work waits in its queue and costs nothing there.

Your originals take the space they take. On top of them, with the Archive, EiN keeps, in the data folder's files-volatile , the thumbnails, posters, storyboards and the AV1 versions of videos it makes for the browser, which it can make again if they are lost. In EiN's terminal, df shows each storage tier's free space, how much of the disk its own files take, how fast it grows a day, and when it will be full at that rate, with the size of the database and its largest tables: # in EiN's terminal df The same figures are on the Status , and top 's Disk panel shows them live. Files and storage explains the tiers. The container engine keeps the images, the build's scratch files and the database in its own storage, usually ~/.local/share/containers for rootless podman and /var/lib/docker for Docker, which may be another disk than your data folder. Each update builds new images, and setup.sh removes the ones they replaced once the new EiN answers; a build's intermediate stages and other images without a name stay. To see what the images take, and to remove the unnamed ones no container uses: # on the machine EiN runs on podman system df podman image prune With Docker, write docker for podman . podman image prune removes only images without a name that no container uses; the database is a folder of yours and is never touched by it. Never add --volumes to a prune: on an installation whose EIN_DB_DIR is empty, the volume ein_db is your database.

With the Archive, the database grows by about 120 KB for each photo or video it indexes: the file's node, its renditions, its metadata, faces and the vectors search uses. The audit trail adds about 45 KB more for the records of the pipelines that worked on the file. It keeps them for good, and after 14 days it compresses them to about 6 KB ( Trace a result back to its cause ). So plan on 170 KB a file while an import runs; two weeks after it, the database is near 130 KB a file. An exact copy of a file that is already there costs about 5 KB. PostgreSQL also needs room of its own to clean up and rebuild indexes, so keep at least 10 GB free on the disk the database is on. Before a large import, multiply its number of photos and videos by 170 KB: 100,000 files need about 17 GB, plus those 10 GB. When the data folder's disk is too small for it, put the database on another disk with the installer's --db-dir , as Move the data folder to another disk describes; df in EiN's terminal shows the database's size.

Whether the machine is big enough shows in whether it keeps up with the work: Where What it tells you The Status 's badge Healthy : nothing is waiting. Catching up : work is waiting and some of it, or a pipeline instance, finished in the last hour. Stuck : work is waiting and none finished in the last hour. Needs a person : a check failed The Status 's Work tab Where the work is, each line of work, what is left of it, how fast it goes, and when it will be done top The processor, EiN's memory and the event loop's lag, the disks, and the work, live host-metrics EiN's processor and memory use now and over the last 6 hours ( --window in minutes) pool-stat The backlog, rates and policy of each line of work in the queues, and each worker's slots and line gauges What the running services report beside the machine's figures, such as the card's memory ems-status With the ems module: the media service's models, what it is running, its queues and the memory of its model processes Catching up after an import is normal; the time it takes depends on the machine and on how much there is. A machine that is too small shows as a Work tab whose time to completion keeps growing while new files come in, or as containers stopped at their memory limits. Health and status explains the badge, the checks and the tabs.

The Status page reads Stuck. Nothing has finished in the last hour. Read the checks under the badge on the Overview tab: they name the kind of work that is not moving and why, with the Archive often the media service not answering. Troubleshooting goes through the causes. Videos in the Archive never get their browser version. Check that Media worker budget is 2 or more, and on the Work tab whether transcode is waiting. Without a graphics card, a long video takes many minutes to encode. A container restarts on its own. Look for Memory cgroup out of memory in the kernel log as in When a container reaches its limit , and raise that container's limit. The whole machine slows down or stops responding during an import. The containers together are using more memory than the machine has. Lower the limits so that they fit the machine, or leave out the language model, and lower the processing settings while the import runs. Searches are slow while an Archive import runs. Lower Model requests in flight and Media worker budget for the duration of the import, as in Keep the interface quick during heavy work . The disk fills up. Run df in EiN's terminal to see which tier grows, and podman system df on the machine to see what the container engine's storage takes. EiN has no command that moves the data folder; Your data: backup, moving and removing explains how.

The graphics card : what the card speeds up and how the media service and the language model share it. Installing in detail : the containers, .env and the installer's checks. Configuration : where settings live and what a change restarts. Processing and pipelines : what the pipelines do with each file, and the engine's settings. The media service and The language model : the two optional services. Health and status : the badge, the checks and the Work tab. Settings : every Processing setting with its default.

This page is for the person who runs EiN on their own machine. It covers how to bring EiN and its services up to date, what an update touches and what it keeps, how to see which version runs, and what to do when an update goes differently.

EiN has no releases and no version numbers to choose between. An update downloads the images GitHub builds each night from the newest commit of each repository, and starts them in place of what ran before; a change made today reaches an update tomorrow. The engine downloads only the layers of an image that changed, so an update of the media service is usually far smaller than its 30 GB. What it updates depends on what is installed: Repository What it is Updated when As deploy ~/ein itself: setup.sh and the compose files always, first git pull of ~/ein core EiN: the tree, the shell, the Web UI always the image ghcr.io/einhq/core:main db PostgreSQL with TimescaleDB, pgvector and PostGIS always the image ghcr.io/einhq/db:main ems the media service, which the Archive needs with the media service the image ghcr.io/einhq/ems:main llm the language model's chat template, for the Assistant with the language model its source, fetched into ~/ein/src GitHub builds the database's image again every week too, so an update also brings PostgreSQL's and its extensions' minor releases. Installed from another organisation with --source , an update fetches the sources of core, db and ems into ~/ein/src instead and builds the images on your machine, the media service's in about an hour ( Where the sources come from ). The language model's server is not built: it is llama.cpp's ready-made image, named by a fixed digest in compose.llm.yaml . It changes only when that file does, which is when the deploy repository is updated. Modules are not part of this. They live in the data folder and are updated separately, on Settings → Modules ; see Update a module . Only a module the new EiN cannot run is replaced, at its start ( below ).

Back up. An update cannot be undone: there is no command to go back to the previous version, and the database is changed in place when the new EiN starts. Your data says what to copy and why the database and the data folder go together. Make sure the admin password is one you know. A first one setup.sh made is INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in ~/ein/.env until you delete that line; one you chose at the install is not kept there. An older .env has no such line, and the random password a new EiN printed to its log goes when an update makes the containers again. Check that the container engine has room. An update downloads the new images while the old ones are still there, and removes the old ones only once EiN is up again; the media service's image is about 30 GB. podman system df shows the space images take.

Run the installer again, as your own user, on the machine EiN runs on: # on the machine EiN runs on, as your own user curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash It asks nothing, and you need no options: those you chose before are kept in ~/ein/.env . If EiN lives somewhere other than ~/ein , name that folder with --home , as in curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --home /srv/ein . What you will see: The installer checks the machine against the system requirements again, with the media service and the language model counted when .env has them. When a check fails it stops here and changes nothing; Installing in detail explains each check. Updating /home/anna/ein from https://github.com/einhq/deploy : it runs git pull --ff-only on the folder, which brings the newest setup.sh and compose files. It runs ~/ein/setup.sh , which prints its steps: == Getting the images == Starting EiN Waiting for EiN to answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/; its first start takes a minute or more EiN is up at http://ein:8080/ Removed the images this update replaced, which freed 31GB EiN starts again when the machine does. The modules installed: archive 0.4.0 (v0.4.0) ems 0.1.2 (v0.1.2) archive 0.3.1 is installed and needs core API ^0.7.0, and this core provides 0.8.0 The list at the end is each module installed, with its version and the release it was installed at, followed by what EiN's start logged about a module it could not install or run, here the Archive it moved to a release it runs. With the language model, or from another source, == Fetching the sources comes first, with a line for each repository fetched: its name, the commit it is now at and that commit's date. Between the steps the container engine prints its own download, build and start output, and while it waits, setup.sh shows EiN's newest log line every 10 seconds. The download happens while the old EiN keeps running. A build from another source that fails is tried once more, since a download it needs, such as the documentation from GitHub, fails now and then; when it fails again, setup.sh stops there and EiN goes on running as it was. EiN is down from the moment its container is made again until the new one answers, which is usually a minute or two, and longer when modules have to be set up or their pages built again. setup.sh waits up to 10 minutes for EiN to answer on its port.

~/ein/setup.sh without the installer downloads and restarts in the same way, and skips the machine checks. It brings ~/ein itself up to date first, with git pull --ff-only , and when that brought a new commit, it says Updated /home/anna/ein to …; running its setup.sh and goes on with the new one: # on the machine EiN runs on, as your own user ~/ein/setup.sh ./setup.sh --only core updates one service, core , ems , db or llm , and restarts only that one, leaving the others running. Every run of setup.sh is an update, also one that only adds or removes an option, such as ./setup.sh --ems . To apply a changed line of .env without updating, run podman compose up -d in ~/ein instead; Configuration explains it. One setup.sh runs in ~/ein at a time. A run goes on when the SSH connection that started it drops, so one started again meanwhile says Another setup.sh is running in /home/anna/ein; waiting for it to end and begins once the first has ended. Note setup.sh keeps to the container engine EiN was installed under, which .env names in EIN_ENGINE . Run with --engine naming the other one, it stops instead of building a second, empty EiN. See Keep to one engine .

p.h: What an update changes and what it keeps
p.x: Changes Stays as it is The files from the deploy repository in ~/ein .env : your options, settings and passwords The sources in ~/ein/src , each moved to its newest commit The database, in the folder EIN_DB_DIR names The images, downloaded or built again, and the ones they replaced removed; the layers that did not change stay The data folder: your originals, renditions and the model file Every container, made again from the new images The installed modules, in the data folder's modules folder, but one the new EiN cannot run compose.override.yaml , written again from .env Settings changed in the Web UI or the terminal, which are in the database The container logs, which go with the old containers The SSH host key, kept in the tree setup.sh makes every container again from the new image even where compose sees no change, with --force-recreate (under podman-compose, it takes them all down and starts them one by one), and with --remove-orphans , so a service whose option you turned off stops.

p.h: What happens when the new EiN starts
p.x: EiN does the rest of an update itself, at its start: It brings its database tables up to date. There is no separate migration step to run. It installs a module that EIN_MODULES names and that is missing. It does not update modules that are installed already and that it can run. It replaces a module installed at a release written for a module API it does not provide, as after an update that changed that API, with the newest release of the module's repository that it can run, and the modules that one needs the same way. That release can be older than the newest published, when the module has moved on to a newer EiN. It sets up every module again, in dependency order, and builds a module's pages again when what they are built from has changed. A module with no release the new EiN can run stays as it was and does not set up, and its pages and commands are missing until a release that fits is published and installed. setup.sh ends with the lines EiN logged about it; When a module does not work lists the messages.

In the Web UI, open the profile menu at the top right and choose About EiN . The Core tile shows core's version, and below it the commit EiN was built from and that commit's date; hold the pointer over it for the full time. The Module API tile shows the version modules build on, and Services shows what installed modules add, such as the media service's version and commit with the ems module and the media service installed. In the terminal, system-info prints the same, with each module's commit, here on an EiN with every module installed: # in EiN's terminal system-info host 4e1d7c9b2a60 uptime 4m core 0.1.0 (3f2a9c1, 2026-10-24) api 0.7.0 modules archive 5d81b2e04, assistant 1c9e7a352, ems 77f0ad913 postgres 18.1 deno 2.9.6 Core's version stays 0.1.0 from one update to the next; the commit is what tells two builds apart. A short uptime confirms that EiN restarted. host is the name of EiN's container, which compose makes up, not the machine's name. The reference has the command.

p.h: Check that all is well after an update
p.x: In ~/ein , podman compose ps shows every container up, and db , and ems when it is installed, healthy. In EiN's terminal, health says whether the system is healthy or catching up; Health and status explains its checks. Open Settings → Modules and look for a module with a badge instead of its version, then choose Install beside the filter and look under Updates . Update the modules there; see Modules .

p.h: Free the space old images take
p.x: setup.sh removes the images an update replaced, EiN's, the database's and the media service's, once the new EiN answers, and says so: Removed the images this update replaced, which freed 31GB . It keeps one that a container still uses, and an update whose EiN did not come up keeps them all. --only does the same for the one service it updates. A build from another source can leave other images without a name behind, such as its intermediate stages. Remove those with: # on the machine EiN runs on podman image prune With Docker, docker image prune . It removes only images no container uses and that have no name, so your running EiN, the database and the data folder are not touched.

The commands are written for podman; with Docker, write docker compose for podman compose . What you see What to do The installer reports a check as missing and stops Nothing was changed. Fix what it names, or update with setup.sh alone, which does not check. git pull stops with a message about local changes, or setup.sh says ~/ein could not be brought up to date A file from the deploy repository in ~/ein was changed. git -C ~/ein status shows which; put back the original with git -C ~/ein checkout -- <file> and move your change into .env . fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting. , or a message about local changes, after a source line A repository under ~/ein/src was changed or moved to another commit by hand. git -C ~/ein/src/<name> status shows what; git -C ~/ein/src/<name> checkout -- . and git -C ~/ein/src/<name> switch main put it back. The download or the build stops with no space left on the device The container engine's storage is full. Free the space old images take (above), or see podman system df . setup.sh: the images did not build, so EiN runs on as it was; the build's output is above Nothing was changed. When the build's output shows a download that failed, run setup.sh again later; otherwise the output names what stopped the build. setup.sh: EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ in 10 minutes: podman compose logs core Read the log it names. podman compose ps shows whether db became healthy; EiN does not start before it. Troubleshooting covers what the log may say. EiN does not take your admin password and has none of your content It runs on an empty database, such as one under the other container engine. See Keep to one engine . A module is still the old version setup.sh does not update modules, and EiN's start replaces only one it cannot run. Use Update on Settings → Modules . A module's pages or commands are gone, and Settings → Modules shows a badge on it It does not fit the new EiN, and EiN found no release of it that does. The lines at the end of setup.sh 's output say why; When a module does not work explains each message. With the ems module, the media service's tile in About EiN says Not answering The media service is still starting or failed to. podman compose logs ems ; The media service helps further. If an update leaves EiN in a state you cannot fix, the way back is the backup you made before it: restore it as Your data describes.

Installing in detail : the installer, setup.sh , the files in ~/ein and running compose day to day. Modules : updating, pinning and removing modules. Your data : what to back up before an update, and how to restore it. Services and logs and Troubleshooting : when something is wrong after an update.

t: Your data: backup, moving and removing

p.x: This page is for whoever runs EiN on its machine: what makes up an installation's data and where each part is, how to back it up and restore it, how to move EiN to another disk or machine, how to get your files out in a form you can read without EiN, and how to delete things, free space and remove EiN altogether. EiN has no backup or export command of its own. Everything below uses the container engine, PostgreSQL's own tools and ordinary copying, run on the machine EiN runs on. The commands are written for podman, run in ~/ein . With Docker, write docker for podman and docker compose for podman compose , and see Under Docker for the one difference that matters.

An installation keeps its data in two places: the data folder, which holds the database too, and ~/ein/.env . Part Where What it holds Back it up? db , the database the data folder, or the folder EIN_DB_DIR names every node of the tree: names, folders, links, permissions, accounts and settings, the albums, people and faces of the Archive, and small content such as comments and keys Yes, as a dump files the data folder, ~/ein/data unless EIN_DATA names another your originals Yes old the data folder files kept from an older installation; empty unless you put files there When it holds anything modules the data folder the installed modules Yes; it is small, and a module installed from Settings → Modules is installed again only by hand files-volatile the data folder with the Archive, the thumbnails, video renditions, face crops and the other renditions it makes from the originals Optional: EiN can make them again, but over a large archive that takes days and needs the media service mqtt the data folder with --automation , the MQTT broker's accounts, hashed, and what the devices announced No; setup.sh writes the accounts again from .env , and the devices announce themselves again when they connect llm the data folder with --llm , the language model, downloaded at its first start No; it is downloaded again ~/ein/.env ~/ein your options, the lines you added, and the passwords made at the install Yes src/ , compose.override.yaml ~/ein the sources and the options as services No; setup.sh makes them again Installing in detail shows how the folders are mounted into the containers.

p.h: Why the database and the files belong together
p.x: The files folder does not hold your files by name. Each file is stored under the id of its node, in a folder named after the last two characters of the id, such as files/7K/01JA3W6Q0V3XG0M2ZK8Q5T7R7K . What a file is called, who may see it and, with the Archive, which album it is in and whose face is in it are all in the database. Neither half is any use without the other, and they must come from the same moment. When something is deleted for good, EiN removes its bytes from the data folder, so a database restored from an older backup than the files points at files that are gone; files newer than the database are simply not in the tree. Take both while EiN is stopped, and restore both together. The database password in .env , POSTGRES_PASSWORD , is kept nowhere else. The restore below does not need it, as it loads the dump into a fresh database, but containers made again on the existing database folder cannot reach the database without it. Keep a copy of .env with every backup.

Do this before every update and on a schedule of your own. The example writes the backup to /mnt/backup/ein , a disk other than the one EiN runs on. Stop EiN, but not its database, so nothing changes while you copy: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose stop core The Web UI, SSH and SFTP are down until step 5. Find the database's container and dump the database, with the TimescaleDB version it was made with: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein mkdir -p /mnt/backup/ein db=$(podman ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=ein --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=db) podman exec " $db " psql -U ein -d ein -tAc "SELECT extversion FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'timescaledb'" > /mnt/backup/ein/timescaledb-version podman exec " $db " pg_dump -U ein -d ein -Fc > /mnt/backup/ein/ein-db.dump The dump is PostgreSQL's custom format and includes the small content EiN keeps in the database. It is much smaller than the files; df in EiN's terminal shows the database's size. Copy .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein cp . env /mnt/backup/ein/env Copy the data folder, leaving out what is not worth keeping: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein rsync -a --delete --exclude /llm --exclude /db ~/ein/data/ /mnt/backup/ein/data/ --exclude /db leaves out the database's own folder: the dump of step 2 is its backup, and the folder belongs to the database's user, which your own cannot read. With the Album folders module, add --exclude /files/albums too: its folders are second names for the originals in files , which rsync -a would copy once more, and EiN makes them again. Add --exclude /files-volatile to leave out the renditions as well; see Make the renditions again for what that costs at a restore. If you chose another data folder at the install, give its path instead of ~/ein/data/ . Start EiN again: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose start core A backup tool that copies the whole data folder as root, such as one that backs up the whole machine, takes db too. That copy is a database only when the database was stopped while it was taken ( podman compose stop db , then podman compose start db ); the dump is one either way. rsync --delete makes the copy the same as the data folder, so something deleted by mistake is gone from the copy at the next run. To keep older backups, write each run to a folder of its own, such as /mnt/backup/ein/2026-10-25 , or use a backup tool that keeps versions, such as restic or Borg, on the dump, .env and the data folder. Warning Never start a dump just before an update or a restart. EiN changes its database tables when it starts, and a dump in progress holds them, so EiN waits for the dump and the update looks as if EiN does not come up. Take the dump while EiN is stopped, as above, or while it is already running.

Docker runs the containers as root, so the files in the data folder belong to root on the machine. Run the rsync of step 4, and of a restore, with sudo . Under rootless podman they belong to your own user, and no sudo is needed.

A restore loads the dump into an empty database and puts the files back beside it. On the machine the backup came from, start at step 3. On a new machine, or after reinstalling, start at step 1. Install EiN with the same options as before, such as --ems --module archive , as Install EiN describes. The installer starts an empty EiN with a new admin password; that password stops mattering after the restore, when the accounts from your backup apply. When setup.sh made it, delete its INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD line from the new .env then, or setup.sh keeps showing a password that no longer signs in. Compare the new ~/ein/.env with the copy in your backup, and copy over the lines you added yourself, such as CFG_ settings, ports or memory limits. Keep the new POSTGRES_PASSWORD and EMS_KEY : the new database was made with them. Check EIN_GPU too, which says whether this machine has a graphics card for EiN; see The graphics card . Stop EiN and find the database's container: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose stop core db=$(podman ps -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=ein --filter label=com.docker.compose.service=db) Replace the database with the dump: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman exec " $db " dropdb -U ein --force ein podman exec " $db " createdb -U ein ein podman exec " $db " psql -U ein -d ein -c "CREATE EXTENSION timescaledb VERSION ' $(cat /mnt/backup/ein/timescaledb-version) '" podman exec " $db " psql -U ein -d ein -c "SELECT timescaledb_pre_restore()" podman exec -i " $db " pg_restore -U ein -d ein < /mnt/backup/ein/ein-db.dump podman exec " $db " psql -U ein -d ein -c "SELECT timescaledb_post_restore()" dropdb deletes the database EiN was running on; --force first ends the connections still open to it, such as the health check that connects every few seconds. TimescaleDB asks for the same version the dump was made with, and for timescaledb_pre_restore() and timescaledb_post_restore() around the restore. EiN brings TimescaleDB and the other extensions up to the newest version the image has when it next starts. Put the files back, so that the data folder holds exactly what the backup holds: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein rsync -a --delete --exclude /llm --exclude /db /mnt/backup/ein/data/ ~/ein/data/ --exclude /db keeps the database you restored in step 4. This also removes the few files the empty EiN of step 1 wrote, which the restored database knows nothing of. Start EiN with the restored data and any lines you changed in .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d Sign in with an account from your backup, and choose Status under System in the sidebar: the Storage card shows the data folder and the database's size, and the badge above the title turns to Healthy once the work after the start is done. Health and status explains what you see. With the Archive, if you left out files-volatile , make the renditions again now, as the next section says. Until then, pictures and videos have no thumbnails or previews.

With the Media module installed, the regenerate command makes the renditions of every picture, video and recording under a folder, and with the Archive, regenerate-face-crops --missing the face crops. After a restore without files-volatile , the database still records the renditions, so add --force to make them although they seem to exist: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator nohup regenerate --force /archive The face crops go a page at a time: regenerate-face-crops --missing --limit 1000 prints where the next page starts, and --after with that id goes on from there, until it says nothing is left. nohup lets it run on when you close the terminal and logs it under /var/logs/jobs . It needs the media service, and over a large archive it takes as long as the first processing did. regenerate --force '/archive/albums/Summer 1987' does one album first, so you can check the result.

Moving is a backup on the old machine and a restore on the new one: On the old machine, back up EiN to a disk you can take along, or to a folder you then copy to the new machine with rsync -a over SSH. On the new machine, follow Restore a backup from step 1, giving the paths where the backup is. Point the family's bookmarks, phones and SFTP clients at the new machine's address. EiN's SSH host key, /etc/ssh_host_key in the tree, moves with the database, so SSH and SFTP clients see the same key as before. The old machine keeps running until you stop it. Stop it after the move, with podman compose down in ~/ein , so no one goes on adding pictures there. If CREATE EXTENSION in step 4 says that TimescaleDB has no installation script for the version, the new machine's database image no longer carries the version the old one used. Update the old EiN first, so both run the same image, as Updating describes, and take the backup again.

p.h: Move the data folder to another disk
p.x: The data folder can be moved on the same machine, such as to a larger disk mounted at /srv/ein-data : Stop EiN and remove its containers: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose down down keeps the database and the data folder; it removes the containers, which the last step makes again. Copy the data folder to the new place, keeping its owners and times: # on the machine EiN runs on podman unshare rsync -a ~/ein/data/ /srv/ein-data/ podman unshare lets the copy read the database's folder, which belongs to one of your subordinate ids. Under Docker, use sudo rsync -a . Change the lines EIN_DATA and EIN_DB_DIR in ~/ein/.env to the new path: # ~/ein/.env EIN_DATA =/srv/ein-data EIN_DB_DIR =/srv/ein-data/db Leave EIN_DB_DIR as it is if it names a folder outside the data folder, or is empty. Make the containers again with the new folder: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d Check that your files, and with the Archive their pictures and thumbnails, show before you delete the old folder. EiN stores no path of the machine in its database, only paths inside its containers, so nothing else needs changing. To put the database on a disk of its own, such as an SSD, stop it, copy its folder as in step 2 to an empty folder, and run ./setup.sh --db-dir /srv/ein-db . An installation whose EIN_DB_DIR is empty keeps the database in the volume ein_db , in the container engine's storage: ./setup.sh --db-dir ~/ein/data/db moves it into the data folder, and while the database is still in the volume, setup.sh stops and prints the commands that copy it there first.

p.h: Get your files out without EiN
p.x: The data folder holds your files under ids, not names, so copying it gives you nothing you can browse. To get files out with their names and folders, take them out through EiN: In the Web UI , with the Archive installed, select pictures in an album or the grid and choose Download in the selection bar. One file downloads as itself, several as one zip named after the album, of up to 5000 files. See Albums . Over SFTP , copy whole albums or the whole archive with scp -r , sftp or a graphical client, or mount EiN with sshfs and copy with rsync or a file manager. SSH and SFTP shows how. As folders on the machine EiN runs on , with the Album folders module: every album of the Archive is a folder of its pictures in files/albums in the data folder, for a file manager or a shared folder, kept up to date as the albums change. From EiN's terminal , scp -r copies a folder to another machine, such as a NAS, if you are in the group ssh . Reaching other machines covers keys and addresses. This copies one of the Archive's albums: # on your own computer scp -P 2222 -r "helen@ein.local:/archive/albums/Summer 1987" ~/Pictures/ Such a copy holds the original files, as they were added. What EiN worked out or was told about them, such as the Archive's faces, people, places, descriptions and album membership, stays in EiN: an album's pictures are links to the files, and what belongs to a photo is in a hidden folder beside it, which a recursive copy leaves out. What the tree looks like over SFTP explains both. A copy like this is a way to take your pictures elsewhere, not a backup of EiN.

In EiN's terminal, df shows each part of the data folder, how full its disk is, how fast it grows and when it fills, and the database's size and its largest tables; the storage cards on the Status page's Overview show the same. # in EiN's terminal df tier disk 41% used 1.1 TB free full in ~212d tier volatile 41% used 1.1 TB free full in ~212d database 6.2 GB root_nodes_attr 2.1 GB root_nodes_audit 1.6 GB root_nodes_lnk 812 MB root_nodes 540 MB root_pools_job 230 MB disk is files and volatile is files-volatile . When they are folders on one disk, as in a default install, they show the same free space. du measures part of the tree, such as du -sh /archive . On the machine itself, du -sh ~/ein/data/* shows each folder of the data folder, and podman system df what the images and the database volume take in the container engine's storage. Each update downloads new images and removes the ones they replaced; podman image prune removes other images without a name that nothing uses any more.

What you delete in the Web UI goes to the deleter's trash first and keeps its room on the disk until it leaves the trash: after 30 days, or the number of days set in CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS ( Days in the trash , under Settings → System ). Only then does EiN remove the files from the data folder. Your profile, favourites and trash explains the trash, and which ways of deleting skip it. To free the room at once, an administrator can empty every account's trash: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator trash empty --all Add --older-than 7 to empty only what was deleted more than seven days ago. Either way it cannot be undone. To remove Do this Files and folders, and the Archive's pictures, albums, people and the like Delete them in the Web UI, then empty the trash; see Your profile, favourites and trash . An account Delete account… removes its home folder at once, without the trash, and passes everything it owned elsewhere to another account; see Accounts and groups . A module Remove in Settings → Modules ; see Modules . The media service or the language model ~/ein/setup.sh --no-ems or --no-llm stops it and keeps its data. Then podman image rm ghcr.io/einhq/ems:main frees the media service's image of about 30 GB ( localhost/ein-ems when it was built from your own source), and removing ~/ein/data/llm the model. Deleting an account does not delete what it owned, such as pictures in the Archive: it passes to the account you choose. To remove them, delete them before or after.

There is no uninstall script. Removing EiN and everything in it takes these steps; back up first if there is anything you want to keep. Stop EiN and remove its containers and its database: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose down The database stays in db in the data folder until step 4. If EIN_DB_DIR in .env names a folder outside it, remove that folder with podman unshare rm -rf and its path (under Docker, sudo rm -rf ); if it is empty, the database is the volume ein_db : podman volume rm ein_db . Either deletes the database for good: every name, album, person, account and setting. Remove the images: # on the machine EiN runs on podman image rm ghcr.io/einhq/core:main ghcr.io/einhq/db:main podman image rm ghcr.io/einhq/ems:main # if you installed the media service podman image rm localhost/ein-core localhost/ein-db localhost/ein-ems # if they were built from your own source podman image prune The language model's image is llama.cpp's, from ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp ; podman images lists it if you want it gone too. Under podman, setup.sh turned on podman-restart.service and lingering for your user, so that EiN starts at boot (see Installing in detail ). With EiN's containers gone they start nothing of EiN's; if no other container of yours needs them, turn them off: # on the machine EiN runs on, as your own user systemctl --user disable podman-restart.service loginctl disable-linger Remove the installation and the data folder, which holds your originals: # on the machine EiN runs on podman unshare rm -rf ~/ein podman unshare lets it remove the database's folder, which belongs to one of your subordinate ids. If you chose another data folder at the install, remove it as well; EIN_DATA in .env names it, so read that line before you remove ~/ein . Under Docker the files belong to root, so use sudo rm -rf . Warning With an empty EIN_DB_DIR , podman compose down -v removes the database volume in the same step as the containers. Use it only when you mean to delete the database.

What you see What to do db=$(…) is empty, and podman exec says it needs a container The database is not running. Start it with podman compose up -d db , and check podman compose ps . Under Docker, use docker ps in the db=$(…) line. CREATE EXTENSION says there is no installation script for the version The database image does not carry the TimescaleDB version the dump was made with; see Move EiN to another machine . With the Archive, after a restore, pictures show without thumbnails The renditions were not restored. Make the renditions again . After a restore, some pictures open as a broken image Their files are missing from the data folder: the files and the database came from different moments. Restore both from the same backup. A module is missing after a restore It was installed from Settings → Modules and its folder was not restored. Install it again there; see Modules . rsync says permission denied Under Docker the data folder belongs to root; run it with sudo . The update after a backup reports that EiN did not come up A dump was still running when EiN started. Wait for it to finish, then podman compose restart core . Troubleshooting covers problems that are not about the data.

Installing in detail : the files in ~/ein , the data folder and .env . Updating : what an update changes and keeps; back up before it. Files and storage : how EiN stores file content, and its tiers. Health and status : the Storage card and when a disk fills. Your profile, favourites and trash : the trash, from the user's side. SSH and SFTP : copying files in and out.

This page is for whoever runs EiN, when something does not work after the install: EiN does not start or answer, nobody can sign in, or work stops getting done. Core's problems come first; after them, the problems that belong to a module are grouped under its name, for you to skip when you have not installed it: the Archive 's pictures without thumbnails, the Assistant that stays silent, and the Media service . Each section says what you see, how to find the cause and what to do, and links the page that covers the topic in full. For problems during the first install, see Install EiN . The commands on the machine are written for podman and run in ~/ein , where the installer put EiN. With Docker, write docker compose where they say podman compose .

Three places tell you most of what is wrong. Look at them in this order. The containers. On the machine EiN runs on, see whether every container is up and whether the database, and the media service when it is installed, are healthy: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose ps podman compose logs -- tail 100 core # the end of EiN's log; db, and ems or llm when installed, for the others A container that shows Up for only a few seconds, again and again, stops and is started again by its restart policy. Its log says why. The Status page. When the Web UI opens, sign in as an administrator and choose Status under System in the sidebar. The badge above System status gives the verdict: Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person . Below it, the Overview tab lists each check that is not fine, with its reason. The Services tab shows each of EiN's own services, and the Log tab its Recent problems and the live log. Health and status explains every tile. The badge in the header is the verdict of the health checks; anything other than Healthy is listed on the Overview tab with its reason. health in EiN's terminal. The same verdict and every check, fine or not, in text. On an EiN with the ems module installed, it may read: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator health needs a person: 1 check failed fail failed work 2 instances failed again after three more runs and need a person (pipeline-instances --status failed) warn ems http://ems:8181 is not answering; work that needs it waits The first line is the verdict; each line after it is a check, failures first. A check names the command that shows more. Verdict What it means healthy Nothing is waiting and no check failed. catching up Work is waiting and getting done. The line says how many jobs wait and, when it can, when the slowest kind is done. stuck Work is waiting and none was done in the last hour. See Work does not get done . needs a person At least one check failed. Its line says what failed and which command to run. Inside EiN, the system log is /var/logs/system , which dmesg prints; it starts empty at each start of EiN. Each service writes its own log to /var/logs/services/<name>/stdout.log and stderr.log , which start empty each time the service starts: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator dmesg -n 50 --level=warn # the last 50 warnings and errors tail /var/logs/services/pipeline-engine/stdout.log # one service's log Services and logs covers both kinds of log and the services that write them.

p.h: EiN does not start or does not answer
p.x: EiN answers on port 8080 only once its database is up and its start is through: it installs the modules EIN_MODULES names that are missing, sets every module up, and only then starts its services, the Web UI and SSH among them. While it does, the browser cannot connect. A start that installs modules over a slow connection takes minutes. What you see What to do podman compose ps shows core as Created or not at all, and db as starting or unhealthy EiN waits for the database to answer a query. Read podman compose logs db . A first start of the database restarts it once, which takes a little while. EiN's log stops after Connecting to database... , and the container starts over EiN could not reach the database; it waits up to 60 seconds for a connection. Check that db is up and healthy, and read its log. password authentication failed for user "ein" in EiN's log POSTGRES_PASSWORD in ~/ein/.env is not the password the database was made with, usually because .env was deleted and setup.sh wrote a new one. Put back the .env from your backup; the database keeps the password it was made with. Your data says why .env belongs in every backup. The log shows the modules being installed, and nothing answers yet EiN is downloading modules. Wait, and follow it with podman compose logs -f core . some modules could not be installed or replaced; continuing boot in the log EiN could not download a module, often for want of a connection to GitHub, or found no release of an installed one that it can run. EiN starts without it; the mod install: lines at the end of setup.sh 's output say which and why. Install or update it from Settings → Modules once EiN is up. module setup completed with failures; continuing boot in the log A module's setup failed and the others carried on. See When a module does not work . setup.sh: EiN did not answer at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ in 10 minutes: podman compose logs core Read the log it names, then go through the lines above. When EIN_BIND is an address other than 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1 , EiN is running and setup.sh only looked in the wrong place: see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A port is already in use when the containers start Another program, or an EiN under the other container engine, has port 8080 or 2222. See Keep to one engine , or choose other ports in .env . After an update, an empty EiN where your admin password does not work The update ran under the other container engine, with an empty database of its own. See Keep to one engine . EiN is not running after the machine restarted Under podman, podman-restart.service starts it at boot, and under rootless podman only for a user who lingers. Start it with podman compose up -d , and see Start EiN when the machine boots . EiN answers on the machine itself, but not from another computer Open ports 8080 and 2222 in the machine's firewall, and try the machine's IP address instead of a name ending in .local . See Open the ports in the firewall . A container that keeps starting over without a clear message in its log may be running out of memory: each has a limit, 6 GB for EiN unless EIN_MEMORY in .env sets another. The machine's kernel log records a container stopped for that reason ( journalctl -k | grep -i oom on most systems). Performance and sizing says how to raise the limits.

What you see What to do setup.sh showed no admin password at the end setup.sh shows a password it made, from INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD in ~/ein/.env . A password you chose at the install it never shows: it says Sign in as admin with the password you chose. and removes the line once EiN has taken it. Otherwise the line is gone because you deleted it, or because .env was written before setup.sh kept the password there. Then a new EiN made a random one and wrote it to its log once, as Admin password set to: ; find it with podman compose logs core | grep 'Admin password set to' . The log is gone once the containers have been made again, by an update or by podman compose down , and an EiN whose database was there before keeps the password it had. The admin password is lost Once changed, nothing keeps it; the INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD line in .env holds only a first one setup.sh made, which works only until it is changed, and a password you chose at the install is not kept at all. A member of the group sudo signs in, chooses Administer… in the account menu, and sets a new one on the Users tab of Settings , under Password , or types admin and then user-passwd admin in the terminal. EiN has no way to reset it from the machine, so let a second person administer before you need it. Someone's sign-in fails with the right password Their account may be disabled, or have no password yet ( Needs a password ): send them a sign-in link . "too many failed sign-ins; try again in" and a number of seconds Wait that long. When it happens to everyone behind your HTTPS proxy at once, EiN sees all of them as one address: see How EiN slows down password guessing . Signing in works, but the next page asks you to sign in again The browser uses http:// while the proxy says https , so the browser does not send the cookie back. Open the https:// address. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . SSH warns that the host key has changed The key is kept in EiN's database and stays across updates; it changes only when EiN was installed afresh. Remove the old key from your ~/.ssh/known_hosts once you know that is what happened. See SSH and SFTP .

What you see What to do The page frame loads but stays empty, and the terminal does not connect The interface talks to EiN over a WebSocket, which something in between does not pass, usually an HTTPS proxy. See What EiN needs from the proxy . The Status page shows an offline badge The page lost its connection to EiN and is reconnecting; the figures are from the last update. It reconnects by itself once EiN answers. When it does not, see EiN does not start or does not answer . Status and Nodes are missing from the sidebar They are for administrators. A member of sudo chooses Administer… in the account menu first. A module's pages do not appear after it was installed Reload the page. When they still do not appear, look for mod: ui-build failed: in the output of the install, and see Modules . Large uploads fail behind a proxy, often with 413 The proxy limits the size of a request. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access .

Everything EiN does after a file arrives is pipeline work, done in the background: with the Archive, everything from thumbnails to faces to transcriptions. Processing and pipelines explains how it is run; this section is about finding why it stopped. Start with health , or the Overview and Work tabs of the Status page. Each check that is not fine points at one of the cases below.

A failed run is run again by itself, after 1 hour, 6 hours and 24 hours. The pipeline-pruner service does this, so nothing needs doing while health says: warn failed work 3 failed instances, run again on their own after 1 h, 6 h and 24 h When a run has failed again after those three, it is left for a person, and the check fails: fail failed work 2 instances failed again after three more runs and need a person (pipeline-instances --status failed) List the failed instances, and look at one: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pipeline-instances --status failed pipeline-status < id > pipeline-status shows each step of the instance and the error of the one that failed. Fix the cause the error names: a full disk, a module that needed an update or, with the Archive, a media service that was down. Run the work again. One instance at a time, from the pipeline's current definition: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pipeline-rerun < id > Or every failed instance the automatic reruns would still take, at once rather than after its wait: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pipeline-heal --now # shows what it would do pipeline-heal --now --apply # does it A step that failed on its input, such as a file no program can open, is not run again, since every run would meet the same bytes. health counts those as input , and they need nothing from you.

p.h: Waiting work that does not drain
p.x: What health says What it means and what to do stuck: … jobs waiting, none done in the last hour Work waits and nothing takes it. The checks below the verdict say which kind; look there. … waiting, and no worker offers this kind No running service takes this kind of work. The Status page shows it in red as Work that nothing will run , with the pipelines that queue it. Usually a module's service has stopped: see A service has stopped . Work that nothing will run says no defined pipeline queues this kind any more The jobs belong to a pipeline that changed or is gone. If it queues the step under another kind now, run the pool cancel command the message shows; if it is no longer defined, run pipeline-prune . See Work that nothing will run . … waiting, the oldest for …, and the workers that take it are idle Work waits while the workers that take it do nothing: EiN is not handing it out. Read the Log tab for why, and restart EiN. … running steps silent for … or more: … Steps that started but have said nothing for a long time. A long video can take that long. When one is truly stuck, stop it and run it again with Restart on the step, or pipeline-step-restart <pipeline>/<id> <step> . … entries dropped after their delivery attempts (queue-dead /var/queues/…: --retry or --drop) Events a queue gave up delivering. Look at them with queue-dead <path> , then put them back with queue-dead --retry <path> once the cause is fixed, or remove them with queue-dead --drop <path> . With the Archive, a kind can also wait for the media service; see Media service . pipeline-overview and pool-stat show the counts behind these checks, and top shows them live. pipeline-repair finds instances marked finished while steps of theirs still wait, and with --apply sets them running again; run it without --apply first to see what it would change.

EiN runs its own services inside its container: the Web UI, SSH, the pipeline engine, and each module's. A service that stops on its own is started again, but after three restarts within a minute EiN leaves it failed . See which services run: # in EiN's terminal service-list --detail Read the failed one's log, /var/logs/services/<name>/stderr.log and stdout.log , to see why it stopped. Start it again, on the Status page's Services tab with its Start button, or in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator service-start trash-purger A service shown as disabled has no buttons on the Status page; enable it first with service-enable <name> . Restarting EiN, podman compose restart core , starts every enabled service again. Services and logs lists the services and what each does.

Two places fill up, and they may be on different disks: Where How to see it The data folder, EIN_DATA : originals, renditions and, with --llm , the language model df in EiN's terminal: free space per storage tier, the size of its files, its growth per day, when it fills, and the size of the database The container engine's storage: the images podman system df on the machine To make room: Trashed files are removed for good after CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS , 30 days unless changed. An administrator can empty it sooner, trash empty --all --older-than 7 for what everyone trashed over a week ago. setup.sh removes the images an update replaced once the new EiN answers. Other images without a name, such as a build's intermediate stages, stay in the container engine's storage; podman image prune removes them. Performance and sizing says how much room EiN needs.

What changed What to do A setting on Settings → System Choose Restore inherited value under it, or run config unset <KEY> in the terminal. See Configuration . A line in ~/ein/.env Undo it and run podman compose up -d . An update See Updating . A module was installed, updated or removed See When a module does not work .

When you ask someone for help, these say what you run and what it is doing: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator system-info # host, uptime, core's version and commit, each module's commit, PostgreSQL and Deno health # the verdict and every check dmesg --level=warn # warnings and errors since EiN started # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose ps podman compose logs -- tail 200 core Read the logs before you send them on: they name your accounts, paths and addresses.
With the Archive installed:

p.h: Thumbnails, faces and text are missing
p.x: The Archive's thumbnails, video renditions, faces, picture vectors, transcriptions and the text of documents all come from the media service, a container of its own. When it is missing or not answering, the work waits for it and nothing fails. See whether EiN reaches it: # in EiN's terminal ems-status ems-status shows its version, every model and its state, what it is running and what it is degraded in. On the Status page, the Media service tab shows the same. When health says http://ems:8181 is not answering; work that needs it waits : It was never installed. The Archive needs it. Add it with ~/ein/setup.sh --ems ; its image is about 30 GB. It is starting. Its health check gives it two minutes to start. podman compose ps shows its state. It stopped. Read podman compose logs ems , and start it again with podman compose up -d . Once it answers, the waiting work goes on by itself. Files that never got their renditions can be given them again: # in EiN's terminal regenerate /archive/albums/cornwall-1968 # what is missing regenerate --force /archive/albums/cornwall-1968 # everything again
With the Assistant installed:

The chat shows one of three cards when a question gets no answer: Card What it means Assistant unavailable "The assistant is not available right now." The language model could not be reached within CFG_LLM_WAIT , 180 seconds unless changed, or the assistant is not set up. No answer "The assistant could not answer this question." The model ran but gave up on this question. Ask it in other words. Answer too long "The answer was too long to finish. Ask for less, such as the last 20 rows." For Assistant unavailable , ask EiN whether it reaches the model: # in EiN's terminal llm-status --checks What it says What to do … is not answering; the chat cannot answer until it does With --llm , read podman compose logs llm : at its first start it downloads its model, several GB, and answers only after that. Without --llm and without a hosted model, there is no model: add one with ~/ein/setup.sh --llm . … does not offer …; the chat's questions to it fail The hosted provider has no model by the name in CFG_LLM_MODEL . Set a name it offers. The language model covers running the model yourself or using a hosted one.

These apply with the media service and the ems module installed, which the Archive needs. The media service covers more. What you see What to do unresolvable CDI devices nvidia.com/gpu=all when the containers start The container engine cannot hand the graphics card to the media service or the language model. See The graphics card . health says … waiting: EMS has not been able to run it for … For half an hour the media service has been busy, could not load what the work needs, or could not reach the files. What it answered is under Where the work is on the Work tab. EiN keeps trying on its own. See Thumbnails, faces and text are missing . A waiting step's error ends fuse: mount failed: Permission denied (files_unavailable) The media service cannot mount the files of its requests: under Docker, AppArmor denies it. Run ./setup.sh again. See The media service . health says http://ems:8181 is not answering; work that needs it waits The media service was never installed, is starting or has stopped. See Thumbnails, faces and text are missing . A fail check named ems gpu The card the media service is meant to have is gone. See The graphics card . Lines beginning ems-link: down and ems-link: up in the ems-link service's log say when the media service went away and came back. When the media service is updated, the ems-link service runs the failed instances again at once ( pipeline heal --now --apply ), all but those that failed on their input or were left for a person, since a new build is the likeliest fix.
