Everything EiN keeps is a node: a photo, an album, a person, an account, a log, a command. This page takes one node apart, says what each part means and how to look at it in the Web UI and the shell, and explains what a node's type decides. It is for anyone who wants to understand what they see in ls -l , in Nodes or in a node's Properties . The examples come from the Wrenfield family's archive. Its paths, such as /archive/albums and /archive/people , and the types album and person exist with the Archive installed; what the page says about nodes is core's and holds for every type.

p.h: What a node is made of
p.x: Every node has the same five parts, whatever its type: Part What it is How to see it Id A fixed identifier of 26 letters and digits, given when the node is made. It stays the same when the node is moved or renamed. info , stat Type A word that says what the node is: file , directory , album , person . Set when the node is made. info , ls -l Properties What every node has, as a file on a computer does: owner, group, mode, access list, times and link count. props , ls -l Attributes What this node's type needs: a photo's size, checksum and capture time; a person's names and dates. attrs Name and place The name the node has in the folder that holds it. A node does not store its own name; the folder does. ls , find Some types also hold content : a file its bytes, a log its lines, a queue its messages, a position its shape on the map. And any node can hold children , a file included. A node keeps its id, type, properties and attributes; its name belongs to the folder that holds it. Take a photo from the Wrenfield family's album: # in EiN's terminal info /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg id: 01JA7Q3M5X8R2C4V6B9N0P1T2W type: file The path names the photo; the id names the node behind it. resolve-id goes the other way, from an id back to the node's path: # in EiN's terminal resolve-id 01JA7Q3M5X8R2C4V6B9N0P1T2W

The Nodes page browses the whole tree. It is in the sidebar under System , for administrators. Open System → Nodes . Go to the node, by its folders or by typing its path in the address bar. Choose Properties in the node's context menu, or press Alt + Enter . A person is a node like any other, with folders of her own beneath her. The properties dialog has three tabs: General shows the node's Id , Type , Links , Created , Changed and Modified , a file's Mimetype and Size , a link's Link to , and the Mode , Owner and Group , which you can change there and save with Apply . Attributes shows the attributes, a Key and a Value to a row. If you may change the node, you can edit a row, remove it or Add one, and save with Apply , or Reset to go back to what is stored. The Attributes tab beside the listing shows them as JSON instead, saved with Save ; when you may not change the node it says You can read these attributes but not change them. Sharing is the Share dialog's body; Permissions in depth explains it. Everyone else meets nodes through the pages modules make for them: with the Archive, an album's page shows an album node and the files in it, a person's page a person node and what links to it.

Five commands show a node, each a different amount of it. All of them take a path. Command What it prints info The id and the type. props The properties. attrs The attributes. stat All of it: id, type, properties and attributes. ls -l One line for each node in a folder: type, mode, links, owner, group, size, time and name. info , props , attrs and stat print YAML with the keys in alphabetical order, and JSON with JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front. A person's attributes, for example: # in EiN's terminal attrs /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield born: '1934-08-22' died: '2021-01-17' fullname: Margaret Wrenfield gender: female name: Peggy Wrenfield ls -l starts each line with the node's type, so it shows at a glance what a folder holds: # in EiN's terminal ls -l /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield directory rwxrwxr-x 1 admin users 2 14 Mar 2026 09:12:40 children directory rwxrwxr-x 1 admin users 1 14 Mar 2026 09:12:41 partners The size column is a file's size in bytes, and for every other node the number of children it has. A + after the mode says the node has an access list, and a link ends with -> and where it points. Names that start with a dot are left out unless you add -a . Note In these commands -L means do not follow a link: stat -L shows the link itself, stat without it the node the link points to. That is the opposite of stat -L on Linux. The command reference has every option of stat , props , attrs , info and ls .

Properties are the same for every type. props prints them under these names: Property General shows it as What it is uid Owner The account that owns the node, by number. gid Group The node's group, by number. mode Mode The permission bits, as chmod writes them: 0750 or rwxr-x--- . props prints the number in decimal, so 0755 shows as 493 . acl (the Sharing tab) The access list: more users or groups, each with bits of their own. Absent when there is none. birthtime Created When the node was made, and by whom. changetime Changed When its properties last changed, and by whom. modtime Modified When its attributes last changed, and by whom. count Links How many folders hold the node. Usually 1; more when it has hard links. softlink Link to Where a softlink points. Only on links. tier (beside Type ) Where a file's bytes are stored: disk , volatile or db . Fixed when the file is made. Each time is a pair of the account's number and the moment, in milliseconds since 1970. ls -l shows the later of the changed and modified times, with owner and group by name. Owner, group, mode and access list decide who may read or change the node. Permissions in depth explains them and the commands that change them: chmod , chown , acl and share-set . Links are explained in Links , and the tiers in Files and storage .

Attributes hold what a node's type needs, as JSON values: text, numbers, lists and objects. Each type has its own: Type Attributes it carries, for example file name , mimetype , size , sha256 ; a photo also takenAt , its capture time person name , fullname , birthname , born , died , gender , contact , description album name , the title shown on its page, which may differ from the folder's name directory often none So /archive/albums/christmas-2019 is the album's path, and Christmas at the cottage , the title on its page, is its name attribute.

Change what a node means through the command or page made for it, when there is one: with the Archive, give Peggy a death date with person-update --died=… or on her page, describe a photo with file-set-description , and rename an album on its page. Those check the value and keep everything that depends on it in step. For anything else, attrs sets and removes attributes directly: # in EiN's terminal attrs -s 'birthname=Margaret Cole' /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield attrs -J 'contact=[{"type":"phone","data":"01632 960 418"}]' /archive/people/helen-okafor attrs -d contact /archive/people/helen-okafor -s key=value sets an attribute to the text after the first = . -J key=value sets it to a JSON value: a number, true , a list, an object. Invalid JSON is refused with invalid JSON for attribute 'key' . -d key removes it. Each option may be given several times. The attributes you do not name are left as they are. The Attributes tab in Properties does the same from the Web UI. Warning attrs writes what you give it without knowing what the type expects. A wrong value, such as a date in the wrong form, can make a page or a pipeline misread the node. Prefer the commands made for the type.

A node's type decides whether it holds content, and of what kind. cat prints it: Type Content file Its bytes: a photo, a video, a text. log Lines with a time each, kept for a retention period. queue Messages waiting to be read; reading one removes it. router Nothing kept: what is written reaches whoever reads now. position A point, a circle or an outline on the map. track Timestamped GPS points. control The states its device reported, a line with a time each. embedding A numeric fingerprint, for similarity search. A directory , album or person holds no content, only attributes and children, and so does a device : what is written to a device or a control goes to the device's driver, which sends it on or reads it into the device's endpoints ( Devices, endpoints and drivers ). Children work the same for every type. With the Archive, a photo keeps what EiN works out about it beneath itself: Child What it holds thumbnails/ Smaller renditions, a video's poster and storyboard metadata/exif The metadata read from the file, an exif node regions/ A media-region node for each face or box on the photo position Where the photo was taken, a position node # in EiN's terminal ls /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg Deleting a node deletes its children with it: rm refuses a node that has children unless you add -r . Names are unique within a folder, so a folder cannot hold two children of the same name. How the tree is laid out, folder by folder, is in The tree .

The type is a plain word stored on the node, and it decides three things: What the node holds. Whether it has content, and what attributes it is expected to carry. How EiN treats it. A softlink is followed to its target; a queue hands out its messages in order; a session disappears when its connection ends; a file is shown as a picture, a video or a text by its mimetype. Where it shows. The Archive's pages list album , person , location , camera and track nodes; the search box's @ completes the names of all but tracks, and labels'. find -type person finds a type anywhere in the tree. A node's type does not change after it is made. To turn a folder into an album, for example, make a new album and move the files into it.

Core has its own types: the ones every installation needs, such as file , directory , softlink , user , group , log and queue . Modules add theirs: the Archive brings album , person , location , camera , media-region , exif and album-profile . A module describes its types in its manifest, with a label, a description and a category; The module manifest shows how. A type is not registered anywhere before it is used. mknode -t <type> makes a node of any type, and a module's commands are often built on it: person-create makes a person node with mknode -t person and its attributes. A type no installed module describes still works; it is simply undescribed. The types fall into three groups: Group What is in it Content What the archive is made of: files, positions and tracks, and with the Archive albums, people, locations, cameras and faces. Structure How the tree is arranged: directories, links, accounts and groups. System How EiN runs: commands, logs, queues, pools, routers, sessions, terminals, embeddings, share links, devices and their controls.

Node types describes every type of an EiN with all its modules. Your own installation lists what it has, with how many of each: In the Web UI, open System → Documentation and choose Node types . Each type shows its label, its description, the module it comes from and how many are in the tree. A type that no installed module describes, perhaps left by a module since removed, is listed under Also in the tree . In the terminal, run docs node-types . Each line has the type, its count, the module it comes from ( core for core's own) and its description. Your installation's own list of types follows the modules installed and counts what is in the tree.

info , stat or attrs answers Node not found or Access denied for operation 'r' . The path is wrong, or the node is one you may not read. EiN leaves out what you may not open, so a node can exist and still not be found by you; Permissions in depth explains why. stat shows a different node than the one you named. The path is a link, and stat follows it. Add -L to see the link itself. attrs changes the target, not the link. It too follows the link and changes the target. Add -L to change the link node. mknode answers missing type . It needs -t and a type. mknode answers tier is not an attribute; use --tier . The storage tier is a property: give it with --tier=disk , --tier=volatile or --tier=db . The Attributes tab is read-only. You may read the node but not change it.

How EiN works : the ideas EiN is built on, in one page. The tree : every standard path and what is there. Links : softlinks and hard links. Files and storage : where a file's bytes are kept. Changes and pipelines : what happens when a node is made or changed. Permissions in depth : owner, group, mode and access lists. Node types : every type, described. Commands by task : the commands that work on nodes.

Everything EiN holds has a path in one tree, from / down. This page walks through the standard paths: what lies where, who owns each part, which parts modules add, and which parts are stored somewhere else. Read it when you browse in the terminal, over SFTP or on the Nodes page and want to know what you are looking at. The examples use folders such as /archive/albums and /archive/people , which exist with the Archive installed; an EiN without modules has the rest of the tree as described.

A fresh installation has eight folders at the top: # in EiN's terminal ls / archive dev etc groups home tmp usr var Each holds one kind of thing, and the kind is the reason a path sits where it does: Folder What it holds Who writes there /archive What EiN is for: labels, and with the Archive albums, people, locations and cameras Everyone with an account, as each folder's sharing allows /home One folder per account: its settings, shell history, favourites, trash and, with the Archive, its staging Each account in its own folder /groups One folder per group given a shared home: what its members have in common The group's members, each in their own group's folder /etc Accounts and groups, the system's settings, the services EiN runs and the navigation of the Web UI The administrator, and commands such as config set /var What the system writes as it runs: logs, sessions, share links, queues, pools and pipeline runs EiN itself /usr Code and read-only files: the commands, the modules and the built-in guide Nobody by hand; an update or mod install replaces it /dev The devices that report to EiN or are switched from it, the channels facts about changes are announced on, and /dev/null EiN itself: its drivers, and device-create for the members of the devices group /tmp Scratch space that does not outlast a restart Everyone Each folder at the top holds one kind of thing, and modules add their folders beside core's. The administrator owns / and the system folders, most of them with the mode 0755 : every account may read and pass through them, and only the administrator changes them. Your own data lives in /archive and in your home. Permissions in depth lists the owner and mode of each standard folder.

/archive holds what someone would be upset to lose. Core makes /archive and the label tree; every other folder in it comes from a module. Each module names the folders its content lives in, and setting the module up creates the ones that are missing. Removing a module never removes them, since they hold the content. Path What is there From /archive/albums Albums, and the photos, videos, recordings and documents in them Archive /archive/people People, each with folders such as children, partners, homes, events and cameras Archive /archive/people/unknown People face recognition found but nobody has named yet; naming one moves it up into /archive/people Archive /archive/locations Locations, each with its outline on the map as a child position node Archive /archive/cameras Cameras, phones and scanners; a phone's links the device it is part of as a child device link Archive /archive/tags Labels: one folder per label, holding a link to everything that carries it Core So an instance without the Archive has /archive/tags and nothing else under /archive . A folder that already exists is left as it is, whoever owns it. /archive itself has the mode 0771 : everyone may pass through, but only the users group, which every account belongs to, may list it. The folders a module makes are 0775 , owned by admin with the group users , so everyone with an account may add content there. What each album, person or location then shows to whom is its own sharing; see Sharing . With the Archive, a photo is a node with children of its own: what EiN works out about it, such as its EXIF, its thumbnails and the faces found on it, is kept beneath the photo and goes with it when it is moved or deleted. Nodes and node types describes what a node holds.

Every account has a home, /home/<username> , made with the account. Helen Okafor's account helen has /home/helen . In the terminal ~ stands for it, and cd alone goes there. You land in it when you log in over SSH or SFTP. Your home is yours, in your own group, with the mode 0751 : others may pass through to something inside it you have shared, and can list nothing. What is made in it takes that from it, so nothing there is shared with others until you share it. Path in your home What it is From .config Your preferences, as CFG_USER_… settings; see Your profile Core .bashrc Your own shell settings, read by every shell you open; see The shell language Core .bash_history The commands you have typed Core stars/ Your favourites, as links to what you hearted Core .trash/ Your trash: each entry holds the node you moved there until you restore it or it is emptied Core .ui/nav.json Your changes to the sidebar and top bar; see Your sidebar and top bar Core .ssh/ Your SSH keys: authorized_keys for signing in, and the keys and known_hosts the ssh command uses Core .chats/ Your conversations with the assistant, private to you Assistant staging/ Uploads waiting for you to sort them; see Sorting in staging Archive Most of these appear only once something needs them. Names starting with a dot are left out by ls ; ls -A , or its alias la , shows them. With the Archive, your staging folder has the mode 0700 , and its files stay out of everyone else's view, search included. It has four folders of its own: Path in staging/ What it holds files/<category>/ The files to sort, by category; uploads go to files/inbox/ albums/<category>/ The groups staging suggests for each category journal/ What you decided in staging routes/ GPX files waiting for the device they belong to Neither your trash nor, with the Archive, your staging is part of the library: search, and the Archive's Media and Year pages, map and On this day , leave out everything in them.

A group the administrator has given a shared home has a folder here, /groups/<group> . Everyone with an account is in the users group, which has one from the start: /groups/users is the household's. The administrator gives other groups one, such as /groups/family ; see Accounts and groups . A group's home belongs to the group, with the mode 0770 : its members read and write everything in it, and nobody else sees it. What is made in it, however deep, stays the whole group's. ls /groups therefore lists the homes of your own groups and nothing else. Modules keep a group's things here, such as its lists in todos/ with Todo . .ui/nav.json holds the group's changes to the sidebar and top bar, and .ui/nav.d the entries of the modules kept to the group; see Your sidebar and top bar .

/etc holds what a person declares: the accounts, the settings and what runs. The administrator owns it. Path What it is /etc/users/<name> An account, as a user node holding its password and the link to the person it is /etc/groups/<group> A group; its members are links in users/ beneath it /etc/config The system's settings, as CFG_… lines, written by Settings and config set /etc/keys The secret settings, such as API keys, readable by the administrator alone /etc/config.d/<module> A module's own settings file, linked in from the module /etc/environment The settings the deployment started EiN with, written again at every start /etc/bashrc Read by every shell: aliases, the history size, and the lines that read the settings files /etc/layout The folder variables, such as LOGS_PATH , written at every start and read by /etc/bashrc /etc/services The services EiN can run ( available/ ) and those it starts ( enabled/ ) /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json Each module's sidebar and top-bar entries /etc/ui/nav.json The administrator's changes to the navigation, laid over every module's /etc/fstab Mounts recorded with mount --save , mounted again at every start /etc/frozen-uploads The types of upload that are frozen as they arrive /etc/ssh_host_key The SSH server's host key /etc/init , /etc/files The scripts EiN runs as it starts With the assistant installed, /etc/assistant-prompt.md holds the instructions the assistant is given, and /etc/assistant.d/<module> what each module tells it. Configuration explains how the settings files combine, and Accounts and groups the accounts.

/var is the machine's own state, written by EiN as it runs. Every folder in it is made at start, so ls /var reads the same on a fresh instance as on one that has run for a year. Path What it is /var/logs/system The system log /var/logs/metrics Measurements of the machine and of EiN over time, for the Status page /var/logs/services/<name> Each service's output /var/logs/jobs/<pid> The output of a job started with nohup /var/sessions The open sessions: one node per session, from a browser or over SSH /var/links Share links: one node per link that opens something without an account /var/queues Queues of events waiting to be handled, the pipeline engine's in pipeline-engine /var/pools Pools of jobs waiting for a worker, such as the Archive's for the media service /var/pipelines/definitions The pipelines the modules define /var/pipelines/instances The pipeline runs, finished and in progress /var/www The sites the web server serves, as links to the Web UI /var/lib/modules The modules mod install installed, one folder each Changes under /var are left out of the audit trail. Changes and pipelines follows work through the queues and pools, and Services and logs shows how to read the logs.

/usr holds code and files nobody edits. An update of EiN replaces what core brings, and mod install what a module brings. Path What it is /usr/bin Core's commands, one command node each: /usr/bin/ls is the ls command /usr/lib Core's other files: its bash commands in core/bin , its services, and the Web UI /usr/modules/<name> Each installed module, a link to its folder in /var/lib/modules /usr/docs/guide This guide, bundled with EiN, which Documentation in the sidebar shows Your PATH holds /usr/bin , /usr/lib/core/bin and each module's bin folder, so a module's commands run by name as soon as it is set up. Modules explains where installed modules are kept.

/dev holds the devices: each sensor, plug, button, phone or GPS logger EiN knows is a folder /dev/<device> , its readings, positions and switches the nodes in it. A driver makes the devices it finds, and members of the devices group make the others with device-create . /dev itself stays the administrator's, with the mode 0755 ; a device is the administrator's and the group devices ', 0770 , read by its members and by whoever a member shares it with. Devices, endpoints and drivers describes them. Beside the devices are EiN's own nodes. /dev/events and /dev/pipeline-events are router nodes: modules announce the facts they derive from changes to the tree on /dev/events , and the pipeline engine announces its own progress on /dev/pipeline-events ; see Changes and pipelines . Both are the administrator's alone, with the mode 0700 . /dev/null works as on Linux: reading it gives nothing, and what is written to it is thrown away. /tmp is open to everyone, with the mode 0777 , and is kept in memory: what you put there is gone when EiN restarts. A file directly in /tmp that has not changed for a day is removed before that; Hours in /tmp , CFG_TMP_RETENTION_HOURS , sets how long. Use it for files you need only for a moment.

p.h: Find a folder by its variable
p.x: Every shell has a variable for each standard folder, so a script does not have to spell the path out. On an EiN with the Archive installed: # in EiN's terminal cd $LOGS_PATH ls $ARCHIVE_PATH echo $HOME albums cameras locations people tags /home/helen Variable Path ARCHIVE_PATH /archive TAGS_PATH /archive/tags HOMES_PATH /home GROUP_HOMES_PATH /groups HOME your own home ETC_PATH /etc USERS_PATH /etc/users GROUPS_PATH /etc/groups SERVICES_PATH /etc/services VAR_PATH /var LOGS_PATH /var/logs SESSIONS_PATH /var/sessions LINKS_PATH /var/links QUEUES_PATH /var/queues POOLS_PATH /var/pools PIPELINES_PATH /var/pipelines WWW_PATH /var/www MOD_INSTALL_PATH /var/lib/modules USR_PATH /usr BIN_PATH /usr/bin LIB_PATH /usr/lib MOD_PATH /usr/modules DOCS_PATH /usr/docs TEMP_PATH /tmp Environment variables lists them all with the rest of the shell's environment.

p.h: Parts of the tree that live elsewhere
p.x: Most of the tree is kept in PostgreSQL, but a folder can be a mount : its contents come from somewhere else, and its path looks like any other. mount without arguments lists them: # in EiN's terminal mount / pg rw 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /etc/files filesystem r 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /tmp memory rw 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /tmp/dev-modules filesystem r 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /usr/bin command r 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /usr/docs/guide filesystem r 3 Oct 2026 09:14:04 /usr/lib filesystem r 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 /var/lib/modules filesystem rw 3 Oct 2026 09:14:02 Type Where its contents are pg The database: the root, and everything not mounted elsewhere filesystem A folder on the machine's disk, such as the built-in guide or the installed modules command EiN's own commands, as nodes memory EiN's memory, gone at a restart sftp A folder on another machine, reached over SFTP r marks a mount nobody can write to, whatever the modes say. Only the administrator mounts and unmounts. Reaching other machines shows how to mount a folder of another machine, and Files and storage where the bytes of the files in the database's part of the tree are kept.

The tree looks the same through every interface, and each shows you only what you may read. In the terminal , cd moves around, ls lists a folder, ls -l adds each node's type, mode, owner, group, size and time, and find searches under a path: # in EiN's terminal cd /archive/people ls -l find /archive/people -maxdepth 1 - type person | wc -l du -chs /archive/albums/christmas-2019 The terminal has more commands for getting around, and The shell language how paths with spaces and wildcards work. On the Nodes page , a file manager over the whole tree. Administrators find it as Nodes under System in the sidebar; its address is /system/nodes , and /system/nodes?path=/archive/albums opens it at a given folder. The Nodes page shows the tree as it is, with each node's type, mode, owner and group. Click a segment of the path above the list to go up to it, or click beside the segments to type a path and press Enter . Up and Home beside it go to the folder above and to your home. Double-click a folder, or press Enter , to go into it. Click a node to select it; Ctrl and click adds or removes one, Shift and click takes a run, Ctrl + A takes them all. On a touch screen, press and hold a node to start picking: a tap then adds or removes one, until none is left selected. Right-click a node, or press and hold a selected one on a touch screen, for Open , Cut , Copy , Paste , Rename , Delete , New directory , Properties and Open terminal here . Tools at the top right opens a pane with the selected node's Preview , Attributes and Sharing ; Split opens a second list beside the first. Properties ( Alt + Enter ) shows and changes a node's owner, group and mode; Permissions in depth describes it. Over SFTP , the tree is a set of folders and files you can open in a file manager or with sftp and scp , as SSH and SFTP describes.

p.h: What you see is yours to see
p.x: A folder lists only what you may read. Something private to someone else is not listed to you at all, so two people can see the same folder differently, and a folder can look empty to you and not be. An administrator sees everything. Permissions in depth has the rules, and Links explains the links that put one node in several folders, such as a label's or a favourite's.

ls /archive shows only tags . The Archive module is not installed. An administrator installs it on Settings → Modules ; see Modules . A file I put in /tmp is gone. /tmp is kept in memory and emptied when EiN restarts, and a file left directly in it is removed after a day. Keep what you need in your home or, with the Archive, in an album. mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount . Mounting is for the administrator. A folder holds more than I see, or will not be deleted. Something in it is hidden from you. Ask its owner or an administrator; Sharing explains why. I cannot find something I deleted. If you moved it to the trash, it is under Trash in your account menu and in ~/.trash , and no list or search shows it until you restore it; see Your profile, favourites and trash . What rm deleted is gone.

Nodes and node types : what a node is and holds. Links : softlinks and hard links, which put one node in several places. Files and storage : where the bytes of files are kept on disk. Changes and pipelines : what happens when something in the tree changes. Permissions in depth : owners, groups, modes and access lists. Node types : every type of node. Environment variables : every variable, the folder variables among them.

A link lets one node be in more than one place in EiN's tree. This page explains the two kinds, softlinks and hard links, where EiN makes them for you, and what moving, deleting and the trash do to them. It is for anyone who works in the terminal , over SFTP or in the Nodes explorer, and wants to know why things in the tree are where they are. Links are core's. The examples use folders such as /archive/albums and /archive/people , which exist with the Archive installed, and the Archive makes many of the links you meet. Note A share link , the address you send to someone without an account, is a different thing. Sharing covers it.

Softlink Hard link What it is A node of its own, of type softlink , that holds the path of another node The same node under a second name, in a second folder Made with ln -s <target> <link_name> , ln -s over SFTP, and EiN itself ln <target> <link_name> Can point at nothing Yes: its target may be missing or gone No: it is the node Deleting it Removes the link, never its target Removes one name; the node goes with its last name Used by EiN Everywhere one thing belongs in several places Nowhere by itself Almost every link you meet in EiN is a softlink. When this documentation says "link" without more, it means a softlink.

A softlink stores a path, nothing else. Opening it opens the node at that path: ls , cat , cd and the Web UI all go through to the target, as they do on Unix. If the target has links of its own on the way, those are followed too, up to 40 in a row; past that EiN stops with too many levels of symbolic links . The path is kept exactly as it was given: An absolute target, starting with / , means the same node wherever the link is. A relative target is read from the folder that holds the link. EiN uses one for enabled services: /etc/services/enabled/<name> points at ../available/<name> . EiN does not check that the target exists when you make a softlink, so a link can point at nothing from the start.

p.h: Where EiN makes softlinks for you
p.x: You make most links without typing ln : a button in the Web UI or a command writes them. What you do The link it makes Put a label on something ( Labels ) A link in /archive/tags/<label>/ to what carries it Heart a picture ( Favourites ) A link in /home/<you>/stars/ to the picture Put someone in a group ( Accounts and groups ) A link in /etc/groups/<group>/users/ , named after the account, to /etc/users/<account> With the Archive installed, its pages and commands make these too: What you do The link it makes Add a picture to an album from elsewhere ( Albums ) A link in the album, named after the picture, to where the picture lives Choose an album's, person's, location's or camera's cover coverPhoto in it, to the picture Set an album's Previous album or Next album previous and next in the album, and the matching one back in the other album Add a parent, partner or child ( Family tree ) A pair: one in parents/ , children/ or partners/ of each person, pointing at the other Add a home or a resident A pair: one in the person's homes/ , one in the location's residents/ Link a picture to a location ( Locations ) location in the picture, to the location Choose Written by on an event ( Albums ) writer in the event, to the person A linked picture is never copied. With the Archive, one photo in five albums is one node with five links to it, so a date, a place, a face or a label given to it shows in all five. One picture, many places: everything that points at it is a softlink, and the picture itself lives in one folder.

A pair of softlinks, one on each side, ties two nodes together; with the Archive, that is how two people are related and who lived where. Each half knows where the other half is, so the two stay together: Removing a relation with unrelate , or with the Archive's pages and person-remove , removes both halves. When one side is deleted for good, the relations-guard service removes the other half. With the Archive, when a person is moved, or merged into another with person-merge , the pairs follow. You can make a pair of your own between any two nodes with relate . It puts the links in a relations/ folder of each node, named <label>-<name of the other> : # in EiN's terminal relate /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield /archive/people/helen-okafor godmother --reverse goddaughter Created bidirectional relation: /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield <-godmother/goddaughter-> /archive/people/helen-okafor unrelate /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield/relations/godmother-helen-okafor removes both halves again. relate refuses a pair that is already there with relate: relation already exists: and the path.

A hard link gives a node a second name. Both names are the same node: the same id, the same owner and mode, the same content and children. Nothing marks one name as the original. # in EiN's terminal ln /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg /home/helen/20191225_155434.jpg Each node counts its names. The count is the third column of ls -l , and Links in the Nodes explorer's Properties ; a node with one name shows 1 . Removing a name with rm lowers the count, and the node itself is deleted only when its last name goes. rm -r on a folder that still has another name removes only that name and leaves everything in it. EiN makes no hard links of its own, and the Web UI has no way to make one. ln refuses one between two different stores, for example into a mounted folder of another machine, with cannot link across different VFS backends , and SFTP has no hard links. Warning A hard link can make a node visible where its other path is closed. A node with a name in an open folder can be reached through that name, whatever the folder of its other name allows. Permissions in depth explains why.

In the terminal. ls -l ends a softlink's line with -> and its target. find -type l lists the softlinks under a folder. Commands follow softlinks unless you ask them not to: Command Without -L With -L ls Lists what the link points at Lists the link itself stat , info Show the target Show the link, its target in softlink chmod , chown , acl , attrs , props Act on the target Act on the link -L means "do not follow" in EiN, which is the opposite of GNU ls -L . # in EiN's terminal ls -l /archive/tags/sailing stat -L /archive/albums/christmas-2019/coverPhoto EiN has no readlink command, and nothing lists the links that point at a node. In the Nodes explorer. A softlink shows a link icon, with → and its target after its name. Select it and choose Properties ( Alt + Enter ) to see Link to with the target and Links with the count of names. A person's folder holds folders of relation links and a cover link; the arrow shows where the link points. Over SFTP. Softlinks are symbolic links: ls -l in sftp shows them as links, following one takes you to the target, and ln -s makes one. How a recursive copy treats a link depends on your SFTP client. SSH and SFTP has the rest.

p.h: Make and remove links in the terminal
p.x: Make a softlink with ln -s , the target first: # in EiN's terminal ln -s /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg /home/helen/favourite.jpg Check it with ls -l /home/helen . The line for favourite.jpg ends with -> /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg . Remove it with rm /home/helen/favourite.jpg . That removes the link only; the picture stays. If the name is taken, ln stops with ln: failed to create link '<name>': File exists . ln -f replaces what is there. Unlike GNU ln , an existing folder as the second argument is not a place to put the link in: name the link in full. For links that EiN keeps track of, use the command that owns them rather than ln and rm . A label lives on the node that carries it, and searches read it there, so the link in /archive/tags/ alone does not label anything: To change Use Labels label add , label remove Favourites star , star -d Relations between nodes relate , unrelate Family ties and homes, with the Archive the person-… commands in Family tree, events and homes An album's cover, with the Archive album set <album> cover <picture> Group membership group-add-member , group-remove-member

When a node moves, every softlink that points at it, or at anything under it, is re-pointed to the new path in the same step. With the Archive, an album can therefore be moved without losing its cover, its labels, its place in other albums or anyone's favourites. This holds for mv , for Rename and Paste in the Nodes explorer, and, with the Archive, for filing pictures from staging into an album. Merging people or duplicates moves the links to the one that is kept. Two kinds of softlink are not re-pointed: one with a relative target, which keeps its text as it was; any link when you move with mv --no-relink , which leaves them all on the old path. One mv re-points at most 100,000 links. A move that more links point into is refused with more than 100000 links point into the moved paths; move fewer at a time . mv says nothing about the links on success. Run as JSON_OUTPUT=1 mv … , its answer counts them in relinked . With the Archive, renaming an album in Edit album changes only its name on the page; its folder keeps its first name, so no link needs to change.

What happens to links depends on how a node goes. Your profile, favourites and trash lists which actions use the trash. What you do The link you act on Links pointing at the node With the Archive, remove a picture from an album ( Remove ) That album's link goes Others are left alone; the picture stays where it lives Move a node to the trash — Left as they are. They point at nothing while it is in the trash, and work again when you restore it Delete for good, or empty the trash — Label links and the other half of every pair are removed by relations-guard . Covers, album links and favourites are left pointing at nothing rm a softlink The link goes — rm a node with hard links One name goes — While something is in the trash it is gone for everyone, including through the links to it. A node with a hard link elsewhere is different: moving one of its names to the trash leaves it reachable by its other name.

What you see What it means What to do Node not found: and a path, when you open a link The link points at nothing: its target was deleted, is in someone's trash, or was moved with --no-relink Restore the target from the trash, point the link again with ln -sf , or remove it with rm too many levels of symbolic links Links point at each other in a loop, or a chain is longer than 40 Look at the targets with ls -l and correct one A label is still listed with nothing behind it A link in /archive/tags/<label>/ points at something gone label prune removes every label link that points at nothing The other half of a family tie is missing One half was removed while relations-guard was not running With the Archive, person-check /archive/people reports broken ties; remove the tie and add it again Labels or relation halves stay after something is deleted for good The relations-guard service is stopped An administrator checks it with service-status ; see Services and logs ln: failed to access '<target>': No such file or directory A hard link needs an existing target Check the path, or make a softlink with -s Access denied for operation when you follow a link A softlink is not a way in: you need access along the target's own path Ask the target's owner to share it

Nodes and node types : what a node is, the softlink type among them The tree : the folders the links live in and point into Files and storage : what a file node holds Albums : adding, removing and deleting pictures Permissions in depth : why a softlink grants nothing and a hard link can Commands: ln , mv , relate , label Node types : the reference entry for softlink

This page explains how EiN keeps the content of files: what a file node records about its bytes, where the bytes are kept on the machine, and what copying, moving and deleting do to them. It is for anyone who wants to know where their photos are, and for the administrator who looks after the disk. Files and their storage are core's. The examples use a photo in an album, /archive/albums/christmas-2019 , a path that exists with the Archive installed, and what the Archive makes from a file is marked as such.

p.h: A file is a node with bytes
p.x: A photo, a video, a recording, a scanned letter and a text you write in the editor are all nodes of type file . Like every node, a file has a name in its folder, an owner, a group, permissions and an id. What sets it apart is that it holds bytes, and its attributes describe them: Attribute What it is name The file's name. mimetype What kind of file it is, such as image/jpeg or video/mp4 . Supported files explains how EiN tells. size The size of the content in bytes. sha256 The SHA-256 checksum of the content. writtenAt When the content last changed. description A description, when someone wrote one. sourceId On a file EiN made from another one, such as a thumbnail, the id of the file it was made from. frozen When true , the content cannot be written, in EiN or on the disk. See Frozen files . A media file carries more once the Archive has read it, such as the time it was taken and its orientation; Nodes and node types describes a node part by part. The bytes are kept apart from the node and are found by the node's id, not by its name or path. Renaming a file or moving it to another folder changes the tree and leaves the bytes where they are, however large the file is. To see a file's attributes, ask for the node in JSON and pick them out: # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 stat /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg | jq '.attrs | {name, mimetype, size, sha256, writtenAt}' { "name" : "20191225_155434.jpg" , "mimetype" : "image/jpeg" , "size" : 4182311 , "sha256" : "9f2c41d07a6e3b58c1d4e2f09a7b36c5d18e4f20b9a63c7d5e1f08a2b4c69d3e" , "writtenAt" : "2025-12-27T18:04:11.402Z" }

p.h: What a file keeps beneath it
p.x: Any node can have children, and a file uses this to keep what EiN works out about it. With the Archive, a photo holds: Child What it is metadata/ What was read from the file, such as its EXIF in metadata/exif and the text read from it thumbnails/ The sizes the Web UI shows, and for a video or recording the versions a browser plays regions/ The faces found on it and the boxes people drew position Where it was taken, when that is known comments/ The comments people wrote on it These are nodes like any other, and many of them are files with bytes of their own. The original's bytes are never changed: when you turn a picture or correct its date, EiN changes what it keeps beside the file, not the file. Deleting the file deletes everything beneath it. Over SFTP these children are in a hidden folder named after the file with _ added, as SSH and SFTP describes.

EiN keeps the bytes of files in three places, called tiers. Each file's bytes are on exactly one: Tier What goes there Where it is in a standard install disk Your originals: every file you upload or write, unless it belongs to another tier files in the data folder volatile What EiN makes from another file and can make again: with the Archive, thumbnails, playable videos and recordings, face crops files-volatile in the data folder db Small content that belongs with the database: the settings file, comments, SSH keys and known_hosts , the host keys of EiN's SSH server, password hashes, /etc/fstab , and with the Archive the events in a person's story, the text read from pictures and documents, and staging's record of what you sorted Large objects in PostgreSQL, in the data folder's db EiN decides the tier when the file is made: A file that names the file it was made from in sourceId goes on volatile , unless it is frozen. Everything else goes on disk . Content that belongs with the database is put on db by the command that writes it. The tier is fixed once the file exists, because the bytes stay where they were first written. Trying to change it fails with storage tier is set once at creation and cannot be changed . To make a file on a tier of your choosing, give it when you make the file: # in EiN's terminal mknode -t file /home/anna/notes/recipes.txt --as mimetype=text/plain --tier db --tier takes disk , volatile or db ; see mknode . Because the volatile tier holds only what EiN can make again, it can sit on a faster or cheaper disk than your originals. The deployment sets the two places with FILE_ROOT_PATH and VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH ; when the second is not set, both tiers share the first. Environment variables lists both.

In a standard install, the data folder is ~/ein/data unless you chose another place at the install. EiN sees its folders at fixed paths inside its container: Folder in the data folder Path inside EiN What it holds files /files the disk tier: your originals files-volatile /files-volatile the volatile tier: thumbnails and other renditions old /old files kept from an older installation, which EiN reads but never writes; empty unless you put files there The media service, which the Archive needs, mounts none of these folders: it reaches the files of each request through EiN, which serves it those files alone, by names of their own, while the request runs. A tool there reads only the part of a file it needs, so the files on the disk and volatile tiers are not copied before it starts. It may read your originals but never write them. Installing in detail has the whole layout, and The media service how the two share it. Inside files and files-volatile , each file's bytes are stored under its node id, in a folder named after the id's last two characters: files/ ├── 1C/ │ └── 01JFX7Q2M8K4T6V9B3N5R0WD1C ├── 7H/ │ ├── 01JFX7Q3A2P9S4D8F6G1J5K07H │ └── 01JG2B8E5C7X1Z3V6N9M4Q2R7H … There are no file names, albums or folders here; they are in the database. To find where one file's bytes are, ask file-stat for its path: # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 file-stat /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg | jq -r .path /files/1C/01JFX7Q2M8K4T6V9B3N5R0WD1C The path is the one inside EiN's container; on the machine it is the same file under the data folder, here ~/ein/data/files/1C/01JFX7Q2M8K4T6V9B3N5R0WD1C . A file on the db tier has no path. Warning Leave the folders in the data folder to EiN. A file changed there by hand no longer matches the size and checksum its node records, and a file deleted there leaves a node whose content is gone. Copy files in through the Web UI, SFTP or the terminal instead. The data folder and the database belong together: the folders hold bytes named by ids, and only the database knows which id is which photo, in which album, owned by whom. Neither is any use without the other. Your data says what to back up and how to move EiN to another machine.

p.h: Size, checksum and when the content changed
p.x: EiN keeps a file's size , sha256 and writtenAt up to date as the bytes are written, whichever way they come in: an upload, SFTP, the editor or a shell redirect such as > . You never run anything to bring them up to date. Attribute What depends on it size Listings, du , and a download's length sha256 With the Archive, finding exact copies of a file ( Duplicates ), noticing that a file arriving in staging is already in the archive, and telling the Archive that a file's content changed so it reads it again writtenAt The modification time SFTP reports, so a backup tool or rsync sees a photo as unchanged while EiN is still working out its faces and description writtenAt is when the bytes last changed. A node also has a modification time of its own, which moves whenever any attribute changes; that is why SFTP reports writtenAt instead. A client that sets the time, such as put -p in sftp or rsync -t , sets writtenAt . While content is being written somewhere other than from the start in order, the checksum is cleared, and EiN reads the finished file back once to measure it. A file whose writing stopped part-way has no checksum rather than a wrong one. Adding to the end of a file that already has content, such as echo line >> notes.txt , clears the checksum and leaves it cleared: measuring it would read the whole file every time a line is added. size and writtenAt still follow, and the next write that replaces the content, or file-sync , gives the file a checksum again. Three commands look at the bytes themselves rather than at what the node records: Command What it does file-stat <path> The size, times, permissions and path of the bytes as they are stored. -f also measures the checksum and the type, which reads the whole file. file-sync <path> Measures the size, checksum and type of the bytes and writes them onto the node. For a file whose bytes changed without EiN seeing it. mime <path> The type the node records, the type its name suggests and the type its first bytes say. See file-stat , file-sync and mime .

p.h: How bytes come in and go out
p.x: Every way in writes through the same place, so each one records size, checksum and time, and checks your permissions the same way. Way What happens to the bytes An upload in the Web UI Stored as a new file. An upload never replaces a file: when the name is taken, it is stored as IMG_0001 (2).jpg , then IMG_0001 (3).jpg , and so on. A picture, video or recording is frozen once it has arrived. With the Archive, Getting your photos in has the ways to upload. Saving in the editor Replaces the content of the file you opened. See The editor . SFTP, scp and sshfs Written as on any SFTP server, and frozen as an upload is. See SSH and SFTP . A shell redirect, cp , unzip Written by the command, in EiN's terminal or over SSH. unzip refuses an archive whose files would not leave a tenth of their size free. Download in the Web UI The original's bytes, exactly as they were uploaded. Downloading several files at once One zip of at most 5000 files, made while it downloads. The files are stored in it, not compressed, since photos and videos are compressed already.

A frozen file keeps the content it arrived with. EiN refuses to write it, and its bytes on the disk are read-only as well, so a program on the machine that reaches them cannot change them either: a photo editor saving into one of the album folders , say. Everything else about the file can still change: its name and folder, its attributes, what EiN keeps beneath it, and it can be deleted. What is frozen: An upload in the Web UI, with POST or PUT on /file/… , or over SFTP, scp and sshfs, whose type /etc/frozen-uploads lists. As EiN comes, that is every picture, video and recording except an SVG; text, documents, scripts and settings files stay writable. The file is frozen once the whole of it has arrived, so an upload that stopped part-way can be sent again. A file taken out of an uploaded zip , with unzip --as-upload , whose type /etc/frozen-uploads lists, as if it had been uploaded on its own. With the Archive, a zip or a Google Takeout export uploaded into staging is taken apart this way. A copy of a frozen file , made with cp . A file marked by hand , with attrs -J frozen=true <file> . What EiN writes itself is not frozen by /etc/frozen-uploads : a file made in the terminal or with a redirect, the files unzip takes out of a zip without --as-upload , and everything EiN makes from a file, such as its thumbnails. /etc/frozen-uploads lists one type per line. image/* stands for every type of picture, and a ! in front leaves a type out: # /etc/frozen-uploads, as EiN comes image/* video/* audio/* !image/svg+xml The administrator may change it with edit ; it applies to the next upload. An empty file freezes no upload. Configuration files says more. To change a frozen file, lift the mark first. Only someone who may change the file can: # in EiN's terminal attrs -d frozen /archive/albums/christmas-2019/20191225_155434.jpg On the disk, a frozen file's bytes lose their write permissions, 0644 becoming 0444 , and lifting the mark gives the owner's back. A file whose bytes are kept elsewhere, behind a link, such as files kept from an older installation in old , is left as it is.

What happens to the bytes depends on the command: What you do What happens to the bytes Rename or move a file, mv Nothing. The node keeps its id, and its bytes stay where they are. Move a file into or out of a mount (see below) The file is copied to the other side and then removed, so it gets a new id and its bytes are written again. Copy a file, cp A new node with a copy of the bytes. The copy takes as much space again, and has the same checksum. Make a hard link, ln The same node under a second name. There is one copy of the bytes. Make a softlink, ln -s , or, with the Archive, add a picture to an album from elsewhere A link that points at the file by its path. It has no bytes of its own. Put a file in the trash The file moves into your trash with its bytes, and comes back whole when you restore it. Delete a file, rm , or empty the trash The node goes, with everything beneath it. Its bytes are removed once the last name the node has is gone. What is in your trash keeps its room on the disk. It is removed for good once it has been there longer than Days in the trash , CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS , 30 days unless the administrator changes it. rm , a file removed over SFTP and Empty trash do not wait; what they delete is gone at once. Links explains what deleting does to the links to a file, and Your profile, favourites and trash shows the trash in the Web UI.

p.h: Mounts: parts of the tree kept elsewhere
p.x: Most of the tree is stored in PostgreSQL, with its files' bytes on the tiers above. A few parts of it are kept elsewhere, each mounted at a path the way a disk is mounted on Linux. mount with no arguments lists them, with rw or r for whether they can be written: # in EiN's terminal mount The mounts every EiN makes at its start: Path Kind What it is / pg The tree itself, in PostgreSQL, with the three tiers /usr/bin command EiN's built-in commands, one node each /usr/lib filesystem Core's own files, read-only /etc/files filesystem The scripts EiN runs at its start, read-only /tmp memory Scratch space, held in memory. It is empty again after every restart. /tmp/dev-modules filesystem Modules that come with the deployment itself, read-only /var/lib/modules filesystem The modules installed with mod install , in the data folder's modules folder /usr/docs/guide filesystem This guide, as EiN was built with it, read-only A filesystem mount shows a folder of the machine, and an sftp mount shows a folder of another machine. Both are mirrors: their files are the other side's files, and nothing is stored about them in EiN. A file in a mirror cannot have children, so EiN makes no thumbnails, reads no dates and finds no faces in them, and changes in an sftp mount start no pipelines at all. With the Archive, to bring files from a mount into the archive, copy them into staging. Only the administrator mounts and unmounts. Reaching other machines shows how to mount a folder of another machine and keep the mount across restarts, and The tree describes every standard path.

p.h: See how much space is used
p.x: df shows how full the disk under each tier is, how fast it is filling and when it will be full, and the size of the database: # in EiN's terminal df tier disk 12% used 801 GB free full in ~912d tier volatile 12% used 801 GB free full in ~912d database 3.4 GB In a standard install the two folders are on one disk, so they show the same figures, and full in appears once EiN has measured the disk long enough to see it fill. The Storage card on the Status shows the same; see Health and status . du adds up the sizes of the files under a path, including what each file keeps beneath it, such as its thumbnails. It counts a file reached by two names once and does not follow softlinks, so a picture added to an album from elsewhere is counted where it lives. It counts only what you may read. # in EiN's terminal du -sh /archive/albums/christmas-2019 1.8 GB /archive/albums/christmas-2019 Your data shows how to measure the data folder from the machine itself, and Delete things and free space how to make room.

What you see Why What to do With the Archive, a picture's thumbnail is missing although the picture was read long ago Its rendition was never finished, or its bytes on the volatile tier are gone. Run regenerate --force on the picture or its album. See regenerate . A file's size or checksum is wrong after it was changed outside EiN The bytes changed without passing through EiN, so the node was not told. Run file-sync on the file. file is frozen and cannot be modified , an upload refused with 403, or Permission denied over SFTP The file is marked frozen , so its content cannot be written. Leave its content as it is, or upload the new version under another name. Someone who may change the file can lift the mark with attrs -d frozen <file> ; see Frozen files . storage tier is set once at creation and cannot be changed A command tried to move a file to another tier. Copy the content into a new file made with --tier , then remove the old one. a filesystem is mounted at /mnt/nas when removing or moving a folder A mount stands on that folder or below it. Unmount it first with unmount , or unmount --save to keep it from coming back at the next start. mount: permission denied, only admin is allowed to mount Only the administrator mounts. Ask the administrator. df says no disk sample yet — is metrics-sampler running? The service that measures the disk has not taken a sample yet, or is not running. It takes its first sample as it starts, so wait a minute. If it stays, see Services and logs . unzip says not enough space The files in the zip would not leave a tenth of their size free. Free space on the disk, or expand the zip on a machine with room and copy the files in. Troubleshooting covers a disk that has filled up and other problems of the whole installation.

This page follows a change through EiN, from the moment a node is saved to the finished work it sets off: the events every change announces, the facts a module derives from them, the pipelines that act on those facts, and the audit trail that leads back from each result to the change that caused it. It is for administrators who want to understand what the Status shows, and for anyone writing a module or a pipeline of their own. The machinery is core's: the events, the engine, the pools and the audit trail. Core ships no pipelines and announces no facts, so the examples come from the Archive : its facts, pipelines, workers and paths such as /archive/albums exist with it installed.

When EiN saves a change to the tree, it announces it as an event. Six kinds exist: Event What happened The event names created A node was made the node updated A node's attributes, bytes or permissions changed the node deleted A node's last name went, and the node with it the node moved A node was moved or renamed the node child-attached Something was put into a folder, by making, linking or moving it the folder child-detached Something left a folder, by removing, unlinking or moving it the folder Each event goes out under a key made of the node's type and the event, system.vfs.<nodeType>.<eventType> : a photo's new size is system.vfs.file.updated , a photo added to an album system.vfs.album.child-attached . Whoever listens binds only the keys it cares about, so a listener for files never hears about the thousands of small writes a busy system makes elsewhere. Only the administrator binds a queue, a log or a track to keys (their routingKeys attribute), or sets the key of a router (its routingKey ), as EiN's services and pipelines do: a message goes to whoever is bound, whether or not they may read the node it is about, so anyone else is refused with Access denied for operation 'change routingKeys' (or 'change routingKey' ). The event is sent only after the change is saved: nothing reacts to a change that did not happen. The same write also leaves a record in the audit trail, in the same transaction, so a record exists exactly when the change does. Trace a result back to its cause shows how to read it.

A raw event says that a node changed. Most work needs to know something more specific: that a new photo has arrived and has not been read yet, or that its metadata is now there. Modules state this as facts , named like media.file.discovered or media.metadata.extracted , each about one node, its subject. A module that states facts runs a service for it, a bridge: the Media module 's media-bridge for the facts of a media file itself, and the Archive's archive-bridge for its own. A bridge listens for the raw events its rules need, reads the node as it is now, and writes the facts that follow to /dev/events . Because the bridge reads the node rather than trusting the event, a fact always describes the tree as it is, whatever order the events arrive in. And because pipeline steps only write to the tree and the bridge derives the facts from what they wrote, the facts cannot disagree with what is stored. Some of the facts the Media module announces: Fact Announced when media.file.discovered A photo, video or recording has its bytes and no metadata yet media.file.content-changed The bytes of a file already read have changed media.metadata.extracted A file's metadata has been read media.renditions.made A file has every rendition the rendition table names for it And some of the Archive's: Fact Announced when media.metadata.interpreted The Archive has worked out when a file was taken and where media.face.detected A face has been found on a picture (one fact per face) media.faces.completed Face detection is done for a picture, also when it found none media.transcript.generated A video or recording has its transcript media.position.available A file has a GPS position media.album.members-changed An album's photos changed location.changed A location was made, its shape drawn, or a photo linked to it by hand staging.category.changed The files in a staging category changed A fact is a line of JSON. Announcing one is writing that line to /dev/events ; there is no separate command for it. /dev/events is the administrator's alone, to write and to read, as is /dev/pipeline-events : a fact starts pipelines, and it may be about anyone's files. An automation of the administrator's raises one with an event out node , and anyone's automation hears those about the nodes its owner may read: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator echo '{"id":"e1","type":"media.file.discovered","subject":"/archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987/IMG_0042.jpg","time":1790000000000,"data":{"mimetype":"image/jpeg"}}' > /dev/events subject is the node the fact is about, and data carries whatever a pipeline needs to decide whether it applies, such as the file's type. Core announces no facts of its own; without a module the only events are the raw ones.

p.h: A pipeline says what to do with a change
p.x: A pipeline is a YAML definition with three parts: the trigger it waits for, the steps it then runs on the subject, each step a shell command, and options for how it is scheduled. This is the Archive's media-faces , which finds the faces in a picture: name: media-faces description: Detect faces in an image and crop each one trigger: on: media.metadata.interpreted wants: archive match: mimetype: image/* skipIfAttr: facesAt steps: detect-faces: command: detect-faces $NODE_PATH description: Face detection plus a cropped image per face pool: media kind: faces priority: 100 requires: models: 1 options: maxAttempts: 3 priority: 10 It reads: when the Archive has worked out from a file's metadata when and where it was taken, the file is a picture, the folder it lies in wants the Archive's work, and its faces have not been looked for yet, run detect-faces on it, in the media pool, as a job of kind faces that needs one model slot. A module ships its pipelines in its pipelines/ folder, and mod setup registers each one when the module is set up, at every start of EiN. A registered pipeline is a link in /var/pipelines/definitions/<name> to its YAML file. The engine reloads the definitions whenever anything there changes, so a new or changed pipeline takes effect without a restart. Core ships no pipelines. Modules covers installing and removing the modules that bring them. # in EiN's terminal: the pipelines this EiN has pipeline list

A trigger takes one of two forms, never both: Form Keys Starts on A fact on: <fact> or a list of facts a fact on /dev/events ; the preferred form A raw change event: <event> , nodeType: <type> a raw event, such as event: updated with nodeType: file A definition with several ways to start writes triggers: with a list instead of trigger: . Each alternative has its own guards, and the first that matches starts the pipeline. The guards decide whether a matching event starts anything. The engine tests them cheapest first, so most events are turned away without starting a process: Key Starts the pipeline only when match every named field matches its glob, or one of a list of globs: mimetype: 'image/*' unless not every named field matches: nodePath: '/var/**' leaves a whole subtree alone wants the folder the subject lies in wants one of these families of work: wants: renditions (below) allowDerived true lets a derived file, such as a thumbnail or a face crop, start it; without it derived files never do skipIfExists the path does not exist: $NODE_PATH/metadata/exif skipIfAttr the subject does not already have this attribute set: skipIfAttr: textIndexedAt filter this shell script exits 0 skipIf this shell script does not exit 0 In match and unless , a field names a value the event carries: mimetype , nodePath , or any key of a fact's data . In a path field, * matches within one name and ** crosses / , so /home/*/staging/** is everything in each person's staging folder. A trigger may also set priority and vars for the runs it starts.

A folder can say which families of work it wants for what lies under it, with its processing attribute: a list of family names, such as ["renditions"] . The nearest folder with one decides, so a folder inside another can ask for more or for less. With none above a file, every family is wanted; an empty list wants none. A trigger names its family with wants , a list meaning any of them, and starts only where the folder wants one; a trigger that names none starts wherever its event says. The modules name the families of their own pipelines: the Archive's are in Processing pictures . Only the folder's owner or an administrator sets or clears it: attrs -J 'processing=["renditions"]' /home/helen/screenshots # sizes and playable copies, nothing else attrs -d processing /home/helen/screenshots # every family again pipeline start starts a pipeline on a file whatever its folder says.

Each step is a command with a name. Steps without dependsOn start together; a step with dependsOn: [other] waits for those steps to complete. A step's condition is a shell test that decides, when the step's turn comes, whether it runs or is skipped. Key What it does command The command to run. Required description What the step does, shown on the pipeline's page dependsOn The steps that must complete first condition A shell test; the step is skipped when it fails pool Hand the step to a pool of workers, such as media , instead of running it in the engine kind The kind of job in the pool, which decides which worker takes it. Defaults to the step's name requires What the job needs of a worker's capacity: cpu: 1 , models: 1 priority The job's priority in the pool, higher first. Overrides the pipeline's exclusive A name; at most one job with it runs in the whole pool at a time A command and its tests see the subject's path as $NODE_PATH . A run started by a fact also has $EVENT_TYPE , $EVENT_ID , $EVENT_SOURCE , the whole data as JSON in $EVENT_DATA , and each key of data as $EVENT_<NAME> in capitals, with _ between words: data.mimetype is $EVENT_MIMETYPE and data.filePath is $EVENT_FILE_PATH . The guards of a raw-event trigger also see $MIMETYPE , $NODE_TYPE and $EVENT_TYPE ; the steps of a run it starts get $NODE_PATH alone. The name is $NODE_PATH and not $PATH , which the shell needs for finding commands. In a command , write $NODE_PATH bare: EiN substitutes the path already quoted, so a name with spaces is safe. In filter , skipIf and condition the path is an ordinary shell variable, so quote it yourself: info "$NODE_PATH/exif" .

Option What it does Default maxAttempts How many times a step is run before the run fails 3 priority The pipeline's place in line, higher first, among steps waiting to run 0 coalesce What a trigger for a subject whose run is still going does: drop it, or rerun once the run ends drop debounceMs How long a trigger waits before it becomes a run, so a burst of changes to one subject is one run none entryPoint Marks the pipeline every other one waits on, so the Status can say how far an import has got none A definition can also declare vars: with a default for each, which its commands use like $NODE_PATH . pipeline start <name> <path> --var NAME=VALUE changes one for a single run, and the values a run started with are kept on it.

p.h: From a change to a run
p.x: Between a fact and the work it starts, EiN keeps everything it has not done yet as nodes, so nothing is lost when it restarts: The queue. The pipeline engine reads the facts, and the raw events its definitions ask for, from a durable queue, /var/queues/pipeline-engine . A change that arrives while the engine is stopped waits there. The trigger pool. For each pipeline whose trigger and guards match, the engine adds a job to /var/pools/triggers , keyed by the pipeline and the subject. A subject announced ten times while it waits is still one job, and one run. The run. The engine claims those jobs and turns each into an instance , a run of the pipeline on that subject, at /var/pipelines/instances/<pipeline>/<id> . The id is the subject's node id, so a node has at most one instance of each pipeline: a later run replaces the earlier one. The engine takes turns between pipelines, so a long queue of one kind of work does not hold back the others. The steps. The engine starts each step whose dependencies are met. A step without pool runs inside the engine, at most CFG_PIPELINE_MAX_CONCURRENT at a time. A step with pool becomes a job in that pool, such as /var/pools/media , and a worker that has room for it runs it. Pipeline steps change the tree, and those changes are events too. A step that writes to its own subject would start its own pipeline again; the engine recognises this and drops a trigger for a subject whose run of that pipeline is still going, or ended less than five seconds ago. A change after that starts a fresh run. A pipeline whose subject collects many changes, such as an album whose photos keep arriving, sets coalesce: rerun instead: every trigger during a run then adds up to one more run when it ends. A file a step makes from another file, such as a thumbnail, a face crop or a video rendition, records where it came from. Such a derived file starts no pipeline unless the trigger says allowDerived: true , so a face crop is never searched for faces of its own. If the subject is deleted while its run is going, the run is cancelled: its remaining steps are skipped and their pool jobs dropped. A step that was running when it went, and failed for want of it, is skipped too, not failed or retried.

Instance Meaning queued Unfinished, with nothing executing: its steps wait in a pool or on other steps running At least one of its steps is executing right now completed Every step completed or was skipped failed A step ran out of attempts, or failed on its input cancelled Stopped by an administrator, or because its subject was deleted Step Meaning pending Waiting for the steps it depends on queued Ready, waiting for a place in the engine waiting Handed to a pool, waiting for a worker to take it running Executing now completed Finished with exit status 0 failed Out of attempts, or failed on its input skipped Its condition said no, or its run was cancelled After a large upload most instances read queued : the pools work through them a few at a time.

The steps that take real time, reading metadata, making thumbnails, finding faces, transcribing, go to a pool rather than running in the engine. A pool is a node holding jobs, each with a kind, a priority and what it requires. Workers, each a service, offer the pool their free capacity and take the best job that fits: the highest priority first, the oldest among equals. The Media module runs two workers on /var/pools/media , for the lines of work (kinds of job) the modules name for them. With the Archive: Service What it runs Paced by media-worker Reading metadata, thumbnails, renditions, fingerprints, zips, matching faces; the media service makes the pictures Media worker budget , CFG_CPU_SLOTS models Requests to the media service's models: faces, picture and text vectors, text in pictures, transcripts, voices Model requests in flight , CFG_MODEL_SLOTS A third worker, models-second , takes the same model work as models in the reverse order. It is off until Second models worker's slots , CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS , is above 0. Most of these steps are calls into the media service , which does the heavy work; EiN decides what to ask for and stores the answers. A worker holds a lease on each job it runs; if the worker stops, the lease runs out and the job goes back to the pool for another. Media explains how to size the workers.

With the Archive installed, an upload sets off this chain. Each arrow is a fact, and each fact starts its own pipelines: You upload IMG_0042.jpg to an album. When its last byte is written, EiN records its size, checksum and type, an updated event. media-bridge sees a photo with bytes and no metadata and announces media.file.discovered . media-ingest runs exif-extract , which reads the camera, its clocks and its GPS fix and writes them under the photo as metadata/exif . That write becomes media.metadata.extracted , which starts media-stills (the display sizes), the Media module's media-fingerprint (the fingerprints that find copies), and the Archive's media-interpret (when the photo was taken, and where); for a picture also the Media module's media-embed-picture (search by what is in the picture) and media-ocr (text in the picture); for a video media-embed-picture , media-transcode and media-transcribe ; for a recording media-transcode and media-transcribe . They run side by side. Once a file has every rendition the rendition table names for it, it is marked so, which becomes media.renditions.made . media-interpret writes the photo's date and its position, and its last write becomes media.metadata.interpreted , which starts media-faces for a picture, media-video-faces for a video, and media-camera when the metadata names the camera that made the file. media-faces writes each face it finds under the photo, which becomes media.face.detected and starts media-face-assign , matching the face to a person. A GPS position becomes media.position.available , which starts media-geocode for the address, and location.point.changed , which links the photo to the location that contains it and starts media-weather for the weather it was taken in. No stage waits for the one before it to finish; each waits for the fact it needs. Nothing in the chain waits for "the previous step". Each stage waits for a fact, so each can be run again, put first or given its own workers without touching the others. Getting your photos in describes what you see in the interface while this happens. The Media module's pipelines and the Archive's, and what starts them: Pipeline Starts on What it does media-ingest media.file.discovered Reads a file's metadata; every other media pipeline waits on it media-reindex media.file.content-changed Reads the metadata again when a file's bytes changed media-stills media.metadata.extracted , media.renditions.stale A photo's sizes, a video's poster frames and hover clip, a recording's waveform media-transcode media.metadata.extracted , media.file.turned , media.renditions.stale Video and audio the browser can play, a video's storyboard and chapters media-interpret media.metadata.extracted When a file was taken and where, from its metadata, a sidecar and its name media-fingerprint media.metadata.extracted , media.fingerprints.stale The fingerprints that find copies, look-alikes and photo stacks media-faces media.metadata.interpreted , for a picture Finds the faces in a picture and crops each one media-video-faces media.metadata.interpreted , for a video Finds the faces a video shows, and when media-face-assign media.face.detected Attaches a found face to a person media-embed-picture media.metadata.extracted ,
