that made it media-damage media.metadata.interpreted , for a scan, and media.damage.missing How faded, dusty, scratched, blurred and shaken a scan is media-restore media.restore.requested A restoration asked for in the background, into a copy among the versions media-camera-cover media.renditions.made , for a video Offers the video's poster frame to its camera as a cover media-geocode media.position.available The address of a file's GPS position media-weather location.point.changed , media.weather.owed The weather at a photo's position and date location-link-point location.point.changed Links a photo to the location containing its position location-upkeep location.changed Redraws a location and links the photos inside it again media-album media.album.members-changed An album's stacks, time span, cover and matching profile media-duplicates media.duplicates.stale Decides a staged file's duplicate findings again document-index a file updated or moved , media.text.missing Extracts the text of PDFs, text and word-processor files for search staging-unzip a file updated in a staging category Expands a zip beside itself and removes it staging-sidecars staging.sidecars.arrived Pairs sidecar files with their files staging-organize staging.category.changed Suggests groups for a staging category again staging-retime staging.retime.requested Dates staged files by their category's time rules track-stage a file updated in staging Turns a GPX file into its track's route Staging and importing for administrators explains the staging pipelines in detail.

A step fails when its command exits with a status other than 0. What happens next depends on the status: Exit status Means What EiN does 75 A service the step needs cannot do it now: the media service is busy, loading a model, restarting or unreachable The step goes back to wait without spending an attempt. In a pool the job waits 30 seconds, doubling up to 10 minutes, while its kind's other jobs run; after five jobs are refused in a row, each for the first time, the whole kind rests as long, until one succeeds. A step the engine runs itself waits five minutes 65 The input is the problem, such as bytes no decoder can open The step fails at once, whatever attempts are left, and is never run again by itself any other The step itself failed One attempt is spent; the step runs again until maxAttempts is used up, and then the instance fails So, with the Archive, a media service that is down for an hour fails nothing: its work waits and starts again when it answers. A failed instance is not the end either. Once an hour, or as often as CFG_PIPELINE_PRUNE_INTERVAL says, the pipeline-pruner service runs pipeline heal --apply , which runs each failed instance again an hour after it failed, then after six hours, then after a day. One that still fails is marked as needing a person and left alone; one that failed on its input is never run again. The same service removes finished instances, keeping the newest 2000 of each pipeline, and leaves failed ones for you to look at. No step is stopped for taking long: a long step is working, and stopping it would throw the work away. A step that says how much of its work is done shows it under Ongoing on the Processing page . A running step that has written nothing and moved no progress for 30 minutes ( CFG_PIPELINE_STEP_QUIET_MS ) is listed as quiet, and you decide whether it is stuck. Some gaps no change announces: a file whose pipeline never ran, work an outage lost, vectors from a model the media service no longer runs. The Archive's media-heal service looks for these and announces each as a fact for the pipeline that fills it, once that pipeline has nothing waiting.

The Status in an administrator's sidebar shows the state of all this in one word at the top: Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person . Its Work tab draws where the work is, from not started through in line to running, and lists every pipeline with how much of its work is not started, in line, running, failed, done and cancelled, how much arrives and finishes per hour, and what is executing now. Health and status explains the words and the figures. Choose a pipeline in the list to open its page. It shows the pipeline's trigger, its steps and its priority, and its instances, with tabs All , Running , Completed , Failed and Cancelled . An administrator can select instances and choose Rerun , Cancel or Remove , or remove finished ones with Prune . Choose an instance to see each step, its status, how long it took and, for a failed step, its error; Retry runs a failed or skipped step again. The same is in the terminal. The commands that only read can be run by anyone; those that change something are for administrators: # in EiN's terminal pipeline overview # counts, queues and what is running pipeline instances -s failed media-faces # failed runs of one pipeline, newest first pipeline status media-faces/< id > # one run: its subject, its steps and their state # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pipeline start media-faces /archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987/IMG_0042.jpg pipeline rerun media-faces/< id > # a fresh run from the current definition pipeline restart media-faces/< id > # run only the failed steps again pipeline cancel media-faces/< id > An instance id is the subject's node id; pipeline instances lists them. Write it as <pipeline>/<id> to say which pipeline's run you mean. pipeline start starts a run directly, without the trigger's guards, so it works on a file the guards would turn away. A run started that way has no fact behind it, so a step that reads $EVENT_* gets nothing; pipeline start warns when a step of the pipeline needs one. Processing and pipelines is the administrator's guide to all of this, and Commands lists every pipeline and pool command with its options.

p.h: Add a pipeline of your own
p.x: A pipeline of your own is a YAML file anywhere in the tree, registered with pipeline define . This one marks every photo that arrives in the Wrenfield albums as not yet reviewed: name: mark-unreviewed description: Mark each new photo in the Wrenfield albums as not reviewed trigger: on: media.metadata.extracted match: nodePath: '/archive/albums/wrenfield-*/**' mimetype: 'image/*' skipIfAttr: reviewed steps: mark: command: attrs -s reviewed=no $NODE_PATH It waits for the Media module's fact media.metadata.extracted , so it needs the Media module, which comes with the Archive and with Recipes; on an EiN without modules, a trigger waits for a raw change instead, such as event: updated with nodeType: file . Save it, for example as /home/helen/pipelines/mark-unreviewed.yaml , with the editor or over SFTP . Register it as an administrator: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator pipeline define /home/helen/pipelines/mark-unreviewed.yaml Defined pipeline 'mark-unreviewed' A definition EiN cannot read gives pipeline-define: and the reason, such as invalid pipeline: missing steps or step 'mark' depends on unknown step 'read' . Upload a photo to one of the albums. The pipeline appears on the Work tab of the Status once it has run. Running pipeline define again with the same name replaces the definition; new runs use it, and pipeline rerun brings an existing run up to it. pipeline undefine mark-unreviewed removes it and cancels its running instances. A step can run any command on the path, a module's included; keep steps safe to run twice, since a step that is interrupted runs again. Writing a module shows how to ship pipelines with a module.

p.h: Trace a result back to its cause
p.x: Every write a run makes is recorded in the audit trail with the run it came from and the write that started it. So from any thumbnail, face or transcript you can find the change that caused it, and from a change everything it set off. Reading the trail is for administrators: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator: what changed under a photo, with details audit -v /archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987/IMG_0042.jpg With -v , each record shows its id, the session or pipeline run it came from ( sid pipeline:media-faces/<id> ), its cause , and each value it changed as from → to . Pass a record's id to audit --cause=<id> to list every write its pipelines made. Writes under /var , where instances, queues and pools live, are not recorded, nor are session and terminal writes. What a run makes belongs to whoever made the subject, so a thumbnail of Helen Okafor's photo is hers. The audit command lists every filter. The trail is kept for good, so every node keeps its whole history, whoever or whatever wrote it. The writes of runs are most of it, about ninety records for each photo an import indexes, so records older than 14 days are compressed, to about a seventh of their size. audit reads the last 14 days unless you give it --all or a time range with --since and --until . A node's history ( --id ), one record ( --record ), what a write set off ( --cause ) and a session's writes ( --sid ) are found in the whole trail, and as quickly. Reading older records only by path or user takes longer: the trail has to be read through for them. # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator: every change under an album, however old audit --all /archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987

Core brings no pipelines. Without a module, EiN keeps what you give it and works nothing out. A change made while a module's pipeline is not defined is not caught up when it is defined: pipelines act on changes as they happen. The Archive's media-heal finds most such gaps for media; for anything else, start the runs with pipeline start . A step is not stopped for running long, and there is no time limit to set.

A device is something outside EiN that reports or can be told what to do: a temperature sensor, a plug, a button, a phone that says where it is, a GPS logger whose files you copy in. EiN keeps each one in the tree at /dev/<device> , with what it reports and what it can be told as files under it. This page explains how that is laid out, how a device's readings get in and go out, and what moves them. Read it before writing to devices from the terminal or a script, or, as the administrator, before binding a queue to them. Devices covers the pages, and Devices and their keys who may do what.

Devices sit directly under /dev , beside EiN's own null and event routers. A device is a node of the type device , a folder, and its endpoints are the nodes in it, much as Linux shows a device's values as files in a folder under /sys : /dev/ ├── events EiN's own: where changes are announced ├── null EiN's own: reads nothing, swallows what is written ├── hall-plug/ a device, found by a driver │ ├── switch-0 a control: on or off │ ├── switch-0-power a log of readings, in W │ └── switch-0-energy a log of readings, in Wh ├── porch-button/ │ └── input-0 a log of events: single, double, long └── ruby-phone/ a device made by hand, driven by core's tracker ├── .key its device key └── position a track of positions A device's name is lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, made from what the device or a person calls it: Ruby phone becomes ruby-phone . The names null , events , pipeline-events , tty , stdin , stdout and stderr are EiN's own and are refused. The name is what commands, automations and routing keys use; the device's label is what the pages show, and can be changed without touching the name. What a device says about itself is in its attributes: Attribute What it holds label What the pages call it class What it is: phone , tracker , plug , switch , light , button , sensor , boat , … driver The driver that reads and writes it; none for a device whose endpoints are written to manufacturer Who made it model Its model firmware The firmware it runs, when it says serial Its serial number mac Its network address online Whether it answers now, when its driver can tell config What a person gave its driver when making it ( device-create --config ) attrs /dev/hall-plug prints them, and device-show prints the device with each of its endpoints.

An endpoint is one thing a device reports or is told. There are four types: Type What it is Reading it gives Writing it log A series of values, or of events Each value with its time A value, kept as the next entry track A series of positions Each position with its time A position, kept as the next one control A value written to change the device, a switch The states the device reported, in order A value, checked and sent to the device through its driver stream A live picture, a camera's A JPEG of it now, from its driver Refused: nothing of a stream is kept A log of events is a button's: each entry is a press, such as single , double or long , rather than a state, and the same press twice is two entries. Into any other log a driver puts a value only when it differs from the one before (see How often a reading is kept ). A stream keeps nothing. Each read is a new picture, which the device's driver takes from the camera then: cat /dev/front-door/main > door.jpg saves one, and /file/dev/front-door/main is one in a browser. The device's page plays it live. Its attributes say what it is: codec , width , height , fps and audio , as far as the driver knows them. A control is not a store of what you wrote. Writing on to /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 sends it to the plug; what reading the control gives is what the plug then reported it was. Until it reports, the control remembers what was asked, who asked and when (its requested attribute), and the device's page shows the switch as asked, waiting for the device. A press is remembered only once the driver took it: one it refuses, such as pausing a speaker that plays nothing, is answered with the driver's error and leaves the page's "pressed … by …" as it was. What a control takes is its schema: Schema It takes Example bool on or off ( true , false , 1 , 0 , yes , no ), or toggle , the opposite of now a relay, a lamp number A number, within the control's least and greatest and in its steps a thermostat's 21.5 enum One of the control's options a heat pump's eco text Any line a display's message momentary press : something the device does once, with no state a restart, a chime toggle needs a state the device has reported; before the first, it is refused. A value the schema does not take is refused with what it would take, such as hall-plug/switch-0 takes on, off or toggle, not '7' , and nothing is sent. An endpoint carries attributes of its own: its label , unit ( °C , W ), deviceClass (what is measured: temperature , power , door , motion ), retention (how long its entries are kept, such as 365 day or forever ), minInterval , and for a control its schema . An endpoint whose category is diagnostic or config tells of the device itself, such as its own temperature or its Wi-Fi signal, and the pages put it apart. One the device announced in a way its driver cannot read is marked supported: false and keeps nothing; one the device no longer announces is marked retired , and keeps its history.

A driver is what turns a device's own language into endpoints and back: it reads what the device sends and appends it to the endpoints, and it sends the device what is written to its controls. A device names its driver in its driver attribute. Driver Comes with What it drives tracker EiN itself A phone, a GPS tracker or a logger: what it posts, or a GPX file written to it, becomes its position track webhook EiN itself A button, a sensor or a script that posts to an address: each field it sends becomes a reading ha-discovery the Automation module Anything that announces itself over MQTT the way Home Assistant reads: ESPHome, Zigbee2MQTT and others shelly the Automation module Shelly's second generation and later, over MQTT shelly-gen1 the Automation module Shelly's first generation (Plug S, 1, 1PM, 2.5, i3, Dimmer, Bulb, RGBW2), over MQTT virtual the Automation module No hardware: readings worked out from other devices' and controls that hold what is set; see Virtual devices rtsp the Automation module A camera that sends its picture over RTSP: its streams; see A camera onvif the Automation module A camera that speaks ONVIF: its streams, its motion and people seen, its presets and moves; see An ONVIF camera devices --drivers lists the drivers running now, with the module each comes from and how many devices it drives. A module's drivers run while its service does: when the service is stopped, a write to one of their devices is refused with <device>'s driver <driver> is not running , and the device's Info tab says (not running) beside the driver. Most drivers find their devices: a sensor announces itself on the MQTT broker, and its driver makes the device and its endpoints within seconds. A phone or a GPS logger announces nothing, so a member of the devices group makes it by hand with device-create , naming its driver: # in EiN's terminal device-create 'Ruby phone' --driver tracker --class phone The driver gives the new device what it has from the start, here an empty position track. A device made without a driver has no endpoints of its own and takes nothing written to the device itself. A driver that reaches its device at an address asks for it with --config , one name=value each, which devices --drivers lists for every driver. What the driver declares secret, a password, is kept apart from the device's attributes, in its .secret , which the administrator alone reads; the rest is in its config attribute, which everyone who may read the device sees. The driver must be running when the device is made, so that EiN knows which is which.

tracker reads everything a phone or a GPS tracker sends, and adds each position that has a time to the device's position track: what Traccar Client posts, as JSON; the OsmAnd protocol, a query such as ?lat=59.32&lon=18.07&timestamp=1794132000 , sent by OsmAnd, older Traccar Client versions and many hardware trackers; a GPRMC sentence, ?gprmc=$GPRMC,… ; a GPX file, as a logger or a tracking app saves it; EiN's own positions, a line of JSON each: {"lat": 59.32, "lng": 18.07, "ts": "2026-11-08T09:00:00Z"} . A position at a time the track already has is not added twice, so sending the same file again adds nothing.

webhook reads what a device or a script posts in the shapes webhooks take, and keeps each field as a reading on the endpoint of that name, a log made the first time the field comes. Each reading is kept and published on the bus as a driver's are: a value that repeats the last one is not kept again, and a number comes at most once every minInterval of its endpoint. Posted Readings a JSON object, {"temperature": 21.4, "door": "open"} temperature 21.4, door open a JSON object within one, {"bme280": {"humidity": 40}} bme280-humidity 40 a JSON list of objects each object's fields, in turn a form, or the address's query, ?battery=81&event=single battery 81, event single a bare value or a line of text, 21.4 value 21.4 nothing at all, as a button calling its address call true , an event Names. A field's name is made an endpoint's: lower case, anything but letters, digits, - and _ a - . A field with no name left, or holding a list, is not read; the answer says which. Values. JSON's numbers, true , false and text are kept as they are. A form's or a query's text that is a number, true or false is taken as one; 0042 stays text. Time. A field ts , time or timestamp that reads as a time, a date or epoch seconds or milliseconds, is when the post's readings were made, not a reading. Without one, they are kept with the time they arrived. Events. A button's press is news each time, the same one twice included. The fields named in the device's events setting are kept that way, given when the device is made: device-create 'Porch' --driver webhook --config events=button . The answer says how many readings were new, such as {"taken": 2, "message": "2 of 2 readings new"} .

The machine EiN runs on is a device too, /dev/<machine> , named after the machine without its domain, of class host . Nobody makes it: the metrics-sampler service writes its readings through the host driver, and makes the device and each endpoint the first time it has a reading for it. After device-forget it is made again at the next reading. Only the administrators see it ( Devices for administrators ). Endpoint Reading How often Kept cpu The share of all the machine's processor cores in use, in % 15 seconds 30 days load The 1-minute load average 15 seconds 30 days memory-used The share of the machine's memory in use, in % 15 seconds 30 days <zone>-temperature Each thermal zone the kernel has, such as x86_pkg_temp , in °C 15 seconds 30 days <disk>-used The share of each disk in use, such as sda1-used , in % 15 minutes 365 days memory-total The machine's memory, in GB 15 minutes 365 days uptime Days since the machine started 15 minutes 365 days These are the whole machine's, whatever runs on it: the media service and the database load it from containers of their own. EiN's own share is on the System status page. A disk is each filesystem on a block device that EiN's container sees, once, wherever it is mounted. The load, the temperatures, the total and the uptime are about the machine itself ( diagnostic ), so the card shows the CPU. In an installation made with setup.sh , the machine's name is EIN_HOSTNAME in .env , which setup.sh writes ( Installing in detail ).

What is written to the device itself, /dev/<device> , is raw input for its driver: a GPX file, a tracker's post, whatever the driver reads. What is written to an endpoint is a value in EiN's own form. Both work the same from the terminal, over SFTP, and over HTTP: # in EiN's terminal cat ~/summer-walk.gpx > /dev/old-logger # raw input: the tracker driver reads the GPX echo on > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 # a value for a control, sent to the plug echo 41.5 > /dev/garden-sensor/soil-moisture # a value appended to a log cat /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 # the states the plug reported tail -f /dev/hall-plug/switch-0-power # each new reading, until Ctrl+C A write to a device or a control is answered when its driver has taken it: echo fails at once when the value is refused or the driver is not running, and a control's write that the device has not taken within 10 seconds fails with <device> did not answer within 10 s . A write to a log or a track endpoint appends to it, with > as with >> : an endpoint keeps its history, unlike a file or a log elsewhere in the tree, which > empties first. A value written to a log endpoint by hand, a number, true or false , or a word, is kept as {"value": …} , as a driver's readings are, so the device's page and device-history read it; a line that is a JSON object is kept as it is. Every log a driver makes has this from its valueField attribute, and a log made by hand under a device gets it with attrs -s valueField=value <log> . A value written by hand is neither throttled nor published on the bus: only what a driver appends is. A control takes > ; >> on a control would append a state as if the device had reported it, which only the administrator may do. Over HTTP the device's file in the tree takes the same writes at /file/dev/<device> and /file/dev/<device>/<endpoint> , where a body of a bare value, such as 21.4 , is kept as {"value": 21.4} . A device cannot sign in, so it sends its device key with them, which opens its own folder for these writes and nothing else; see Devices and their keys .

Every reading a driver keeps is also published on a routing key, a name a message goes out under, which any queue or log bound to it gets a copy of. Only the administrator binds one, since a queue bound to dev.# hears every device whoever may read it; the automations of the Automation module read them for everyone else, each only what its owner may read: Routing key What comes on it dev.<device>.<endpoint> Each new value of the endpoint: a reading, a press, a state the device reported, a position dev.<device> The device coming online or going offline A message is a line of JSON that says whose it is, so it can be read without its key: {"device":"hall-sensor","endpoint":"temperature","value":21.4,"unit":"°C","at":"2026-11-08T07:42:10.512Z"} {"device":"porch-button","endpoint":"input-0","value":"single","event":true,"at":"2026-11-08T18:03:55.120Z"} {"device":"ruby-phone","endpoint":"position","fix":{"lat":59.3251,"lng":18.0711,"speed":1.2},"at":"2026-11-08T12:10:04.000Z"} {"device":"hall-plug","online":false,"at":"2026-11-08T22:15:02.004Z"} value is a number, a word, or true and false for on and off; event marks a press; fix is a position, its speed in metres per second; at is when it was read. A reading the device replayed, as an MQTT broker does with the last one after EiN reconnects, also has "retained": true . A GPX file with thousands of positions publishes only its newest. In a key, * stands for one part and # for any number of them, none included: dev.*.temperature is every endpoint called temperature , and dev.hall-plug.# everything the hall plug says, its coming and going included.

A queue bound to keys keeps every message that comes on them until it is taken, whether or not anyone is reading. The administrator makes one for what they want, such as every press of the porch button: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mkqueue -k 'dev.porch-button.#' ~/presses queue-peek ~/presses # the next ones, left in the queue cat ~/presses # takes them out as it prints them Remove it with rm ~/presses when you no longer want it, or it keeps filling.

A log keeps what comes on its keys as entries with their times, for as long as you say: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mklog -k 'dev.*.temperature' -r '90 day' ~/temperatures log-read ~/temperatures --since 1d log-read ~/temperatures --since 30d --bucket 1d --field value --agg max

p.h: How often a reading is kept
p.x: A driver hands EiN every reading it hears, and EiN keeps and publishes it only when it is news: A value the same as the endpoint's last is not kept again. A number is kept at most once every minInterval seconds, the endpoint's own attribute. One that comes sooner waits for the end of the interval, and only the newest of those is kept, so the last of a burst is never lost. On and off, words, positions and every press are kept as they come. A sensor that reports its power every second therefore costs a row every ten seconds or so while it changes, and none while it holds still. The Automation module gives the endpoints it makes a minInterval from its Seconds between readings setting.

Every command an EiN with all its modules has: 454 of them. Each module's page describes its commands in full; this page lists them by what they are for, in a line each.

Each command is shown with how it is typed: share-link [--expires=<string>] [--never] [--session] <subcommand> <target> <target> is something you give, [...] may be left out, and ... may be given more than once. --name=<value> takes a value after an equals sign, which a value starting with a minus needs ( --lng=-3.7 ); -x is a short option. administrators only marks a command only the administrator may run; visitors too , one a visitor browsing without signing in may run. answers JSON marks a command whose answer comes as JSON with JSON_OUTPUT=1 in front of it, which is what the Web UI reads. A command of a family, such as mod-install or user-passwd , can be typed as two words where the family has a command of its own: mod install archive . In the shell, <command> --help says the same as these pages, for what is installed there; the documentation page in the Web UI has them too.

All 224 in full . -iname -path -ipath GLOB, -regex -iregex RE on the whole path, -type f|d|l| , -empty, -size [+-]N[cwbkMG], -user -group NAME, -uid -gid N, -newer PATH, -mmin and -mtime [+-]N), operators (! -not -a -o Command What it does ems-files Serve the media service the files of its requests in flight over SFTP, the only way it reaches EiN's files (the ems-files service) ems-files-grant Names for paths through ems-files for a while, and the EMS-Files header that reaches them, to try a media service's way to EiN's files by hand. ems-gpu The GPU of an instance of the media service now, with the last six hours of utilization and VRAM, from its machine device. ems-instance The media service's instances: list them and what each serves, or add, change or remove one beside the primary. ems-link Watch every instance of the media service: log when one comes or goes, run failed work again when one's build changes, and keep the primary's card at the share CFG_EMS_CARD_SHARE_MB names (the ems-link service) ems-memory The memory of the media service's machine now, with the last six hours, and what EMS holds of it. ems-models What the media service held over the last hours, a sample a minute, with the work EiN had waiting beside it. ems-sampler Drive the machine each instance of the media service runs on as a device, and sample what it holds (the ems-sampler service) ems-status Show media service health: version, every model and its state, what is executing, degradation, worker memory and queues. ems-text-embed Texts as vectors, by EMS's current text model, to compare by meaning.

Command What it does compute-fingerprint Compute the fingerprints that find copies of a media file: SSCD for pictures and video keyframes, chromaprint for sound. detect-chapters Find a video's cuts and write them as its chapters (metadata/chapters) embed-picture Embed a photo or a video's keyframes for search by what is in the picture. exif-extract Read a media file's metadata: the probe's dump and what it says of the file under metadata/exif, and its mimetype, dimensions, angle, duration, codec and whether it can be decoded on the file. Each module's hold command runs first, and a file it holds is not read unless forced. file-crop Cut a part of a picture out at its own resolution, into a new file. file-restore Restore a photo into a new version beside it: faded colours back, dust and scratches filled, blur taken out, grain lessened. file-set-text Write the text in a picture by hand, in place of what was read from it. file-set-text-language Set the language the text in a picture is written in (or auto), and read the picture again in it. file-set-transcript Write what is said in a video or a recording by hand, in place of the transcript, from WebVTT on stdin. find-damage Read how faded, dusty, scratched, blurred and shaken a picture is, and keep it on the file to find those worth restoring. fingerprints-scan Announce every picture, video and recording that was never fingerprinted to the end: it has no fingerprintedAt. generate-derivatives Generate web derivatives (still pictures, transcoded renditions, a document's PDF) for a media file or a document. index-document Extract text content and generate embedding for a document file. media-bridge Derive the facts of a media file itself from VFS mutations: arrived, changed, turned, removed, read, its renditions made, its text and transcript, and the unread files a moved directory carried (long-running) media-pool-kinds The kinds of work a worker of the media pool takes, from the modules' drop-ins, as pipeline-worker's flags. media-reembed Embed the extracted texts, transcripts and hand-written descriptions already stored into the current text space, from the stored text alone. pictures-scan Announce every photo and video whose picture vectors are not the model EMS embeds with now: its marker is missing or names another model. promote-exif-attrs Copy width/height/duration from a file's exif node onto the file node. read-text Read the text written in a picture and keep it for search. regenerate Regenerate web derivatives for media files under a path. renditions-scan Announce every file whose renditions are not those the rendition table names now: its marker is missing or names another table, or a rendition was refused under a CPU budget EMS no longer runs. text-scan Announce every file whose text, transcript or text vectors are missing or not what EMS makes now, found by their markers. transcribe-file Transcribe audio or video into a timed WebVTT node with chunk embeddings.

Command What it does events-todo Home's events from the todo lists: open items due around a day that are yours, given to you or to nobody. todo-about List the items not done, on every list you can see, that are about a path: that link to it, such as a picture, an album or a person. With no path, every item that links to anything; with --done the done ones too. todo-add Add an item to a todo list, a markdown file named for when it was added, with the day it is due and who is to do it if you like. todo-archive Put done todo items away in their list's archived/, which is no column of the board. todo-move or todo-done --undo takes one out again. todo-done Mark a todo item done, with who did it and when, moving it to the list's done/; with --undo, not done again and back in the list's Todo. todo-item Show one todo item: its title, description, due day, who is to do it, its column and its links. todo-items Show a todo list's board: its columns, Todo (the list itself), each folder in it, then Done (its done/), and the items of each in their order. archived/ is left out. todo-link Link a todo item to what it is about, such as a picture or an album: a softlink under the item's file, named as what it points at. rm takes one away. todo-list-create Make a todo list, a folder named by its title: your own, in ~/todos, or with --group one every member of the group shares, in the group's shared home. todo-lists List the todo lists you can see: your own, then those in the shared homes of your groups. todo-members List who an item of a todo list may be given to: the members of the list's group, or you for a list of your own. todo-mine List what is left for you to do: items not done given to you on any list, and your own lists' items not done given to nobody, soonest due first, each with its column; with --done the done ones too. todo-move Move a todo item to another column of its list's board, at its end, or put it just before or just after another item, numbering that column's items in their new order. Into done/ it is marked done, out of it not done. todo-set Change a todo item's title, its description, the day it is due, or who is to do it.

Ensure path is abspath. reads only abspath <path> Argument What it is <path> the path to make absolute.

Show who signed in or out, opened a share link or downloaded what, from where, and when (administrators only) administrators only · reads only access-log [--user=<string>] [--event=<string>] [--sid=<string>] [--from=<string>] [--link=<string>] [--record=<string>] [--since=<string>] [--until=<string>] [--after=<string>] [-n <string>] <path> Argument What it is <path> only downloads and share links of this path or below it. Option What it does --user=<string> only events of this user (name or uid) --event=<string> only this event (repeatable): sign-in, sign-in-failed, sign-out, elevate, elevate-failed, link-open, download, download-archive. --sid=<string> only events of this session or SSH connection, as audit -v shows it. --from=<string> only events from this client address. --link=<string> only events through this share link (its id) --record=<string> only the record with this id. --since=<string> from this time on (ISO date/time or epoch ms) --until=<string> before this time (ISO date/time or epoch ms) --after=<string> only the records after this record id, oldest first: pass the last id read to follow the log. -n <string> at most this many records, the latest, or with --after the first (default: 100) access-log --event sign-in-failed --since 2026-11-01 access-log /archive --event download --event download-archive access-log --user anna -n 20

Remove access-log records older than a given age, so the access log does not grow without bound (administrators only) administrators only · changes things access-log-purge [--older-than=<string>] Option What it does --older-than=<string> remove the records written longer ago than this, e.g. 90d. access-log-purge --older-than 90d

Display or modify a node access control list. reads only acl [-m <string>] [-x <string>] [-b] [-r] [-L] <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node. Option What it does -m <string> add or modify an entry (u: : or g: : ) -x <string> remove an entry (u: or g: ) -b remove the user and group entries (share links stay: share-link removes them) -r apply to the whole subtree, skipping nodes that hold their own access. -L do not follow symbolic links.

Become the administrator in this terminal, for a member of the sudo group (user-elevate) changes things admin admin admin --off With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; this terminal acts as the administrator until admin --off or signing out.

Display or set node attributes. reads only attrs [-L] [-s <string>] [-d <string>] [-J <string>] <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node. Option What it does -L do not follow symbolic links. -s <string> set attribute as string. -d <string> unset attribute. -J <string> set attribute as JSON. attrs /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg attrs -s 'description=Ett exempel' /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : every attribute on the node, or nothing when setting one.

Show who created, changed, moved, linked or removed which node, and when (administrators only). Reads the last 14 days unless given --all, a time range, or a record, node, session or cause to find. administrators only · reads only audit [--user=<string>] [--id=<string>] [--record=<string>] [--sid=<string>] [--no-pipeline] [--cause=<string>] [--op=<string>] [--since=<string>] [--until=<string>] [--type=<string>] [--after=<string>] [--all] [-n <string>] [-v] <path> Argument What it is <path> only writes to this path or below it (moves match on either side) Option What it does --user=<string> only writes by this user (name or uid) --id=<string> only writes to this node id. --record=<string> only the record with this id. --sid=<string> only writes of this session, SSH connection or pipeline run, as -v and access-log show it. --no-pipeline leave out the writes of pipeline runs: only what people, imports and services wrote. --cause=<string> only writes set off by the write with this record id: what its pipeline runs wrote. --op=<string> only this operation: create, update, move, link, unlink, delete. --since=<string> from this time on (ISO date/time or epoch ms) --until=<string> before this time (ISO date/time or epoch ms) --type=<string> only writes to nodes of this type (repeatable) --after=<string> only the records after this record id, oldest first: pass the last id read to follow the trail. --all read the whole trail, not only the last 14 days: slower, and slowest with only a path to narrow on. -n <string> at most this many records, the latest, or with --after the first (default: 100) -v show each record's id, session or pipeline run, cause, and the values it changed.

Pattern scanning and text processing language (fields, patterns, arrays, printf) reads only awk [-F <string>] [-v <string>] [-f <string>] <PROGRAM> <FILE>... Argument What it is <PROGRAM> awk program, e.g. '{ print $1 }' or 'BEGIN { FS=":" } $3 > 10 { n++ } END { print n }'; omit when using -f. <FILE>... files to process, or var=value assignments (reads stdin if no files) Option What it does -F <string> field separator (a character, "t" for tab, or a regex) -v <string> assign var=value before the program starts (repeatable) -f <string> read the program from this file (repeatable)

Strip directory and suffix from filenames. reads only basename [-s <string>] [-a] [-z] <NAME> [<SUFFIX>] Argument What it is <NAME> the path to extract basename from. [<SUFFIX>] optional suffix to remove. Option What it does -s <string> remove a trailing SUFFIX. -a support multiple arguments. -z end each output line with NUL, not newline.

Print nodes' contents, one after the other: a text file, a log (one JSON entry a line), a position or an embedding (JSON), a camera's stream (a JPEG of it now) reads only cat [-s] [-l] [-t] [--timestamps] [<path>...] Argument What it is [<path>...] nodes to output, one after the other; without one, or for -, stdin is copied. Option What it does -s small media preview (mediaLines / 2) -l large media preview (mediaLines * 2) -t log: each entry's time (ISO 8601, UTC) first, a tab, then the entry. --timestamps log: each entry's time (ISO 8601, UTC) first, a tab, then the entry. cat /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/notes.txt cat -t /archive/people/Anna_Exempel/measurements/weight With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the node's contents; with -t on a log, lines like 2016-09-04T16:13:27.739Z {"value":83.4}.

Change file mode bits. changes things chmod [-L] [-r] <mode> <path> Argument What it is <mode> mode to set. <path> node(s) to change. Option What it does -L do not follow symbolic links. -r apply to the whole subtree, skipping nodes that hold their own access.

Change file owner and group. changes things chown [-L] [-r] <usergroup> <path> Argument What it is <usergroup> user or group to set. <path> node(s) to change. Option What it does -L do not follow symbolic links. -r apply to the whole subtree, skipping nodes that hold their own access.
Clear the terminal screen. reads only clear

Manage comments on a node (list, add, remove) reads only comment [--body=<string>] <subcommand> <path> <slug> Argument What it is <subcommand> list | add | remove. <path> node the comment belongs to. <slug> comment slug (remove) Option What it does --body=<string> comment body (add); - reads it from stdin.
Spec-driven completion helpers. completion <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.

Complete a person, location, album or device by name. reads only completion-entity [--kind=<string>] [--limit=<string>] <query> Argument What it is <query> the partial name typed so far. Option What it does --kind=<string> restrict to these kinds, comma-separated: whichever the installed modules declare (person, location, album, device) --limit=<string> maximum suggestions (default 8)
Autocomplete a group. reads only completion-group [--word=<string>] Option What it does --word=<string> Word to autocomplete.
Autocomplete a path. reads only completion-path [--word=<string>] Option What it does --word=<string> Word to autocomplete.

Autocomplete a command. reads only completion-subcommand [--word=<string>] <command> Argument What it is <command> Command to which the subcommand belongs. Option What it does --word=<string> Word to autocomplete.
Autocomplete a user. reads only completion-user [--word=<string>] Option What it does --word=<string> Word to autocomplete.
Read and change system and personal settings. visitors too config <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.
Print the effective value of one setting; for a key, only whether it is set. reads only config-get <key> Argument What it is <key> setting name.
List settings with their effective values. visitors too · reads only config-list [--scope=<string>] Option What it does --scope=<string> limit to 'system' or 'user' settings.
Copy settings from this process's environment into /etc/environment. changes things config-publish
Change a setting and restart the services that read it only at start. changes things config-set <key> <value> Argument What it is <key> setting name. <value> new value.
Reset a setting to its default. changes things config-unset <key> Argument What it is <key> setting name.

Copy files and directories. changes things cp [-r] [-f] <source> <dest> Argument What it is <source> source file(s) or directories to copy. <dest> destination: an existing directory (or other node that is not a file) to copy into, or the path of a single source, replacing a file there. Option What it does -r copy directories recursively. -f replace a node of the same name in the destination directory; a file named as DEST is replaced without it. cp /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007_copy.jpg cp -r /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_A /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_B With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing.

Remove sections from each line of files. reads only cut [-d <string>] [-f <string>] [-c <string>] [-s] <FILE>... Argument What it is <FILE>... files to cut, one after the other (stdin if omitted, or for -) Option What it does -d <string> use DELIM instead of TAB for field delimiter. -f <string> select only these fields (e.g., -f1, -f1-3, -f1,3) -c <string> select only these characters (e.g., -c1-5) -s do not print lines not containing delimiters.

Print or set the system date and time. reads only date [-d <string>] [-u] [-I <string>] [-R] <+FORMAT> Argument What it is <+FORMAT> output format (strftime-style) Option What it does -d <string> display time described by STRING, not now. -u print or set UTC time. -I <string> output in ISO 8601 format (date, hours, minutes, seconds, ns) -R output in RFC 5322 format.

detach a job so it keeps running after the shell closes. changes things detach [--list] <job> Argument What it is <job> job spec (%n), job number, or pid; defaults to the most recent job. Option What it does --list list detached jobs system-wide instead, from their records under /var/logs/jobs.

Show what a device's driver was given, or change it (name=value, name= to take one away) and have the driver take it up; changing is for members of the devices group. reads only device-config <device> [<field>...] Argument What it is <device> the device's name. [<field>...] name=value for its driver; name= takes it away; none shows the config. device-config front-door device-config front-door password= 'n3w pass' device-config front-door sub= With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceConfigAnswer.

Make a device by hand, which no driver announces: a phone or GPS logger (--driver tracker), something that posts its readings to a webhook (--driver webhook) changes things device-create [--label=<string>] [--class=<string>] [--driver=<string>] [--manufacturer=<string>] [--model=<string>] [--config=<string>] <name> Argument What it is <name> what to call it; its name under /dev is made from it. Option What it does --label=<string> what its page calls it, when not the name. --class=<string> what it is: phone, tracker, boat, car, sensor, …. --driver=<string> the driver that reads what is written to it: tracker, webhook, or a module's (devices --drivers) --manufacturer=<string> who made it. --model=<string> its model. --config=<string> name=value for its driver; again for each. device-create 'Ruby phone' --driver tracker --class phone device-create 'Old logger' --driver tracker --class tracker --model 'eTrex 30' device-create 'Porch' --driver webhook --class button --config events=button With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceCreated: device, path.

Remove a device and everything under it, its history included; for members of the devices group. changes things device-forget <device> Argument What it is <device> the device's name. device-forget old-sensor With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : { device, forgotten }.

An endpoint's history, oldest first: a log's or control's values, or with --bucket summed up per interval; a track's fixes. reads only device-history [-n <string>] [--since=<string>] [--until=<string>] [--bucket=<string>] [--agg=<string>] <endpoint> Argument What it is <endpoint> / , or its path under /dev. Option What it does -n <string> at most this many values or intervals, the latest (100 when not given) --since=<string> from this time on: ISO 8601, or a duration such as 24h or 7d meaning that long ago. --until=<string> before this time, as --since takes it. --bucket=<string> sum the values up per interval of this length: 10m, 1h, 1d; a day is a calendar day. --agg=<string> with --bucket, how: avg, min, max, sum, count, first, last (avg when not given); on and off count as 1 and 0. device-history hall-sensor/temperature -n 10 device-history hall-plug/power --since 7d --bucket 1h device-history ruby-phone/position --since 1d With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceHistory.

The key that lets a device write to /file/dev/ without signing in, and the URL a phone or tracker is given: shown, made new (--new) or taken away (--off) changes things device-key [--new] [--off] [--origin=<string>] <device> Argument What it is <device> the device's name. Option What it does --new make a new key; a URL given out before stops working. --off take the key away: nothing writes to the device without signing in. --origin=<string> this EiN's address as the device reaches it ( https://ein.example ), for the whole URL and a QR code. device-key ruby-phone device-key ruby-phone --new --origin https://ein.example device-key old-sensor --off With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceKeyAnswer.

Name a device or one of its endpoints, as its page and cards show it; for members of the devices group. changes things device-label <target> <label>... Argument What it is <target> or / . <label>... the name to show. device-label hall-plug 'Hall lamp' device-label hall-sensor/temperature 'Hall temperature' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : { path, label }.

A device and each of its endpoints: a log's or control's latest value, a track's fixes, a stream's size and codec, and whether you may write a control. reads only device-show <device> Argument What it is <device> the device's name, or its path under /dev. device-show hall-plug device-show /dev/ruby-phone With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceInfo.

Every device under /dev you may see, or those a word names: its name, label, whether it answers and its main value; or the drivers. reads only devices [--online] [--class=<string>] [--drivers] [<word>...] Argument What it is [<word>...] only the devices whose name or label holds this word, or any of several: lamp, hall. Option What it does --online only the devices that answer now. --class=<string> only the devices of these classes, separated by commas: host,storage. --drivers the drivers running now instead: core's, and those modules' services registered. devices devices lamp devices --online devices --class host,storage devices --drivers With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : DeviceSummary[], or with --drivers DriverSummary[].
Free space per storage tier, the size of its files, its growth per day and when it fills, and the database size and its largest tables. reads only df
Strip last component from file name. reads only dirname [-z] <NAME> Argument What it is <NAME> the path to extract directory from. Option What it does -z end each output line with NUL, not newline.

Print system log. reads only dmesg [-n <string>] [--level=<string>] [<path>] Argument What it is [<path>] log node path (default: /var/logs/system) Option What it does -n <string> show last N lines. --level=<string> only lines at this level or above: debug, info, warn, error.
Describe what this installation is made of: its commands, node types and environment variables. docs <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.

List every command on your PATH with its full spec and the module it comes from. reads only docs-commands docs commands With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per command: name, module (core or the module whose bin it is) and its whole spec.

List the environment variables EiN and its modules read, with their values in this shell. reads only docs-env docs env docs env | grep PATH With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per variable: key, kind, description, default, owner module, and its value in this shell where it has one.

Commands by what they do, best first: by the command CFG_COMMAND_FINDER names, else by their words. reads only docs-find [--limit=<number>] <words>... Argument What it is <words>... What the command should do. Option What it does --limit=<number> How many commands.

List every node type, described or in use, with what it is for and how many exist. reads only docs-node-types docs node-types With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per type: type, count, and label, description, category and owner module where it is described.

Estimate file usage in node structures. reads only du [-c] [-h] [-s] [<path>] Argument What it is [<path>] one or more structures to measure (default: .) Option What it does -c print a grand total. -h print sizes in units of 1024 (e.g. 1.5 KB) -s print only a total for each argument. du -sh /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the size of each path, and a total with -c.
Edit a text file, with syntax highlighting and checks for JSON, YAML, bash and Markdown. changes things edit <path> Argument What it is <path> path to file to edit.
Print environment variables. reads only env

What falls on the days around a date, from every events-* command on PATH. reads only events [--today=<string>] [--days-ahead=<number>] [--days-past=<number>] [--limit=<number>] [--source=<string>] Option What it does --today=<string> the date to look around, YYYY-MM-DD (default today, UTC) --days-ahead=<number> how far forward to look (default 30) --days-past=<number> how far back to look (default 7) --limit=<number> entries returned across all providers; milestones, then the nearest, survive the cut (default 16) --source=<string> ask only this provider, the name after events- such as anniversaries (repeatable) events events --days-ahead 0 --days-past 0 events --today 2026-12-24 --days-ahead 7 events -- source anniversaries -- source todo With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the entries of every events-* provider, or of those --source names, in the window, in date order: the day, what, whether it is a milestone, the node it is about, which provider, and the route that draws it.

Bucket counts (per year, per kind) for sizing search filters. reads only facets [--kind=<string>] [--from=<string>] [--to=<string>] Option What it does --kind=<string> restrict to content kinds: photo, video, audio, document, or node types. --from=<string> only count media taken at/after this date. --to=<string> only count media taken before this date, exclusive. facets --kind photo --from 2015 --to 2020 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : per-year and per-kind counts for the filters given.

Stat for on disk file. reads only file-stat [-f] <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node. Option What it does -f return full information, including mimetype, sha256, much slower. file-stat /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the file's size, mode and times as they are on disk.

Sync for on disk file. changes things file-sync <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node. file-sync /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; the node's size and checksum are brought in line with the bytes on disk.

Search for nodes under a path, as GNU find does: starting points, then an expression of tests (-name -iname -path -ipath GLOB, -regex -iregex RE on the whole path, -type f|d|l| , -empty, -size [+-]N[cwbkMG], -user -group NAME, -uid -gid N, -newer PATH, -mmin and -mtime [+-]N), operators (! -not -a -o and parentheses), options (-maxdepth -mindepth N, -depth) and actions (-print -print0 -printf FORMAT -prune -quit -delete, -exec CMD {} ';' and -exec CMD {} +); -printf knows %p %f %h %P %d %s %y %m %u %g %U %G %t %c and %Tk %Ck %Bk for k in @YymdHMSFTDab+; the flags below are the same tests. reads only find [--name=<string>] [--iname=<string>] [--type=<string>] [--maxdepth=<string>] [--mindepth=<string>] [<path>] Argument What it is [<path>] starting point, printed itself at depth 0; several may be given (default: .) Option What it does --name=<string> match the name by glob pattern (-name) --iname=<string> match the name by glob pattern, ignoring case (-iname) --type=<string> node type: f, d, l or one such as person; several comma-separated (-type) --maxdepth=<string> descend at most this many levels: 0 is the starting point alone (-maxdepth) --mindepth=<string> match nothing shallower than this level: 1 leaves out the starting point (-mindepth) find /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 -name '*.jpg' - type f find /archive/people -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 2 - type person find /home/anna/staging -name '.tmp*' -prune -o - type f -mmin -60 - print find /home/anna/staging - type f -size +10M - printf '%s %p\n' find /home/anna/staging -name '*.tmp' - exec rm {} + With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : every path -print selects; in JSON each with its type, name and number of children. With -printf, -print0 or -exec the output is text.

Find positions whose shape contains a point. reads only find-containing [--lat=<string>] [--lng=<string>] [--limit=<string>] <lat> <lng> Argument What it is <lat> latitude of the point. <lng> longitude of the point. Option What it does --lat=<string> latitude, as --lat= — required form for a negative coordinate. --lng=<string> longitude, as --lng= — required form for a negative coordinate. --limit=<string> max results (default: 10)

Find positions near a position node, by distance. reads only find-nearby [--radius=<string>] [--limit=<string>] <path> Argument What it is <path> path of a position node. Option What it does --radius=<string> search radius in meters (default: 10000) --limit=<string> max results (default: 10)

Find similar nodes by embedding. reads only find-similar [--limit=<number>] <path> Argument What it is <path> path of embedding node. Option What it does --limit=<number> at most this many matches. With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the nearest embeddings with their similarity and paths, as JSON (SimilarAnswer).

Wrap each input line to fit a width (fold -w1: one character per line) reads only fold [-w <number>] [-s] [-b] <FILE>... Argument What it is <FILE>... files to fold (reads from stdin if omitted) Option What it does -w <number> width in columns (default 80) -s break at the last blank that fits. -b count characters, not columns (tabs count one)
List the gauges running services draw beside the host's (a card's memory, say) reads only gauges

Search for patterns in input. reads only grep [-i] [-v] [-c] [-n] [-o] [-E] [-F] [-q] <PATTERN> <FILE>... Argument What it is <PATTERN> the pattern to search for. <FILE>... files to search (stdin if omitted, or for -) Option What it does -i ignore case distinctions. -v select non-matching lines. -c print only a count of matching lines. -n prefix each line with line number. -o show only the matching part of lines. -E interpret pattern as extended regexp. -F interpret pattern as fixed string. -q quiet mode, exit with 0 on match, 1 otherwise. grep -n exempelord /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/notes.txt With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the matching lines.
Manage groups. group <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.

Add a user to a group; to users (everyone), put back an account taken out of it. administrators only · changes things group-add-member <group> <user> Argument What it is <group> group to add the user to. <user> user to add to the group.

Create a new group. administrators only · changes things group-create [--gid=<string>] [--title=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--home] <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> name of the group to create: lower-case letters, digits and . _ -, starting with a letter or _. Option What it does --gid=<string> numeric group ID. --title=<string> display title for the group. --description=<string> description of the group. --home give it a home its members share, as group-home does.

Delete a group: what it owned goes to another group, and ACL entries naming it are dropped. administrators only · changes things group-delete [--to=<group>] [--force] [--remove-home] <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> name of the group to delete. Option What it does --to=<group> group that takes over the nodes it owned (default admin) --force delete it even if it is a primary group; those users go back to their own group. --remove-home delete it even if it has a home, which goes to the administrator's trash.
Check if a group exists. reads only group-exists <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> group name to check.

Give a group a home, a directory its members share and nobody else sees, or with --off move it to the administrator's trash. administrators only · changes things group-home [--off] <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> the group. Option What it does --off take the group's home away, into the trash.
Display group information. reads only group-info <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> group name to look up.
Check if a user is a member of a group. reads only group-is-member <group> <user> Argument What it is <group> group to check if the user is member of. <user> user to check.

List the groups; as JSON with each one's description, built-in role and whether it has a home. reads only group-list [--members] Option What it does --members also list the usernames linked into each group, where the caller may see them (a primary group's users are not linked)

List members of a group. administrators only · reads only group-members [--limit=<string>] <group> Argument What it is <group> group to list members of. Option What it does --limit=<string> maximum members to return (1-50)

Remove a user from a group; from users (everyone), take the account out of what is shared with every account. administrators only · changes things group-remove-member <group> <user> Argument What it is <group> group to remove the user from. <user> user to remove from the group.
Resolve group name to GID or vice versa. reads only group-resolve <gid_or_groupname> Argument What it is <gid_or_groupname> gid (numeric) or group name to resolve.

Update a group's title or description; its gid is fixed when it is created. administrators only · changes things group-update [--title=<string>] [--description=<string>] <groupname> Argument What it is <groupname> name of the group to update. Option What it does --title=<string> set display title. --description=<string> set description.

Output the first part of files, logs, or stdin; on a queue, the next entries without consuming them. reads only head [-n <string>] [-c <string>] <path> Argument What it is <path> file, log or queue node to read (stdin if omitted, or for -) Option What it does -n <string> print the first NUM lines instead of the first 10 (-NUM works too) -c <string> print the first NUM bytes. head -n 20 /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/notes.txt With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the first lines of the file.
Say whether the system is healthy, catching up, stuck or needs a person, and the checks that decide it. reads only health

The machine's CPU and memory, this container's share of each, and event-loop lag now, with their recent history from metrics-sampler. reads only host-metrics [--window=<string>] Option What it does --window=<string> Minutes of history (default: 360)

Start an HTTP server. administrators only · changes things http-server [--port=<string>] <path> Argument What it is <path> path to serve as root, "default" in root will be used as the default host. Option What it does --port=<string> port to use.
Display node ID and type. reads only info [-L] <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node. Option What it does -L do not follow symbolic links.

Lightweight JSON processor. reads only jq [-r] [-e] [-c] [-C] [-M] [-S] <filter> <FILE>... Argument What it is <filter> jq filter expression (e.g., .field, .field.nested, .[] | .name, startswith("x")); . if omitted. <FILE>... files of JSON texts (one, or JSON Lines), each text filtered in turn (stdin if omitted, or for -) Option What it does -r output raw strings, not JSON texts. -e exit with status 1 if output is null or false. -c compact instead of pretty-printed output. -C colorize JSON output even when not on a terminal. -M do not colorize JSON output. -S Output the fields of each object with the keys in sorted order.

Manage labels/tags (add, remove, list, prune) reads only label <subcommand> <path> <label> Argument What it is <subcommand> add | remove | list | prune. <path> node path. <label> label name(s) label add /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg exempeletikett label list /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : for list , the labels on the node; for add and remove , nothing.

List labels (all, or of a node); search --tag finds what carries one. reads only labels [<path>] Argument What it is [<path>] node path (optional) labels labels /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : without a path, every label in use with how many nodes carry it ({ label, count }); with one, the labels on that node.

Create links between files. changes things ln [-s] [-f] <target> <link_name> Argument What it is <target> target of the link. <link_name> name of the link to create. Option What it does -s make symbolic links instead of hard links. -f remove existing destination files. ln -s /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg /home/anna/favourite.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing.

Append a JSON entry to a log, optionally at an explicit (backdated) timestamp. changes things log-append [--data=<string>] [--at=<string>] <log> <data> Argument What it is <log> VFS path to the log node. <data> JSON entry (alternative to --data); - reads it from stdin. Option What it does --data=<string> JSON payload for the entry; - reads it from stdin. --at=<string> ISO timestamp to backdate the entry to.

Read a log by time: the entries written in a range, or with --bucket the range summed up per interval (an average an hour, a maximum a day), as a chart wants it. reads only log-read [--since=<string>] [--until=<string>] [-n <string>] [--bucket=<string>] [--field=<string>] [--agg=<string>] [--tz=<string>] <log> Argument What it is <log> VFS path to the log node. Option What it does --since=<string> from this time on: ISO 8601, or a duration such as 24h or 7d meaning that long ago. --until=<string> before this time, as --since takes it. -n <string> at most this many entries or intervals, the latest (10000 when not given) --bucket=<string> sum the entries up per interval of this length: 5m, 1h, 1d. --field=<string> with --bucket, the field to sum up, dotted (usedBytes, host.availableBytes); the entry itself when not given. --agg=<string> with --bucket, how: avg, min, max, sum, count, first, last (avg when not given) --tz=<string> with --bucket, the time zone a day or an hour is counted in (the system's when not given) log-read /var/logs/metrics/cpu --since 1h log-read /var/logs/metrics/memory --since 7d --bucket 1h --field usedBytes --agg max With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : LogReadEntries { entries: [{at, data}] }, or with --bucket LogReadBuckets { buckets: [{at, value, count}] }.

Authenticate as a user. visitors too · changes things login [--session] <username> [<password>] Argument What it is <username> user to login: a username, or the e-mail address of an account. [<password>] password (optional, prompts if not provided) Option What it does --session login session not just shell.
Log out of the current session. visitors too · changes things logout [--session] Option What it does --session logout session not just shell.

List directory contents. reads only ls [-l] [-a] [-A] [-r] [-L] [-C] [-d] [-1] [-h] [--limit=<string>] [--after=<string>] [<path>...] Argument What it is [<path>...] paths to list, each under its own header when there are several. Option What it does -l use a long listing format. -a do not ignore entries starting with . -A do not ignore entries starting with . except for . and .. -r reverse order while sorting. -L do not follow symbolic links. -C include each entry's own child names (extra lookup, JSON output only) -d list each path itself, not what a directory holds. -1 list one entry per line, also on a terminal. -h with -l, print file sizes in units of 1024 (e.g. 1.5 KB) --limit=<string> list one page of this many entries, in the store's name order. --after=<string> with --limit, the page after this name: the last one of the page before. ls -l /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files ls /archive/people ls -d /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 /archive/people ls -l -- limit 200 --after IMG_0412.jpg /home/anna/staging/files/inbox With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the directory's entries; for several paths, an object of each path's entries; with -d, the paths themselves.

Who is in a container: an album's members by its rules, or a directory's media. reads only members <path> Argument What it is <path> The container. members /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 members /archive/tags/segling With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : every member's path, node id and, for a member held by a link, the link; with a type's own command (members- ), also which member stands for a folded group.

Sample EiN's own resources, storage and workload into /var/logs/metrics, and the machine's readings into its device /dev/ (long-running) administrators only · changes things metrics-sampler [--interval=<string>] Option What it does --interval=<string> Seconds between ticks (default: shortest series cadence)
Show stored, extension-based and content-sniffed mimetype of a node. reads only mime <path> Argument What it is <path> path to node.
Create a buffer node. changes things mkbuf mkbuf /tmp/exempelbuffert With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; the buffer node is created.
Create a directory node (-p to create parents) changes things mkdir mkdir -p /archive/albums/Nytt_Exempelalbum/files With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; the directory is created.

Create an empty text file node (what touch does elsewhere) changes things mkfile <target> Argument What it is <target> VFS path for the new file. mkfile /home/exempel/anteckning.txt With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; an empty text file node is created.

Create a log node. changes things mklog [--routing-keys=<string>] [--retention=<string>] <target> Argument What it is <target> VFS path for the log node. Option What it does --routing-keys=<string> , -k Comma-separated routing keys to bind to. --retention=<string> , -r Retention policy (default: forever, e.g. 7 day, 100 entries)

Create new or ensure node. changes things mknode [-p] [-t <string>] [--under=<string>] [--tier=<string>] [--as=<string>] [--an=<number>] [--aj=<string>] [--al=<string>] [-m <string>] [-o <string>] [-g <string>] <path>... Argument What it is <path>... node path to create; repeatable. Option What it does -p if the path already exists, do nothing. -t <string> type of node to make, required. --under=<string> existing node the path must sit under; bounds what -p may create. --tier=<string> storage tier for a file's bytes: disk, volatile or db; fixed once created. --as=<string> set attribute as string. --an=<number> set attribute as number. --aj=<string> set attribute as JSON. --al=<string> set attribute as comma-separated list. -m <string> mode to set. -o <string> owner as uid or user name. -g <string> group as gid or group name.

Create a pool node. changes things mkpool [--aging-seconds=<string>] [--aging-boost=<string>] [--aging-max=<string>] [--lease-ms=<string>] [--max-attempts=<string>] <target> Argument What it is <target> VFS path for the pool node. Option What it does --aging-seconds=<string> , -a Queue age per aging step (0 disables aging) --aging-boost=<string> , -b Effective-priority points per aging step. --aging-max=<string> , -m Total aging cap; keep below the gap between priority lanes. --lease-ms=<string> , -l Default lease duration in ms. --max-attempts=<string> , -n Default attempts before a job fails.

Create a queue node. changes things mkqueue [--routing-keys=<string>] <target> Argument What it is <target> VFS path for the queue node. Option What it does --routing-keys=<string> , -k Comma-separated routing keys to bind to.

Create a router node. changes things mkrouter [--routing-key=<string>] <target> Argument What it is <target> VFS path for the router node. Option What it does --routing-key=<string> , -k Routing key for fan-out broadcasting (required)
Module management. mod <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.
Pre-fetch a module's TypeScript command dependencies. administrators only · changes things mod-cache <name> Argument What it is <name> Module name (directory name under /modules)

Say which groups a module is kept to, or keep it to some groups, or make it everyone's again. administrators only · reads only mod-groups [--everyone] <name> <group>... Argument What it is <name> The module. <group>... Keep it to these groups: on their PATH and in their navigation alone, its commands refused to anyone else. Option What it does --everyone Make it everyone's again. mod groups archive mod groups archive family friends mod groups archive --everyone With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The module and the groups it is kept to, none when it is everyone's.
Show module information. reads only mod-info <name> Argument What it is <name> Module name.

Install modules from their repositories, or update them, with the dependencies they lack, and set them up: one install at a time, which goes on when the session ends. administrators only · changes things mod-install [--force] [--missing] [--groups=<string>] [--no-setup] [--background] <module>... Argument What it is <module>... A published module by name (archive), or its repository ( https://github.com/einhq/module-archive ), either with @branch, @tag or @commit (its id whole, or its first seven characters or more); without one, its newest release (v tag) that this core can run, or its default branch when it has none. Option What it does --force Fetch again what is installed at the same commit, and update even when an installed module does not accept the new version. --missing Install only modules not installed, or installed at a release this core cannot run, leaving any other installed one as it is without asking its forge. --groups=<string> Keep the modules named to these groups, comma-separated, as mod groups does; the dependencies it installs with them are everyone's. --no-setup Put the modules in place without setting them up or starting their services, as boot does before its own mod setup --all. --background Start the install and return at once; mod status says how far it has got.
List installed modules, those kept to groups only for their members and administrators. reads only mod-list [--long] Option What it does --long Show detailed information.
Uninstall a module. administrators only · changes things mod-remove [--force] <name> Argument What it is <name> Module name. Option What it does --force Skip confirmation prompt.

The published modules: each module-* repository of the module sources (CFG_MODULE_SOURCES), with its version and whether it is installed. reads only mod-search <words>... Argument What it is <words>... Words the name or description must hold.

Set up a module already in the modules directory. administrators only · changes things mod-setup <name> Argument What it is <name> Module name (directory name under /modules), or --all for every module in dependency order.

Say how far the module install running now has got, or what the last one came to. reads only mod-status [--follow] Option What it does --follow Say what the install says until it ends, and exit as it does.

Mount a filesystem. changes things mount [--save] [-a] <path> <type> <options> Argument What it is <path> mount point, made as a directory when it is missing. <type> type: memory, pg, filesystem, command, sftp. <options> k=v,... — any: readonly, noaudit (paths, separated by : , whose writes the audit trail skips), nopublish (its events reach no queue, so no pipeline or service bound to one sees them); sftp: host, port, user, path, key (identity file), hostkey (SHA256:… to pin), uid, gid. Option What it does --save also record the mount in /etc/fstab, so boot mounts it again. -a mount every /etc/fstab entry not mounted yet. mount mount --save /mnt/nas sftp "host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos" mount /mnt/backup sftp "host=backup.example.com,port=2222,key=/home/admin/.ssh/backup,readonly" mount -a

Move or rename files and directories, re-pointing the softlinks at each moved path or anywhere under it (and a relation link’s peerLink with them) changes things mv [--no-clobber] [--no-relink] <source> <dest> Argument What it is <source> the files or directories to move; several go into DEST, which must exist. <dest> destination: an existing node that is not a file to move into, or the new path of a single source, replacing a file there. Option What it does --no-clobber Do not overwrite an existing file - fails if destination already exists (-n) --no-relink Leave the softlinks that point at or under each moved source on its old path. mv /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/nytt_namn.jpg mv /home/anna/staging/files/inbox/upload-2026-10-16 /home/anna/staging/files/scans/ With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : in JSON mode, MvAnswer: how many sources moved, how many softlinks were re-pointed, and each source that did not move with why. Exits non-zero only when no source moved.

What has been added lately, newest first, from every news-* command on PATH. reads only news [--limit=<number>] Option What it does --limit=<number> entries returned, across all providers (default 8) news news -- limit 20 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the newest entries of every news-* provider together: when, what, who did it, the node it is about, which provider, and the route that draws it.
run a command detached, immune to shell hang-up, logging to /var/logs/jobs. changes things nohup <command> Argument What it is <command> the command (and args) to run detached.

What the archive has from a calendar day (MM-DD, default today) in earlier years, from every onthisday-* command on PATH. reads only onthisday [--limit=<number>] [<day>] Argument What it is [<day>] day as MM-DD (default today, UTC) Option What it does --limit=<number> entries returned across all providers (default 8) onthisday onthisday 06-21 -- limit 20 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the entries of every onthisday-* provider, newest year first: the year, what, the node it is about, which provider, and the route that draws it.

A search's words read as filters — subjects, an area, years, kinds — by the command CFG_SEARCH_PARSER names, or as words when it names none. reads only parse-search [--rules] <words>... Argument What it is <words>... What was typed into the search box. Option What it does --rules The parser's fast pass only, without its model.
Manage pipelines. pipeline <subcommand> Argument What it is <subcommand> Subcommand to run.
Cancel a running pipeline. administrators only · changes things pipeline-cancel <id> Argument What it is <id> Instance ID.
Register a pipeline definition from a YAML file. administrators only · changes things pipeline-define <path> Argument What it is <path> Path to pipeline YAML file.
Run the pipeline engine (long-running) administrators only · changes things pipeline-engine

Rerun failed instances after a growing wait, and mark those that keep failing for a person. administrators only · reads only pipeline-heal [--apply] [--now] [--limit=<number>] Option What it does --apply Rerun and mark (default is a dry run) --now Skip the waits: the cause is known to have passed. --limit=<number> Failed instances to look at, oldest first (default 500)

List pipeline instances — running, failed or completed — newest first. reads only pipeline-instances [-s <string>] [--limit=<string>] [--after=<string>] [<name>] Argument What it is [<name>] Pipeline name (optional, repeatable) Option What it does -s <string> Filter by status. --limit=<string> Page size (default 100) --after=<string> Keyset cursor from a previous page ( : )
List pipeline definitions. reads only pipeline-list
Pipeline workload summary: instance counts (running, failed, completed), queue depths, active instances, completion rate. reads only pipeline-overview
