POSTGRES_POOL_RESERVED 4 Of those, connections background work may never take, so an interactive command never waits behind a crawl. 0 is first come, first served. POSTGRES_LISTEN_POOL_MAX 4 Connections kept apart for change notifications, which hold theirs for good. TRUSTED_PROXIES Addresses, separated by commas, of proxies whose X-Forwarded-For and Forwarded headers name the client, besides this host's loopback, which is always believed. setup.sh sets 10.0.2.2 under rootless podman's slirp4netns, where a proxy on the machine reaches EiN from there. FILE_ROOT_PATH ./files Host directory where file content is stored. VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH FILE_ROOT_PATH Host directory for content that can be made again — thumbnails, crops, transcodes — so it can live on a faster or cheaper disk. DOCS_PATH ./guide Host directory mounted as the guide at /usr/docs/guide: the documentation at einhq.eu, as the image bundles it or a checkout of the site. Without one the Docs page links to einhq.eu. In a shell the same name is the tree path /usr/docs. DEV_MODULES_PATH ./modules The deployment's modules: a folder of module checkouts mounted read-only at /tmp/dev-modules and linked into /usr/modules. A name here wins over an installed module of the same name. In a shell the same name is that tree path. MODULE_INSTALL_PATH ./modules-installed Host directory mod install puts modules in, mounted read-write at /var/lib/modules. A folder of the host mounted into the container keeps the installed modules when the container is replaced. INSTALL_MODULES Modules boot installs with mod install when they are not installed: names or repository addresses, separated by spaces. One installed already is left as it is, unless this core cannot run it: at each boot an installed module written for another module API is replaced by the newest release this core runs. mod install and the settings page update them. INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD The admin account's first password, set at the first start of a new instance. Without it that start sets a random one and prints it to the log once. Changing it later does nothing; the account's password is changed in Settings or with user-passwd . TZ the host's zone Time zone for log lines, "today", and which year a date late on New Year's Eve belongs to. LOG_LEVEL INFO How much the process logs: DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR. LOG_MODULES Per-component log levels over LOG_LEVEL, such as ssh-server:DEBUG,pipeline:WARN. EXTERNAL_COMMANDS_CONFIG external-commands.json File listing the host programs shell commands may run. COMMAND_LOOKUP_TTL_MS 5000 How long a command name found on PATH is remembered before it is looked up again. DEBUG_LOCKS Set to 1 to record who holds each lock and warn about one held for more than five seconds.

Where the tree keeps each kind of thing, exported for every shell, so cd $LOGS_PATH works wherever the folder lives. Variable Default What it is ARCHIVE_PATH The archive: everything people put in and look at. TAGS_PATH Labels, one directory per label holding links to what carries it. HOMES_PATH One home directory per user, owned by the user. GROUP_HOMES_PATH One shared home per group given one, which only its members see. ETC_PATH System configuration: settings, groups, services, boot scripts. USERS_PATH The accounts: one user node per account, the administrator's. GROUPS_PATH Groups. SERVICES_PATH Service definitions. INIT_FILES_PATH Files installed into the tree at boot. INIT_PATH Boot scripts. VAR_PATH What the system writes as it runs. LOGS_PATH Logs and metrics. SESSIONS_PATH Open sessions. LINKS_PATH Share links: one node per link that opens an album without signing in. QUEUES_PATH Queues. PIPELINE_QUEUE_PATH The queue the pipeline engine works from. POOLS_PATH Job pools. PIPELINES_PATH Pipeline definitions and running instances. WWW_PATH Web pages served over HTTP. MOD_INSTALL_PATH The modules mod install installed, each linked into /usr/modules. USR_PATH Code and read-only payload. BIN_PATH Built-in commands. LIB_PATH Core's other files: its shell commands, its services and the Web UI. MOD_PATH Installed modules. DOCS_PATH This documentation. TEMP_PATH Temporary nodes. DEV_MODULES_PATH The deployment's modules, mounted read-only. VAR_DIRS The directories under /var, as names separated by spaces, for boot scripts to loop over.

What EiN exports for every shell at its start besides the folders: the built-in accounts, the host folders its storage is on, and the ports the deployment gave it. Variable Default What it is ADMIN_USERNAME The built-in administrator account. ADMIN_GROUPNAME Its group. ADMIN_UID Its user id. ADMIN_GID Its group's id. GUEST_USERNAME The account a visitor who has not signed in acts as. GUEST_GROUPNAME Its group. GUEST_UID Its user id. GUEST_GID Its group's id. USERS_GROUPNAME The group every account belongs to: what "everyone" means when sharing. USERS_GID Its id. CFG_HTTP_PORT 8080 The port the Web UI listens on, as the deployment set it, which the http-server service reads at its start. In the installer's container it is always 8080: the machine publishes EIN_HTTP_PORT from .env onto it. It is not a setting, since only the deployment knows which port reaches it. CFG_SSH_PORT 2222 The port the SSH and SFTP server listens on, as the deployment set it, which the ssh-server service reads at its start. In the installer's container it is always 2222: the machine publishes EIN_SSH_PORT from .env onto it. EIN_PATH_EXPORTS The layout variables as export lines, written into /etc/layout at boot. EIN_FILE_ROOT_PATH Where file content is stored on the host, as FILE_ROOT_PATH gave it: what the dashboard reports disk use for. EIN_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH The same for content that can be made again. EXTERNAL_FILE_ROOT_PATH FILE_ROOT_PATH as boot received it, for the init scripts. EXTERNAL_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH as boot received it. EXTERNAL_DOCS_PATH DOCS_PATH as boot received it: what is mounted at /usr/docs/guide. EXTERNAL_DEV_MODULES_PATH DEV_MODULES_PATH as boot received it. EXTERNAL_MODULE_INSTALL_PATH MODULE_INSTALL_PATH as boot received it. DEV_MODULES Which of the modules in DEV_MODULES_PATH boot links, when set: the test harness names the modules a test loads. Unset, it links them all. HEADLESS Set to 1 by the test harness, which serves HTTP itself: boot leaves the HTTP and SSH servers disabled and links no browser shell.

Set by the server that opened the shell: the Web UI, the terminal panel or SSH. Variable Default What it is USER Your user name. HOME Your home directory, holding your settings (.config) and shell history. PATH Where commands are looked up, first directory first: core's commands, then each installed module's bin directory. TMPDIR Where commands put temporary nodes. PWD The directory you are in. OLDPWD The directory you were in before, where cd - goes. UID Your user id. GID Your primary group's id. SID The session this shell belongs to. PID The running command's own id, its name and a unique suffix. TTY_NAME The terminal this shell is attached to, when it has one. TERM The terminal type an interactive shell reports to programs. HOSTNAME The host name shown in the prompt. COOKIE_NAME The browser cookie that carries a web session.

Nobody sets these for you. Export one in a shell, or put it in front of a command, to change how commands behave there: JSON_OUTPUT=1 ls . Variable Default What it is JSON_OUTPUT Set to 1 and commands answer in JSON instead of text. The Web UI runs every command this way. MEDIA_LINES 20 How many text lines tall cat draws a picture in a terminal. SEARCH_TRACE Set to 1 and search reports how long each of its sources took. CFG_PASSWORD_HASH_LOGN 16 The scrypt work factor for new password hashes, as a power of two. Lowered by the test tier, where the passwords protect nothing; leave it unset anywhere else. NOMINATIM_SEARCH_URL https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search Where geocoding asks Nominatim for an address, as geocode-location and location-region do. Point it at your own server to avoid the public one's rate limit. From the archive module. NOMINATIM_REVERSE_URL https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/reverse Where Nominatim is asked for the address at a point: a picture's street address (geocode-position), and the town around a stay that has no harbour, island or bay nearby (track-places). From the archive module. OVERPASS_URL https://overpass-api.de/api/interpreter https://overpass.private.coffee/api/interpreter Where track-places asks OpenStreetMap's Overpass API for the harbours, islands and bays a track stayed at: one or more endpoints, separated by spaces, tried in turn. Point it at your own server to avoid the public ones' rate limit. From the archive module. SMHI_METOBS_URL https://opendata-download-metobs.smhi.se/api/version/1.0 Where weather asks SMHI's meteorological observations for the weather stations and their hourly values. From the archive module. OPEN_METEO_ARCHIVE_URL https://archive-api.open-meteo.com/v1/archive Where weather asks Open-Meteo's historical weather API for the hourly weather of places with no SMHI station near them. From the archive module. OPEN_METEO_FORECAST_URL https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast Where weather-forecast, and the dashboard's weather card, ask Open-Meteo's forecast API for the weather now and in the days ahead. From the archive module.

Set for each step of a pipeline by the change that started it. Variable Default What it is NODE_PATH The node the event is about. EVENT_TYPE What happened, as a dotted name such as media.metadata.extracted. EVENT_ID The event's id. EVENT_SOURCE What raised the event, such as archive-bridge. EVENT_DATA The event's details as JSON. Each field is also its own variable: mimetype becomes EVENT_MIMETYPE, deviceSerial EVENT_DEVICE_SERIAL. CFG_EMS_INSTANCE Which instance of the media service a step calls (ems-instance list): set by the pool worker for another instance on each step it runs; unset, the primary. From the media service module.
Every node has a type, which decides what it holds and how it behaves. These are the 32 types of an EiN with all its modules. Nodes and node types explains what a node is.

What the archive is made of: what people add, and what EiN works out about it. Type What it is Lives under Module album Album A collection of photos and videos that behaves as a directory. It holds its files, and links the ones added to it from elsewhere. It remembers its cover, the time span of its media, and the stacks of similar photos taken in a row. /archive/albums Archive album-profile Album profile A summary of a library album's members — their times, days, places, people and a few pictures that stand for how it looks — kept beside it as its .profile child, which staging matches suggested groups against. Archive camera Camera A camera or phone, matched by make, model and serial number. Knows its time zone, so photos without one get their capture time right. One that is part of a device that records where it was, a phone, links the device as its child device, and its track is the device's. /archive/cameras Archive exif EXIF The metadata read from a media file — camera, picture, exposure, its clock readings and GPS fix — kept as a child of the file. Media file File Stored bytes with a name, a mimetype, a size and a checksum: a photo, a video, a document, an event text. Media files carry what was read from them (capture time, orientation, faces) and hold their derived pieces — thumbnails, captions, EXIF — as children. Core location Location A location under /archive/locations: its name, the address it was written down with and how that was geocoded, the people who lived there and the photos linked to it. Where it is on the map is its child named position, a point, circle or outline. /archive/locations Archive media-region Region A box on a photo, kept under the photo's regions/ directory: a face the detector found, a box someone drew, or a tag imported from the old archive. It carries who is in it. A region that shows a usable face has the face's vector as a child named embedding, and only those take part in face recognition. Archive person Person Someone in the archive, with names, dates of birth and death, and contact details. Parents, children and partners are links between people; the photos they appear in are found by their faces. /archive/people Archive position Position A point on the map with an optional radius or outline. A photo, a location or an event keeps where it is as a child named position. Core recipe Recipe A recipe in /archive/recipes: its title, the servings it is written for, its ingredients and steps in sections, the categories it is in, the language it is written in and the page it was taken from. Its pictures are files in its pictures/ directory, one of them its cover. /archive/recipes Recipes track Track The route something travelled: timestamped GPS points, live or from GPX files, summarised by their extent and time span. A device under /dev keeps its position as one, its position endpoint. Core

How the tree is arranged: folders, links, and what holds other nodes. Type What it is Lives under Module directory Directory A folder that holds other nodes. The archive roots — albums, people, locations, devices and labels — are directories. Core group Group A set of users, under /etc/groups. A node's group, and any group in its ACL, decides who besides the owner may read or change it. Core softlink Softlink A pointer to another node by path, followed transparently. Album covers, pictures added to an album, labels and the relations between people and locations are all softlinks. Core user User An account that can sign in, under /home. Owns nodes, belongs to groups, and keeps its settings and shell history in its home directory. Core

How EiN runs: its commands, logs, queues and the other parts of the system that are nodes too. Type What it is Lives under Module command Command A built-in shell command, carrying its own description, arguments and flags. Commands a module adds are files in the module's bin directory instead. Core control Control An endpoint of a device that is written to change it: a switch, a dimmer, a setpoint. What is written goes to the device's driver; what is read are the states the device reported. Core device Device Something that reports or can be switched, under /dev: a phone, a sensor, a plug, a camera. Its endpoints are its children, logs, tracks, controls and streams, and what is written to the device itself goes to its driver, which reads it into them. Core device-key Device key The key a device carries to write to /file/dev/ without signing in, as a phone posting its position does: the device's child .key, readable by the administrator alone. device-key makes, shows and takes it away. Core embedding Embedding A numeric fingerprint of an image, a face or a text, kept for similarity search: what finds photos by what they show and faces of the same person. Core log Log An append-only record of entries kept for a retention period, such as the system log under /var/logs. A device's readings and events are logs under it, one an endpoint. Core null Null /dev/null: reading it gives nothing and what is written to it is thrown away, for output nobody wants. Core pool Pool Background jobs waiting for a worker with the right resources, under /var/pools. pool stat shows what is waiting. Core queue Queue A durable first-in, first-out buffer; reading an entry removes it. The pipeline engine takes its work from one. Core router Router A live broadcast channel: what is written reaches every current reader and nothing is kept. /dev/events is one. Core session Session A signed-in connection — a browser, an SSH login, a service — under /var/sessions. Removed when it ends. Core share-link Share link A link that opens an album, and what it holds, to whoever has it, without signing in; under /var/links, with when it expires and how often it was opened. share-link makes, lists and turns them off. Core stream Stream An endpoint of a device that is a live picture, a camera's. Nothing is kept of it: reading it gives a JPEG of it now from the device's driver ( cat /dev/front-door/main > door.jpg ), and the device's page plays it live. Core tty Terminal An interactive terminal belonging to a session, with its size and working directory. Core user-invite Sign-in link A link an administrator makes for an account, with which its person chooses their own password once at /invite/ before it expires: the account's child .invite, readable by the administrator alone. user-invite makes, shows and takes it away. Core

Every file that configures EiN, where it lives, what writes it and what reads it: the installation's files on the machine EiN runs on, and the files in EiN's own tree. This page is for administrators, and for anyone who wants to know which file a setting or a habit of the shell comes from. There are two places to look: On the machine EiN runs on , in the folder EiN was installed in ( ~/ein with the installer): .env , the compose files and setup.sh . They decide what runs and with which environment, and change only when you edit them or run setup.sh . In EiN's tree , under /etc and in each home: ordinary files kept in the database, which you read with cat and change with edit in EiN's terminal. They survive a restart and an update like the rest of the tree. How the settings in these files combine, and how to change a setting without touching a file, is on Configuration . Every setting is listed on Settings , and every other variable on Environment variables .

The installer fetches the deployment into ~/ein and runs setup.sh there. After the first run the folder holds: Path Made by What it is .env setup.sh , the first run The settings and passwords of this installation, and the environment of EiN and the media service. Yours to edit. compose.yaml the deployment EiN and its database, the base of every installation. compose.ems.yaml the deployment The media service, which the Archive needs, added with --ems . compose.llm.yaml the deployment The language model the Assistant uses, added with --llm . compose.override.yaml setup.sh , every run The options chosen in .env , as compose services. Written again on every run; do not edit it. setup.sh the deployment Brings this folder up to date, fetches the sources, writes .env and compose.override.yaml , pulls the images or builds them from your own source, and starts them. src/ setup.sh The sources it fetches: ems and llm when those options are on, and core and db from any source but GitHub's einhq , which it builds with ems . data/ setup.sh Your files and the database, unless EIN_DATA named another folder at the install. See The data folder . The files from the deployment are replaced when setup.sh brings the folder up to date at the start of every run, so changes belong in .env , not in compose.yaml . setup.sh --help lists its options, and Installing in detail explains each. The database is in data/db , or in the folder setup.sh --db-dir named. Your data: backup, moving and removing says how to keep it.

.env is read in two ways. Compose reads it to fill in compose.yaml , and EiN's and the media service's containers get every line of it as their environment. setup.sh writes it once, with mode 0600 , and from then on changes only the lines its options set: EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM , EIN_MODULES , EIN_SOURCE , EIN_SOURCE_KEY and EIN_DB_DIR , and adds EIN_ENGINE to a .env written before it had that line. It also moves EIN_HTTP_PORT or EIN_SSH_PORT to the next free port when another program holds it, and with a Forgejo or Gitea source keeps CFG_MODULE_SOURCES and CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY in step with EIN_SOURCE . The file the installer writes looks like this, with your own values: # ~/ein/.env, on the machine EiN runs on COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME =ein EIN_ENGINE =podman EIN_EMS = 0 EIN_LLM = 0 EIN_GPU = 0 EIN_MODULES = "" EIN_DATA =/home/helen/ein/data POSTGRES_PASSWORD =… EMS_KEY =… TZ =Europe/London INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD =… EIN_BIND = 0.0 . 0.0 EIN_HTTP_PORT = 8080 EIN_SSH_PORT = 2222 # CFG_LLM_URL=https://api.openai.com # CFG_LLM_KEY= # CFG_LLM_PROVIDER=OpenAI # CFG_LLM_MODEL= EIN_SOURCE =https://github.com/einhq EIN_SOURCE_KEY = EIN_DB_DIR =/home/anna/ein/data/db Line What it does Explained on COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME ein , the name of the containers, network and volumes. EIN_ENGINE podman or docker , the engine setup.sh picked at the install and keeps to. Installing in detail EIN_EMS 1 runs the media service. --ems and --no-ems set it. The media service EIN_LLM 1 runs the language model. --llm and --no-llm set it. The language model EIN_GPU 1 gives the graphics card to the media service and the language model. The first run sets it when it finds a card with its CDI file. The graphics card EIN_MODULES The modules EiN installs at its start when they are missing, separated by spaces. --module adds a name. Modules EIN_DATA The data folder, as an absolute path. Installing in detail POSTGRES_PASSWORD The database's password, made at the install. EMS_KEY The media service's key, made at the install. Both EiN and the media service get it. The media service TZ The time zone, taken from the machine at the install. Environment variables INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD The admin account's first password, made at the install. EiN takes it at its first start only; setup.sh prints it at the end of every run until you delete the line, once you have changed the password. Install EiN EIN_BIND The address the ports are published on. 127.0.0.1 keeps them to the machine. Ports, HTTPS and remote access EIN_HTTP_PORT The machine's port for the Web UI. Ports, HTTPS and remote access EIN_SSH_PORT The machine's port for SSH and SFTP. Ports, HTTPS and remote access CFG_LLM_… The Assistant's settings for a hosted language model in place of --llm , commented out until you use it. The language model EIN_SOURCE The organisation the sources are cloned from. --source sets it. Installing in detail EIN_SOURCE_KEY The token that reads the source's repositories when they are private. A --source on another host empties it, unless EIN_SOURCE_KEY in the environment gives a new one. Installing in detail EIN_DB_DIR The database's folder, db in the data folder; --db-dir sets another. Empty keeps it in the engine's volume ein_db . Installing in detail Lines you can add: Line Read by What it does CFG_… EiN Gives a setting its value, shown as From deployment . See the exceptions below. EMS_… the media service Configures the media service. EIN_MEMORY , EMS_MEMORY , LLM_MEMORY compose The most memory each container may use: 6g , 16g and 10g unless set. LLM_GGUF_REPO , LLM_GGUF_FILE , LLM_IMAGE , LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB compose The language model's file, image and share of the card. TRUSTED_PROXIES EiN The addresses of proxies whose forwarding headers name the visitor, by commas. See Ports, HTTPS and remote access . Four settings are fixed by compose.yaml , which wins over .env : CFG_HTTP_PORT ( 8080 ), CFG_SSH_PORT ( 2222 ), and the ems module's CFG_EMS_URL ( http://ems:8181 ) and CFG_EMS_KEY (the value of EMS_KEY ). A line for them in .env changes nothing. The Assistant's CFG_LLM_URL is read from .env and is http://llm:8190 when the line is missing. With --llm , compose.override.yaml also sets CFG_LLM_CARD to card or cpu after EIN_GPU . To apply a change to .env : # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d # or: docker compose up -d Under podman-compose, a container that podman compose up -d makes again has no swap limit, which setup.sh gives each one: the media service's idle models then go to swap, and a search waits for them. Running ./setup.sh makes the containers again with it, and applies .env too, but also fetches and builds the newest sources; Updating explains it. After a change to EIN_EMS , EIN_LLM or EIN_GPU , run setup.sh , since only it writes them into compose.override.yaml . Warning .env holds the database password and the media service's key, and no other file keeps them. Keep a copy of it with your backups.

setup.sh writes this file from .env on every run, and every compose reads it beside compose.yaml on its own, so podman compose up -d starts the same services as setup.sh does. Under podman, with the media service, the language model and a card, it reads: # Written by setup.sh from the options in .env and the container engine; edit those and run # setup.sh again. services: db: restart: always ein: environment: CFG_LLM_CARD: card restart: always ems: extends: { file: compose.ems.yaml , service: ems } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always llm: extends: { file: compose.llm.yaml , service: llm } devices: [ nvidia.com/gpu=all ] restart: always Under podman every service gets restart: always , the policy podman starts again at boot; under Docker those lines are left out. A change made by hand is gone at the next run of setup.sh .

EIN_DATA is the folder for what is yours outside the database. setup.sh makes its subfolders, and the containers mount them: Folder Mounted in EiN at What it holds files /files The originals. old /old Older originals. files-volatile /files-volatile Renditions EiN can make again: thumbnails, crops, transcodes. modules /modules-installed The modules EiN installed, which it sees in its tree at /var/lib/modules . llm not in EiN; the language model's /models The downloaded model. The media service, when installed, mounts none of these folders: it reaches the files of each request through EiN's ems-files service. Files and storage explains how the tree's files map to these folders.

These files are nodes in the tree, so they live in the database and survive a restart, an update and a new container. Read them in EiN's terminal with cat , and change them with edit or the code editor on the Nodes page, as far as your rights allow. Path Written by Read by Mode /etc/bashrc core at the first start, then the administrator every shell, when it opens 0644 /etc/bashrc.d/<group> the administrator, mod setup the group's members' shells, when they open 0644 /etc/layout boot, at every start /etc/bashrc /etc/environment boot, at every start /etc/bashrc 0644 /etc/config.d/<module> mod setup , as a link to the module's file /etc/bashrc /etc/config Settings → System , config set /etc/bashrc 0644 /etc/keys Settings → System , config set , for keys EiN itself, never a shell 0600 ~/.config Profile → Preferences , config set /etc/bashrc 0600 ~/.bashrc you your terminal and SSH logins ~/.bash_history your shell your shell /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json mod setup , as a link to the module's file the sidebar and top bar /etc/ui/nav.json the administrator the sidebar and top bar /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json the group's members the group's members' sidebar and top bar /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.d/<module>.json mod setup , as a link to the module's file, for a module kept to the group the group's members' sidebar and top bar /etc/modules/<module>.groups mod groups , mod install --groups , Settings → Modules mod setup and the shell, for who has the module 0644 ~/.ui/nav.json you your sidebar and top bar /etc/fstab mount --save , unmount --save boot, with mount -a 0600 /etc/frozen-uploads core at the first start, then the administrator an upload over the web or SFTP, unzip --as-upload 0644 /etc/ssh_host_key , .pub the SSH server, at the first start the SSH server 0700 ~/.ssh/… you, ssh-keygen , ssh the SSH server, ssh , scp , mount 0700 /etc/users/ , /etc/groups/ the account and group commands every sign-in and access check /etc/services/ service add , service enable , mod setup service start-all at boot /etc/files/ , /etc/init/ boot boot /etc/assistant-prompt.md mod setup , once; then the administrator the Assistant, when installed /etc/assistant.d/<module>/ mod setup , as a link to the module's folder the Assistant, when installed A blank mode is the default the folder gives a new file. ~ is your home, /home/<your username> .

Five files hold the values of settings, each an ordinary shell file of export lines: # /etc/config export CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS= '14' export CFG_MODULE_SOURCES= 'https://github.com/einhq https://forge.example:3000/family' File Holds /etc/environment The CFG_… variables EiN's container was started with, written whole at every start. A value the deployment stops passing is gone from it. A key is never written here. /etc/config.d/<module> A module's own choice of values: a link to the module's etc/config , made by mod setup and removed with the module. The Archive's names CFG_SEARCH_PARSER , the assistant's CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL and CFG_COMMAND_FINDER , the media service's CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER . /etc/config The administrator's values for system settings. Made by the first config set ; until then it does not exist. ~/.config One person's values for personal settings, the CFG_USER_… ones and HISTSIZE . Made by the first config set of that person. /etc/keys The keys to other services saved on the Settings page or with config set : CFG_MODULE_SOURCES_KEY , and with their modules CFG_EMS_KEY and CFG_LLM_KEY . Owned by admin , and sourced by no shell. A key from .env is never written to any file. /etc/bashrc sources the first four in that order, so the last one wins: a person's own value, then the administrator's, then a module's, then the deployment's. How the layers combine shows the whole order with the badges of the Settings page. config set rewrites a line in place and keeps the rest of the file as it was. When you edit /etc/config or ~/.config by hand, nothing checks your values and nothing is restarted; Edit the settings file by hand says what that means.

/etc/bashrc is sourced by every shell EiN opens: a terminal tab, an SSH login, a command sent over SSH, a service, a pipeline step. It is copied from core's own file at the first start, and from then on it is the administrator's: an update does not replace it. With the Archive installed it reads, in this order: #!bash alias la= 'ls -A' alias ll= 'ls -al' alias whoami = 'user whoami' alias id = 'user id' export HISTSIZE=1000 # Configuration layers: the deployment's first, then the modules', the system's, and personal last, # so a personal setting wins. 10_config.sh adds these to an existing /etc/bashrc, which boot # never replaces. case ": $PATH :" in *:/usr/modules/archive/bin:*) ;; *) export PATH= " $PATH :/usr/modules/archive/bin" ;; esac [ -r /etc/layout ] && source /etc/layout [ -r /etc/environment ] && source /etc/environment for f in /etc/config.d/*; do [ -r " $f " ] && source " $f " ; done [ -r /etc/config ] && source /etc/config [ -n " $HOME " ] && [ -r " $HOME /.config" ] && source " $HOME /.config" Each other module with a bin/ folder, such as the ems module, has a PATH line of its own beside the Archive's. Boot and mod setup keep some lines in it, whatever else you change: mod setup adds a PATH line for each module that has a bin/ folder, once. Boot adds the line that sources /etc/layout , once. At every start, boot moves the four lines that source the settings files to the end, so they come after anything you add. /etc/layout exports where each folder of the tree is, such as ETC_PATH and LOGS_PATH , and where the data folders are on the machine ( EIN_FILE_ROOT_PATH , EIN_VOLATILE_FILE_ROOT_PATH ). Boot writes it whole at every start; leave it alone. Folders in the tree lists the variables. A change to /etc/bashrc reaches every shell before its next command, an open terminal tab included; a command already running keeps what it started with. Put aliases and settings of your own in ~/.bashrc instead, which is yours alone.

File What it is ~/.bashrc Your own aliases, functions and variables, read after /etc/bashrc by a terminal tab and an SSH login, not by a command sent with ssh host 'command' . A line that fails does not stop the shell from opening. ~/.bash_history Your command history, the file HISTFILE names. HISTSIZE sets how many commands are kept. ~/.config Your personal settings; see The settings files . EiN reads no ~/.bash_profile or ~/.profile . Keep your settings in ~/.bashrc shows what to put in it.

The sidebar and the top bar are put together from four layers of JSON, each changing only what it names: File Who writes it Who it is for /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json each module, linked by mod setup ; EiN's own is /etc/ui/nav.d/ui.json everyone /etc/ui/nav.json an administrator everyone /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json the group's members the group's members ~/.ui/nav.json you you only A module kept to some groups has its file linked in /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.d/<module>.json in each of its groups' homes instead, read for the group's members, and for an administrator, alongside /etc/ui/nav.d . The files in /etc/ui/nav.d are links to the modules' files, and an update replaces them; put changes in /etc/ui/nav.json , a group's /groups/<group>/.ui/nav.json or ~/.ui/nav.json , which exist only once someone writes them. Your sidebar and top bar describes the format and its fields.

/etc/fstab lists the mounts EiN makes again at every start, one per line: the mount point, the type and the options, separated by spaces. A field with a space in it is in double quotes, and a line starting with # is a comment. /mnt/nas sftp host=nas.local,user=anna,path=/srv/photos,key=/home/admin/.ssh/nas mount --save adds or replaces the line for its mount point, and unmount --save removes it, keeping every other line and comment. The file is made with mode 0600 , since it names other machines and their users. When it is missing, boot mounts nothing. Mount a folder of another machine explains the options.

/etc/frozen-uploads says which uploads are frozen as they arrive: a file uploaded in the Web UI or copied in over SFTP whose type it lists can no longer be written, in EiN or on the disk, and so can one unzip --as-upload takes out of an uploaded zip, as the Archive's staging does. One type per line; image/* stands for every subtype, a ! in front leaves a type out that another line takes in, and # starts a comment. It is copied from core's own file at the first start, and from then on it is the administrator's: # /etc/frozen-uploads image/* video/* audio/* # An SVG is a text file that can hold a script. !image/svg+xml An upload reads the file as it is then, so a change applies to the next one and freezes or thaws nothing already there. An empty file freezes no upload; a missing one is copied again at the next start. What EiN writes itself is never frozen by it.

File What it is /etc/ssh_host_key , /etc/ssh_host_key.pub The SSH server's host key, an ed25519 pair made at the first start. Kept in the tree, so it stays the same across updates and new containers. ~/.ssh/authorized_keys The public keys that may sign in as you over SSH and SFTP, one a line. SSH and SFTP explains the modes it needs. ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 , id_ecdsa , id_rsa Your own keys, for ssh , scp and ssh-copy-id to other machines, made with ssh-keygen . ~/.ssh/config Settings per machine for ssh and scp , in OpenSSH's format. ~/.ssh/known_hosts The host keys of the machines you have accepted. Lines written by OpenSSH work as they are. ~/.ssh is made with mode 0700 the first time a command needs it. Reaching other machines covers the client files.

These are kept by commands, not edited as text: /etc/users/<name> is an account, with its password in .password and, with the Archive, a link to the person it is. /etc/groups/<group> is a group, with links to its members in users . Accounts and groups and the user and group commands change them; Permissions in depth gives their modes. /etc/services/available/<name> is a link to a service's folder, which holds its start.sh , and /etc/services/enabled/<name> marks it to start at boot. A module's service that is a single script gets a folder of its own in /etc/service-scripts/<name> . Each service writes its output to /var/logs/services/<name>/stdout.log and stderr.log . Services and logs explains the service commands.

/etc/files is the folder of boot scripts that ships with EiN, mounted read-only, and /etc/init holds a link to each script boot runs, in name order. They are EiN's own; to change what happens at start-up, use the settings, /etc/fstab or a service instead.

With the Assistant installed: File What it is /etc/assistant-prompt.md The instructions the language model is given at the start of every chat. Copied from the assistant module once and never replaced, so you can edit it. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/prompt.md What a module tells the model about its part. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/tools The commands the module offers the model as tools, one a line; # starts a comment. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/examples Questions the chat suggests asking, one a line. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/cards.json The cards an answer may carry under it, drawn from the module's own pages. /etc/assistant.d/<module>/eval.json The questions agent-eval asks to test the assistant. Each /etc/assistant.d/<module> is a link to the module's etc/assistant.d , so an update of the module replaces it; only /etc/assistant-prompt.md is yours to change. Because an update does not replace that file either, a new version of the assistant's own instructions does not reach an installation where it already exists. Teaching the assistant describes these files for module authors.

When a module is set up, at every start and after mod install , mod setup puts the module's files in place: From the module In the tree How etc/config /etc/config.d/<module> Linked, and removed with the module. etc/<name>.d /etc/<name>.d/<module> Linked, and removed with the module. ui/nav.json /etc/ui/nav.d/<module>.json Linked, and removed with the module. any other etc/ file /etc/<file> Copied once. A file already there is left as it is. bin/ a PATH line in /etc/bashrc Added once. services/ /etc/services/available , enabled Registered and enabled. The linked files always show the module's current version. A copied file is yours after the first setup, which is why mod setup prints etc/<file> already exists, skipping for it later. The module manifest and Writing a module describe a module's folders.

The files in EiN's tree are in the database, so a backup of the database keeps them all: /etc/config , /etc/fstab , the host key, everyone's ~/.ssh and ~/.bashrc . On the machine, keep .env and the data folder besides. Your data: backup, moving and removing says how. EiN has no command that exports its configuration files on their own; copy one with cat or over SFTP when you want it apart.

p.h: When a file does not do what you expect
p.x: What you see Why, and what to do A CFG_… line in .env has no effect The setting is set on the Settings page or chosen by a module, both of which win; it is one of the four compose.yaml fixes; or the container was not made again with podman compose up -d . A change to compose.override.yaml is gone setup.sh writes it on every run. Change the options in .env , or with setup.sh , instead. A change to /etc/config , ~/.config or /etc/bashrc does not show in the terminal A command that was already running keeps the environment it started with; the next command reads the change. A service's own loop keeps it too until the service restarts. A service still uses the old value after a hand edit A hand edit restarts nothing. Restart the service from Services and logs , or save the setting on the Settings page, which does. could not write … when you save You may read the file but not change it. /etc is the administrator's; a member of the sudo group becomes the administrator with admin , as Accounts and groups explains. A photo uploaded again over an earlier one is refused The earlier one is frozen, as /etc/frozen-uploads says. Upload it under another name, or lift the mark with attrs -d frozen <file> first; see Frozen files . A line you added to /etc/environment or /etc/layout is gone Boot writes both files whole at every start. Put the value in /etc/config , or the CFG_… line in .env . A saved mount is not there after a start Run cat /etc/fstab to check its line and mount -a to try again. An SFTP mount whose host key is neither in known_hosts nor pinned with hostkey= is not connected at start-up.

Configuration : the Settings page, config set and how the layers combine. Settings and Environment variables : every setting and variable. Installing in detail : setup.sh , its options and variables. The editor : edit , for the files in the tree. Your sidebar and top bar : the navigation files. Reaching other machines and SSH and SFTP : the SSH files and /etc/fstab .
Every key EiN's Web UI knows, by the part of the screen it works in. Each section links the page that explains that part in full; this page is for looking a key up.

p.h: See the keys where you are
p.x: Press ? anywhere outside a text field, or choose Shortcuts in the account menu. The Keyboard shortcuts dialog opens, listing the keys that work anywhere under Anywhere , the keys that open a page under Go to , and a group for each part of the screen that has keys of its own while that part is on screen: Pictures for a grid of pictures and Nodes , and with the Archive installed Lightbox , Video and Audio for the viewer, Staging and Memories . Press ? again or Esc to close it. The ? dialog lists only the keys of what is on screen now. Some pages also show their keys at the foot of the page while you work, such as the Archive's Sort tab in staging; each key there is a button too. How to read the keys on this page: Ctrl in a shortcut marked "( ⌘ on a Mac)" is ⌘ on a Mac. The Keyboard shortcuts dialog shows the key your computer has. Alt is ⌥ on a Mac. The terminal's command line and the editor in the terminal use Ctrl on a Mac too, never ⌘ . A letter key works without Shift unless the table says Shift . Core's keys come first on this page. The keys a module brings are grouped under the module after them, Archive and Assistant ; they work only with that module installed. Keys typed into a text field are the field's. A page's single-letter keys and ? do nothing while you type in a box; Ctrl + K , the terminal's Alt keys and the Alt keys of the sidebar and top bar work there too, except on a Mac, where ⌥ with a letter types a character in a box.

Keys What they do Ctrl + K ( ⌘ + K on a Mac) Opens the finder: search, or go to a page or, with the Archive, a person or album; type > for commands. In its dialog form, pressed again, closes it. ? Opens or closes the Keyboard shortcuts dialog. Alt + T Shows or hides the terminal. Alt + N Adds a terminal tab. Esc Closes a dialog, or a page shown full screen, such as the viewer. Where a dialog or the viewer covers the search box, Ctrl + K opens the finder as a dialog of its own. Finding your way around shows the dialog, and Search and the finder the finder.

The main pages of the sidebar have a key that opens them, as choosing the entry does. The keys rest while a dialog or the viewer is open, which have keys of their own. Keys What they do Alt + H Opens Home . Alt + S Opens the Search page. The Archive's pages have keys too, under Anywhere with the Archive , and the Assistant's Chat under Anywhere with the Assistant . On a computer, holding the pointer over an icon of the narrowed sidebar shows its key, such as People (Alt+P) , and the finder shows each page's key beside its row.

A sidebar entry, a top-bar button or a row of one of its menus can have a key, from a module or from your own navigation file. Alt + R for the Archive's Random album is the only one a published module ships with. Each such key is listed under Anywhere in the Keyboard shortcuts dialog and shown in the button's tooltip, such as Random album (Alt+R) . Your sidebar and top bar shows how to give an entry a key, change one, or take one away. These keys are EiN's own and no sidebar or top-bar entry can take them: Ctrl + K , ? , and Alt with T , N , M , W , ← , → , ↑ or ↓ .

In the finder ( Search and the finder ): Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Light the row above or below. Enter Opens the lit row. With words typed, the first row, the search, is lit from the start. Esc Closes the list. In the search box of the Search page, and of the Archive's Media page: Keys What they do Enter Runs the search. ↑ ↓ in the @ list Light a thing to pick, such as a person, place or album. Enter or Tab in the list Picks the lit row, which becomes a chip. Esc in the list Closes the list without picking.

Wherever pictures stand in a grid: search results, and with the Archive an album, Media or a person's pictures. Albums describes selecting in full. Keys What they do Shift +click Selects everything from the last picture picked to this one. Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) Adds a picture to the selection, or takes it out. Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Selects every picture the page has loaded. Esc Clears the selection. With the viewer open, closes the viewer instead. Enter or Space Opens the picture that has the keyboard's focus.

While a folder listing of the Nodes explorer has the keyboard. The tree says what the nodes are. Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Move the selection to the row above or below. Shift + ↑ Shift + ↓ Extend the selection. Ctrl + ↑ Ctrl + ↓ Move without selecting, to pick rows one by one. → / ← Open / close the row's folder in place. In the icons view the arrows move by the tiles on screen instead. Space Opens or closes the row's folder in place. Enter Go into the row. Alt + Enter Properties Backspace Up a level. F2 Rename. Enter keeps the new name, Esc gives it up. Delete Delete, after asking. Only where you may write. F5 Reload the listing. Ctrl + H ( ⌘ + H on a Mac) Show or hide names that start with a dot. Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Select every row shown, open folders included. Ctrl + C ( ⌘ + C on a Mac) Copy. Ctrl + X ( ⌘ + X on a Mac) Cut. Only where you may write. Ctrl + V ( ⌘ + V on a Mac) Paste into the folder shown. Only where you may write. Tab With two panes, moves the keyboard to the other pane. In the address bar above a listing, Enter goes to the path typed and Esc puts back the path you were at. The explorer's code editor saves with Ctrl + S ( ⌘ + S on a Mac); Esc closes it only when nothing is unsaved. The editor covers it.

On the Trash page ( Your profile, favourites and trash ): Keys What they do ↑ ↓ Move the selection. Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) Add a row to the selection. Shift +click Select a range. Enter Opens or closes a row that holds several things. Delete Delete for good , after asking. F5 Reload the list.

The terminal's own keys work whether you are typing in it or not, with Alt alone, without Ctrl , Shift or ⌘ . The terminal explains them. Keys What they do Alt + T Show or hide the terminal Alt + N New tab Alt + W Close the tab you are typing in; never the last one Alt + M Fill the window, or go back to half of it Alt + ← / Alt + → Previous / next tab Alt + ↑ / Alt + ↓ A tenth of the window shorter / taller Note On a Mac, ⌥ with a letter types a character of its own (⌥T types †), so ⌥T, ⌥N, ⌥W and ⌥M may not reach the terminal. Use the terminal button in the top bar and the buttons in the tab bar instead. ⌥ with an arrow key works. The command line is edited with bash's keys: Tab completes, ↑ and ↓ walk your history, Ctrl + R searches it (and does not reload the page; F5 does), Ctrl + C stops a command, and Ctrl + D ends the input of the command reading the terminal, or on an empty line the shell. Edit the command line has the full list. Ctrl + Z does not pause a command. In an ssh session to another machine, ~ then . at the start of a line cuts the connection; see Reaching other machines .

edit opens a file in the terminal. Its keys are Ctrl on a Mac too. The editor has every key. Keys What they do Ctrl + S or Ctrl + O Save Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + X Leave; asks first if anything is unsaved Ctrl + F Find Ctrl + G Go to a line, or line:column Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Y Undo / redo Ctrl + K / Ctrl + U Cut the line / paste what was cut Esc or Ctrl + C Cancel a question
These keys work with the Archive installed.

Keys What they do Alt + I Opens Media . Alt + Y Opens Year . Alt + G Opens the Map . Alt + A Opens Albums . Alt + P Opens People . Alt + L Opens Locations . Alt + R Opens an album at random, as Random album in the top bar does. These are sidebar and top-bar keys, so they can be changed or taken away; see Keys for top-bar buttons .

The time scrubber at the right of a long list ( Scroll through time ), on the albums page, in a media timeline and in staging, takes keys once you move to it with Tab : ↑ and ↓ step to the time before or after, Home and End go to the first and the last.

While a photo, video or recording is open. Viewing photos, videos and recordings explains each. Keys What they do ← / → Previous / next file, also during a slideshow. i Shows or hides the details panel. Not for a visitor who came by a share link. f Shows or hides the face boxes with their names. t Shows or hides the text in the picture, when it has some. s Adds the file to your favourites, or takes it out. + or = Zooms in a step (photos and videos, not during a slideshow). - Zooms out a step. 0 Fits the whole picture again. Esc Closes what lies over the picture first: the enlarged map, the text dialog, drawing a face box. Then stops a slideshow. Then closes the viewer. In the Who is this? box of an unnamed face, Enter names it. In the Text in the picture dialog, Enter saves and Shift + Enter starts a new line. While a dialog lies over the viewer, the viewer's keys rest. Videos and recordings Keys What they do Space or k Plays or pauses (videos and recordings). j / l Back / forward 10 seconds (videos and recordings). Shift + ← / Shift + → Previous / next chapter, when the video has chapters. m Mutes or unmutes. c Turns subtitles on or off, when the file has a transcript. p Turns picture-in-picture on or off, where the browser has it. Move to the timeline, or a recording's waveform, with Tab to use these: Keys What they do ← ↓ / → ↑ Back / forward 5 seconds. Page Down / Page Up Previous / next chapter, or a tenth of the file back / forward without chapters. Home / End The start / the end. On the volume slider, after Tab : ← ↓ and → ↑ change the volume by 5 percent, Page Down and Page Up by 20 percent, Home silences it and End turns it full up. A click on the timeline or the slider leaves the keyboard where it was, so ← and → still step between files.

On Home , while On this day plays as a story ( Memories, news and events on Home ): Keys What they do → Next picture; after a year's last, the next year; after the last, closes. ← Previous picture. Space Pauses or plays. Esc Closes the story.

People and faces explains each place. Where Keys What they do Unidentified people Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Ticks every loaded card. Esc Clears what is ticked. Reviewing an unidentified person Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) Picks every face and recording shown. Shift +click Picks a range. Esc Closes an open photo first, then clears what is picked, then closes the review. Enter in the name box Names the person. Split a person Esc Closes an open photo first, then the dialog. A person's faces The keys of pictures in a grid .

On a computer, ? , or Keyboard shortcuts at the foot of the column beside the stream, lists them under Staging , a section for each place the cursor can be. The keys do nothing while you type in a field or a dialog is open, and there are none on a phone. Sorting in staging explains what each does to a group. On a group: Keys What they do J / K Next / previous group Shift + J / Shift + K , or Shift + ↓ / Shift + ↑ Select on to the next / previous group Enter The proposal N New album from the group P New private album A Add to album… B Into the target, or Choose a target… when there is none Shift + B Choose the target 1 2 3 Into that candidate album , / . Highlight the candidate above / below R Not the highlighted candidate C Compare with the highlighted album, or narrow the column again X Discard L Later, or back to its lane Z Undo E Rename T Set the time of every picture, or of the selected ones M / Shift + M Merge into the group above / merge the group below in [ / ] Previous / next day or month of the group ← → ↑ ↓ Step through the pictures O Open the first picture On a picture (after an arrow key), on a day or month (after [ or ] ), or with pictures selected: Keys What they do Space Select the picture, or the day's pictures O Open the picture S Split the group before them; in a lane, make them a new group < / > Move them to the group above / below G Move them to a group… Enter N P A B X Act on the day or the selected pictures only Esc Back to the group, or clear the selection With a selection that reaches past the open group, Enter asks to accept the proposals of every group in it, N , P , A , B and X act on the whole selection, L puts the groups aside, and Esc clears it. < , > , [ and ] work on any keyboard layout, also where you type them with AltGr or Option. With a mouse, drag across the stream to select the pictures and groups the box touches. Esc while dragging drops the box and puts the selection back as it was. In the dialogs these keys open: Add to an album and Choose the target : with nothing typed, 1 , 2 and so on pick the suggested album of that number. Move to a group : ↑ and ↓ light a group, Enter takes it. Renaming a group: Enter keeps the name, Esc gives it up.

On the Duplicates tab and in its compare dialog ( Duplicates ): Where Keys What they do Duplicates tab J / K Mark the next / previous set Enter Remove the marked set's copies C Compare the marked set Z Undo the last removal of this visit Comparing a set ← / → Move between the files K Keep the file in focus instead (staged files only) Enter Remove the others X Not duplicates (look-alikes only) Esc Close without changing anything
These keys work with the Assistant installed.
Alt + C opens the Chat page, as its entry in the sidebar does.

In the chat box ( Chatting with the assistant ), Enter sends the question and Shift + Enter starts a new line. The comment box on a file and the Text in the picture dialog work the same way. The side drawer the chat opens in can be made wider or narrower from the keyboard: move to its edge ( Resize side panel ) with Tab , then ← makes it 20 pixels wider and → 20 pixels narrower.

The focus is in a text field. Click an empty part of the page, or press Esc in a search box to leave it, and press the key again. Pages such as People and Albums put the focus in their filter box; on a Mac that holds the sidebar's keys too. The key belongs to something else on screen. A dialog over the page takes the keyboard: the viewer's keys rest while a dialog lies over it, staging's keys rest while a dialog is open, and the keys that open a page rest while a dialog or the viewer is open. Press ? to see which groups are active. The browser or the computer keeps the key. Some browsers keep Ctrl + W , Ctrl + Q or Ctrl + S for themselves; the editor in the terminal also takes Ctrl + O and Ctrl + X . A sidebar or top-bar key you set is missing. A key two entries ask for goes to the first in the sidebar's order, then the top bar's, and EiN's own keys are never given away. Your sidebar and top bar helps find out why. On a phone or tablet there is no keyboard to press; the keys need a computer. EiN on a phone covers the gestures instead.

Every page of EiN's Web UI has an address of its own, and most of what a page shows, such as the tab, the filters, the year or the part of the map, is written into that address. This page lists the addresses and their parameters, so you can bookmark a view, send someone a link to it, or type one in. It is for anyone who uses EiN in a browser, and for administrators who link to EiN from elsewhere.

An address is the place EiN is reached at, then a path, then sometimes a query: http://ein.local:8080/people/helen-okafor?tab=faces └──── where EiN is ──┘└────── path ──────┘└─ query ─┘ The path says which page: /people/helen-okafor is Helen Okafor's page, one of the Archive's. The query, after ? , says how the page looks: tab=faces opens it on Faces . Several parameters are joined with & . A part that holds a path in the tree, such as an album's, is URL-encoded: / becomes %2F and a space %20 . EiN writes these addresses itself when you move around; you only meet the encoding when you type one by hand. Copy the address from the browser's address bar to share or bookmark what you see. Someone who opens it sees the same page, as far as their own permissions let them. The pages come from EiN itself and from its modules . Core's addresses come first on this page; after them each module's addresses and parameters are grouped under it: the Archive , the Assistant and the media service . A module that is not installed brings none of its addresses, and opening one shows Nothing here .

p.h: Pages, dialogs, the side panel and full screen
p.x: The same address can be shown four ways. Which one depends on how you open it, not on the address: Shown as How you get there Is it in the address bar? A page The sidebar, a link, or typing the address Yes, as the path A dialog over the page Entries of the top bar's Create New menu, About EiN in the account menu No The side panel beside the page The top bar's Chat button No Full screen A picture, video or recording opened from a grid, a memory on the home page Yes, as ?fullscreen= Modules give the entries: with the Archive, Create New → Person opens /people/new in a dialog, and typing /people/new into the address bar opens the same form as a page. In the same way, with the Assistant, /chat is the side panel from the top bar and a full page from the sidebar. On a phone, what would open in the side panel opens in a dialog instead. Finding your way around shows each of these. Full screen is the one kind that lives in the address. When you open a picture from one of the Archive's albums, the address keeps the album and adds the picture: /albums/%2Farchive%2Falbums%2FMalpas%201979?fullscreen=%2Fmedia%2F%252Farchive%252F… Back closes the picture and leaves you on the album, and a reload or a shared link opens the album with the picture over it. Opened by its own address, /media/<path> , the picture is the page.

Address What it shows Who can open it / Home Everyone who can browse /login The sign-in page Everyone /s/<token> Where a share link lands, see Share links Everyone /search Search , see Search and the finder Everyone who can browse /stats Statistics Everyone who can browse /docs Documentation , see Links into the documentation Everyone who can browse /profile Profile : your account, preferences and security Signed in /settings Settings Signed in /trash Your Trash Signed in /about About EiN ; from the account menu it opens in a dialog Signed in /devices Devices , see Devices Signed in; a visitor sees no device /devices/<name> One device, for example /devices/hall-plug Signed in /system Dashboard , see Health and the dashboard In the sidebar for administrators /system/nodes Nodes , the node explorer In the sidebar for administrators /system/pipelines/<pipeline> One pipeline and its recent runs, for example /system/pipelines/media-faces Reached from the Dashboard /system/pipelines/<pipeline>/<id> One run of a pipeline Reached from the pipeline's page "Everyone who can browse" means signed-in users, and also visitors who have not signed in when the administrator turns on CFG_GUEST_BROWSING . A page marked "Signed in" always asks a visitor to sign in first. What each person then sees on a page follows the permissions on the nodes behind it; see Permissions in depth .
A parameter that is missing, or holds a value the page does not know, is ignored: the page opens as it would without it. You never get an error for a mistyped parameter.

Pages with tabs keep the open tab in tab . An address without tab opens the first one. Page Values of tab (default first) /profile account ( Account ), preferences ( Preferences ), security ( Security ) /settings system ( System ), users ( Users ), groups ( Groups ), permissions ( Permissions ), modules ( Modules ) /system overview ( Overview ), work ( Work ), ems.media-service ( Media service , with the ems module), services ( Services ), log ( Log ) /devices/<name> overview ( Overview ), history ( History ), info ( Info ), and the tabs modules add by their id: archive.trips ( Trips , with the Archive) A module's pages keep their tabs the same way; their values are under the module below. On Settings , the first four tabs are for administrators. Anyone else who asks for one of them gets Modules , and an administrator who names no tab gets System .

Search keeps its whole search in the address, so a search can be linked to and survives a reload; the Archive's Media page takes the same parameters. The parameters are named after the flags of the search command. Parameter What it holds Example q The words searched for q=sailing kind Kinds, separated by commas: photo , video , audio , document , person , location , album , camera , track kind=photo,video tag Labels, separated by commas tag=beach subject A person, location or camera that must be in it, as <kind>:<name> or a path; repeat it for several, all of which must be there subject=person:helen-okafor subject-name Every subject of a kind whose name matches the words, as <kind>:<words> ; repeatable subject-name=person:Wrenfield from , to The first and last year, both included from=1975&to=1985 bbox A rectangle on the map: north, south, east, west bbox=50.3,50.2,-5.0,-5.1 circle A circle on the map: latitude, longitude, radius in metres circle=50.263,-5.051,2000 poly A polygon: at least three latitude,longitude pairs separated by ; poly=50.3,-5.1;50.3,-5.0;50.2,-5.0 under Only what one album or folder holds, by path under=/archive/albums/Malpas 1979 like Pictures that look like this one, by path like=/archive/…/IMG_0412.jpg sort score , time (oldest first), -time (newest first) or name sort=-time The kinds person , location , album , camera and track , and a subject , find something only with the Archive installed. With it, for example, every picture and video of Helen Okafor from the 1980s, newest first: /media?kind=photo,video&subject=person:helen-okafor&from=1980&to=1989&sort=-time Only one of bbox , circle and poly applies. Search with no parameters shows its landing page rather than searching for everything.

Page Parameter What it does /settings?tab=modules module The module open, for example module=archive /settings?tab=modules section Its tab: dependencies , services , pages , commands , settings or types ( Overview when left out) /settings?tab=modules published=1 Install a module : the modules published for installing /settings?tab=users user The account open, by username /settings?tab=groups group The group open, by name /settings?tab=users , ?tab=groups new=1 The form for a new account or group /system/nodes path The path open in the explorer, for example path=/archive /devices q The filter typed into the page's own search box /devices/<name> endpoint On History , the endpoint charted, by its name, for example endpoint=switch-0-power /docs find The words in the documentation's search box /login next Where to go after signing in

The Documentation section has its own addresses. The reference pages are drawn from the installation you are on, so they list exactly what it has. Address What it shows /docs The guide's overview /docs/<path> One guide page, by its URL-encoded path under /usr/docs/guide /docs/commands Every command, see also Commands /docs/settings Every setting with its current value, see also Settings /docs/environment The environment variables, see also Environment variables /docs/node-types The node types, see also Node types /docs/modules What is installed /docs/modules/<name> One installed module, for example /docs/modules/archive The reference pages have an anchor for every entry, which scrolls to it and marks it for a moment: Entry Address A command /docs/commands#cmd-<name> , for example /docs/commands#cmd-share-link A setting /docs/settings#set-<KEY> , for example /docs/settings#set-CFG_GUEST_BROWSING A node type /docs/node-types#type-<type>

A visitor who opens a page they must sign in for is sent to the sign-in page, with the address they asked for in next : /login?next=%2Fpeople%2Fhelen-okafor%3Ftab%3Dfaces After signing in they land on that page. next only leads to a page on the same EiN; anything else leads to Home . Someone already signed in who opens /login goes straight on to next , or to Home .

A share link has the form /s/<token> , for example http://ein.local:8080/s/ followed by a long string of letters and digits. You make one with Share in the interface, see Sharing , or with share-link create in the terminal. Opening it shows Opening what was shared with you… and then the page of what was shared, such as the album's address. Where visitors may not browse, the visitor stays on what the link opens: other pages ask them to sign in. A link that has expired or been turned off shows This link no longer works with a Sign in button.

Besides the pages, EiN's web server answers a few addresses that programs use rather than people. You meet them in links to files, in scripts, and in a reverse proxy's configuration ( Ports, HTTPS and remote access ). Address Method What it does /file/<path> GET , HEAD The bytes of a file in the tree, read with the permissions of whoever asks /file/<path> PUT Stores the body at exactly that path, creating or replacing the file /file/<directory>/?name=<name> POST Stores an upload under a name nothing in the directory has yet: name , else name (2) , name (3) and so on /archive POST Collects a selection of files for a download as one zip /archive/<token> GET Downloads that zip /file/dev/<device> PUT , POST Raw input for the device's driver, such as a tracker's position, a GPX file or a webhook's post, signed in or with the device's key; see Devices and their keys /file/dev/<device>?key=<key>&… GET The same from a device that sends only GET s, such as OsmAnd or a button calling an address: its query is the input /file/dev/<device>/<endpoint> POST A value: appended to a log or a track, or written to a control /__shell The connection the Web UI talks to EiN over; a proxy must pass it on as a WebSocket Any other path that is not a file of the Web UI returns the interface itself, which then shows the page or Nothing here . A visitor who is not signed in where visitors may not browse gets sign in first from /file/ and /archive/ .

These addresses exist with the Archive installed. Addresses with <name> take the name of the node in the tree. A person's or a place's is its name in lower case with hyphens: Helen Okafor is /people/helen-okafor . A camera's keeps its capitals and has _ for spaces, such as /cameras/Canon_EOS_5D_Mark_III . Addresses with <path> take the node's whole path, URL-encoded.

Address What it shows /media Media : every picture, video, recording and document, see Media, Year and labels /media/<path> One file in the viewer, see Viewing photos, videos and recordings /year Year /timeline Opens /year , keeping the query /map Map , see Locations and the map /albums Albums , see Albums /albums/<path> One album, for example /albums/%2Farchive%2Falbums%2FMalpas%201979 /people People , see People and faces /people/<name> One person, for example /people/peggy-wrenfield /people/unknown The people EiN has seen or heard but nobody has named /family A family tree of chosen people, see Family tree, events and homes /locations Locations /locations/<name> One location /cameras Cameras , see Cameras /cameras/<name> One camera /favourites Your Favourites ; signed in only, see Your profile, favourites and trash /duplicates?path=<path> The copies of a node, see Duplicates

These are the forms of the top bar's Create New menu. They open in a dialog from the menu and as a page by their address. All of them need you to be signed in. Address Form /albums/new Create Album /people/new Create Person /locations/new Create Location /cameras/new Register Camera ; ?name= , ?make= , ?model= and ?serial= fill in its fields

All of these need you to be signed in. Sorting in staging and Getting your photos in explain the work itself. Address What it shows /staging Staging : your categories, or the one category when you have only one /staging/import Import media , also from Create New /staging/categories/new New category /staging/categories/<name> Category settings for one category /staging/routes Routes waiting for a device , see GPX files in staging

Some addresses are pieces that other pages draw inside themselves: a section of Statistics , an entry in the home page's news, a group on the Search page's landing. Each opens as a page of its own too, which is mostly useful for linking to it. Address Drawn in /stats/life-events Statistics , the Events section /explore/people , /explore/locations , /explore/years , /explore/labels The Search page before you search /looks-like?path=<path> The Search page, when you search for one label /memories/<MM-DD>?year=<year> Full screen from the home page: one calendar day across the years, starting at year /start/upload Home , while there is no news yet /news/album , /onthisday/media , /events/anniversary Entries of the home page; the home page writes their parameters /map/pins Pins on a small map, under an answer in the chat /trips?device=<path> The Trips tab of a device's page, for a device with a track, see Trips

The Media page takes the parameters of Search . Tabs Page Values of tab (default first) /people/<name> timeline ( Timeline ), info ( Info ), media ( Media ), faces ( Faces ), voices ( Heard in ), family ( Family ), homes ( Homes ) /albums/<path> media ( Media ), map ( Map ), info ( Info ) /locations/<name> info ( Info ), timeline ( Timeline ), media ( Media ), residents ( Residents ) /cameras/<name> info ( Info ), media ( Media ) /staging sort ( Sort ), duplicates ( Duplicates ), files ( Files ), done ( Done ) Map The Map page keeps where you look, the layers and the filters in the address. What is at its default is left out, so a plain /map stays plain. Parameter What it holds Default c The centre, as latitude,longitude z The zoom level layers Layers shown, separated by commas: media , locations , tracks ; or none All three from , to The first and last year No limit base The background: Map , Dark map or Satellite Map q Words to search for person , location , tag Only what has this person, location or label /map?c=50.26300,-5.05100&z=13&layers=media,tracks&from=1979&to=1979&base=Satellite Other parameters Page Parameter What it does /year year The year shown, for example year=1979 ; this year when left out /people , /albums , /locations , /cameras q The filter typed into the page's own search box /people/<name> faces=doubtful On Faces , only the faces somebody marked as doubtful /people/unknown sort faces (the default) or created /people/unknown min Seen at least this many times: 0 , 2 , 5 , 10 or 50 /people/unknown person The unknown person open for review /staging c The category, by name, for example c=inbox /staging lane On Sort : sort ( To sort ), everyday ( Everyday ), undated ( Needs a date ), clutter ( Clutter ), later ( Later ) /staging order=new On Sort : newest first /staging g On Sort : the group open, for example g=auto-2019-06-14 /staging dir , view=folder On Files : the folder open, and the folder view /staging/categories/new kind , move The kind of the new category, and a staged folder to move into it

These addresses exist with the Assistant installed. Address What it shows /chat Chat with your latest conversation, see Chatting with the assistant /chat/<id> One conversation; the address follows when you switch conversations /chart A chart the chat draws under an answer; its parameters come from the chat /about/language-model The language model, as About EiN shows it

The ems module, which the Archive brings along, adds these; see The media service . Address What it shows /system/media-service The media service, the Media service tab of the Dashboard /system/gpu The graphics card, a part of the Dashboard 's overview /about/media-service The media service, as About EiN shows it

p.h: When an address does not open
p.x: What you see What it means What to do Nothing here and "There is no page at …" No page has that path: a typing mistake, or a page of a module that is not installed Check the address; Go back or Go home The sign-in page The page is for signed-in users, or visitors may not browse Sign in; you go on to the page afterwards This page did not load The page's code could not be fetched, often because EiN was updated while the tab was open Choose Reload Something broke on this page The page failed while drawing; the error is shown below the message, and under it the error's stack, the components it was thrown in, the page and the browser Choose Reload ; if it keeps happening, choose Copy details for the report and see Troubleshooting This link no longer works A share link that expired or was turned off Ask for a new link, or sign in In a dialog or the side panel the same messages appear smaller, with Close in place of Go home . After an administrator installs or updates a module, its pages reach the browser once EiN has rebuilt them with ui-build , which it does after mod install , mod setup and mod remove , and when it starts. An open tab picks them up when you reload it.

Finding your way around : the pages, dialogs and side panel these addresses open. Sharing : making and turning off share links. Search and the finder : the search the /search parameters describe. Your sidebar and top bar : which entries open which address. Keyboard shortcuts . The module manifest : how a module adds its own addresses.

This page defines the words the EiN documentation uses, in alphabetical order, for anyone who meets one and wants to know what it means. Each entry is short and links the page that explains the topic in full. A few words mean two things in EiN, depending on where you meet them: an event is a change to the tree or a dated note on a person, a group is a set of accounts or a suggested album in staging, and a link is a softlink, a hard link or a share link. Each meaning has an entry of its own. Most words are core's and hold on every EiN. A word that belongs to a module starts its entry with the module's name in italics, such as Archive. , and means something only with that module installed. A · B · C · D · E · F · G · H · I · J · L · M · N · O · P · Q · R · S · T · U · V · W

Further users and groups that a node grants access to, beyond its owner and group, each with its own read, write and execute, such as group:family:rwx . It is optional. The Share dialog fills it in for you; acl and share-set set it in the terminal. See Permissions in depth .

A person who can sign in, with a username, a password and a home folder. Each account is a user node under /etc/users , belongs to groups and has a personal group named like itself. EiN starts with two accounts, admin and guest . See Accounts and groups .

A sign-in of a member of the sudo group that acts as the administrator for a while. It starts with Administer… in the account menu, or admin in a terminal for that terminal alone, and ends with Leave admin mode , or admin --off . See Finding your way around .

The admin account, uid 0 , which passes every permission check, as root does on Linux. A member of the sudo group in admin mode passes them too. Some commands and pages, such as Nodes and Dashboard , are for administrators only. See Permissions in depth .

Archive. A node of type album that gathers the photos, videos and recordings of one occasion. It holds the files uploaded into it and links to pictures added from elsewhere, and keeps its cover, its time span and its stacks. Albums are under /archive/albums . See Albums .

The first module, archive , and what it adds: albums, people and their family tree, locations, cameras, the trips of the devices that travel, labels, staging, and the pipelines that process media. Its parts of the tree are /archive/albums , /archive/people , /archive/locations and /archive/cameras . Without it, EiN keeps what you give it and works nothing out. See The Archive and Modules .

The chat that answers questions about what the archive holds and about EiN, by running EiN's commands as you. A command that would change something waits until you press Run . It comes with the assistant module and needs a language model. See The Assistant and Chatting with the assistant .

A named value a node carries besides its name and permissions: a photo's size, checksum and capture time, a person's names and dates. The node's type decides which attributes it has. attrs shows them in the terminal. See Nodes and node types .

A record of every write to the tree: who created, changed, moved, linked or removed which node, when, and what changed. The audit command reads it, for administrators only. Writes under /var and terminal sessions leave no record. See Commands .

The lowest place in the order of the pipeline engine's work. With the Archive, work on a staging category of the Google Photos export or Scans kind runs there unless you change it, so what people upload in the meantime is processed first. See Processing and pipelines .
Archive. Several shots taken a moment apart. A burst is not a duplicate: EiN folds it into a stack and removes nothing. See Duplicates .

Archive. What took a picture: a camera, phone, scanner or camcorder, matched by its make, model and serial number. A registered camera dates the pictures it took in its own time zone, and a phone's camera can link to the phone as a device, whose track says where it was. Cameras are under /archive/cameras . See Cameras .

Archive. A folder of your staging area that keeps one source together, such as a Google Photos export, a box of scanned prints or a phone. Its kind ( Inbox , Google Photos export , Scans , Phone , Camera , Messaging , Screenshots or Other ) decides how its files are grouped, dated and ordered for processing. See Sorting in staging .

One part of an installation, run by podman or Docker with compose: ein (EiN itself), db (PostgreSQL), and if you chose them ems (the media service) and llm (the language model). Only ein has ports open to other machines. A container is not a service. See How EiN works .

An endpoint of a device that is written to change it: a switch, a dimmer, a thermostat's target. echo on > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 sends on to the plug, and reading the control gives the states the device reported. See Devices, endpoints and drivers .
EiN without modules: the tree, the shell and its commands, the pipeline engine, accounts and sharing, and the frame of the Web UI. Core brings no pipelines of its own. See How EiN works .

Archive. The picture that stands for an album, a person, a location or a camera on its card and in its header. A cover is a softlink to one of the pictures, for a person to one of their face crops. See Albums and People and faces .

The administrator's page that sums up the system's state in one verdict ( Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person ) with tabs for the checks, the work waiting, the services and the log, and with the ems module the media service. See Health and the dashboard .

The folder on the machine's disk that holds your files: the originals in files , the renditions EiN makes from them in files-volatile . It is ~/ein/data unless you chose another at install. The database is in it too, in db . See Files and storage .

Archive. The panel beside a photo, video or recording in the viewer, with its date, place, people, labels, camera and the text read from it. i opens and closes it. See Viewing photos, videos and recordings .
