Something outside EiN that reports to it or can be switched from it: a sensor, a plug, a button, a phone that says where it is, a GPS logger. Each is a folder under /dev , such as /dev/hall-plug , holding its endpoints, and has a page under Devices . A driver finds it, or a member of the devices group makes it. See Devices .

The key a device carries to write to EiN without signing in, as a phone posting its position does: it opens /file/dev/<device> of that one device for writing, and nothing else. device-key and the device's Info tab make, show and take it away. See Devices and their keys .
Archive. The staging decision that sends a group's files to your trash instead of filing them. It can be undone. See Sorting in staging .

What turns a device's own messages into its endpoints and sends it what is written to its controls. EiN's own tracker drives phones and GPS loggers; the Automation module brings drivers for MQTT devices. See Devices, endpoints and drivers .

Archive. A file that is the same picture as another. An exact copy is the same bytes and is kept once; a look-alike is the same picture in other bytes, marked with how alike the two are, for you to decide. A burst is not a duplicate. See Duplicates .

A list of numbers that stands for a picture, a face, a voice or a text, so that similar things have similar numbers. Search by meaning, finding faces of the same person and searching with a picture all compare embeddings. The media service makes them. Also called a vector. See Search and the finder .
Media service. The media service. The name is short for EiN Media Service.

One thing a device reports or is told, a node under the device: a log of readings or presses, a track of positions, or a control . It is written <device>/<endpoint> , such as hall-sensor/temperature . See Devices, endpoints and drivers .
The announcement that a node was created, changed, moved or deleted, made once the change is saved. Pipelines start from events. See Changes and pipelines .

Archive. A dated note on a person, an album, a location or a camera: a wedding, a move, a birth. A person's event has the type Generic , Birth , Death , Marriage or Engagement . See Family tree, events and homes .

Archive. The metadata a camera or phone writes into a picture: the camera, the time it was taken, the exposure and often where. EiN reads it on arrival and keeps it under the file as metadata/exif . See Dates and places of pictures .
A picture you have marked with a heart. A favourite is a softlink in the folder stars in your home folder, so hearting a picture never copies or moves it. See Your profile, favourites and trash .

A node of type file : stored bytes with a name, a mimetype, a size and a checksum. A photo, a video, a recording and a document are files. With the Archive, a media file keeps what EiN works out about it as children: metadata/ , thumbnails/ , regions/ . See Files and storage .

Archive. The staging decision that moves a group's files into the library, as a new album, a new private album or into an album that exists. Only filing makes your uploads visible to anyone else. See Sorting in staging .

The box in the middle of the top bar, Search for anything . It finds pages, and with the Archive albums, people and places, as you type, and Ctrl + K puts the cursor in it from anywhere. See Search and the finder .

Archive. A short summary of a file's picture or sound that finds copies in other bytes, such as a smaller version or a re-encoded video. EiN makes one once a file's metadata is read and compares it to find look-alikes. See Duplicates .
Archive. The photo a stack shows as its tile in an album's grid. Make front in the viewer chooses another. See Albums .

A set of accounts, kept under /etc/groups . Every node has one group, and an access list can name more. EiN starts with the groups admin , users , ssh , sudo and guest , and every account has a personal group. See Accounts and groups .

Archive. A suggested album: files in a staging category that the organizer put together because they belong to one occasion, folder or year. You file, discard or put aside each group. See Sorting in staging .

Whoever opens EiN without signing in. The guest can sign in or open a share link and nothing more, unless an administrator turns on Visitors may browse ; then the guest sees what is granted to the guest group. The guest never changes anything. See Permissions in depth .
The same node under a second name in another folder, as on Unix. Unlike a softlink, it is not a node of its own. See Links .
What the health command and the Dashboard report: a verdict, Healthy , Catching up , Stuck or Needs a person , and the checks behind it. See Health and the dashboard .
Your own space in the tree, /home/<username> : your settings, shell history, favourites in stars , your trash and, with the Archive, your staging area. See The tree .
Archive. The staging category every account has, which cannot be removed. Uploads land in it unless you choose another category. See Sorting in staging .

One run of a pipeline on one node, with its steps and their status. A pipeline runs at most once per node at a time. The Work tab of the dashboard lists instances, and pipeline-status prints one. See Processing and pipelines .

Archive. The record of every staging decision, in staging/journal in your home folder, each with the plan that undoes it. The Done tab and staging undo undo an entry. See Staging and importing for administrators .

One word, such as sailing , put on a picture, an album, a person, a location or a camera. The same word is the same label across the archive. A label is a folder under /archive/tags holding a link to everything that carries it. See Media, Year and labels .
Archive. A part of a staging category's stream of groups: To sort , Everyday , Needs a date , Clutter and Later . Not to be confused with the bulk lane of processing. See Sorting in staging .

Assistant. The model the assistant asks, either in the llm container on your machine or at a hosted provider with an OpenAI-compatible API. Everything except the chat works without one. See The language model .

Archive. A named place, such as "Highbury", with an address, a description, labels, the people who lived there, and a point, a circle or a polygon on the map. Pictures whose position falls inside a circle or polygon are linked to it. Locations are under /archive/locations . See Locations and the map .
A node that keeps lines appended to it for a time, such as the system log /var/logs/system . See Services and logs .

Archive. A file that shows the same picture as another in other bytes: a smaller version, a re-save in another format, a mild crop. EiN marks it with how alike the two are and suggests which to keep. See Duplicates .
A module's mod.json , which names the module and says what it needs. See The module manifest .

Media service. The container, ems , that holds every media tool and model EiN uses: it reads metadata, makes thumbnails and video renditions, finds faces, voices and text, transcribes speech and makes the embeddings search compares. It keeps no data of its own. The Archive needs it. See The media service .
The permission bits of a node: read, write and execute, once for the owner, once for the group and once for everyone else, written as 0750 or rwxr-x--- . chmod changes it. See Permissions in depth .

A folder with a manifest that adds to EiN what its folders hold: commands, services, pipelines, pages and sidebar entries, settings, node types and documentation. The published modules are archive , assistant and ems . An administrator installs them on Settings → Modules or with mod install . See Modules .
A folder of another machine, reached over SFTP, shown at a path in the tree. An administrator makes one with mount . See Reaching other machines .
Archive. The timeline on Home of the albums people made lately. See Memories, news and events on Home .

Anything EiN keeps: a photo, an album, a person, an account, a log, a command. Every node has a type, a name in its folder, an owner, a group, a mode and the attributes its type needs, and any node can have children. See Nodes and node types .
What decides what a node holds and how EiN treats it, such as file , album , person or log . Core has types of its own and modules add theirs. See Node types .
Archive. The row on Home with a ring for each year that has pictures taken on today's date. A ring opens that day's memories story. See Memories, news and events on Home .

Archive. The part of the Archive that sorts the files in your staging area into groups, within a few minutes of their arrival. It leaves alone a group you have edited. The staging-organize pipeline runs it, and the staging-organizer service asks for a run of what it missed. See Sorting in staging .
The account a node belongs to, usually whoever created it. The owner's bits in the mode say what the owner may do. chown changes it. See Permissions in depth .
Where a node is in the tree, from / , as a file has: /archive/albums/christmas-2019 . See The tree .

Archive. Someone in the archive, with names, dates and contact details, under /archive/people . Parents, children and partners are links between people, and the photos a person is in are found by their faces. See People and faces .
The group every account made on the Users tab or with user-create gets, named like the account: the account helen has the group helen . See Accounts and groups .

A definition of the change it waits for and the steps, each a command, that it then runs on the node that changed. Modules bring pipelines; core brings none. See Changes and pipelines and Processing and pipelines .

A node under /var/pools holding long-running jobs that wait for a worker with room for them. The Archive's media steps wait in /var/pools/media , where the Media module's workers media-worker , models and models-second take them. pool stat shows what is waiting. See Processing and pipelines .
Archive. Where a photo, a location or an event is on the map, kept as its child named position : a point, with a radius or an outline for a location. See Dates and places of pictures .
A node that holds messages in order until they are read; reading one removes it. The pipeline engine takes its work from /var/queues/pipeline-engine . See Changes and pipelines .

Archive. A box on a photo, kept under the photo's regions/ : a face the detector found or a box someone drew. It says who is in it. In the viewer a face box no person is assigned to reads Unassigned . See People and faces .

Archive. A version of a file that EiN makes for showing it: a thumbnail, a display size, or a video or recording the browser can play. Renditions are kept in files-volatile in the data folder and can be made again from the original. See Files and storage .
A node that passes what is written to it to everyone reading at that moment and keeps nothing, such as /dev/events . See Node types .

A long-running job inside the ein container, a shell script EiN runs as the administrator: the web server, the SSH server, the pipeline engine, the pool workers and tidying loops. Core brings nine, and modules add theirs. A service is not a container. See Services and logs .
A signed-in connection, a browser, an SSH login or a service, kept under /var/sessions and removed when it ends. See Accounts and groups .

A named value that changes how EiN works, such as CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS . System settings, named CFG_… , are changed by an administrator on Settings → System ; personal ones, named CFG_USER_… (and HISTSIZE ), by each person under Profile → Preferences . Both can be changed with config set . See Configuration and Settings .

An address that opens one node, such as an album, and what it holds, to anyone who has it, without an account. It expires after 30 days unless you choose another time, and Delete link stops it at once. Share links are kept under /var/links . See Sharing .

Who can see and change a node, such as a folder or, with the Archive, an album, a person, a location or a camera, set in words with Share : Can view or Can edit for people and groups, and links for people without an account. It sets the same mode and access list as chmod and acl . See Sharing .
EiN's command language: bash syntax, run inside EiN, where the files and folders are the nodes of the tree. The terminal, SSH and the assistant all run it. See The shell language .
The panel at the right of the screen, where the chat opens. See Finding your way around .

The column of entries down the left of every page. Core gives Home , Search , Devices , Settings , Statistics and Documentation , and for administrators Nodes and Dashboard , and modules add theirs. See Your sidebar and top bar .

A node that points at another node by its path; opening it opens what it points at. Labels and favourites are softlinks, and with the Archive so are album covers, pictures added to an album from elsewhere and relations between people. Moving a node re-points every softlink to it. See Links .
Archive. Similar photos taken in a row, folded behind one tile in an album's grid, with the count in its corner. No file moves, and a stack belongs to one album. See Albums .

Archive. Your private inbox for uploads, /home/<username>/staging , where files wait, seen only by you, until you file them into an album or discard them. It comes with the Archive. See Sorting in staging .

One command in a pipeline. The pipeline engine runs short steps itself and puts long ones as jobs in a pool. Its status is pending , queued , waiting , running , completed , failed or skipped . See Processing and pipelines .
The panel that drops down over the page with a shell of your own in each tab. The top bar's terminal button or Alt + T opens it. See The terminal .
The bar across the top of every page, with the finder, Create , the terminal button and the account menu. See Finding your way around .

Where a device has been: positions with their times, sent live or read from GPX files, kept as one of the device's endpoints, such as /dev/sailboat/position . A device's History tab draws it on a map, and with the Archive its Trips tab cuts it into trips. See Devices .

Where what you delete in the Web UI waits, in .trash in your home folder, for 30 days unless the administrator set another number in CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS . rm and Delete on the Nodes page do not use it. See Your profile, favourites and trash .
The one hierarchy of nodes that holds everything in EiN, from / : /archive , /home , /etc , /var , /usr , /dev and /tmp . See The tree .

Archive. A stretch of a device's track from where it lay still to where it lay still again, found by EiN and kept up to date as the track grows, on the device's Trips tab. A trip can be made an album. See Trips .
Archive. A person recognition started for a face or a voice that matches nobody, with a placeholder name such as Unknown 4XK9QM , waiting for someone to say who it is. See People and faces .
Archive. The full-screen view of one photo, video or recording, with the details panel beside it. See Viewing photos, videos and recordings .
Archive. The coloured word under an album's title that says how visible it is: Public , Restricted or Private . An album everyone with an account can see has none. See Sharing .
The setting under Settings → Permissions , CFG_GUEST_BROWSING , that lets people who have not signed in see what is granted to the guest group. It is off unless set. See Guest .

A service that takes long jobs from a pool when it has room. The Media module brings three, all on /var/pools/media : media-worker , for work done on this machine such as thumbnails and transcoding, and models , for work done by a model in the media service such as finding faces, with models-second , off unless CFG_MODEL_SECOND_SLOTS is set above 0, beside it. See The workers , and Processing and pipelines for workers in general.

A module is how EiN learns to do something new: its commands, pages, background services, settings and pipelines come in one folder that you can install on any EiN. This page is for developers. It walks through a small module from its first file to publishing it, and shows where each kind of part goes.

A module is a folder with a mod.json at its top, kept in a repository of its own named module-<name> . Core knows no module by name: the Archive , the Assistant and the media service client, ems ( The media service ), are modules like the one you write, and you can read their repositories to see any part on this page at full size. When EiN sets a module up, it finds most of what the module brings by where it is in the folder. The manifest says who the module is, what it shares with other modules, and what it adds to machinery core already has. Nothing in the manifest is code. In the module What EiN does with it at setup mod.json Reads and checks it; refuses the module when it is wrong bin/ Adds the folder to every shell's PATH ; each file is a command, in bash or TypeScript services/<name>/ Registers and enables a background service: start.sh with a config.json ; a single script services/<name> is wrapped in a folder of its own pipelines/*.yaml Registers each pipeline definition ui/ Bundles the pages mod.json names; links ui/nav.json as the module's sidebar and top-bar entries ui/index.html Links a built ui/ as a site of its own, /var/www/<name> etc/config Links it as /etc/config.d/<name> : the module's own choice of settings etc/<x>.d/ Links it as /etc/<x>.d/<name> , for the module that reads that folder; mod install restarts the services that read it when it changes ( dropIns ) etc/ (anything else) Copies it into /etc when it is not there yet; never overwrites lib/ , types/ , test/ Nothing; ordinary source, reached through the manifest's imports and exports uninstall.sh Runs it when the module is removed EiN finds most of a module by where each part sits in its folder; mod.json says the rest. The module manifest describes every field of mod.json . This page uses the few a first module needs.

You need: An EiN you are the administrator of, to install the module on while you work. A test installation is better than the one holding your family's archive. A place for the module's files that you can edit, on the machine EiN runs on. For publishing, a repository on GitHub, Forgejo or Gitea. You do not need a copy of EiN's source to write a module: EiN bundles a module's pages and runs its TypeScript itself. To type-check a module and run its tests you work inside a checkout of core, which Building from source sets up. There is no command that makes a new module for you. Start from the folder below, or copy a small published module such as module-ems and cut it down.

This page builds recipes , a module that keeps the Wrenfield family's recipes as nodes under /archive/recipes , with a command to add one, a command to list them and a page that shows them: module-recipes/ ├── mod.json ├── bin/ │ ├── recipe-add a command in bash │ └── recipe-list a command in TypeScript ├── ui/ │ ├── nav.json its sidebar entry │ └── pages/ │ └── recipes.tsx its page └── docs/ └── index.md its guide The module's name is lower case, digits and hyphens. It is the folder's name under /usr/modules , the owner EiN shows beside its commands and settings, and the prefix of its import aliases ( @recipes/… ).

Start mod.json with who the module is and the core it is written for: { "name" : "recipes" , "version" : "0.1.0" , "description" : "The family's recipes: who cooked what, for how many" , "author" : "Ruby Wrenfield" , "license" : "MIT" , "coreApi" : "^0.6.0" , "roots" : [ "/archive/recipes" ] , "nodeTypes" : [ { "type" : "recipe" , "label" : "Recipe" , "category" : "content" , "root" : "/archive/recipes" , "description" : "One dish: its title and how many it serves." } ] , "ui" : { "routes" : { "/recipes" : "ui/pages/recipes.tsx" } } } Field What it does here name The module's name; it must match the folder it is installed in version Its semver version, which other modules' dependencies ranges are checked against description One sentence for mod list , Settings → Modules and the documentation coreApi The range of core's module API the module is written against; mod setup refuses it when this core does not satisfy it roots Folders under /archive the module's content lives in; setup creates a missing one and nothing ever removes one nodeTypes The node types it defines, for the documentation; one with a root is what an @ in the search box completes to ui.routes Its pages, each route with the file that draws it mod info on any installed module shows the range it asks for under Core API , followed by the core API this EiN provides, which system-info also shows on its api line. A module without coreApi still installs, with a warning.

A file in bin/ that starts with #!bash is a command written in EiN's shell language. The arg builtin declares its arguments, which gives it --help , Tab completion and an entry in the command reference, the same as EiN's own commands. Write bin/recipe-add : #!bash arg --desc "Add a recipe" arg --effect write arg '<title>' string "The dish, as the family calls it" arg -s --serves number "How many it serves" arg --example "recipe-add 'Apple cake' --serves 8" arg --returns "nothing; the recipe node is created." arg -- export name=$( echo " $TITLE " | tr ' ' '_' | tr - cd 'A-Za-z0-9_-' ) mknode -t recipe "/archive/recipes/ $name " --as "title= $TITLE " --as "serves= $SERVES " || exit 1 echo "added /archive/recipes/ $name " arg --export reads the arguments and sets $TITLE and $SERVES . A command run this way runs with the access of whoever runs it, like any script. The shell language lists every form arg takes. Say what the command does to the system with arg --effect read or write . With the Assistant installed, the assistant runs a read command at once and shows a write to the person first; a command that says nothing is treated as a write.

A file in bin/ that starts with #!ts is a TypeScript command. Its default export is a function that takes the command object and returns an exit code, and carries a spec that describes it. Write bin/recipe-list : #!ts import type { CmdReturn , Command } from '@ein/client' ; const ROOT = '/archive/recipes' ; const recipeList = async ( cmd : Command ): CmdReturn => { const entries = await cmd. sys . vfs . children (cmd. access , ROOT ). catch ( () => []); const recipes = entries . filter ( ( entry ) => entry. node . type === 'recipe' ) . map ( ( entry ) => ({ path : ` ${ROOT} / ${entry.name} ` , title : String (entry. node . attrs . title ?? entry. name ), serves : String (entry. node . attrs . serves ?? '' ), })); if (cmd. json ) await cmd. writeJSON (recipes); else for ( const recipe of recipes) await cmd. writeLn ( ` ${recipe.title} (serves ${recipe.serves || '?' } )` ); return 0 ; }; recipeList. spec = { name : 'recipe-list' , effect : 'read' as const , description : 'List the recipes, with how many each serves' , args : [], flags : [], examples : [ 'recipe-list' ], returns : 'One entry per recipe: path, title and serves.' , }; export default recipeList; A #!ts command runs inside EiN's own process, with all of its permissions. EiN therefore runs one only from a module under /usr/modules , where only the administrator can put files. The same file anywhere else, a home folder included, stops with a #!ts command runs only from a module in /usr/modules and status 126 . A person's own commands are bash scripts. Module code imports from core only @ein/client , the module API. What a command uses most: Member What it is cmd.args The words after the command's name; read flags from them with parseArgs cmd.json True when the caller wants JSON, as the Web UI and JSON_OUTPUT=1 do cmd.writeLn , cmd.writeJSON , cmd.writeError Write a line, a JSON answer, or a line on stderr cmd.stdin Standard input: for await (const line of cmd.stdin.lines()) , or all of it with cmd.stdin.text() cmd.execute(script, { stdin }) Run a shell line and get its code , stdout and stderr ; quote paths with shq , and pass text as stdin cmd.progress(fraction) Say how much of the work is done, 0 to 1; a pipeline step shows it under Ongoing, and it keeps it off quiet cmd.sys.vfs The tree, read and written with cmd.access , the caller's access: nodes, their content, queries and searches cmd.env , cmd.cwd The caller's environment, settings included, and working folder cmd.interrupted , cmd.onInterrupt Whether the person pressed Ctrl + C , and a handler for it And the parts of spec : Field What it says name The command's name, the same as the file's description What it is for, in one line, for --help , the command reference and the assistant args Each positional argument: name , type ( string , path , user , group , command , number , subcommand ) and description flags Each flag: name , type ( bool for a switch) and description effect read or write ; a reading command marks the arguments or flags that make it a write with writes examples One or two real command lines returns What it answers with under JSON_OUTPUT=1 , in a sentence admin true when only an administrator may run it; for anyone else it is left out of completion and the reference json false for a command that writes text even when JSON is asked for A command may import packages through the manifest's imports , such as "@std/path": "jsr:@std/path@^1.1.3" , and files of its own through aliases named after the module, such as "@recipes/store": "./lib/store.ts" . A file outside the module is reached only through another module's exports (see Use another module ).

p.h: Try the module on your EiN
p.x: With the standard installation, EiN keeps the modules it installs in modules/ in its data folder, ~/ein/data/modules unless you chose another data folder, which EiN sees as /var/lib/modules . Put the module's folder there under the module's name, and make its commands executable: # on the machine EiN runs on cp -r ~/src/module-recipes ~/ein/data/modules/recipes chmod 755 ~/ein/data/modules/recipes/bin/* Link it among the installed modules and set it up: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator ln -s /var/lib/modules/recipes /usr/modules/recipes mod setup recipes Setup says what it did, with lines like these: Setting up module 'recipes'... roots: /archive/recipes Added /usr/modules/recipes/bin to PATH Linked navigation at /etc/ui/nav.d/recipes.json Module 'recipes' setup complete recipes: built, 3.1 KB in 820 ms The last lines come from bundling every module's pages, one line per module. Try the commands. mod setup added bin/ to PATH in /etc/bashrc , which every shell reads again before its next command, an open terminal tab included: # in EiN's terminal recipe-add "Peggy Wrenfield's apple cake" --serves 8 recipe-list recipe-list -- help Reload the web page. Settings → Modules lists recipes as Active , and its panel shows what it brings. Restarting EiN does step 2 for you: at every start EiN links each folder in /var/lib/modules that has a mod.json and sets every module up, in the order of their dependencies. Warning mod remove recipes deletes a module's folder in /var/lib/modules along with its link. Keep your working copy, and its git history, somewhere else and copy it in.

p.h: Change it and see the change
p.x: What you have to do after an edit depends on what you changed: You changed To see it A file in bin/ Nothing: the next run uses it A file in lib/ that a #!ts command imports mod setup recipes , which drops the commands EiN has loaded mod.json : settings, node types, roots, indexes mod setup recipes A new file in services/ or pipelines/ mod setup recipes , then service start <name> for a new service A page, or anything it imports ui-build recipes , then reload the web page ui/nav.json Reload the web page EiN keeps a loaded TypeScript command against its file alone, so an edited lib/ file reaches a command when the command's own file changes, after mod setup , or after EiN restarts.

p.h: Add a page and a sidebar entry
p.x:
A module's pages are React components. EiN bundles them itself, from the module's files, whenever modules are set up; there is no build step on your side and nothing is fetched from the network. Name each route and the file that draws it in mod.json , as above: "ui": { "routes": { "/recipes": "ui/pages/recipes.tsx" } } . A route is a path below / , of literal and :param segments, such as /recipes/:name . Write the page. Its default export is the component: import { Stack, Table, Title } from '@mantine/core'; import { EmptyState, PageLoader } from '@ein/ui/components'; import { useCommand } from '@ein/ui/hooks'; type Recipe = { path: string; title: string; serves: string }; export default function Recipes() { const { data, loading, error } = useCommand('recipe-list'); if (loading) return ; if (error) return {error.message}; if (!data?.length) return Add one with recipe-add.; return ( Recipes {data.map((recipe) => ( {recipe.title} {recipe.serves} ))}
); } useCommand runs a command in the reader's own shell, as JSON, and keeps its answer. A page reads and changes the tree only through commands, which is why each part of a module that the Web UI shows has a command behind it. Give it a sidebar entry in ui/nav.json : { "sidebar" : [ { "id" : "recipes.list" , "section" : "browse" , "label" : "Recipes" , "icon" : "tools-kitchen-2" , "to" : "/recipes" , "order" : 60 } ] } Run ui-build recipes and reload the web page. Recipes is in the sidebar's Browse section. A page imports only what the Web UI lends it, its own files, and anything at all with import type : Import What it is react , react-dom React, the one the Web UI runs @mantine/core , @mantine/dates , @mantine/hooks The Mantine components the interface is built with react-router-dom Routing: Link , useParams , useNavigate , useSearchParams and the like @preact/signals-react , @hello-pangea/dnd Signals, and drag and drop @ein/ui/components , @ein/ui/hooks , @ein/ui/lib , @ein/ui/signals , @ein/ui/theme The interface's own parts @ein/paths Core's path names Your module's files, CSS and CSS modules included By relative path or through its imports Anything else stops the build with a message naming the file and the import. A page writes a date or a time with formatDateTime , formatDate or formatTime from @ein/ui/lib , which take the options toLocaleString takes, or with dateTimeFormat where it needs an Intl.DateTimeFormat . They follow the reader's Date and time format ; toLocaleString and a bare Intl.DateTimeFormat follow the browser's language instead, which gives an English browser a 12-hour clock.

p.h: Where an entry opens a route
p.x: A module gives the Web UI entries and routes, nothing more. Each entry says where its route opens: Entry Where it appears sidebar In a section of the sidebar ( main , explore , browse , system ); needs section , label , icon and to topbar A button in the top bar, or a row of a dropdown it names as parent , such as ui.create , the Create menu panels Inside another page, at a slot it names, such as system.tabs (a tab of the Status ), device.tabs (a tab of a device's page) or nodes.tools A top-bar entry's action is { "navigate": "/recipes" } for the page, { "dialog": "/recipes/new" } for the dialog over it, { "drawer": … } for the side drawer and { "fullscreen": … } for over everything; { "run": … } runs a command line instead, and with navigate beside it goes where the command's answer says. Each entry's id is <module>.<name> . icon is a Tabler icon name. admin: true shows an entry to administrators only, signedIn: true to people who are signed in, group: "<group>" to that group's members and administrators. ui-nav prints the navigation as the reader gets it, with a warning for each entry it left out and why. The administrator and each person can move, rename and hide a module's entries; Your sidebar and top bar shows how. To make nodes of your type into links wherever EiN shows them, in search results, completions and the node explorer, name the route that opens one in mod.json : "ui": { "open": { "recipe": "/recipes/{name}" } } . {name} is the node's last path segment, {parent} the one before it and {path} its whole path. Files of your own under a folder open the same way by the folder: "/etc/things/": "/things/{rest}" ( ui.open ). A page that draws something to drag and zoom, as a map or a diagram, takes the gestures from usePanZoom in @ein/ui/hooks : dragging, pinching, the wheel about the cursor and a double tap, with ignore for what on the drawing keeps a press to itself, such as a card dragged on it. The family tree draws with it, and so does the Automation module's graph.

A module owns settings by listing them in mod.json under config.options . Setup adds them to Settings and config ; the values live in /etc/config and each person's ~/.config , and every shell sees them as environment variables. "config" : { "options" : [ { "key" : "CFG_RECIPES_DEFAULT_SERVES" , "scope" : "system" , "type" : "number" , "default" : "4" , "label" : "Servings when none is given" , "description" : "How many a recipe serves when it was added without saying." , "group" : "Recipes" } ] } A command reads it as $CFG_RECIPES_DEFAULT_SERVES , or cmd.env.CFG_RECIPES_DEFAULT_SERVES . A user setting is named CFG_USER_… , and a key to another service is a secret named CFG_…_KEY , which no shell sees. The module manifest lists every key of an option, and Configuration explains how the values are layered. A module that wants a setting, its own or core's, to have a value of its choosing writes it in etc/config , as export KEY='value' lines. Setup links the file as /etc/config.d/<name> ; a value the administrator sets wins over it. The ems module's names its text embedder this way: export CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER= 'ems-text-embed'

A service is a script EiN keeps running: a folder services/<name>/ with a start.sh and a config.json . Setup registers and enables it; EiN starts the enabled services when it starts, and service start <name> starts one now. { "description" : "Checks the recipes every hour" , "restartPolicy" : "on-failure" } # services/recipe-check/start.sh while true ; do recipe-list > /dev/null sleep 3600 done Key What it does description One line for the Status 's services and service list restartPolicy on-failure , always or never ; with a restart policy EiN starts a failed service again maxRestarts How many restarts within restartWindow before the service stays failed; 3 by default restartWindow That window, in milliseconds; 60000 by default stopTimeout How long a stopping script may take before it is closed, in milliseconds; 5000 by default env Environment variables for the script statusCommand A command answering the service's health in one line, shown beside its status checkCommand A command answering checks for health , as JSON [{ name, state, reason }] with ok , warn or fail gaugeCommand A command answering meters for top and the Status , as JSON [{ label, percent?, value }] workClass background for a service whose work may wait behind people's: its database connections leave some free for them Module services use "restartPolicy": "on-failure" . A service whose name the module stops shipping is stopped and removed at the next setup. Services and logs shows where a service's output goes.

A pipeline runs commands when something happens in the tree, such as a photo's metadata being read. Each file in pipelines/ defines one: name: recipe-photo description: Link a photo of a dish to its recipe trigger: on: media.metadata.extracted steps: link: command: recipe-link $NODE_PATH description: Find the recipe the photo shows options: maxAttempts: 2 priority: 5 The events come from the modules that emit them: media.metadata.extracted is the Media module's, so this module would list media in its dependencies . Changes and pipelines explains triggers and steps, and Processing and pipelines how to watch them run. A definition the module stops shipping is removed at the next setup.

p.h: Plug into search, the home page and other places
p.x: Core asks for some things by a command's name, so a module provides them by naming a command in bin/ after them. No manifest field is involved, and core never names your module: Command name What core does with it search-<x> search asks it for hits; it answers --kinds with what it finds ( { "kinds": ["recipe"] } ) news-<x> The home page's news: what was added lately, --limit N events-<x> The home page's coming events, --today YYYY-MM-DD --days-ahead A --days-past P --limit N onthisday-<x> The home page's "on this day", MM-DD --limit N members-<type> How a node of that type lists its members, for search --under and members subject-<kind> The media a subject has, for search --subject <kind>:<ref> Each is run with JSON_OUTPUT=1 and answers a shape that @ein/api or @ein/client declares. These prefixes are reserved: a command so named is asked, so do not use them for anything else. For the home page, each entry carries a title , the route of your own page that draws it, and the path of the node it is about. Other jobs only one command may do are chosen by a setting the module sets in its etc/config : CFG_SEARCH_PARSER reads the words typed in the search box, CFG_COMMAND_FINDER finds commands by what they do, and CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL and CFG_TEXT_EMBEDDER name the commands a module runs for a language model or text vectors. The settings are in the settings reference . With the Assistant installed, what the assistant knows about your module's commands, and how to give it more, is in Teaching the assistant . A module that brings a kind of device registers a driver from one of its services; see Writing a driver .

With the Dashboards module installed, a person puts cards on a dashboard from those the installed modules offer. A card is a route of your module drawn inside a tile, and the module offers it in etc/dashboard.d/cards.json , which mod setup links as /etc/dashboard.d/<module>/cards.json . Nothing else is needed: the dashboard names no module, and your module does not depend on it. The Todo module's list card: [ { "name" : "list" , "label" : "Todo list" , "description" : "One list's items not done yet, late ones first and then by when they are due." , "icon" : "list-check" , "color" : "yellow" , "route" : "/cards/todo/list" , "size" : [ 4 , 5 ] , "min" : [ 3 , 3 ] , "params" : { "type" : "object" , "required" : [ "list" ] , "properties" : { "list" : { "type" : "string" , "format" : "path" , "title" : "List" , "x-choices" : { "command" : "todo-lists" , "value" : "path" , "label" : "title" } } , "who" : { "type" : "boolean" , "title" : "Who is to do each" , "default" : true } } } } ] Field What it is Default name Lower case letters, digits and - ; the card is <module>.<name> required label What the picker and the tile's header call it required route The route that draws it, without a query; one of your ui.routes required size [columns, rows] a new one takes, of a dashboard 12 columns wide required min The smallest [columns, rows] it may be made [1, 1] description One sentence in the picker the label icon A Tabler icon name puzzle color A Mantine colour name, the kind colour of what it shows gray frame titled draws a header with its icon and title above the route; plain gives the route the tile titled params A JSON Schema of an object: what a person sets, passed to the route in its query no settings Each parameter has a type ( string , number , integer , boolean or array of strings or numbers), and may have a title , description , default , minimum , maximum , and enum or oneOf ( { "const": …, "title": … } ) for a fixed choice. format picks the input: path for a node, markdown , timezone , date or time . x-choices lists the choices from a read command: the form runs command as the person editing, with JSON_OUTPUT=1 , and takes value and label from each entry of its answer, or of the list at the key path items when the answer is not a list; {other} in command is another parameter's value, so "command": "device-show {device}", "items": "endpointList" lists a chosen device's endpoints. where keeps the entries whose fields have one of the given values: "where": { "type": "control" } lists only its controls. dashboard-card-add checks a card's values against its params before it puts it on. The route is drawn with the values in its query, /cards/todo/list?list=%2Fgroups%2F…&who=true , a list as the key repeated. Keep card routes under /cards/<module>/ , a first segment none of your pages use, and draw them to fill the tile: the tile is a size container, so cqmin units and clamp() scale text with it. A card reads its own data as whoever looks at the dashboard and keeps itself current, with useNodeEvents for what changes by events or usePolledCommand for what changes on a clock. On a screen opened from a display link nobody is signed in ( isAuthenticated is false): draw no controls there and link nowhere, since every write is refused. dashboard-cards lists what the modules offer and says what in a list could not be read.

A module's documentation in EiN comes from what it already declares: each command's spec or arg lines, each setting's label and description , and in mod.json its nodeTypes and the environment variables it reads other than its settings, under environment . docs commands , docs node-types and docs env read them from the installed modules, and so do the reference pages of this site. A guide for the people who use the module, written for them rather than for developers, goes in its repository, beside mod.json . The modules published with EiN have theirs here, in this site's Modules part, which EiN carries offline in Documentation .

A module shares files by naming them in exports , and another module imports them only if it lists the first in dependencies : "dependencies" : { "archive" : "^0.1.0" } With that, recipes may import what the Archive exports, as @archive/<name> , and run its commands. Nothing else of the Archive's is reachable. A dependency is checked at setup: it must be installed, at a version in the range, and it is set up first. mod install installs a missing dependency along with the module. mod info archive lists what the Archive exports and which installed modules depend on it. To share your own files, export them: "exports": { "./api": "./lib/api.ts" } is imported elsewhere as @recipes/api . By convention ./api holds the types of what your commands answer as JSON, imports nothing but other such files, and is what your own pages import too.

A module's tests run inside a checkout of core, with the module in its modules/ folder; see Building from source . There, deno task sync:modules writes the module's deno.jsonc from its mod.json (never edit that file), deno task check type-checks it, and deno task test:one modules/recipes/test/ runs its tests. A test imports @ein/testing and runs commands in an EiN with the module set up: import { assertEquals } from '@std/assert' ; import { createTestContext } from '@ein/testing' ; const testCtx = createTestContext ({ modules : [ 'recipes' ], boot : true }); Deno . test ({ name : 'recipes' , sanitizeResources : false , sanitizeOps : false }, async () => { await testCtx. setup (); const client = await testCtx. server . createShellClient (); await client. exec ( "recipe-add 'Apple cake' --serves 8" ); const recipes = await client. execJson <{ title : string }[]>( 'recipe-list' ); assertEquals (recipes. map ( ( recipe ) => recipe. title ), [ 'Apple cake' ]); }); The tests in core check what every module must keep to: a module imports from core only @ein/client , @ein/api , @ein/paths and, in pages, the interface's parts, and runs another module's commands only when it depends on it.

Push the module to a repository named module-recipes , with mod.json at its top. Commit the commands with their execute bit ( git update-index --chmod=+x bin/* ): EiN installs each file with the mode the repository gives it. Release versions as tags v<version> , such as v0.1.0 , and raise version in mod.json with each: the minor when you add something another module may come to rely on, the major when something they use changes. Without a ref, mod install takes the highest of them, and the default branch only while there is none. Install it on any EiN by its address, with a branch, tag or commit after @ if you want one: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install https://forge.example:3000/wrenfield/module-recipes@v0.1.0 EiN fetches the commit from the forge, checks the module as setup would, puts it in place, sets it up and starts its services. To let administrators install it by name, they add your organisation to Module sources , CFG_MODULE_SOURCES . Then mod install recipes finds it, mod search lists it and Settings → Modules offers Install and Update . Modules covers sources that need a token. When EiN's module API changes in a way that breaks modules, a module whose coreApi range the new EiN does not satisfy is refused at setup with needs @ein/client ^0.5.0, this core provides 0.6.0 . Publish a version written for the new API, with its coreApi raised. An EiN that is older than the API a release asks for still installs your module by name: mod install without a ref takes the newest release whose coreApi it satisfies.

mod remove recipes asks before it removes anything, runs the module's uninstall.sh if it has one, then takes back what setup did: its commands leave PATH , its services are stopped and removed, its pipelines, settings, navigation and guide are unlinked, and its pages are rebuilt without it. The module's content stays: its roots under /archive , and the values of its settings in /etc/config , which come back if the module is installed again.

mod setup names each problem; mod list --long and the module's panel in Settings → Modules show them afterwards. What you see What to do mod setup: module not found: /usr/modules/recipes The link in /usr/modules is missing; make it as in Try the module mod setup: no mod.json found in /usr/modules/recipes mod.json must be at the folder's top recipes: needs @ein/client ^0.7.0, this core provides 0.6.0 coreApi asks for another version of the module API than this EiN has recipes: requires module 'archive' (^0.1.0), which is not installed Install the dependency, or remove it from dependencies recipes: export './api' points at a missing file: ./lib/api.ts Fix the path in exports recipes: ui.routes['/recipes'] must be a .tsx page: ui/pages/recipes.ts A page is a .tsx file ui-build: recipes: …: '…' is neither lent by the shell nor the module's own The page imports a package the interface does not lend; see the table in Add a page recipe-list: command not found mod setup has not run since bin/ was made, or the file is not in bin/ ; run mod setup recipes Access denied when someone else runs a command The file has no execute bit; chmod 755 it, and commit the mode The sidebar entry does not appear Run ui-nav and read its warnings: a missing field or an unknown section leaves an entry out A page shows an error inside the frame Its bundle failed to load or the page threw; run ui-build recipes and read its output, then the browser's console Troubleshooting covers problems that are not the module's.

The module manifest : every field of mod.json Writing a driver : bringing a kind of device to EiN Teaching the assistant : making the assistant use your module's commands Building from source : a checkout of core to type-check and test modules in Modules : installing, updating and removing modules as an administrator The shell language : the language bash commands and services are written in Changes and pipelines : how work follows a change in the tree Nodes and node types : what a node and its attributes are Core commands : mod setup and the other mod commands

Every module has a mod.json at its root: who the module is, what it shares with other modules, and what it adds to what core already has. This page is the reference for each field, for the developer writing a module. Writing a module explains how a module is put together; this page is what to look up while you write its manifest. Nothing in a manifest is code. What a module does lives in its folders ( bin/ , services/ , pipelines/ , ui/ , etc/ ), and mod setup finds those by where they are. The manifest names the module, lists its settings and node types, and declares what core should create or register for it.

A module that adds a few commands, one setting and one page needs little more than this: { "name" : "letters" , "version" : "0.1.0" , "description" : "Letters: scanned letters, who wrote them and to whom" , "coreApi" : "^0.7.0" , "dependencies" : { "archive" : "^0.1.0" } , "exports" : { "./api" : "./lib/api.ts" } , "imports" : { "@letters/parse" : "./lib/parse.ts" , "@std/path" : "jsr:@std/path@^1.1.3" } , "config" : { "options" : [ { "key" : "CFG_LETTERS_OCR_LANGUAGE" , "scope" : "system" , "type" : "select" , "choices" : [ "en" , "sv" ] , "default" : "en" , "label" : "Letter language" , "description" : "The language a scanned letter is read in." , "group" : "Letters" } ] } , "ui" : { "routes" : { "/letters" : "ui/pages/letters.tsx" } } } letters is an invented module, shown for the shape. The ems module's manifest is a real one with the same parts and no dependencies: a name, a version, a description, coreApi , four exports, its imports, seven settings and three pages.

Field What it is When it matters name the module's name, its directory and its alias prefix always version its semver version, checked against dependents' ranges mod setup description one sentence shown wherever the module is listed display author , license free text display coreApi the range of core's module contract it is written against mod setup exports the files other modules may import loading, type checks imports its own private aliases and external packages loading, type checks dependencies the modules it needs, with version ranges mod setup config.options the settings it owns mod setup dropIns the drop-in folders its services read, and which to restart mod install , mod remove environment environment variables it reads that are not settings documentation nodeTypes the node types it defines; with a root , what @ completes to documentation, runtime roots folders directly under /archive its content lives in mod setup indexes database indexes on node attrs its queries need mod setup ui.routes its pages, by route ui-build ui.open which route opens a node of a type ui-build , browser ui.shareLinks which nodes the Share dialog offers a link for browser EiN runs mod setup --all at every start, for every installed module in dependency order, so a field read by mod setup takes effect the next time EiN starts or the next time you run mod setup <name> . "Loading, type checks" means the field is read when the module's TypeScript is loaded, and by deno task check through the module's generated deno.jsonc . ui-build bundles the modules' pages; mod setup runs it after it has set modules up.

The module's name. It must be the name of the directory the module is installed in, /usr/modules/<name> , because dependencies and import aliases are both found by directory name. Use lower case letters, digits and hyphens: only such a name can be imported as @<name>/… . The name is also the owner shown beside the module's settings, node types and commands, the prefix of its aliases (everything archive shares is imported as @archive/… ), and the name its navigation, settings and documentation are linked under.

The module's version, in semver: "0.1.0" . A module that depends on this one names a range, and mod setup refuses the dependent when the installed version is outside it. Step it as a caret range reads it: below 1.0.0, raise the minor when something a dependent uses changes or goes, and the patch for anything else; from 1.0.0, the major and the minor. Tag each released version v<version> in the module's repository, such as v0.1.0 , which is what mod install <name>@v0.1.0 installs.

Free text. description is shown by mod list --long and mod info , on Settings → Modules and on the documentation's modules page. Write it as what the module is, for a reader: the Assistant's is "Assistant: answers questions by running EiN's commands for the user, with what the installed modules offer it".

The range of core's module contract the module is written against, as a semver range: "^0.7.0" . Core's side of it is MODULE_API_VERSION in src/modules/types.ts , at present 0.12.4 ; system-info shows it on its api line. The contract is what a module may use from core: @ein/client , @ein/api , @ein/paths and the Web UI's kit, @ein/ui/* . Core's src/client/contract.snapshot lists every symbol in it, and a test fails when the contract changes without the version and the snapshot changing too. Below 1.0.0 the minor is the breaking part: ^0.6.0 accepts 0.6.x and nothing else. mod setup checks the range: Manifest What mod setup says no coreApi letters: no coreApi declared, assuming 0.6.0 , and it goes on a range that does not parse letters: coreApi is not a valid semver range: … , and it refuses a range core does not satisfy letters: needs @ein/client ^0.6.0, this core provides 0.5.0 , and it refuses

p.h: What a module shares and uses
p.x: exports , imports and dependencies decide what the module's TypeScript may import and which other modules' commands it may run. One function in core, src/modules/resolve.ts , applies the rule for the loader that runs #!ts commands, for deno task sync:modules and for the boundary test, so what type-checks, what runs and what the test allows are the same. A bare specifier in a module's source is looked up in this order: the module's own imports , longest key first, the way an import map resolves; the module's own exports , under @<name>/… ; the exports of a module listed in dependencies , under @<dependency>/… ; core's own map: @ein/client , @ein/api , @ein/paths and @ein/testing , which no manifest restates. In a core checkout, each module is a Deno workspace member with a deno.jsonc that deno task sync:modules writes from its mod.json . Never edit that file: change mod.json and run the task again. Building from source covers the checkout.

The module's public interface, "./<name>": "./<file>" . Another module imports the file as @<module>/<name> , and only when it lists this module in its dependencies . Nothing else in the module can be reached from outside it. An export is also usable inside the module under the same alias. "exports" : { "./people/api" : "./lib/people/api.ts" , "./people/genealogy" : "./lib/people/genealogy.ts" , "./paths" : "./lib/paths.ts" } A key is ./<name> , or ./<area>/<name> in a module made of several areas as the Archive is, in lower case with hyphens. The target is a path inside the module, starting with ./ , and the file must exist: mod setup refuses export './api' points at a missing file: ./lib/api.ts . Exports the modules use by convention: ./api , or ./<area>/api in a module with areas: the types of what the module's commands answer under JSON_OUTPUT=1 , for its own pages and for other modules. These files import only other API files, so a page can import them without type-checking the whole module. ./testing : a stand-in other modules' tests may use. The media service client exports its fake media service this way.

What the module's own code uses: private aliases into its own files, and external packages. "imports" : { "@assistant/agent" : "./lib/agent.ts" , "@std/assert" : "jsr:@std/assert@^1.0.16" , "mdast-util-from-markdown" : "npm:mdast-util-from-markdown@^2.0.3" } Name a private alias after the module, @<name>/… , as you would an export; it is private because it is not in exports . A target is a path inside the module starting with ./ , or a package: jsr: , npm: , node: , http: , https: or data: . It is never a path into another module; that is what dependencies and the other module's exports are for. An alias reaches below itself only when its key ends in / or it maps to a jsr: or npm: package. @archive/timeline mapped to a file says nothing about @archive/timeline/facets , which needs an entry of its own. Deno applies the same rule.

The other modules this one needs, as name and semver range: "dependencies": { "ems": "^0.1.0" } . A dependency is: checked by mod setup : it must be installed, at a version in the range; set up first, since modules are set up in dependency order; a cycle is reported as mod setup: dependency cycle, skipping: a -> b -> a and none of its modules is set up; the only way to import another module's exports ; required to run another module's commands. Core's boundary test reads command names from execute(…) calls, pipeline command: lines and shell scripts, and fails on a call into a module that is not listed. Problem What mod setup says the module is not installed letters: requires module 'archive' (^0.1.0), which is not installed the range does not parse letters: dependency 'archive' has an invalid semver range: … the installed version is outside it letters: requires 'archive' ^0.2.0, but 0.1.0 is installed the dependency's own version is not semver a warning, … has an unparseable version '…', not checked , and it goes on An import of another module's file gets a message of its own when the module runs or is checked: … imports '@archive/paths' but does not list 'archive' in its dependencies , or … '@archive/x' is not exported by 'archive' (exports: …) , which lists what it does export.

The settings the module owns. mod setup adds them to EiN's table of settings and mod remove takes them out, so they appear on Settings → System , under Profile → Preferences for personal ones, and in config list , without core knowing them. Configuration describes how an administrator sees and changes them. The values are never in the manifest. They live in /etc/config for system settings and in each person's ~/.config for personal ones, and every shell sees them as environment variables. { "key" : "CFG_MODEL_SLOTS" , "scope" : "system" , "type" : "number" , "default" : "2" , "label" : "Model requests in flight" , "description" : "How many model-bound media steps (faces, picture vectors, text in pictures, text vectors, transcripts, voices) EiN keeps in flight against the media service at once. …" , "group" : "Processing" , "restarts" : [ "models" ] } Key What it is key the environment variable: CFG_… for a system setting, CFG_USER_… for a personal one scope system (one value, set by an administrator) or user (each person their own) type string , number , boolean , select , mode , user , group , secret or locale (a language tag such as en-SE ): the control, and what config set accepts choices the allowed values, required for select default what applies when nothing is set; always a string, never written to a file label the setting's name on the Settings page description what the setting does, for the person reading the Settings page; say what changes, not how it is implemented group the category it is listed under on the Settings page restarts the services that read it when they start, restarted when it changes restartNote shown instead of restarting, for a service that cannot be restarted from a page emptyMeans what an empty value means, when empty is a choice rather than "not set" The example is the Media module's CFG_MODEL_SLOTS . Settings lists every setting the installed modules declare, with its default. The names and the scope must agree: a user setting is named CFG_USER_… (the one exception is HISTSIZE , which bash owns), and a system setting is not; a secret is a key to another service. It is named CFG_…_KEY , a name only a secret may have, it is a system setting, and its default is "" . No shell sees it, and the Settings page says only whether it is set. The Assistant's CFG_LLM_KEY is one. A malformed setting does not stop the module. mod setup prints a warning such as letters: option 'CFG_LETTERS_X': type 'select' needs choices and leaves that setting out. A key that core or another module already registered is also left out, and the first owner keeps it. When that owner drops the setting, by an update that no longer declares it or by being removed, the module that was left out gets it: a setting moves from one module to another that way, whichever of the two is set up first.

p.h: A module's own choice of values
p.x: A module that wants a setting, its own or core's, to have a value of its choosing writes it in etc/config , a shell file of export KEY='value' lines. mod setup links it as /etc/config.d/<name> and mod remove removes the link. The Archive's is: # Read what is typed into the search box as filters: people, locations, years, kinds. export CFG_SEARCH_PARSER= 'archive-parse' The file is read before the administrator's /etc/config , so a value set on the Settings page wins, and the Settings page shows a value that came from the file as the module's.

A module can read a folder the other modules put files in: mod setup links each module's etc/<x>.d/ as /etc/<x>.d/<module> , and the module that reads /etc/<x>.d takes what is there. A service that reads such a folder as it starts names it here, with the services to restart when what is there changes: "dropIns" : { "media-worker.d" : { "restarts" : [ "media-worker" ] } , "media-models.d" : { "restarts" : [ "models" , "models-second" ] } } The example is the Media module's: its workers take the kinds of work the modules name in /etc/media-worker.d and /etc/media-models.d . mod install restarts the services named that run once it has put in place a module whose drop-ins in the folder are new or changed, after every module is set up, so they find them linked; an update that leaves its drop-ins as they were leaves them running. mod remove restarts them when it removes a module that had some there. A drop-in changed by hand needs service restart . The field needs core's module contract 0.12.4 or later.
These two fields describe; they do not change what EiN does, apart from root below. mod setup warns about an entry it cannot use and leaves it out of the documentation.

Environment variables the module reads that are not its settings, documented for docs env and the Environment variables page: { "key" : "NOMINATIM_SEARCH_URL" , "kind" : "option" , "default" : "https://nominatim.openstreetmap.org/search" , "description" : "Where geocoding asks Nominatim for an address, as geocode-location and location-region do. Point it at your own server to avoid the public one's rate limit." } key , kind and description are required, default is what the reader falls back to when the variable is not set, and kind says how the variable reaches whatever reads it: kind How it is set option nobody sets it for you; export it in a shell to change how a command behaves deployment the EiN process's own environment, read once at start session set for every shell by the server that opened it path the tree's layout, exported at start system the rest of what EiN exports at start for scripts pipeline set for a pipeline step by the event that started it A module almost always means option .

The node types the module defines, described for docs node-types and the Node types page. A node type exists as soon as a node carries it; one that is used but described nowhere is still listed, with its count and no description. { "type" : "album" , "label" : "Album" , "category" : "content" , "root" : "/archive/albums" , "description" : "A collection of photos and videos that behaves as a directory. …" } type , label , description and category are required. category is content (what the archive holds), structure (what organises it) or system . plural names several of them ("People"; the label with an s when it is left out), and searchable: true offers the type on the Search page as a choice of what to show, which needs a root and a type the search command knows. A type whose nodes live directly under one folder names that folder as root , and that makes it something an @ in the search box completes to. Typing @hel lists the names, matching what you typed, of the nodes of every such type directly under its root, so Helen Okafor's person node comes up. mod setup registers the types with a root and mod remove drops them. When two modules give the same type a root, the first one set up keeps it.

The folders directly under /archive that the module's content lives in. The Archive's are: "roots" : [ "/archive/people" , "/archive/locations" , "/archive/cameras" , "/archive/albums" , "/archive/sources" ] Each must be /archive/ followed by one name of lower case letters, digits, _ and - , starting with a letter. mod setup creates a missing one, owned by the administrator and the users group, with mode 771: anyone else, someone holding a link included, reaches what is shared with them under it but cannot list it. Nothing removes one, so removing a module does not delete its content. Name the roots in your module's own code too, so its dependents can use them: the Archive exports them as @archive/paths .

Database indexes on node attributes, for the queries the module's data is asked. mod setup creates each one that is missing. "indexes" : [ { "name" : "camera_taken_utc" , "on" : [ "cameraPath" , "takenAtUtc" ] , "partial" : "cameraPath" } , { "name" : "spoken_text" , "on" : [ "text" ] , "partial" : "text" , "using" : "trigram" } , { "name" : "duplicate_deferred" , "on" : [ "duplicate.deferred" ] , "using" : "statistics" } ] Key What it is name lower case letters, digits and _ , starting with a letter; the index is named <attrs table>_<name>_idx on the attributes, in order; a dotted path reaches into a nested attribute ( relation.from ) partial index only the nodes where this attribute is set: small and cheap for an attribute few nodes have collation bytes (the default), en or sv : the order the values are kept in, which must be the order a query asks for to use the index using trigram or statistics , below using: "trigram" makes a trigram index over one attribute's text instead. It serves a search for a substring anywhere in the text, and no order, so it takes one attribute in on and no collation . using: "statistics" makes no index at all, only the database's statistics on one attribute, for a condition no index serves that the planner would otherwise misjudge, such as asking for nodes that lack an attribute few nodes have. It takes one attribute and neither collation nor partial . If any of nodeTypes ' roots, roots or indexes is malformed, mod setup warns, for example letters: index 'Taken': invalid name 'Taken' (lower case, digits, _) , and none of the three is used: no root is created, no index is made and no type completes after @ .

The module's pages: each route with the file that draws it, relative to the module's root. "ui" : { "routes" : { "/cameras" : "ui/camera/pages/cameras.tsx" , "/cameras/:id" : "ui/camera/pages/camera.tsx" } } A route is a path below / made of literal and :param segments; / itself is the home page, which belongs to the Web UI. The page is a .tsx file inside the module, and its default export is the page's component. If ui.routes is present it must hold at least one route. ui-build bundles the pages inside the running EiN whenever modules are set up or removed, and the browser loads a module's bundle the first time one of its routes is opened. When two modules give the same route, the module whose name sorts later is left out: its pages are not served and ui-build reports /cameras is archive's route already . A route at the exact path of one of the Web UI's own pages is never reached, since the interface's own is matched first. How a route is shown, as a page, in a dialog, in the side drawer or full screen, is decided by the entry that opens it in the module's ui/nav.json , not by the route. Writing a module covers navigation entries.

Which route opens a node of a type, so the Web UI can link nodes it finds but does not know: search results, completions in the header, and Open in the node explorer. "open" : { "person" : "/people/{name}" , "album" : "/albums/{path}" , "camera" : "/cameras/{name}" } Placeholder Replaced by {name} the node's last path segment {parent} the segment before it {path} the node's whole path Each is URI-encoded. A route must start with / and use no other placeholder. A type that no installed module names is shown without a link. A key that is a folder, starting and ending with / , opens whatever is under it, whatever its type: a module's own files that are plain files to EiN, such as YAML it keeps under /etc . It may also use {rest} , the path below the folder without its extension, and the longest folder a node is under wins over its type: "open" : { "/etc/automations/" : "/automations/{rest}" } /etc/automations/hall-light.yaml then opens at /automations/hall-light , and a deeper /etc/automations/upstairs/hall.yaml at /automations/upstairs%2Fhall . Core opens a device at its page itself, and a log , track or control directly under a device at its device's page, so a module names no route for those; a module adds a tab to the device page with a device.tabs panel instead ( A tab on the device page ).

Which nodes the Share dialog offers a link for, and how the link opens them. Keys are as ui.open 's: a node type, or a folder ending with / . "shareLinks" : { "album" : { "shows" : "node" , "noun" : "album" } , "/archive/dashboards/" : { "shows" : "account" , "noun" : "dashboard" } } Field What it is shows node : the link shows the node and what it holds, as an album's does. account : the link signs in read-only as an account the person sharing picks, a display link, as a dashboard's does on a wall screen noun What the dialog calls the node: "Anyone with the link can see this album" A node no installed module names here is shared with people and groups only. Sharing describes both kinds of link, and Show a dashboard on a screen a display link. The field needs core's module contract 0.14.18 or later.

p.h: What mod setup finds without a field
p.x: Some of what a module brings is found by where it is in the module, not by a field in mod.json : In the module What mod setup does with it bin/ adds it to every shell's PATH ; each file is a command, a shell script or #!ts TypeScript services/<name>/ registers and enables a service from its start.sh ; a service the module no longer ships is retired pipelines/*.yaml defines each pipeline; one the module no longer ships is undefined ui/nav.json links it as /etc/ui/nav.d/<name>.json : its sidebar, top-bar and panel entries, each opening a route ui/index.html links ui/ as a site under /var/www/<name> etc/config links it as /etc/config.d/<name> : the module's own choice of setting values etc/<x>.d/ links it as /etc/<x>.d/<name> , for whichever module reads /etc/<x>.d/* ( assistant.d , dashboard.d ) the rest of etc/ copies each entry into /etc when it is not already there; never overwrites lib/ , types/ , test/ ordinary source, reached through imports and exports deno.jsonc generated from mod.json by deno task sync:modules ; never edited Commands are also found by name. Core runs a module's command when it is named after a role: members-<type> for what a node of that type holds, subject-<kind> for search --subject , search-* providers for the search box, and news-<x> , events-<x> and onthisday-<x> for the home page's sections. Writing a module gives each role's arguments and answer. Teaching the assistant covers what a module gives the assistant through etc/assistant.d .

mod setup checks the manifest before it changes anything, since the commands, services and pipelines it registers are live the moment they land. Put the module in place, or change its mod.json . In EiN's terminal, as an administrator, set it up again: # in EiN's terminal mod setup letters Read what it prints. On success it lists what it did and ends with Module 'letters' setup complete . What goes wrong falls in two kinds: Kind What it covers What happens Error the directory name, coreApi , dependencies , exports , imports , ui , and a field of the wrong shape ( config.options , nodeTypes , environment , indexes or roots that is not a list) the module is not set up at all; each problem is printed as mod setup: letters: … Warning a missing coreApi , a malformed setting, node type, environment variable, index or root the module is set up without the entry; the warning is printed A module installed under another directory name is refused with letters: must be installed as /usr/modules/letters, the directory named after it . When a later step fails, for example a service that cannot be added, mod setup ends with mod setup: module 'letters' setup incomplete . mod list shows afterwards how each module's last setup went, and Settings → Modules shows the same for each module. Modules describes both, and mod-setup and mod-info the commands. In a core checkout, deno task check type-checks the modules against their manifests, and core's tests include the boundary test and a check that each deno.jsonc matches its mod.json .

A driver teaches EiN a kind of device: it turns what such a device sends into endpoints under /dev/<device> , and sends the device what is written to its controls. Core has two drivers of its own, tracker , for phones and GPS loggers, and webhook , for anything that posts its readings; the Automation module brings three for MQTT devices. This page is for developers who write one in a module. It assumes Writing a module , and Devices, endpoints and drivers for what a device, an endpoint and a control are.

Direction What happens Through Device to EiN The driver hears the device, makes the device and its endpoints when they are new, and appends each reading ensureDevice , ensureEndpoint , append , online Written to EiN What a person, a script or the device itself writes to /dev/<device> reaches the driver as raw input the driver's input EiN to device A value written to one of the device's controls, checked against its schema, reaches the driver to send on the driver's write A driver that finds its devices, such as one listening on a broker, makes them itself. One whose devices announce nothing, such as core's tracker , waits for a person to make one with device-create <name> --driver <driver> , and gets its setup called to give it its first endpoints.

A driver is registered by a service of its module, in EiN's own process, and lives as long as the service runs. The service's start.sh runs a #!ts command that registers the driver and waits until the service is stopped: #!ts /** * weather-bridge — the weather-bridge service: registers the weather-json driver until stopped. */ import type { CmdReturn , Command } from '@ein/client' ; import { weatherDriver } from '@weather/driver' ; const weatherBridge = async ( cmd : Command ): CmdReturn => { const devices = cmd. sys . devices ; if (!devices) { await cmd. writeError ( 'weather-bridge: this EiN keeps no devices\n' ); return 1 ; } const stopped = new Promise < void >( ( resolve ) => cmd. onInterrupt (resolve)); const unregister = devices. registerDriver ( 'weather-json' , weatherDriver (cmd, devices)); await cmd. writeLn ( 'weather-bridge: driving weather-json' ); try { await stopped; } finally { unregister (); } return 0 ; }; weatherBridge. spec = { name : 'weather-bridge' , admin : true , daemon : true , effect : 'write' as const , json : false , description : 'Drive weather stations that post their readings as JSON (the weather-bridge service)' , examples : [ 'service restart weather-bridge' ], }; export default weatherBridge; # services/weather-bridge/start.sh weather-bridge cmd.sys.devices is core's device API, ModuleDevices in @ein/client . A service runs as the administrator, so cmd.access writes any device; pass it to every call. registerDriver answers a function that unregisters the driver; while it is unregistered, a write to one of its devices is refused with <device>'s driver weather-json is not running , and the device's page says (not running) . A driver's name is lower-case letters, digits, - and _ , and a second registration under the same name replaces the first.

registerDriver(name, driver) takes an object with these members: Member Needed What it is description yes One line for devices --drivers module no The module that brings it, for devices --drivers config no What a person gives when making a device with it: { name, label, type, required? } , type being string , number or url input(raw) no Raw input written to one of its devices; without it, its devices take none write(cmd) no A value written to one of its devices' controls, to send to the device setup(name) no A person made one of its devices with device-create --driver : give it the endpoints it has from the start forget(name) no One of its devices is being forgotten: let go of whatever would make it again, such as a retained announcement on a broker. Called before it is removed Core awaits each hook while the write that caused it waits, so whoever wrote hears at once whether it was taken. A hook refuses by throwing: the message reaches the writer, as echo 's error in the terminal or as the body of a 400 over HTTP, after the device's name (and the control's, for a write ).

What is written to /dev/<device> , from the terminal ( cat ride.gpx > /dev/old-logger ), over SFTP, or over HTTP to /file/dev/<device> , arrives whole, once the writer closes, as a DriverInput : Field What it holds device The device's name path /dev/<device> attrs The device's attributes: its label , class , config and the rest bytes What was written contentType The type it came with over HTTP; unset from the terminal or SFTP query The query it came with over HTTP, without ? or the device's key; a GET with the key brings only this by Who wrote it: an account's name, or device:<name> for a write made with the device's key It answers an optional { taken, message } , which an HTTP writer gets back as JSON: how many values were new, and a word for whoever sent them.

A value written to a control arrives as a DriverWrite once core has checked it against the control's schema , so value is already what the control takes: true or false for bool , a number within its limits for number , one of its options for enum , a line for text , press for momentary , with toggle turned into the opposite of the state the device last reported. Its fields are device , endpoint , path , the device's attrs , the control's endpointAttrs , value and by . Send it, and return once the device or its broker has taken it. Do not append the new state here: append what the device reports back, which is what reading the control gives. Until then the control's requested attribute holds what was asked, by whom and when, and its page shows it as waiting for the device. A write that has not returned after 10 seconds is answered <device> did not answer within 10 s .

What a driver hears it writes through the same ModuleDevices : Call What it does ensureDevice(access, name, attrs) Makes /dev/<name> when it is missing, else sets the attributes given where they differ. A label is set only when the device is made, so a person's device-label is kept. Answers the path ensureEndpoint(access, device, name, type, attrs, mode?) Makes the endpoint log , track or control when it is missing, else sets the attributes given where they differ; refuses one of another type. Answers the path removeEndpoint(access, device, endpoint) Removes an endpoint and its history: one the device no longer has, or one that changed type append(access, device, endpoint, value, { at?, retained? }) A reading for a log or a control, or a position { lat, lng, alt?, speed?, course?, accuracy? } for a track: kept, and published on dev.<device>.<endpoint> .
