Highlight the candidate above / below R Not the highlighted candidate C Compare with the highlighted album, or narrow the column again X Discard L Later, or back to its lane Z Undo the last decision of this visit E Rename T Set the time of every picture M / Shift + M Merge into the group above / merge the group below in [ / ] Previous / next day or month of the group Arrow keys Step through the pictures O Open the first picture Shift + J / Shift + K Select on to the next / previous group On a picture (after an arrow key), a day or month (after [ or ] ), or selected pictures: Key What it does Space Select the picture, or the day's pictures O Open the picture S Split the group before them; in a lane, make them a new group < / > Move them to the group above / below G Move them to a group… Enter N P A B X Act on the day or the selected pictures only Esc Back to the group, or clear the selection With the arrow keys on a single picture and nothing selected, Enter , N , P , A , B and X still act on the whole group. < , > , [ and ] work on any keyboard layout, also where you type them with AltGr or Option.

The organizer's groups are suggestions. When one is wrong, change it. Every change but a rename says so in a message with Undo , and every change is listed on the Done tab, where Undo takes it back. To Do this What happens Split a group Split here on a day or month, or S on a picture, a day or a selection That picture and the ones after it become a group of their own: "“A week in London” split in two". You cannot split before the first picture. Move pictures to a neighbour Select them, then < or > They join the group above or below. Move pictures to any group Select them, then G The Move to a group dialog: the five groups on each side, Find a group by name , or New group ("A group of their own, named by their dates"). Make a new group New group of N pictures under the open group; in a lane, New group on a day or S The pictures become a group of their own, named by their dates. Merge two groups M ( Merge into “…” , the group above) or Shift + M ( Merge “…” in , the group below) One group. It keeps a name a person gave; otherwise a name that says what or where rather than bare dates; otherwise the larger group's. Break up a group Not a group… in the ⋯ menu or the column The Not a group? dialog: the photos go back to their lanes, Everyday and the like, and the organizer does not suggest them as a group again. No photo is removed. Rename E , Rename in the ⋯ menu, or double-click the open group's name Type the name and press Enter ; Esc keeps the old one. Keep a group exactly as it is ⋯ → Open as an album page , then ⋮ → Keep album as is The organizer leaves the group and its files alone. Let the organizer manage album hands it back; Sort in Staging returns to the group in the stream. You can also drag pictures, or a whole group by its grip ⠿, onto another group's header to move or merge them. In a Scans category, groups are runs of scans in their folders, not events: split or merge them instead of using Not a group… , which is refused there.

The organizer looks at a category again a couple of minutes after its files change, and when you choose Group now . Groups can change while files are still arriving and being read, which is what Still indexing warns of. The stream follows along: a group that changes is read again, and one that is removed disappears. What you decide is kept through every one of those runs: Your changes of the groups (splits, moves, new groups, merges, Not a group , names) are kept on every run until you undo them. On the Done tab all but a rename carry the badge kept : "The organizer keeps this change on every run until it is undone". A group whose pictures you changed by hand shows Yours , and the organizer leaves it as it is. Not this album keeps that album away from those photos until you undo it. A group put aside stays in Later until you bring it back. If the organizer changed a group while you were deciding on it, your decision is refused with "it changed while you were deciding; look again". The group comes back with Retry and Dismiss ; look at it again before you decide.

The Files tab shows the category one folder at a time. The line at the top leads back up to the category; subfolders are cards with the number of entries in each. Media shows every picture, video and recording in the folder and its subfolders, by day. Select pictures to use Add to album , Set time , and, when you may change them all, Set location and Label . Folder lists every entry of the folder, whatever its type (a PDF, a sidecar file), as the Nodes page does, filling the page below its header: details, list or icons, sorted by a click on a column's name, a folder opened in place with its arrow or gone into with a double click or Enter , and a panel beside it that previews the entry you are on. It stays within the category: Up stops at it and Home goes back to it. Select entries with a click, Ctrl or Shift and a click for more, or Ctrl + A (on a phone, press and hold one, then tap the others); the top of the panel then offers Move to folder… , Move to category… and Discard… for them, and Delete discards them too. To move or discard a folder or files, use the ⋯ on a folder's card, the Actions button for the folder you are in, or the panel beside a selection in Folder : Move to folder… moves it to another folder of the same category. Move to category… moves it into another category (offered when you have more than one). It first leaves the groups of its old category, and its files are dated again by the new category's rules. Discard… moves it to your trash. In the move dialog, choose the Category , step into a folder, and optionally type a name under Into a new folder here . The line under it says where it goes, for example "Into Scans › box-3. Links to them, in albums and suggested groups, follow them." Choose Move here . The Discard dialog says: "They go to your trash, kept together as one entry on the Trash page. Undo, here or on the Done tab, puts them back where they were." Choose Discard ; the message has Undo . An empty category says "Nothing in Box 3 yet" (with its own name) and offers Import media , and the folder to copy into over SFTP.

p.h: Done: what you decided, and Undo
p.x: The Done tab lists what was decided in the category, newest first, 50 at a time ( Show older for more). At the top: "N filed · M discarded". Everything shows every decision; Regrouping shows only the changes you made to the groups. Each row shows when it happened and what it was: "86 files → Christmas at the cottage" with the album as a link, "12 files discarded", "Split “A week in London”", "“Christmas Eve · 24 Dec 1975” is not for Christmas 1975", and so on, with the groups it touched. Badges: only you for a private album, kept for a change the organizer keeps, in part for a decision that stopped part-way. Each row has Undo , or "undone" and the time once it is undone. Undo puts things back: filed files move back into staging, and an album the decision made is removed once it is empty; discarded files come back from the trash, as long as they are still there; the groups get their pictures back, and a change of the groups stops applying; Not this album gives the group its candidates back. The message says "Undone:" and what was undone. A file that was moved after the decision stays where it is: "Undone in part: some files have moved since, and stay where they are". In the Sort tab, Z undoes the decisions of this visit, newest first; one still waiting to be carried out is cancelled instead. With nothing left, it says "Nothing to undo from this visit; the Done tab lists every decision." Later is not listed on Done ; bring a group back from the Later lane instead.

On a phone the Sort tab has no keys, no column beside the stream and no selecting of several groups. Tap a group to open it. Each closed group has its proposal (or New album… ) as a button under its pictures, and the ⋯ menu on each group has every action. More on EiN on a phone .

What you see What it means What to do No groups yet The files are still being read, or the organizer has not grouped them yet Wait a few minutes, or choose Group now under the tab names Still indexing on a group Some of its pictures are still being read Decide later, or go ahead; the group may still change "it changed while you were deciding; look again" The organizer changed the group after you opened it Look at the group, then Retry , or Dismiss "You can't add to “…”." The album is one you may only look at Choose another album, or ask whoever owns it "No proposal: N, A, B or X." EiN has nothing to suggest Choose yourself: a new album, any album, the target, or discard Remove category is greyed out The category still holds files Move or discard its files first "Undone in part: …" Some files were moved after the decision Look for them in the place they were moved to The commands behind these pages, for use in the terminal, are under staging in the Archive commands .

This page is for anyone sorting new pictures in staging. It covers how EiN tells exact copies, look-alikes and bursts apart, where it marks them, and how you remove the copies you do not want. The version you keep is filled in with anything the copies held that it lacks. Everything here happens in your own staging area, before pictures join the shared library. How pictures get there is on Getting your photos in , and the rest of staging is on Sorting in staging .

EiN sorts "the same picture twice" into three kinds and treats each one differently. An exact copy is kept once, a look-alike is yours to judge, and a burst is a stack, never a duplicate Kind What it is When EiN finds it What happens Exact copy The same file, byte for byte: the same photo uploaded twice, or a second copy of an export As the file is read on arrival One copy is kept. The others are not processed, and each one shows its original's picture Look-alike The same picture in other bytes: a smaller version a phone app or cloud service saved, a re-save in another format, a mild crop, a video or recording encoded again Once the file is prepared and its fingerprint is made Marked with how alike the files are, for example "97% alike". EiN suggests the better one, and you decide Burst Several shots taken a moment apart When the pictures are grouped Not a duplicate. The shots are folded into a stack, and nothing is removed EiN compares each new file with the library photos you can open and with the rest of your own staging area, across all your categories. A copy in someone else's staging area, or in a library album you cannot open, does not count. EiN does not take two shots for one picture when their times tell them apart: Two photos whose camera clocks (or GPS times) are a second or more apart are two shots. A copy that EiN placed in another time zone than its original is not, since its camera's clock read the same. Two photos from one camera, of one size and taken in the same second, are two shots when the camera recorded different fractions of that second. When it recorded the same fraction, they are one picture: an edit keeps the time, so a black-and-white or mirrored copy is a look-alike of its photo, even though it looks less alike than a smaller version does. Without a fraction to tell, such photos are one picture only if they are as alike as a re-saved copy. A crop that cuts away most of the picture is not found, and a picture turned on its side often is not. A picture that looks like thirty or more other files, such as a dark frame or a test chart, counts as alike to none of them.

p.h: An exact copy shows its original
p.x: When a file arrives that is an exact copy of one you can open, in the library or earlier in your staging area, EiN does not process it. It makes no previews, finds no faces and adds nothing to search. Taking in a second copy of a large export therefore costs a moment per file, not minutes. While it stays a copy: the Duplicates tab shows it with its original's picture and size, since the bytes are the same; it joins no suggested group in Sort ; the Media view of the Files tab leaves it out (the Folder view lists every file, copies too); it does not count among the files being prepared. Among identical files in your staging area, the one that arrived first is the original. When you file an original into the library, its copies still in staging become copies of the library photo. When a copy no longer has an original you can open, EiN processes it where it is, like any new file. If you discard the original in staging, this happens at once, and the copy is then grouped like any other file. If the original goes some other way, for example when someone deletes it from the library, it happens within the hour.

In the open group, a picture that copies or looks like another one carries a badge in its corner: Badge Tooltip Means ⧉ "In the library already: compare" It is a copy or look-alike of a photo in the library 2× "Another one here is the same picture: compare" It is a copy or look-alike of another staged photo Click a badge to open Compare for that picture. The open group's header also gets a chip with the totals, for example "⧉ 4 in library · 2× 1". Its menu has these items: Compare opens the first marked picture side by side with its matches. Keep the library copies removes the group's pictures the library already has. It removes only those that need no look: exact copies, and smaller versions of a library photo (see Remove all for what counts). Look-alikes that need a look stay in the group. Select these selects the marked pictures, so you can act on them together. It is offered on a computer. When at least four in five of the open group's pictures are copies or smaller versions of library photos, the group's proposal becomes Keep the library copies · N photos go , marked sure (●●●). Enter removes them, and the rest of the group stays to be sorted. The message says, for example, "12 photos of “Cornwall, summer 1968” removed", with Undo .

In the Media view of a category's Files tab, tiles carry the same ⧉ and 2× badges. A photo that is kept over copies left out of the list also gets 2× , so you can see that it has copies. Click the badge to compare.

When you open one of your own staged pictures in the viewer , its details panel says which sets it belongs to, with one of these lines: "A copy of a library photo" or "A copy of a photo in this import" "Looks like a library photo" or "Looks like a photo in this import" "Kept over 2 copies" or "Kept over 1 look-alike" Under the line are the set's other files as thumbnails, with the kept one marked Kept , and why it is kept. Compare opens the files side by side, and for look-alikes Not duplicates keeps them apart. If you remove the picture you are viewing, the viewer closes.

A burst is not a duplicate, so it has no set to remove. In a suggested group, consecutive photos that look alike and were taken within seconds of each other are folded behind one tile, which shows a stack icon and the number of shots. Each album makes its own stacks the same way once the pictures are filed. The files never move. You can choose the front photo or keep one out of a stack: see Albums . How alike and how close in time the shots must be are two settings an administrator can change, Stack similarity ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_THRESHOLD , 0.75 by default) and Stack time gap (seconds) ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_MAX_GAP_SECONDS , 10).

Open Staging , choose a category, and select the Duplicates tab, the second tab after Sort . The number on the tab counts the category's exact copies. Look-alikes are counted inside the tab. The tab reads what EiN already found while the files arrived, so it opens at once however large the category is. At the top, a switch shows four lists, each with its count: List What it holds When it is empty Copies of library photos Staged photos with the same bytes as a photo in the library "No photo of this category is a copy of one in the library." Copies within this import Staged photos with the same bytes as another staged one, which arrived first "No photo of this category is a copy of another one here." Like library photos Staged photos that are the same picture as a library photo, in other bytes "No photo of this category looks like one in the library." Alike within this import Staged photos that are the same picture as each other "No two photos of this category look like one picture." "This import" means your staging area: an original in another of your categories counts too. A category's tab lists the copies that lie in that category. The tab opens on the first list that has something in it. The lists hold videos and recordings as well as photos.

The tab shows one card per set : the file kept and the files it would replace. The card heading says what the set is, for example "2 copies of a library photo", "1 copy of a photo in this import", "1 photo like a library photo" or "2 photos alike in this import". Beside it, a set of look-alikes shows how alike they are ("97% alike"), and every set shows how much space removing the copies frees. Each file is a tile with a label in its corner: Label Means Keep · library The kept file is a library photo. The album holding it is named under the tile Keep The kept file is one of your staged photos Drop This file goes to your trash when you remove the set Elsewhere A file of the set that this removal leaves alone, for example a copy in another category (dimmed) Under each tile are its picture size, file size and the time it was taken. A copy that holds something the kept file lacks says so, for example "gives description, labels". Under the tiles, one line says why the kept file is kept and what it gains, for example "kept: it is in the library · the kept one gains: description, star". Yellow lines warn of anything to look out for. They are listed under When something looks wrong .

A library photo is always kept: nothing in staging removes or changes a library photo, except to fill it in. Between your staged files, EiN keeps these: In a set of exact copies, the file that arrived first ("kept: it came first"). In a set of look-alikes, the better picture, by the first of these rules that tells two apart: Rule What the line says More pixels "kept: it has more pixels (4032×3024 over 1600×1200)" A better format: RAW, then HEIC, then TIFF or PNG, then JPEG, then WebP, then GIF "kept: its format is better" A surer time: typed in by hand, then GPS, then the camera's clock, then a sidecar, then the file name "kept: its time is surer" The larger file "kept: it is the larger file" A name that is not a copy's, such as one without (2) , a trailing -1 or copy "kept: its name is not a copy’s" Otherwise, the one that arrived first "kept: it came first" When you pick another one yourself, the line says "kept: you chose it".

Removing a set merges the copies into the kept file before they go. The kept file is filled in, never overwritten . From the copies it takes a description, a time typed in by hand, a place or a sidecar when it has none, the labels and your star when it lacks them, and the copies' people, comments and albums. The line "the kept one gains: …" lists what it will get. The copies then leave your suggested groups. When the kept file is staged in the same category, it takes a copy's place in its group. The copies go to your trash together, as one entry.

p.h: Remove the copies of one set
p.x: Open Staging , choose the category, and select the Duplicates tab. Choose a list at the top. Look at a set. If you are not sure which file is better, click Compare . Click Remove 1 copy (for exact copies) or Remove 1 photo (for look-alikes). The button gives the number of files that go. The set leaves the list at once, and a message says how many files were removed, for example "2 removed", with Undo . While removals are still running, "◌ 2 applying" shows at the top. To keep a different staged file, click Keep this one under its tile. It is offered in sets within this import and in sets of look-alikes. EiN keeps that file and removes the other staged files of the set. A library photo stays whichever file you pick. On a computer you can work through the list with the keyboard: Key What it does J / K Mark the next or previous set Enter Remove the marked set's copies C Compare the marked set Z Undo the last removal of this visit Clicking a set marks it too. All keys are on Keyboard shortcuts .

Compare opens a set's files large, side by side. You can open it from the Duplicates tab, from a badge in Sort or on the Files tab, and from the viewer. The dialog is titled Copies or Look-alikes . Under the title, the set's likeness and why the kept file is kept appear, for example "97% alike · kept: it has more pixels (4032×3024 over 1600×1200)". Each file is labelled Keep · library , Keep , Drop , Library (a library photo that stays) or Stays . Under each are its picture size, file size, the time it was taken, the camera, and how alike it is. When a file has exact copies of its own, "and 2 byte copies" says so: they go with it when it is removed. Key What it does ← / → Move between the files K Keep the file in focus instead (staged files only) Enter Remove the others X Not duplicates (look-alikes only) Esc Close without changing anything The buttons at the bottom do the same: Not duplicates (for look-alikes), Cancel and Remove the others . On a phone, tap a file to focus it and use the buttons.

p.h: Say that two pictures are not duplicates
p.x: Look-alikes can be wrong: two photos of the same view, or two shots of one moment that the camera did not time apart. Click Not duplicates on the set, in Compare or in the viewer. The set leaves the list, and the message "Kept apart: not duplicates" has Undo . EiN remembers the choice on each staged file and never pairs those files again. This choice is not listed on the Done tab, so the message's Undo is the only way back in the Web UI. Exact copies cannot be kept apart, since their bytes are the same.

p.h: Remove a whole list at once
p.x: Three lists have a button at the top that resolves every set needing no look: List Button What it removes Copies of library photos Remove all N copies… Every copy Copies within this import Remove all N copies… Every copy but the one kept Like library photos Remove all smaller versions… Only staged photos that are smaller versions of a library photo, at least 95% alike, and that cannot be two shots of a burst Alike within this import has no such button: those sets are for you to look at one by one. Choose the list and click its Remove all button. Read the dialog, for example Remove all copies of library photos? It explains that each copy goes to your trash once the kept file is filled in. It also says that a set whose kept file is gone, or that you cannot fill in, is left as it is. Click Remove 120 copies (or Remove them for smaller versions), or Cancel . A bar shows the progress, for example "Removing copies of library photos: 40 copies so far, 80 left". Stop ends the run once the batch being removed is done; the button reads Stopping… until then. When the run ends, one message says how many copies were removed and has Undo for the whole run. Each set is checked again right before it is removed, so a set that changed meanwhile is left alone.

Nothing is deleted outright. Every removal can be taken back: with Undo in the message that follows it; with Z on the Duplicates tab or in Sort , for removals made during this visit; from the Done tab, where each removal is one entry, for example "3 copies of 2 photos removed", with Undo . See Sorting in staging . Undo brings the copies back where they were, with their places in their groups, and they are listed as copies again. What the kept file gained stays, since it overwrote nothing. Each removal is also one entry on your Trash page, named for example "Duplicates from Phone: 3 copies". Undo is the better way back, because it also puts the copies back into their groups. The Trash page is described on Your profile, favourites and trash .

What you see What it means What to do "perhaps two shots of a burst: same size, same camera, same second" The files may be two shots rather than one picture twice Compare them. If they differ, click Not duplicates "a staged one has more pixels than the library’s" Your new file is larger than the library photo, but the library photo is still the one kept To keep both, click Not duplicates and file your photo like any other. You can then remove the smaller one from its album yourself, as Albums describes "files in other folders stay" A copy lies in another category Remove it from that category's Duplicates tab "its original is gone or changed: nothing is dropped" The kept file is no longer there with the same bytes. Remove is greyed out Nothing to do. EiN checks every finding each hour, and the set changes or goes away "you cannot write the kept one, which would gain from the copies" You may not change the library photo, and a copy holds something it would gain. Remove is greyed out Ask someone who may change that photo, or, if what the copy holds does not matter, discard it on the Files tab (its Folder view lists copies too) "it changed: look again" The set changed after the page read it Open the tab again "look-alikes are for you to look at: Remove all leaves them" Remove all skips this set Look at it and use Remove , Keep this one or Not duplicates The message "Left as it is: …" after Remove The set changed before the removal ran, so nothing was removed. This also happens after Keep this one on the only staged photo beside a library photo, since nothing else is left to remove Look at the set again. To keep both pictures, use Not duplicates A copy you expected is not listed It is in someone else's staging area, in an album you cannot open, or not prepared yet Look-alikes appear once the file is prepared; see Getting your photos in

The Duplicates tab compares new files with the library. It does not look for copies among photos that are already in the library, and EiN has no page that does this for family members. An administrator can look for them with the Duplicates tool on the Nodes page, or with duplicates and merge-duplicates in the shell. The web uploader sends every file, even one the library already has, and EiN then sets the copy aside without processing it. You do not need to check for copies before you upload.

Everything the tab does is a staging subcommand you can run yourself in EiN's terminal : # in EiN's terminal staging duplicates inbox --counts # copies and look-alikes in the inbox, by kind staging duplicates inbox --exact -- where library # the sets of copies of library photos staging dedupe inbox --apply --exact -- where library --dry-run # what Remove all would do staging separate <file> <other> # these files are not duplicates staging dedupe must be run by the owner of the staging area, since the copies go to their trash. Every flag is in the staging reference , and the administrator's side of staging is on Staging and importing for administrators .

Every picture in EiN gets a date when anything can tell it one, and a place when it was taken with GPS or someone gives it one. This page is for family members who fix when and where pictures were taken: where EiN finds both, how to correct them, and what happens to scans and to pictures nobody has dated.

p.h: Where you see a picture's date and place
p.x: Open a picture in the viewer. On a computer the date and the place sit in the bar under the picture; on a phone the date is centred over the top of the picture and the bar at the foot keeps the place. The date is written as precisely as it is known: "Saturday, 16 June 1956, 14:03:11" for a full time, "1975" for a picture known only to a year, "August 1968" for one known to a month. A picture with no date shows none. Point at the date for a tooltip. It names where the date came from (the time source), any note someone left with it, and the time in your own time zone when the picture was taken in another ("… your time"). The place is the name of the location the picture is linked to, else its street address, else its city and country. The details panel ( Details (i) , or i ; on a phone, swipe up) shows more. Its place section has the location's name as a link, the street address and a small map with Enlarge map . The Details row near its foot, folded until you click its icon, holds Taken at (the date exactly as stored, with its time zone), Taken at (UTC) and Time source . Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers the rest of the panel. In an album the pictures are laid out in sections by day. One known only to a year sits under a heading with only the year; one with no date comes after the dated ones, under Undated . A person's, location's or camera's Media tab lists undated pictures after the rest too. The Media feed lists pictures by date, so it leaves out a picture that has none.

EiN looks at up to five sources for a picture's date and takes the first one that has it. The Time source says in words which one it was. The first source on the ladder that has a date decides; a scan waits until a person gives it one Order Source Time source reads What it is 1 Set by hand entered by hand A date someone gave with Set time or file-set-time . It always wins, and it may be as vague as a year. 2 A sidecar or Google Photos from Google Photos or a sidecar A date a photo editor or scanning program wrote into an XMP sidecar, or a date someone changed in Google Photos before exporting. 3 GPS from GPS The GPS receiver's clock, the one source that knows the exact moment. 4 The camera's clock from the camera clock The date and time the camera or phone wrote into the file, or a video's recording time. 5 The file name from the file name A date the name spells, such as IMG_20190601_123456.jpg , for files from a staging category whose names count as dates. When none of them has a date, the picture is undated. EiN never dates a picture by when it was uploaded or when the file was last changed. A sidecar is a small file beside a picture that says things about it: the JSON Google Photos writes for each photo of a Takeout export, or the .xmp file a photo editor writes. EiN pairs sidecars with their pictures as they arrive in staging, in every kind of category but Messaging and Screenshots. Getting your photos in and Supported files say which names it understands. A few rules decide the close cases: A GPS time far from the camera's clock is ignored. More than 26 hours apart, the GPS time is taken for an old position the receiver kept reporting, and the camera's clock dates the picture. Google Photos' time counts as a person's date only when it differs. More than 26 hours from the camera's clock (or, for a picture without one, from when it was uploaded to Google), it is a date someone set there, and it comes second on the ladder. Closer than that, it is Google's reading of the camera's clock: the picture keeps the camera's time, Google's time tells EiN which time zone the clock was in, and Time source reads "from Google Photos or a sidecar". A GPS time still comes first then, and a camera that recorded its own time zone keeps "from the camera clock". File names count only where a staging category says so , and only the names a phone, a messenger, a screenshot tool or a desktop uploader writes. A name that dates a picture before 1995 is not believed, and a scanner's running number such as IMG_20190601_0001.jpg is no date. A scanner's clock never dates a picture once the scanner is registered as a camera with Scanner or digitizer turned on (see Cameras ). A GPS time in the file still counts.

p.h: Date scans of old prints and slides
p.x: A scanner writes the day of the scan into the file, and a scanning app on a phone adds where the scan was made. Neither says when the picture was taken. When files arrive in a staging category of the kind Scans , EiN marks them as scans and sets aside the scanner's clock, the GPS time and position, the file name, and a Google Photos time that agrees with them. A scan is dated only by a date a person gives it: with Set time , with file-set-time , in an XMP sidecar, or by changing it in Google Photos. Until then it is undated, rather than dated to the day it was scanned. A date in an XMP sidecar keeps the precision it was written with: 1985 , 1985-06 , 1985-06-12 or a time. A date the scan application marks approximate, as when someone typed "ca. 1985", is shown as ~1985 in the viewer and its details panel, and pointing at the date says "approximate". A date set by hand replaces it and is exact. Time source on a scan adds "a scan: its scanner’s clocks are not when it was taken". The mark goes with the file when it is filed into an album, so the scan stays undated there until someone dates it. To bring in a box of scans: Open the Create menu (the plus in the top bar) and choose Import media . Under Into which category? , choose your Scans category, or New category with What it holds set to Scans and a name under Called , such as "Box 3". Press Choose files or Choose a folder , then Upload , which shows the number of files. Scans that already arrived in the Inbox can be moved: on the Inbox's Files tab, open the folder's ⋯ menu, choose Move to category… , pick the Scans category and press Move here . EiN dates the moved files again by the scans' rules, in the background. Sorting in staging explains categories and the Files tab. Note A scan uploaded straight into an album, or copied into one over SFTP, is not marked: no staging category's rules apply there. For those, register the scanner as a camera with Scanner or digitizer turned on. Saving that setting re-dates the files already linked to it and says "Removed scanner dates from N linked files." Helen Okafor scanned the family's slides of "Cornwall, summer 1968" in March 2012. Uploaded into a Scans category, they wait undated until she gives them a date. Uploaded straight into an album from an unregistered scanner, they would all show March 2012. In a Scans category the Sort tab keeps the scans in runs, by folder and file name, under To sort , dated or not. Once most of a run has dates set by hand, its name gains their years, and a run splits where two neighbouring scans were given different years.

Each staging category has two time rules, which come with its kind ( What it holds ): whether its files are scans, and whether a date in a file name counts. What it holds Treated as scans File names count as dates Inbox no yes Google Photos export no no Scans yes no Phone no yes Camera no no Messaging no yes Screenshots no yes Other no no Files that move into a category with other rules are dated again by that category's rules, in the background. A move within a category, or between two with the same rules, changes nothing. Category settings has no switch for the two rules. Changing What it holds there resets them, together with the category's other settings, to those of the kind you chose. In the terminal, staging category <name> --digitized on|off and staging category <name> --filename-dates on|off change one rule and date the category's files again before they answer. A date set by hand outranks both rules.

p.h: Give pictures that need a date a date
p.x: Staging shows what has no date. A category's card on the Staging overview, and the strip above the category's tabs, has a bar whose Needs a date part counts the pictures read without a date. On the category's Sort tab, the Needs a date lane holds groups of undated pictures, named like "Undated · Peggy's shoebox", and groups of pictures dated only to a year or a month, named like "1987 · Peggy's shoebox". In a Scans category the scans stay in their runs under To sort instead, as described above. Open Staging , then the category, then its Sort tab. Choose Needs a date in the row of lanes above the groups. The row appears when more than one lane has groups, each lane with its number of groups. Open a group: click it, or move to it with J and K . Press T , or open the group's ⋯ menu and choose Set the time… . To date only some of its pictures, select them first; T then sets the time of those. In the Set time dialog, set Start time and the order (see the next section), then press Set time on N files . A picture dated only to a year or a month keeps that date unless you click its row first (see the next section), so a group named like "1987 · Peggy's shoebox" needs a click on each row you want to date. Until you do, the button is off and the dialog says "These pictures are known only to a year or a month and keep that date. Click a row to give it a time." EiN confirms with "The time is set on N photos of “ ”". Within a few minutes the organizer puts the pictures into groups by the dates you gave them: an event, a trip, or a year's Everyday lane. On a phone there are no keys; tap the group and use its ⋯ menu. You can also file a Needs a date group as it is, undated, with New album… , Add to album… or the other decisions of the Sort tab. Its proposal is the category's album when the category has one; otherwise there is none. Pictures already in the library have no lane. An album lists its undated pictures last, under Undated : select them there and use Set time . In the terminal , search --undated lists everything undated in the library that you may see.

p.h: Set the time of several pictures at once
p.x: Set time is in the selection bar that appears when you select pictures: on an album page, the Media page, a person's, location's or camera's Media tab, and the Files tab in staging. On a narrow screen it is under Actions . It is offered only when you may change every selected picture. In staging's Sort tab, T opens the same dialog. The dialog is titled Set time , with the number of files under it. Order decides which picture comes first: Current time (the default; earliest first, undated last), Name (by file name, IMG_2 before IMG_10 ) or Manual . Drag a row by the grip at its left to reorder; dragging switches to Manual . Start time is the time the first row gets. It starts at the earliest date in the batch, or at today's date and time when none of the pictures has one. Each row shows the picture, its name, its current date or "No date", and after the arrow the time it will get. The times are worked out from the top: The first row gets Start time . Each following row gets the time of the row before it plus the gap between their current times. Where either of the two has no date, or your order puts a later picture before an earlier one, the gap is one minute. Pictures taken in the same second stay in the same second. Changing a row's time pins it: that row keeps your time and the rows after it follow on from it. The round arrow at the end of a pinned row ("Unpin — follow the row above again") lets it follow the row above again. A picture known only to a year or a month keeps its date. Its row reads " — unchanged", with the tooltip "Keeping this date as it is. Give it a time to replace it.", and the rows after it follow the last row that took a time. Click it to give it a full time instead. Press Set time on N files , where N counts the pictures that get a time; one that keeps its vague date is left out. Each picture's date becomes one entered by hand, with the time of day included, also for a picture that was known only to the day. Albums holding the pictures update their date range. Warning The dialog shows and writes times in your browser's time zone. For a picture taken in another time zone, such as on a trip abroad, the time after the arrow can differ by some hours from its current date before you change anything. Compare the rows before you press Set time on N files . Some ways to use it: The camera's clock was wrong , an hour behind after a trip or never set at all: select that camera's pictures, keep Current time , and set Start time to the right time of the first picture. The others move by the same amount and keep their spacing. Scans of an album, in page order : select them, choose Name , and set Start time to the day. They spread a minute apart in scan order, so they stay in that order everywhere. Undated pictures where you know the time of some : set Start time , then change the rows whose time you know. The rows between follow on from them. One picture : select only that one.

p.h: Give a picture a vague date
p.x: A date can be as vague as it really is: a year ("1975"), a month ("August 1968") or a day. EiN keeps it that way and never adds a day or an hour nobody knew. The Set time dialog writes full times only, so a vague date is given in the terminal with file-set-time . Open the picture in the viewer and open the details panel. Unfold the Details row near its foot by clicking its icon, and click the path under Path . A terminal tab opens, standing in the picture itself, so . names the picture. Type file-set-time , the picture and the date: # in EiN's terminal, opened from Path file-set-time . 1968-08 EiN answers with the date the picture has and where it came from: /archive/albums/Cornwall, summer 1968/scan0004.jpg: 1968-08 (manual) The date can be 1968 , 1968-08 , 1968-08-14 , 1968-08-14T15:30 or 1968-08-14T15:30:00 , and the last two may end in a time zone, +01:00 or Z . The year must lie between 1826 and next year; anything else is refused with "file-set-time: not a capture time: ". More forms, run in the folder that holds the pictures ( cd .. from the picture): # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-time scan0004.jpg 1968-08 scan0005.jpg 1968-08 --note "Peggy remembers the August heatwave" for f in scan00*.jpg; do file-set-time " $f " 1968; done file-set-time --clear scan0004.jpg Several pictures go in one call as pairs of picture and date. If one date is wrong or one picture is missing, nothing is written. --note keeps a reason with the date. It shows beside the time source, in the date's tooltip and under Time source . --clear takes away a date set by hand, and its note. The picture falls back to the next source on the ladder, or to no date. The Web UI has no button for this.

A picture is shown at the time on the clock the photographer was reading. A photograph taken at noon in Wellington reads 12:00, whoever looks at it; when your own time zone differs, the date's tooltip adds the same moment in yours ("… your time"). EiN works out the time zone of a picture from: the time zone the camera recorded in the file, as many phones do; the difference between the GPS time and the camera's clock, rounded to whole hours; the difference between Google Photos' time and the camera's clock, for a picture from a Takeout; the Timezone of the registered camera that took it, which knows the summer time of the year the picture was taken in. A picture none of these places carries no time zone. It is shown at the camera's time without a "your time" line, and EiN reads it in the archive's own time zone, which is the time zone of the machine EiN runs on ( TZ , under Environment variables ). When a camera's pictures come out hours off: The camera's clock was set to another zone , for one bought abroad or kept on home time during a trip: give the camera the Timezone its clock was set to. For a registered camera, open its page, press Edit and set Timezone ; saving re-dates the pictures linked to it and says "Re-dated N linked files." Register an unregistered one from the Cameras page with its Timezone , which links its pictures and dates them by it. Cameras has the details. A phone's videos are off by exactly its time zone : turn on Video times in UTC for that phone. Phones keep their videos' recording time in UTC. The clock was wrong by some amount , a day ahead or some minutes fast: open the camera's page, press Edit and set Clock is off by , from the date it was wrong if not for all its pictures (see Clocks, time zones and scanners ). For a few pictures, use Set time as described above. A time from the Set time dialog carries no time zone and is read in the archive's time zone, so a picture from a trip abroad that you re-time loses its "your time" line. In the terminal you can give the zone with the time: # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-time DSCF0412.JPG 1996-02-03T14:30+13:00

p.h: Where a picture's place comes from
p.x: A picture gets its place from the first of these that has one: A place set by hand, with Set location , in Edit file or with file-set-position . It replaces anything the file carries, and EiN reading the file again never puts the GPS position back over it. The GPS position in the file. The place in its sidecar: an XMP sidecar's, or a Google Photos Takeout's. A scan's own GPS position is where it was scanned, so EiN ignores it, and a Takeout's place for a scan too, unless someone set that place in Google Photos. A position of exactly 0,0, in the sea off West Africa, is what a camera or phone writes when it has no GPS fix, and Google Photos when it has no place. EiN takes it for no place, in the file and in a sidecar alike, and Set location refuses it. Street addresses. EiN looks up each picture's position once in OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service, which turns coordinates into a street address. Only the coordinates are sent, never the picture. The address shows in the place section of the details panel, and in the viewer's bar when the picture is linked to no location. It can arrive a while after the picture: Nominatim answers one question a second, and a lookup that fails is asked again later. Locations. When a picture gets a position, EiN links it to the location whose shape contains the point, the nearest one when several do. A shape is a circle or a polygon drawn for the location, or the circle a location gets from its address or from its pictures. A location that is only a point, because coordinates were typed or clicked when it was created, contains nothing, so no picture joins it by itself. When a location's shape changes, the library's pictures inside it are linked to it and those left outside are let go. The link gives the picture the location's name in the viewer and puts it on the location's Media tab. A link someone made by hand, or one brought in from an older archive, is never replaced. Locations and the map shows how to draw a location's shape. A track's route is drawn beside the pictures on the map and on an album's Map tab (see Trips ). EiN does not use it to give pictures a position.

Select the pictures in a grid: an album, the Media page, your favourites, a person's, location's or camera's Media tab, the pictures behind a pile on the map, or the Files tab in staging. Press Set location in the selection bar. It is offered only when you may change every selected picture. The dialog asks "Where was this taken?", or "Where were these taken?" for several. Choose the place in one of two ways: Under A known location ("Pick one, or click the map"), pick a location. The list holds the locations that have a place on the map, and picking one moves the point to it. Under On the map ("Click where it was taken, or type the coordinates."), click the map, or type Latitude and Longitude . Press Set location . EiN confirms with "Location set on N files". The hint at the foot of the dialog says what happens: "This replaces whatever position the files carry, for the map and for searching by location." Picking a known location gives the pictures that location's point. They are linked to the location, and show its name, when the point lies inside its circle or polygon.

p.h: Change or clear the place of one picture
p.x: Open the picture in the viewer and open the details panel. Click the cog at the top of the panel and choose Edit . The Edit file dialog opens, with Description and the labels on one side and the place on the other, starting at the picture's point. To move the point, pick under A known location , click the map under On the map , or type Latitude and Longitude . The hint reads "The new location replaces the position the file carries, for the map and for searching by location." To take the place away, press Clear location . The hint reads "The file will have no location, for the map or for searching by location." Press Save . The cog menu has Edit when you may change the picture. Clear location removes the point, whether the GPS or a person put it there, and the picture's link to a location, however it was made. EiN reads a file's GPS position when it takes the file in, so the picture stays without a place. To clear several pictures at once, use file-set-position with --clear in the terminal.

The terminal does the same work with commands, and some of it only there: Task Command Give pictures a date, as vague as it is file-set-time <file> <date> [<file> <date> …] [--note <text>] Take away a date set by hand file-set-time --clear <file>… List what is undated in the library search --undated Set the place of pictures file-set-position <file>… --lat=<n> --lng=<n> Clear the place of pictures file-set-position <file>… --clear Link a picture to a location by hand ln -s -f /archive/locations/<location> '<file>/location' Look up a picture's street address again, as an administrator geocode-position -f '<file>/position' Date a staging category's files again by its rules staging retime [<category>] Change a category's time rules staging category <name> --digitized on|off or --filename-dates on|off Write a negative coordinate with = , as in --lng=-5.066 : on its own, -5.066 would be read as an option. # in EiN's terminal, in the album's folder file-set-position P1000412.JPG P1000413.JPG --lat=50.153 --lng=-5.066 Set location 50.153,-5.066 on /archive/albums/Peggy's Falmouth/P1000412.JPG Set location 50.153,-5.066 on /archive/albums/Peggy's Falmouth/P1000413.JPG

A scan shows the day it was scanned. It did not arrive in a Scans category, and its scanner is not registered as one. Give it its date with Set time , which outranks the scanner's clock; move its folder into a Scans category while it is still in staging; or register the scanner with Scanner or digitizer . A picture has a date you did not expect. Look at Time source under Details . "from the file name" means its category reads dates from names; "from the camera clock" with a wrong year means the camera's clock was wrong. All pictures from one camera are some hours off. Set the camera's Timezone , or for a phone's videos turn on Video times in UTC , as described under Time zones . A clock that was simply wrong, by a day or some minutes, takes Clock is off by . Set time is not in the selection bar. You may not change every selected picture: select only pictures you may change, or ask whoever owns the others. Your favourites and the pictures behind a pile on the map do not offer Set time at all; select the pictures in their album instead. The times after the arrow in Set time are hours off before you change anything. The pictures were taken in another time zone than your browser's; see the warning under Set the time of several pictures at once . The street address still names the old street after you moved the point. EiN looks up an address once per picture and does not look again when the point moves. An administrator can look it up again in the terminal with geocode-position -f '<file>/position' . A picture is on the map but has no street address. The lookup has not run yet, or the machine EiN runs on cannot reach nominatim.openstreetmap.org . It is asked again later. The picture is not linked to the location you picked. That location is a single point, which contains nothing. Draw a circle or a polygon for it, as Locations and the map describes, and the pictures inside join it. The picture still names its old location after you moved it. Its link was made by hand, and EiN never replaces such a link. In Edit file , press Clear location and Save , then open Edit file again and set the point. file-set-time answers "not a capture time". Write the date as YYYY , YYYY-MM , YYYY-MM-DD , YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM or YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS , with a year from 1826 to next year.

An album gathers the photos, videos and recordings of one occasion: a summer, a trip, a birthday. This page is for everyone who browses and organises the family's pictures. It covers finding an album, making one, filling it, changing it, and acting on the pictures in it.

Choose Albums in the sidebar, under Browse . The page lists every album you may see, with their number under the title, for example 29 albums . Each card shows the album's cover, its name, its dates and how many items it holds. Each card shows: the album's cover, with the number of items it holds in the corner; its name; its dates, from the first picture to the last, or the span someone set (see Change an album's name, description and dates ); its labels, if it has any. Rest the pointer on a card to read the album's description. A card with a photo icon instead of a picture belongs to an album with nothing to show yet, such as one that holds only documents. To narrow the list, type in Filter albums… . It matches the album's name as you type. Case and accents do not matter, and every word must appear, in any order: wellington christmas finds "Christmas in Wellington". The × in the box clears it. When nothing matches, the page says No albums found matching "<what you typed>" . Sort orders the cards. EiN remembers your choice in this browser. Choice Order Newest first (the default) The albums with the latest dates first Oldest first The albums with the earliest dates first Name (A-Z) Alphabetical by name Most items The albums holding the most pictures first Sorted by date, the page has a rail at its right edge, Scroll through time , that marks the years with albums; drag along it to jump through them. The list holds the albums people made. The albums that staging suggests for your uploads stay in your staging area until you file them, so they are not here. On an archive with no albums yet, the page says No albums yet and, if you are signed in, offers New album .

Random album , the button with two crossing arrows beside the search box in the top bar, opens an album picked at random. Alt + R does the same from anywhere, on a Mac from anywhere outside a text field. It picks among the albums people made that you may open, never a staging suggestion. To find one particular album, start typing its name in the search box at the top ( Ctrl + K , or ⌘ + K on a Mac). Search and the finder covers that, and the Search page, which also finds albums by what their pictures show.

You need to be signed in. Choose Create , the plus in the top bar, then Album . On an empty Albums page, New album does the same. Create Album opens. In Name , type what the album is called, for example Sailing in the archipelago . If you like, write a Description . It takes Markdown, so you can use headings, lists and links. Choose Create . EiN makes the album and opens it, empty. Add pictures to it as Add pictures to an album describes. The name is also the album's folder in the tree, /archive/albums/<name> , so two albums cannot share a name. If one is taken, the dialog shows an error in red and makes nothing. You can also make an album while adding pictures to it: in Add to an album , type a name no album has and choose New album “ ” . And when you sort your uploads in staging, filing a group into an album of its own makes one. An album you create starts out shared the way your albums are by default. An administrator sets that for everyone, and you can change it for yourself with How widely what you create is shared under Profile → Preferences . Sharing explains both, and how to share one album differently with Share .

An album opens on its pictures, one section for each day they were taken. The header holds, from the top: links to the previous and next album, when the album is part of a series; the album's dates; its name, over its cover; its description; a chip that says how widely it is shared (visitors do not see it; Sharing explains the colours); its labels. Choosing one searches for everything that carries it. If you may change the album, the header also has Upload , Share and Edit , and under ⋮ the items Add event and Move to trash , and Hide RAW files while the album has camera RAW files that a picture of the same name can take ( Hide RAW files ). On a phone they are all under ⋮ . If you may only look at the album, none of them is there. With the default sharing, everyone with an account sees every album and only its owner changes it, so on someone else's album you usually have none of these buttons. Below the header are three tabs: Media , where the album opens, Map and Info . An album made of a trip has a fourth, Trip , after Media . The tab you choose goes into the page's address ( ?tab=map , ?tab=info , ?tab=trip ), so a link can open the album on it.

Show narrows the grid to one kind: All , Images , Video , Audio or Documents . It offers only the kinds the album holds, and is not there at all when the album holds one kind. Sort puts the pictures Oldest first (the default) or Newest first . EiN remembers the choice in this browser, for every album. Folders inside the album come first, as square cards (see Folders inside an album ). The pictures follow in sections, one for each day they were taken. The heading of a day gives its date and how many pictures it has. An album with pictures from more than 240 different days is shown by month instead, and one with more than 240 months by year. Pictures with no date at all are gathered under Undated . What the tiles show: a video or a recording shows its length; a video plays a short silent preview when the pointer rests on it, or on a touch screen when it scrolls into view; a stack of similar photos shows how many it holds (see Stacks of similar photos ); a heart marks a picture in your favourites; a lock marks a picture that keeps its own sharing; you see it if you may change the album. Notes added with Add event appear among the days (see Add a note to a day ). Once the album holds more than 120 pictures and notes, a Scroll through time rail at the right lets you jump through its days. Choose a picture to open it in the viewer. The viewer walks the album in the order the grid shows, and after the last picture it goes on to the first. Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers it.

An album made of a trip has a Trip tab (see Make a trip an album ). At the top are the trip's dates, an Ongoing badge while it lasts, the device's track, which links to its device's Trips tab, how many days it took and its length, in nautical miles for a boat and kilometres for anything else. Under them is where it started and ended, and the farthest place it stayed at, and the weather over the whole trip. Each day of the trip has a card of its own: the date, the first and last time in the track's time zone (UTC for a track without a Timezone ), the day's length, where it started and where it ended, and the day's weather. The album's notes from that day stand under it, as on the Media tab: this is the trip's logbook. Add note on a day's card writes a note dated on that day, as Add event does; the pen on a note changes it. Under the days, Stays lists the places the trip stayed at, when it arrived and when it left. A place that is a location links to it. The weather is there unless an administrator has turned off Look up the weather (see The weather at a place and time ). It is the weather where the track was at each whole hour of the day: the mean wind in metres per second, the strongest hour's when it was stronger, and where the wind mostly blew from; the coldest and the warmest hour; and the mean cloud cover. For example Wind 5.5 m/s, at most 9, from SW · 14 to 19 °C · 40 % cloud . While the trip is ongoing, the tab follows it as the track's points come in.

The Map tab puts the album's pictures where they were taken, with the routes recorded while it lasted. The Map tab shows the album's pictures that have a position, and the routes the album's devices recorded during its dates. The map opens fitted to both, and fills the window below the tabs: opening the tab shrinks the album's header down to its row of tabs, and the map grows upward into the room without moving, so the mouse wheel over the map zooms it rather than scrolling the page. Scroll up over the tabs to bring the header back. The album's devices are those the cameras that took its pictures are part of, such as a phone, and any device added to it, such as a GPS tracker carried on the trip; a route someone else recorded on the same days stays off the map (see Choose which devices the map shows ). A picture on its own is drawn as its thumbnail; choose it to open it in the viewer. Pictures close together form a pile with a count. Choose it to list them in N photos here . Choosing never zooms. Zoom with the mouse wheel or a pinch; the map has no zoom buttons. The layers button in the corner switches between Map , Dark map and Satellite . The routes come from the album's whole span, so widening its dates in Edit album brings in the journey there and back. When nothing has a position and none of its devices recorded a route, the tab says so and names the devices, for example Nothing in this album has a position, and Ruby's phone recorded no route while it was taken. An album with no devices at all says Nothing in this album has a position, and it has no devices whose routes to show. Dates and places of pictures shows how to give pictures a place, and Trips how a route gets in.

The Info tab sums up who and what is in the album, each with a link. Section What it shows Album Name , When (its dates), Holds (for example "31 photos · 6 videos") and On the map : All of them , or how many of how many About The description Comments What people wrote about the album, as in the viewer ( The details panel ): everyone who sees the album reads them, and if you may change it you write one and delete your own People The people in its pictures, most often first Places The locations its pictures are linked to Cameras The cameras that took its pictures, most pictures first Devices The devices whose tracks the Map tab draws: those the cameras of its pictures are part of, then those added to the album Photographers The people who took them Labels The labels its pictures carry, with how many carry each Each name opens its page. In People , Places and Cameras , the number beside a name searches the album for the pictures that have it. In Devices , the number is how many of the pictures the device's cameras took, and a device added to the album says added instead. In Labels , a label searches the album for that label. People , Places , Cameras and Photographers show their first 10, then Show all N and Show fewer ; Devices and Labels show them all. When nobody is tagged and nothing is linked to a location or a camera, the tab says so. Comments is there when the album has some, or when you may change it.

p.h: Choose which devices the map shows
p.x: An album's devices start as those the cameras that took its pictures are part of, such as a phone (see A phone that records where it was ). A camera whose pictures join later, say from an import, brings its device onto the list as soon as they are in the album, and a route the device records later shows on the map. You can add a device no camera of the album is part of, such as a GPS tracker, and take off one whose route does not belong. You can do this if you may change the album. Open the album and choose the Info tab. In Devices : to add one, choose it in Add a device to the map , which lists the devices that keep a track; to take one off, choose × beside it ( Take off the map ). With no device, the section says "No devices: the map shows no routes." A device that a camera of the album's pictures is part of and that was taken off is listed under Taken off the map , and stays off when more of that camera's pictures join the album. Choose + beside it ( Put back on the map ) to put it back. Only the map is changed: the pictures stay in the album, linked to their camera.
There are two ways: upload files from your computer or phone straight into the album, or add pictures that are already in EiN.

You can do this if you may change the album. Open the album. Choose Upload and pick the files. Or drag files from your computer and drop them anywhere on the page: while you drag, the page says Drop files to upload and, under it, Into and the album's name. Follow the upload under the Uploads button, which appears in the top bar as soon as you drop or pick the files; while a large drop is still being read, it says "Reading the dropped files…". It shows each upload's progress, with Cancel while files are going up, Retry failed when some failed, and Clear . The files go straight into the album; they skip staging . They are shared as the album is: whoever can see the album can see them. A file whose name the album already has is stored under a numbered name beside it; nothing is replaced. Upload takes files, not folders, and the files of a folder you drop go into the album without their folder. On a phone, the picker offers your photo library and camera beside your files. When the upload ends, the album shows the files. Each one shows a placeholder until EiN has made its thumbnail, and goes to its day once its date has been read, which can take a few minutes after a large upload. Getting your photos in explains what happens to each file and why it takes a while. Tip For a card full of pictures you have not sorted, use Create → Import media instead. Those files wait in your private staging area, where EiN suggests albums for them and nobody else sees them until you file them. Getting your photos in compares the ways in. A suggested album from staging takes no uploads.

p.h: Add pictures that are already in EiN
p.x: Select the pictures, in any grid: an album, the Media page, a person's page, a search. Select pictures shows how. Choose Add to album in the selection bar. In the viewer, the same is in the cog menu. Add to an album opens. In Find an album, or name a new one , type part of the album's name, then choose it from the list. The list holds the albums you may change. An album whose whole name you type but cannot change is listed greyed out, marked View only . To put the pictures in an album that does not exist yet, type its name and choose New album “ ” . EiN says what it did, for example 12 added to Christmas in Wellington , adding 3 already there when some were in it before, and offers Undo . The pictures are not copied. Each stays where it lives, and the album gets a link to it, so one picture can be in several albums at once. A date, a place, a name on a face or a label given to it shows in every album it is in. The one exception is a file from your staging area: it moves into the album, and the message adds N moved out of staging .

p.h: Change an album's name, description and dates
p.x: Choose Edit in the album's header. Edit album opens. Field What it does Name What the album is called everywhere. Required. Description Text about the album, in Markdown. It shows under the title and on the Info tab. Labels The album's own labels. Pick one in use or type one; a space starts the next label. Starts and Ends The album's span, as YYYY-MM-DD . See below. Previous album and Next album Its neighbours in a series. Type part of an album's name to find one, or clear the field for none. Choose Save . EiN says Album saved . Renaming changes the name on every page. The album's folder in the tree keeps its first name, so links to the album, and to the pictures in it, keep working. The span. An album's dates are those of its first and last picture. Starts and Ends let you reach out past them, to cover the journey there and back: the dates show on the card and over the title, the Albums page sorts by them, and the Map tab draws the routes recorded within them. You cannot move them inside the pictures: Starts stops at the first picture's day and Ends at the last one's. The line under the fields says what the pictures span, for example "The media run from 2025-08-04 to 2025-08-10. Reach out past them to cover the journey there and back." To let the span follow the pictures again, clear the field or set it back to the pictures' own day. An album whose pictures have no dates has only the span you set; the line then reads "Nothing in the album is dated yet; the span is what you set here." An album made of a trip spans the trip too, from its first point to its last, so it has dates before it has any pictures. A series. Albums of one summer after another, or the parts of a long journey, can lead from one to the next. Pick the album before this one in Previous album , or the one after it in Next album ; the album you pick links back to this one by itself. The header then shows a small pill for each neighbour, with an arrow, its cover and its name, above the dates. Rest the pointer on it to see a larger cover, and choose it to go there.

The cover is the picture on the album's card and behind its title. Open the album and select one picture. It can be one that lives in the album or one added to it from elsewhere. Choose Set as cover in the selection bar. The header changes to the picture at once. Set as cover is in the bar only if you may change the album, and it works with exactly one picture selected; with more it is greyed out. A person's page has the same button for the person's picture. An album without a cover of its own is given one by EiN: one of its own pictures, picked at random, a photo before a video or a recording. A cover you choose is never replaced. If the cover picture is deleted, the album shows another of its pictures in its place.

When someone takes several shots of the same moment, EiN folds them into a stack in the album: one tile, the stack's front photo, with a count in its corner. The other photos are still in the album; the stack only hides them from the grid. No file moves. Photos are stacked when they follow one another, look alike, and were taken at most 10 seconds apart. An administrator can change both limits under Settings → System , in the Albums group: Stack similarity ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_THRESHOLD , 0.75) and Stack time gap (seconds) ( CFG_ALBUM_STACK_MAX_GAP_SECONDS , 10). A stack belongs to one album. The same photos can be a stack in one album and separate in another. To look through a stack, open its tile. The details panel of the viewer has a section headed with the count, for example 5 stacked photos , and a thumbnail of each photo, the front marked Front . Choose a thumbnail to see that photo. If you may change the album and every photo in the stack, the section has these buttons: Button What it does Make front Makes the photo you are looking at the one the grid shows. Keep separate Takes this photo out of stacks in this album. The section then reads Kept separate . Allow stacking On a photo kept separate: lets it be stacked again. To stack photos yourself, select two or more in the album and choose Stack in the selection bar. If one of them is already in a stack, the others join it and its front stays the front. Selecting a stack's tile selects its front photo only, so Download , Delete and the other actions of the bar act on that one photo.

An album can hold folders, for example one for each day of a long trip. They show as square cards above the pictures, with the folder's name and how many entries it holds. If you may change the album, a lock on a card marks a folder that keeps its own sharing. Choose a card to open the folder. It opens like an album page of its own, with the same tabs. The album's grid shows only the pictures at the album's own level: open a folder to see what is in it. An album that holds only folders says No media here — open a folder above. The Web UI shows folders but has no button that makes one. They come from an import, from copying folders over SFTP , or from mkdir in the terminal . Once a folder is there, open it and choose Upload to upload into it, or move pictures into it with mv in the terminal: Move to album moves pictures into an album itself, not into one of its folders. The selection bar's Stack , Set as cover and Share are offered in the album itself, not in its folders.

p.h: Add a note to a day
p.x: A note tells what happened on a day of the album: who arrived, where you sailed, why it rained. In the album's header, choose ⋮ , then Add event . Add event opens. Date is filled in with the first day of the album's pictures that has no note yet; change it as you like, as YYYY-MM-DD . Write the note in Description . Written by is you, when your account is linked to a person; choose someone else if they wrote it. Choose Add event . The note appears among the pictures, at its day, signed with the writer's name. If you may change it, a pencil on the note ( Edit event ) opens it again, with Delete to send it to the trash; EiN says Event moved to the trash and offers Undo .

You select pictures to act on several at once: download them, add them to another album or move them there, give them a date or a place, delete them. Choosing a day's heading selects all of that day; the bar at the foot acts on the selection. To Do this Select one picture Point at it and tick the checkbox in its corner. On a touch screen, press and hold it; the phone gives a short buzz. Add or take away one picture Ctrl +click it ( ⌘ +click on a Mac). Once anything is selected, a plain click or tap does the same. Select a run Shift +click: everything from the last picture you picked to this one, across days too. Select a whole day Choose the date in the day's heading. Its count then reads, for example, 24 / 24 . Choose it again to deselect the day. Select everything Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac). Clear the selection Esc , or the × at the right end of the selection bar. While anything is selected, every picture shows its checkbox, and a plain click selects instead of opening. Ctrl + A takes the pictures the page has loaded; in a long album, scroll to its end first to take them all. With the viewer open, Esc closes the viewer and leaves the selection alone. A picture that has the keyboard's focus opens with Enter or Space . ? lists these keys with the others; see Keyboard shortcuts .

As soon as one picture is selected, a bar floats at the foot of the page with the count, for example 24 selected , and buttons for what you can do. On a narrow screen, or when there are more buttons than the window has room for, they fold into one Actions menu. Which buttons you see depends on the page and on what you may change. On an album page, in order: Button What it does Shown Favourite / Unfavourite Adds the pictures to your favourites, or takes them out when every one is there already. EiN says, for example, 12 files added to favourites , with Undo . Your profile, favourites and trash has the Favourites page. When you are signed in Download Saves the original files: one file as itself, several as one zip named after the album. Always Add to album Adds the pictures to another album, as above . When you are signed in Move to album Moves the pictures out of this album into another one, as below . On an album you may change Set time Gives the pictures a date and time. Dates and places of pictures covers the dialog. When you may change every selected picture Stack Stacks the pictures, as above . Needs two or more. On an album you may change Set as cover Makes the picture the album's cover. Needs exactly one. On an album you may change Share Shares the pictures Like the album , or gives them Their own sharing , for example to keep a few private in a shared album. Sharing covers the dialog. Greyed out when the selection holds a picture only added here from elsewhere: that picture has the sharing of the place it lives. On an album you may change Set location Says where the pictures were taken. Dates and places of pictures covers it. When you may change every selected picture Label Adds labels to the pictures, in Add labels . Media, Year and labels covers labels. When you may change every selected picture Delete (red) or Remove (orange) Takes the pictures out of this album, as the next section explains. When you may change every selected picture that lives in the album Other pages have most of the same buttons. Stack , Set as cover and Share are the album's own; a person's page has Set as cover too.

A picture in an album either lives there, because it was uploaded or filed into that album, or it was added to the album from elsewhere, and only a link to it is there. The last button of the selection bar treats the two differently: Delete sends a picture that lives in the album to your trash. It leaves every other album it was added to as well, and comes back to all of them if you restore it. Remove takes a picture that was only added to the album out of it. The picture stays where it lives, and in any other album it is in. One picture, many places: Delete acts on the picture itself, Remove only on this album's link to it. The tiles look alike either way; the button tells you which you have. It reads Remove , in orange, when every selected picture was only added here. When any of them lives here it reads Delete , in red: the pictures that live here go to the trash, and the ones only added here are taken out of the album. Neither asks first. EiN says what it did, for example 3 moved to the trash, 2 taken out of this album , and offers Undo , which brings back the deleted pictures and puts the links back. Deleted pictures wait in your trash, under your picture in the top bar → Trash , for 30 days by default ( CFG_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS ); after that they are gone for good. Your profile, favourites and trash covers the Trash page, and Links what deleting and the trash do to links. When you delete a picture, what EiN worked out about it, such as faces and a transcript, goes with it, and comes back with it if you restore it.

Select the pictures in the album, or in one of its folders. Choose Move to album in the selection bar. Move to an album opens. Before you type, it lists the albums you moved or sorted pictures into lately; choose one, or press its number. Otherwise type part of an album's name in Find an album, or name a new one and choose it from the list, or type a name that is not taken and choose New album “ ” to make that album. The pictures leave this album and go into the other album itself, not into one of its folders. EiN says, for example, 12 moved to Erik's archipelago , and offers Undo , which moves them back. Every link to a moved picture keeps working: in other albums it was added to, as an album's cover, as a favourite. A picture that was only added to this album from elsewhere is not moved: it stays where it lives, and is added to the other album instead of this one. A picture the other album already has is taken out of this one, and not added twice. When the other album only had it added, the picture now lives there instead. A picture whose name is taken in the other album gets a number after its name, as IMG_0412 (2).jpg . A picture you may not move stays, and the message says why, for example 2 could not be moved: … . Move to album is offered on an album you may change, not on a suggested album from staging, whose pictures you file in the Sort stream . The album you move the pictures to must be one you may change as well. A moved picture keeps the sharing it had. To give it the sharing of the album it moved into, select it there, choose Share , then Like the album and Save . In the terminal , album move does the same: # in EiN's terminal album move "/archive/albums/Erik's archipelago" "/archive/albums/Sailing in the archipelago/IMG_0412.jpg"
