What you did How to undo it Favourite or Unfavourite Undo in EiN's message, or the other button Add to album Undo in EiN's message takes the pictures out again, and files from staging go back to it. An album made in the same step may stay behind, empty; move it to the trash if you do not want it. Move to album Undo in EiN's message moves the pictures back. An album made in the same step stays behind, empty; move it to the trash if you do not want it. Delete or Remove Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page for what was deleted Move to trash on an album Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page Delete on a note Undo in EiN's message, or Restore on the Trash page Edit album No undo: open Edit and change it back Set as cover Choose another picture as the cover Stack Keep separate on each photo, in the viewer's details Hide RAW files No undo; each RAW file can still be downloaded from Versions in the viewer's details

A camera that saves each shot twice, as a RAW file and a JPEG of the same name ( IMG_1234.CR2 and IMG_1234.JPG ), puts two pictures in the album for each shot. EiN files such a RAW under its JPEG by itself two minutes after it is uploaded ( Camera RAW ). One it did not file, because its JPEG came later or it was there before EiN did this, is filed from the album's menu. In the album's header, choose ⋮ , then Hide RAW files . The number after it says how many RAW files have a picture of the same name. The item is there only while there are some, and only if you may change the album. EiN says, for example, 12 RAW files filed under their pictures . If some stay, because no picture has their name, or two do, it adds how many. A RAW file filed under its picture: leaves the album, search and the timeline; the picture stands for the shot; is listed under Versions in the viewer's details panel , where its name downloads it; loses the faces found on it, since the picture has the same ones. A person who was only in those faces, and has no name, goes with them.

p.h: Move an album to the trash
p.x: In the album's header, choose ⋮ , then Move to trash . Nothing asks first. EiN takes you back to the Albums page and says, for example, Sailing in the archipelago moved to the trash , with Undo , which puts the album back and returns you to it. The album waits in your trash with everything that lives in it, and you can restore it from the Trash page for as long as the trash keeps it. The pictures that live in the album leave every other album they were added to, until you restore it. The pictures that were only added to it stay where they live.

When you upload into your staging area, EiN groups the files and suggests albums for them. Those live in your staging area, only you see them, and you decide them on the Staging page. You can open one as an album page ( Open as an album page in staging). It then shows why its pictures were grouped, with Sort in Staging to go back to it, a match percentage, and under ⋮ the choice Keep album as is or Let the organizer manage album . It has no Upload and no Move to trash , and Edit changes only its name and labels. Sorting in staging covers all of it.

What you see Why What to do No Upload , Share or Edit on an album You may look at the album but not change it. Ask its owner, or an administrator, to share it with you so that you can edit it. See Sharing . A placeholder where a picture should be, after an upload Its thumbnail is not made yet. The media service makes it, after the pictures uploaded before it. Wait. Getting your photos in explains why it takes time. Uploaded pictures are not on their day yet Their dates have not been read yet. Reload the page a little later. An album has no dates on its card None of its pictures has a date, no span is set, and it is not a trip's. Set Starts and Ends in Edit album , or give the pictures a time with Set time . Share in the selection bar is greyed out The selection holds a picture that was only added to this album; it has the sharing of the place it lives. Select only pictures that live here. Share the others where they live. Set as cover is greyed out It needs exactly one picture selected. Select one. Stack is greyed out It needs two or more. Select more. The last button reads Remove , not Delete Every selected picture was only added to this album. Remove takes them out of this album only. To delete a picture, go to the album where it lives. A picture is gone from an album nobody changed Someone deleted it where it lives, or moved that album to the trash. It comes back to every album when it is restored from the trash of whoever deleted it. Nothing in this album has a position, and … recorded no route while it was taken. on the Map tab No picture has a place, and none of the album's devices recorded a route within its dates. Give pictures a place with Set location ( Dates and places of pictures ), widen the album's dates, or add the device that recorded the route ( Choose which devices the map shows ). A route recorded on the trip is not on the Map tab No camera of the album's pictures is part of its device, or the device was taken off the map. Add the device in the Info tab's Devices ( Choose which devices the map shows ), or link the phone's camera to its device ( A phone that records where it was ). This album holds more than 20,000 entries; 20,000 of them are shown. An album page shows at most 20,000 pictures. Split it into folders or several albums, or search inside it. album: Node already exists in parent … with name: … when you create an album An album or folder of that name is already in /archive/albums . Choose another name.

Everything on this page is a command underneath, and the terminal runs the same commands. A few of them: # in EiN's terminal album create "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" --description "Christmas with Helen and the children" album add "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" "/archive/albums/Ruby's Wellington/IMG_2231.jpg" album set "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" spanStart 2025-12-18 album set "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" next "/archive/albums/Ruby's Wellington" album-stack refresh "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" --dry-run -v album-device-list "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" album-device-add "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" gps-tracker album-device-rm "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington" ruby-phone album-random An album's path is its folder, /archive/albums/ and the name it was created with; renaming it does not change the path. A device is its name, its path under /dev , or a track of it. album , album-stack , album-device-list , album-device-add , album-device-rm and album-random have every option in the archive's commands .

Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer an album's pictures open in. Sharing : who sees an album, share links, and keeping some pictures private. Getting your photos in : every way files get in, and what happens to them. Sorting in staging : your private inbox and the albums it suggests. Dates and places of pictures : Set time and Set location . Links : how one picture can be in several albums. Album folders : with that module, the albums as folders of files on the machine EiN runs on.

The viewer shows one photo, video, recording or document at a time, large, with what EiN knows about it beside it. This page is for everyone who looks at pictures in EiN, on a computer or on a phone: how to open the viewer and move through files, what the details panel tells you, and how to work with faces, text in pictures, playback, transcripts, documents and slideshows.

Click any picture in a grid: an album, the Media page, a person's Media tab, your Favourites , a search result. The picture grows out of its tile and fills the screen over the page. With the keyboard, move to a tile with Tab and press Enter or Space . While you are selecting pictures, a click ticks a tile instead of opening it; Albums explains selecting. The viewer walks the list you opened it from, in that list's order. A search hit on something said in a video or a recording opens it at the moment the words are spoken; see Search and the finder . Each file in the viewer has its own address: the page's address with the file added in its fullscreen parameter ( …?fullscreen=%2Fmedia%2F… ), or, opened on its own, /media/ followed by the file's path. You can copy it from the browser's address bar and send it to someone who may see the file. Stepping to another file replaces the address once you stop on it, instead of adding to the browser's history, so one press of the browser's Back button closes the viewer and returns you to the page underneath.

The viewer on a computer. The bar under the picture gives the position in the list, the date and the place; the details panel beside it says who took it, who is in it and how old they were that day. On a computer: Top left : the close button (×). Top right : the details button (ⓘ, tooltip Details (i) ), which shows or hides the details panel , and beside it Chat , where the assistant module is installed, which opens the assistant in a drawer beside the picture, or as a dialog over it in a window narrower than 992 pixels. You can ask it about the picture you are looking at; see Chatting with the assistant . Left and right edges : arrows to the previous and the next file. The bar under the picture , from left to right: where you are in the list, such as 24 of 26 . The Media page leaves this out, because it loads its feed a part at a time and does not know the whole count; the date and time the picture was taken, such as Saturday, 27 December 2025, 13:16:18 ; the place: the name of the location the picture is linked to, or else the street address read from its GPS position; the heart, Favourite (s) , when you are signed in; Start slideshow ; More (⋮).

The date is shown as precisely as it is known, and no more. A picture known only to the year shows 1975 , one known to the month shows March 2004 , and neither is given an invented day or hour. A date known only approximately shows a tilde, ~1985 . Point at the date to see where it came from: from the camera clock , from GPS , entered by hand , from Google Photos or a sidecar or from the file name . A scan adds a scan: its scanner’s clocks are not when it was taken . A picture taken in another time zone is shown at the time on the photographer's clock, and the tooltip adds the same moment in your own time, such as 27 Dec 2025, 01:16 your time . Dates and places of pictures explains which date a picture gets and how to change it.

More (⋮) at the right end of the bar holds what you do to the view rather than to the file: Row What it does Pin faces / Unpin faces ( f ) Shows every face box with its name, or hides them again. It reads No faces , greyed out, when none were found. For photos and videos. Show text / Hide text ( t ) Lays the text read from the photo over it. Shown only when text was read. Edit text / Add text Opens the text for writing by hand. Shown on photos you may change. Fullscreen / Exit fullscreen Gives the viewer the whole screen. Download Saves the original file to your device. The file name at the top of the details panel downloads the original too. To download several files at once, select them in the grid and use Download in the selection bar.

p.h: Move between files and close the viewer
p.x: Next file : → , the arrow at the right edge, or swipe left on a touch screen. Previous file : ← , the arrow at the left edge, or swipe right. The list goes round: after the last file comes the first again, and before the first comes the last. While the next picture slides in, the position, the date and the place turn to it once it covers more than half the screen. A swipe you take back before letting go turns them back. To close the viewer, press × at the top left, press Esc , use the browser's Back button, or on a phone swipe down on the picture. The picture shrinks back into its tile, so you see where you were in the grid. Esc first closes whatever lies over the picture: the enlarged map, the text dialog or Edit faces . During a slideshow it stops the slideshow. Only then does it close the viewer.

Photos and videos zoom; recordings do not, and nothing zooms during a slideshow. To With a mouse and keyboard On a touch screen Zoom in or out at a spot Turn the mouse wheel over the spot Pinch Zoom in on a spot, or back out Double-click a photo Double-tap Zoom in a step + or = Zoom out a step - Fit the whole picture again 0 Double-tap Look around a zoomed picture Drag it Drag with one finger Each file opens fitted to the screen. On a touch screen, swiping to the next file waits until the picture is back at its fitted size; until then a one-finger drag moves around the picture. Over text laid on the picture, the mouse wheel scrolls the text; hold Ctrl to zoom instead.

Key What it does ← / → Previous / next file i Show or hide the details f Show or hide the faces t Show or hide the text in the picture s Favourite or unfavourite + or = Zoom in - Zoom out 0 Fit the picture Esc Close: first a layer over the picture or a slideshow, then the viewer Videos and recordings have keys of their own; see Play a video . Press ? to see the shortcuts that work where you are, and see Keyboard shortcuts for every key in EiN.

The viewer takes its phone layout on any touch screen, and in any browser window 768 pixels wide or narrower. On a phone the details are a sheet you pull up from under the picture with a swipe. The date sits in a dark pill centred over the top of the picture, with the time beneath it. The bar under the picture keeps only the position in the list and the place. ⋮ in the top right corner holds Favourite , Start slideshow , the rows of the More menu and Chat . The details panel is closed when the viewer opens. Held upright, swipe up on the picture to pull up the details sheet over the bottom half, and swipe down on it to put it away. Held sideways, the details open as a panel on the right: press Show details beside ⋮, or swipe up, and swipe the panel to the right to close it. Edit faces is not offered on a phone held upright. Gesture What it does Swipe left / right Next / previous file Swipe up Open the details Swipe down Close the details; with the details closed, close the viewer Pinch, or double-tap Zoom a photo Drag with one finger on a zoomed photo Look around it Tap a pinned face Open the person's page, or name an unnamed person A swipe that starts at the very edge of the screen is left to the phone itself, so its own Back gesture closes the viewer. Turning the phone sideways makes the viewer fullscreen, and turning it upright again leaves fullscreen. An iPhone has no fullscreen for web pages, so there the viewer stays as it is. EiN on a phone covers the rest of the interface on a small screen.

On a computer the details panel opens on the right each time you open the viewer. Press the details button (ⓘ) or i to close it while you look; it stays closed until you close the viewer. On a phone you pull it up, as described above. Each part of the panel is a row with an icon at its left. A row appears only when it has something to show. Click a row's icon to fold the row to a single line with its name, and how many it holds when it is a list, such as People · 3 ; click the icon or the line to unfold it. Which rows are folded is remembered in this browser, for the next picture and the next visit. From the top: Row What it shows The file The file name, which downloads the original, and its size. Under it a line of facts: 3200 × 2400 · 7.7 MP · ISO 100 · 1/250 s ; a video adds its length and frame rate, and a recording its length, kbps, kHz and mono or stereo ; a document shows its first page's size in millimetres, such as 210 × 297 mm . Then the sharing chip, which says who can see the file ( Sharing ), and the file's labels; a label opens a search for it ( Media, Year and labels ). The cog at the right opens the cog menu . Description What someone wrote about the file. Copies in staging Only for a file of yours still in your staging area: its exact copies and look-alikes. See Duplicates . Transcript For videos and recordings with speech: what is said, line by line. See Read along with a transcript . Camera The camera that took it, linking to its page; Owned by whoever owned it then, with the years; Shot by the photographer, when someone has said who. Without a registered camera, the make and model the file names. See Cameras . Albums Every album the file is in, with its cover. A file can be in several albums without being copied. People Everyone recognised or tagged in the picture, with their age that day. See People in the picture . Place The location the file is linked to, as a link, the street address, and a small map. Enlarge map opens a large map of the spot. Weather For a file with a place and a date: the weather that hour, such as 14.5 °C · Wind 4 m/s, from SW · 40 % cloud , and under it where that came from, an SMHI station or Open-Meteo. See The weather at a place and time . Stack For a photo stacked with others in this album: N stacked photos , or Kept separate , with a thumbnail of each and Front on the one the album shows. Click a thumbnail to see it in the viewer. Make front , Keep separate and Allow stacking are there when you may change the album and every photo in the stack. See Albums . Versions For a file with other versions, such as the camera RAW of a JPEG or a restored copy: each one's name, which downloads it, with its kind of file and size; a restored copy also what was done to it, Compare , and Show this copy or, for the one shown, Show the original . See Camera RAW and Restore a faded or damaged photo . Similar Up to 12 pictures that look most like this one, nearest first, leaving out the picture itself and the rest of its stack. Click one to walk these pictures in the viewer. Show all opens the Media page with every picture like it. Not shown for recordings. Comments Comments on the file, with who wrote them and when: the full name set on their account (its username when it has none), beside the picture of the person the account is linked to ( Your picture and the person you are ). Everyone who can see the file reads them. If you may change the file, write one in Add a comment… , which grows as you add lines, and press the send button inside it ( Comment ) or Enter ; Shift + Enter starts a new line. The bin beside a comment of your own ( Delete comment ) asks Delete comment? and removes it when you press Delete . Details The machine-written facts, folded until you open it. See The Details section . EXIF Every tag the file carries, one per row, or No EXIF recorded . Folded until you open it.

Each person has a badge with their age on the day the picture was taken: 69 years , or 8 months for a child under one. A ~ in front, as in ~44 years , marks an age that is approximate because only the year or month of the person's birth is known, or only about when they were born. There is no age when the picture has no date, or the person has no birth date or one only before or after a year. Pointing at a name lights up that person's face box on the picture, and pointing at a box lights up the name. Click a name to open the person's page. Point at a name for a moment and a card opens above it. It shows the person's picture, larger, with their full name, the years of their life, where they live now and the start of their description, as on their page; for a face nobody has named yet, the face itself. Under that is what you can do with the face: Show at 0:42 on a video (see Faces in a video ), and Not sure this is them? when you may change the picture. Moving the pointer onto the card keeps it open; moving away closes it. On a phone there is nothing to point with, so the actions are small buttons at the end of the row instead. If you are not sure a face really is the person named, press Not sure this is them? (the question mark on a phone). The card asks Not sure this is <name>? , still under their picture to compare with, and you either: say who it is: pick someone, or type a name and choose New person: <name> , and press Move ; or press Mark as doubtful to leave it to somebody who knows. The face stays the person's, marked as doubtful until somebody answers, here or on the person's Faces tab (see Doubtful faces ). press Make unknown when it was named by mistake and you do not know who it is. The face leaves the person and is listed again as a face nobody has named yet, such as Unknown 8F3C81 , to be named later. A doubtful face always has an orange question mark at the end of its row. Press it, or point at the name and press Is this them? in the card. It asks Is this <name>? and shows who marked the face, such as "peggy is not sure.": Yes : it is them. The face stays theirs, as a person's decision, and the doubt goes. No, it is… : pick who it is instead, or a new name, as above, and press Move . Withdraw : takes your doubt back without answering it. Make unknown : it is not them, and you do not know who it is either; as above. Readers who may not change the picture see the orange question mark and who marked the face, but cannot answer. Faces that recognition has grouped as one person but nobody has named yet are listed with a crop of the face and a placeholder name, such as Unknown 8F3C81 . Click one to open the review over the viewer, where you name them or say they are someone you already have. People and faces describes the review and how recognition works. A scanned print. The camera row names the scanner it was digitized on, and the two faces nobody has named yet wait under placeholder names; clicking one opens the review where you say who it is.

Details , near the bottom of the panel, holds the facts a reader seldom needs. It is folded until you click its icon, and then stays open for the next picture and the next visit, like any row. Row What it shows Path Where the file is in EiN's tree, such as /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg . Click it to open a terminal tab at the file ( The terminal ). Visitors who are not signed in see the path as text. Text in image The text read from the picture. Text language The language the text was read in, and how sure the reading was. If you may change the file, a menu to choose another; see Read the text in a picture . Type The kind of file, such as image/heic . Taken at The capture time exactly as stored, such as 2025-12-27T13:16:18+13:00 . Taken at (UTC) The same moment in UTC. Time source Where the date came from, in words, and any note left with it. Damage For a scan, what EiN found it has: faded colours, dust, scratches, out of focus, camera shake, or none. See Find the scans worth restoring . Restoring A restoration asked for many photos at once that has not been made yet, or why it could not be. See Restore many photos at once . Created , Modified The file's created and modified times. Hashes Fingerprints of the file's bytes, such as sha256 .

p.h: Change a file from the cog menu
p.x: The cog at the top right of the details panel ( Edit media ) opens a menu. It is there when you may change the file, and for any signed-in reader for Add to album . Row Who sees it What it does Edit Readers who may change the file Opens Edit file : description, labels and location. See below. Share Readers who may change the file Opens the Share dialog for this file. See Sharing . Add to album Signed-in readers Opens Add to an album . Type part of an album's name to find it, or a name that is not taken to make an album by that name. The file is linked into the album, not copied; a file from your staging area moves into it instead. A message such as 1 added to Christmas in Wellington offers Undo . Edit faces Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos, not on a phone held upright Draw, move or remove face boxes. See Draw or correct a face box . Edit subtitles , Add subtitles Readers who may change the file, on videos and recordings Opens what is said, line by line, beside the video or recording, to correct it. See Correct the subtitles . Restore… Readers who may change the file, on JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP and BMP photos Makes a restored copy beside the photo: faded colours back, dust and scratches filled, blur taken out, grain lessened. See Restore a faded or damaged photo ; to restore many at once, Restore many photos at once . Remove a blemish… Readers who may change the file, on JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP and BMP photos Paint over a spot, a stain or a tear to have it filled, in a copy beside the photo. See Remove a blemish . Rotate left , Rotate right Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos Turns the file a quarter turn. Mirror horizontally Readers who may change the file, on photos and videos Flips the file left to right. A tick shows while it is mirrored. A turn or a flip is kept on the file, for everyone who sees it. EiN moves the face boxes with the picture and makes the smaller versions it shows again. A video is re-encoded by the media service, which takes a while; until it is done the video plays the old way round. To undo a turn, turn it back. The rotate and mirror rows are not offered for a file that cannot be decoded. There is no cropping and no colour editing in EiN; Restore… makes a copy and leaves the photo as it is.

p.h: Change the description, labels or location
p.x: In the cog menu, choose Edit . The Edit file dialog opens, with the file name under its title. In Description , write what the picture shows or what you know about it. Formatting such as bold and lists is kept. In Labels , pick a label in use or type one. A space starts the next label. To set where it was taken, pick a place in A known location , or click the spot in On the map , or type its coordinates there. The dialog warns: "The new location replaces the position the file carries, for the map and for searching by location." To take the location away, press Clear location . The dialog warns: "The file will have no location, for the map or for searching by location." Press Save . It stays greyed out until you have changed something; Cancel closes the dialog without saving. The date is not changed here. To change when pictures were taken, select them in the grid and use Set time in the selection bar; see Dates and places of pictures .

Face boxes stay hidden until you point at a face; then that face's box and name appear. Pin faces in the More menu, or f , shows every box with its name. They stay pinned as you move from file to file, until you unpin them or reload the page. On a touch screen, where nothing can be pointed at, pinning is the way to see the boxes. With the faces pinned, click a named box to open that person's page. Unpinned, a box is part of the picture: a click or a double-click on a face does what it does anywhere else on the picture, so zooming in on a face never opens the person by accident. With the faces pinned, click the box of an unnamed person to open a small field, Who is this? . Type a name and press Enter or the tick. This gives them a name as a person of their own. If they are someone already in the archive, click their placeholder name in the details panel instead and choose the person in the review. A face that belongs to nobody reads Unassigned . A dashed box is a tag: "Tag: a box with a name, not used to recognise faces". It says who is there without helping to recognise them in other pictures. A box drawn by hand is a tag, and so is a found face whose box someone has moved or resized.

p.h: Draw or correct a face box
p.x: Use Edit faces when recognition missed a face, drew the box in the wrong place, or matched the wrong person. It is offered on photos and videos you may change, except on a phone held upright. On a video it pauses the video, and you draw on the frame on screen; the large play button leaves the picture while you draw, and the one on the bar still plays. A box you draw on a video belongs to that moment and shows from half a second before it to half a second after. A box already there can be chosen and removed or given to someone else, but not moved or resized. In the cog menu, choose Edit faces . The bar under the picture reads Draw a new box or select a face , and every box shows. To add a face, drag a box over it. To change a face, click its box. Drag the box to move it, or drag one of the round handles on its edges and corners to resize it. The bar reads Adjust the box, change who it is, or remove it . Under the box, choose: Done to save the box; Cancel to drop your changes to it; the person's name (tooltip Change who this is ) to say who the face is, in the dialog described below; Remove , then Confirm remove , to take the face away. A box you drew is given an unidentified person of its own, and the review opens so you can name them or say they are someone already in the archive. A found face whose box you move or resize keeps its person, but becomes a tag and no longer helps recognition. To leave Edit faces , choose it again in the cog menu, press × in the bar under the picture, or press Esc . The dialog for a face's name is Who is this? , with Now marked as Helen Okafor or Not marked as anyone under the title: Someone I know : pick the person in Who it is , then press Move . Someone new : "the face becomes a new unidentified person, for you to name now or later". Press Move . Let recognition decide : the face is matched again against everyone else. Press Match again . The bar then says what happened, such as Recognition matched the face to Ruby Wrenfield. , Recognition made the face a new unidentified person. or Recognition left the face unassigned: too small or unclear to start a new person. This choice is not there for a tag, which recognition cannot match. Changes you make to faces are decisions by a person, and later recognition runs leave them alone; see People and faces .

p.h: Restore a faded or damaged photo
p.x: A scanned print or slide often shows its age: colours turned red, yellow or pale, specks of dust, scratches and cracks, film grain, a picture out of focus or blurred by a moving camera. Restore… in the cog menu makes a restored copy of the photo with the media service . The photo itself is never changed: the copy is kept beside it as one of its versions. In the cog menu, choose Restore… . Tick what to restore: Faded colours brings back the colours and contrast of a print or slide whose dyes have faded. It is ticked to begin with for a scan, a file from a staging category that holds scans. A black-and-white print toned brown comes out grey. Dust and scratches finds specks, scratches and cracks and paints them over from what is around them. Dark marks too also looks for damage darker than the picture, such as black specks on a print. Quick fill suits dust and thin scratches; Careful fill takes longer and suits creases, tears and torn corners. Blur sharpens a photo that is Out of focus or blurred by Camera shake , the camera moving as it was taken. It brings back detail the blur softened: shake is mended well, a slightly soft photo a little, and detail lost in a photo far out of focus does not come back. Grain and noise smooths film grain and the scanner's noise, by as much as the slider says. Grain is part of a photograph: at half strength about half of it is left. Choose Restore . The dialog waits while the media service works: seconds for a small photo, a minute or two for a large scan. The restored copy then opens beside the original. Finding dust and scratches is a guess, and it sometimes takes a detail of the picture for damage: a button, a highlight in an eye, a thin line. Turn on Show what was taken for damage to see, in red over the original, everything that was painted over, and compare the two before you keep the copy. When it took the wrong things, or missed some, correct its marks and fill again: Choose Correct the marks . The original opens with the marks over it in red. With Erase , brush the marks off what is not damage; with Paint , brush over damage that was missed. Size sets the brush, and the arrow takes back the last stroke. To reach dust a pixel or two across, zoom in: the wheel, two fingers or the buttons in the corner zoom, and a drag with the right mouse button or two fingers moves the picture. Zoomed in, the part in view sharpens to the photo's own resolution a moment after it holds still, and the marks are shown exactly as they are kept. Choose Fill again . A new copy is made with the same colours, fill and grain, filling exactly what is marked now, and it takes the place of the copy you corrected. Back returns to the comparison without filling. Keep closes the comparison and leaves the copy among the photo's versions, named restored-1.png ( .tif for a TIFF), then restored-2.png , and so on. Show this copy makes the copy the picture EiN shows; see below. Show the original turns it back. Discard deletes the copy, and shows the original again if the copy was shown. Download saves the copy. A copy carries the photo's metadata: when and where it was taken, the camera, its description and colour profile, and which way up it is shown. It also says it was restored: its XMP history names each step, with the program that made it and when, and its IPTC digital source type says composite with trained algorithmic media when the careful fill painted it, and algorithmically enhanced otherwise. In the details panel, Versions lists each restored copy with what was done to it, and Compare opens the comparison again.

A kept copy stays among the photo's versions, and the photo goes on showing the original. To see the copy instead, choose Show this copy under it in Versions , or in the comparison. The copy is then the picture in Media , in albums, search results and the viewer, and as an album's cover. Under the photo's name the details panel says "Shown as its restored copy", with Show the original one click away. Only one copy is shown at a time, and only someone who may change the photo can choose it. Everything else still comes from the original: the faces found in it, the text read from it, what it looks like for Similar and search, its duplicates, and the file you download by its name. Correcting the marks of a shown copy shows the new copy in its place. Other people's browsers may show the original for up to an hour after the switch, until their copy of the picture expires. Restoring needs the media service with its restoration models, and someone who may change the photo. Running out of time or a picture the media service cannot read ends with a message, and no copy is kept.

EiN looks at every scan as it arrives, a file from a staging category that holds scans, and notes how faded, dusty, scratched, out of focus and shaken it is. The details panel says what it found under Damage : for example "Faded colours, dust", or "None found". On the Media page, Damage lists the scans found Faded , Dusty , Scratched , Out of focus or with Camera shake ; see Find damaged scans . Faded is a print or slide whose colours Faded colours would change a lot. A photo whose colours are meant to be strong or dark, a sunset or a room lit by candles, can be found faded too. Dusty and Scratched are specks and long thin marks on the smooth parts of the picture, such as a sky or a wall, where they show most. Marks among leaves, grass or a crowd are not counted, since the picture's own thin light details look like them there. Out of focus is a picture with no sharp part anywhere. A portrait with a soft background, or a soft subject such as a face or a cup of coffee, has a sharp part somewhere and is not found. Camera shake is a picture whose edges are blurred one way and sharp the other, as a camera that moved leaves them. It only notes: nothing is restored until you ask. Scans already in the archive are looked at by the media pass that runs every hour, and a scan's colours are looked at again after the media service measures them another way.

Select the photos on the Media page, for example everything Damage found Faded , and choose Restore… in the selection bar. Tick what to restore as for one photo: with Faded chosen, Faded colours is ticked, with Dusty or Scratched Dust and scratches , with Out of focus or Camera shake Blur , set to the same. Choose Restore and EiN restores them in the background, one after another, while you go on with something else: a few seconds each for a small scan, a minute or more for a large one. Each photo gets its restored copy among its versions, as one restored on its own does, to compare and keep or discard. Until its turn comes, its details panel says "Queued, waiting its turn" under Restoring . A photo the media service could not restore says why there instead, and is not tried again until you ask once more. Files of the selection that cannot be restored, such as videos or HEIF photos, are left out, and the dialog says how many.

A spot, a stain or a tear on any photo can be painted over and filled from what is around it, with the careful fill Restore… uses for creases and tears. In the cog menu, choose Remove a blemish… . With Paint , brush over the blemish; Erase takes paint away again, Size sets the brush and the arrow takes back the last stroke. The picture zooms and moves as it does while correcting the marks. Choose Fill . The copy then opens beside the original, as a restored copy does, to keep or discard, and its marks can be corrected and filled again the same way.

p.h: Read the text in a picture
p.x: EiN reads the text in photos: letters, postcards, signs, printed pages, and handwriting in English, Swedish and Finnish. The media service does the reading in the background. A picture still in your staging area is read once it is filed into an album. Show text lays the words read from Peggy's postcard over the picture. The pencil at its top right opens the text for correcting. Show text , in the More menu, or t , darkens the picture and lays the text over it in a typewriter face. Long text scrolls. The row is there only when text was read. The text stays shown as you move from picture to picture, until you close the viewer, so you can page through a scanned letter. It is hidden during a slideshow. Hide text , or t again, takes it away. The text is also under Text in image in the Details section , and search finds pictures by it; see Search and the finder .

p.h: Correct the text, or add it by hand
p.x: In the More menu, choose Edit text , or Add text when nothing was read. With the text shown, the pencil at its top right does the same. The dialog Text in the picture opens: the picture on the left (above, on a narrow screen), which you can zoom to read closely, and a text box on the right. Type or correct the text. Shift + Enter starts a new line. Press Save , or Enter . Saving empty text removes it. What you write replaces what was read. It is offered on photos you may change. Saving does not wait for the media service: when it is away, the text is saved at once and search finds it once the service is back.

p.h: Read the text again in another language
p.x: When the reading came out wrong because EiN took the text for another language, choose the language yourself: Unfold Details near the bottom of the details panel: click its icon. In Text language , choose the language. The menu starts at Automatic , which shows what was detected, such as Automatic: English (93%) , and offers Swedish, Finnish, English, Danish, Norwegian, German and French. EiN reads the picture again in that language, and the text follows after a while. Choose Automatic to let EiN tell the language again. Readers who may not change the file see the language without the menu.

A video starts playing when it opens. If your browser blocks that, press play. On a computer, click the picture to pause or play, and double-click it to go fullscreen. A large play button sits in the middle while the video is paused. The controls fade while the video plays and come back when you move the mouse. Control Key What it does Play / Pause Space or k Plays or pauses. Back 10 s j Goes back ten seconds. Forward 10 s l Goes forward ten seconds. Previous chapter , Next chapter Shift + ← , Shift + → Jumps between chapters, when the video has them. Mute / Unmute m Turns the sound off or on. The slider beside it sets the volume, where the browser lets a page do that. The clock Where you are and how long the video is, such as 0:42 / 2:11 , and Chapter 2 of 5 when it has chapters. Subtitles (CC) c Shows or hides subtitles, when the video has a transcript. The tooltip names the language: Subtitles: English (c) . Picture-in-picture p Plays the video in a small window that stays on top, where the browser offers it. Cast to a screen Sends the video to a television or other screen. Shown only while your browser finds one. Fullscreen Gives the player alone the whole screen, with its controls and subtitles. The volume you set is remembered in this browser for the next video or recording. There is no control for the playback speed. On a phone, tap the picture to show or hide the controls. Three buttons sit over the middle of the picture: back ten seconds, play or pause, and forward ten seconds, or previous and next chapter when the video has chapters. More (⋮) on the bar holds Picture-in-picture and Cast to a screen… , where the browser offers them. There is no mute button: use the phone's own volume buttons. On an iPhone, Fullscreen opens Safari's own player, which shows the subtitles when they are on. Elsewhere, a wide video put fullscreen with the player's button turns the screen sideways where the browser allows it.

Click or drag on the timeline to jump. Pointing at it shows the time there and, once the media service has made the video's storyboard, a small frame from that moment. The media service finds the cuts in a video and makes each scene a chapter. A video whose file names the camera or phone that recorded it is taken to be one take, so there only a clear cut makes a chapter, not a lamp switched on, the exposure changing or a dark moment. Chapters show as pieces of the timeline with gaps between them; a video with too many to fit gets a small tick at each start instead. Pointing at the timeline shows the chapter too, such as 1:24 · Chapter 3 . Previous chapter more than two seconds into a chapter goes back to its start, and otherwise to the chapter before. Move to the timeline with Tab to use the keyboard on it: ← and → go back and forward five seconds, Page Down and Page Up go to the previous and next chapter (or a tenth of the video, without chapters), and Home and End go to the start and the end.

A video or recording with a transcript has the CC button. Subtitles start on; once you turn them off, they stay off for the next video or recording in this browser, until you turn them on again. When two or more people speak, each line starts with the speaker's name, in a colour of their own. A voice nobody has named is called Speaker 1 , Speaker 2 and so on.

The face boxes follow the faces as the video plays, and Pin faces works as it does on a photo. In the details panel, point at a person or an unnamed face and press Show at 0:42 in the card above it. Just above the button the card says when they are on screen, for example On screen 0:00–0:39, 0:42–1:28 . The video pauses on the frame where the face is seen most clearly and keeps a box on the face from there. While it does, a lit button at the end of the row reads Stop following Ruby Wrenfield : press it, or Stop following in the card, to let go. On a phone the button is always in the row.

A recording plays against a picture of its sound. The transcript beside it follows along, and clicking a line jumps there. A recording starts playing when it opens. Its picture is the waveform of the sound, and the waveform is the timeline: the part already played is brighter, a line marks where you are, and a click or a drag on it jumps there. A large play button sits on it while the recording is paused. Under it are play or pause ( Play (Space) , Pause (Space) ), Back 10 s and Forward 10 s , mute and the volume slider (not on a phone), and the clock; at the right end Subtitles (CC) when it has a transcript, Picture-in-picture where the browser offers it, and Fullscreen . With subtitles on, the line being said shows between the waveform and the buttons. Space or k plays and pauses, and j , l , m , c and p work as on a video. Move to the waveform with Tab to use the same keys as on a video's timeline.

The media service writes down what is said in videos and recordings, and works out who speaks when. The transcript appears near the top of the details panel, under the file. Each line starts with its time. The line being said is in bold and is kept in view as it plays. Click a line to jump to that moment. Where the voice changes, the line carries the speaker's name. Above the lines is a chip for each voice, such as Speaker 1 · 1:38 : who it is and how long they speak in the file. The small play button on a chip ( Hear Speaker 1 ) jumps to the start of that voice's longest turn. Click a chip to say who it is. A named voice opens the person's page. An unnamed one opens the review, where you name them or say they are someone already in the archive. A voice that belongs to nobody yet becomes an unidentified person of its own first; this needs permission to change the file. A transcript can also read No speech was detected. , or Transcript unavailable. when it could not be loaded.

The transcript is written by a machine, and it mishears: a name, a word in a dialect, a line it invents over a quiet stretch, or one it never heard. You can correct it on a video or a recording you may change. In the cog menu at the top right of the details panel, choose Edit subtitles , or Add subtitles when there are none. The dialog Subtitles opens where the viewer was playing, and pauses it: the video (or the recording's waveform) on the left, above a timeline that shows where every line lies, and the lines on the right (below, on a narrow screen). The line being said is drawn over the picture as it reads now, with your changes, and tinted in the list. Correct a line by typing in it. Each line has its start and end, which you can type ( 1:23.4 , or seconds such as 83.4 ), and a play button that plays just that line and stops. The line you are in has buttons to start or end it at the playhead, split it at the cursor, join it with the next line, and delete it. Add line puts a new line at the playhead. Press Save , or Ctrl + Enter . An empty line is left out. A line that ends before it starts is marked in red and must be fixed first. The keys work while you type in a line, so you can listen and write at once: Key What it does Ctrl + Space , Alt + K Play or pause. Outside a text box Space and k do too. Alt + J / Alt + L Back or forward two seconds. Alt + P Play the line, from its start to its end. Alt + I / Alt + O The line starts, or ends, at the playhead. Alt + N A new line at the playhead. Alt + S Split the line at the cursor. Alt + ↑ / Alt + ↓ The line before, or after. Closing with changes not saved asks first. What you save is what the subtitles, the transcript in the details panel and search show from then on, and EiN keeps it: the file is not transcribed again, not even when the media service's transcription improves. The speakers stay as they were. Saving does not wait for the media service: when it is away, the lines are saved at once and search finds the new words once the service is back. For a recording or video you reach from a search for words that are said in it, the viewer opens at the moment they are said.

A document opens in the viewer to be read: a PDF in your browser's own PDF reader, with its pages, zoom, search and printing; a Word ( .docx or .doc ), OpenDocument or RTF file the same way, as the PDF EiN made of it; a plain text file, a Markdown note or an HTML page as its text. A long one shows its first 256 KB; Download has the rest. While the PDF reader has the keyboard, the arrow keys move through the document; click the bar under it to move between files with them again. On a phone, where a browser often cannot show a PDF inside a page, the viewer shows the first page and Open the document , which opens the PDF on its own. In a slideshow a document shows its first page. A document whose PDF EiN has not made yet, or one it cannot open, shows its first page or an icon and says so. Use Download in the More menu to open it on your device.

Open the picture to start from, in the album or list you want to show. Press Start slideshow (the play button in the bar). On a phone it is in ⋮. It is greyed out when the list holds only one file. The browser goes fullscreen, if it allows that; if not, the slideshow runs in the window. The close button, the arrows, the details panel and the face boxes go away, and the bar lies over the bottom of the picture. Pinned face names stay on and follow the picture. Each photo stays on screen for Seconds per slide , 3 unless you change it, and fades into the next. With Ken Burns effect on, as it is unless you turn it off, each photo slowly pans and zooms. Videos and recordings play to their end before the next file. One that will not play is skipped after one slide's time. The slideshow follows the list's order and goes round from the last file to the first, until you stop it. There is no shuffle. ← and → still step back and forward. While it runs, the screen is kept from going to sleep. To stop the slideshow, click the picture, press Esc , or leave fullscreen. To change the timing or turn the pan and zoom off, open your picture at the top right, choose Profile , then the Preferences tab, and look under Playback : Setting What it does Default Seconds per slide How long each photo is shown in a slideshow. 3 Ken Burns effect Slowly pan and zoom each photo during a slideshow. on They are yours alone and do not change anyone else's slideshows. See Your profile, favourites and trash , and in the settings reference CFG_USER_SLIDESHOW_SECONDS and CFG_USER_KEN_BURNS .

Press the heart in the bar, or s ; on a phone choose Favourite in ⋮. The heart turns red. Press it again ( Unfavourite ) to take the picture out of your favourites. Your favourites are your own: open your picture at the top right and choose Favourites to see them all, by day. To heart many pictures at once, select them in the grid and use Favourite in the selection bar. Visitors who are not signed in have no favourites and see no heart. See Your profile, favourites and trash .

p.h: What you see depends on who you are
p.x: You are What differs Signed in, and may change the file Everything on this page. Signed in, and may only see the file The cog menu holds only Add to album . You read comments but cannot write them, and see the text language without the menu. No Edit text , Edit subtitles , Edit faces , rotate or mirror. A visitor who is not signed in No heart, no cog menu and no sharing chip. Path is plain text. Someone who opened a share link The pictures without the details panel; the details button and i are not there. Sharing explains who can see what.

p.h: When something is not as expected
p.x: A picture you added a moment ago has no thumbnail, faces, text or transcript yet. The media service works through added files in the background, and the viewer fills in as each step finishes. Until it is done, an administrator sees the Status read Catching up . Text in pictures waits until the file leaves staging. See Getting your photos in . "This rendition could not be played. It may still be transcoding." The version of the video or recording that the browser plays has not been made yet, or failed. Wait a while and open it again. "This browser or device cannot play AV1, the format this video is in." EiN makes its playable videos in the AV1 format, and this browser or device cannot decode it. Use a current browser on another device, or Download the original. "This file cannot be played" , with "The original is damaged, so no preview or playable version could be made from it." The uploaded file itself cannot be read; the reason is under the message. Download it to check the file on your own device. A document says "EiN cannot show this document here". A Word, OpenDocument or RTF file is shown as the PDF EiN makes of it, and that PDF is not made yet, or the file cannot be opened. Wait a while and open it again, or use Download in the More menu to open the file on your device. Its text can still be found with search; see Supported files . Show text is not in the More menu. No text was read from this picture, or it is a video or a recording. Add the text yourself with Add text , if you may change the file. Start slideshow is greyed out. The list holds only one file. Open the viewer from an album or a longer list. The date or the place is wrong. See Dates and places of pictures .

What the viewer shows and changes can also be done in EiN's terminal : Command What it does media-details <file> Everything the details panel shows about a file. file-set-description --text '…' <file> Sets or clears the description. file-set-text --text '…' <file> Writes the text in a picture by hand. file-set-text-language <file> <code|auto> Reads the text again in a language. file-set-transcript <file> < subtitles.vtt Writes what is said in a video or recording, as WebVTT, by hand. file-set-orientation --rotate cw <file> Turns a file; ccw and 180 too, and --toggle-mirror flips it. star <path> , star -d <path> Marks a favourite, or takes it away. # in EiN's terminal media-details /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg file-set-text-language /archive/albums/cornwall-1968/img20120303_133900582.jpg en

The Media page shows every photo, video, recording and document you may see, and searches them. The Year page shows what one year of the archive holds. Labels are words you put on pictures and albums so that you can find them again. This page is for everyone who browses the archive.

Open Media in the sidebar. The page is headed Media , "Photos, videos, audio and documents", with a search box and its controls under the title. With nothing typed in the box, the Media page is a feed of everything you may see, newest first. The page works in two ways: With the box empty, it is a feed : everything you may see, newest first, in sections by date. With anything typed or picked in the box, it is a search : the best matches first, in one grid without dates. See Search from the Media page .

Each section is headed by its date, such as "29 June 2026", and the number of pictures in it. As you scroll, the date of the section you are in stays at the top of the page. Click a date heading to select everything under it. Click it again to clear the selection. A picture known only to a year, such as a scan dated 1975, sits under the year alone. Pictures with no date at all come last, under Undated . Dates and places of pictures explains where dates come from. Above the feed, a row of round rings shows this day in earlier years: one for each earlier year with pictures taken on today's date, marked "1 year ago", "12 years ago" and so on. A ring plays that year's pictures as a story. Memories, news and events on Home describes it. Once the feed holds more than 120 pictures, a time rail runs down the right edge of the page. Drag it to move through the years; the feed loads the pictures from the date you drag to. Click a picture to open it in the viewer, where the arrows walk through the feed. The viewer's "N of M" counter is not shown here, because the feed loads part of the archive at a time. Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers the viewer. On a phone, in the Default layout, pinch the grid to fit between 2 and 5 pictures across. Files in your staging area are not in the feed, and not in the page's searches, until you file them into an album. See Sorting in staging .

Layout decides how the feed is drawn: Layout How the feed looks Default By day, each picture at its own shape, in rows that fill the width. Days By day, in square tiles: three across on a phone, more on a wider screen. Months By month, in square tiles: five across on a phone, more on a wider screen. Good for getting around a large archive. A search is one grid without dates, so Layout is hidden while you search. Your choice is remembered in this browser, not for your account: another computer or phone starts with Default .

Turn on Show only mine to see only the files you added yourself, the ones uploaded or imported under your account. It narrows searches from the box as well as the feed. With nothing of yours to show, the page says "Nothing you have added yet." The switch is off by default, and like the layout it is remembered in this browser. Visitors who have not signed in do not have it.

Show keeps one kind of file: Choice What is shown All Photos, videos, recordings and documents. Images Photos. Video Videos. Audio Recordings. Documents PDF, Word, OpenDocument, RTF, Markdown, HTML and plain text files. Choosing a kind keeps the feed: the videos alone are still newest first, by date. The kind goes into the page's address ( /media?kind=video ), so a link you copy opens the same view. A document's tile is a picture of its first page, and the viewer shows the document to read ( Read a document ); Supported files lists which ones EiN reads the text of.

Damage keeps the scans EiN found worn: Faded , Dusty , Scratched , Out of focus or with Camera shake , or Any condition for everything. EiN looks at every scan as it arrives, a file from a staging category that holds scans, and photos from a camera or a phone are never in these lists. The choice becomes a chip in the box, such as Faded , and the page turns into a search; remove the chip with its ×, or choose Any condition , to return. Select what you find and choose Restore… to restore them all in the background ( Restore many photos at once ). Find the scans worth restoring says what each one means. On a phone, Damage folds into the button with a sliders icon with the other choices.

When the pictures shown carry labels, a row of label pills appears above them, each with the number of pictures that carry it. Click a pill to keep only those pictures: the label becomes a #label chip in the box, and the page turns into a search. Click another pill to narrow further, to pictures that carry both labels. Remove a chip with its × to widen the view again. A label that every picture shown already carries would narrow nothing, so it is left out of the row, as are the labels you have already chosen. Labels explains how pictures get them.

Type in the box, where it says "Filter the media — “Anna sailing 2011”, or type @ to pick someone", and press Enter . On a computer the box has the keyboard as soon as the page opens, so you can start typing at once. Words find pictures by what they show, by the text written in them and by what is said in recordings and videos. "Christmas tree" finds Christmas pictures from every decade, whether or not anyone labelled them. A year in what you type becomes a chip, such as "1998" or "from 2010", and a kind of file, such as "videos", sets Show . With a language model set up, the names of people and places become chips too. @ opens a list of people, locations, labels, cameras and albums. Pick one to keep only the pictures that have it: @Peggy Wrenfield , @The cottage at Malpas , #sailing . The picture button beside the box, Search with a picture , finds what looks like a picture from your device, such as a photo of an old print. The results are one grid, best matches first. Each tile shows its score as a percentage, measured against the best match, which is 100%. The search is kept in the page's address, so you can send someone the link and it opens the same search. Remove the chips and empty the box to return to the feed. Search and the finder explains the rest: how the box reads a sentence, the Interpreted filter beside the box, what needs the media service and what a language model adds.

Select pictures as you would in an album: hover over a picture and tick its box, Shift +click to select a range, Ctrl +click ( ⌘ +click on a Mac) to add or remove one, Ctrl + A to select everything loaded, and Esc to clear. On a touch screen, press and hold a picture. ? lists these keys, and Albums describes selecting in full. A bar at the bottom says how many are selected and offers what you may do with them: Button What it does Shown when Favourite / Unfavourite Hearts the pictures, or takes them out of your favourites when all of them are hearted. You are signed in. Download Downloads one file as itself, several as one zip file. Always. Add to album Links the pictures into an album you choose, or one you name there. You are signed in. Set time Sets when the pictures were taken. See Dates and places of pictures . You may change every selected file. Restore… Restores the photos in the background, each into a copy among its versions. See Restore many photos at once . The selection holds a JPEG, PNG, TIFF, WebP or BMP photo, and you may change every one. Set location Sets where they were taken. See Dates and places of pictures . You may change every selected file. Label Puts labels on them. See Put labels on pictures . You may change every selected file. Delete Moves them to your trash, with Undo in the message that follows. You may change every selected file. On a phone, or when the window has no room for them all, the buttons fold into one Actions menu. Your favourites and your trash are described in Your profile, favourites and trash .

Upload , at the top right of the page, picks files to send, and Upload a folder , under ⋮, picks a whole folder. You can also drop files anywhere on the page: the screen says "Drop files to upload" and "Into staging, folders and all". All three send the files to your staging area, into today's folder of your inbox, and not into the library. They appear on the Media page once you have filed them into an album. You need to be signed in to upload. Getting your photos in explains every way in and what happens to a file afterwards.

Open Year under Explore in the sidebar. The page is headed Year , "Everything from one year", and opens on the current year, or on the year its address names: /year?year=1968 opens 1968. The histogram shows which years hold anything; the slider and the arrows move between them.

There are three ways to move, and they work together: The arrows beside the year. ‹ and › step one year earlier or later. « and » jump to the nearest earlier or later year that holds anything, which saves stepping through the empty years between sparse decades. Pointing at « or » names the year it jumps to, for example "Previous year with entries: 1983", or says "No earlier entries" when there is none; with Albums or People chosen under Show , it counts those instead. The histogram behind the header. Each year that holds anything has a faint bar, taller the more it holds; the chosen year's bar is drawn in blue. The bars grow with the square root of the count, so a year with two albums is still visible beside one with a hundred. The slider along the foot of the header. It has one step for each year that holds anything, plus the current year, so empty years take no room. A few of the years are written under it. Drag the handle and the year at the top follows. The year is kept in the page's address, so you can link to it, and a reload opens the same year. Visiting many years does not fill the browser's history: one press of Back leaves the Year page. The Years section of the Search page lists every year with something in it and opens it here.

The year shows two kinds of card: Albums that hold pictures taken that year. An album with pictures from one December and the January after appears in both years. The card is the one the Albums page draws: the cover, the name, the dates and the number of items. An album with no dated pictures appears in no year, and suggested albums in your staging area do not appear. People born or died that year. A person's card has the badge Born , or Died , with their age added when their birth date is known: Arthur Wrenfield appears in 2014 as Died, aged 83 . Click a card to open the album or the person. Two controls at the right of the box arrange the cards: Control Choices Show All , Albums , or People (births and deaths). Sort Oldest first (the default), Newest first , Name (A-Z) or Most items . With Most items , people come after the albums. Both are remembered in this browser. The histogram and the jump arrows follow Show : with People chosen, they show the years with births and deaths. On a phone, Show and Sort fold into one button with a sliders icon. When a year holds nothing, the page says "Nothing from 1957." and the histogram shows which years do.

p.h: Narrow the year to a person, a place or a label
p.x: The box under the year, "Narrow the year — type @ for a person, location or label", keeps only what has to do with one person, one location or one label. Type @ and the first letters of the name, for example @pegg . Pick Peggy Wrenfield from the list with the mouse, or with the arrow keys and Enter or Tab . Press Enter . The name becomes a chip in the box, and the year keeps: Chip What the year keeps A person Albums holding pictures of them, and their own birth or death. A location Albums holding pictures taken there. A label ( #sailing ) Albums holding pictures that carry the label. You can have one person, one location and one label at a time; picking a second person replaces the first. Words typed without @ keep the cards whose title or description contains them. Remove a chip with its × to widen the year again. The histogram and the jump arrows follow the box as well, so they show the years where that person, place or label appears. When the year you are on has nothing that matches, the page says "Nothing from 1968 matches — the histogram shows the years that do." Use « or » to jump to the nearest year that does. The box narrows what you see without changing the address: a reload, or a link you send, shows the whole year.

A label is one word, such as sailing or christmas , that you put on a picture, an album, a person, a location or a camera. A label stays one word: spaces and commas in what you type start the next label, and a slash becomes a hyphen. Labels are shared across the archive, so the labels anyone has used are offered as you type, and the same word is the same label wherever it is. Labels show under the name of what carries them: in an album's, a person's, a location's or a camera's header, and in the viewer's details panel.

Select the pictures, on the Media page, in an album, or on a person's, a location's or a camera's Media tab. Press Label in the bar at the bottom. In Add labels , type the labels. "Pick a label in use or type a new one. A space starts the next label." Press Add labels . Label is offered only when you may change every selected file. To put labels on a single picture you have open, use its cog menu in the viewer: Edit opens Edit file , which has a Labels field.

p.h: Put labels on an album, a person, a location or a camera
p.x: Each of these has a Labels field in its edit dialog, opened with Edit in its header: Edit album , Edit person , Edit location and Edit camera . Add a label by typing it, take one off with the × on it, and save the dialog. You see Edit only where you may change the thing. The edit dialogs are also the only place in the Web UI where you take labels off. There is no button that takes a label off many pictures at once; in the terminal, label remove does it for one node at a time.

Where you look decides what you find: Where What it finds Click a label wherever it is shown The Search page for that label: albums holding a picture that carries it, and any album, person, location or camera that carries it itself. The Media page: pick the label with @ , or click its label pill The pictures that carry the label. The Year page: pick the label with @ The albums of that year holding pictures that carry it. An album's Info tab, under Labels The album's pictures that carry each label, with their count. See Albums . The Labels section of the Search page, before you search Every label in use, most used first, each with its count. A label on an album finds the album on the Search page, but the Media and Year pages look at the pictures themselves: a picture carries a label only when it was put on the picture. The Search page's Labels section also lists suggested labels, drawn outlined with a sparkle: words that at least five pictures look like but that nothing carries yet. Pointing at one says, for example, "A suggested label: 12 pictures look like it, and nothing carries it yet". The words come from a list of things a family archive shows, such as beach , wedding or christmas , in the archive's language ( en or sv , the setting CFG_LANGUAGE ).

Every label is also a folder: /archive/tags/<label> holds a link to each picture, album, person, location or camera that carries the label. You can look through it in the terminal, for example with ls /archive/tags/sailing . Links explains links in the tree. A label is kept on the node that carries it: the label pills count it there, and a search for the label finds it there. The link in the folder is for looking through, so a link added or deleted by hand labels nothing and unlabels nothing. The dialogs, label add and label remove keep the folder in step, so put labels on and take them off with those. When something labelled is deleted, its link in the folder goes with it, and label prune clears any link left pointing at nothing. A label is listed while at least one thing carries it.

p.h: Let EiN suggest where a label belongs
p.x: When you are signed in and the Search page or the Media page asks for exactly one label, a bar headed Looks like and the label appears above the results. EiN learns what the label looks like from the pictures that carry it, and suggests other pictures and albums that look the same. Search for one label, for example by clicking sailing on an album, or by picking #sailing on the Media page. On the Looks like sailing bar, press Show . While EiN learns, the bar says "Learning what sailing looks like…". Look through the suggestions: pictures and albums that do not carry the label yet, the most alike first. Select the pictures that belong and press Label sailing , or select the ones that do not and press Not sailing . An album's card has its own Label and Not sailing buttons. EiN learns from each answer: the model and the suggestions are worked out again at once, and what you marked as not the label is left out of the suggestions from then on. Show all opens the Media page with every picture that looks like the label and does not carry it yet, the most alike first, under the chip Looks like sailing . Hide folds the bar. When the model is good enough to stand on its own, the bar says how many pictures it would add, for example "40 more look like it", before you open it. For a suggested label that nothing carries yet, the bar opens by itself, because the suggestions are all there is. Under the bar, one line says how far to trust the suggestions: What the bar says What it means "Learned from N pictures in N labeled files and albums. Of the labeled pictures held back, it finds N% again." EiN hid some of the labelled pictures while learning and checked how many it found again. The higher, the better. "… Label a few more for it to measure how well it finds them." Too few pictures carry the label to check the model. It still suggests. "Suggested from what "a photo of a christmas tree" looks like. Label pictures of it and it learns from them instead." A suggested label: nothing carries it yet, so EiN goes by what the words describe. "Nothing with this label has a picture to learn from." The label is only on people, places or cameras, or on pictures the media service has not looked at yet. "The pictures held back were not found again, so what this label names does not seem to show in the pictures: a person, a trip or a time rather than something seen." The label names something you cannot see, so EiN offers no suggestions. Show what it would suggest shows them anyway. "Nothing else looks like sailing" means that no picture outside the label is alike enough, apart from those marked as not it. Learning works from what the media service has worked out about each picture, so a picture it has not looked at yet is neither learned from nor suggested. Besides the learning you start from the bar, the archive's label-models service relearns every label, and every suggested word, once an hour when something has changed: when pictures gained or lost the label, when something was marked as not the label, or when a week has passed. The Web UI has no button to take back a Not ; in the terminal, label-model unreject does.

What you see What it means, and what to do Incomplete answer : "The content match did not answer in time, so these are filename matches only. Try again in a moment." The media service did not answer the search in time, so only file names were searched. Try again shortly. If it keeps happening, tell whoever looks after EiN; The media service is theirs. "No person or location filter matched … — searched those words as description instead." The Media page found no person or place by that name, and searched the words as text. Pick the person with @ instead. "No match for @… — searched as plain text instead." The same on the Year page. Pictures you uploaded are missing from the Media page Files sent with Import media or the Media page's Upload wait in your staging area until you file them into an album; see Sorting in staging . A file that is still being prepared shows a placeholder until its thumbnail exists. An album is missing from a year None of its pictures is dated in that year. Check the pictures' dates; see Dates and places of pictures . "The histogram counts only the first N matches." There is more than the histogram counts, so its bars show part of it. The cards for the chosen year are complete. "Nothing matches that filter." No picture meets every chip. Remove a chip, or choose All under Show . Label , Set time or Delete is missing from the selection bar You may not change every selected picture. Select only your own, or ask the person who shared them. The layout, Show only mine or the Year page's Show and Sort are different on another device They are remembered per browser, not per account.

The Media page, the Year page and labels all run ordinary commands, which you can run yourself in the terminal : # in EiN's terminal search --tag sailing --kind photo,video # pictures that carry a label search 'christmas tree' --kind photo # pictures by what they show search --has damage=faded --kind photo # the scans found faded timeline --year 1968 --kind album,auto-album,birth,death # what the Year page shows for 1968 labels # every label in use, with its count label add '/archive/albums/Summer 2020' sailing # put a label on an album label remove '/archive/albums/Summer 2020' sailing ls /archive/tags/sailing # the label's folder label-model show sailing # how well the label is learned timeline also takes --person , --location and --tag , as the Year page's box does. The full options are in the reference for search , label , labels , timeline and label-model , and Commands by task lists more.

With the Archive installed, EiN searches your photos, videos, recordings and documents, down to what is in a picture and what is said in a recording, and finds the albums, people, locations and cameras they belong to. This page is for everyone who searches the archive in a browser. The finder in the top bar and the Search page itself are EiN's own, and Search and the finder covers them.

Page Where you find it What it finds Search Search under Explore in the sidebar, or Search for "…" in the finder Albums, people, locations and cameras: the things pictures belong to Media Media in the sidebar, or Pictures of "…" in the finder The photos, videos, audio recordings and documents themselves Both pages have the same kind of search box. You can write a sentence, pick something exactly with @ , and see what the box understood as chips you can remove one by one. The address in the browser holds the whole search, so a search can be linked, and the browser's Back and Forward step through your searches. Every search finds only what you are allowed to see. Files still in your staging area are left out until they are filed ( Sorting in staging ).

p.h: Find photos, videos, recordings and documents
p.x: The Media page shows everything as a feed, newest first, until you ask it something. Then it turns into a search, with the best matches first in one grid. Open Media in the sidebar. Click the box, Filter the media — “Anna sailing 2011”, or type @ to pick someone , and type what you are looking for, for example Christmas tree . Press Enter , or click the arrow at the end of the box. The results take the place of the feed, the closest first. Each tile shows a match percentage, and a video its length. To see one kind only, choose it under Show : All , Images , Video , Audio or Documents . Click a tile to open it in the viewer . To go back to the feed, empty the box, press Enter and remove any chips with their ×. Nothing in these pictures carries a label or a description: EiN finds the tree by what the pictures show.

p.h: What your words are compared with
p.x: Each search looks in several places at once and puts the results together: What is searched How Try it in the Wrenfield demo What a photo shows, and what a video shows in its frames By meaning; nothing needs a label or a description first Christmas tree , harbour Text in pictures: printed and handwritten letters, postcards, recipe cards, signs By meaning and by its exact words the cottage is ours finds Peggy's postcard from Cornwall in 1968; self-raising flour finds her recipe for scones What is said in videos and recordings By meaning and by its exact words the knife's gone blunt finds Arthur carving the goose at Christmas 1998 Documents: PDF, Word ( .docx ), OpenDocument ( .odt ) and plain text By what their text is about Christmas letter finds the family newsletter from 2019 Descriptions someone wrote By meaning File names By the name; an underscore and a space count alike DSC_0215 , IMG_0525 A match in something said opens the video or recording at the moment the words are said, not at the start. A name said once in an hour of tape is found by its words. Write what you remember being said as a sentence: when half or more of its longer words are said in one of the recordings that match it best, that recording counts as an exact match and comes near the top. Documents have no preview in EiN and show as plain tiles; Supported files lists which files EiN reads text from.

When words or a picture rank the results, each tile shows a percentage. The best match is always 100%, and every other result shows how it compares with that best one. The number tells you how a result ranks within this search; it is not a measure of how sure EiN is, and the same picture can show a different number in another search. A search of chips alone, such as a person, a label or a year, has nothing to rank by: a picture is either in it or not. Its results show newest first, without percentages, and with the date rail beside them when they span enough dates.

Show only mine (only when you are signed in) limits the page, both the feed and a search, to the files you added yourself. EiN remembers the choice in this browser, not in your account. The Media page's other controls, its layouts and label pills, are covered in Media, Year and labels .

p.h: Write what you are looking for
