p.x: You can type a whole sentence. When you press Enter , the box turns what it understands into chips, each with its own × to remove it, and keeps the remaining words as the description it searches for by meaning. It reads in two passes. Years and kinds , at once, in English and Swedish: A year, such as 1968 . Before or after one: before 1980 or until 1980 , after 2010 or since 2010 , and the Swedish före , innan , efter and sedan . Two years make a span: 1990 1999 . Years from 1800 to next year are read. A kind: photos , pictures , images , videos , films , movies , clips , recordings , audio or documents , and Swedish words such as bilder , foton , filmer , ljud , inspelningar and dokument . On the Media page a kind sets Show ; on the Search page, albums , people and locations do. People, places and words that describe the picture , a moment later, when your EiN has a language model (the assistant module sets one up). A small spinner in the box shows that it is reading. The search already runs on the first pass meanwhile, and runs again when the model has found more. A name that belongs to one person becomes that person. A name several people share becomes a chip ending in … , meaning every person whose name contains it. A place becomes one of your locations , or, for a country or a city that is not one, an Area chip covering it. me ( mig ) is you, and a relative of yours, such as my mother or min mammas syster , is whoever your family tree says that is. Both need your account to be linked to your person in the archive (your account menu then has a Me row; your administrator makes the link, see Accounts and groups ). Without the link, or when the tree records no such relative or more than one, or the search names two relations, the yellow note names the word and it is searched as words; name the person instead. show me at the start of a search asks for nobody. Some examples on the Media page of the Wrenfield demo: videos 1998 sets Show to Video and adds the chip 1998 , leaving the box empty: every video from 1998. Peggy 1968 adds 1968 at once. With a language model, Peggy then becomes @Peggy Wrenfield , and the box is left empty: every picture of Peggy from 1968. Peggy at the cottage at Malpas in 1968 gives the same two chips and @The cottage at Malpas , so only the pictures that have all three are left. Christmas 1975 adds 1975 and looks through that year's pictures for what looks like Christmas. Without a language model, only years and kinds are read, and the rest is searched as words describing the picture. A name that matched nobody is searched as words too, and a yellow note says so: No person or location filter matched … — searched those words as description instead. The Search page puts it as No person or location matched … — searched as plain text instead. Close the note with its ×. Tip Write a place the way it is named in EiN, or pick it with @ . A word that is only part of a location's name, such as cottage alone, is not taken as that location; the model may then look it up as an area on the map instead. The Interpreted filter shows what happened. A second search adds to the chips already there rather than replacing them. To widen a search, remove a chip; to start again, remove them all.

Chip What it means @Peggy Wrenfield One person, location or camera, picked with @ or understood from your words @Okafor… Every person whose name contains these words Area An area on the map, such as a country or a city 1968 , 1990–1999 , from 2010 , up to 1980 A year, a span of years, or a limit #harbour A label @Christmas 1998 An album: only what is in it (Media page) Looks like harbour Pictures that look like the pictures carrying that label Similar , with a small picture Pictures that look like that picture

Beside the box, the Interpreted filter button (an ⓘ icon) opens an account of what is being searched. It appears once there is something to explain, and not on a phone. Row What it shows Description (q) The words searched for by meaning, or none Looks like (like) The picture searched with, in place of words Names (subject-name, AND words) Partial names, and the people each one matched Exact (subject) The people, locations and cameras picked exactly Area An area on the map Date (from/to) The year or years Labels (tag) The labels Album/directory The album searched in On the Search page it adds a line saying that people, locations, dates and cameras are what a picture has, so an album matches when it holds a picture that does. Open it when a search brings back something unexpected. A word you meant as a description may have been taken as a place, or the other way round; remove that chip and search again.

Type @ and the start of a name. A list opens with the matching people, locations, labels and cameras (on the Media page, albums too), each with its kind beside it. The list matches the start of each word of a name, in order, and lets you skip words: @peg wren finds Peggy Wrenfield. Pick one with the arrow keys and Enter or Tab , or click it. The box writes @Peggy Wrenfield . Add more words or picks, and press Enter . Each pick becomes a chip. Esc closes the list without picking. An @ word you type without picking from the list stays in the box as ordinary words, and the yellow note mentions it. The Year page and the Map have boxes of their own that take @ for a person, a location or a label; see Media, Year and labels and Locations and the map .

When words fail you, search with a picture instead: an old print you are holding, or a place you are standing in. On the Media page, click the button beside the box, Search with a picture . Choose a picture on your device, or on a phone take one with the camera. The page shows the pictures that look most like it, nearest first, and the box shows the chip Similar with a small copy of your picture. Chips and Show narrow the answer the same way they narrow words. Typing words and pressing Enter replaces the picture with your words. The picture goes to your EiN and nowhere else, turned upright and made smaller first. EiN keeps it in /tmp , never adds it to the archive, and removes it after 24 hours (the Hours in /tmp setting, CFG_TMP_RETENTION_HOURS ). If it cannot be sent, a red message says the picture could not be sent , followed by the HTTP status. To find pictures like one that is already in the archive, open it in the viewer . Its details panel shows Similar , a strip of the nearest pictures, and Show all opens the same search on the Media page.

Above the results, a row of label pills shows the labels the results carry, each with a count. Click one to add it to the search as a chip, such as #harbour . A label that every result carries is left out, as it would narrow nothing. A label shown anywhere else in EiN, on a picture or an album, opens the Search page for that label when you click it. When you are signed in, a search for exactly one label also offers the pictures that look like that label but do not carry it yet; Media, Year and labels explains how to label them and teach EiN what the label means.

p.h: Find albums, people, locations and cameras
p.x: The Search page finds the things pictures belong to. The Search page explains its box, Show and Sort ; with the Archive, Show offers All , Albums , People , Locations and Cameras , and an album's card also shows its dates and how many files it holds. What each kind is found by: Kind Found by Try it in the Wrenfield demo Albums Name, description, and what their pictures show album christmas sets Show to Albums and finds the Christmas albums, such as Christmas 1975 and Christmas in Wellington People Name; every word must match the same person. A first name and surname find them without their middle names, or with one half of a double surname helen okafor Locations Name falmouth Cameras Name, make, model or serial number lumix finds Peggy's Lumix A person's name typed in whole words, even without the middle names, finds the person ahead of the albums named after them and of the pictures with their name written in them: helen okafor puts Helen before an album called Helen Okafor in Falmouth and before a letter she signed. A person, location, year, camera or label in the search narrows albums by their pictures: @Peggy Wrenfield 1968 finds the albums holding a picture of Peggy taken in 1968. A label matches an album that carries it or holds a picture that does. A year alone also matches an album whose name carries it: album christmas 1975 finds Christmas 1975 even when its scans have no date.

p.h: Start from people, places, years and labels
p.x: Before you type, the Search page offers places to start: the people and locations with the most pictures, every year, and the labels. Before you type, the Search page shows your Recent searches ( Before you search ), and under them the Archive's rows: People : the people in the most pictures. Locations : up to 16 locations that have a place on the map, as small maps, those placed from the most geotagged pictures first. Years : every year with something in it, each opening that year on the Year page . Labels : every label, the most used first, then suggested labels marked with a sparkle: words that at least five pictures look like although nothing carries them yet. Pointing at one shows A suggested label: N pictures look like it, and nothing carries it yet . See all beside People, Locations and Years opens the People , Locations or Year page. A section with nothing to show is left out. With the assistant installed, it can search for you too: ask it in Chat , and an answer that comes from a search offers Show in search to open it on the Search or Media page.

p.h: What needs the media service and a language model
p.x: EiN's media service reads every picture, recording and document as it arrives, and turns your words into something it can compare with them when you search. A language model reads names out of a sentence. Your administrator installs both; see The media service and The language model . What you do Needs Finding albums, people, locations and cameras in the finder The Archive alone Finding files, albums, people, locations and cameras by name; @ picks; labels; years and kinds read from a sentence The Archive alone Finding pictures by what they show; text in pictures and speech by meaning; documents; albums by what their pictures show The media service, answering when you search Searching with a picture you choose The media service, answering when you search Finding text in pictures and speech by their exact words The media service to have read them once; not when you search Reading people, places and descriptive words from a sentence, and me or my mother A language model A file is found by what it shows or says only once the media service has looked at it: a picture added a few minutes ago may not turn up by meaning yet. Your administrator's Status page reads Catching up while that work goes on. If your administrator chose a hosted provider for the language model, the words you type into a search box are sent to that provider to be read. A place in your words that is none of your locations is looked up on OpenStreetMap's address service, Nominatim, to find its area.

p.h: When the media service is not answering
p.x: On the Media page a yellow note appears above the results: Incomplete answer The content match did not answer in time, so these are filename matches only. Try again in a moment. More lines under it can name other parts that did not answer, such as the picture match. The results come only from what EiN can match without the media service, such as file names. A search with a picture finds nothing, and its line in the note says why. Wait a moment and press Enter in the box again. The media service may be busy or starting. If the note keeps coming back, tell your administrator. Anyone signed in can check first: About EiN , in the menu under your picture, shows the Media service tile as Not answering while it is down. Your administrator finds more on the Status page's Media service tab, and The media service covers what to do. Elsewhere you see no note, only less: the Search page still finds albums, people, locations and cameras by name, but not albums by what their pictures show. When the language model is slow or away, you see no error either: the search keeps the years and kinds it read and searches the rest of your sentence as words.

The search command answers the same questions as the two pages, in EiN's terminal : # in EiN's terminal search "Christmas tree" --kind photo search --subject-name person:peggy --from 1968 --to 1968 search --occasion midsummer --from 1995 --to 2000 The first finds photos by what they show; the second lists everything with a person whose name contains Peggy, taken in 1968; the third what was taken at midsummer in each of the years 1995 to 2000. --occasion knows the days of midsummer , easter , christmas , new-year , walpurgis , national-day and lucia in every year, also by their Swedish names ( midsommar , påsk , jul , nyår , valborg , nationaldagen ), and without --from and --to it looks in every year. The assistant uses it when you ask in Chat for pictures from a holiday. Without --kind , search finds every kind at once, and a person's name finds the person first and the pictures they are in after them: search "Peggy Wrenfield" puts Peggy ahead of every photo of her, even one named after her. Its options are in the command reference , the Archive's providers behind it, such as search-media , are in Archive commands , and Commands by task lists the archive's other search commands.

Search and the finder : the finder in the top bar and the Search page. Media, Year and labels : the Media feed, the Year page and labels. Locations and the map : finding pictures by place on the map. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer and its Similar strip. The media service : what reads your pictures, recordings and documents.

EiN finds the faces in your photos and videos and the voices in your recordings, and groups the ones that belong to the same person. This page is for everyone in the family who names those people, corrects what recognition got wrong, and browses a person's pictures.

You do not have to tag anyone for recognition to start. Every photo, and frames sampled through every video, is searched for faces as it arrives, and every face that is found goes through the same three-way decision: It joins a person when it looks enough like faces of that person in other photos, and the comparison clearly favours that one person over everyone else. That person may be named or still unidentified. It starts an unidentified person when it matches nobody, but is clear and large enough to be worth treating as someone new. That person gets a placeholder name such as Unknown 4XK9QM and waits on the Unidentified people page for someone to say who it is. It stays unknown when it is too small or too unsure to start anyone. In the viewer its box reads Unassigned . The next photo of the same stranger finds the first one, sees that it already belongs to an unidentified person, and joins that person instead of starting another. So when you name an unidentified person you name every face in the group at once, and new pictures of them join the named person by themselves from then on. Two faces in the same photo are never made the same person automatically. Voices work the same way across recordings and the sound of videos: a voice that matches nobody starts an unidentified person when it speaks for at least 10 seconds in all in one recording, and two voices in one recording are never made the same person. In a video, a face seen speaking in step with a voice counts as evidence of who is speaking. Recognition decides on its own, and anything a person decides afterwards is kept. The work is done by the media service on your own machine; no photo, face or voice is sent anywhere to be analysed. Without the media service no faces are found, and they are found once it runs again. After a large import it takes a while for every picture to be looked at; the Status reads Catching up until it is done (see Health and status ). Faces are found in the pictures waiting in your staging area too, before you file them into albums.

With the Automation module's cameras, the media service watches every camera as it sends its picture, and the faces it sees go through the same decision as a photo's. Within a second or so of someone coming into view, the face is compared with every face that belongs to someone, and the camera's Faces log says who it is, or unknown ; an automation can take that, such as an unknown face at the front door at night. Once the person has gone, the clearest picture of their face is filed under the camera, on its page in Cameras , where it joins a person, starts an unidentified one, or stays unknown, as any photo's face does, beside a video clip of the visit. So someone the camera keeps seeing is named once, on the Unidentified people page, and known from then on. Every face every camera sees is looked at; there is no camera left out and nobody who is not looked for. The pictures stay on your machine, as everything the media service does. When an update of the media service brings other face models, EiN looks for the faces in every picture and video again by itself, after the new pictures waiting for theirs. Each face it finds again keeps the person it had, and a face a person named that the new models no longer find stays as a box with its name. Until a picture has had its turn, its faces keep their names but are not compared with any others, since two models' fingerprints of a face cannot be compared.

Open People in the sidebar, under Browse . Everyone with a name, the most pictured first; the button at the top leads to the people still waiting for one. The header counts the named people ( 19 people ). The filter box ( Filter people… ) matches the name and the full name as you type. N unidentified opens the people recognition found but nobody has named yet. It is there only when there are some. On a phone it is an icon with the count as a badge. Sort offers Most pictured (the default), Name (A-Z) and Name (Z-A) . Your choice is remembered in this browser. A name that starts with ? , a placeholder for someone known only from a family record, sorts after the real names. Each card shows the person's cover picture, their name and how many pictures they are in, or their full name when they are in none. Click a card to open the person's page . The number on a card counts the files of the library the person is seen or heard in: a picture with their face or a box naming them, or a recording with their voice. A picture with two of their faces counts once, as does a recording they speak in many times. Files still waiting in someone's staging area count once they are filed, and files in a trash count again once they are restored. When nobody has been named yet, the page says No people yet and "Face recognition finds people in the pictures; name them under Unidentified, or add someone here." with a New person button. You can also find a person from the search box in the top bar, or with @ and their name on the Search, Media, Year and Map pages; see Search and the finder .

Click N unidentified on the People page, or open /people/unknown . Each card is one person recognition put together; typing a name in its box names every face in it. The page is headed Unidentified people : "Faces and voices recognized as the same person, but nobody has said who they are." Under it, N unidentified says how many there are, and N loaded how many the page has fetched so far. Sort offers Most found (the default) and Newest . Found shows only people found at least so many times: Any count , 2+ times , 5+ times , 10+ times or 50+ times . A face and a recording the voice is heard in count one time each. Each card shows one large glimpse and up to three small ones: the best faces first, then round play buttons that play the voice's longest turn. A voice heard in a video shows the video in its button: the moment the person speaks, those moments one after another while the pointer rests on it, and what is on screen as you listen. The badges say N faces and heard in N (recordings). A face or recording on a file in a trash is left out of both, and of the glimpses, until the file is restored. Load more (N of M) at the foot fetches the next cards. Both choices are kept in the address, so a link opens the same view. To name someone from their card: Click in the card's Who is this? box and type the name, for example Ruby Wrenfield . Once you type, the box lists the matching people who already have a name, the best match first: the name exactly as typed, then names holding every typed word whole, then names where a typed word only starts or is inside a word ( Johan in Johansson ). A match in someone's full or birth name comes after the same match in the name they go by. Press Enter , or click one of the listed people, which adds this person to them at once. While it is saved, the box shows a spinner and the card fades in and out until it leaves the page. What happens depends on the name: A new name names the person. They move to the People page with every face and voice they hold, and a message says Named Ruby Wrenfield . The name of someone who already exists adds the faces and voices to that person instead of making a second one, and the message says Added to Ruby Wrenfield . The name must match exactly, apart from capital letters, so pick it from the list rather than typing it differently. Tip Before you name a card you are unsure of, open it. A card shows at most four glimpses; the review shows every face and recording, which is where you notice that two people were put together. When nobody is waiting, the page says "Nobody unidentified. Everyone recognized so far has a name." With a Found filter on, it says, for example, "Nobody unidentified found 5 or more times."

p.h: Look at everything before you decide
p.x: Click a card, anywhere but its name box and its tick box, to open the review. Its title is the placeholder name, with the N faces and heard in N badges beside it. At the top, the Who is this? box ("A new name, or someone you already have") works like the card's. Its button reads Name , or Add to <name> when the name is someone who already exists. Not a person beside it is described in Say what is not a person . Faces shows every face of this person. Click a face to see the photo it came from, large, over the review; its arrows, or ← and → , step through the photos of the faces shown. Load more (N of M) fetches more when there are many. Voice ("heard in N recordings") shows a tile for each recording the voice is heard in. The round button plays the voice's longest turn there, with the video's frames in it for a video, and Open in the lightbox opens the recording at that moment; the review steps aside while the viewer is open and is back as you left it when you close it. Pick all picks every recording. To pick faces or recordings, tick the box in their corner. Once something is picked, a click on a face picks it too instead of opening its photo; Shift +click picks a range, and Ctrl + A ( ⌘ + A on a Mac) picks everything shown. Esc closes an open photo first, then clears what is picked, then closes the review. The review has its own address, /people/unknown?person=<id> , so you can send it to a relative who may know who it is.

p.h: Take some faces out (Split off, Move to…)
p.x: When the review shows faces of more than one person, pick the ones that do not belong. A bar appears with N faces picked and these actions: Action Dialog What it does Split off as someone new Split off N faces? → Split off The picked faces and recordings become a new unidentified person of their own, for you to name afterwards or add to someone. Move to… Move N faces to someone? , then Who they are → Move They move to the named person you pick, and count as decided by a human, so no later pass moves them again. Not a person N faces: not a person? → Unassign and lock They lose their identity and are locked, so recognition leaves them alone. Nothing is deleted. Clear Unpicks everything. When you have picked everything the person holds, Split off as someone new and Move to… are greyed out, with the note "That is everything they have. To give all of it to someone, name them or add them to someone above instead. Not a person removes them."

Recognition sometimes joins two people through one weak resemblance, and four glimpses on a card will not show it. With three faces or more, the review has an Adjust group threshold switch beside Faces (and with three recordings or more, one beside Voice ): Turn on Adjust group threshold . EiN compares every face of this person with every other ("Comparing every face against every other"), once. Drag the How alike slider. The faces are laid out in groups, Largest group first, then Group 2 and onward, each with its number of faces. The slider starts where the comparison suggests the groups part. Tick a group's box to pick all of it, then use Split off as someone new , Move to… or Not a person as above. Only the 30 largest groups are shown; the rest are counted under them ("Move the slider left to bring them up here."). A box someone drew by hand has nothing to compare and is in no group.

p.h: Fold several unidentified people into one
p.x: Recognition often splits one person into a large group and a few small ones. To join them: On the Unidentified people page, tick the box in the corner of each card. Once one is ticked, a plain click on a card ticks it too; Ctrl + A ticks every loaded card and Esc clears. In the bar at the bottom, press Merge . It needs two cards or more. The dialog Merge N into one person? names the one that survives: the card with the most faces, or the older one when two have as many. "<name> survives with all N faces. It keeps its own entry and stays unidentified — name it afterwards." It lists the others with their faces. Press Merge . The other entries are removed, and their faces are marked as decided by a human, so no later pass undoes it. Name the person that is left, from its card or its review. The Web UI merges only unidentified people. To fold one named person into another, for example a second Ruby made by a typo, use person-merge in the terminal : faces, voices, events, relations and every other link move to the person you keep, and the other is removed. --dry-run shows what would move without changing anything. # in EiN's terminal person-merge --dry-run /archive/people/ruby-wrenfeld /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield person-merge /archive/people/ruby-wrenfeld /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield The last path is the person who stays. See person-merge in the command reference.

p.h: Say what is not a person
p.x: A poster, a statue, a doll, a pattern in the wallpaper or the back of a head can all be taken for a face. Saying so keeps recognition from trying again: Several cards at once: tick them on the Unidentified people page and press Not a person in the bar. One person: press Not a person at the top of their review. The dialog ( Not a person? , or N: not a person? for several) says what happens: every face and recording they hold loses its identity and is locked, so recognition leaves it alone from now on, and the entry is removed. "The photos and recordings themselves are untouched." Confirm with Not a person . Some faces of one person: pick them in the review and press Not a person in the bar under it. The dialog ( N faces: not a person? ) locks only those, and the person keeps the rest. Confirm with Unassign and lock . For faces wrongly given to someone who already has a name, use Not a face on their Faces tab .

p.h: Name a face in the viewer
p.x: You can also name people while you look at a picture. The viewer describes it fully; in short: Press f , or choose Pin faces in the More (⋮) menu, to show every face box with its name. Hovering a box, or a name in the details panel, lights up the other. With the faces pinned, click a named box to open that person's page. Click the box of an unidentified person to get a Who is this? box: type the name and press Enter or the check mark. This always makes a new person, even when someone of that name exists; to add the faces to someone who already exists, use the review instead. In the details panel, under the people in the picture, an unidentified person is listed by a crop of their face and their placeholder name. Click it to open their review over the viewer. On a computer, Edit faces in the cog menu lets you select a box and press its name ("Change who this is"). The Who is this? dialog offers Someone I know (pick them under Who it is ), Someone new (a new unidentified person, for you to name now or later) and, for a face recognition found, Let recognition decide (matched again against everyone except the person it is on now). Confirm with Move or Match again . This is also how you give a name to a face marked Unassigned . In Edit faces you can also drag a new box around a face recognition missed. It becomes a new unidentified person, and its review opens for you to name it. A box drawn by hand names the person in that picture, but is not used to recognise them in others. Edit faces is offered on a computer, on photos you may change.

Someone who is in no picture yet, a great-grandparent for the family tree for example, can be added by hand: Open Create (the plus in the top bar) and choose Person , or press New person on an empty People page. In Create Person , fill in Name (required), and if you like Full name and Gender ( Female , Male , Other or Unknown ). Press Create . The new person's page opens. Look on the People page first, so that you do not add someone who is already there: the dialog does not look for someone of the same name. The address of the new page is made from the name, and if a person already has that address the dialog shows an error instead; give the new person a name that tells the two apart. Later faces only join a person through faces that already belong to them, so a person made by hand gets pictures once you give them a face: add an unidentified person to them by typing their name, or move faces to them with Move to… or Someone I know .

Click a person on the People page, a name in the viewer, or a person in search results. The header places a person in time; the tabs hold everything else. The header shows: their cover picture and name, the full name under it, and "Born as <birth name>" when that is different; a life line: "1934 – 2021 · died aged 86" for someone who has died, "Born 1958 · 68" for someone living. A ~ before the age means it is approximate, because the birth date has no day or is uncertain; an uncertain year reads "~1890", "before 1900" or "after 1900" (see Uncertain dates ); where they live now, linking to the location, their contact details (not on a phone; the Info tab lists them), and how many photos they are in, over which years ("34 photos · 1968–2025"); allergies, marked with a warning sign, their labels, and the description. If you may change the person, the header has Share and Edit , and under ⋮ Add event , Split faces… (administrators only) and Move to trash . Share shares the person's page and what hangs off it, not the photos they are in; see Sharing . Move to trash returns you to the People page with "<name> moved to the trash" and Undo . Tab What it shows Timeline Their life by year, the latest first: birth and death, events, moves, partnerships, their children's births, and the albums they appear in. Info Everything recorded about them: Person (Name, Full name, Born as, Gender, Born, Died, Age or Age at death, Photos), Contact , Allergies , Homes with the years, Family (each relative by role), About , Comments (as in the viewer's details panel : everyone who sees the person reads them, and if you may change the person you write one and delete your own) and Sources , the files that describe them (see Bring in a family tree from a GEDCOM file ). Media Every photo and video they are in, newest first, with the time rail at the side for jumping through the years. Faces Every face of theirs, as a grid of crops. See Correct a person's faces . Heard in Every recording they speak in. See Recordings a person is heard in . Family The family tree. See Family tree, events and homes . Homes Where they have lived, with the years. See Family tree, events and homes . The open tab is kept in the address ( ?tab=faces , ?tab=voices and so on), so you can link straight to it. When there is nothing to show, the Timeline says "Nothing recorded for <name> yet. Add an event to record something.", and the Media tab "No photos of <name> yet. They appear here once tagged, or once a detected face is assigned to them." On the Media tab you can select pictures as in an album. If you may change the person, Set as cover in the selection bar makes the one selected picture their cover; Set time changes the capture time of pictures you may change (see Dates and places of pictures ). On a phone, the tabs show only their icons, except the one that is open, and the header's buttons fold into ⋮. On a phone the same page fits one column; the tab icons are in the same order as on a computer.

The Faces tab shows every face assigned to the person, as crops in a grid. Click a crop to open the photo it came from in the viewer; the arrows step through the photos in the order of the grid. While there are more faces than are loaded, a note says "N of M loaded", and more load as you scroll. A wrong face stands out among the right ones; select it and say who it really is. Select faces as you select pictures in an album: hover a crop and tick its box, Shift +click for a range, or long-press on a phone. The selection bar then offers: Download : the selected crops, as one zip named "<name> faces" when there are several. Set as cover : makes the one selected crop the person's picture. Not <name> : takes the faces off this person. Is <name> : only in the Doubtful view, described below. Not <name> opens the dialog Not <name>? , with the number of faces under its title and four choices: Choice What happens Let recognition decide (the default) Each face is matched again against everyone except this person. It joins whoever it looks like, or becomes a new unidentified person. It is never put back on this person. Someone I know The faces move to the person you pick under Who it is . One new unidentified person All the faces are the same person, not yet named. Name them later from the unidentified list. Not a face They lose their identity and are locked, so recognition leaves them alone from now on. Press Move , or Unassign and lock for Not a face . After Let recognition decide , a short report ( Faces moved ) says where the faces went, for example "2 faces matched to Peggy Wrenfield", "3 faces became unidentified people" or "1 face left unassigned — too small or unclear to start a new person". Press Done . If a face that was the person's cover leaves them, they get a new cover from their remaining faces.

Somebody who is not sure a face is the person can mark it as doubtful in the viewer (see People in the picture ), or with the face-doubt command. The face stays the person's until somebody answers. When a person has doubtful faces, the Faces tab shows a switch: All faces or Doubtful (N) , "Faces somebody is not sure of, or that look more like somebody else". Each doubtful crop is badged with who marked it, for example "asked by peggy". Choose Doubtful (N) . Select the faces that are someone else and press Not <name> . Select the faces that are right and press Is <name> . They stay, as a person's decision. When none are left, the tab says "No doubtful faces of <name> left."

p.h: Recordings a person is heard in
p.x: The Heard in tab lists, under "Heard in N recordings", a tile for each recording the person speaks in, those they speak most in first. The round button on a tile plays their longest turn in that recording; for a video it shows the video's frames of that turn. Hovering the name shows the recording's date and how long they speak in it ("speaks 1:42 in it"), and Open in the lightbox opens the recording at their turn. To take a recording off the person, tick its tile and press Not this person (N) . Their voice in it loses its identity and is locked, so recognition does not give it back. Nothing asks first. If the person speaks in no recording, the tab says "Not heard in any recording yet." Naming a voice in a transcript, and seeing who speaks when, is in the viewer .

p.h: Split a person who is really two
p.x: Naming an unidentified person approves every face in it. If it turns out to have held two people, an administrator can take them apart with Split faces… under ⋮ on the person's page. The dialog Split <name> compares the person's faces with each other, more strictly than recognition did. Drag the Similarity slider until the people come apart; the badge says how many groups there are. One group , Split in two , Suggested and Split off all but the largest are shortcuts. For each group, choose Keep , Split off (a new unidentified person; not offered for a group of one face), Merge into… (pick a named person) or Not a person . Every group starts on Keep . Click a face to see the photo it came from, over the dialog; its arrows then step through that group, which is the way to check that the same person keeps turning up. Read the summary at the foot, for example "40 faces stay · 1 new unidentified person", and press Apply to N groups . At least one group has to stay: moving all of them is a rename, not a split. Only the 30 largest groups get a card; the smaller ones stay as they are. A box drawn by hand has nothing to compare and stays where it is.

Press Edit on the person's page to open Edit person . Leave an optional field empty to remove it. Field What to enter Name The name shown everywhere. Required. Full name Their whole name, shown under the name. Birth name The name they were born with, shown as "Born as". Gender Female , Male , Other or Unknown . Born , Died A year, a month or a day: 1934 , 1934-05 or 1934-05-20 , and beside it On , or About , Before or After when the date is uncertain. Without a day, their age is shown as approximate. Contact information Add contact adds a row with a Type (for example "Email, phone, address…") and the Details . An e-mail address becomes a link that writes to it, and a phone number one that calls it. Allergies Shown with a warning sign in the header. Description Free text, with Markdown. Labels Words to find the person by. A space starts the next label. Press Save . If something is missing, the dialog says "a name is needed" or "each contact needs both a type and details". Events, parents, partners, children and homes are not in this dialog; see Family tree, events and homes .

Old records often say only roughly when something happened. Beside Born , Died and an event's Date , choose how sure the date is: Choice Means Shown as On it happened then 1890 About around then, give or take ~1890 Before at the latest then before 1900 After at the earliest then after 1900 An uncertain date is placed on the timeline at its year, under "about", "before" or "after", and the header and the Info tab show it as above; a card in the family tree, short of room, writes <1900 and >1900 . It makes no birthday or memorial on the Home page, since the day is not known. An age worked out from a date About a year is shown with a ~ ; a birth or death only Before or After a year gives no age at all. Typing a new date in Edit person keeps the choice beside it; in the terminal, person-update --born alone makes the date exact, and --born-qualifier about (or before , after ) qualifies it.

A named person without a cover gets one by themselves: the crop of one of their own faces. Faces someone named or confirmed come first, then photos where they are the only face, then clear faces looking into the camera, then the largest. A cover you choose yourself, with Set as cover on the Faces or Media tab, is never replaced by another pick. A cover is replaced only when it no longer works: the picture is gone, or it is the crop of a face that has since been taken off the person, because their card would then show somebody else.

p.h: What EiN keeps of your decisions
p.x: Recognition only decides about faces nobody has decided about. Anything a person says is kept, and no later automatic pass undoes it: You Afterwards Name an unidentified person Their faces count as named by a human. New faces that look like them join them by themselves. Add someone to an existing person, or Merge The faces are marked as decided by a human. Move to… , Someone I know The faces stay with the person you picked. Split off as someone new , One new unidentified person The faces stay together as the new person. Not a person , Not a face , Not this person The faces and voices are locked without a name. Let recognition decide The faces are never matched back to the person you took them from. Is <name> , Yes to Is this <name>? The faces are marked as decided by a human, and the doubt goes. Set as cover Your cover stays, as long as the picture is there and the face is still theirs. Changing the recognition settings does not touch these decisions either.

No faces are found at all. Recognition needs the media service. Ask your administrator to check the Status ; see The media service . A face in a photo has no box. Faces that are very small, blurred or turned far away are not kept. Draw a box around it with Edit faces in the viewer, as described in Name a face in the viewer . One person is spread over many unidentified cards. Tick the cards and merge them , or type the same name into each card's box. An unidentified person holds two people. Open the review and use Group similar faces . For a named person, an administrator uses Split faces… . A person has someone else's faces. Open their Faces tab, select the wrong ones and press Not <name> . A person's card shows more pictures than their page. The card counts faces and voices, so each recording the person is heard in counts too. An action fails. The reason appears in red under the bar or in the dialog. A change you are not allowed to make, to a picture or a person you may only view, is refused; ask whoever owns it, or your administrator. Recognition is too eager or too cautious. An administrator can tune it under Settings → System , in the groups Faces and Voices . Changes apply to faces and voices decided from then on. Setting Default What it decides Face match threshold 0.55 How similar two faces must be before one is attached to a known person. Higher makes fewer wrong matches and more unknown faces. Face winner margin 1.2 How far the leading person must outweigh the runner-up. Higher leaves close calls unknown. Confidence to start a new person from a face 0.7 How sure the detector must be before a face that matches nobody starts a new person. Size to start a new person from a face (px) 48 How large such a face must be: its shorter side, in pixels of the displayed photo. Minimum face confidence , Minimum face size (px) , Maximum head turn (degrees) 0.7, 24, 80 Which detections are kept as faces at all. Speech to start a new person (seconds) 10 How long a voice that matches nobody must speak in one recording, in all, before it starts a new person. Every setting is described in the reference, under Faces and Voices .

This page shows how to record how the people in your archive are related, what happened in their lives and where they lived, and what EiN makes of it: the family tree, the timelines, and the birthdays and anniversaries on the Home page. It is for the family members who keep these records, and it says which parts need an administrator.

Everything on this page hangs off a person's page or a location's page. In the Web UI, two of the controls are shown only to an administrator: What Where Who sees the controls Parents, partners and children the person's Family tab administrators only A person's homes the person's Homes tab administrators only A location's residents Residents on the location's Info tab anyone who may change the location Events of a person ⋮ → Add event on the person anyone who may change the person Born and died Edit on the person anyone who may change the person Events of an album, a location or a camera ⋮ → Add event on its page anyone who may change it People, relations, events from a GEDCOM a .ged file uploaded to staging, then Review and import anyone who may change those people An administrator is someone signed in as admin , or a member of the sudo group who has chosen Administer… in the account menu and entered their password again. See Accounts and groups . Who may change a person or a location is a matter of its sharing; see Sharing . Everyone else reads the tree, the homes and the timelines like any other page, and sees no ⋯ menus on the tree's cards and no Add home button. Note The administrator rule belongs to the Web UI only. The same changes are ordinary commands in the terminal , and the assistant can propose parents, partners and events for you; there they need permission to change the people they touch, not administrator rights. See In the terminal .

Open a person and choose the Family tab. The address ends in ?tab=family , so you can link to someone's tree directly. Generations are rows and couples sit side by side, so the tree reads like a family tree on paper. The tree is drawn the way family trees usually are: Generations are rows. Parents and grandparents are above, children and grandchildren below. Couples sit side by side , joined by a line. When the partnership has dates, the year it began is written over the line and the year it ended under it. Each card shows the person's picture, their name and their years: 1934 – 2021 , b. 1958 for someone with only a birth date, d. 2011 for someone with only a death date. The person the page is about has an outlined card and a bold name. Click a name to open that person's page. The tree shows only people you may see. Someone whose page is hidden from you is left out, with the lines to them.

A large family would not fit on a screen, so the tree opens with two generations up and two down from the person, and the partners of everyone drawn. A card with more family behind it has a round chevron on its edge: at the top when there are more parents ("Show <name>'s parents"), at the bottom when there are more children ("Show <name>'s children"). Click one and the tree loads one more generation that way: the parents above the card, or the children below it. The chevron then turns round ("Hide <name>'s parents" or "Hide <name>'s children"), and clicking it folds those relatives away again. Two things are not drawn until you ask: Brothers and sisters. The tree walks up from the person and down from the person, so their siblings appear once you open the chevron on one of their parents' cards. A partner's own family. A husband's or wife's parents belong to another tree. Open the chevron on the partner's card to bring them in.

The tree moves inside its own box, as a map does, so the rest of the page stays where it is. Drag it with the mouse or one finger. Scroll over it to zoom around the pointer, or pinch with two fingers or on a trackpad. A double click or double tap on the space between the cards zooms in there; hold Shift to zoom out. The buttons in the box's top right corner: Button What it does Full screen Opens the tree in a window that fills the screen; Leave full screen closes it. Fit the whole family Shrinks the drawing until all of it fits the box. Centre on this person Moves back to the person the page is about. Hidden while the whole family is fitted.

There is no brother or sister relation to record. Two people are siblings when they share a parent: give both the same two parents and they are brother and sister, give them one parent in common and they are half-siblings. In-laws and step-parents also follow from the ties you record: the partner of someone's parent is their stepfather or stepmother, and the parent of someone's partner is their father-in-law or mother-in-law. Set each person's Gender with Edit (see Edit a person ) so that EiN can say father or mother rather than parent.

p.h: Add a parent, partner or child
p.x: You need administrator rights for this in the Web UI; see Who may change what . Open the person's Family tab. Find the card of the person you are adding to. It can be any card in the tree, not only the person the page is about. Click ⋯ on that card and choose Add parent , Add partner or Add child . The dialog asks the question: "Whose child is <name>?", "Who is <name> with?" or "Who is a child of <name>?". Leave Someone already here selected and pick the person in Who . Type part of a name to narrow the list. For a parent or a child, choose the Kind . For a partner, choose the Relationship and, if you know them, the dates in From and Until . Press Add . The tree, the person's header and their timeline are read again at once. The tree keeps every chevron you opened, so the new relative appears where they belong; a branch whose card the edit took off the tree closes. Each tie joins two people. Add child gives the child one parent: if both partners of a couple are the child's parents, add the child from the other partner's card as well, or add the second parent from the child's own card. Adding a partner links no children. To add someone who is not in the archive yet, a great-grandmother for example, choose Someone new and type their name: they are created as with Create → Person (see Create a person by hand ) and linked in the same step.

Kind Use it for Blood A birth parent. This is the default. Adoptive A parent by adoption, as Jon and Kiri Wrenfield are to Leo. Step A step-parent you want drawn as a parent, above the child. Foster A foster parent. The tree draws every kind of parent alike. The kind shows in the words EiN uses for the tie, such as "adoptive father" or "stepmother", when the assistant or person-how-related says how two people are related. A step-parent does not have to be recorded as a parent at all: the partner of a parent is already a stepfather or stepmother.

Relationship is Partner or Married . From and Until take a year, a month or a day: 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . Leave Until empty while the two are together. The dates do more than label the line in the tree: From puts "<A> and <B> married" (or "became partners") on both people's timelines on that date. Until puts "<A> and <B> parted" on both timelines. Leave it empty when the partnership ended with a death: the death date already ends the anniversaries, and an Until on the day of death makes both timelines say the two parted that day. From with a full date makes the anniversary come round on the Home page: "Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married". A partnership dated only to a year or a month, such as Thomas Wrenfield and Rachel Moore's from 2008-05 , has no day to come round on. See Birthdays, memorials and anniversaries . To add or correct the dates of a partnership that is already recorded, choose Add partner again, pick the same partner, and fill in From or Until . EiN updates the dates of the partnership you have instead of adding a second one, and keeps its Relationship as it was. To change the Relationship or to clear a date, remove the relation and add it again.

Problems show in a red box in the dialog, which stays open so you can correct them. People are named there by the last part of their page's address, such as helen-okafor . Message What it means "pick somebody, or create them" Who is empty. "person-set-parent: refusing to add parent: <a> is a descendant of <b>" The tie would make someone their own ancestor. Check who is the parent. "person-set-parent: <a> is already a parent of <b>" The tie is already there. "person-set-partner: <a> and <b> are already partners" The partnership is already there, and no dates were given to update. "person-set-partner: invalid from date '…' (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])", or the same with to A date is not written as a year, a month or a day. "person-set-partner: partnership end is before start" Until is earlier than From .

On the Family tab, click ⋯ on the card of one of the two people and choose Remove a relation… . The dialog lists their ties to the people on screen, such as "Arthur Wrenfield — partner" or "Helen Okafor — child". Choose one. Press Remove . The tie goes both ways, so this removes it from both people. Neither person is deleted, and nothing goes to the trash: to undo it, add the relation again, with its kind and dates. Only ties to people drawn in the tree are offered. If the dialog says "Nothing to remove — no relations of theirs are on screen.", open the chevrons until the other person's card is shown.

There is no page in the Web UI that answers this. Ask the assistant , for example "How is Ruby related to Peggy?". Its answer can carry a small tree of only the people on the line between the two, with a Full screen button. In the terminal , person-how-related answers in English or Swedish: # in EiN's terminal person-how-related /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield person-how-related /archive/people/erik-wrenfield /archive/people/rachel-moore Ruby Wrenfield is Peggy Wrenfield's granddaughter Rachel Moore is Erik Wrenfield's stepmother Add --lang sv after the two people for the Swedish word.

An event is a dated note on a person: a wedding, a move abroad, a graduation, a birth or a death. Open the person's page, click ⋮ in the header and choose Add event . Choose the Type : Generic , Birth , Death , Marriage or Engagement . Type the Date as 1956 , 1956-06 or 1956-06-16 . Beside it, On says it happened then; choose About , Before or After when that is all you know (see Uncertain dates ). A birth or death sets the same on Born or Died . Write the Description , with Markdown if you like. Its first line becomes the event's title on the timeline. Written by names the person who wrote the text. It starts as you, when your account is linked to a person; clear it or pick someone else. Press Add event . It becomes available once there is a date or a description. Type What else it does Generic Nothing more: it is an entry on the person's timeline. Birth With a date, it sets the person's Born , replacing what was there. Its description joins the "<name> was born" entry on the timeline. Death With a date, it sets the person's Died , replacing what was there. Its description joins the "<name> died" entry. Marriage Counts in the Marriages by month chart on the Statistics page. It does not record a partnership; see Record a wedding . Engagement Counts in the Engagements by month chart. Things to know: An event without a date is kept but placed on no timeline , since there is nothing to place it by. Give it a date to see it. Without a description , the timeline shows a name made from the type and the date, such as marriage-1956-06-16 . Write a first line that says what happened. A person's events cannot be changed or removed in the Web UI once added. An administrator, or anyone who may change the person, can do it in the terminal: the events are files in the person's events folder. # in EiN's terminal ls /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield/events trash put /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield/events/event-1999 trash put moves the event to your trash, where you can restore it; see Your profile, favourites and trash .

A wedding is best recorded in two parts, because each part feeds a different place: The partnership , with Add partner , Relationship Married and the full date in From . It puts the wedding on both people's timelines and brings the anniversary to the Home page every year. A Marriage event , if you have more to say, with the same date and a description such as "Married at Islington Town Hall". It carries the story, and counts in the Statistics chart. When the event and the partnership fall on the same day, the timeline of the person who has the event shows the two as one entry; the partner's timeline shows the partnership.

p.h: Events of albums, locations and cameras
p.x: Albums, locations and cameras have Add event under ⋮ too, for someone who may change them. Their events are always generic, and need both a Date and a Description . On an album , the date starts as the first day with pictures and no event yet. The event stands as a note among that day's pictures, signed "— <writer>", or with the name of the account that added it when it has no writer. If you may change it, a pencil on the note opens Edit event , where you change the date, the text or the writer and press Save , or press Delete . A deleted event goes to your trash, and the message "Event moved to the trash" has Undo . On a location or a camera , the event appears on its timeline, on its Info tab. It cannot be changed in the Web UI afterwards.

A person's Timeline tab is put together from what is recorded about them and their family. You do not add entries to it directly. Her death, her moves and the end of her marriage all come from records on her page and her family's, not from entries typed into the timeline. Entry Where it comes from "<name> was born", "<name> died" Born and Died , with any Birth or Death event The event's title Their dated events "<name> moved to <location>", "<name> left <location>" Their homes, on the Moved in and Moved out dates "<A> and <B> married", "became partners", "parted" Their partnerships' From and Until "<child> was born", with "Child of <name>" Their children's Born An album The albums with pictures of them A location's timeline, on the left of its Info tab, shows its residents moving in and out, its own events and the albums with photos taken there. When it has none, it says "Nothing recorded at <location> yet. Residents with dates, and albums with photos taken here, appear on its timeline." A person's Born and Died also put them on the Year page for those years, with a "Born" or "Died, aged N" badge; see Media, Year and labels .

Where someone lived is one record seen from two sides: the person's Homes tab lists their homes, and Residents on each location's Info tab lists the people who lived there. A change on either side shows on both.

p.h: Add a home to a person
p.x: You need administrator rights for this in the Web UI. Open the person's Homes tab. It says "Where <name> has lived, and when." Press Add home . Choose Location already here and pick it in Location , or choose New location and type a Location name . Fill in Moved in and, if they left, Moved out : 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . Leave Moved out empty while they live there. Press Add home . A new location made here has only its name. It has no place on the map until someone opens it and gives it an address or a position; see Locations and the map . Each row shows the location, which opens its page, and the dates as they were entered: 1956 – 1999 , since 1983 , until 1999 , or dates unknown . A home with a moved-in date and no moved-out date is marked current . Homes without a moved-out date come first, then the others, the latest move first. To correct the dates , press the pencil on the row, change Moved in or Moved out , and press Save changes . The dates you leave are the new ones: emptying Moved out makes it a current home again. To remove a home , press the bin on the row, then Remove under "Remove <location> from this home history?". The location itself stays. A person with no homes shows "No homes recorded."

p.h: Add a resident to a location
p.x: Residents on a location's Info tab works the same way, from the other side, and anyone who may change the location can use it. Open the location. Residents is on the right of the Info tab, the tab it opens on. Press Add resident beside the heading. Choose Person already here and pick them in Person , or choose New person and type their Name . A new person made here is an ordinary person on the People page. Fill in Moved in and Moved out , and press Add resident . The pencil and the bin on each row correct the dates and remove the resident, as on the Homes tab; the question there is "Remove <name> from the residents of <location>?". A location with nobody recorded shows "No known residents."

The dates are what turn a home into moves: A home with a moved-in date puts "<name> moved to <location>" on the person's timeline and on the location's. A moved-out date adds "<name> left <location>". A home without dates says where someone lived and nothing about when. It is listed on the Homes and Residents tabs as dates unknown and on the person's Info tab, but on no timeline. A home without a moved-out date counts as where the person lives now, even with no dates at all: the person's header shows it, and the location's header lists them under its current residents. Give a moved-out date to every home somebody has left.

The form stays open with the reason in a red box: Message What to do "pick a location, or create one", "pick somebody, or create them" Pick one in the list, or switch to New location or New person . "a location name is needed", "a name is needed" Type the name. "that name has no letters or digits to make a path from" Use a name with letters or digits in it. "person-set-home: --from '…' is not a date (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])" Write the date as 1972 , 1972-05 or 1972-05-20 . "person-set-home: moved out … before moving in …" Moved out is earlier than Moved in . "person-set-home: … already exists (use --update to change the dates)" The home is already recorded. Close the form and use the pencil on its row.

p.h: Bring in a family tree from a GEDCOM file
p.x: A GEDCOM file ( .ged ) is the file genealogy programs and family tree websites export a family tree as. Upload one into your staging area, by Import media , the Media page's Upload or SFTP (see Getting your photos in ). Nothing is imported yet: the file waits, and the Staging page says so in a yellow Needs you box. Review and import opens the family tree (see Look over a family tree before it is imported ), where you can say who each person is before anything is written. When you press Import , EiN brings in the people and families in it: Who each person is. EiN looks for each person in the file among the people of the archive, by any of their names: the name they go by, their full name or the name they were born with. An initial stands for a given name it begins, so "Harold J R Wrenfield" can be the file's Harold James Robert Wrenfield. A first name, the surname and the year of birth together are enough, as are a first name and the full date of birth, or two given names or more and the surname written out in full. Two spellings of one name, such as Eriksson and Ericsson or Thompson and Thomson, are read as one (see Spellings of a name ); a person who fits only that way is found when the day of birth is the same as well, and otherwise suggested. A person known only by a first name is found when a parent, partner or child of theirs in the file has been found and is related to them the same way in the archive. A date or a gender that disagrees rules a person out, and when two people fit equally well, neither is chosen. Whatever you chose on the family tree comes first. Everyone else gets a page , named by the name they went by and the surname they had last, with their full name, the name they were born with, gender, and the dates of birth and death. A date the file gives only roughly is kept as such: "about 1890" as About 1890, "before 1900" and "after 1900" as Before and After , and "between 1885 and 1889" as about 1887 (see Uncertain dates ). What a person is missing is filled in. A full name, birth name, gender or date the archive does not have yet is taken from the file, and so are their notes, as the description on their Info tab; nothing the archive already has is changed. Parents and partners are added where the archive does not have them yet: a marriage with its date, an adoption or a foster child as such (see Parent kinds ). A child who has two parents already gets no third, and nobody becomes their own ancestor. Events are added : christenings, occupations, emigrations, censuses, burials and the other events and facts the file gives, each as an event on the person, with its place and notes as its text. A birth, death, marriage or divorce becomes an event only when the file says where it happened or has a note on it, since the dates are on the person and the partnership already; a marriage or divorce the file dates only roughly becomes one too, since a partnership's dates are exact. A wedding goes on one of the two partners. An event the person has already, of the same kind on the same day, is not added again, and a person has one birth and one death. A place that is a location in the archive gives the event that location's position on the map: the whole place, or its first part, such as "Lower Wrenfield" for "Lower Wrenfield, Kent", must be the name of exactly one location. A residence at such a location becomes a home , with the moved-in and moved-out dates of a "from … to …" period; a residence anywhere else is an event. EiN makes no locations of its own from the file. The file is kept in /archive/sources/genealogy/ and every person it describes lists it under Sources on their Info tab, where you can download it. The file is read as you: someone you may not change is still recognised, but nothing is written on them, and a relation that would need writing on them is left out. Uploading the same file again finds the same people and adds nothing, and so does a newer export of the same tree from a program that gives each person a lasting identifier. When EiN has made two pages for one person after all, fold them together with person-merge (see People and faces ).

p.h: Look over a family tree before it is imported
p.x: Review and import on the Staging page opens the family tree waiting there, drawn over the whole window as one tree with the archive's own people; the header counts them by what becomes of them. Each card is a person in the file, and its coloured stripe says what the import would do with them: Stripe Says Means Green Found in the archive EiN takes them to be this person of the archive; the card's last line names them. Blue Chosen by you You said who they are. Orange To decide People of the archive could be them, or have a like name, and EiN chose none, so a new page would be made. Purple New person Nobody in the archive fits; they get a page of their own. Red Left out You left them out: no page, and none of their relations. Grey Only in the archive Not in the file: a parent, partner or child, in the archive, of someone found there. A person who is found brings their family in the archive along, so the file's relations and the archive's meet on their card, and you can see whether the two trees agree. When the file holds families not related to each other, or people related to nobody else in it, a switch at the top of the tree picks which to show. Select a card and a panel floating over the tree, at its right (over its lower part on a phone), shows what the file says of them next to what the archive has, marking with + what the import would add; it never changes what the archive has already. Under Who is this? are the people who fit, best first, then people of a like name: those who share a given name and the surname but have a word in their names the file does not, such as a nickname, marked "a like name" and never chosen for you. Each has This is them , and: Someone else in the archive… picks anyone else. New person makes them a page of their own, whoever they fit. Leave out brings in neither them nor their relations. Let the import decide takes back your choice. Selecting a grey card offers the other way round: Is one of the file's individuals says which person in the file they are. A choice shows at once, so you can go straight on to the next person, while the tree is read again behind it ("Reading the tree again…"): saying who one person is can settle their relatives too, so a child known only by a first name is found once their parent is. Your choices are kept in your browser until you import. Import brings the file in with them; Move to trash under ⋮ removes the file without importing it.

Names were written many ways before spelling settled, and are still: Eriksson, Ericsson and Erikson; Olsson, Ohlson and Olsen; Gustaf and Gustav; Thompson and Thomson; MacDonald and McDonald. When EiN compares the names in a family tree file with the archive's, it reads every word through a set of spelling rules first, and two words that come out the same are one name. The rules cover Swedish and English names alike: ck , ch , q and a hard c are read as k , an h after the first letter is dropped, a doubled letter is one, -sen is -son , ph is f , th is t , w is v , z is s , mac is mc , a final e is dropped, and a few more. A person who fits only by spelling is found when their day of birth is the same too. Otherwise they are suggested under Who is this? , marked "a like name", for you to choose. An administrator can add rules. Every file in /etc/name-spellings.d is read; the archive's own are in /etc/name-spellings.d/archive/spellings , which shows how they are written, and are replaced when the Archive module is updated, so add yours in a file of your own beside them, such as /etc/name-spellings.d/local . Each line is a rule, <from> -> <to> : <from> a regular expression over one word in lower case without accents (Öberg is read as oberg), <to> what it becomes, empty to drop it. # starts a comment. Your files are read before the archive's, so a rule of yours sees the name as it is written: # in EiN's terminal, as an administrator cat /etc/name-spellings.d/archive/spellings echo 'ie$ -> e # Rosie, Rose' >> /etc/name-spellings.d/local echo '^petrus$ -> per # Petrus, Per' >> /etc/name-spellings.d/local The rules are read each time a family tree is matched, so a new rule counts at once. A rule that is not a regular expression stops the match with the file and the line, such as "/etc/name-spellings.d/local:2: '(ck' is not a regular expression".

p.h: Import a GEDCOM file in the terminal
p.x: gedcom-read says who each person in a file would be, and gedcom-import brings it in. The same choices as on the family tree are flags that name a person by their record in the file (its xref, such as @I3@ ): --match @I3@=ruby-wrenfield says who they are, --new @I4@ makes them a new person, and --skip @I9@ leaves them out. With --dry-run , gedcom-import writes nothing: # in EiN's terminal gedcom-read " $HOME /staging/genealogy/wrenfield.ged" gedcom-import " $HOME /staging/genealogy/wrenfield.ged" --match @I3@=ruby-wrenfield --dry-run gedcom-import " $HOME /staging/genealogy/wrenfield.ged" --match @I3@=ruby-wrenfield Run on a file outside staging, gedcom-import keeps a copy and leaves your file where it is.

p.h: Birthdays, memorials and anniversaries on the Home page
p.x: The Events panel on the Home page lists what comes round in the next 30 days and what came round in the last 7, under Today , Coming up and Recently . It is filled from the dates on this page, so what it shows depends on what you record: On the Home page Comes from Needs Birthdays: "<name> turns N", or "would have turned N" after their death the person's Born a full date, 1934-08-22 , not an uncertain one Memorials: "N years since <name> died" the person's Died a full date, not an uncertain one; only on round years Anniversaries: "<A> and <B> — N years married" or "… years together" a partnership's From a full date; Married says married, Partner says together A date known only to the year or the month never comes round, since it has no day. Round years, the 5th, 10th, 15th and 20th and then every 10th, are shown in bold, and they are kept first when there are more than 16 entries. Birthdays stop after the 110th. An anniversary comes round up to the year of the Until date or of the first partner's death, and for 75 years at most. Someone born on 29 February appears only in leap years. Birthdays and memorials come from the people on the People page. Memories, news and events on Home describes the panel itself, and the Statistics page with its charts of births, engagements, marriages and deaths by month.

Everything on this page is also a command, which an administrator or a power user can run in the terminal or over SSH . The commands need permission to change the people and locations they write to; they do not ask for administrator rights. # in EiN's terminal person-set-parent /archive/people/leo-wrenfield /archive/people/kiri-wrenfield --kind adoptive person-set-partner /archive/people/jon-wrenfield /archive/people/kiri-wrenfield --kind married --from 1996-02-03 person-set-home --from 1996 /archive/people/jon-wrenfield /archive/locations/Kelburn person-add-event -- type marriage -- date 1956-06-16 --body 'Married at Islington Town Hall' /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield person-family-tree /archive/people/peggy-wrenfield Give person-set-parent , person-set-partner and person-how-related the two people first and the flags after them: placed before the people, a flag's value is taken for a person. Command What it does person-set-parent Adds a parent; the child comes first. --kind blood|adoptive|step|foster . person-set-partner Adds a partnership, or updates the dates of one. --kind partner|married , --from , --to . person-remove Removes the tie between two people, from both sides. person-set-home Records a home with --from and --to ; --update rewrites the dates of one already there. person-remove-home Removes a home, from both the person and the location. person-add-event Adds an event to a person, album, location or camera. person-info Shows a person's dates, relatives, homes and events, the undated ones too. person-family-tree Prints ancestors and descendants as text. person-how-related Names how two people are related. person-timeline Prints a person's timeline. person-check Looks for broken ties, impossible dates and loops in the tree: person-check /archive/people . gedcom-read Says who each person in a GEDCOM file would be, and who else could be them. gedcom-import Brings in a GEDCOM file: people, relations, events and homes. --dry-run writes nothing. source-list Lists the files a person was read from, such as a GEDCOM file. events Prints what the Home page's Events panel shows. You can also tell the assistant a parent, a partnership or an event the archive should record, for example "Leo was adopted by Jon and Kiri". It proposes the command, and nothing changes until you press Run ; it runs as you, with your permissions. Homes are not among the commands it is pointed to, so record those on a person's Homes tab or under a location's Residents .

There is no ⋯ on the cards, or no Add home button. These are shown only to administrators. Ask one to make the change, or, if you are in the sudo group, choose Administer… in the account menu first. A relative is missing from the tree. Open the chevron on the nearest card that is shown; siblings and a partner's family appear only then. If there is no chevron, the tie is not recorded, or the relative's page is hidden from you. A birthday or anniversary does not show on the Home page. Check that the date has a day, that it falls within the next 30 days or the last 7, and for an anniversary that the partnership has a From date. When more than 16 entries fall in the window, the rest are left out; round years are kept first. A GEDCOM file made a second page for someone already in the archive. Their names or dates in the file and in the archive differ, or two people in the archive fit equally well. Fold the new page into the old one with person-merge . A dry run ( gedcom-import --dry-run ) shows beforehand whom EiN will find. A GEDCOM upload stays in staging. EiN found no people in it: it is not a GEDCOM file, or one with nothing in it but the header. A move is not on the timeline. The home has no dates. Press the pencil on its row and fill in Moved in . Someone shows a home they left long ago as where they live. That home has no moved-out date. Add one.

This page is for everyone in the family who works with places: the homes, cottages, churches and towns where pictures were taken and people lived. It covers the Locations page, creating a location and drawing where it lies, how pictures join a location by themselves, the weather at a place and time, and the Map page, where pictures, locations and GPS tracks are drawn together. How one picture gets its position, and how you correct it, is on Dates and places of pictures .

A location is a named place in the archive, such as "The cottage at Malpas", "Highbury" or "London". It has a name and, if you give them, an address, a city and a country, a description, labels and the people who lived there. Where it lies on the map is one of three shapes: Shape What it is Where it comes from Pictures inside join it Point One spot, with no size Coordinates typed or clicked when the location is created No Circle A centre and a radius Drawn by hand, or worked out from the location's address or linked pictures Yes Polygon An outline with three or more corners Drawn by hand Yes A location with a circle or a polygon does work for you: Pictures whose position falls inside it are linked to it. The viewer shows the location's name for them, and its Media tab lists them. Typing @ and the location's name finds those pictures in search and on the map, and narrows the Year page to what holds them. An album's Info tab lists the locations of its pictures under Places . Staging names the albums it suggests after the location most of their pictures are linked to, or else the nearest location within 500 m. People's homes are locations too, so a location's page shows who lived there; see Family tree, events and homes . Locations are kept under /archive/locations in the tree .

Open Locations in the sidebar, under Browse . Each card shows where the place lies and where that position came from. The header counts the locations, for example "16 locations", and has these controls: Control What it does Filter locations… Narrows the cards as you type, by name and address. Case and accents do not matter. Show All (N) or Needs location (N) , the locations with no place on the map. It appears only while at least one location has none. Sort Name (A-Z) or Name (Z-A) . This browser remembers your choice. Each card shows a small map of where the location lies, or a crossed-out pin when it has no place yet, then its name, its address and one of these badges: Badge Means set by hand Someone drew its shape or typed its coordinates from N photos Its circle was worked out from N geotagged photos linked to it from address Its circle comes from looking up its address N suggestions The address lookup found candidates but was not sure; you pick one on its page Click a card to open the location. A location has no cover photo to choose in the Web UI; its card shows the map. With no locations at all, the page says "No locations yet" and "Homes, churches, summer houses: locations where people lived or pictures were taken.", with a New location button when you are signed in. A filter that matches nothing says No locations found matching "<text>" .

You need to be signed in. Press the plus ( Create ) in the top bar and choose Location . On an empty Locations page, New location does the same. See The Create menu . The Create Location dialog opens with a map beside the fields. Type a Name , for example The cottage at Malpas . It is the only field you must fill in.
