If the place has an address, type it under Address as it was written down: street and number, postcode and town. The hint reads "Looked up on the map when no coordinates are given, and again whenever it is edited." If you know exactly where it is, click the map under Coordinates , or type Latitude and Longitude . A marker shows the spot. Press Create . The location's page opens. What happens next depends on what you gave: Coordinates make the location a point, set by hand. An address you typed is kept as written and not looked up. An address and no coordinates : EiN looks the address up in the background, a few seconds after you press Create . Reload the location's page to see the answer: a circle with a radius of 50 m on the building, a list of suggestions to choose from, or still "No location set yet." when nothing matched. See Where a location's position comes from . Only a name : EiN looks up the name the same way. A name such as Falmouth brings suggestions at best, because a name has no house number or postcode to confirm the answer. Tip A point is an exact spot with no area, so no picture joins it. For a home, a church or a town, give the location a circle or a polygon; see Draw a circle or a polygon . A point can be turned into a circle there too. If the dialog says "Give both latitude and longitude, or neither.", fill in the other half or empty both. The page's web address is made from the name, /locations/the-cottage-at-malpas for the example, so two locations whose names give the same web address cannot both exist. When the dialog reports an error for that reason, choose another name.

p.h: Where a location's position comes from
p.x: A location gets its place on the map from the first of these that gives one: Set by hand. A circle or polygon drawn in Edit location , or coordinates given when the location was created. Nothing else ever moves it. Its pictures. When at least two geotagged pictures are linked to the location directly, by hand in the terminal, EiN puts a circle around them, as wide as they spread. A picture far from the rest is left out, and pictures spread wider than 25 km give no circle. Pictures that joined the location because they lie inside its shape do not count. Where a track stayed. A location EiN made for a stay in a track (see Places a track stayed at ) has a circle with a radius of 150 m around where the track lay. Its pictures replace it once they give a circle. Its address. EiN asks OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service where the address is, or where the name is when there is no address. EiN uses the answer by itself only when the answer is a building, the house number or postcode you wrote agrees with it, and no answer that ranks almost as high lies more than 250 m away. The location then gets a circle with a radius of 50 m, and its City and Country are filled in. A less certain answer is kept as up to five suggestions for you to choose from. Source Badge on the card Line on the Info tab Set by hand set by hand "Set by hand" Its pictures from N photos "Derived from N geotagged photos spread over N m" A stay from a track "A stay on a track" Its address from address "Geocoded from the address" An address is looked up in Sweden first, and in the rest of the world when Sweden has no match. A location with only a name is looked up worldwide. For a place abroad, write the town and the country in the address, so that a street of the same name in Sweden does not win. When you change the address of a location that was placed from its address, EiN looks up the changed address. If it cannot be placed with certainty, the location loses its old position and shows suggestions instead, or "No location set yet." when nothing matched. A location placed from its pictures stays where its pictures are, and a location set by hand keeps its shape whatever the address says.

Where a track lay still, EiN puts the stay at a location, so that its trips say where they went (see Trips ). Each stay goes to the first of these: A home base. A stay at one of the track's home bases is at that home's location. A location near it. A stay within 150 m of a location's position is at that location: a harbour you have stayed at before, or a location you made yourself. A new location. Otherwise EiN makes a location there and names it after what OpenStreetMap has within 500 m: a marina or harbour first, then a boatyard (a name ending in "varv"), then an island or islet, then a bay, the nearest of each kind. A harbour named only "Gästhamn", "Småbåtshamn", "Marina" or a similar word is passed over. With none of these near, the location is named after the town or village around it. The next stay within 150 m of it is at it too. A new location gets a circle with a radius of 150 m, so the pictures taken inside it join it as pictures join any location (see How pictures join a location ). When you rename such a location in Edit location , your name stays, whatever track stays there later. Out at sea, where nothing has a name, a stay gets no location. When a lookup fails, because OpenStreetMap's services are busy or out of reach, the stay is looked up again the next time the track's trips are found again. EiN keeps what the services answered, in /archive/sources/places , so each place is asked about once. It asks OpenStreetMap for the harbours, islands and bays of an area about 5 km across at a time, and every later stay in that area, in any track, is named without going online. So is a place where nothing had a name, and a location you deleted that a stay needs again. Only track-places --rename asks again.

p.h: The weather at a place and time
p.x: EiN can look up what the weather was at a place and an hour: the air temperature, the wind's speed and the direction it blew from, and how much of the sky was covered by cloud. It can also tell the weather ahead ( The weather ahead ). Every lookup sends the place and the date to a weather service; an administrator who does not want that turns off Look up the weather ( CFG_WEATHER ) in Settings → System , under Places . Each value comes from the first of these that has it: The nearest SMHI weather station that measured it then, if one is within 30 km. SMHI is the Swedish meteorological institute, so this is the weather actually observed, in Sweden and just across its borders. Not every station measures everything: the wind may come from one station and the cloud from another, a little farther away. SMHI station distance ( CFG_WEATHER_SMHI_KM ) sets how far a station may be; 0 leaves SMHI out. Open-Meteo , for everywhere else and for an hour the station missed. It gives ERA5, a reconstruction of the weather from 1940 until a few days ago, for squares of 0.25 degrees, about 28 km from north to south. It is close to what was observed over open country and the sea, and less so in mountains and along a broken coast. The value is the one of the whole hour nearest the time asked about. A time still to come has no weather. weather with --to answers every hour from one time to another, and with --days every hour of the last few days, at most 31 days, a line each, the way a log is printed. That is what the assistant draws a chart of when you ask for the temperature over a week. --place names the place instead of its coordinates, and sends the name to Nominatim to find it: # in EiN's terminal weather 57.71 11.97 2026-10-30T00:00 --to=2026-11-06T00:00 weather --place=Göteborg --days=7 EiN keeps what the services answered in /archive/sources/weather : a station's values a year at a time, and Open-Meteo's a month at a time. The first lookup near a station fetches its whole history of that measurement, which can take a minute; every later hour there, in any year, is answered without going online. Answers kept there can be deleted: they are asked for again when needed. A photo or video with a place and a date gets the weather of that hour at that place, shown under the map in the viewer's details ( The details panel ). It is looked up once the picture's place is known, and again when someone moves the picture. A picture whose date changed, and the pictures already in the archive, get theirs from the background check that closes the gaps the pipelines missed ( Close gaps the pipelines missed ). In the terminal, weather-photo '<file>/position' looks one up, and -f looks it up again. A track's trips get their weather this way too: each whole hour of a trip, the weather where the track was then, summed up for each day and for the whole trip on the album made of it ( The Trip tab ). A trip is looked up once it has been found in the track, and again for a week after each day, since the last hours are sometimes observed later.

weather-forecast gives the weather at a place now and ahead: the kind of weather, the temperature and what it feels like, rain and snow with the chance of any, the wind and its gusts, and the sunrise and sunset of each day. It reads the hours from the one under way ( --hours , 24 unless you give it) and the days from today ( --days , 7 unless you give it, at most 16), in the place's own time. It comes from Open-Meteo's forecast, which takes the best of the national weather models for the place, and needs the same Look up the weather setting as the rest. The forecast is kept for ten minutes, so many screens showing it ask once. The weather card for a dashboard ( On a dashboard ) shows it. # in EiN's terminal weather-forecast --place=Göteborg --days=3 --hours=12 weather-forecast --lat=48.85 --lng=-3.01

The header shows the location's name and address, the people who live there, and its labels. If you may change the location, it also has Share , Edit and a ⋮ menu with Add event and Move to trash . On a phone all of these are in the ⋮ menu. Sharing a location works as for anything else; see Sharing . The Info tab puts who lived here, and when, beside where the place lies and the shape that decides which pictures belong to it. Tab What it shows Info The location's timeline, and beside it its place, everyone who has lived there and its description. The page opens here. Map The location's shape and the pictures linked to it, on a map that fills the window Media The pictures linked to the location, newest first, in month sections The page's web address keeps the tab, for example /locations/the-cottage-at-malpas?tab=media , so you can link straight to it.

On the left is the location's timeline : its residents moving in and out, its own events and the albums with photos taken there, newest first. When it has none, it says "Nothing recorded at <location> yet. Residents with dates, and albums with photos taken here, appear on its timeline." On the right, and above the timeline on a phone: Place lists the address as written, the full address the lookup found when that differs ( Found as ), the city and country, and the Position : the coordinates of its centre with On the map , which opens the Map tab, and where the position came from, such as "Set by hand". Area gives the shape: "Circle, radius 300 m", "Polygon, 6 corners", or "A point, which holds no pictures". Photos counts the pictures linked to the location and the years they span. Residents lists everyone who has lived there, with their dates; see Residents and events . With nobody recorded, it says "No known residents." About shows the description, when there is one. A location with no place says "Not placed yet" under Position . If you may change the location, Location on map beside it opens Edit location . When the lookup left suggestions, it says how many, with a link to them on the Map tab; see Pick from suggested locations .

The Map tab draws the location's shape on a map that fills the window. The Map tab shows the location's circle, polygon or point and the pictures linked to it that have a position. The map opens fitted to both and fills the window below the tabs, as an album's Map tab does: opening it shrinks the header down to its row of tabs, so the mouse wheel over the map zooms it rather than scrolling the page. Scroll up over the tabs to bring the header back. A picture on its own is drawn as its thumbnail; choose it to open it in the viewer. Pictures close together form a pile with a count. Choose it to list them in N photos here . The layers button in the corner switches between Map , Dark map and Satellite . A location with no place, no suggestions and no pictures with a position says "No location set yet." instead of a map. If you may change the location, Location on map under it opens Edit location .

The Media tab lists every picture linked to the location; see How pictures join a location . You can select pictures and open them in the viewer as in an album, and the selection bar offers Set time . With nothing linked, the tab says "No photos here yet. Geotagged photos inside its area are linked to it automatically." For a location with no place yet, it says "No photos here yet. Once it has a location, geotagged photos inside its area are linked to it automatically."

When the lookup found candidates but was not sure, the location's Map tab shows numbered pins and, over the foot of the map, a Suggested locations list: "Geocoding was not confident enough to place this automatically. Pick the right one, or set it by hand." Each row has the place's full name, its kind (such as city or house ) and its coordinates. Pointing at a row lights up its pin, and the other way round. The Info tab says how many there are under Position , with a link to them. Open the location's Map tab. Click the numbered pin that looks right, or its row in the list. The location gets a circle with a radius of 50 m at that spot, marked "Geocoded from the address", and the suggestions disappear. If none of them is right, press None of these — place it by hand under the list. It opens Edit location , where you draw the shape yourself. Only someone who may change the location can pick a suggestion. Everyone else sees the list.

p.h: Draw a circle or a polygon
p.x: You need permission to change the location. Open the location and press Edit , or Location on map when it has no place yet. The Edit location dialog has the fields on one side and On the map on the other. Choose Circle or Polygon above the map. Draw the shape: Circle : click the map to place the centre. The circle starts with a radius of 250 m. Drag the pin to move it, and drag the round handle on its right-hand edge to make it larger or smaller. Polygon : click the map once for each corner. Drag a corner to move it, click one of the small handles halfway along a side to add a corner there, and right-click a corner to remove it. A polygon needs at least three corners. Press Save . The hint under the map repeats how the chosen mode works. When the location has suggestions, they show on this map as numbered pins, for reference only. After Save , the location is "Set by hand". Within a few seconds, the library's pictures inside the shape are linked to it, and pictures it no longer covers are let go. Open the Media tab to see them. Make the shape cover everywhere pictures of the place were taken: the garden, the jetty below the house, the whole village. A circle from an address is only 50 m around the building. Good to know: Switching between Circle and Polygon clears what you drew. To start a shape again, switch to the other mode and back. Clicking the map does not move a circle that is already there. Move it by its pin. A location that is a point opens as a circle of 250 m around it. Move the pin or the handle and press Save , and the location becomes that circle. The dialog cannot take a location off the map. That is done in the terminal; see In the terminal . If saving fails, the dialog stays open with the reason: "a polygon needs at least three corners" or "a location needs a name".

p.h: Change a location's name, address or description
p.x: Press Edit on the location. The Edit location dialog has these fields beside the map: Field Notes Name Required. A changed name shows everywhere; the page's web address stays the same. Address "As it was written down. A changed address is looked up on the map again, unless the location was set by hand." City Filled in when EiN places the location from its address by itself. You can type it yourself. Country As for City . Description Free text, with Markdown. Labels One word each. A label on a location opens a search for that label when clicked. Emptying a field other than Name removes it. Save stays greyed out until you change something. After an address change, EiN says "Saved. The new address is looked up in the background; a location set by hand is kept." Reload the page after a few seconds to see where the lookup put it.

You do not file pictures into a location. EiN links them by these rules: A picture inside a shape is linked to it. A picture in the library with a position, from its GPS or set by hand, that falls inside a location's circle or polygon is linked to that location. This happens when the picture gets its position, and again whenever the location's shape changes. A picture has one location. When it falls inside several shapes, as a picture taken in Highbury lies inside both Highbury and London, it goes to the location whose centre is nearest. London's Media tab therefore does not list the pictures linked to Highbury. A point contains nothing. A location that is only a point collects no pictures. A changed shape moves the links. Pictures the shape no longer covers are let go, or go to another location that covers them. A link made by a person stays. A link made by hand in the terminal is never replaced by one of these. To put pictures in a location, give them a position inside it. Select them, press Set location and choose the location under A known location : the pictures take the location's centre as their position, and join it when it has a circle or a polygon. The steps are in Set the place of pictures .

Residents on the Info tab lists everyone who has lived at the location. Anyone who may change the location can add residents and correct their dates there with Add resident , choosing Person already here or New person and giving Moved in and Moved out . A resident without a Moved out date counts as living there, is marked current when it has a Moved in date, and appears in the header. The same records are a person's homes, seen from the other side: see Add a resident to a location . Under ⋮, Add event writes a dated note on the location, which appears on its timeline on the Info tab. A location's event needs both a Date and a Description ; see Events of albums, locations and cameras .

p.h: Move a location to the trash
p.x: If you may change the location, open ⋮ and choose Move to trash . EiN returns you to the Locations page and says "<name> moved to the trash", with Undo . You can also restore it from Trash in the account menu, for as many days as an administrator keeps the trash; see Your profile, favourites and trash .

Open Map in the sidebar, under Explore . The map fills the page, with no header. Pictures, locations and the routes of the tracks share one map, narrowed by the search box and the years under it. The map draws three things: Pictures with a position that you may see, gathered into piles. Pictures in staging are left out until they are filed. Locations that have a place, as pins. GPS tracks , the routes of the devices' tracks . Opened from the sidebar, the map starts over Gothenburg in Sweden, whatever your pictures show. Zoom out to find them, or keep a bookmark of the view you use; see Share or bookmark a view .

Drag the map to move it, and zoom with the mouse wheel or by pinching. The map has no zoom buttons, and clicking a pile never zooms: it opens the pile. A small spinner under the buttons in the top-right corner shows while the map reads what is in view after you move it. It does not show while the map follows a live track.

A single picture is drawn as its thumbnail, and pointing at it shows its file name. Click it to open the viewer . The arrow keys then move through the other single pictures on the map. A pile is several pictures close together, drawn as one of them with the count on it. Pointing at it says "N photos — click to browse". Click it to open N photos here : the pictures behind it in month sections, with the spot's coordinates under the title. Open one in the viewer, or select pictures as in an album. The browser's Back, or a phone's back gesture, closes it and leaves you on the map. List the N photos in this view , the button with four squares in the top-right corner, opens every picture in view the same way, titled "N photos in this view". It shows while pictures are drawn and the view holds some. Piles depend on the zoom: zoom in, and a pile splits into smaller piles and single pictures.

p.h: Locations and tracks on the map
p.x: Location pins stand at each location's centre. Click a pin to open the location's page. The pins are hidden while the search box narrows the map; the years do not hide them. Tracks are routes recorded by trackers, phones and GPS loggers, as coloured lines, one colour per day. Each track has three colours of its own that its days take in turn, so two days in a row differ, and other tracks use other colours. Pointing at a line shows the track's name and the day. Where a track lay still, it ends on that spot and leaves from it later, without the wandering its GPS recorded meanwhile; see The route on the map . Tracks are always drawn in full: the years and the search box narrow the pictures only. Where tracks come from, GPX files among them, is on Trips .

A track that a tracker or a phone is adding its position to as it moves is live while its last point is under four hours old. The map then draws a pin where it is now and extends its line as new points arrive, without a reload. Pointing at the pin shows the track's name, its speed in km/h and how long ago the point was taken ("12 km/h · 40 s ago"). The live tracks are also listed in the top-left corner, each with its colour, name, speed and age. Click a name to open its device's page. Click Follow (the crosshair beside a track), or the track's pin, and the map moves along with it, keeping its newest point in view; zooming does not stop it. Drag the map, or click Follow again, to stop. A track drops out of the list four hours after its last point. Live tracks are drawn with the other tracks: they show while Show is on All or Tracks .

The funnel button at the top of the right-hand corner is the Show menu: Choice Draws All Pictures, locations and tracks Media Pictures only Locations Location pins only Tracks Tracks only While one layer is chosen, the button shows that layer's icon instead of the funnel.

The button under it, Map style , opens a column of previews, each showing the place you are looking at in one style. Pointing at a preview names it, and clicking it changes the map: Style What it is Map OpenStreetMap's street map with OpenSeaMap's buoys, lights and beacons, the default Dark map A dark grey map from Esri Satellite Aerial photographs from Esri The Map tabs of a location and of an album have their own style button in the corner, with the same three styles.

Under the search box is a slider for the years, with the first year of the range drawn at its left and the last at its right. Drag either handle, and the map reads again when you let go. While the slider narrows the map, the two years turn white; with both handles at the ends, nothing is narrowed. Only years with pictures take room on the slider, so the decades most pictures come from get most of its length.

The box at the foot of the map reads "Search this view — type @ for a person, location or label". Type what you are looking for. Words find pictures by what they show or contain, as on the Media page. @ opens a list of people, locations and labels to pick from: type @peg and choose Peggy Wrenfield, for example. Press Enter or the arrow at the right of the box. Nothing changes while you type. The map then draws only the matching pictures in view and hides the location pins. For words, the 500 best matches in view are drawn. The box takes one person, one location and one label; when you pick a second person, the last one counts. A location finds the pictures linked to it. Except on a phone, an info icon beside the box shows what the box understood. To show everything again, empty the box and press Enter . Finding pictures by what they show needs the media service; see What needs the media service and a language model .

The address bar holds the whole view, so a bookmark or a link you send opens the same map, and a reload keeps it. These parts of the address are the map's: Part What it holds c The centre, as latitude and longitude z The zoom layers Which of media , locations and tracks are on; absent for all from , to The years base The map style; absent for Map q , person , location , tag What the search box holds For example, /map?c=50.244,-5.027&z=14&layers=media&from=1968&to=1975 shows the pictures taken around the cottage at Malpas from 1968 to 1975. Every address of the Web UI is listed on Addresses in the Web UI .

p.h: Where the maps and addresses come from
p.x: The map pictures, the address lookups and the weather come from outside services. Your photos, videos and recordings are never sent to them. What From What is sent The Map style, and the small maps on cards OpenStreetMap's tile servers, tile.openstreetmap.org Your browser asks for the map squares of the area you look at The sea marks on the Map style and cards OpenSeaMap, tiles.openseamap.org The same The Dark map and Satellite styles Esri, server.arcgisonline.com The same A location's position from its address OpenStreetMap's Nominatim, nominatim.openstreetmap.org The machine EiN runs on sends the location's address, or its name Pictures' street addresses Nominatim The machine EiN runs on sends each picture's coordinates The names of places a track stayed at OpenStreetMap's Overpass API, overpass-api.de , and Nominatim The machine EiN runs on sends the corners of each new area, about 5 km across, and the point of a stay with no harbour, island or bay near it The weather at a place and time, unless turned off SMHI's observations, opendata-download-metobs.smhi.se , and Open-Meteo, archive-api.open-meteo.com The machine EiN runs on asks SMHI for its list of stations and a station's values, which says roughly where; it sends Open-Meteo the place, to 0.25 degrees, and the month Without an internet connection, the maps have no background, while pins, thumbnails and tracks are still drawn, and addresses cannot be looked up. For administrators: the public Nominatim service answers one request a second, and EiN paces its own requests to that, and its Overpass requests to one every 1.1 seconds. The environment variable NOMINATIM_SEARCH_URL points the address lookups at another Nominatim server, such as one of your own, and NOMINATIM_REVERSE_URL the lookups from coordinates. OVERPASS_URL lists the Overpass servers, separated by spaces, which EiN takes in turn when one is busy. SMHI and Open-Meteo are asked at most once a second each; SMHI_METOBS_URL and OPEN_METEO_ARCHIVE_URL point the weather lookups at other servers. See Environment variables .

Locations are ordinary nodes, and these commands work on them in the terminal . Each links to its reference entry. Task Command List the locations with their coordinates location-list See a location's shape position-get <location> Give a location a point or a circle ( --polygon for a polygon) position-set <location>/position --lat=… --lng=… [--radius=…] Take a location off the map position-set <location>/position --clear Mark a shape as set by hand, as Save does geocode-location <location> --drawn Look an address up again, even for a placed location geocode-location --force <location> Place a location again from its pictures or its address location-locate --force <location> Change the name, address, city, country or description location-update Link the pictures inside a location's shape at once location-link-media --location <location> Put a track's stays at locations, and name the new ones track-places <track> , --dry-run to see them first Look the names of a track's stay locations up again track-places <track> --rename , which asks the services again; names changed by hand are kept The weather at a place and time weather <lat> <lng> <time> , such as weather 59.33 18.07 2024-07-14T15:00 To turn the point "Islington Town Hall" into a circle with a radius of 150 m, the way the dialog does it: # in EiN's terminal position-set /archive/locations/Islington_Town_Hall/position --lat=51.5416 --lng=-0.1028 --radius=150 geocode-location /archive/locations/Islington_Town_Hall --drawn Write negative coordinates with = , as --lng=-0.1028 , so they are not read as an option; for weather that is weather --lat=50.24 --lng=-5.03 1972-08-12T14:00 . A time without an offset, such as +02:00 , is UTC. How to link one picture to a location by hand is in Dates and places of pictures .

A location stays at "No location set yet." The lookup found nothing for its address. Edit the address so it has a house number, a postcode, the town and, abroad, the country, or draw its shape yourself. It shows suggestions although the address is right. The address has no house number or postcode to confirm the answer, or two places share the name. Pick the right one, or press None of these and draw it. Its circle is on the wrong building or in the wrong town. Draw it yourself with Edit . A shape set by hand is never moved by a lookup. Pictures taken there are not on its Media tab. Look for the cause in this order: the location is a point, which contains nothing: give it a circle or a polygon; the pictures have no position: give them one with Set location , as in Set the place of pictures ; they lie inside another location whose centre is nearer, such as a house inside a town, and are on that location's Media tab; they were linked to another location by hand or by the import, which is never replaced; they are still in staging: file them into an album first; you drew the shape a moment ago: wait a few seconds and open the Media tab again. The page shows the old position after you changed the address. The lookup runs in the background. Reload the page after a few seconds. A location set by hand does not move for an address. Edit, Share and the ⋮ menu are missing. You may not change this location. Ask whoever owns it to share it with you; see Sharing . The map is grey, with thumbnails and pins but no streets. Your browser cannot reach the tile servers: you are offline, or a network filter blocks tile.openstreetmap.org or server.arcgisonline.com . The Map page shows no pictures. It opens over Gothenburg; zoom out. Check that Show is on All or Media , that the year slider's handles are at the ends, and that the search box is empty. The location pins are gone from the map. The search box narrows the map, or Show is on Media or Tracks . A track ignores the year slider. Tracks are always drawn in full; only the pictures are narrowed. A live track's pin stays where it was. Its last point is older than you expected: the tracker or phone has stopped sending, or cannot reach EiN. The age beside its name says when the point was taken. weather answers "weather lookups are turned off". An administrator has turned off Look up the weather ; turning it on again lets EiN ask. The weather of a place in Sweden comes from Open-Meteo. No SMHI station within 30 km measured that value at that hour: the stations near it opened later, closed earlier, or did not measure it. Older stations often measured wind only three times a day. The first weather lookup near a station takes a minute. It fetches the station's whole history; later lookups there are immediate. The map jumps back after you zoom. You are following a track; drag the map or click Follow to stop.

Dates and places of pictures : a picture's position, street address, and Set location Family tree, events and homes : homes, residents and events Trips : the tracks the map draws, and their trips Search and the finder : finding pictures by location with @ Albums : an album's Map and Info tabs Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the place section of the details panel

A camera is what took pictures for your archive: a camera, a phone, a scanner or a camcorder. This page is for family members and administrators who register cameras, say who owned them and set their clocks right. Where a phone or a GPS tracker went is its device's track, on Devices and Trips .

p.h: What registering a camera gives you
p.x: EiN reads the camera's name out of every picture, but until the camera is registered that is all it knows: the viewer shows the make and model the file names, and nothing else. Once a camera is registered, the pictures it took are linked to it, and: the viewer's camera line names the camera, links to its page and says who owned it (see The details panel ); the camera's page gathers everything it took, who owned it and when, and the device it is part of, such as a phone, if it has one; an album's Info tab lists the cameras that took its pictures, and its Map tab draws the tracks of the devices they are part of (see Albums ); the Search page finds cameras and narrows albums by them, and @ in a search box picks one to keep the pictures it took (see Search and the finder ); the camera's Timezone , Clock is off by , Scanner or digitizer and Video times in UTC settings correct the dates of every picture it took.

When a file arrives, EiN reads what the camera wrote into it: the make (the EXIF tag Make ), the model ( Model ) and, when the camera writes one, its serial number ( SerialNumber , InternalSerialNumber or DeviceSerialNo ). Some camcorders write the make and model as DeviceManufacturer and DeviceModelName instead. These three together are the file's fingerprint , and EiN looks for the registered camera that has the same one: a camera with the same serial number; otherwise, a camera with the same make and the same model, also when the file carries a serial number that no camera has. The camera's name plays no part. The make and model are compared exactly as the camera writes them, so a camera registered with the make Nikon does not match files that say NIKON CORPORATION . EiN does this when it first reads the file, when you register the camera and when you change its make, model or serial number: registering a camera, or giving it a new fingerprint, links the files already in the archive that carry it. Link existing media on its page looks again for any it missed (see Link the files a camera missed ). Two things a fingerprint cannot do: Tell two phones of the same model apart. A serial number identifies one camera body; a make and model identify only a model line, and most phones write no serial number. If two people in the family have the same phone model, EiN cannot tell their pictures apart, and all of them are linked to one of the two cameras. Match a file that names no camera. Many messaging apps remove the make and model from the pictures they send, and a file without them matches nothing. You can link such files by hand in the terminal (see From the terminal ). A camera's fingerprint has nothing to do with the fingerprints EiN takes of the pictures themselves to find copies; those are described in Duplicates .

A camera on the network that the Automation module drives ( A camera ) is a device under Devices , and the archive makes it a camera here too, linked to the device, the first time it sees a face. Under it, in faces/ with a folder a day, is the picture of each face the camera saw, as the face was clearest, named for the time it was seen. Those pictures are the archive's like any other: their faces join people or start unidentified ones ( Faces a camera sees ), and they turn up in search. Beside them, in clips/ with a folder a day, is a video of each visit: the camera's sharpest stream from five seconds before a face came into view until ten seconds after the last face was gone, named for the time it starts. Someone who stays is one clip, up to two minutes. The video is the camera's own picture and sound, not made again, and it is the archive's like any other: it gets its stills, a version the browser plays, the faces in it and a place on the timeline at the time it was recorded. Nothing is recorded between visits. Two settings on the camera, in Edit camera (see Change a camera's settings ), decide the clips; its page shows them under Clips : Clips : Around a face (the default), Around a face or motion , where anything that moves in the picture makes a clip too, or Off . Keep clips (days) : how many days of clips are kept, 30 unless you change it. Every hour, the days older than that are removed; 0 keeps every clip. The faces' pictures are kept whatever it says. camera-clip front-door in the terminal records a clip now, from five seconds ago until ten seconds on ( --post 30 for thirty), filed with the others; an automation can run it, such as when the doorbell is pressed.

Open Cameras in the sidebar, under Browse . Every registered camera with the picture that stands for it; the badges show at a glance which ones carry a serial number, a time zone or the scanner setting. The header counts the registered cameras ( 13 cameras ). The filter box ( Filter cameras… ) matches the name, make, model and serial number as you type. Show switches between Registered (N) and Unregistered , the cameras EiN has seen in the pictures that match no registered camera. Sort offers Name (A-Z) (the default), Name (Z-A) and Make / model . Your choice is remembered in this browser. It has no effect on the unregistered list. Each card shows the camera's cover, its name, its description or else its make and model, and badges: the serial number, the time zone, scanner and video UTC . Click a card to open the camera's page . When nothing is registered yet, the page says No cameras registered yet : "The cameras and phones that took the pictures. Unregistered lists the ones the archive has already seen." with Show unregistered and, when you are signed in, New camera .

p.h: Register a camera EiN has already seen
p.x: The quickest way to register a camera is from the pictures it took. On the Cameras page, choose Show → Unregistered . The first time in a visit, EiN looks through the files it has read for cameras that match nothing registered. The list reads: "Cameras found in the indexed media that match nothing in the registry. Registering one lets its photos be linked to it, and its timezone and owners apply." Find the camera. Each card shows a suggested name (the model, with the make in front when the model does not start with it, such as Canon EOS 7D or Panasonic DMC-TZ1 ), the make and model, the serial number when there is one, and how many files it took ( N files ). The cameras with the most files come first. Click Register on its card. The Register Camera dialog opens with Name , Make , Model and Serial number filled in from the files. Change Name to what the family calls the camera, such as David's 7D . Leave Make , Model and Serial number as they are: they are what the files are matched on. Under Timezone , choose the time zone its clock was set to, and turn on Scanner or digitizer or Video times in UTC if they apply (see Clocks, time zones and scanners ). Click Register . The files the camera took are linked to it and dated by its settings, and the camera's page opens. The more files carry its fingerprint, the longer this takes: some minutes for a camera with tens of thousands of pictures. Rescan at the top of the unregistered list looks again, for instance after a large import. When every camera is registered, the list says "Every camera the media names is registered (N files matched)." With many unknown cameras it shows the most used ones and says "Only the most-used cameras are listed; there are more."

p.h: When a card says "registered as …, but unmatchable"
p.x: Sometimes a camera with that name already exists, but without the make, model or serial number its files carry, so nothing is matched to it. Its card then has the badge registered as <name>, but unmatchable and the button Add fingerprint instead of Register , because registering would make a second copy of a camera EiN already knows. Click Add fingerprint . EiN writes the make, model and serial number from the card into the existing camera and links the files they identify. When it is done, a message says "Linked N files to <name>." or "<name> now carries the fingerprint, but no unclaimed files matched it." This is quick for a camera with a serial number and slow for one known only by its make and model, which can take minutes in a large archive. The button is there only if you may change that camera; otherwise the card has no button.

Register a camera by hand when EiN has not seen it in any picture yet: a scanner before the scans arrive, or a camera whose files you are about to import. Open the Create menu (the plus in the top bar) and choose Camera , or click New camera on an empty Cameras page. The Register Camera dialog opens. Fill in the fields below. Only Name is required. Click Register . The camera's page opens. With a serial number, or both a make and a model, the files already in the archive that carry them are linked to it first. Field What to enter Name What the family calls it, such as Helen's scanner . The name also gives the camera's folder in the tree, so two cameras cannot have the same name. Make "As the camera writes it in exif: what files are matched on." For example Canon . Model "As the camera writes it in exif." For example Canon EOS 5D Mark III . Serial number "Tells one body apart, where make and model tell only the model." Optional. Timezone "The zone its clock was set to." Optional. Scanner or digitizer "Its EXIF camera dates describe digitisation, not when the photograph was taken." Video times in UTC "Its videos keep their recording time in UTC, as phones do." To copy the make and model exactly, open a picture the camera took in the viewer and open Details at the foot of the details panel. Among the EXIF tags it lists are Make , Model and, when the camera writes one, SerialNumber (see The Details section ). A camera without a serial number and without both a make and a model is never matched to any file. Its page says so: "No serial and no make/model — nothing is matched to this camera automatically; camera-link --camera links files to it by hand." Anyone signed in can register a camera. Changing it afterwards, with the buttons this page describes, is offered to whoever may change it, which the camera's Share dialog shows and sets (see Sharing ).

Click a card on the Cameras page, or the camera's name in the viewer. The page's address is /cameras/ and the camera's folder name, such as /cameras/ruby-iphone for Ruby's iPhone, and the Media tab adds ?tab=media . A camera registered in the Web UI is named after itself, with _ for spaces and no punctuation: David's 7D would be /cameras/Davids_7D . Under the name, the header shows the current owners (up to three, then "and N more"), how many files the camera took and in which years, such as 75 files · 2025–2026 ( N+ files when counting stopped at its limit), and the camera's labels. For those who may change the camera, the corner has Share and Edit , and the ⋮ menu has Add event and Move to trash . On a phone they are all under ⋮. A phone's camera: who owns it, the albums it took pictures for, and the phone it is part of. Tab What it shows Info The page opens here: the camera's timeline, and beside it its settings, owners, device and description (see below). Media Every file linked to the camera, by date. Select pictures to act on them from the selection bar, for example Add to album or Set time (see The selection bar ). On the Info tab, the timeline on the left is the camera's history: when each owner started and stopped using it, the events written on it, and the albums holding pictures it took. When it has none, it says "Nothing recorded for <camera> yet. Owners with dates, and albums with photos it took, appear on its timeline." On the right, and above the timeline on a phone: Camera lists Make, Model, Serial number, Timezone, "Clock off by" with the date it applies from, "Capture dates: Scanner dates suppressed" for a scanner and "Video times: UTC"; with nothing but a name it says "Nothing recorded beyond the name." Under them is Link existing media (see Link the files a camera missed ). Owners lists everyone who has owned it, with the dates (see Say who owned a camera ). Device links to the device the camera is part of, such as the phone, or says "It is part of no device." (see A phone that records where it was ). It is left out for those who may not change the camera when there is no device. About shows the description, when there is one. A camera whose clock was wrong by the same amount for all its pictures, or from some date on, is corrected with Clock is off by (see Clocks, time zones and scanners ). For a few pictures, the Media tab is the place: select them and use Set time , as Dates and places of pictures describes. Move to trash sends the camera to your trash, and the message's Undo brings it back (see Your profile, favourites and trash ).

p.h: Link the files a camera missed
p.x: Files are linked to their camera when EiN first reads them, when the camera is registered and when its make, model or serial number is changed. A file can still miss its camera, such as one that was read while linking was not running. Open the camera's page. The Info tab opens. Click Link existing media under Camera . The text under it explains: "Files are linked to their camera when they are indexed, when it is registered and when its make, model or serial number is changed. This looks again for the files that carry its fingerprint and are linked to no camera, such as one indexed while linking was not running." Wait for the message, such as "Linked 412 files and updated dates on 37.", or "Nothing new to link or update — every matching file already has this camera policy." Linking also dates the files again by the camera's settings, which is what "updated dates" counts. Files that are already linked to another camera are left with it. The button is shown only to those who may change the camera, and only when the camera has a serial number or both a make and a model. A camera that has both is looked for both ways. The more files carry its fingerprint, the longer it takes: some minutes for a camera with tens of thousands of pictures.

On the camera's page, click Edit . The Edit camera dialog opens. Change what you need: Name , Make , Model , Serial number , Timezone (a list of time zones you can type in, such as Pacific/Auckland ), Clock is off by and its From , Scanner or digitizer , Video times in UTC , Description and Labels ; and, for a camera that is a device with a stream, Clips and Keep clips (days) (see A security camera ). Click Save . A changed Timezone , Clock is off by , Scanner or digitizer or Video times in UTC re-dates every file already linked to the camera, and the page says "Re-dated N linked files.", or "Removed scanner dates from N linked files." when you turned the scanner setting on. A changed Make , Model or Serial number links the files already in the archive that carry the new fingerprint and are linked to no other camera, and the page says "Linked N files.", or "Linked N files and updated dates on M." when linking also re-dated files of the camera. A camera with a serial number is linked quickly; one known only by its make and model can take minutes in a large archive, and Save waits for it. Files linked under the old fingerprint stay linked.

Four settings tell EiN how to read a camera's dates. Each one applies to the files linked to the camera, and changing it re-dates them. Timezone : the time zone the camera's clock was set to. A camera's clock writes a time without a zone, and EiN reads it in this zone, with the summer time of the year the picture was taken. A zone the camera wrote into the file itself comes first. Without a Timezone , EiN uses the archive's own time zone. Set it for a camera bought abroad, or one left on home time during a trip: Helen's Coolpix stayed on London time when she took it to Wellington, and with its Timezone set to Europe/London , EiN reads its clock as London time and gets the moment of each picture right. Leave it empty for a phone, whose clock follows the local time wherever it is: its pictures carry their own zone or a GPS time, and the few that carry neither are read in the archive's time zone. Clock is off by : how far the camera's clock was ahead of the right time, such as +23h 2m for a clock set a day ahead and a little slow, or -5m for one five minutes behind; d , h , m and s count days, hours, minutes and seconds. EiN takes it off each picture's time before reading it in the camera's Timezone , or the archive's. Under From , give the date the clock was off from ( 2017 , 2017-06 or 2017-06-20 ), or leave it empty for all its pictures. Saving adds the setting to the ones before: a picture from before its date keeps the earlier setting, and 0 from a date says the clock was put right then. Edit shows the latest one, and the Info tab lists it. To find the amount, compare one of its pictures with another camera's from the same moment. Scanner or digitizer : the camera's clock records when a file was scanned, not when the photograph was taken, so EiN dates pictures neither by it nor by a date in the file names it gives them. Pictures with no other date stay undated until someone gives them one. Files brought in through a staging category of the kind Scans are treated as scans whatever camera made them; this setting matters for scans uploaded straight into an album, copied in over SFTP, or already in the library. Video times in UTC : phones keep their videos' recording time in UTC. Turn this on for a phone whose videos come out off by its time zone. Dates and places of pictures explains how EiN chooses a picture's date and time zone, and Date scans of old prints and slides how scans are dated. A camera's Timezone is about its clock alone. The days of a device's trips are cut in its track's own time zone, set on the device's Trips tab (see How a device travels ).

A camera can have several owners over the years. The viewer lists them under the camera's name, each with the dates, such as Owned by Ruby Wrenfield (2023–), so you can tell whose camera it was when a picture was taken. Open the camera's page. Owners is on the right of the Info tab, the tab it opens on. Click Add owner beside the heading. Under Person , choose the person. Fill in From and To as a year, a month or a day: 2005 , 2005-06 or 2005-06-20 . Leave To empty while they still own it, and leave both empty if you do not know the dates. Click Add owner . The list shows the current owners first, then the earlier ones, with their dates: "2019 – 2023", "since 2019", "until 2023", or "dates unknown". A current owner with a start date has the badge current . Use the pencil beside an owner to change the dates ( Save changes ), and the bin to remove them; EiN asks "Remove <person> as an owner of <camera>?" before it does. With no owner, it says "Nobody is recorded as owning this." An owner without a To date counts as a current owner, in the page's header and under Owners . Dated ownership appears on the camera's timeline, on the Info tab, as "<person> started using <camera>" and "<person> stopped using <camera>". A date that is not a year, month or day is refused with a message ending in "is not a date (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])". The owners' homes also count as the home bases of the track of the camera's device while the track has none of its own (see Home bases ).

p.h: A phone that records where it was
p.x: A phone can keep where it was as well as take pictures: it posts its position as it moves, or leaves a GPX file of its route. That route is the track of the phone as a device (see Where tracks come from ), and the phone's camera is part of that device. Link the camera to the device, and: the camera's page links to the device, under Device on the Info tab; an album with pictures the camera took draws the device's track on its Map tab (see Choose which devices the map shows ); a GPX file that names the camera, by its name, its make and model, or its serial number, goes to the device when it is dropped in staging (see GPX files in staging ); while the device's track has no home bases of its own, the homes of the camera's owners count (see Home bases ). To link it: Open the camera's page. Device is on the right of the Info tab, with the line "A phone's camera is part of the phone, whose track says where its pictures were taken." Click Set device , choose the device in the list ( Pick a device ), and click Set . The list holds the devices that keep a track. Change device picks another, and the cross beside the device ( Take the device away ) takes the link away; the device and its track stay as they are. Both are offered to those who may change the camera. A camera that records nowhere, such as Helen's Coolpix or a scanner, needs no device. A phone that is not a device yet is made by a member of the devices group (see A phone or a GPS tracker ).

p.h: Write something on a camera's timeline
p.x: To keep a story with a camera, such as where it was bought or when it broke, add an event: On the camera's page, open the ⋮ menu and choose Add event . Fill in Date (such as 2005-06-15 ) and Description ("What happened"). Both are needed. Written by is you unless you choose someone else. Click Add event . The event appears on the camera's timeline, on its Info tab. Events are described in full in Family tree, events and homes .

The picture on a camera's card and behind its page's header is its cover: the newest picture linked to it, by the date it was taken. The cover moves on by itself as newer pictures are linked. A camera that took only videos, such as a camcorder, gets the poster frame of its newest video once that video has been processed; recordings are never used. The card of a camera with no pictures shows a placeholder with its initials. The Web UI has no button to choose a camera's cover. In the terminal you can link a picture as the camera's coverPhoto yourself, and a cover chosen this way is kept. In the demo, Ruby's iPhone is the folder /archive/cameras/ruby-iphone : # in EiN's terminal ln -sf /archive/albums/wellington-christmas-2025/IMG_0650.HEIC /archive/cameras/ruby-iphone/coverPhoto To go back to the automatic cover, remove the link with rm /archive/cameras/ruby-iphone/coverPhoto and run camera-cover /archive/cameras/ruby-iphone .

What you see Why What to do The viewer shows only a make and model where the camera's name should be. The camera is not registered, or the picture was read while linking was not running. Register it from Unregistered , or click Link existing media on its page. A camera's Media tab says "Nothing is linked to this camera yet: no file carries its make and model or serial number. If files from it are missing, “Link existing media” on its Info tab looks again." No file names this camera as the camera has it, or its files were read while linking was not running. Compare its Make and Model with the Make and Model in a picture's Details , and Edit them to match; saving links the files. Otherwise click Link existing media on the Info tab. The Media tab says "Nothing is linked to this camera yet, and nothing can be: give it a serial number, or both a make and a model." The camera has no fingerprint. Edit it and fill in Make and Model exactly as the files have them; saving links the files. Link existing media finds nothing, but pictures from the camera are missing from its page. The make or model differs from what the files say; the files are linked to another camera; or they name no camera at all. Compare with the Make and Model in the viewer's Details . For files linked elsewhere or naming no camera, use camera-relink --force or camera-link --camera in the terminal. Pictures from two people's phones are mixed up on one camera. The phones are the same model and write no serial number. EiN cannot tell them apart. Link one person's pictures by hand with camera-link --camera . A camera's pictures are some hours off. Its clock was set to another time zone. Set its Timezone ; see Clocks, time zones and scanners . A phone's videos are off by exactly its time zone. The phone keeps video times in UTC. Turn on Video times in UTC for it. Scans are dated to the day they were scanned. The scanner is not registered with Scanner or digitizer . Register it with the setting on, or turn it on in Edit camera . Registering says camera-create: /archive/cameras/…: already exists . A camera with that name exists already. Punctuation such as an apostrophe is left out of the folder name, so Davids 7D and David's 7D clash. Choose another name, or open the existing camera. An album's map does not draw the route a phone recorded. The phone's camera is not linked to its device. Set device on the camera's Info tab; see A phone that records where it was . Edit , Link existing media , Add owner or Set device is missing. You may not change this camera. Ask the person who registered it, or an administrator.

Each camera is a folder under /archive/cameras ; ls /archive/cameras lists their names, and the link to the device a camera is part of is its child device . The commands below are in the archive command reference , and every one takes --help . Those that start with camera- can also be typed as two words: camera info is camera-info . Task Command List the cameras camera-list List the cameras seen but not registered camera-scan Find cameras by name, make, model or serial number search-camera <words> Which camera a make and model, or a serial number, is matched to camera-match --make <make> --model <model> , or --serial <serial> Register a camera camera-create --name <name> --make <make> --model <model> , with --serial , --timezone , --digitizer or --quicktime-utc Change a camera's settings camera-update <camera> --timezone <zone> , or --clear <field> Say how far a camera's clock was off, from a date camera-update <camera> --clock-offset=+23h2m --clock-from=2017-06 ; camera-info lists the settings Say what a security camera's clips are around, and keep them camera-update <camera> --clips face , motion or off , and --clip-days <days> (0 keeps them) Record a clip of a security camera now camera-clip <device> , with --post <seconds> Show a camera and its owners camera-info <camera> A camera's history camera-timeline <camera> Link the files a camera's fingerprint matches camera-relink <camera> ; --dry-run reports first, --force takes files from another camera, --all does every camera Date a camera's files again by its settings, linking nothing camera-relink <camera> --reapply Link files to a camera by hand camera-link --camera <camera> <file or folder>… Add an owner, or change the dates camera-set-owner <camera> <person> --from <date> --to <date> , with --update to change Remove an owner camera-remove-owner <camera> <person> Link a camera to the device it is part of, or take the link away camera-device <camera> <device> , or <camera> --off ; a device is its name, its path under /dev , or a track of it Bring a camera's automatic cover up to date camera-cover <camera> , or --all The pictures a camera took search --subject camera:<camera> --kind photo Registering Jon's camera and making him its owner: # in EiN's terminal camera-create --name "Jon's X-Pro1" --make FUJIFILM --model X-Pro1 --timezone Pacific/Auckland camera-set-owner /archive/cameras/Jons_X-Pro1 /archive/people/jon-wrenfield --from 2014 camera-create prints the camera's folder, /archive/cameras/Jons_X-Pro1 , and how many files it linked. See Commands by task for the rest of the archive's commands.

Trips : where phones and GPS trackers went, and their trips. Dates and places of pictures : how a picture's date, time zone and place are chosen. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the camera line in the details panel. Albums : the cameras on an album's Info tab.

A device that travels, such as a phone, a GPS tracker on a boat or a logger carried on walks, keeps where it was as a track: positions with their times. The Archive cuts the track into trips, says where they stayed and what the weather was, draws the route on its maps, and makes a trip an album, all on the device's Trips tab. This page is for family members and administrators who bring routes in, correct trips and make albums of them. The devices themselves are EiN's own, on Devices ; what took the pictures is on Cameras .

A track is a device's endpoint of the type track under /dev : the position that EiN's tracker driver keeps for a phone, a GPS tracker or a logger. Its positions come in two ways: Posted as the device moves. A phone with Traccar Client, or a tracker on a boat or in a car, posts its position to EiN with the device's key (see Report from a phone ). From GPX files a logger or a tracking app saved: written to the device, uploaded on its Trips tab, or dropped in staging (see GPX files ). A member of the devices group makes the device first, saying how it travels when it always travels the same way: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create Sailboat --driver tracker --class boat device-create 'Ruby phone' --driver tracker --class phone A track is named by its device's label: the sailboat's is called Sailboat. A phone that takes pictures as well is a camera too, and linking the camera to its device ties the two together (see A phone that records where it was ).

A device with a track has a Trips tab on its page, after Overview , History and Info . Its address is the device's page with ?tab=archive.trips , such as /devices/sailboat?tab=archive.trips . An album's Trip tab and a track's entry on a timeline open the device's page on it; a live track on the Map page, Device on a camera's Info tab and a device in an album's Info tab open the device's page as it opens. Each trip found in the track is a card, newest first, ready to become an album. At its top, Trips , Travel and Fixes choose what it shows: View What it shows Trips The view it opens on: the trips found in the track, newest first (see Trips ) Travel How the device travels, its home bases and its description (see below) Fixes The route on a map, with the positions EiN left out (see The route on the map ) Those who may change the track also get Upload GPX and How it travels beside them. That is the device's owner, whoever made it, and the administrator, who owns the devices a driver found; Devices and their keys says more. On Travel : Travel lists Travels as (its own setting, or the device's class, such as "Boat (the device's class)", or "Not set (read as a car)"), Timezone ( UTC when none is set), how many Positions it holds, the days it was Recorded over, such as "12 Jun 2025 – 3 Aug 2025", and its Path in the tree, such as /dev/sailboat/position . Home bases , where arriving ends a trip (see Home bases ). About shows the description, when there is one.

A device moves as a boat, a car, a bike or on foot, and that says which units its track is shown in: a boat's distances in nautical miles and its speeds in knots, everyone else's in kilometres and km/h. It also says what lying still looks like when the track is drawn (see The route on the map ): a boat lies still within 80 m for 15 minutes, a car or a bike within 50 or 30 m for 10 minutes, someone on foot within 25 m; and a jump faster than 50 knots, 250, 100 or 40 km/h is a GPS error. How it travels is the track's Travels as setting, or, while that is not set, the device's class when the class is boat , car , bike or foot . A track with neither is read as a car. A phone, carried on a sailing holiday and in the car alike, is best left as it is, and a tracker that stays on the boat made with --class boat . Its Timezone is the time zone its trips are cut into days in: a day ends at midnight there, and the times of its trips are on that clock. A track without one has its days in UTC. To change them: On the device's Trips tab, click How it travels . The How it travels dialog opens. Choose Travels as : "How it travels, which tells its stops from drift and its trips from rests. A boat’s track is shown in knots and nautical miles, the others’ in km/h and km. Without one, the device’s class says it." Choose Timezone , "The zone its trips are cut into days in.", from a list of time zones you can type in, such as Europe/Stockholm . Clear it for UTC. Write a Description if you like, and click Save . A changed Travels as or Timezone finds the track's trips again from the start, and so does a changed class of its device while Travels as is not set.

A track's home bases are the places it belongs: the boat's home berth and winter yard, the house where the car is parked. Arriving at one ends a trip. Home bases on the Travel view of the device's Trips tab lists them, each linking to its location, under the line "Where it belongs: a home berth, a winter yard, the house. Arriving at one ends a trip." Click Add home base , choose a location in the list ( Pick a location ), and click Add . A place that is not a location yet is added on the Locations page first (see Locations and the map ). Click the cross beside a home base to remove it. While a track has no home bases of its own, the homes of the owners of the cameras linked to its device count instead: each place an owner lived while they owned the camera, for the years both are true (see A phone that records where it was and Homes and residents ). It then says "None set, so the homes of the owners of its cameras count:" and lists them with those years, such as "2010 – 2020". With no such home either, it says "None set, and no owner of a camera linked to the device has a home recorded." As soon as the track has one home base of its own, the owners' homes no longer count. Adding and removing are offered to those who may change the track, and each finds the track's trips again from the start.

A track shows on the Fixes view of its device's Trips tab, on the Map page with its Tracks layer (see Locations and the map ), and on the Map tab of an album whose dates it falls in, when its device is on the album's list: a camera that took some of the album's pictures is linked to the device, or the device was added to the album (see Choose which devices the map shows ). A GPS tracker takes no pictures, so add it to the albums of the trips it was carried on. The device's own History tab draws its positions too, for a day, a week, a month or a year ( Devices ). Fixes draws the route on a map that takes most of the window below the device's header, each day in its own colour, as an album's Map tab does. A panel floats over the foot of the map with what the route adds up to: Figure What it is Points How many recorded positions the track holds, without those EiN rejected (see below). Days On how many days it recorded. Distance The length of the route, added up day by day, so the gap between one day's end and the next day's start is not counted. In nautical miles for a boat, in kilometres otherwise (see How a device travels ). Avg speed The average speed while it moved, in knots for a boat and km/h otherwise. Time lying still, jumps nothing could make, and gaps of more than an hour between two points are left out. Duration The time from the first point to the last, in hours and minutes. It includes the time between trips, so a track that holds several trips shows the whole span. While a tracker lies still, its GPS keeps wandering: around a berth or a parking space it records a tangle of positions, now and then one far out that it never went to. EiN draws neither. Where the track stayed in one place, at walking pace or slower, the line ends on the middle of where it lay and later leaves from there, and a position it could not have reached so fast is left out, unless you accepted it (see Reject or accept a position by hand ). What counts as staying and as too fast follows how its device travels (see How a device travels ). The Points figure still counts every recorded position, while Distance leaves the wandering out. The Map page and an album's Map tab draw tracks the same way. A GPS can also be wrong for longer than one position. A receiver that loses most of its satellites can draw a smooth route hundreds of kilometres away for minutes, and a phone that loses its fix falls back to a position a cell or a network gave it, sometimes the same one over and over. EiN keeps every position it is given, and as it adds them to a track it rejects such runs: a stretch the track jumps out to and back from, faster than anything on the ground or the water goes (over 600 km/h for more than a kilometre), within two hours; a position it jumps back onto exactly, to the last decimal, after being away from it longer than it was there. A rejected position is not drawn, counted in Points or used for trips. A jump that does not come back, as when a logger starts again somewhere else, keeps its positions, and the line is broken there instead of drawn across. A route flown with the logger on is neither: every one of its steps is fast. The same rules apply however the positions arrive: a GPX file uploaded or staged, or a phone tracking live. track-read --rejected reads the rejected positions too, marked, and track-read --only-rejected reads them alone. A long track is drawn from a thinned copy, and its distance then comes out a little shorter than the route really was. EiN draws a track on the maps; it does not use it to give a position to pictures that have none. To place those, see Dates and places of pictures . A track with no positions yet says Nothing recorded yet : "Its route appears here once a GPX file it was recorded in is uploaded, or the device reports where it is.", with Upload GPX under it for those who may change it.

p.h: Reject or accept a position by hand
p.x: The rules can be wrong both ways: a glitch they miss stays on the map, and a real stretch they reject, such as a flight with the logger off that lands near where it left, is left out. On Fixes the rejected positions are drawn faintly in red, each with a dot, and the panel over the map says how many there are. Click near a position, drawn or rejected, and the panel says when it was recorded and what EiN made of it. If you may change the track, it also offers: Reject , on a drawn position: it is left out, whatever the rules say, and so are the other drawn positions within 40 m of it that day (the day in UTC, as the track colours it). A point on the drawn line often stands for several positions recorded close together, and one taken away would let the next take its place. The panel says how many there are, and the button reads Reject all and the number. Over 25 is a place the track stayed at, not a glitch, and then Reject takes the one position alone. Accept , on a rejected one: it is drawn, whatever the rules say. When it is one of a run of rejected positions, Accept all takes the whole run. Undo , on a position you rejected or accepted: it goes back to what the rules make of it. Undo all N that day , on a position you rejected, when you rejected others that day: every position rejected by hand that day goes back to the rules. Positions you accepted stay accepted. A position rejected by hand is left out before the rules judge the positions around it, so the line can break somewhere else once it is gone. The track's trips are found again ten minutes later, as when points arrive. To do the same for a time span, use track-mark with --reject , --accept or --clear : # in EiN's terminal track-mark sailboat --from 2025-07-01T13:00:00Z --to 2025-07-01T15:30:00Z --accept --from and --to are both optional: without them the whole track is marked, so track-mark sailboat --clear hands every position back to the rules. --near <lat,lng> marks only the positions within 40 m of a point ( --within sets another distance in metres), and --marked reject or --marked accept only those you rejected or accepted. Undo all N that day is this: # in EiN's terminal track-mark sailboat --from 2025-07-01T00:00:00Z --to 2025-07-02T00:00:00Z --marked reject --clear

A tracker or a phone that posts its position as it moves adds it to its track as it comes (see Report from a phone ). While its last point is under four hours old, a Live line tops the panel with its speed in km/h and how long ago that point was taken ("12 km/h · 40 s ago"). The map then draws a pin where it is now and extends the route as points arrive. Click Follow , the crosshair at the end of that line, and the map keeps the newest point in view until you drag it. The Map page follows live tracks the same way; see Follow a track live .

A GPX file is the format GPS trackers and tracking apps save routes in. EiN reads the recorded track points of the file, each with its time; points with a time the track already has are not added twice, so bringing the same file in again changes nothing. A point without a time is left out, since EiN cannot tell when the track was there. A GPX file goes to a device: written to it, cat summer.gpx > /dev/sailboat in the terminal, the device's driver reads its points into the track (see GPX files on the Devices page). The Archive adds two ways, below, and keeps every GPX file it brings in in the track's routes folder, such as /dev/sailboat/position/routes/ , linked from the track's own sources folder. The same file brought in twice, byte for byte, is kept once.

p.h: Upload a GPX file to a device
p.x: If you know which device a file was recorded on, upload it on that device's page: Open the device's Trips tab. Upload GPX is at its top, beside the views. Click Upload GPX and choose one or more .gpx files. The file picker offers GPX files only. Wait for the message: "N new points added to the track", or "The track already had every point in it", followed by "; N without a time left out" when some were. A file that cannot be added gets a message of its own, starting with its name; the others are added all the same. The button is offered to those who may change the track. The file is kept with the track under its own name, in its routes folder.

A GPX file that arrives in your staging area, by Import media , the Media page's Upload or copying over SFTP (see Getting your photos in ), is not treated as a picture. EiN reads which device the file names and gives the route to that device; the file then moves out of staging into the device's track's routes folder. The file names its device in its creator attribute or in one of its <name> entries. It matches a device when one of these holds, as whole words, the device's label, its manufacturer and model together, or its serial number, or the name, the make and model together, or the serial number of a camera linked to the device (see A phone that records where it was ). Capital letters and punctuation do not count, and a name shorter than three letters never matches. A file whose creator reads Garmin eTrex 30x joins the device made with --manufacturer Garmin --model 'eTrex 30x' , one whose creator reads Apple iPhone 15 joins the phone whose camera has the make Apple and the model iPhone 15 , and one named Sailboat joins the sailboat. Either of these places counts: <gpx version="1.1" creator="Apple iPhone 15"> <metadata><name>Sailboat</name></metadata> <trk><name>Sailboat</name> …</trk> </gpx> A <name> inside a track point is a waypoint's label and does not count. Many apps write their own name as the creator ( Track Logger 2.1 ) and no device anywhere; such a file waits for you to choose its device, as below. When a file names no device, or more than one, it waits for you: Open Staging in the sidebar. A yellow box titled Needs you says "1 GPX file waits for the device it belongs to." (or how many), whichever category the file was dropped on. The box is on the overview, not on a category's page. Click Choose device . The page Routes waiting for a device opens, with your staging area's routes folder listed below its header as on the Nodes page, and a panel beside it. Click a file to see in the panel what it says about itself: its Name and Description , its Tracks , its Creator , when it was Recorded (first and last point, in UTC, and how long between), its Points , its Size , and under Matches the devices it names, or "no device it names". The arrow keys move from file to file. Select the files of one device: Ctrl and click adds or removes one, Shift and click takes a run of them, Ctrl + A takes them all. On a phone, press and hold a file, then tap the others. At the top of the panel, choose the device in the Device they come from list and click Import ( Import 3 files with three selected). Each route joins that device's track and its file moves out of the list into the track's routes folder. A file that cannot be read stays, and the panel names it and why. Back to staging returns to the staging page. On a narrow screen the panel is below the list. In the terminal, gpx-info says the same of any GPX file without importing it: gpx-info /home/<you>/staging/routes/*.gpx . If the device does not exist yet, have a member of devices make it first (see Where tracks come from ) and open the page again; a waiting file is not tried again by itself. Waiting files are kept in your staging area's routes folder, /home/<you>/staging/routes/ . Sorting in staging describes the staging area.

EiN cuts a track into trips by itself, and the Trips view of the device's Trips tab lists them, newest first. A trip runs from where the track lay still to where it lay still again: Arriving at one of the track's home bases ends a trip, once it has been there half an hour or the track ends there. Passing by does not. Staying anywhere else longer than three days ends a trip too (two days for a bike or on foot), as does a gap of that long with no points at all. A trip that never gets 500 m from where it started is not a trip, and is left out. How near a place has to be to count as the same place depends on how the device travels : within 1 km for a boat, 500 m for a car, 300 m for a bike and 200 m on foot. Each trip's card shows its dates, an Ongoing badge while it has not ended and its last point is less than two days old, how many days it took, its length, how far from its start it got, and where it started and ended: the location of the stay, such as a harbour, an island or your home, or "a point on the way". The farthest place it stayed at is named too. Click a name to open its location. How stays get their locations and names is on Places a track stayed at . A stay of two hours or more across midnight is an overnight stay; it does not end the trip. A trip that is an album names it under Album ; see Make a trip an album . Click N legs to see the trip day by day: each day's date, its first and last time, its length, and where the day ended. A day's length runs from where the day before ended, so a drive across midnight counts, and the days add up to the trip's length. Days follow the track's Timezone , so a day ends at midnight there, and the times are on that clock; a track without one has its days and times in UTC. The trips are kept up to date as the track grows: ten minutes after points arrive, EiN finds them again from where the last finished trip ended, puts the new stays at locations, and, unless weather lookups are turned off, gives each trip and day the weather along the track, which an album made of the trip shows ( The Trip tab ).
