Changing how the device travels (its Travels as or its class), its time zone or its home bases finds them again from the start. Find trips again does it at once. When the track has no trips, the view says No trips : "Nothing in the track went 500 m or more from where it started.", or, before they were ever looked for, "Trips are found in the track once it has fixes, and kept up to date as it grows.", with Find trips for those who may change the track.

EiN may end a trip where you do not: a weekend at home in the middle of a holiday, or a long wait for weather in a harbour. Those who may change the track can correct it: Join to the trip before , on a trip's card, makes it and the trip before it one trip, whatever ended the first. The card then says Joined on and the day, with Part again to undo it. Start a trip here , beside a day in a trip's legs, makes that day the first day of a trip of its own. Join to the trip before on the new trip undoes it. The trips are found again at once. The changes are kept with the track, in its tripEdits setting, and hold when the trips are found again later.

p.h: Move a trip to another device
p.x: A trip recorded on the wrong device, such as a phone posting the sailboat's trip while it was the car's tracker that should have, can be moved to the right one. Those who may change the track click Move to another device… on the trip's card, pick the device under Device in Move the trip to another device ("Its positions, first to last, leave this device's track for the other's, and the trips of both are found again."), and click Move . The list holds every other device with a track. Positions you rejected or accepted by hand keep that. The positions recorded where the trip began and ended stay, as does any GPX file the trip was read from, in this track's routes folder. To move another stretch, use track-move with the time span, naming the devices: # in EiN's terminal track-move ruby-phone sailboat --from 2025-07-01T06:00:00Z --to 2025-07-03T18:00:00Z A position at the very same moment as one the other track has already is dropped, and the other track keeps its own.

A trip EiN finds is only a proposal until you make it an album. Those who may change the track see, on each trip's card: New album… , which opens Create Album to ask what the album is called. The name starts as the farthest place the trip stayed at when that place has a name; the trip's dates are the album's span, not part of its name. Create makes the album in /archive/albums and opens it. Put in an album… , which opens Put the trip in an album . Before you type, it offers the albums whose dates overlap the trip and whose map draws this device's track (see Choose which devices the map shows ); their number keys pick them. Type part of a name to find any album you may change, or type a new name and press New album “…” to make an album of the trip under that name. Choosing an album makes it the trip's. An album that already holds another trip is refused with a message saying so. Either way the device is added to the album's devices, so its Map tab draws the route, and the album spans the trip even before it has any pictures. The card then names the album under Album , with Take off the album to undo it; the album and its pictures stay, and so does the device on its list. A trip is one album's, and an album holds one trip. Each time the trips are found again, or their stays put at locations, the album follows: it grows while the trip is ongoing, and its stays get their locations. The album holds on to its trip when the device or its track is moved or renamed. The album gets a Trip tab: the days, the distance in the track's units, where it stayed, and each day's notes. See The Trip tab . Those who may only look at the track see the albums the trip may belong to under Maybe in .

What you see Why What to do A device has no Trips tab. It has no track: it is a sensor or a plug, or a tracker made without --driver tracker that has had no position yet. Make a phone or a logger with device-create <name> --driver tracker ; see Where tracks come from . The Trips view says No trips though the track has positions. Its trips have not been found yet, or no part of the track went 500 m or more from where it started. Click Find trips , or Find trips again . A trip ends at home in the middle of a holiday, or two trips should be one. Arriving at a home base, or staying somewhere longer than three days, ends a trip. Click Join to the trip before on the second trip's card. A trip's days end at the wrong hour. The track's Timezone is not set, so its days are cut in UTC, or it is set to another zone. Click How it travels and choose the Timezone its days belong in. A trip is listed under the wrong device. The phone or tracker that recorded it posted to another device, or its GPX file was given to the wrong device. Click Move to another device… on the trip's card; see Move a trip to another device . How it travels , Upload GPX or Add home base is missing. You may not change this track: it is the device's owner's. Ask whoever made the device, or an administrator. Upload GPX gives a message ending in "no track points found". The file holds no recorded track points, only a planned route or waypoints. Use the file that was recorded while it moved. Upload GPX gives a message ending in "none of its N track points has a time". The file's points carry no times: a route drawn on a map, or a file the program saved without them. Use the file that was recorded while it moved, or export it again with times. A GPX file dropped in staging waits, though its device exists. The file names neither the device nor a camera linked to it, or it names more than one device. Click Choose device under Needs you on the Staging page; see GPX files in staging . The phone reports nothing to the track. It cannot reach EiN over HTTPS from where it is, its key was renewed or taken away, or tracking is off in Traccar Client. See Report from a phone and Ports, HTTPS and remote access . A GPX file sits in an album as an ordinary file. It was uploaded straight into the album, where GPX files are not read as routes. Upload it on the device's Trips tab, then delete the file from the album.

Every track command takes a track by its path, or by its device or a camera linked to the device, by its path or its name: sailboat is /dev/sailboat/position . A track's routes folder holds the GPX files it was read from, its homes folder links its home bases, and its .trips keeps its trips. The commands below are in the archive command reference , and every one takes --help ; the devices' own commands are on Devices . Task Command List the devices' tracks, with their name, kind, positions and span track-list , or track-list <folder> for those under one folder Find tracks by name or description search-track <words> Change how a device travels track-update <track> --kind boat ( car , bike , foot ), --timezone <zone> or --description <text> , or --clear <field> List a track's home bases track-home <track> ; with none of its own, the homes of its cameras' owners and the years they count Add or remove a home base track-home <track> --add <location>… or --remove <location>… ; a location is its path, or its folder name Read a track as the maps draw it track-read <track> --still ; without --still every recorded position, --max-speed <m/s> to change what is too fast Give a GPX file to a device cat <gpx> > /dev/<device> ; track-stage <gpx> --track <device> , which moves the file to the track's routes , or track-import <device> <gpx> , which keeps a copy there Add a position by hand track-append <track> --lat=<lat> --lng=<lng> --ts <time> See what GPX files hold, without importing gpx-info <gpx>… : name, tracks, creator, points and their time span, size, and the devices each names List the GPX files a track was read from source-list /dev/sailboat/position Find a track's trips track-trips <track> , --full from the start, --dry-run to see them without keeping them List a track's trips trip-list <track> Put a track's stays at locations, and name the new ones track-places <track> ; see Places a track stayed at Give a track's trips and days their weather track-weather <track> , --full to look every trip up again, --dry-run to see what it would look up Join a trip to the one before, or part one trip-edit <track> <trip> --merge , or <track> <day> --split Make a trip an album, or take it off trip-album <track> <trip> --new , --album=<album> , or --detach Reject or accept positions by hand, or hand them back to the rules track-mark <track> --reject , --accept or --clear , with --from , --to , --near <lat,lng> and --marked reject Move a stretch of a track to another device track-move <track> <to-track> --from <time> --to <time> Link a camera to the device it is part of camera-device <camera> <device> , or <camera> --off Put a device on an album's map, or take it off album-device-add and album-device-rm <album> <device>… ; see Albums Make a phone's or a tracker's key, or renew or take it away device-key <device> , with --new or --off ; see Report from a phone Making Jon's GPS logger, which he walks with, and adding a route copied into your home folder: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create "Jon's eTrex" --driver tracker --class foot --manufacturer Garmin --model 'eTrex 30x' track-update jon-s-etrex --timezone Pacific/Auckland track-stage " $HOME /tararua-walk.gpx" --track jon-s-etrex device-create prints the device's path, /dev/jon-s-etrex , and gives it its track, /dev/jon-s-etrex/position ; --class foot says how it travels. track-stage moves the GPX file to the track's routes folder once its points are in the track. See Commands by task for the rest of the archive's commands.

Devices : the device pages, a phone as a tracker, and GPX files written to a device. Cameras : the phones and cameras that took the pictures, and the devices they are part of. Locations and the map : the Map page and its Tracks layer, and the places trips stayed at. Albums : an album's Map and Trip tabs. Getting your photos in : every way files, GPX files among them, get into EiN. Sorting in staging : the staging area where waiting routes are.

t: Memories, news and events on Home

p.x: With the Archive installed, Home shows pictures taken on this day in earlier years, the albums people made lately, and the birthdays and anniversaries around today, and the Statistics page shows when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall. This page is for everyone who uses EiN. Home's layout and the rest of the Statistics page are EiN's own, and Home and statistics covers them. News lists the albums made lately and Events what comes round in the next month. On this day is missing here because nothing was taken on that date in earlier years. The Archive fills all three of Home's sections. Like everything on Home, they show only what you may see: an album or a person that is not shared with you does not appear.

On this day is a row of round pictures, one for each year that has pictures taken on today's date, newest year first, up to 8. Under each ring it says how long ago that was, such as "1 year ago" or "12 years ago", and the year. The picture in the ring is the first one taken that day. This year counts too, so a picture taken today has a ring of its own, "0 years ago". When there are more rings than fit, swipe the row sideways, or scroll it with a trackpad. The row counts pictures in albums only. Pictures still in your staging area, and pictures with no date, are not part of it, and neither are pictures you may not see. When no year has anything for today, the section is not shown at all. The same rings stand above the feed on the Media page; see Media, Year and labels .

Press a ring. The story opens over the whole window, on black. At the top, a thin bar for each picture of that year fills as the picture shows; each picture stays 5 seconds. Under the bars it says how long ago it was, such as "7 years ago", and the date, such as "25 December 2019". The story plays that year's pictures in the order they were taken, up to 24 of them, then moves on to the next earlier year with pictures from this day, through up to 30 years that have pictures. After the last picture of the oldest year, it closes. To With a finger or the mouse With the keyboard Go to the next picture Tap or click anywhere but the left third → Go back a picture Tap or click the left third ← Pause, and play again Hold your finger or the mouse button down, and let go to play on; or press Pause , then Play Space See the pictures in the viewer Open in the lightbox Close the story Close Esc Open in the lightbox opens the story's pictures, from every year, in the viewer at the picture you were on, with the details panel and everything else the viewer offers; see Viewing photos, videos and recordings . A few things work differently from a slideshow in the viewer: The 5 seconds are fixed. Your Seconds per slide preference applies to the viewer's slideshow only; see Watch a slideshow . Each picture pans and zooms slowly whatever your Ken Burns effect preference says. On a device set to reduce motion, the pictures stay still. A video shows as a still from it, and a recording as an empty slide. Use Open in the lightbox to play them. While a picture is still loading, its bar waits, so a slow picture still gets its full time. While the story plays, your screen is kept from going to sleep.

News is a timeline of the albums people made lately, newest first, up to 8. Each entry reads "<who> added <album>", for example "Helen Okafor added Christmas in Wellington", with how long ago under it: It says When the album was made "just now" less than an hour ago "3h ago" less than a day ago, in hours "yesterday" one day ago "4 days ago" up to a week ago "2 weeks ago" up to a month ago a date, such as "12 Jul 2025" longer ago, in your browser's date format Under it is a row of the album's pictures, as many as fit and at most five, the last one marked with how many more the album holds, such as +21 . Click the album's name or any of the pictures to open the album. Beside each entry is the portrait of the person whose account made the album, when the account is linked to a person in the archive; otherwise a picture icon. See Your profile, favourites and trash . What makes an entry: An album is made. Every way of making one counts: Create → Album , New album while adding pictures, and filing a group from staging as a New album or New private album . See Create an album and Sorting in staging . The time is when the album was made. Adding pictures to an album, renaming it or changing its dates does not bring it back to the top. Only albums in the album list count : folders inside an album, and the albums staging suggests to you, do not. An album moved to the trash leaves the news. When nothing has been added yet, News says "Nothing has been added yet" and "What people add shows up here.", and when you are signed in the Archive offers Import media under it; see Import media .

Events is a card of what comes round every year, for the days around today. How the card groups its entries, how far it looks and how it says when each falls are on Home and statistics . Each entry shows the face of the person it is about, or both partners' faces for a wedding anniversary. Click it to open the person's page.

Kind Comes from When it shows It reads Birthday A person's Born date Every year, up to the age of 110 "Helen Okafor turns 68"; after the person's death, "Arthur Wrenfield would have turned 95" Memorial A person's Died date Only in milestone years "5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died" Wedding anniversary The From date of two partners' relation Every year, up to and including the year the relation ended ( Until ) or the first of the two died, and for at most 75 years "Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married"; "… years together" for Partner , "… years engaged" for a relation whose kind is engaged Each of them needs a full date, with year, month and day. A date known only to the year or the month, such as 1934 or 1934-05 , has no day to come round on, so it makes no entry. Someone born on 29 February has a birthday entry in leap years only. The first entry is the first anniversary: nobody "turns 0". Birthdays and memorials are read from the people on the People page. A Marriage event on a person's page does not make an anniversary; the From date on the partner relation does.

A milestone is the 5th, 10th, 15th and 20th year, and then every 10th: 30, 40, 50 and so on. A milestone shows in bold, and milestones are the entries kept when the card runs out of room. Memorials appear only on milestones; birthdays and wedding anniversaries appear every year.

In the Wrenfield family's archive, the Events card on 20 January 2026 shows four entries, the milestones in bold: Group Entry When Coming up Grace Price turns 40 in 5 days Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married in 2 weeks Thomas Wrenfield turns 65 in 4 weeks Recently 5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died 3 days ago

Birthdays and memorials: open the person, press Edit , and type Born or Died as a full date, such as 1958-05-03 . See Edit a person . Wedding anniversaries: give the partner relation a From date, such as 1996-02-03 , when you choose Add partner on the person's Family tab, and an Until date if it ended for another reason than a death. Choose Married under Relationship for "years married". In the Web UI this takes an administrator. To date a partnership that is already recorded, choose Add partner again and pick the same partner. See Partnerships and their dates .

p.h: Life events on the Statistics page
p.x: The Archive adds the Events section to the Statistics page , above EiN's own Nodes section. Each chart folds every year into twelve months, so you see when in the year births, weddings and deaths fall. It has four charts: Births by month , Engagements by month , Marriages by month and Deaths by month . Each has a bar for every month from Jan to Dec, counting all years together, as the line "All years" under it says. Rest the pointer on a bar to read its count, such as "Mar: 2". The number at the top right is the total. It also counts dates known only to the year, which are in no month's bar, so the bars can add up to less than the total. Births and Deaths count the Born and Died dates of people. Engagements and Marriages count the Engagement and Marriage events written on people's pages. A wedding written on both spouses counts twice, and a partnership dated only by a From date on the relation does not count. See Record a wedding .

With Dashboards installed, the Archive offers three cards for a dashboard: Card What it shows Picture of the day One picture filling the card, the same all day or changing each hour: from This day in earlier years , from An album you choose, or from The newest pictures Birthdays The birthdays in the Days ahead , nearest first, with each face, the age and the days left; choose Show to add wedding anniversaries and memorials. As on Home, it lists only the people shared with you Weather The weather at a Place , given by name or as coordinates such as 57.71, 11.97 : now, and as the card has room, the next hours in a row under it and up to Days ahead days, under it or beside it on a wide card On a screen opened from a display link they show what the link's account may see. The weather is the place's own forecast, read every fifteen minutes, with the hours and days in the place's time ( The weather ahead ); it says so when Look up the weather is turned off.

What you see Why, and what to do On this day is missing No picture in the albums you may see was taken on today's date in another year. Pictures still in staging and pictures without a date do not count; file them into an album and check their dates, see Dates and places of pictures . A picture turns up under the day before or after The day is counted in UTC, so a picture taken close to midnight can fall on the neighbouring day. A picture known only to a year or a month counts from the start of that period, so it can turn up on 1 January or the first of the month, or the day before in a time zone east of UTC. The story says "Nothing was taken on this day in earlier years." There are no pictures you may see from that date, for example when the story was opened from a link for another day. An album you added pictures to is not in News News shows when an album was made, not when pictures were added to it. An entry reads "Somebody added …" EiN could not tell which account made the album, for example because that account is gone. A birthday or memorial is missing The Born or Died date needs a day, the person must be on the People page, and birthdays stop at 110 years. Memorials show only in milestone years. The card also holds at most 16 entries, milestones first. A wedding anniversary is missing The partner relation needs a From date with a day. Anniversaries stop after the relation's Until year, after the year one of the two died, and after 75 years. A Marriage event alone does not make one. Events is a day out, or On this day shows yesterday's pictures Home takes today's date from your computer or phone. Check its date and time zone. The Marriages chart shows twice as many weddings as there were Each wedding was written as an event on both spouses, and each event counts. See Life events on the Statistics page .

Home's onthisday , news and events commands gather what every installed module offers; Home and statistics shows how to run them. The Archive's part comes from onthisday-media , news-albums and events-anniversaries . events --today 2026-01-20 in the Wrenfield family's archive prints the example above. A * marks a milestone: 2026-01-17 3d ago * 5 years since Peggy Wrenfield died 2026-01-25 in 5d * Grace Price turns 40 2026-02-03 in 14d * Jon Wrenfield and Kiri Wrenfield — 30 years married 2026-02-19 in 30d Thomas Wrenfield turns 65 onthisday prints one line for each year, such as 2019 Pictures taken on 25 December 2019 , and news one line for each album, such as 2026-10-11 18:02 Helen Okafor added Christmas in Wellington . The Archive has more commands about the family's dates: # in EiN's terminal timeline --kind birth,death,anniversary # the family's history, looking back from today dayinhistory 12-25 --years 20 --per-year 1 # the pictures of a day, by path anniversaries --days-ahead 60 --kind birthday # the birthdays in the next two months, with ages person-stats # the counts behind the Statistics page's Events charts timeline is the archive's history, newest first: albums, births, deaths, birthdays, wedding anniversaries, events, moves and GPS tracks. It looks back from today, never ahead, and stops a person's birthdays at their death. By default it lists only milestone birthdays and anniversaries; --birthdays all and --anniversaries all list every year. --kind , --year , --person , --location and --tag narrow it. The full options are in the reference for timeline , dayinhistory , person-stats , onthisday-media , news-albums and events-anniversaries .

Home and statistics : the Home page and the Statistics page themselves. Family tree, events and homes : dates of birth and death, partners and their dates, and events on a person's page. Media, Year and labels : the Media feed with the same rings, and the Year page. Viewing photos, videos and recordings : the viewer and its slideshow. Albums : making the albums that fill News. Sharing : who sees which albums and people.

EiN keeps any file you give it. What it works out from a file depends on what kind of file it is: a photo gets thumbnails, faces and a date, a video also gets a version your browser can play, and a document has its text read for search. This page is for everyone who brings files into EiN. It lists the formats EiN recognises, what it makes from each, and what happens to the rest.

p.h: What EiN does with each kind of file
p.x: Kind Formats What EiN works out Photos JPEG, HEIC, PNG, TIFF, WebP, AVIF, GIF, BMP, camera RAW date, place, camera, thumbnails, faces, text in the picture, what it shows, look-alikes Videos MP4, MOV, M4V, MTS and M2TS, MPG, AVI, MKV, WebM, 3GP, FLV date, place, camera, a playable version, a preview clip, chapters, faces, what is said and who says it, look-alikes Recordings M4A, MP3, WAV, FLAC, Ogg and Opus, AMR date, a playable version, a picture of the sound, what is said and who says it, the same recording twice Documents PDF, Word, OpenDocument, RTF and plain text a picture of the first page, a version to read in the viewer, the text for search; the text of scanned pages too Sidecar files Google Takeout JSON, XMP nothing of their own: they give their picture its date, place and caption GPS tracks GPX the route, added to the track of the device it was recorded on Family trees GEDCOM the people, their relations, events and homes, found among the archive's people or added Zip files ZIP in staging, expanded into the files it holds Everything else any file kept as it is, and nothing more The work happens in the background after a file arrives, and each part shows up when it is done; Getting your photos in explains the order. A file you upload into staging is read once it arrives, but the text in pictures and documents is read only when you file it into an album.

p.h: How EiN tells what a file is
p.x: EiN looks at the first bytes of a file, not at its name. A JPEG photo named IMG_0412.png is still a JPEG photo, and a file with no extension at all is recognised the same way. It makes no difference whether the file came in with Import media , an upload into an album, by dropping it on a page, or over SFTP . A program that copies a file over SFTP under a temporary name, such as IMG_0412.jpg.filepart , and renames it when it is done gets the type the final name gives. The name decides in three cases, because the bytes say too little: Camera RAW files. Most RAW formats look like a TIFF picture from their first bytes, so EiN goes by the extension, such as .NEF or .CR3 . Capital or small letters do not matter. Sidecar files. A text file ending in .json is JSON data, and one ending in .xmp is an XMP sidecar, not a document to read. Office files. Word, Excel and PowerPoint files, OpenDocument files and EPUB books begin like any zip file, and the old Word, Excel and PowerPoint formats ( .doc , .xls , .ppt ) all begin alike, so EiN goes by the extension, such as .docx or .odt . Once the media service has read a photo, video or recording, the type it reports is the one EiN keeps. To see what EiN made of a file, run mime in the terminal; see In the terminal .

EiN recognises JPEG, HEIC and HEIF (what iPhones take), PNG, TIFF, WebP, AVIF, GIF and BMP, and the camera RAW formats below. For each photo, EiN: reads its date, its GPS position and the camera or phone that took it; see Dates and places of pictures and Cameras ; makes thumbnails and screen-sized copies in the AVIF format: a square of 320 pixels, and copies that fit inside 512, 800, 1,600 and 2,560 pixels. These copies are never larger than the photo, so a small one gets only the sizes up to its own; finds the faces in it ( People and faces ); reads any text in it, printed or handwritten, so that search finds it ( Read the text in a picture ); works out what it shows, so that you can search for "a dog on a beach"; takes a fingerprint, which finds copies, look-alikes and bursts ( Duplicates ). Text in a photo is read, handwriting included, and search finds the picture by it.

EiN takes the RAW files of these cameras: Extension Camera .cr2 , .cr3 , .crw Canon .nef , .nrw Nikon .arw , .sr2 Sony .raf Fujifilm .orf Olympus .rw2 , .raw Panasonic .pef Pentax .dng Adobe DNG, used by many cameras and phones .x3f Sigma .mrw Minolta .dcr , .kdc Kodak .3fr Hasselblad .iiq Phase One .erf Epson .srw Samsung .rwl Leica A RAW file gets everything a JPEG gets. EiN develops it for the thumbnails; a RAW file whose sensor data cannot be read is shown from the JPEG preview the camera put inside it. Faces and text are read from that preview too. When the camera saved a JPEG beside the RAW, under the same name ( IMG_1234.CR2 and IMG_1234.JPG ), EiN files the RAW under the JPEG two minutes after it arrives, which leaves the JPEG time to arrive too. The RAW is then a version of that JPEG: the album, search and the timeline show the JPEG alone; the viewer lists the RAW under Versions in the details panel , where its name downloads it; the faces found on the RAW are deleted, since the JPEG has the same ones. A person who was only in those faces, and has no name, goes with them. A RAW whose JPEG came later, or that was uploaded before EiN did this, is filed with Hide RAW files in its album's menu, or with raw --sort . A RAW with no JPEG of its name stays a picture of its own, and so does one with two pictures of its name in the folder (a JPEG and a HEIC, say), since EiN cannot tell which it belongs to. A RAW that arrives again after it was filed, as an import run a second time can bring it, takes the place of the version already under its JPEG when the two hold the same bytes; when they differ it stays where it is, and the sort says the version already exists. When EiN finds a RAW of its own to be a duplicate of another picture, it suggests keeping the RAW, as the better format ( Which copy is kept ).

EiN recognises MP4, MOV (what iPhones and many cameras record), M4V, MTS and M2TS (AVCHD camcorders), MPG, AVI, MKV, WebM, 3GP and FLV. For each video, EiN: reads its date, its GPS position and the camera or phone that recorded it; makes a still for its tile and the poster shown before it plays, from a second in. When that frame shows nothing, such as black, white or a tape's blue screen, the still comes from further into the video; makes a version your browser plays, at most 1920 × 1080 pixels, in the AV1 format inside an MP4 file, with the sound at 128 kbit/s; makes a silent clip of up to 20 seconds that plays when you point at the tile, starting where the still was taken. A video shorter than 2 seconds gets none: its still already shows it all; makes the small pictures you see when you move along the timeline, and finds where one shot cuts to the next, which become its chapters ( Play a video ); finds the faces in it, and works out what it shows; writes down what is said in it and recognises who says it, so that search finds the words and the viewer can show subtitles; takes a fingerprint, which finds copies and look-alikes. The viewer plays the AV1 version, not the original. A browser or device that cannot play AV1 says so; the original can still be downloaded. If a video is too long or too heavy for the media service to convert within its limits, which can happen on a machine without a graphics card, it gets no playable version. Use Download to watch it on your own device.

EiN recognises M4A (what phone voice memos are), MP3, WAV, FLAC, Ogg and Opus, and AMR. M4B audiobooks count as recordings too. For each recording, EiN: reads its date, where the file has one; makes a version your browser plays: AAC at no more than 128 kbit/s and 44.1 kHz, in an .m4a file; draws a picture of the sound, its waveform, which is the recording's tile and what you see while it plays; writes down what is said in it and recognises who says it ( Listen to a recording ); takes a fingerprint of the sound, which finds the same recording twice. A recording shorter than about 2.5 seconds gets none. A recording's tile and player show a picture of its sound, and the transcript beside it is searchable.

EiN reads the text of PDF files, Word ( .docx ) and OpenDocument ( .odt ) files and plain text files, so that search finds a document by what it is about: a search for Christmas letter finds the family newsletter of 2019. See Search and the finder . PDF. EiN reads the text the PDF holds. A page with almost no text, such as a scanned letter, is read as a picture instead, handwriting included. At most 40 pages of one PDF are read this way; the pages after that keep only the text they hold. Plain text. Any file that is text, whatever its name: .txt , a Markdown note, an HTML page. An SVG drawing is text too, so EiN treats it as a document, not as a picture. Word and OpenDocument. A .docx or .odt file. A document's text is read once the file is in an album or elsewhere in the library, not while it waits in staging. Files in folders whose name starts with a dot, such as the trash, are not read. EiN also draws the first page of a PDF, Word ( .docx and old .doc ), OpenDocument, RTF or plain text file, which is its tile in an album and on the Media page, and makes a PDF of a Word, OpenDocument or RTF file once, which the viewer shows. The viewer shows a PDF as it is and plain text as text ( Read a document ). A document EiN cannot open keeps a plain tile; use Download to open it on your device. The Documents choice on the Media page also lists Markdown and HTML files, which the viewer shows as text. EiN does not read the text of RTF files and old Word ( .doc ) files: search finds them by their file name only. To have their text read, save them as PDF or .docx first.

A sidecar is a small file beside a picture that says things about it: the JSON file Google Photos writes beside every photo and video of a Takeout, such as IMG_0001.jpg.supplemental-metadata.json ; the XMP file a photo editor or a scanning tool writes, IMG_0001.jpg.xmp or IMG_0001.xmp . A sidecar is not a picture or a document of its own. In staging, EiN pairs it with its picture and moves it under it, and the picture takes its date, its place where the file has no GPS position, and its caption. A Google Takeout export shows what each part of a Takeout becomes. A sidecar that matches no picture stays where it is, among the category's Other files .

A GPX file is a route recorded by a GPS tracker, a watch or a tracking app. In staging it is not a picture: EiN gives it to the device the file names, whose track takes its points, and the file moves to the track's routes folder, where the track links it. On a device's Trips tab you can upload GPX files to it directly. See GPX files in staging and Upload a GPX file to a device .

A GEDCOM file ( .ged ) is a family tree as genealogy programs export it, in any of the character sets they write: UTF-8, UTF-16, ANSEL or ANSI. In staging it is not a document: it waits for you to look over its family tree beside the archive's, and then EiN finds each of its people among the archive's people or makes them a page, adds the parents and partners, the events, the homes and the notes it gives, and keeps the file in /archive/sources/genealogy/ , where every person it describes links it. Its text is not made searchable. See Bring in a family tree from a GEDCOM file .

A zip file that you upload or copy anywhere into a staging category is expanded once its upload has ended: what it holds goes into the folder the zip lies in, and the zip is removed. Outside staging, for example uploaded into an album, a zip stays a zip. Zips and Google Takeout exports has the details. Only zip files are expanded. A .tar , .7z or .rar archive is kept as it is, and so is an office file such as a .docx , .xlsx or .odt , though it is a zip inside.

Any other file is kept as it came, with its name and size, and nothing is made from it. In staging it counts among the category's Other files , and the Folder view of the Files tab lists it, where you can move or discard it ( Sorting in staging ). It does not appear on the Media page, in albums' grids or in search by content. You reach it over SFTP or in the terminal , and an administrator also on the Nodes page. Some media formats are among these, because EiN does not recognise them from their first bytes: Format Usual extension Windows Media video and audio .wmv , .wma AIFF audio .aif , .aiff AAC audio outside an M4A file .aac JPEG XL .jxl To have EiN work with such a file, convert it on your own computer first: a video to MP4, a sound to M4A, FLAC or WAV, a JPEG XL picture to JPEG or PNG.

p.h: Your originals stay as they are
p.x: EiN never changes the bytes of the file you uploaded. Thumbnails, playable versions, transcripts, read text and everything else it works out are kept beside the file. When you correct a date, turn a picture or write its text by hand, EiN changes what it keeps, not the file. Download in the viewer, and the file name at the top of its details panel, always give you the original.

p.h: When a file does not show up as expected
p.x: What you see Why What to do A new picture shows a plain tile with a picture icon Its thumbnails are not made yet. Wait. A large import keeps the media service busy for a long while. A file you uploaded into staging is counted under Other files EiN did not recognise it as a picture, video or recording: a document, a sidecar, or a format from the table above. Look at it in the Folder view of the Files tab. Convert an unrecognised media file and upload it again. A video or recording says "This file cannot be played" The file is damaged: nothing can read it. The reason is under the message. Download it and check it on your own device. A video says "This browser or device cannot play AV1, the format this video is in." The browser cannot play the format EiN makes playable videos in. Use a current browser, or Download the original. A document is not found by its words It is still in staging, or it is a format whose text EiN does not read. File it into an album. Save an RTF or .doc file as PDF or .docx . A RAW file is shown as an ordinary picture with no RAW detail Its sensor data could not be read, so it is shown from the preview inside it. Nothing is lost: the original is kept, and Download gives it to you. Viewing photos, videos and recordings covers the viewer's other messages.

mime shows the type EiN stored for a file, the type its name suggests, and the type its first bytes say, and whether it counts as camera RAW: # in EiN's terminal mime "/archive/albums/Christmas in Wellington/IMG_0412.HEIC" stored: image/heic ext: image/heic content: image/heic raw: no A file whose stored line says application/octet-stream was not recognised; one that says application/zip is kept as a zip. Two commands do a file's reading again, for a file you may change: Command What it does exif-extract -f <file> Reads a photo's, video's or recording's metadata again, and dates and places it again from what it read. A file marked as unreadable is tried again. index-document -f <file> Reads a document's text again. Every command and its options are in the Media module's command reference and the core command reference .

Viewing photos, videos and recordings : how each kind of file is shown and played. Search and the finder : finding files by what they show, say and contain. Duplicates : copies and look-alikes, and which format is kept. Files and storage : how EiN stores files and what it keeps beside them. The media service : the part of EiN that does the reading.

This page is for the administrator of an EiN with the Archive installed. It covers the work the Archive does on every photo, video, recording and document that arrives: its pipelines, the workers that run them and the commands that run the work again. How much runs at once is set on the Media module's page. The pipelines run in core's engine. Processing and pipelines covers the engine itself: watching the work on the Status and in the terminal, failed work and how it is run again, the bulk lane, and the engine's own settings.

When a file arrives, the Media module reads its metadata first ( Reading a file ). Then the Archive's media-interpret works out from it when the file was taken and where, side by side with the thumbnails, picture vectors, fingerprints, text and transcripts; faces and the camera that made the file wait for the date and place. Changes and pipelines follows one upload from start to finish. The Archive runs these services for its processing: Service What it does archive-bridge Turns changes into the events the Archive's pipelines wait for media-heal Starts a pass of the media-heal pipeline when one is due (see Close gaps the pipelines missed ) The steps themselves are run by the Media module's workers, which take the kinds of work the Archive names for them: media-worker the rest, such as dating and placing files, matching faces, duplicates and staging; models the work done by a model in the media service , such as finding faces or transcribing speech, and models-second the same beside it when it is on. The workers lists the kinds. Its other services, which keep albums, person covers, label suggestions and staging up to date, are listed in Services and logs . Most of the model work and much of the media work are calls into the media service: without it, those steps wait, and their kinds show waiting for EMS on the Status .

Pipeline What it does Kind of work media-interpret When a photo, video or recording was taken and where, from its metadata, a sidecar and its name interpret media-faces Finds the faces in a photo and crops each one faces media-video-faces Finds the faces in a video and when each is on screen faces media-face-assign Matches a found face to a person face-assign media-voiceprint Who speaks when in a recording, with a voiceprint per voice diarize media-speaker-assign Decides which person each voice is speaker-assign media-speaker-faces Ties a video's voices to the faces seen speaking them, once its faces are found diarize , speaker-assign media-camera Links a file to the camera or phone that took it run by the engine media-camera-cover Offers a video's poster frame to the camera that took it, once its renditions are made run by the engine media-geocode Looks up the address of a file's GPS position run by the engine media-weather Looks up the weather a photo was taken in, at its GPS position and its date run by the engine media-album An album's stacks, time span, missing cover and profile, when its members change run by the engine media-duplicates Decides the duplicate findings of a staged file again, or once its fingerprints are in dedupe location-link-point Links a photo to the location that contains its GPS point run by the engine location-upkeep Redraws a location and relinks the photos inside it when it or its photos change run by the engine document-index Extracts the text of a document and makes it searchable run by the engine staging-unzip Expands a zip that lands in a staging category, then removes the zip unzip staging-sidecars Pairs Takeout and XMP sidecars with their files sidecars staging-organize Plans a staging category's suggested groups again organize staging-retime Dates staged files again by the rules of the category they were moved into retime track-stage Gives a GPX file dropped in staging to the device it was recorded on run by the engine track-trips Finds a track's trips again after points arrive, names the places it stayed, and looks up their weather run by the engine gedcom-stage Moves a GEDCOM file dropped in staging to genealogy/ , to be looked over and imported run by the engine media-heal Goes through the albums or a staging area and announces the files missing work the other pipelines should have done run by the engine

Each media pipeline belongs to a family of work, which it names with wants , so a folder can ask for only some of it ( Which processing a folder wants ): Family What it covers Pipelines renditions A picture's sizes, a video's poster frames, hover clip, playable copy, storyboard and chapters, a recording's playable copy and waveform the Media module's media-stills and media-transcode picture-vectors Searching by what is in a picture the Media module's media-embed-picture text The text written in a picture, and a document's text the Media module's media-ocr , document-index and media-embed-text transcripts What is said in a video or recording the Media module's media-transcribe and media-embed-text fingerprints The fingerprints that find copies, look-alikes and photo stacks the Media module's media-fingerprint archive The date and the place, faces and voices and who they are, duplicates, the camera, the weather, a scan's damage media-interpret , media-damage , and the face, voice, camera, geocoding, weather and duplicate pipelines above The Media module's media-ingest and media-reindex name no family, since every family needs what they read, and nor do the pipelines that work on the Archive's own folders and on the devices' tracks: albums, staging, tracks and places. A folder with processing set to ["renditions"] gets its pictures read and their sizes made, and no dates worked out, no faces, text, picture vectors or fingerprints. A staging area wants every family but text : its files get everything else while they wait, and their text is read once they are filed into a folder that wants it.

The thumbnails, display sizes and playable copies of the Archive's pictures, videos and recordings, and the pipelines that make them, media-stills and media-transcode , are the Media module's: The renditions it makes . The Archive's own are a picture's face crops, which detect-faces cuts, file-set-orientation cuts again when a picture is turned, and regenerate-face-crops --missing cuts where a crash left one empty.

Every kind of work above that is not run by the engine goes as a job into the pool /var/pools/media , where the Media module's workers take it: the Archive names its kinds for them. media-worker takes the Archive's unzip , interpret , face-assign , speaker-assign , dedupe , retime , organize and sidecars , beside the Media module's own ingest , stills , transcode and fingerprint ; models takes the Archive's faces , diarize and damage , beside the Media module's shots , embed-picture , ocr , embed-text , transcribe and restore , and models-second the same kinds in the reverse order. How much of it runs at once is set there, in How much runs at once .

You want to Run Run one pipeline on one file pipeline-start media-faces /archive/albums/christmas-2019/IMG_2041.jpg Transcode a video again although it has renditions pipeline-start --var FORCE=-f media-transcode /archive/albums/christmas-2019/MVI_0412.mp4 Announce files the Archive never saw, or that are missing work media-scan /archive/albums Embed the stored texts and transcripts again, as they are media-reembed Encode the face crops again without finding the faces again regenerate-face-crops --limit 200 Cut the face crops a crash left empty, or never cut regenerate-face-crops --missing --limit 200 media-transcode , media-transcribe , media-embed-picture and media-ocr declare FORCE , which -f makes them redo work already done. pipeline-start is core's, media-reembed the Media module's, and the others the Archive's, which Archive commands lists with their options.

media-scan walks a folder and announces each file that was never taken in, or that lacks something a pipeline should have given it: its date and place, faces or voices, its address, or the weather it was taken in. Each pipeline then skips what is already done. What describes a file is the Media module's to keep current, in every folder: renditions , picture vectors , fingerprints and text, transcripts and their vectors . The media-heal pipeline runs media-scan for you over /archive/albums and over each user's staged files, /home/<user>/staging/files , whose faces staging uses to suggest groups. Each pass is one instance, which shows under Ongoing on the Status with how far through its folder it has come; it is housekeeping, not work waiting, so health does not count it. A pass holds back a gap whose pipeline already has work waiting, so it never repeats what is already on its way, and announces the rest: a long queue of one kind of work, such as faces, does not keep voices or transcripts from being found. It announces every gap as it finds it, so the work it starts shows on the Status page and in health until it is done. It remembers where it is every thousand files, so a restart of EiN does not send it back to the beginning. When a pass ends, the Output of its step says how many files it went through, how many gaps it announced and which kinds it held back. A pass that fails is a failed instance, run again like any other failed work . The media-heal service says when a pass is due. It looks every CFG_MEDIA_HEAL_INTERVAL seconds (900) and, unless a pass is running, starts one over the first folder, the albums before the staging areas, whose pass is due: one runs at a time. A folder's pass is not due when its last one failed, or when every kind of gap it would look for has work waiting. The kinds a folder's last pass held back get a pass of their own once their pipelines have nothing waiting. After a pass that finds nothing and holds nothing back, that folder rests for CFG_MEDIA_HEAL_REST seconds (21600, six hours). media-heal -n says whether a pass is due now, and media-heal --rest 0 starts one without waiting out the rest. Faces are compared with the models the media service runs now, so a scan needs the service to answer. While it does not, a pass ends without going through the archive, and the service starts it again at its next look, rather than going on without those checks. Run by hand, media-scan goes on and names the kinds of gap it could not check; scan for those again with --only and --restart once the service is back. Run it by hand after installing the Archive on files that were already there, or to look at one folder: # in EiN's terminal media-scan -n /archive/albums/christmas-2019 # only report what it would announce media-scan /archive/albums/christmas-2019 A run examines up to 20000 files ( --scan-limit ) and announces up to 1000 ( --limit ), and remembers where it stopped, so the next run goes on from there; --restart starts from the top. It announces fewer as running media-ingest instances and waiting triggers add up, and nothing once they reach 500 ( --max-active ).

p.h: Large imports and the bulk lane
p.x: Work on a staging category of the Google Photos export or Scans kind runs in core's bulk lane , below all other work, so what people upload in the meantime is processed first. Any category can be put in that lane with staging category <name> --lane bulk , which applies to work announced from then on. Staging for administrators covers categories.

Processing and pipelines : the engine, failed work, and watching it all. The media service : where the model work and much of the media work runs. Supported files : what the Archive reads and makes of each kind of file. Staging for administrators : categories and their lanes. Troubleshooting : when photos do not get thumbnails, faces or dates. Archive commands : every command the Archive adds.

This page is for the administrator who looks after the staging areas where everyone's uploads wait: how they are laid out, the background work that reads and groups what arrives, how to plan an import of tens of thousands of files, the finer settings of a category, and the staging command for checking and repairing a person's staging area. How family members upload and sort is on Getting your photos in and Sorting in staging .

Every account has its own staging area in its home, /home/<username>/staging . Files wait there, seen only by their owner, until the owner files them into an album or discards them. The Archive module provides staging; without the archive module there is none (see Modules ). /home/helen/staging/ files/<category>/… the staged files, in any folders below a category albums/<category>/<slug> the suggested albums (groups) for that category's files journal/<id> one entry per decision, with the plan that undoes it routes/ GPX files waiting for the device they belong to genealogy/ GEDCOM files waiting to be looked over and imported Part What it is files/inbox The default category. It is always there and cannot be removed; uploads from the Media page go here. files/<category> Any other category, one folder each. Its name is its key and never changes. Its settings are kept on the folder. albums/<category>/ The groups the organizer suggests, as albums whose members are links to the staged files. It also holds the organizer's checkpoint, .organizer . journal/ Every decision: filing, discarding, removing copies, changing the groups and "not this album". Entries are never deleted; each is undone from the Done tab or with staging undo . routes/ GPX files that name no device EiN knows, or more than one, until their owner says which device they belong to. genealogy/ GEDCOM family trees, until their owner has said who the people in them are and imported them. Every directory of a staging area is mode 0700 and owned by the account, and staging/ is marked unlisted. Nobody else can open it, find it in a search or see it on the map, and the library's own views (the Media page, the map, On this day, search) leave it out even for its owner until the files are filed. The administrator passes every permission check, other people's staging included, as root does; Permissions in depth explains why the 0700 folder is enough. The background work runs with administrative access, so it reads and processes staged files like any others. EiN sets no limit on how much one person's staging area holds. Staged files take room on the same disk as the library; df in the terminal shows the free space.

p.h: When a staging area is set up
p.x: A new account has no staging area until one of these sets it up: the person opens Staging in the Web UI, or drops files on a page that uploads into staging; the staging-organizer service, which sets up every account's staging area once an hour; you, with staging init . Someone who wants to copy files in over SFTP before opening Staging finds no /home/<username>/staging yet. Have them open Staging once, or set it up for them: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator staging init --user ruby ruby: 7 created, 0 repaired, 0 adopted, 0 moved, 0 groups, 0 routes, 0 relinked staging init makes the directories with their modes and owner, marks staging/ unlisted, sets its processing to every family but text (so a staged file's text is read once it is filed), and makes the Inbox. It also puts right what is out of place, moving each thing with every link to it following, so albums and suggestions keep pointing at it: Found What staging init does A folder directly under files/ Adopts it as a category of the generic kind ( Other in the Web UI), named after it. A file directly in files/ Moves it into files/inbox/unsorted/ , or the folder --loose-batch names. A group directly in albums/ Moves it into albums/inbox/ . A GPX file waiting for a device Moves it into routes/ . A name already taken where something moves gets -2 , -3 . Run again, it finds nothing to do. Option What it does --user <name> Sets up that person's staging area. Without it, your own. --all Every account's. --loose-batch <name> The Inbox folder that loose files of files/ move into, instead of unsorted . --idle-minutes <n> Leaves a loose file of files/ where it is when it changed within the last n minutes, so a copy still being written is not moved. The service passes 360 . --layout-only Makes the directories and categories and moves nothing. The Staging page runs this. --dry-run Says what it would do and does none of it.

Nothing in staging needs you to start it. Each step below is a pipeline that starts on its own when files arrive or change, or a service that runs on a timer. All of them run in EiN's pipeline engine, which Processing and pipelines covers. Pipeline or service Starts when What it does staging-unzip A zip anywhere in a category has finished uploading Expands it into the folder it lies in ( unzip -n --as-upload , which freezes what /etc/frozen-uploads lists, as an upload), then removes it. One zip at a time. staging-sidecars A Google Takeout JSON or an XMP file lands in a category that pairs sidecars, about 30 seconds after the last one Pairs each sidecar with its photo or video ( media-sidecars ), which gives the picture its date, place and caption. One run at a time. media-ingest , media-interpret and the media work A file lands Checks whether it is an exact copy, which then waits unread; reads its metadata, then dates and places it by the category's time rules; then the thumbnails, faces, fingerprints and the rest, through the media service . staging-retime Files move into a category with other time rules, about 10 seconds after the last one Dates them again by the rules of the category they are in now ( staging retime ). staging-organize A category's files arrive, leave, move or are read, or someone asks for a run; held two minutes Plans the category's groups again where its files changed, and writes what differs ( staging organize ). track-stage A .gpx file lands anywhere in staging Writes it to the device it names, whose driver reads its points into the device's track, and moves the file to the track's routes/ ; one that names no device, or several, waits for its owner. gedcom-stage A .ged file lands under files/ Moves it to genealogy/ , where it waits for its owner to look it over and import it ( gedcom-import , which moves it to /archive/sources/genealogy/ and imports as the staging area's owner). staging-organizer (service) Every 15 minutes Asks for an organizer run of each category that something waits for, and matches the groups due a match against the library's albums. staging-organizer (service) Every hour Sets up every account's staging area and moves a file copied loose into files/ , once nothing has changed on it for six hours, into files/inbox/unsorted/ ( staging init --all --idle-minutes 360 ); and checks every duplicate finding against where its file is now ( staging duplicates --repair --all ). The organizer reads what changed since its last run and plans only that again. A run while another is going folds into one more run, so a large upload does not queue thousands of them. A category gets a full build on its first run, when its grouping settings change, and once a week. Text in pictures and documents is the one piece of work that waits: it is read when a file is filed, not while it is staged. To see the work, look at the Status ( Health and status ), or in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal health pipeline-instances -s failed staging-unzip service-status staging-organizer

p.h: Look at a person's staging area
p.x: staging status reads a staging area without changing it: per category, its media, its other files (anything that is not a picture, video or recording), those still being read and those without a date. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator staging status --user helen inbox: 1204 media, 37 other, 212 indexing, 18 undated google-photos: 48210 media, 1391 other, 30544 indexing, 66 undated 1 route(s) waiting for a device 1 family tree(s) waiting to be imported A staging area that was never set up answers helen: not initialized; run staging init . With JSON_OUTPUT=1 the answer also holds the bytes, each category's organizer summary, the exact copies by where their originals are, and how many files were filed and discarded. Other commands that only read: Command What it shows staging category <name> --user <name> One category: what it is called, its kind, its default album, whether it is in the bulk lane, its media. staging journal [<category>] --user <name> The decisions, newest first, 50 a page, with the totals filed and discarded. staging detect --user <name> What the newest folders in the Inbox look like: a Google export, scans, a phone and so on. staging duplicates --counts --user <name> How many copies and look-alikes the staging area holds, by where the originals are. staging check --user <name> What breaks the layout's rules (see Put a staging area right ).

A browser upload suits a few thousand files. For a whole Google Takeout, a scanned collection or years of a phone's pictures, copy the files in over SFTP and let EiN work through them. Check the disk. Run df . The files need their own size, and a zip needs room for what it holds and a tenth more while it is expanded. A zip that does not fit is left as it is. Make a category for the source , of the kind closest to it. On the Staging page this is the New category card; in the terminal, as the person or for them: # in EiN's terminal staging category google-photos --create --kind google-photos --user helen The Google Photos export and Scans kinds put their files in the bulk lane: their reading, thumbnails, faces and the rest wait behind all other work, so what anyone uploads to an Inbox meanwhile is ready first, and the import goes on whenever nothing else waits. Copy the files into the category's folder , never into files/ itself. Keep a folder above the event folders: a folder's name becomes a suggested album only when it lies two or more levels below the category. # on your own computer scp -P 2222 takeout-001.zip takeout-002.zip helen@ein.local:/home/helen/staging/files/google-photos/ Zips can go in as they are: each is expanded where it lands, and the parts of one Takeout fill one tree. Getting your photos in has the details the person copying needs, and SSH and SFTP the connection. Let it run. staging status --user helen shows how many files are still being read. The Status reads Catching up while work waits and gets done. A file that is an exact copy of one its owner can already open is recorded as a copy and processed no further, so a second copy of an export costs little. Sort. The groups appear on the category's Sort tab as the files are read; its owner files them as Sorting in staging describes. Tip One category per source keeps an export's files together and lets its kind decide how they are dated and grouped. A source already copied into the Inbox can be moved into a category of its own afterwards, with Move to category… on the Files tab or staging move ; the files are dated again by the new category's rules. How fast the work goes depends on the machine and the graphics card; see Performance and sizing .

p.h: Change the finer settings of a category
p.x: The Web UI changes a category's name, kind and default album. The rest of its settings are changed with staging category . A person may change their own categories; an administrator may change anyone's with --user . Option Values What it decides --kind <kind> inbox , google-photos , scans , phone , camera , messaging , screenshots , generic What it holds; only the Inbox is of the inbox kind. A new kind resets every other setting, the label too, to that kind's, but for the default album and what the same command sets. --label <text> The name the pages show. --destination <album> an album's path The library album its files are filed into by default. --no-destination clears it. --strategy <strategy> events , folders , none How its files are grouped: by time and place, by folder and runs of file names, or into monthly lanes only. --significance <level> fewer , normal , more How readily a day becomes a group of its own rather than part of an Everyday lane. --digitized on|off on , off On: the files are scans, and no clock recorded while digitizing them (the scanner, a GPS fix, the file name) dates them. --filename-dates on|off on , off On: a date the file name spells, such as IMG_20190601_123456.jpg , dates a file when nothing better does. --lane <lane> normal , bulk bulk runs the work on its files below all other work. It applies to work announced from then on, within a minute; work already queued keeps its place. --sidecars <mode> pair , ignore Whether Google Takeout JSON and XMP files arriving from then on are paired with their files. --create Makes the category. Its name is lowercase letters, digits and dashes. --remove Removes it. Only an empty category other than the Inbox can be removed. What each kind starts with: Kind Grouping digitized filename-dates Lane Sidecars inbox events off on normal pair google-photos events off off bulk pair scans folders on off bulk pair phone events off on normal pair camera events off off normal pair messaging none off on normal ignore screenshots none off on normal ignore generic events off off normal pair A change of --digitized or --filename-dates dates the category's files again before the command answers. A change of --strategy or --significance asks for an organizer run, which regroups the files within minutes. # in EiN's terminal staging category inbox --significance more --user helen staging category old-phone --lane bulk --user helen inbox: Inbox (inbox); 1204 media, changed group old-phone: Old phone (phone), bulk lane; 8730 media, changed lane Dates and places of pictures explains what the time rules mean for the person sorting.

staging check lists what breaks the layout's rules and changes nothing. It checks up to 20,000 of the groups' links. # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator staging check --user helen 0 problem(s); 3120 link(s) checked Each problem is a line <code>: <path>: <detail> : Code What it means missing A directory of the layout is not there. not-directory Something other than a directory stands where one should be. mode , owner A directory has another mode than 0700 , or another owner. not-unlisted staging/ is not marked unlisted, so the library's views would show it. processing staging/ wants other processing than staging's, such as text. loose-entry Something lies directly in files/ or albums/ . no-inbox The Inbox category is missing. orphan-albums A folder of groups has no category. cross-category A group links to a file outside its own category. dangling-link A group links to nothing. waiting-route A GPX file waits for its device outside routes/ . staging init --user <name> puts right all but the two kinds of link. A group's broken links are put right by the next full organizer run, which you can start at once: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator staging organize inbox --user helen --full Other repairs, each for one person with --user or, where marked, everyone with --all : Command When to use it staging organize [<category>…] --full The groups look wrong or stale. Plans the whole category again instead of what changed. --dry-run says what it would do. --all for everyone. staging organize [<category>…] --queue Asks the pipeline for a run instead of running one here; this is the Group now button. staging retime [<category or folder>] Dates look wrong after files were moved or settings changed. Dates the files again by their category's rules. --dry-run counts and writes nothing. staging duplicates --repair Copies are marked against the wrong original after files were moved outside staging. The service does this every hour. --all for everyone. staging duplicates --refresh [<folder>] Files have no duplicate finding. Has each one checked again, 5,000 a call; --force checks every file, --dry-run counts them. media-sidecars <folder> Sidecars were not paired, for example in a category set to ignore that you have since set to pair . A second run finds nothing to do. media-scan /home/<name>/staging/files Files stay unread after a crash, with the media service answering and nothing waiting. Announces the files that miss work. Run it only when the engine is idle: while work waits, it announces again what is already on its way.

--user <name> makes any staging subcommand act on that person's staging area, which only an administrator may; a member of the sudo group must first elevate with Administer… in the account menu, or admin in the terminal ( Permissions in depth ). --all works only for init , organize , match and duplicates --repair ; any other subcommand answers, for example, staging status: --all is only for init, organize, match and duplicates --repair; name one user with --user . A decision you make in someone's staging area, such as staging discard or staging promote , goes into their journal and shows on their Done tab, where they can undo it, and so can you: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator staging journal inbox --user helen -- limit 10 staging undo 01JA2B3C4D5E6F7G8H9J0K1M2N --user helen Removing copies is the owner's alone: the copies go to the trash of whoever runs it, so staging dedupe for someone else answers staging dedupe: staging dedupe moves copies to your own trash: run it as helen . Archive commands lists every subcommand and option.

A person's /home/<name>/staging does not exist. Their staging area is not set up yet. Run staging init --user <name> , or have them open Staging once. A zip is still a zip. Look at the failed staging-unzip runs with pipeline-instances -s failed staging-unzip and pipeline-status <id> . The step's error says why: not enough space: … when the disk lacks room for what it holds and a tenth more, refusing entry '…': it would land outside … for an unsafe archive, or a file of another size is there when a file of that name is in the folder already. Free space or move the clashing file, then expand it by hand: unzip --as-upload -d <folder> <zip> goes on where the last run stopped, freezing what the run would have, and -o writes over the files there. Files stay "being prepared" for hours. A large import takes hours, and a bulk-lane category waits behind all other work. If staging status shows the indexing count not going down at all, see whether the media service answers ( The media service ) and whether the Status says Stuck . The Sort tab stays at "No groups yet" though the files are read. Ask for a run with staging organize <category> --user <name> --queue ; it answers helen/inbox: run asked for at … . If no groups come, run it here without --queue to see its answer or its error, and look at service-status staging-organizer . Scans have dates they should not have, or phone pictures lack them. The category has the wrong time rules for its files. Change them with --digitized or --filename-dates , which dates the files again at once. An export's sidecars were not paired. The category is of the Messaging or Screenshots kind, or set to --sidecars ignore . Set --sidecars pair and run media-sidecars on the folder. A person left with files in staging. Deleting an account deletes its home, staging included; see Accounts and groups . File or move what should be kept first.

This page is for power users and administrators who use the Archive from the terminal. Each table row gives a task, a command line that does it, and a link to that command's full entry. The commands come with the Archive and are there once it is installed; The Archive says what it adds, and Commands by task has core's commands and how to read the tables. EiN runs most of the analysis by itself after an upload; the commands here are for looking things up, changing them by hand, and doing one thing again. Albums , People and faces and the other guide pages show the same tasks in the Web UI.
