Manage a user's private staging area: its categories and which one a newly arrived folder looks like it belongs in, their suggested groups and the organizer that makes them, the edits that change them, and the decisions that file them into the library or discard them, each journaled and undoable. reads only staging [--user=<string>] [--all] [--stale] [--since=<string>] [--full] [--queue] [--if-pending] [--at=<path>] [--new] [--to=<string>] [--name=<string>] [--into=<path>] [--share=<string>] [--except=<path>] [--expect=<string>] [--confidence=<string>] [--action=<string>] [--limit=<string>] [--cursor=<string>] [--refresh] [--force] [--repair] [--counts] [--where=<string>] [--keep=<string>] [--apply] [--off] [--exact] [--near] [--loose-batch=<string>] [--layout-only] [--idle-minutes=<string>] [--dry-run] [--create] [--remove] [--kind=<string>] [--label=<string>] [--destination=<path>] [--no-destination] [--strategy=<string>] [--significance=<string>] [--digitized=<string>] [--filename-dates=<string>] [--lane=<string>] [--sidecars=<string>] <subcommand> <path>... Argument What it is <subcommand> One of init , status , check , detect , category , retime , organize , promote , discard , accept , later , undo , journal , move , split , regroup , merge , delete , rename , pin , reject , match , dedupe , duplicates , separate . <path>... a category's name, or suggested groups by path or slug in the default category of --user, as required; detect takes at most 20 folders, of staging or not (by default the folders newly arrived in the default category); organize takes the categories to organize (every one by default); retime takes a category, or a folder or file of one (every category by default); discard also takes staged files and folders; accept takes at most 20 groups (50 with --dry-run), later 100; undo takes at most 20 journal entries; move takes what to move, then the folder; regroup takes the group, then the staged files to move into it (at most 2000), or with --new the files alone; merge takes the group to keep, then the groups to fold into it; rename takes the new name after it; reject takes the group, then the library album it does not go into; match takes groups (every group of the user's by default); duplicates takes a category, a folder of staged files (all of them by default), a suggested group, or staged files (at most 200) for the sets they belong to; dedupe takes the sets to resolve (exact: or near: ), with a category, a folder in one or a suggested group to drop their files from (the default category by default); separate takes a staged file, then the files it is no duplicate of. Option What it does --user=<string> act on this user (defaults to the current user) --all init, organize, match, duplicates --repair: act on every user (administrator only) --stale match: only the groups due a match: none for their members as they are, by another model, or older than a candidate profile. --since=<string> match: only the groups around the days of the library albums whose profile changed after this time. --full organize: plan the whole category again, not only what changed since the last run. --queue organize: ask for a run rather than run one; the organizer's pipeline runs it within minutes. A user may ask for their own categories. --if-pending organize --queue: only for a category something waits for: changes since its last run, edits, a first run, or a week since its last full build (administrator only) --at=<path> split: the first file of the new group. --new regroup: the files make a new group of their own. --to=<string> promote: the directory a new album is made in (default /archive/albums) --name=<string> promote: the new album's title, its path made from it (default the first group's name); split, regroup --new: the new group's name; merge: the kept group's new name. --into=<path> promote: file into this library album instead of a new one. --share=<string> promote: 'private' makes the new album yours alone; 'default' shares it as your new albums are. --except=<path> promote, discard: leave this member in its group, which is then pinned (repeatable) --expect=<string> promote, discard, accept, split, regroup, merge, delete: the member key each group must still have, in group order (repeatable) --confidence=<string> accept: the least sure proposal to apply (high, medium, low; default medium) --action=<string> journal: only decisions of this kind (promote, file, discard, dedupe, edit, reject) --limit=<string> journal: entries per page (default 50, at most 200); duplicates: sets per page (default 50, at most 200); duplicates --refresh: files announced per call (default 5000); dedupe --apply: copies dropped per call. --cursor=<string> journal, duplicates, duplicates --refresh, dedupe --apply: go on after this one's cursor. --refresh duplicates: announce each staged media file whose duplicate finding is missing, from another inbox or for other bytes, for media-duplicates to record; takes a folder of the user's staging files (default all of them) --force duplicates --refresh: announce every staged media file. --repair duplicates: check each duplicate finding against where its file is now, and fix it (with --all, every user's) --counts duplicates: how many staged copies the scope holds, by where their originals lie. --where=<string> duplicates, dedupe --apply: only copies or look-alikes of library photos (library), or of files within the inbox (inbox); both, in that order, by default. --keep=<string> dedupe: keep this staged file (its id) of the one set named, instead of the one the rules keep. --apply dedupe: resolve every set of the scope that resolves unasked, at most 500 sets and --limit copies (default and most 2000) a call. --off pin: unpin, so the organizer manages the group again; later: bring back into its lane; separate: no longer keep the files apart. --exact duplicates, dedupe --apply: only byte copies. --near duplicates, dedupe --apply: only look-alikes: the same picture in other bytes. --loose-batch=<string> init: the default category's folder that loose entries of files/ move into (default unsorted) --layout-only init: make the directories and categories only; move nothing. --idle-minutes=<string> init: leave the loose files of files/ changed within this many minutes, which may still be being copied. --dry-run init, organize, promote, discard, accept, dedupe, duplicates, retime --refresh: say what would be done, and do none of it. --create category: make it, with its directory of groups. --remove category: remove it, which only an empty one other than the default can be. --kind=<string> category: what it holds, which resets its other settings to the kind's (inbox, google-photos, scans, phone, camera, messaging, screenshots, generic) --label=<string> category: what a page calls it. --destination=<path> category: the library album its files are filed into by default. --no-destination category: no default album. --strategy=<string> category: how its files are grouped (events, folders, none): by time and place, by folder and file-name run, or into monthly lanes. --significance=<string> category: how readily a day becomes a group of its own rather than part of an Everyday lane (fewer, normal, more) --digitized=<string> category: on, its files are digitized copies (scans), and no clock recorded while digitizing them (camera, GPS, file name) dates them; off, they do. Its files are dated again. --filename-dates=<string> category: on, a date its files' names spell (IMG_20190601_123456.jpg) dates them when nothing better does; off, names are not dates. from then on. --sidecars=<string> category: whether the Google Photos Takeout JSON and XMP sidecars arriving there are paired with their files (pair, ignore), from then on. staging init --all Option What it does --from=<string> only fixes at or after this ISO timestamp. --to=<string> only fixes before this ISO timestamp. track-move anna-phone sailboat --from=2025-07-01T06:00:00Z --to=2025-07-03T18:00:00Z

Put each of a track's stays at a location, naming the ones it makes after the harbour, island, bay or town there. changes things track-places [--rename] [--dry-run] <track> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. Option What it does --rename ask Overpass and Nominatim again for the names of the stays' locations, except names changed by hand. --dry-run look the places up and show them without making locations or writing .trips. track-places sailboat track-places /dev/sailboat/position --dry-run

Read a track as drawable segments ({segments, points, truncated}) reads only track-read [--from=<string>] [--to=<string>] [--bbox=<string>] [--margin=<string>] [--tolerance=<string>] [--limit=<string>] [--still] [--max-speed=<string>] [--rejected] [--only-rejected] <track> Argument What it is <track> the track to read: the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. Option What it does --from=<string> only fixes at or after this ISO timestamp. --to=<string> only fixes before this ISO timestamp. --bbox=<string> only points near north,south,east,west. --margin=<string> how far outside --bbox to read, as a fraction of it (default 0.25) --tolerance=<string> simplification tolerance in degrees (level of detail) --limit=<string> max points to return. --still drop GPS spikes and draw each stay as two points, by the track's kind. --max-speed=<string> with --still, a jump faster than this (m/s) is a spike (default by the track's kind) --rejected read the fixes the track's rules or a person rejected too, each marked 'rejected'. --only-rejected read the rejected fixes alone, each run of them a segment.

Import a staged GPX file into the device it names, and move the file to its track's routes/; mark it pending when no single device matches, and keep it in its staging area's routes/. changes things track-stage [--track=<path>] [--name=<string>] <gpx> Argument What it is <gpx> VFS path to the GPX file. Option What it does --track=<path> the track it belongs to, instead of the one of the device it names: the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. --name=<string> the name to keep the file under in the track's routes/, instead of its own. track-stage /home/anna/staging/files/inbox/upload-2026-10-16/hike.gpx track-stage /home/anna/staging/routes/hike.gpx --track hiking-gps With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : imported, with the track, the number of new fixes and where the file is kept; or pending, with why.

Derive a track's trips and stays, into /.trips. changes things track-trips [--full] [--dry-run] <track> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. Option What it does --full read the whole track, not only from where its trips are settled. --dry-run derive and show them without writing .trips. track-trips sailboat track-trips /dev/sailboat/position --full --dry-run

Change how a track travels: its kind, the timezone its trips are cut in, its description. changes things track-update [--kind=<string>] [--timezone=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--clear=<string>] <track> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. Option What it does --kind=<string> how it travels, which sets how it is read and the units it is shown in: boat, car, bike, foot. --timezone=<string> IANA timezone its trips are cut into days in, e.g. Europe/Stockholm. --description=<string> free-text note. --clear=<string> remove a field: kind, timezone or description (repeatable) track-update sailboat --kind boat --timezone Europe/Stockholm track-update /dev/sailboat/position --clear timezone

Give a track's trips and their days the weather along it: wind, temperature and cloud cover. changes things track-weather [--full] [--dry-run] <track> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. Option What it does --full sample every trip again, not only those without weather or with a day in the last week. --dry-run look the weather up and count it without writing .trips. track-weather sailboat track-weather /dev/sailboat/position --full With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : TrackWeather: how many days and hours it sampled, how many it left for the next run and why, and how many requests it sent.

Make a trip of a track an album, a new one or one that is there, or take it from its album. changes things trip-album [--new] [--name=<string>] [--album=<path>] [--detach] <track> <trip> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. <trip> the trip: its id from trip-list, or its first day. Option What it does --new make a new album of the trip. --name=<string> the new album's name; by default where the trip got farthest, or the track's name. --album=<path> make this album the album of the trip. --detach take the trip off its album. trip-album sailboat 2025-06-10 --new trip-album sailboat 2025-06-10 --album=/archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 trip-album sailboat 2025-06-10 --detach With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : the album the trip was made, or the one it was taken from.

Join a track's trip to the one before it, or part the track on a day, and derive its trips again. changes things trip-edit [--merge] [--split] <track> <trip> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. <trip> the trip (its id, or its first day) to join, or the day to part on. Option What it does --merge join the trip to the one before it. --split part a trip joined on this day again, or start a trip on it. trip-edit sailboat 2025-06-10 --merge trip-edit sailboat 2025-06-10 -- split

A track's trips and stays, as track-trips last derived them. reads only trip-list <track> Argument What it is <track> the track's path, or a device or a camera linked to one, by its path or its name. trip-list sailboat

Find the voices of an audio or video recording: who speaks when, with one voiceprint per voice. changes things voiceprint-file [-v] [-f] [--no-video] <input> Argument What it is <input> VFS path to an audio or video file. Option What it does -v Verbose output. -f Force re-voiceprinting even if speakers exist. --no-video Skip the faces seen speaking; voices only. voiceprint-file /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/MVI_0042.MOV With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : nothing; one speaker node per voice is written under the file.

The weather at a place and time, or every hour of a span with --to: temperature, wind and cloud cover from the nearest SMHI station, or from Open-Meteo. reads only weather [--lat=<string>] [--lng=<string>] [--place=<string>] [--from=<string>] [--days=<string>] [--to=<string>] <lat> <lng> <time> Argument What it is <lat> latitude (positional; use --lat= if negative) <lng> longitude (positional; use --lng= if negative) <time> when, ISO 8601; UTC unless it gives an offset. Option What it does --lat=<string> latitude, as --lat= , the form a negative one needs. --lng=<string> longitude, as --lng= , the form a negative one needs. --place=<string> the place by name instead of coordinates, as --place=Göteborg: the first hit of a Nominatim search. --from=<string> as a flag: the first hour of a span with --to. --days=<string> every hour of the last days, up to now, instead of and --to. --to=<string> every hour from to this one, at most 744: a line each, TAB {"temperature":…}, as cat -t prints a log. weather 59.33 18.07 2024-07-14T15:00 weather 57.71 11.97 2024-07-08T00:00 --to=2024-07-14T23:00 weather --place=Göteborg --days=7 weather --lat=48.85 --lng=-3.01 2023-08-02T09:30+02:00 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : WeatherReading: each parameter with its value, the hour it holds for and where it came from; one neither source has is left out. With --to, a WeatherReading an hour.

The weather at a place now and in the hours and days ahead, from Open-Meteo. reads only weather-forecast [--lat=<string>] [--lng=<string>] [--place=<string>] [--days=<string>] [--hours=<string>] <lat> <lng> Argument What it is <lat> latitude (positional; use --lat= if negative) <lng> longitude (positional; use --lng= if negative) Option What it does --lat=<string> latitude, as --lat= , the form a negative one needs. --lng=<string> longitude, as --lng= , the form a negative one needs. --place=<string> the place by name instead of coordinates, as --place=Göteborg: the first hit of a Nominatim search. --days=<string> the days ahead from today, 1 to 16 (default 7) --hours=<string> the hours ahead from the one under way (default 24) weather-forecast 57.71 11.97 weather-forecast --place=Göteborg --days=3 --hours=12 weather-forecast --lat=48.85 --lng=-3.01 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : WeatherForecast: the weather now, an entry per hour ahead and per day ahead, each with its WMO weather code, temperature, rain and snow, and wind.

Look up the weather a photo was taken in, at its point and capture time, and write it on its position node. changes things weather-photo [-f] <position> Argument What it is <position> the position node of a file, /position. Option What it does -f Look it up again even when the weather held is for the same point and time. weather-photo /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0007.jpg/position With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : WeatherPhotoResult: the weather written, or why none was.

The Assistant is the module that adds a chat to EiN: you ask in your own words, and it answers by running EiN's commands as you. This page is for anyone deciding whether to install it and for the administrator who does: what it does, what it needs, how to install it and what it adds.

The assistant answers questions about what is kept in EiN, and about EiN itself. To find the answer it runs EiN's own commands as you, with your permissions, and shows you every command it ran. A command that only reads runs at once. One that would change something, such as writing a caption or moving a file, comes to you as a proposal card with the exact commands, which you run or decline: the assistant never changes anything on its own. Chatting with the assistant shows the chat from the user's side. The assistant knows no module by name. Each installed module tells it which of its commands to offer, what to know about its part, which cards to draw under an answer and which questions to suggest; Teaching the assistant describes how.

The assistant works on an EiN with no other module. It then answers from core's commands and its own: what is in a folder or a file, which services are running, how much disk space is used, and charts of what it counted. With the Archive installed, it also searches pictures, people, albums and places, answers questions about family, birthdays and events, proposes captions and events on someone's timeline, and can draw a family tree or a map under an answer. The Archive's search box then reads a sentence typed into it with the assistant's language model too ( The language model ). With Todo installed, it reads your todo lists and what is left for you to do, and proposes adding, ticking off and moving their items. With Dashboards installed, it reads your dashboards and proposes making them, putting cards on them and changing them. With Automation installed, it reads the house's devices, such as how warm it is in the hall and which devices are offline, charts how a reading went, and proposes switching them.

A language model that speaks the OpenAI chat API. The module brings none of its own: The model EiN runs itself , which the installer adds with --llm as a container beside EiN, on the graphics card or the processor. A hosted provider's model , such as OpenAI's, set with four settings in ~/ein/.env . Your questions, and what the assistant reads to answer them, then leave your machine. The language model covers both, and how to check that the model answers. Without a model, the chat waits for one and then says Assistant unavailable . The assistant needs no other module. With the media service and its ems module installed as well, its command search finds commands by meaning rather than by their words ( Find the command you need ).

Install it like any module, in any of three ways: With the installer , at the first install or any time after, together with the model: # on the machine that will run EiN curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- assistant On a machine where EiN runs already, ~/ein/setup.sh --module assistant does the same; add --llm for the model. On Settings → Modules : choose Install beside the filter, then Install on assistant . In EiN's terminal , as the administrator: mod install assistant . Modules explains each way, and how to update and remove a module.

Where What The sidebar Chat , which opens the Chat page with your recent chats The top bar The Chat button, which opens the chat in the side drawer beside the page you are on About EiN , in the account menu A Language model tile: the model's name, and "on this host" or the provider's name Settings → System The Assistant group: the model's address, key, provider and name, where it runs, whether it thinks, how much it may write and how long the chat waits for it ( settings ) Status → Services The llm-link row, which says whether the model answers and where it runs EiN's terminal The commands assistant-chat , assistant-commands , llm-chat , llm-status , agent-eval and assistant-ask ( Assistant commands ) Your conversations are kept as logs in your home folder, under ~/.chats/ ( Where your conversations are kept ).

Chatting with the assistant : asking, reading an answer, running or declining a proposal, and your conversations. The language model : running the model on your machine or using a hosted one, and checking that it answers. Teaching the assistant : how a module offers the assistant its commands, cards and questions, and how to measure it with agent-eval . Assistant commands : every command the module brings. The graphics card the model can run on is covered in The graphics card .

The assistant answers questions about what your family keeps in EiN, and about EiN itself, in your own words. It looks things up by running EiN's own commands as you, shows you every command it ran, and asks you before it changes anything. This page is for everyone who uses the chat. The chat comes with the Assistant module, and this page applies once it is installed. If you do not see Chat in the sidebar, the module is not installed; your administrator can add it (see Modules ). Pictures, people, albums and places come with the Archive : where this page shows them, it assumes the Archive is installed too.

There are three places to open it, and they all show the same conversations. Chat in the sidebar opens the Chat page, with your recent chats in a box beside the conversation. The Chat button in the top bar (a speech bubble) opens the chat in the side drawer, beside the page you are on, so you can ask about that page. Choose the button again to close the drawer. The drawer's title, Chat , is a link ( Open as page ) that opens the same conversation as the full Chat page. On the Chat page itself there is no chat button. In the viewer the top bar is covered, so the viewer has a Chat button of its own at the top right, next to the details button. The drawer then stays open beside the picture, with a Close chat button (×) of its own. In a window narrower than 992 pixels there is no room beside the picture, and the button opens the chat as a dialog over it instead. On a phone the top bar's chat button opens the chat as a dialog that fills the screen; Back or the × closes it. In the viewer on a phone, open the menu at the top right and choose Chat . See EiN on a phone for what else differs. The chat beside the viewer knows which picture is open, so you can ask about it without naming it. You can make the drawer wider or narrower by dragging its left edge; Finding your way around explains the drawer. No keyboard shortcut opens the chat.

Click in the box at the bottom, which reads "Ask about what is kept here — or EiN itself…" ("Ask anything…" on a phone). A click on any empty part of the chat puts the cursor there too. Type your question. Shift + Enter starts a new line; the box grows to eight lines. Press Enter , or click the send button (a paper plane). The answer grows in front of you. It says "Waiting…" at first, "Thinking…" while the language model works out its next step, and "Running commands… 2 done" with the command it is running underneath. The answer's words appear as they are written. An answer takes from a few seconds to a few minutes, depending on how many commands the question needs and how fast your machine runs the language model. While a chat is answering, its box is locked and the send button is grey. There is no button to stop an answer once you have asked. You can start a new chat and ask something else in the meantime. A new, empty chat shows a robot and "Ask about what is kept here, or about EiN itself.", and under it two questions the installed modules suggest, such as "When were we last at the beach?". The assistant answers in the language you ask in, whatever language the archive is kept in or the commands print. A message too short to tell, such as a name or "ok", is answered in the Archive language ( CFG_LANGUAGE ). The chat's own buttons and messages are in English.

p.h: What the assistant knows about the page you are on
p.x: Every question carries what you have in front of you, so you do not have to name it: the date and time, from the clock of the machine EiN runs on, so "this week" and "today" work; the page you have open: its name and the sidebar entry it is under, what it says it shows, which tab is open, and the person, album, place or other thing the page is about; the picture, video or recording open in the viewer. So on Peggy Wrenfield's page you can ask "When was she born?", and in the viewer "Who is in this picture?". A dialog, or the chat itself, is never the page it is asked about. "I", "me", "my" and "we" mean you only when your account is linked to a person in the archive. You can tell: your account menu then has a Me row. Without the link, the assistant says it cannot tell who you are. Your administrator makes the link (see Accounts and groups ). A file you ask it to make without saying where goes in your home folder. The assistant knows nothing from your other chats. Each chat is a conversation of its own. The assistant reads only text: what EiN has recorded about a picture, such as its date, place, the people whose faces are named in it, its caption and any text found in it. It does not look at the picture itself. If nobody has named a face yet, it cannot tell you who that is; see People and faces .

The bulb inside the question box asks the model to think before every step. The answer takes about twice as long, and the assistant picks its commands more carefully. Off, its tooltip reads Think harder (slower) . Click it and it turns yellow: Thinking harder: slower, more careful . It stays on in this browser, for every chat, until you click it again. A question you asked with it shows a small bulb beside it ( Asked with "think harder" ), and the answer shows the model's thoughts. Try it when an answer came back as No answer , or when the commands the assistant ran were not the ones the question needed.

Reading runs at once; anything that would change something waits for you. An answer that needed no command is a plain bubble. An answer for which the assistant ran something, or that has a card, pictures or links under it, is drawn as a timeline, starting with a robot, with a dot for each step: What you see What it is Thought for 1.2s What the model thought before it answered, when it thinks (always with Think harder ). Click to read it. Words between steps What the model said while it worked. Ran 3 commands · 0.4s The commands it ran, folded to one line, with ", 1 failed" when one failed. Click to open: each command shows the line as it ran, how long it took, and what it printed, after the thought that led to it. Long output is folded behind output · N lines ; a failure is shown in red. Waited 42s for the language model to restart The language model was away and came back during the answer. The answer The reply itself, with lists, bold text, tables and links where they help. After the answer A proposal card, a table, cards, pictures, links and Show in search , each described below. Under the answer is the time it took, such as "12.3s"; point at it to see the date and time of the answer. Point at your picture beside a question to see when you asked it. Opening Ran N commands is how you check an answer: you see exactly what the assistant looked up and what EiN told it.

Pictures come as a grid of up to 24 thumbnails under the answer; click one to open it in the viewer . The text says in a sentence what they are rather than listing them. Ask for more in the same chat and the assistant leaves out the pictures it has already shown you there. A plain request for pictures, such as "Show photos of Peggy Wrenfield in Falmouth", is answered straight from a search, without the longer back-and-forth: the answer begins "Here are …", and its two steps, parse-search and search , show as its commands. This happens when Think harder is off and the request starts with words like "show", "find", "get", "photos", "pictures" or "videos", or the Swedish "visa", "hitta" or "bilder", and asks nothing more. A request with "who", "when", "how many", "this" or "my" in it is answered the longer way, through the commands.

Names in the answer are links: a picture opens in the viewer, a person, album or place opens its page, and a web address opens as usual. Under the answer, links to the people, places and folders the answer is about are lined up for you. Before the answer reaches you, EiN checks every link as you: a link to something that does not exist, or that you may not see, is left as plain words.

When the assistant searched, Show in search opens that search with its filters filled in: on the Media page for photos, videos and recordings, and on the Search page when it looked for albums, people, places, cameras or tracks. Use it to see how the assistant understood your question, and to change the filters yourself. Search and the finder explains the filters.

When you ask for a table, or the answer has many rows, the chat draws a table under it. EiN reads the rows from the command itself rather than from the model, so no value is copied wrongly. The table has a title, a header that stays in view as you scroll, and numbers aligned to the right. Under it are the command that printed the rows and how many there are, such as "42 rows", with ", the first 1000 shown" when there are more than 1,000.

Some answers come with a card drawn under them: Card When What it shows Chart When you ask for a chart, a graph or a diagram A line, bar or pie chart of a log's entries, of a series a command prints, such as the weather hour by hour over a week, or of numbers the assistant counted. With fewer than two values it says "Nothing to chart." Family tree For a question about family The tree around a person, or the line of relations between two people. Comes with the archive. Map When you ask where something is, or ask for a map The places and pictures the answer named, pinned where the archive has them. Comes with the archive. A card is drawn as you each time it appears, so it shows the archive as it is when you look, and leaves out anything you may not see.

p.h: When the assistant offers to make a change
p.x: The assistant reads on its own, but it never changes anything without you. When your question needs a change, such as writing a picture's caption, adding an event to someone's timeline, setting someone's parent or partner, or creating, moving or removing a file, it answers "Shall I run this?" and shows a proposal card: a header, Bash , and a title saying what the change does; the exact commands as a small script: set -e first, then each command under its title as a comment line starting with # ; a yellow border while it waits for you; the buttons Run and Decline . Asked "Add to Ruby Wrenfield's timeline that she graduated in December 2021", the card could read: set -e # Add an event (blob) to a person, album, location or camera person-add-event -- date =2021-12 --body= 'Graduated' /archive/people/ruby-wrenfield A command that can say what it would do without doing it, such as automation-new --dry-run , is tried that way before the card is shown. If the try fails, the assistant is told why and corrects the command, so a card does not offer a change that would be refused. To decide: Read the commands. Check the names, dates and paths: the card shows what the assistant understood. If something is wrong, click into the script and change it. The card then says edited ; reset puts the proposal back as it was. Click Run to run the whole script, or Decline to leave things as they are. Run runs the script exactly as the card shows it, as you, as if you had typed it in the terminal . Because of set -e , it stops at the first line that fails; take that line out if you want the rest to run regardless. The card then shows how it went: green Done with "· exit 0" and what the commands printed, red Failed with the exit code and the error, or Dismissed when you declined. The assistant goes on by itself: it reads what happened and takes the next step, which may be another card, or gives its answer. After you decline, it does not propose the same change again in that answer; if you change your mind, ask for it in a new message. Pages open beside the chat show the change at once. A card can be run or declined only once.

Every command the assistant runs, and every script you run from a card, runs as you, with your permissions. It sees what you can see in the browser and nothing more, and a change you may not make fails the same way it would if you made it yourself. In admin mode the assistant reads with the administrator's rights too. What counts as a change is decided by EiN, not by the model. A line runs at once only when every command in it is known to only read and nothing is written to a file; anything else becomes a card. The assistant cannot open the editor, sign in or out, run a service's own program (services are started with service-start , which it proposes like any change), or ask itself a question. Teaching the assistant describes how this works.

p.h: Visitors who have not signed in
p.x: Where the administrator has turned on Visitors may browse (see Browse without signing in ), someone who has not signed in can ask questions too. The assistant changes nothing for them: no proposal card appears, and the answer says that a change needs signing in. A visitor's conversation is kept only in the open page. There are no recent chats, New chat starts over, and the conversation is gone when the page is closed or reloaded.

The Chat page keeps every conversation you have had, newest first, and asks about EiN itself as readily as about what it keeps. Start a new chat with the plus button ( New chat ). Start one for each new topic: the assistant remembers only what was said in the current chat. If the chat you are in has no messages yet, New chat stays in it rather than making another empty one. Titles are the first question, on one line, cut at 60 characters. A chat cannot be renamed. Recent chats : on the Chat page they are in the box at the left, the most recently used first, each with its title, the time (today) or the date, and how many messages it has. The Filter chats… box above them matches titles, not what was said. In the drawer and on a phone, the Recent chats button (a clock) opens the same list as a menu. With nothing to show, the list says "No previous chats", or "No chats match" when the filter finds none. Come back to a chat by its address: the Chat page shows /chat/<id> in the address bar, so you can bookmark a conversation. A chat opens only for you; anyone else who follows the address gets their own latest chat instead. To delete a chat: Open the Chat page from the sidebar. In the recent chats box, click the trash icon ( Delete chat ) beside the chat. Your browser asks Delete “<title>”? ; confirm. The chat is deleted for good: it does not go to the trash . The menu in the drawer and on a phone has no delete button, and a chat cannot be deleted while it is answering.

Each chat is a log in your home folder, under ~/.chats/ . The folder and its logs are yours alone: other users cannot open them. An administrator can, because an administrator's access passes every permission. Chats are kept until you delete them; EiN removes none on its own. A chat's log holds your questions, the answers, the commands that ran and what they printed, so it holds copies of what the assistant read to answer you. From the terminal you can list, read and delete your chats; see assistant-chat : # in EiN's terminal assistant-chat list assistant-chat read < id > assistant-chat delete < id >

With every question the assistant gets the earlier turns of the chat again, but long results from earlier turns go back shortened, and once the earlier turns add up to about 20,000 characters the oldest are dropped. Everything stays on your screen and in the log, but the assistant no longer reads the first questions of a long chat. Start a new chat for a new topic, or say again what matters.

While the language model is starting or restarting, for example after an update or a restart of the machine, the answer says "The language model is restarting; waiting for it…". The chat keeps trying, for three minutes unless your administrator has changed Wait for the language model (seconds) ( CFG_LLM_WAIT ). If the model comes back in time, the answer goes on and its timeline notes how long it waited. Each command gets a minute. When commands take too long, the assistant stops running them and answers from what it has, saying what was slow. When there is no answer, a red card takes its place: Card It says What happened What to do Assistant unavailable "The assistant is not available right now." The language model could not be reached within the wait, a step took longer than three minutes, or your browser lost contact with EiN. Try again later. If it keeps happening, tell your administrator. No answer "The assistant could not answer this question." The model gave up: it kept repeating a command, used commands that do not exist, kept running commands after its 12 for one question, or the chat no longer fit. Ask more plainly, name the person or album, turn on Think harder , or start a new chat. Answer too long "The answer was too long to finish. Ask for less, such as the last 20 rows." The answer was longer than the model may write at once. Ask for less, or ask for a table. Under the text, the card gives the technical reason in small type, such as model service unreachable: http://llm:8190: …; still away after 180s . Pass it on to your administrator if you ask for help. Retry , on the card, asks the same question again as a new message. It works after a reload too. If every question waits the full time and then shows Assistant unavailable , the language model is not running, or none has been set up; that is for your administrator. The language model covers setting it up and Troubleshooting what to check. The assistant can also be wrong while looking sure. It is told to say only what the commands printed, but a small model sometimes picks the wrong command or misreads a result. When an answer matters, open Ran N commands to see what it looked up, or Show in search to see how it read your question.

Usually the language model runs on the same machine as EiN, and nothing you ask leaves it. The chat says nothing about it then. The Language model tile in About EiN , in your account menu, says "on this host" under the model's name. Your administrator can choose a hosted provider's model instead. The chat then shows a line above the question box, with a globe icon, naming the provider, for example: Answered by OpenAI: your questions, and the names, places and search results used to answer them, leave this server. With a provider, what goes there is your questions, what is on your screen (the page's name and the path of the thing or picture it shows), your name, and what the commands printed: names, dates, places, captions, and the text of files the assistant read. Pictures, videos and recordings themselves are never sent. Searches you type as sentences are read by the same model, so they go to the provider too. The language model has the details for administrators.

These work on the demo archive of the Wrenfield family; use the names in your own archive instead. Ask What you get Show photos of Peggy Wrenfield in Falmouth A grid of pictures, straight from a search, with Show in search Who is Helen Okafor? Her dates, parents, partner, children and life events How are Ruby Wrenfield and Helen Okafor related? The answer in words, with a family tree card of the line between them Who are Helen Okafor's grandchildren? A list of names, linked to their pages Whose birthday is coming up? Birthdays, anniversaries and other events around today Who is in this picture, and how old was each of them that day? With a picture open in the viewer: the people named in it and their ages Where were the pictures of Sailing in the archipelago taken? Show me on a map. A map card with the places pinned Add to Ruby Wrenfield's timeline that she graduated in December 2021 A proposal card to run or decline Which services are running? A list or table of EiN's services and how they are doing How much disk space is used? The space used and free, from the machine EiN runs on For more about finding pictures without the chat, see Search and the finder .

The assistant's chat, and the search box when you type a sentence, read people's words with a language model. This page is for the administrator who sets that model up: on the machine EiN runs on, on its graphics card or processor, or at a hosted provider, and how to check that it answers. It applies once the Assistant module is installed.

p.h: What the language model is for
p.x: EiN asks the language model in three places: The chat. Every answer in the chat comes from the model, which runs EiN's commands to look things up. Chatting with the assistant shows it from the user's side. The search box. With the Archive installed, when someone types a sentence, such as photos of Ruby Wrenfield from 1987 , the Archive's search parser asks the model which words are people, places, years and kinds of media. When the model does not answer within 20 seconds, the parser reads the sentence with its own rules instead, so search keeps working without it. Plain picture requests in the chat , such as "Show photos of Peggy Wrenfield from 1990", which go through the same search parser and are answered with one search. All three belong to the assistant module. Without it installed, EiN asks no language model at all; The Assistant shows how to install it. The language model does no media processing. Faces, picture descriptions, transcripts and the vectors that find things by meaning come from the media service , which runs models of its own.

Where How you set it up What it costs On this machine, on the graphics card setup.sh --llm on a machine with an NVIDIA card Part of the card's memory, shared with the media service. Answers in seconds. On this machine, on the processor setup.sh --llm on a machine without a card Memory and processor time. The answers are the same, only slower. At a hosted provider Four settings in ~/ein/.env The provider's charges. Questions, and what the assistant reads in the archive to answer them, leave your machine. The model EiN runs itself is Qwen3.5-4B in llama.cpp's server. The prompts, the chat's shortcuts and the assistant's test questions are tuned for that model, and it is the only one EiN calls tried. Any service that speaks the OpenAI chat API can stand in for it: a hosted provider such as OpenAI, OpenRouter, Mistral or Groq, or a server of your own such as vLLM, Ollama or LM Studio.

p.h: Run the model on your machine
p.x: Add the model on the machine EiN runs on: # on the machine EiN runs on ~/ein/setup.sh --llm setup.sh keeps EIN_LLM=1 in ~/ein/.env , fetches the model's sources into ~/ein/src/llm , adds an llm container, and restarts EiN. When the first install found an NVIDIA card ( EIN_GPU=1 in .env ), the container gets the card. The installer takes the same option: curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- --llm . Wait for the model to download. On its first start the container fetches the model file from Hugging Face into the llm folder of your data folder ( ~/ein/data/llm unless you chose another), a download of several gigabytes. Follow it with: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose logs -f llm The model is ready when the log says the server is listening on port 8190. A later start reads the file from disk and takes a minute or two. Check that EiN reaches it. In EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal llm-status --checks ok llm ours, qwen3.5-4b at http://llm:8190, on the card on the CPU instead of on the card means the model runs on the processor. Check that the model answers explains the other lines you may see. Open the chat and ask something. The first answer after a start can take longer, while the model reads the assistant's instructions for the first time. The commands on this page are written for podman. With Docker, write docker compose where they say podman compose .

What Value Model Qwen3.5-4B-Q8_0.gguf from unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF , named qwen3.5-4b Server llama.cpp's server, a ready-made image pinned to one build Address http://llm:8190 , on the compose network only; nothing outside the containers reaches it Context 32768 tokens: the most of a conversation the model reads at once, cached at 8 bits Requests One at a time; a second question waits until the first is answered Memory At most 10 GB ( LLM_MEMORY ) Thinking Off, unless a question asks for it (the chat's Think harder ) The server keeps what it last read in a cache, so a follow-up question in the same chat reads only the new message. It stays loaded between questions.

p.h: Share the graphics card with the media service
p.x: With the media service on the same card, the two divide its memory. The model leaves the media service LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB of the card, 8800 MB unless you change it, loads as many of its layers as fit in the rest, and runs the others on the processor. It works its part out each time it starts, from what the media service holds then, so it gets the same part whichever of the two started first. On a 16 GB card every layer fits; on a smaller one some run on the processor, and the answers come more slowly. To change the division, set the media service's share 400 MB below the model's reserve, with the slider on the Media service tab or in EiN's terminal, and the reserve in ~/ein/.env , then start the model again: # in EiN's terminal config set CFG_EMS_CARD_SHARE_MB 8400 # in ~/ein/.env LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB = 8800 # what the model leaves the media service of the card # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein podman compose up -d llm The graphics card covers the card itself, and Performance and sizing how much card and memory each part needs.

These go in ~/ein/.env and take effect at the next podman compose up -d . Variable Default What it sets LLM_GGUF_REPO unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-GGUF The Hugging Face repository the model file comes from LLM_GGUF_FILE Qwen3.5-4B-Q8_0.gguf The model file LLM_CARD_RESERVE_MB 8800 How much of the card the model leaves free for the media service LLM_MEMORY 10g The most memory the container may use LLM_IMAGE a pinned llama.cpp build The server's image Warning The container's chat template is written for Qwen3.5, and the server names whatever it loaded qwen3.5-4b . A model of another family needs its own template, which .env cannot choose, and the health check cannot tell that it is not the tried model. Change LLM_GGUF_FILE only to another quantisation of Qwen3.5-4B, or use a server of your own and point EiN at it as described below.

Open ~/ein/.env on the machine EiN runs on. The file has the lines ready, commented out. Remove the # and fill them in: # in ~/ein/.env CFG_LLM_URL =https://api.openai.com CFG_LLM_KEY =<the key the provider gave you> CFG_LLM_PROVIDER =OpenAI CFG_LLM_MODEL =<the model 's name, as the provider writes it> CFG_LLM_URL is the address of the API without /v1 . CFG_LLM_PROVIDER is the name the chat shows. Always set it for a hosted model: while it is empty, EiN treats the model as running on your machine and tells no one that their questions leave it. CFG_LLM_MODEL must be a model the provider offers. Left out, EiN asks for qwen3.5-4b , which a provider does not have. Apply it. If the model was running on your machine, take it out at the same time: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein ./setup.sh --no-llm # removes the llm container and restarts EiN; the model file stays Otherwise podman compose up -d is enough. Check it with llm-status --checks in EiN's terminal: ok llm OpenAI's <model> at https://api.openai.com: questions, and what the assistant reads to answer them, leave this host warn llm model <model> is untried: the prompts, the fast path and the eval set are tuned for qwen3.5-4b; run agent-eval against it before trusting it The second line is expected for every model but Qwen3.5-4B. It is a warning only: the chat answers, but nobody has measured how well. Try a model before you rely on it shows how to measure it. The same settings are on Settings → System , in the Assistant category, for an administrator who prefers the Web UI: Language model address , Language model key , Language model provider and Language model . A value saved there wins over .env and shows the badge Set here ; a value from .env shows From deployment . Restore inherited value goes back to the one from .env . In the terminal, config-set CFG_LLM_PROVIDER OpenAI does the same as saving it on the page ( reference ).

Once CFG_LLM_PROVIDER is set, the chat shows a line above the question box, with a globe icon: Answered by OpenAI: your questions, and the names, places and search results used to answer them, leave this server. What goes to the provider is each question, the page the person is on, their name, and everything the commands print while the assistant looks things up: names, dates, places, captions, and the text of files it reads. Sentences typed into the search box go there too, since the search parser asks the same model. Pictures, videos and recordings are never sent. Tell the people who use your EiN before you switch.

The key is a secret. No shell in EiN sees it, config-get CFG_LLM_KEY says only whether it is set, and the settings page shows Set — type a new one to replace it rather than the key. A key saved on the settings page is kept in /etc/keys , which only an administrator can read; one in .env stays in EiN's own process. EiN sends the key only to the address in CFG_LLM_URL as the system has it, never to an address someone puts in front of a command.

Where What it tells you llm-status Whose the model is and where it runs, from the settings alone, without asking the model llm-status --checks Whether the model answers, whose it is, where it runs, and whether it is the tried model. health reads the same Status → Services , row llm-link The same checks in one line About EiN , in the account menu A Language model tile with the model's name, and "on this host" or the provider's name under it podman compose logs llm The server's own log, for a model on your machine Each service's row carries its status line, such as ems-link's here; llm-link's, further down, says whether the chat's model answers and where it runs. llm-link is not the model itself but a service of the assistant module that watches it. Once a minute it asks the model whether it answers, and writes a line to its log each time the answer changes, so /var/logs/services/llm-link/stdout.log shows when the model went away or came back: llm-link: watching ours at http://llm:8190 llm-link: ours, qwen3.5-4b at http://llm:8190, on the card llm-link: http://llm:8190 is not answering; the chat cannot answer until it does The log starts over each time the service starts. A model that does not answer is a warning in health , never a failure: the archive's work goes on without it. Health and status and Services and logs cover both in general.

All of these are system settings, on Settings → System → Assistant ( Language model command is under Search ), in ~/ein/.env , or with config-set . Configuration explains where a value comes from and which one wins. Setting Label on the settings page Default What it does CFG_LLM_URL Language model address http://127.0.0.1:8190 The API's address, without /v1 . The compose install sets http://llm:8190 . CFG_LLM_MODEL Language model qwen3.5-4b The model name sent with each request. llama.cpp answers with the model it loaded, whatever this says. CFG_LLM_KEY Language model key not set The bearer key a provider expects. CFG_LLM_PROVIDER Language model provider empty The provider's name. Empty means the model runs on this host. CFG_LLM_CARD Where our language model runs empty card or cpu , for the status lines. setup.sh --llm sets it from EIN_GPU . CFG_LLM_THINKING Think before answering empty 1 or 0 turns the model's thinking on or off for every question in the chat that does not ask otherwise. llm-chat , and the search box through it, thinks only when asked with --think . Only llama.cpp reads it; empty leaves it to the server. CFG_LLM_MAX_TOKENS Answer length (tokens) 2048 How much the model may write in one step of an answer. A model that thinks needs more. CFG_LLM_WAIT Wait for the language model (seconds) 180 How long a chat question waits for a model that is restarting or loading before it gives up. 0 gives up at once. CFG_LANGUAGE_MODEL Language model command empty The command the search parser asks. The assistant module sets it to llm-chat ; empty, the search box reads sentences by its rules. A change on the settings page takes effect at the next question; EiN itself does not restart. A change to the address, model, key, provider or Where our language model runs also restarts llm-link . A change in .env takes effect at the next podman compose up -d , unless the same setting has been saved on the settings page.

llm-chat sends one question to the model, with nothing from the archive, and prints the answer. It is the quickest way to see that the model answers and how fast: # in EiN's terminal llm-chat 'Answer in one word: what colour is the sky?' llm-chat --system 'Answer in one word.' 'The colour of grass?' It gives up after 180 seconds ( --timeout ) and does not wait for a model that is restarting. With --think the model thinks first, and the thought counts toward --max-tokens : a thought that uses them all up leaves no answer, and llm-chat fails with the answer was cut off before it began . llm-chat lists its options.

p.h: Try a model before you rely on it
p.x: agent-eval asks the chat the test questions every module ships, against your real archive, and scores whether the model reached the right commands and answered. Run it after switching to another model, and compare it with a run on the default one: # in EiN's terminal agent-eval -- limit 5 --verbose nohup agent-eval --out /tmp/agent-eval.json A full run asks many questions and can take a long time; --out writes the results after every question, so a closed terminal loses nothing. agent-eval lists its options.

Everyone who has signed in can use the chat and the model. People who have not signed in, such as visitors through a share link, may use it only where the archive is open to visitors; otherwise the model refuses them with sign in to use the language model . Permissions in depth covers opening the archive to visitors.

# on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein ./setup.sh --no-llm This removes the llm container and restarts EiN. The model file stays in the llm folder of your data folder, so --llm later starts without downloading it again; delete the folder to free the space. With no model, the chat waits for CFG_LLM_WAIT seconds and then answers Assistant unavailable , and the search box reads sentences by its rules. To remove the chat altogether, remove the assistant module ( Modules ).

What you see What to do Every chat question waits three minutes, then shows Assistant unavailable No model answers. Run llm-status --checks . Without --llm and without a provider in .env , there is no model: add one as above. http://llm:8190 is not answering; the chat cannot answer until it does The container is not running or still loading. Look at podman compose ps and podman compose logs llm . On the first start it may still be downloading the model. The chat says "The language model is restarting; waiting for it…" after a restart The model is loading. The chat waits up to CFG_LLM_WAIT seconds and goes on when it answers. llm-status --checks says on the CPU , or answers are slow on a machine with a card on the CPU means EIN_GPU=0 in .env . Slow answers with a card can also mean the media service left too little of it; podman compose logs llm says how many of its layers fit on the card when it started. See Share the graphics card with the media service and The graphics card . The llm container restarts again and again It is out of memory, or the card filled while it loaded. Look at podman compose logs llm ; give it more with LLM_MEMORY , or leave more of the card free for it. OpenAI does not offer qwen3.5-4b; the chat's questions to it fail CFG_LLM_MODEL is not set, or names a model the provider does not have. Set it to one of the provider's models. A hosted model answers HTTP 401 in the error card's small type The key is wrong or missing. Set CFG_LLM_KEY again. A key saved on the settings page wins over the one in .env . You changed CFG_LLM_URL in .env and nothing changed The setting is saved on Settings → System , which wins. Click Restore inherited value there, or change it there instead. Answer too long in the chat The answer reached Answer length (tokens) . Asking for less usually helps; a higher CFG_LLM_MAX_TOKENS lets the model write more. The chat has no provider line, but the model is hosted CFG_LLM_PROVIDER is empty. Set it, so the people using EiN know where their questions go. Troubleshooting has more, and Chatting with the assistant explains the chat's error cards from the user's side.

The assistant knows no module by name: everything it can do with your module, it learns from a few files your module ships. This page is for module developers who want the chat to answer questions about their part, and for administrators who want to change what the assistant is told. It applies once the Assistant module is installed. What the chat looks like to the people who use it is in Chatting with the assistant . Where the language model runs and how to point EiN at another one is in The language model .

p.h: How the assistant learns about a module
p.x: Each turn of the chat is a short loop. The language model is given a system message and a list of tools, calls one tool at a time, reads what the command printed, and finally answers with a tool called final_answer . At most 12 tool calls are made before the model must answer. Both the system message and the tools are put together from the installed modules each time: The tools are the commands the modules list, each described by its own --help spec, plus find_commands , command_help , run_command and final_answer . The system message is the prompt file /etc/assistant-prompt.md , then what each module says about its part, then a few lines about the question: who is asking, their home directory and the system's language ( CFG_LANGUAGE ), which only a message too short to tell is answered in. The cards an answer can carry, the questions an empty chat suggests and the questions agent-eval asks also come from the modules. A module gives all of this in one directory, etc/assistant.d/ . When an administrator runs mod setup , that directory is linked as /etc/assistant.d/<module>/ , and the setup log says Linked assistant.d at /etc/assistant.d/<module> ( Assistant.d already linked at … when the link is there already). The assistant reads every directory under /etc/assistant.d/ in name order, as the user who is asking. Every file is optional; a module ships only the ones it needs. File What it gives the assistant tools The module's commands that the model may call directly, one name a line. prompt.md What the model should know about the module's part: where things are and which command answers what. cards.json Pages of the module that can be drawn under an answer: a map, a family tree, a chart. examples Questions the chat suggests before anything has been asked, one a line. eval.json Questions with known good commands, for agent-eval to measure the assistant with. The assistant module ships its own drop-in this way (the ls , stat , find and cat tools and the chart card), and so does the Archive (its search, people and location commands, the family tree and map cards). The media service module ships none. modules/<module>/ ├── mod.json ├── bin/ │ └── recipe-search └── etc/ └── assistant.d/ ├── tools ├── prompt.md ├── cards.json ├── examples └── eval.json Because the directory is linked rather than copied, an edit to a file in it is seen without running mod setup again, and mod remove takes the link away. How a module is laid out in general is in Writing a module .

p.h: Offer a command as a tool
p.x: List the commands the model should be able to call directly in etc/assistant.d/tools , one a line. A # starts a comment. A command that two modules list is offered once. # The commands the recipes module offers the assistant's model as tools, one a line. recipe-search recipe-info recipe-add-note The assistant asks each listed command for its spec with JSON_OUTPUT=1 <command> --help and turns the spec into a tool. Nothing about the command is written down twice: what --help says is exactly what the model reads. A listed command that does not answer --help with a spec is left out of the tools, and asked again on the next turn.

p.h: Commands you do not list are still reachable
p.x: You do not have to list every command. The model can search for any command on the asking user's path by what it should do ( find_commands ), read its spec ( command_help ) and run a shell line ( run_command ). Listing a command saves the model those steps and makes it the obvious choice, so list the few commands that answer most questions about your part, and leave the rest to the search. The search ranks commands by their name, description and returns sentence, so a clear description helps there too. Try it from EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal assistant-commands find 'find a recipe by ingredient' The answer lists the best commands with their description, whether they change anything, and a score. An administrator's command ( admin: true in its spec) is only found for administrators, a daemon is never run from the chat, and edit , login , logout , assistant-ask and agent-eval are refused outright. The full list of the command's options is in the command reference .

p.h: Write a spec the model can use
p.x: A small model calls a command exactly as its spec describes it. Give every command you list: Field What the model gets from it description What the command is for, in one sentence. The first line of the tool's description. args Positional arguments, each a property of the tool under its own name, with its description. flags Each flag a property of the tool. type is required: bool makes a switch, any other type takes a value. examples One or two real command lines, without a prompt. Shown to the model under Examples: . returns What the command answers with under JSON_OUTPUT=1 , in a sentence. Shown under Returns: . effect read or write . Decides whether the chat runs a line at once or shows it to the user first. How a spec becomes a tool: A positional argument is required unless the spec marks it optional: true . Mark every argument that may be left out, whatever its description says. An argument marked variadic becomes a list. A flag marked repeatable becomes a list, and each entry is passed as its own --flag=value . Use it where a user might name several things, such as two people in one search. When a short and a long flag have the same description, only the long one is offered. A long flag is always written as --flag=value , so a value starting with a dash (a longitude west of Greenwich) is not read as another flag. A TypeScript command carries its spec as a spec property. This is the Archive's file-set-description : fileSetDescription. spec = { name : 'file-set-description' , effect : 'write' as const , description : "Set a file's hand-written description" , args : [ { name : 'file' , type : 'path' as const , description : 'VFS path to file node' }, ], flags : [ { name : 'text' , type : 'string' as const , description : 'the description; empty clears it, - reads it from stdin' }, ], examples : [ "file-set-description --text 'Ett exempel' /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0042.jpg" , 'cat notes.md | file-set-description --text - /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019/files/IMG_0042.jpg' , ], returns : 'nothing; the description is written.' , }; A bash command declares the same with the arg builtin. This is the Archive's person-create , with some of its options left out: #!bash arg --desc "Create a person node" arg --effect write arg '<target>' path "VFS path for the person node" arg -n --name string "Display name" arg -b --born string "Birth date (YYYY[-MM[-DD]])" arg --example "person-create /archive/people/Disa_Exempel --name 'Disa Exempel' --born 2019-01-01" arg --returns "nothing; the person node is created." arg -- export An optional bash argument ( arg [<name>] type = default "desc" ) is marked optional: true in the spec arg writes, so the model is not told to give one. Check what the model will read with the command's own help: # in EiN's terminal JSON_OUTPUT=1 recipe-search -- help

p.h: Commands that change things become proposals
p.x: The chat never runs a change on its own. Every line the model wants to run, whether a listed tool or a run_command line, is judged against the specs of the commands in it. A line that only reads runs at once and its output goes back to the model. A line that writes ends the turn with a card showing the exact line, and runs only when the user clicks Run , as that user. After Run or Decline the turn goes on, and the model reads what the line printed or that it was declined. So effect matters more than any other field: read : running it never changes anything. write : it changes something every time. A command that does both is read , with what makes it a write marked: a flag with writes: true , an argument with writes: true (any value) or writes: ['create', …] (only those values). In bash: arg --writes <name> [value…] . A flag with dryRun: true reports what the command would do: a line that uses it is a read, even for a write command. A command without effect is judged a write, so the user is asked before it runs even when it only reads. You can see how a line is judged: # in EiN's terminal assistant-commands judge 'recipe-add-note /home/anna/recipes/Bread --text "Less salt"' The answer says read or write , with the reasons. How a command's spec is written in general is in Writing a module .

p.h: Tell the model about your part
p.x: The model knows the node types every EiN has, but nothing about where your module keeps things or which of your commands answers what. Write that in etc/assistant.d/prompt.md . Each module's text follows the prompt file in the system message, in module name order, separated by a blank line. Write it for a small model that reads it before every question: Say where your nodes live, as paths: recipes are /home/<user>/recipes/<Recipe>, each with ingredients/ and notes/ . Name your node types and the attributes that matter, and which command reads them. Map kinds of questions to commands, one bullet each: what the user asks, the command, and how to call it. The Archive's prompt.md is a good model: "Birthdays and anniversaries: events. Never a search bounded by today's date." Say what the model must not do, where it would otherwise guess, such as working out a family relation itself instead of calling the command that walks the tree. Leave out what the tool specs already say. The model reads every flag's description in the tool list; the prompt is for choosing between commands, not for repeating them. Keep it short. Every word is read on every turn, and the model's context is limited.

p.h: Draw a card under an answer
p.x: A card is one of your module's pages, drawn under the answer as a panel. The assistant knows none of them: a module offers its cards in etc/assistant.d/cards.json , a list of objects, and each card becomes an optional property of final_answer . When the model gives that property, what it filled in becomes the page's query string. Field What it is name The card's property in final_answer , such as map . Characters other than letters, digits and _ become _ . route A route of your module's, declared in ui.routes in mod.json , such as /map/pins . description When the card is wanted, and how to fill it in. The model reads this to decide; say "only when the user asks for a map" when that is what you mean. params A JSON Schema of the route's query: type: "object" , properties and required . fill Optional. A parameter filled with the paths of the pictures the answer shows when the model names none: { "paths": "pictures" } . pictures is the only value. This is the Archive's map card: [ { "name" : "map" , "route" : "/map/pins" , "description" : "A map under the answer, only when the user asks where something is or for a map. Name the locations and pictures a result gave you by path, and the areas location-region looked up by the name you gave it; name nothing to pin the pictures the answer shows. The app pins each one where the archive has it: never write coordinates." , "params" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "title" : { "type" : "string" , "description" : "A short title, in the language of the reply." } , "paths" : { "type" : "array" , "items" : { "type" : "string" , "format" : "path" } , "description" : "Locations or pictures a result named." } , "areas" : { "type" : "array" , "items" : { "type" : "string" } , "description" : "Areas location-region looked up this turn: a city, a country." } } } , "fill" : { "paths" : "pictures" } } ] What the model fills in is checked before it becomes a query: A string with "format": "path" must be an absolute path the asking user can see; any other is left out. A number or integer that is not a number is left out. Text is cut at 400 characters, and a list at 100 values. A list of strings or numbers becomes one query value per item ( ?paths=…&paths=… ). A list of objects, or an object, becomes its JSON text in one value, which your page parses. A card with a required parameter missing, or with nothing in its query at all, is dropped. The names answer , paths , links and table belong to final_answer . A card with one of those names, or a name another module already took, is offered as <module>_<name> . The chat stores only the route with its query, and draws it when the message is shown. Your page reads its query (with useSearchParams from react-router-dom ) and fetches what it shows with ordinary commands, as the person looking at it. A card therefore shows what EiN holds when it is drawn, never values the model wrote down, and its address is a page of its own as well. Keep the page compact: it is drawn in the chat's column, between the answer and the next message. How a module declares its pages is in The module manifest . A card is not a table. For many rows, the model uses final_answer 's own table : it names the line that prints the rows, and the chat runs it and draws every row, so your command only has to print them.

An empty chat shows "Ask about what is kept here, or about EiN itself." and, under it, "For example:" with two suggested questions. They come from the modules' etc/assistant.d/examples , one question a line, with # lines as comments: # Questions the chat suggests before anything is asked, one a line. Which recipes use rhubarb? All modules' questions are put together in module name order, and the first two are shown, so with the Archive installed its questions come first. assistant-chat examples prints the whole list.

A change to a spec, a prompt or a card description can make the model better at one kind of question and worse at another. agent-eval asks a set of questions through the chat's own loop, against the real data on the machine, and scores what happened. Nothing is changed: a line that would write is recorded as a proposal, as the chat would show it.

Each module keeps the questions about its part in etc/assistant.d/eval.json : { "note" : "Questions for agent-eval about recipes." , "resolvers" : [ "recipe-search" ] , "questions" : [ { "id" : "find-by-ingredient" , "bucket" : "search" , "lang" : "en" , "ask" : "Which recipes use rhubarb?" , "commands" : [ "recipe-search" ] } , { "id" : "note-on-open-recipe" , "bucket" : "write" , "lang" : "en" , "ask" : "Add a note to this recipe: less salt next time" , "context" : { "node" : "/home/anna/recipes/Bread" } , "commands" : [ "recipe-add-note" ] } ] } Field What it is id A short name for the question, for --ids . bucket A group of questions, for --bucket : search , kin , write , whatever suits your part. lang sv or en : the language the answer must be in. ask The question, as a user would type it. context Optional. What the app shows when it is asked: route , section , title , about , node , or lightbox for a picture open in the viewer. commands The commands that do the job. Reaching any of them counts. An empty list means the question should be answered without a command, like a greeting. proposes Optional. Words the line the assistant proposes must each hold, such as the endpoints of the devices the question names. resolvers At the top level. Commands that turn a name into a path, so calling one of them first is not counted as a wrong first choice.

agent-eval runs in EiN's terminal, as the account you are signed in with. By default it asks as the person linked to that account, as the chat does, so questions with "my" and "I" can be answered. # in EiN's terminal agent-eval -- limit 5 --verbose agent-eval --bucket write agent-eval --print-prompt --verbose prints a line per question as it finishes, such as find-by-ingredient: reached recipe-search via recipe-search . --print-prompt prints the whole system message, with the lines the chat adds about who is asking, their home folder and the system's language, and every tool schema the model is given, and stops. It is the quickest way to see what your prompt.md , tools and cards.json turned into. --fixtures=<path> asks the questions of one file instead of every module's, and --prompt=<path> tries another prompt file without replacing the installed one. --user=<path> asks as another person, by the path of their node. At the end it prints a summary as JSON: the model that answered, how many questions there were, how many reached one of their commands ( reached ) and how many did so first ( firstChoice ), how many were answered and in the right language, how many lines ran, failed or became proposals, of the questions with proposes how many proposed a line holding every word ( proposalsOk of proposalsWanted ), and the time per question, with how much of it the model took. A full run over every module's questions takes a long time. Run it so it survives a dropped connection, and keep the results in a file that is written after every question: # in EiN's terminal nohup agent-eval --out /tmp/agent-eval.json The file holds the summary and, for each question, every call the model made and the conversation exactly as it was sent. The chat's prompts and fast answers are tuned for qwen3.5-4b ; a run names the model that answered it, so you can compare runs on different models. Every option is in the command reference .

You change When the chat sees it A file in etc/assistant.d/ prompt.md , cards.json and the list in tools on the next question. examples the next time the Web UI is loaded. A listed command's spec Specs are kept for ten minutes, so within ten minutes, or at once after EiN restarts. A command found by search The command search asks a command for its spec again once its file has changed, as mod setup and an update do, and finds a new command within a minute. assistant-commands reindex rebuilds the search at once. /etc/assistant-prompt.md On the next question. A chat that is already going on keeps working after such a change. The first turn after it is slower: the new system message and tools replace the old ones at the top of the conversation, and the model reads the whole chat again from the start.

The rules every module's text follows are in /etc/assistant-prompt.md : how to work, the node types every EiN has, which command to use for the system's own questions, how to write the reply, and that the reply is in the language of the user's question. An administrator can edit it in EiN's terminal with the editor : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator edit /etc/assistant-prompt.md The assistant module ships this file and mod setup copies it only when it is not there yet (the setup log says etc/assistant-prompt.md already exists, skipping ). Your edits are therefore kept across updates, and so are the old rules: a newer version of the module's prompt is not installed over yours. To take the module's version, move your file aside and set the module up again: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mv /etc/assistant-prompt.md /etc/assistant-prompt.md.mine mod setup assistant Try a changed prompt before you install it with agent-eval --prompt=<path> . Note Without a readable /etc/assistant-prompt.md the assistant has no system message and cannot answer; the chat says the assistant is unavailable.

Your command never appears in the tools. Run agent-eval --print-prompt . If it is missing there, agent-eval also says agent-eval: <command> did not describe itself; it is offered by nothing : the command is not on the path, or its --help does not answer with a spec under JSON_OUTPUT=1 . Check that mod setup has run, so the module's bin/ is on the path, and that /etc/assistant.d/<module> exists. The model calls your command with a flag as a stray word, or a value as a switch. A flag without a type cannot be told apart. Give every flag one. The model keeps leaving out an argument it needs, or insists on one it does not. Check whether its description says "optional" or "default"; that alone decides whether it is required. Every use of your command asks the user first. Its spec has no effect , or it is write . A command that only reads should say read . A command the model ran is refused as "x is not an EiN command". The model made up a command name. That message, which the model reads, names similar commands it found; a clearer description or an example in prompt.md helps it pick the right one. A card never appears. The model gives a card only when its description says it is wanted. Check the card with agent-eval --print-prompt under final_answer , and check that every required parameter can be filled: a path the asking user cannot see is dropped, and with it a card that needed it.
