Answers are good in one language and poor in another. Add questions in both to eval.json and compare language in the summary.

This page is for power users and administrators who use the assistant from the terminal. Each table row gives a task, a command line that does it, and a link to that command's full entry. The commands come with the assistant module and are there once it is installed; The Assistant says what it adds, Chatting with the assistant covers the chat in the Web UI, and Commands by task has core's commands. Task Command Reference Which language model answers, and whether it does llm-status --checks llm-status Ask the assistant a question assistant-ask 'Which albums is Peggy Wrenfield in?' assistant-ask The same, thinking before each step assistant-ask --think '<question>' assistant-ask Your saved chats assistant-chat list , assistant-chat read <id> assistant-chat Delete a chat assistant-chat delete <id> assistant-chat Find a command by meaning assistant-commands find 'list running services' assistant-commands Whether a command line changes anything assistant-commands judge 'service restart models' assistant-commands Ask the language model one thing, without tools llm-chat 'The colour of the sky?' llm-chat Score the assistant against the modules' questions agent-eval --limit 5 --verbose agent-eval Asked from the terminal, assistant-ask runs nothing that changes things: a change comes back as a proposal, and without --chat nothing is saved.

The commands the assistant module adds. They are there once the module is installed. 6 of them, by name. Every command also says this with --help ; Commands explains how to read an entry. agent-eval · assistant-ask · assistant-chat · assistant-commands · llm-chat · llm-status

Ask the chat's loop the modules' questions against the real archive, and score what happens. reads only agent-eval [--fixtures=<path>] [--bucket=<string>] [--ids=<string>] [--limit=<number>] [--verbose] [--prompt=<path>] [--print-prompt] [--user=<path>] [--out=<path>] Option What it does --fixtures=<path> a file of questions to ask (default: every module's, in its drop-in's eval.json) --bucket=<string> only questions from this bucket. --ids=<string> only these questions, by id, comma-separated. --limit=<number> stop after this many questions. --verbose a line per question as it finishes. --prompt=<path> the prompt file to use (default /etc/assistant-prompt.md) --print-prompt print the system prompt and the tool schemas the model is given, and stop. --user=<path> the person to ask as, by path (default: the person linked to the account running it) --out=<path> write the results here after every question, so a dropped session loses nothing. agent-eval -- limit 5 --verbose agent-eval --bucket kin nohup agent-eval --user /archive/people/anna-exempel --out /tmp/agent-eval.json With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : a summary — the model that answered, how often the right command was reached, how many lines ran, how many proposals held what they should, how many questions were answered — and the turns of each question.

Answer a question about EiN by running its commands (the chat drawer's backend) reads only assistant-ask [--think] [--resume] [--chat=<string>] [--history=<string>] [--context=<string>] [--max-steps=<string>] [--progress=<string>] <message> Argument What it is <message> what the user wrote; none with --resume. Option What it does --think think before every model call: slower, fewer malformed commands. --resume go on with the chat's last turn after the user ran or declined its proposal. --chat=<string> durable chat id; loads and appends history in $HOME/.chats. --history=<string> earlier turns as a JSON array of {role: user|assistant, content}. --context=<string> what the UI shows, as JSON {route?, section?, title?, about?, node?, lightbox?, shown?: [paths already shown]}. --max-steps=<string> tool calls allowed before the model must answer (default 12) --progress=<string> ephemeral turn id whose waiting/thinking phase may be read while this command runs.

List, create, read, or delete durable assistant chats; read a turn in flight; record how a proposal ended; the questions the modules suggest. reads only assistant-chat [--error=<string>] [--results=<string>] [--script=<string>] <action> [<id>] [<message>] [<status>] Argument What it is <action> list, create, read, delete, progress, examples, or outcome. [<id>] chat id for read/delete/outcome. [<message>] outcome: id of the message carrying the proposal. [<status>] outcome: ran, failed, or dismissed. Option What it does --error=<string> outcome: what the failed command said. --results=<string> outcome: JSON array of {command, ok, exitCode?, output}, what each command said. --script=<string> outcome: the block as run, when the user edited it first.

Find a command by what it is for, judge whether a line changes anything, or rebuild the assistant's command index. reads only assistant-commands [--limit=<number>] <action> <text>... Argument What it is <action> find, judge or reindex. <text>... find: what the command should do; judge: the shell line. Option What it does --limit=<number> find: how many commands (default 8) assistant-commands find 'list running services' assistant-commands judge 'service restart pipeline-pruner' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : find: the best commands with name, description, effect and score; judge: read or write with the reasons; reindex: how many commands were indexed.

Ask the assistant's language model one thing, and print what it answers. reads only llm-chat [--system=<string>] [--history=<string>] [--max-tokens=<number>] [--timeout=<number>] [--think] <message>... Argument What it is <message>... what to ask. Option What it does --system=<string> the system text: what the model is and how to answer. --history=<string> earlier turns, as JSON: [{"role":"user"|"assistant","content":"…"}]. --max-tokens=<number> the most the answer may be (default 768) --timeout=<number> seconds to wait for the answer (default 180) --think let the model think before it answers, within --max-tokens and --timeout. llm-chat 'Vad är huvudstaden i Norge?' llm-chat --system 'Answer in one word.' 'The colour of the sky?' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : content, the answer, and model, the model that wrote it.

Whose the assistant's language model is, where it runs, and (with --checks) whether it answers. reads only llm-status [--checks] [--brief] Option What it does --checks The checks health reads: whether it answers, where it is, whether its model has been tried. --brief The checks in one line (used by service-list --detail) llm-status llm-status --checks With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : url, model, kind (ours or external), provider for an external one, card (card or cpu) for ours. With --checks, health's checks.

The Album folders module keeps every album of the Archive as a folder of real files on the machine EiN runs on. Point a file manager, a shared folder or another photo program at it and you browse the albums and their pictures without EiN. The folders follow the albums: an album made, renamed or deleted in EiN, or a picture added or removed, shows there within seconds. The folders only ever show what EiN has. Nothing done to them reaches EiN, and they cannot be changed by hand. To add, sort or remove pictures, use EiN as before.

The module needs the Archive. Install it from Settings → Modules , or in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install album-folders Its service, album-folders , starts at once and makes the folders. Modules covers installing and removing modules.

The folders are in files/albums in the data folder: ~/ein/data/files/albums , unless you chose another data folder at the install ( What makes up your data ). Inside, the albums are laid out as they are under /archive/albums in EiN, folders of albums included: ~/ein/data/files/albums/ ├── Summer 1987/ │ ├── IMG_0412.jpg │ └── IMG_0413.jpg └── Wrenfield farm/ ├── Harvest 1992/ │ └── DSC_1034.NEF └── The new barn/ └── barn.mp4 A folder is named like the album in the tree, which is the name in its address. Changing an album's title on its page does not rename the folder; moving the album to another path, with mv in the terminal, does. Each picture, video and recording of the album is a file under the name it has in the album, a picture added from elsewhere included. An album holding its pictures in a files folder shows them directly in the album's folder. Similar photos stacked into one show as all the photos. An album with nothing in it is an empty folder. Each file is the original itself, not a copy: a second name for the same file in files , called a hard link. The folders take no room of their own, and the files keep their dates and contents as they were added.

Files whose bytes are not on the disk tier. A hard link can only be made to a file on the same disk, so a folder holds only what EiN keeps with your originals, in files . Renditions on the volatile tier and content kept in the database, the db tier, never show up there, nor does a picture made on either of them with mknode --tier . album-folders status counts what it left out. Where the bytes are kept explains the tiers. What EiN knows about the pictures : faces, people, places, descriptions and comments stay in EiN, as do thumbnails and video renditions. The folders hold the originals. Suggested albums in staging, until they are filed as albums.

The folders cannot be changed: nothing can be added, renamed or removed in them. Warning The files in the folders are EiN's own originals, not copies. Whoever may write to a file there writes to the original: a photo program that saves an edit into a picture changes it in EiN, and EiN does not know. Give everyone and every program the folders read-only. A frozen original is read-only on the disk, mode 0444 , and every photo, video and recording that was uploaded or copied in over SFTP is frozen as it arrives. A program can still write to a file that is not frozen, such as one taken out of a zip, and a program that may change permissions can make a frozen one writable again. Under podman, which the installer uses unless told otherwise, the files belong to your own user, who can write to every file that is not frozen. Two ways to give the folders read-only: A shared folder in Samba, with read only = yes : [albums] path = /home/helen/ein/data/files/albums read only = yes A read-only view of the folders elsewhere on the machine, for a program of your own: # on the machine EiN runs on sudo mkdir -p /srv/albums sudo mount -- bind ~/ein/data/files/albums /srv/albums sudo mount -o remount, bind ,ro /srv/albums Under Docker the files belong to root, and other users can read but not change them. Who can see an album in EiN does not carry over: everyone who can read the folders sees every album.

The service follows each change to the albums and brings the folders it touches up to date a couple of seconds after the changes stop. Every hour it also compares every folder with its album, which catches anything a change notice missed, such as one made while the service was stopped. After EiN starts, it compares everything first. A picture deleted from EiN leaves every folder it was in, and only then is its space freed: while a folder still holds a file, the file keeps its room on the disk.

Both are in Settings , under Album folders , and restart the service when changed. Configuration explains settings. Setting Default What it does CFG_ALBUM_FOLDERS_PATH empty Where the folders are, as EiN sees it. Empty means /files/albums , which is files/albums in the data folder. CFG_ALBUM_FOLDERS_INTERVAL 3600 seconds How often every folder is compared with its album, beside following each change. At least 60. A hard link cannot cross from one disk or mount to another, so another location must be inside /files , EiN's view of the files folder.

album-folders status says where the folders are and what the last full comparison found: # in EiN's terminal album-folders status /files/albums: ready last full pass 2026-10-30T21:00:00.000Z, 112 albums: 0 linked, 0 removed, 8410 in place album-folders sync compares them now, every album or the albums under one path, and --dry-run only counts what it would change: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator album-folders sync "/archive/albums/Summer 1987" --dry-run Album folders commands has every option.

The backup copies the data folder with rsync -a , which copies a hard link as a file of its own and so stores every picture in an album twice. Leave the folders out with --exclude /files/albums : EiN makes them again from the albums after a restore.

What you see Why, and what to do holds files but no .ein-album-folders; not taken as the album folders The location already holds files the module did not make. It only takes an empty folder or one it made, since it removes every file there that no album wants. Choose an empty folder. not on the same mount as the stored files CFG_ALBUM_FOLDERS_PATH is outside /files . Choose a folder inside it. … of … files belong to no album; not removing them (--force does) in the log A full comparison would have emptied more than half the folders, which is what an archive not yet in place looks like. If the albums really are gone, run album-folders sync --force . An album's folder is empty The album has no pictures, or none whose bytes are on the disk tier ( What is left out ). A picture is missing in a folder after a change Wait a few seconds, or run album-folders sync with the album's path. What the service did is in /var/logs/services/album-folders/stdout.log , its errors in stderr.log ( Services and logs ).
Albums Your data: backup, moving and removing SSH and SFTP , the other way to browse EiN from outside Modules

The commands the album folders module adds. They are there once the module is installed. 1 of them, by name. Every command also says this with --help ; Commands explains how to read an entry. album-folders

Keep the albums as folders of real files on disk, for browsing outside EiN (status, sync, watch) reads only album-folders [--dry-run] [--force] <subcommand> [<album>] Argument What it is <subcommand> status | sync | watch. [<album>] sync: one album, or a directory of albums, instead of all of them. Option What it does --dry-run sync: count what would be linked and removed, changing nothing. --force sync: go ahead even when more than half the files belong to no album. album-folders status album-folders sync album-folders sync /archive/albums/Exempelalbum_2019 --dry-run With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : for status , the folder and what the last full pass found (AlbumFoldersStatus); for sync , what was linked, removed, kept and skipped (AlbumFoldersSync); watch runs until stopped.

The Todo module keeps lists of things to do: lists of your own that nobody else sees, and lists you share with a group, such as the household's shopping list. Each list is a board whose columns an item moves through, from Todo to Done. An item can have a day it is due and someone to do it, and what falls due shows on Home among the events.
Install it from Settings → Modules , or in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install todo Todo is then in the sidebar. Modules covers installing and removing modules.

p.h: Lists are folders, items are files
p.x: A list is a folder, named by its title, and each item on it is a Markdown file you can read and change in any editor, over SFTP or in EiN's terminal as well as on the Todo page: --- due: 2026-12-01 assignee: helen --- # Renew the passport The old one is in the desk drawer. The first heading is the item's title , and what follows it is its description . The front matter between the --- lines says the day it is due , who is to do it ( assignee ) and its place on the list ( order ). All are optional, and an item with none needs no front matter at all. A new item's file is named for when it was added, such as 2026-11-05-140322.md , so the files sort in the order they came. Any other name works as well: rename a file, or write a text file of your own into the list, and it is an item. Items are in the order their order numbers say, in each column of the list. Dragging an item on the page, or todo-move , numbers the items of the column it lands in from 1 in their new order; an item with no number comes after those that have one, in the order it was added. An item can be about something else in EiN, such as a picture to fix or an album to sort: a softlink under the item's own file points at it, and goes with the item when it is done. When the picture is moved or renamed, the link follows it. A done item is moved to the list's done/ folder. An item in done/ is done whether or not its file says so. Moving it there on the page, or with todo-done or todo-move , also writes done: and done-by: into its front matter, the time and who did it.

A list is a board of columns, and an item is in one of them: Todo is the list's own folder: what is not started yet. ls of a list is its Todo column. Every folder in the list is a column of its own, such as In progress/ or Waiting/ . It is called by its folder's name, unless the folder has a name attribute, which is then its title: attrs ~/todos/Fix/doing -s 'name=In progress' . The columns stand in the order of their order attributes, which moving a column on the page writes, and those without one after them in the order the folders were made. Done is the list's done/ folder, always the last column. A new list has one from the start. archived/ is where done items are put away. It is no column, so they are off the board and out of the counts, but they are still files in the list.

p.h: Your own lists and a group's
p.x: A list is either yours or a group's, and that is decided when you make it: Your own lists are in ~/todos in your home. Nobody else sees them, the administrator aside. A group's lists are in todos/ of the group's shared home , such as /groups/family/todos . Every member of the group can read, add, tick off and change them, and nobody else sees them. Everyone with an account is in users , so a list shared with users is the whole household's. You can share a list only with a group that has a shared home and that you are in. users has one from the start; the administrator gives other groups theirs.

Open Todo in the sidebar. The bar at the top has a tab for Overview and then one for every list you can see, your own marked with a list and a group's with two people; hovering a tab says whose it is. On a phone the tabs scroll sideways. A list's columns fill the page under the bar side by side, a line between each, sharing its width and running to its foot; each scrolls its own cards. When there are more than fit, the board scrolls sideways. On a phone a list reads as a plain list: one row per item, the columns one after the other with no headings, Todo first and Done last. The box at a row's left ticks the item off, moving it to Done ; unticking it in Done moves it back to Todo . A slowly turning spinner after the title says the item is under way: it is in a column of your own, neither Todo nor Done. A chevron after that, when the item has a description, unfolds it. At the right are its due day (or a calendar to give it one) and whoever is to do it. What it links to shows under the title as pictures alone. Hold a row still for half a second to open the item in its dialog; hold it and move to move it. Add an item floats at the foot of the screen, and adds to Todo. Columns are made, renamed and deleted, and done items archived, on a computer, or with the commands below. Make a list : choose ⋮ in the page's bar and New list , type a Title such as Shopping, and under Shared with keep Nobody, it is mine or pick a group. Choose Create list . Add an item : open the list's tab, type in Add an item at the foot of Todo (on a phone, of the screen) and press Enter . The line stays for the next one. Shift + Enter , or pasting several lines, gives it more: the first line is the item's title and the lines after it its description, blank ones at its top and foot left out. Move an item : drag its card to another place in the column, or to another column; a dashed frame shows where it will land. Dropped on Done it is done, and dragged out of Done it is not. On a phone, lifting a row brings up the names of the columns at the foot of the screen: let go over one and the card goes to the end of that column. Assign it : the round button at a card's top right (on a phone, at the row's right) is the face of whoever is to do it, their person's picture or their initials, or an empty circle when it is nobody's. Choose it and, under Assign to , a member of the list's group, or Nobody in particular . Give it a due day : the calendar at a card's top right picks one; once set, the day stands there instead, before the face, and opens the picker again, where No due day takes it away. Read the description : a card shows the first line of its description, with … when there is more. Choose it to read the whole of it, as formatted Markdown, and again to fold it. Change an item : the pencil at a card's top right, or on a phone a long press on its row, opens the item in a dialog: its Title , its Description , written in Markdown (lists, links, bold ; Preview shows how it will look), the day it is Due , and Assign to , where typing a name narrows the members to choose from. Save keeps the change. Link an item : in the same dialog, type in Link to to find a person, a place, an album or the other things the top bar's search finds by name, and choose one; or type a whole path, such as /albums/Summer/beach.jpg , to link a picture or a folder. A link is made as soon as you choose it, and the cross on one takes it away. Delete an item : Delete in the dialog removes it for good, with its links; what they point at stays where it is. Add a column : open the list's tab, choose ⋮ in the page's bar and New column , and type its name; it comes before Done . The pencil in a column's heading renames it, Left and Right move it among the list's own columns, and once no card is left in it, Delete takes it away. Todo stays first and Done last: they cannot be moved, Todo cannot be renamed, Done cannot be deleted, and done and archived are names the list keeps for itself. Delete a list : the cross on its tab, then Delete the list . The list goes for good, with every item on it, archived ones too, and for everyone a group's list is shared with; what the items link to stays where it is. Archive done items : tick the cards in Done you want put away, or the box in its heading for all of them, and choose Archive . They move to the list's archived/ folder. On a computer the due day and the face stand at the right of a card's title, which runs on under them when it is long; while the pointer is over the card its pencil, and its calendar when it has no due day, show beside them. A due day that has passed is red. On a computer a stripe down a card's left edge is coloured by how long it has been on the list: green on the day it is added, then yellow, and red once it is four weeks old; a done card's is grey. Hovering the card says when it was added. An item can be given only to a member of the list's group; on a list of your own every item is yours. Overview is everything of yours, soonest due first: the items assigned to you on any list, and the items of your own lists assigned to nobody, done ones too (archived ones are not). Its columns are those of the lists your items are on, put together by title: Todo , then every other column in the order it is first met, two lists' Ongoing being one column, and Done last. A card names its list with a label at its foot, with the icon of the list's tab, and on a phone a row's title starts with it, Shopping › Milk ; choose the list's name to open its tab. Drag a card to another column to move it there on its own list; a column its list does not have takes no drop. A card's links are listed under its description, each with its picture: a picture's own, an album's cover, a person's, place's or camera's picture. A picture or a video shows as its picture alone, its name said on hovering it; any other link is named too, called what it points at is called, such as an album's title. Choosing one opens it: a picture in the lightbox, an album or a person on their page. A link to something that is gone, or that you may not see, is greyed out.

The todo widget keeps the todos about what you are looking at in reach on every page. Turn it on with the pin in the Todo page's bar, Show the todo widget , and off with the same button, Hide the todo widget ; it is also Todo widget under Profile → Preferences , and it is yours alone, on every device you sign in on. While it is on, a round button floats over every page and over the lightbox; dialogs open over it. Drag it wherever it is out of your way; it stays there on that device. Its badge counts the open todos, on any list you can see, that link to what is on screen: the picture open in the lightbox, or the album, person, place or camera whose page is open. Stepping from picture to picture in the lightbox, the count follows. With none , choosing the button opens New todo item at once, with About what is on screen ticked, so the new item links to it. Adding it leaves you where you were. With some , choosing it slides out a list of them, above the button or below it, whichever way has more room. Tick one to mark it done, choose its title to open it in the item's dialog, or choose New todo about this to add another. Choosing anywhere else puts the list away. On a page about nothing in particular, such as Home or Search, the button has no badge and adds an item that links to nothing.

Home's Events lists the items falling due that are yours to do: given to you, or to nobody on a list you can see. They show from a week before they are due until a week after, beside the other events, and choosing one opens its list. Home and statistics covers the rest of Home.

With Dashboards installed, Todo offers a Todo list card: one list's items not done yet, late ones first and then by when they are due, with who is to do each. Choose the List in the card's settings, and under Show everything not done or only what is due within a week and late. Signed in, a tick on the card marks an item done; on a screen opened from a display link it only shows. Items falling due are also on a dashboard's Coming up card, as on Home.

With the Assistant installed, the chat reads and changes your lists too: ask "what's on the shopping list?", "what do I have left to do?" or "add milk and bread to the shopping list". It finds a list you name among those you can see, and with a list open on the Todo page, "this list" and "add it" mean that one. Reading happens at once; adding, ticking off, moving or changing an item is a proposal card you run or decline.

Every part of the page is a command, and a list or an item is named by its path: # in EiN's terminal todo-lists # every list you can see todo-list-create Shopping --group users # a list shared with users todo-list-create 'Before the trip' # a list of your own todo-add /groups/users/todos/Shopping Milk todo-add ~/todos/ 'Before the trip' 'Renew the passport' --due 2026-12-01 todo-add ~/todos/ 'Before the trip' Pack --description 'Warm clothes, the charger.' todo-items /groups/users/todos/Shopping # the list, its columns and their items todo-item /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md # one item, with its description and links ls /groups/users/todos/Shopping # what is not started, as files todo-done /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md todo-done --undo /groups/users/todos/Shopping/done/2026-11-05-140322.md todo-set /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --assignee helen --due 2026-11-20 todo-move /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --before /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-04-091500.md mkdir '/groups/users/todos/Shopping/In the basket' # a column todo-move /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --column '/groups/users/todos/Shopping/In the basket' todo-archive /groups/users/todos/Shopping/done/2026-11-05-140322.md todo-add ~/todos/Fix 'Straighten the horizon' -- link /albums/Summer/beach.jpg todo-link ~/todos/Fix/2026-11-05-150210.md /albums/Summer # another link todo-mine # what is left for you todo-mine -- done # and what you have done, as Overview shows it todo-about /albums/Summer/beach.jpg # what is left to do about a picture todo-about # every open item that links to anything An item's path is its list's, then its column's folder unless it is in Todo, and then its file's name, which todo-items shows; a done item's is in the list's done/ , an archived one's in archived/ . todo-move --column or todo-done --undo takes an archived item out again. An item's links are under its file, …/2026-11-05-150210.md/beach.jpg , and rm of one takes the link away and leaves the picture. Once ~/todos is there, mkdir in it makes a list as well as todo-list-create does, and cat and any editor read and change an item. Remove an item, or a whole list, with trash put . Todo commands lists every option.

What you see What it means What to do Shared with offers no group None of your groups has a shared home Ask the administrator to give your group one, or share it with users todo-add: 'peggy' is not in the group 'family' An item goes only to a member of the list's group Pick a member, or ask the administrator to add them to the group todo-add: an item on your own list can only be yours A list of your own is nobody else's Make the list a group's to share it A list someone made has no tab It is someone else's own, or of a group you are not in Group changes apply the next time you sign in todo-list-create: there is already a list called … A list's name is its title, and that one is taken Pick another title, or add to the list that is there An item's due day or person is not shown Its front matter is not YAML the module can read Open the file and correct the lines between the --- lines An item due long ago is not on Home Home shows a week back Overview lists every item of yours, overdue or not A folder in the list is not a column Its name starts with a dot, or it is archived Rename the folder

The commands the todo module adds. They are there once the module is installed. 14 of them, by name. Every command also says this with --help ; Commands explains how to read an entry. events-todo · todo-about · todo-add · todo-archive · todo-done · todo-item · todo-items · todo-link · todo-list-create · todo-lists · todo-members · todo-mine · todo-move · todo-set

Home's events from the todo lists: open items due around a day that are yours, given to you or to nobody. reads only events-todo [--today=<string>] [--days-ahead=<number>] [--days-past=<number>] [--limit=<number>] Option What it does --today=<string> the day to look around, YYYY-MM-DD (default today) --days-ahead=<number> how many days ahead (default 30) --days-past=<number> how many days back (default 7) --limit=<number> at most this many (default 16) events-todo --today 2026-11-04 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One events entry per item: title, route, path and date.

List the items not done, on every list you can see, that are about a path: that link to it, such as a picture, an album or a person. With no path, every item that links to anything; with --done the done ones too. reads only todo-about [--done] [<path>...] Argument What it is [<path>...] what they are about. Option What it does --done the done ones as well, those in a list's done/ (not archived/) todo-about /albums/Summer/beach.jpg todo-about With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per item, as todo-items gives them, with listTitle, group, columnTitle and stage (todo, doing or done), list by list in their columns' order.

Add an item to a todo list, a markdown file named for when it was added, with the day it is due and who is to do it if you like. changes things todo-add [--description=<string>] [--due=<string>] [--assignee=<user>] [--link=<path>] <list> <title> Argument What it is <list> the list, by its path. <title> what is to be done. Option What it does --description=<string> what it says under the title, in markdown. --due=<string> the day it is due, as YYYY-MM-DD. --assignee=<user> who is to do it: a member of the list's group, or you on a list of your own. --link=<path> what it is about, such as a picture or an album: a softlink under the item. todo-add /groups/users/todos/Shopping Milk todo-add ~/todos/ 'Before the trip' 'Renew the passport' --due 2026-12-01 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The new item: path, list, title, done, due, assignee and links.

Put done todo items away in their list's archived/, which is no column of the board. todo-move or todo-done --undo takes one out again. changes things todo-archive <item>... Argument What it is <item>... a done item, by its path. todo-archive /groups/users/todos/Shopping/done/2026-11-05-140322.md With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The items as they are now, at their paths in archived/.

Mark a todo item done, with who did it and when, moving it to the list's done/; with --undo, not done again and back in the list's Todo. changes things todo-done [--undo] <item> Argument What it is <item> the item, by its path. Option What it does --undo mark it not done. todo-done /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md todo-done --undo /groups/users/todos/Shopping/done/2026-11-05-140322.md With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The item as it is now, at its new path, with doneAt and doneBy when it is done.

Show one todo item: its title, description, due day, who is to do it, its column and its links. reads only todo-item <item> Argument What it is <item> the item, by its path. todo-item /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The item: path, list, column, title, description, done, doneAt, doneBy, due, assignee, order and links.

Show a todo list's board: its columns, Todo (the list itself), each folder in it, then Done (its done/), and the items of each in their order. archived/ is left out. reads only todo-items <list> Argument What it is <list> the list, by its path. todo-items /groups/users/todos/Shopping With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The list (path, title, group, open, total), its columns (path, title, stage) and their items column by column (path, column, title, description, done, doneAt, doneBy, due, assignee, order, links).

Link a todo item to what it is about, such as a picture or an album: a softlink under the item's file, named as what it points at. rm takes one away. changes things todo-link <item> <path>... Argument What it is <item> the item, by its path. <path>... what it is about. todo-link ~/todos/Fix/2026-11-05-140322.md /albums/Summer/beach.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The item as it is now, with its links.

Make a todo list, a folder named by its title: your own, in ~/todos, or with --group one every member of the group shares, in the group's shared home. changes things todo-list-create [--group=<group>] <title> Argument What it is <title> what the list is called, such as Shopping. Option What it does --group=<group> a group of yours with a shared home, whose members share the list. todo-list-create Shopping --group users todo-list-create 'Before the trip' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The new list: path, title, group, open and total.

List the todo lists you can see: your own, then those in the shared homes of your groups. reads only todo-lists todo-lists With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per list: path, title, group (absent for your own), open, total, and its columns (path, title, stage) in their order.

List who an item of a todo list may be given to: the members of the list's group, or you for a list of your own. reads only todo-members <list> Argument What it is <list> the list, by its path. todo-members /groups/users/todos/Shopping With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per person: username and name.

List what is left for you to do: items not done given to you on any list, and your own lists' items not done given to nobody, soonest due first, each with its column; with --done the done ones too. reads only todo-mine [--done] Option What it does --done the done ones as well, those in a list's done/ (not archived/) todo-mine todo-mine -- done With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per item, as todo-items gives them, with listTitle, group, columnTitle and stage (todo, doing or done).

Move a todo item to another column of its list's board, at its end, or put it just before or just after another item, numbering that column's items in their new order. Into done/ it is marked done, out of it not done. changes things todo-move [--column=<path>] [--before=<path>] [--after=<path>] <item> Argument What it is <item> the item, by its path. Option What it does --column=<path> the column: the list itself (Todo), or a folder in it such as its done/. --before=<path> the item to put it before, in whichever column that is. --after=<path> the item to put it after, in whichever column that is. todo-move /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --column '/groups/users/todos/Shopping/In the basket' todo-move /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --before /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-04-091500.md With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The item as it is now, at its new path, with its column and order.

Change a todo item's title, its description, the day it is due, or who is to do it. changes things todo-set [--title=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--due=<string>] [--no-due] [--assignee=<user>] [--no-assignee] <item> Argument What it is <item> the item, by its path. Option What it does --title=<string> its new title. --description=<string> what the file says under the title, in markdown, in place of what it said; empty for none. --due=<string> the day it is due, as YYYY-MM-DD. --no-due it is due on no particular day. --assignee=<user> who is to do it: a member of the list's group, or you on a list of your own. --no-assignee it is nobody in particular's. todo-set /groups/users/todos/Shopping/2026-11-05-140322.md --due 2026-11-20 --assignee anna With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The item as it is now.

The Recipes module keeps the household's recipes: their ingredients and steps, how many they serve, how long they take, and pictures of the dish. A recipe's page scales the ingredients to the number of servings you want.

Install it from Settings → Modules , or in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install recipes Recipes is then in the sidebar, and Recipe in the top bar's Create menu. It brings the Media module, which reads the recipes' pictures and makes their thumbnails through the media service ; the Archive is not needed. Modules covers installing and removing modules.

Every recipe is in /archive/recipes , one node of type recipe each, named after its title: Wrenfield apple cake is /archive/recipes/wrenfield-apple-cake . Everyone signed in can read the recipes, and everyone with an account can add and change them. A recipe's pictures are files in its pictures/ folder, and one of them is its cover. They are not part of the library: /archive/recipes is marked unlisted, so the library's own views (the Media page, the map, On this day, search's pictures) leave them out, and it wants only renditions , so the pictures get their thumbnails and nothing else, also when the Archive is installed: no dates, faces, text or picture search. The recipes themselves are found by search, by their title and description.

Choose Create → Recipe in the top bar, or New recipe on the Recipes page. Only Title is needed; fill in what you know: Serves : how many servings the amounts are written for. A recipe's page can scale them only when this is said. Time in minutes , Difficulty and Rating . Categories : separated by commas, such as Baking, Dessert . The Recipes page narrows to one. Ingredients and Steps : one per line. A line starting with # names a section, and the lines after it belong to it until the next such line: 4 apples # Batter 2 dl sugar 100 g butter Language : the language the recipe is written in, such as sv for Swedish. EiN's own words stay in yours; a recipe's amounts are written the way its language writes numbers. Taken from : the address of the page the recipe came from. Its page links back to it. Choose Create . Edit on a recipe's page opens the same form; a field you empty is taken away.

Open Recipes in the sidebar and pick a recipe. Type in Filter recipes… to narrow them by title, and use Category and Sort beside it. The − and + beside Ingredients change the number of servings, and every amount EiN could read changes with them: 2 dl sugar for four becomes 3 dl sugar for six. A line without an amount, such as salt and pepper , stays as written. Tap an ingredient or a step to strike it through, to keep your place while cooking. Neither the servings nor what is struck through is saved. Upload in the page's header adds pictures, or drop them on the page. The first becomes the recipe's cover; under the recipe, the star on another makes it the cover instead. Move to trash under ⋮ takes the recipe, with its pictures, into your trash.

The Recipes commands do the same from EiN's terminal: recipe-create , recipe-set , recipe-show , recipe-list , recipe-categories and recipe-cover . recipe-create 'Wrenfield apple cake' --serves 8 --categories 'Baking, Dessert' \ --ingredients $ '4 apples
2 dl sugar
100 g butter' --steps $ 'Slice the apples.
Bake for 40 minutes.' recipe-list --category Baking recipe-show wrenfield-apple-cake

The commands the recipes module adds. They are there once the module is installed. 7 of them, by name. Every command also says this with --help ; Commands explains how to read an entry. recipe-categories · recipe-cover · recipe-create · recipe-list · recipe-set · recipe-show · search-recipe
List the categories recipes are in, with how many are in each. reads only recipe-categories recipe-categories With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per category: name and count, the fullest first.

Make one of a recipe's pictures the one it is shown with; with none named, its first, when it has no cover yet. changes things recipe-cover <recipe> <picture> Argument What it is <recipe> the recipe, by its path or its name in /archive/recipes. <picture> one of its pictures, by its path or its name. recipe-cover apple-cake recipe-cover apple-cake baked.jpg With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The recipe.

Add a recipe: its title, and its ingredients, steps and the rest if you like. changes things recipe-create [--description=<string>] [--serves=<number>] [--minutes=<number>] [--difficulty=<number>] [--rating=<number>] [--categories=<string>] [--lang=<string>] [--source=<string>] [--allergies=<string>] [--ingredients=<string>] [--steps=<string>] <title> Argument What it is <title> what the dish is called. Option What it does --description=<string> a line or two about it. --serves=<number> how many servings the amounts are for. --minutes=<number> how long it takes in all, in minutes. --difficulty=<number> 1 easy, 2 medium, 3 demanding. --rating=<number> how good it is, 1 to 5. --categories=<string> the categories it is in, separated by commas (Dinner, Fish) --lang=<string> the language it is written in, such as sv or en. --source=<string> the address of the page it was taken from. --allergies=<string> what it holds that someone may not eat. --ingredients=<string> the ingredients, one per line; a line starting with # names a section. --steps=<string> the steps, one per line; a line starting with # names a section. recipe-create 'Apple cake' --serves 8 --categories 'Baking, Dessert' --ingredients $ '4 apples
2 dl sugar
100 g butter' --steps $ 'Slice the apples.
Bake for 40 minutes.' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The new recipe: path, title, its facts, ingredients, steps and pictures.

List the recipes, by title or the newest first, in a category or with words in their title. reads only recipe-list [--category=<string>] [--sort=<string>] [--limit=<number>] [--after=<string>] <text> Argument What it is <text> words the title holds. Option What it does --category=<string> only the recipes in this category. --sort=<string> title (the default) or newest. --limit=<number> how many to list, 48 unless said. --after=<string> the next page, as the previous page answered it. recipe-list recipe-list --category Baking recipe-list cake -- sort newest With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : recipes (path, title, description, serves, totalMinutes, difficulty, rating, categories, lang, site), and next when there are more.

Change what a recipe says; a field given empty is taken away. changes things recipe-set [--title=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--serves=<number>] [--minutes=<number>] [--difficulty=<number>] [--rating=<number>] [--categories=<string>] [--lang=<string>] [--source=<string>] [--allergies=<string>] [--ingredients=<string>] [--steps=<string>] <recipe> Argument What it is <recipe> the recipe, by its path or its name in /archive/recipes. Option What it does --title=<string> its new title. --description=<string> a line or two about it. --serves=<number> how many servings the amounts are for. --minutes=<number> how long it takes in all, in minutes. --difficulty=<number> 1 easy, 2 medium, 3 demanding. --rating=<number> how good it is, 1 to 5. --categories=<string> the categories it is in, separated by commas (Dinner, Fish) --lang=<string> the language it is written in, such as sv or en. --source=<string> the address of the page it was taken from. --allergies=<string> what it holds that someone may not eat. --ingredients=<string> the ingredients, one per line; a line starting with # names a section. --steps=<string> the steps, one per line; a line starting with # names a section. recipe-set apple-cake --serves 6 --rating 5 recipe-set apple-cake --description '' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The recipe as it is now.

Show a recipe: its facts, ingredients and steps. reads only recipe-show <recipe> Argument What it is <recipe> the recipe, by its path or its name in /archive/recipes. recipe-show apple-cake With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The recipe: path, title, description, serves, totalMinutes, difficulty, rating, categories, lang, site, source, allergyInfo, ingredients, steps and pictures.

Search recipes by title or description. reads only search-recipe [--kinds] [-l <number>] <query> Argument What it is <query> Search query text. Option What it does --kinds print the content kinds this provider can return, and exit. -l <number> Max results per channel (default 10) search-recipe 'apple cake' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : matching recipes, one row per channel that found it (name, description), best first within each.

The Dashboards module puts cards together on one page: the time, what is coming up, a picture of the day, a device's readings, a todo list. You choose the cards and arrange them, show the page full screen on a screen on the wall, and give that screen a link so it never has to sign in. The cards come from the modules you have installed: each module offers the cards of what it holds, and a dashboard shows whichever you pick. This page is for everyone who uses EiN.

Install it from Settings → Modules , or in EiN's terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install dashboard Dashboards is then in the sidebar, under System , and Dashboard in the Create New menu. Modules covers installing and removing modules.

Choose Create New → Dashboard , or New dashboard on the Dashboards page. Give it a Title , such as "Kitchen", and if you like a Description , such as "By the fridge". Choose its Colour : what its page and its wall are drawn in. Every colour runs all of EiN's colours across it; the others are the colours of what EiN holds, such as People violet or Devices orange . Choose Who sees it : as you share new things, only you, or everyone with an account. The Share button on its page changes that later, as for an album; see Sharing . Choose Create dashboard . It opens, empty, ready to arrange. The Dashboards page shows every dashboard you can see as a tile. Its picture is the dashboard's layout in small, each card in its colour. Type in Filter dashboards… to narrow them by title. Each tile draws its dashboard's layout in small, each card in its colour.

On the dashboard's page, choose Add card (in the ⋮ menu, or the tile at the end while you arrange it). The cards the installed modules offer are listed, each with what it shows and which module offers it. Choose a card. Fill in its settings: what it shows, such as which todo list or which device. A setting with a list to choose from reads it from EiN as you, so it lists what you can see. Give it a Title if you want another than the card's own, and choose its Size . The Preview beside the settings draws the card as it will look, a moment after each change. Choose Add card . It goes on at the end of the dashboard. The cards that come with Dashboards: Card What it shows Clock The time, large, with the day and date under it; another place's time zone, the seconds, and a label if you like Coming up What falls on the days ahead from every module that tells of it: birthdays and anniversaries from the Archive , todos falling due from Todo ; Only from keeps it to some of them On this day Pictures taken on this day in earlier years, a ring for each year, as on Home News What was added lately, such as albums, as on Home Device A device 's readings and switches, each as on its page Reading One reading of a device, large, with how it went over the last hours Note A few words of your own, in Markdown Other modules add their own: the Archive the Picture of the day , Birthdays and Weather , Todo a Todo list , and Automation a Camera and a Button . A card whose module is removed later says so on the dashboard until you take it off. A card holding more than its tile has room for, such as a long Coming up list or a device with many readings, shows it all in turn rather than scrolling: after a few seconds the next row glides in at the bottom while the top one fades out, and after the last the first comes round again, below a thin line. On this day moves sideways in the same way. Rows that fit stand still. Moving the pointer over a card holds it still for a few seconds, and where the computer or phone asks for reduced motion, the rows fade from one to the next instead of gliding. A Note too long for its tile scrolls; make it larger. Cards from Dashboards, the Archive and Todo side by side on one page.

Choose Arrange on the dashboard's page. Each card gets a row of buttons in its top corner and a bracket in its bottom one: ⠿ : hold it and drag the card to another place; the others make room as it passes. Size : Small, Medium, Wide, Tall, Large, Hero or Banner. The bracket in the bottom right corner: drag it to make the card larger or smaller, a cell at a time. The others move aside as it grows, its size in cells shows beside the corner, and it stays as it is when you let go. A card is never made smaller than it can be drawn in. Settings : what the card shows, its title and size, beside a preview, and Take off . × : take the card off. Undo in the message at the foot of the screen puts it back. On a phone, arrows move a card up and down instead of dragging, and Size is how a card is sized. Choose Done when it is as you want it. Cards are laid out in their order from the top left, each in the first place it fits, so a small card fills the gap a large one leaves. On a phone the cards stand in two columns. ⋮ → Settings changes its title, description, colour, how many Columns wide it is (6, 8 or 12; more columns size the cards more finely) and how its wall looks. ⋮ → Make a copy makes another dashboard laid out the same, and ⋮ → Move to trash removes it. Everything changes at once for everyone looking at the dashboard, a screen on the wall included.

Choose Full screen on the dashboard's page. Its cards fill the screen as glass tiles over the pattern in its colour, as large as the screen allows; the pattern lights a tile now and then. The address in the browser now opens it full screen, so you can bookmark it. Full screen, the cards fill the screen as glass tiles, each as large as it allows. Move the pointer to see the buttons in the corner: Fill the screen hides the browser too, Arrange goes back to the page to arrange it, and × (or Esc ) leaves. The pointer and the buttons go after three seconds without moving the pointer. The screen is kept awake where the browser allows it, which over plain HTTP most do not; see Show a dashboard on a screen . ⋮ → Settings → On the wall : Plain tiles, for a slow screen leaves out the blur behind the tiles. Dim from and until dim the wall between two times, such as 22:30 and 06:30, to the Brightness while dimmed . To show a dashboard on a screen nobody signs in at, see Show a dashboard on a screen .

With the Assistant installed, the chat reads and arranges your dashboards too: ask "which dashboards are there?", "make a kitchen dashboard with a clock and the birthdays coming up", "show the hall temperature on this dashboard" or "dim the kitchen wall at night". With a dashboard open, "this dashboard" means that one. It looks up what a card can show, such as a device and its readings, before it sets it. Reading happens at once; making a dashboard, adding, changing or taking off a card, and a display link for a screen are each a proposal card you run or decline.

A dashboard is a YAML file in /archive/dashboards , named by its title: the dashboard Kitchen is /archive/dashboards/Kitchen.yaml . Its file holds its layout, which you can read and change in any editor: columns: 12 wall: dim: { from: '22:30' , to: '06:30' , level: 0.35 } cards: - id: k7q2 card: dashboard.clock size: [ 4 , 3 ] - id: p3mx card: archive.picture size: [ 8 , 6 ] with: { from: onthisday , every: day } - id: t1zz card: todo.list size: [ 4 , 5 ] title: Shopping with: { list: /groups/wrenfield/todos/Shopping } Each card has an id , the card it is ( <module>.<name> ), its size in columns and rows, a title (or false for no header), and with , what it shows. Changing it with the commands rewrites it, without your comments. What cannot be read, such as a card no module offers, is shown on the page while you arrange it. # in EiN's terminal dashboards # the dashboards you can see dashboard-cards --brief # the cards the modules offer dashboard-create Kitchen --color device dashboard-card-add Kitchen dashboard.clock --size 4x3 dashboard-card-add Kitchen dashboard.coming-up --with days=14 --with only=anniversaries dashboard-show Kitchen # its cards and their ids dashboard-card-set Kitchen k7q2 --size 6x3 --to 0 # resize the clock and move it first dashboard-set Kitchen --dim 22:30-06:30@0.3 Dashboards commands lists every flag.

p.h: Offer a card from a module
p.x: A module offers cards in etc/dashboard.d/cards.json ; see Writing a module .

t: Show a dashboard on a screen

p.x: A screen on the wall — a monitor by the front door, a tablet in the kitchen — shows a dashboard full screen and never signs in. You give it a display link : a link that shows the dashboard as an account sees it, so its todo lists, devices and birthdays are filled in, while whoever has the link can change nothing. This page is for whoever sets up the screen; making the account is the administrator's. What a screen shows: the dashboard full screen, filled in as its account sees it.

A display link shows the dashboard, and anything else, as one account sees it. Rather than your own, use an account made for screens, so a screen sees only what it should: An administrator makes an account, such as Kitchen display , in Settings → Users ; see Accounts and groups . It needs no password anyone knows. Put it in the groups whose things the screen shows, such as your household's group for its todo lists, and devices for the devices. Take it out of the Users group: on the account, untick Users under Groups . Every account is in it, and it sees what is shared with everyone with an account, such as most albums and people. Left in, so does the screen. The share dialog says so when the account you choose is still in it. A card showing something the account may not read, such as a device outside its groups, says so on the screen instead. A link never shows things as an administrator, nor as an account in the admin , sudo or ssh groups, nor as a disabled one. Anyone may make a display link as their own account; only an administrator makes one as another account.

Open the dashboard and choose Share . Under Show it on a screen , choose Shows it as : the account for screens. Choosing yourself warns that anyone with the link can read everything you can. Choose how long it Works for . A screen wants No end date , which the dialog offers first. Choose Create link , and copy the address. The link's row then says "Shows it as Kitchen display sees it". A screen reads with the account's groups as they were when it opened the link: after changing them, open the link on the screen again. If the account is later disabled, deleted or put in one of the groups above, the row says "Opens nothing" and why, and the screen shows This link no longer works .

On the screen, open the link. It opens the dashboard full screen. Make the link the browser's start page, so the screen comes back to it after a restart. A browser in kiosk mode, such as chromium --kiosk <link> , also hides its own toolbars. To hide the browser without kiosk mode, move the pointer and choose Fill the screen . What the screen does by itself: It stays on the dashboard: there is no sidebar, and the cards lead nowhere. It follows the dashboard: a card added or moved shows on it at once, and what the cards show is read again as it changes or every few minutes. Nobody has to scroll it: a card with more than fits shows its rows in turn, gliding by slowly. It loads itself again each night at about half past three, to take what an update of EiN brought. It stays signed in through its link for 30 days after it was last used; while it is on, that is for good. If it loses its session, it opens the link again by itself rather than asking to sign in. It is kept awake where the browser allows it. Browsers allow that only over HTTPS: over plain HTTP, turn off the screen's own sleep, or reach EiN over HTTPS; see Ports, HTTPS and remote access . How long a link's session lasts is the administrator's to change: Share link session expiry in Settings , CFG_LINK_SESSION_EXPIRES_SEC .
Choose Delete link in the dashboard's Share dialog. Every screen showing it goes to This link no longer works at once. Deleting the account does the same for every link shown as it.
# in EiN's terminal: a link shown as the account display, with no end date share-link create '/archive/dashboards/Kitchen.yaml' --as display --never share-link list '/archive/dashboards/Kitchen.yaml'

The commands the dashboards module adds. They are there once the module is installed. 9 of them, by name. Every command also says this with --help ; Commands explains how to read an entry. dashboard-card-add · dashboard-card-remove · dashboard-card-set · dashboard-cards · dashboard-copy · dashboard-create · dashboard-set · dashboard-show · dashboards

Put a card on a dashboard. changes things dashboard-card-add [--size=<string>] [--title=<string>] [--no-title] [--with=<string>] [--at=<string>] <dashboard> <card> Argument What it is <dashboard> its title, or its path under /archive/dashboards. <card> the card, as . ; dashboard-cards lists them. Option What it does --size=<string> x , such as 4x3 (default the card's own) --title=<string> its header's title in place of the card's name. --no-title no header at all. --with=<string> key=value: what it shows, as the card takes it; again for each. --at=<string> its place among the cards, from 0 (default the end) dashboard-card-add Kitchen dashboard.clock dashboard-card-add Kitchen dashboard.coming-up --size 4x5 --with days=14 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The card as dashboard-show shows it: id, card, size, title, with, label, icon, color, frame, and route or a problem.

Take a card off a dashboard. changes things dashboard-card-remove <dashboard> <id> Argument What it is <dashboard> its title, or its path under /archive/dashboards. <id> the card's id, as dashboard-show lists it. dashboard-card-remove Kitchen k7q2 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : { ok: true }.

Change a card on a dashboard: its size, title, what it shows, or its place. changes things dashboard-card-set [--size=<string>] [--title=<string>] [--no-title] [--card-title] [--with=<string>] [--without=<string>] [--to=<string>] <dashboard> <id> Argument What it is <dashboard> its title, or its path under /archive/dashboards. <id> the card's id, as dashboard-show lists it. Option What it does --size=<string> x , such as 4x3. --title=<string> its header's title in place of the card's name. --no-title no header at all. --card-title the card's own name in its header again. --with=<string> key=value: what it shows, as the card takes it; again for each. --without=<string> a setting to take away, back to its default; again for each. --to=<string> its new place among the cards, from 0. dashboard-card-set Kitchen k7q2 --size 6x4 dashboard-card-set Kitchen k7q2 --to 0 dashboard-card-set Kitchen k7q2 --with days=7 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The card as dashboard-show shows it.

List the cards the installed modules offer for dashboards. reads only dashboard-cards [--brief] <card>... Argument What it is <card>... only these cards, as . (default every one) Option What it does --brief each card's id, label, description and the names of its settings, without the rest. dashboard-cards --brief dashboard-cards dashboard.coming-up With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per card: id ( . ), module, name, label, description, icon, color, route, frame, size, min, and params, a JSON Schema of what it takes. With --brief: id, label, description, settings (the names in params) and required.

Make a new dashboard laid out as another one. changes things dashboard-copy <dashboard> <title>... Argument What it is <dashboard> the one to copy: its title, or its path. <title>... the copy's title. dashboard-copy Kitchen 'Kitchen, winter' With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The new dashboard, as dashboards lists it.

Make a new, empty dashboard. changes things dashboard-create [--color=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--columns=<string>] [--share=<string>] <title>... Argument What it is <title>... what it is called; its file is .yaml in /archive/dashboards. Option What it does --color=<string> the colour its page and wall are drawn in: mixed, album, person, location, track, camera, device, label, media, staging, system (default mixed) --description=<string> a line about it, under its title. --columns=<string> cells across: 6, 8, 12 (default 12) --share=<string> default (as you share new things), private, shared or everyone. dashboard-create Kitchen dashboard-create 'Living room' --color device --share private With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The new dashboard, as dashboards lists it.

Change a dashboard's title, colour, description, columns or wall. changes things dashboard-set [--title=<string>] [--color=<string>] [--description=<string>] [--columns=<string>] [--effects=<string>] [--dim=<string>] [--no-dim] <dashboard> Argument What it is <dashboard> its title, or its path under /archive/dashboards. Option What it does --title=<string> a new title, which renames its file. --color=<string> its colour: mixed, album, person, location, track, camera, device, label, media, staging, system. --description=<string> a line about it; empty takes it away. --columns=<string> cells across: 6, 8, 12. --effects=<string> full, or light: no blur behind the tiles on its wall, for a slow screen. --dim=<string> dim its wall between two times, to a level: 22:30-06: 30@0.3 . --no-dim never dim its wall. dashboard-set Kitchen --color device dashboard-set Kitchen --title 'Kitchen wall' --dim 22:30-06:30@0.3 With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The dashboard, as dashboard-show answers.

Show one dashboard: its cards, each with the route it is drawn with. reads only dashboard-show <dashboard> Argument What it is <dashboard> its title, or its path under /archive/dashboards. dashboard-show Kitchen With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : The dashboard (as dashboards lists it) with its wall settings, its cards — id, card, size, title, with, label, icon, color, frame, and route, or a problem — and problems read in its file.

List the dashboards you can see. reads only dashboards dashboards With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : One entry per dashboard: path, name, color, description, columns, its cards laid out as tiles (x, y, w, h, color), owner, modified, and whether you may change it.

The Automation module brings the devices in the house that talk MQTT into EiN: sensors, plugs, switches, lights and buttons, such as those running ESPHome and Shelly's. It adds drivers that hear them on an MQTT broker and make each one a device under /dev , with its readings, presses and switches, a driver for cameras whose picture you watch live, and automations : nodes wired together, which switch things and run command lines when a reading, a press, a file coming into a folder or the clock says so. The devices, their pages and their commands are EiN's own, the same for a plug as for a phone: Devices . This page is for the administrator who installs the module and connects the devices, and for the household that uses them. Automations covers making automations.

Part What it is The ha-discovery driver Anything that announces itself over MQTT the way Home Assistant reads it: ESPHome, and Zigbee2MQTT as far as it keeps to that; lights with their brightness and colour The shelly driver Shelly's second generation and later: Plus, Pro, Gen3 and Gen4; relays, lights with their brightness and colour, and covers The shelly-gen1 driver Shelly's first generation: Plug S, 1, 1PM, 2.5, i3, Dimmer, Bulb, Duo, RGBW2 The ipp driver A network printer, asked over IPP: its state, its warnings and how much of each ink or toner is left The cast driver A Google Cast speaker or screen: what it plays, its volume and mute, play, pause and stop The snmp driver A NAS, a router or anything else that answers SNMP: its uptime, load, memory, each volume's use and its temperatures The network driver Anything else on the network: whether it answers, and how fast The http driver A web API that answers JSON, asked at its address for the readings you name, and set at the addresses you name: the weather, the price of electricity, a device on your network with a web API of its own; see A web API The virtual driver Devices whose readings are worked out from other devices' (an average, the most, whether any is on) and whose controls hold what is set; see Virtual devices The rtsp driver A camera that sends its picture over RTSP: its streams, a picture of each now, and the picture live; see A camera The onvif driver A camera that speaks ONVIF, found on the network: its streams as rtsp 's, its motion and the people it sees, and its presets and moves where it turns; see An ONVIF camera The Live tab A camera's picture as it comes, on its device page The Camera and Button cards For dashboards : a camera's picture, and one large button for a control; see On a dashboard The automation-bridge service Hears the broker and runs the drivers The automation-engine service Runs the automations under /etc/automations , each as its owner The group automation Its members make automations automation-status , automations , automation-new , automation-set , automation-check Whether the broker is heard; the automations, making and changing them, and what one would do now Found on the network The devices on the network that are not devices yet, with a button on the Devices page; see Add a device found on the network automation-found , automation-adopt , automation-ignore What is on the network and all it said, adding it as a device, and leaving something out With the Assistant , it also teaches the chat to read the devices and to propose switching them.

An MQTT broker , the server the devices and EiN exchange their messages through, for the devices that speak MQTT: those running ESPHome, and Shelly's of every generation. The installer runs one beside EiN with --automation , in the automation sidecar ; a broker you already run works as well. A restreamer for cameras, which the sidecar has too: it keeps one connection to each camera, and EiN's pages and commands watch the camera through it. Without it a camera gives only its still picture, when it has one. No broker for the rest: printers, Google Cast speakers, NAS boxes, web APIs and anything else on the network are asked by EiN directly, once added, with or without one. Without the installer's broker nothing is found on the network, though, so add them by hand with device-create . Nothing else: neither the Archive nor the media service.

With the installer's broker, add the broker and the module in one run: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein ./setup.sh --automation --module automation On a new machine, name the module to the installer, which makes it the same options: curl -fsSL https://einhq.eu/install.sh | bash -s -- automation . With a broker of your own, install the module alone, from Settings → Modules or in EiN's terminal, and then give it the broker ( A broker you already run ): # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mod install automation The module runs two services: automation-bridge , which hears the broker and drives the devices, and automation-engine , which runs the automations. When automation-engine first starts it makes the group automation , whose members make automations. Modules covers installing and removing modules.

--automation runs the automation sidecar, one container beside EiN on the machine's own network, automation , with three services in it: The MQTT broker , Mosquitto. It takes no anonymous clients. EiN signs in as ein and the devices as device , with passwords setup.sh made at the install and keeps in ~/ein/.env : MQTT_EIN_PASSWORD and MQTT_DEVICE_PASSWORD . A password changed there takes effect at the next ./setup.sh . The devices reach it on port 1883 of the machine ( MQTT_PORT in .env ), on the address EIN_BIND names. It keeps what the devices announce in the data folder's mqtt folder, so it is all there again after a restart. A listener on the machine's own network, which finds the devices that are not on the broker yet: Add a device found on the network . A restreamer , go2rtc, which keeps one connection to each camera EiN has and serves it again, to EiN on port 1984 ( STREAMS_PORT ) and over RTSP on 8554 ( RTSP_PORT ), behind the account ein and STREAMS_PASSWORD from .env . EiN gives it the cameras itself. setup.sh gives EiN the broker's and the restreamer's addresses and passwords itself, and the device account a device added from the network is given: those settings say From deployment on the Settings page and need nothing from you. ./setup.sh --no-automation takes the sidecar out again, and ./setup.sh --only automation updates it alone. Under Docker, and podman run as root, EiN reaches the sidecar at the machine's address on its container network, so the sidecar needs EIN_BIND to be 0.0.0.0 : setup.sh says so when it is not. The devices need the device password. Read it on the machine: # on the machine EiN runs on, in ~/ein grep MQTT_DEVICE_PASSWORD . env Warning The broker speaks plain MQTT, without TLS. Whoever reaches port 1883 with the device password can switch the house's devices and read what they say, and whoever reaches 1984 or 8554 with the restreamer's password watches the cameras. Keep the ports on your home network and never forward them on your router; Ports, HTTPS and remote access lists it with EiN's other ports.

Give EiN the broker's address and an account on it, under Settings → System in the Automation group, or with config set : # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator config set CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_URL mqtt://192.0.2.20:1883 config set CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_USER ein config set CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_KEY 'the password' # the leading space keeps it out of your history MQTT broker takes mqtt://host:1883 , or mqtts://host:8883 for a broker that takes TLS. MQTT password is a key: nobody can read it back, and EiN sends it only to that broker ( Give a key to another service ). Saving any of the three restarts automation-bridge . While MQTT broker is empty no device is heard on a broker, and only the devices EiN asks over the network itself are read.

A device announces itself on the broker, and its driver makes it a device as soon as it hears it: within seconds of the device connecting it is on the Devices page with all it reads and does. Nothing is entered in EiN. A device that is on the network but not yet on the broker is found too, and a Shelly is added from EiN without opening its own web page: Add a device found on the network . The sections after it say how to point each kind at the broker by hand.

p.h: Add a device found on the network
p.x: With the installer's broker, its listener discovery asks the network every two minutes what is there, over mDNS (Bonjour) and SSDP (UPnP), the way phones and computers find printers and speakers, and over WS-Discovery, the way cameras that speak ONVIF are found, and hears what announces itself over mDNS in between. It does not scan addresses: it hears only what announces itself. Each thing that answered is named by what it said, such as a Shelly Plus 1PM, an ESPHome board, a HomeKit or Matter accessory, a Hue bridge, a camera, a speaker, a TV or a printer, and is matched to the devices EiN has already, by its name and its hardware address. When something found can become a device and is none yet, the Devices page's header has a button that says how many, such as 2 found . It opens Found on the network , a card for each, and Add on a card makes it a device: What was found What Add does A Shelly, of any generation EiN sets its MQTT to the broker, with the device account, and restarts it. It is under Devices when it is back, within a minute, with all it reads and switches. A camera that speaks ONVIF Add asks for the account EiN signs in to the camera with, and checks it with the camera: a device of the onvif driver at once, with its streams, its motion and the people it sees, and its presets and moves where it turns ( An ONVIF camera ). A printer A device of the ipp driver at once: its state (idle, printing, stopped), its warnings (such as marker-supply-low-warning ) and a level in % for each ink or toner it reports. A Google Cast speaker or screen A device of the cast driver: player says whether it plays ( idle , playing , paused ) and playing what, as title – artist (app); volume and muted can be set, and play , pause and stop pressed. Anything that answers SNMP: a NAS, a router … A device of the snmp driver: uptime , load , memory-used , for each volume <volume>-used (%) and <volume>-free (GB), and a <sensor>-temperature for each temperature its agent reports. EiN asks with the community SNMP community in the Automation settings, public unless you change it. Anything else: a NAS without SNMP, a TV … A device of the network driver, online while it answers, with its response-time . EiN does not speak its own protocol yet. ESPHome or Tasmota No Add : the line under it says how to point it at the broker, and the sections below say more. A device added from the network follows it to a new address: EiN knows it by its hardware address. A printer is asked every two minutes, a Cast device every 15 seconds and the rest every minute. SNMP is often off on a NAS or a router until it is turned on in its own settings, usually read-only with the community public ; a NETGEAR ReadyNAS has it under System → SNMP . One added before SNMP was on is a network device: forget it and add it again. To see what a device's agent answers beyond what the driver reads, walk it: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of the devices group automation-snmp 192.0.2.40 # its name, description and uptime automation-snmp 192.0.2.40 1.3.6.1.2.1.25.2.3 # its volumes automation-snmp 192.0.2.40 1.3.6.1.4.1 # what its maker adds Choose a card to see all the listener heard of it: what EiN makes of it, each mDNS service with its records, each SSDP answer with what the device's own description says, and the raw message, as it came. For something EiN does not support, it is what there is to go on. Ignore leaves one out of the count and the list; Show Everything finds it again, with Take back . Open opens one that is a device already. Show chooses Can be added (the default), Not a device yet , or Everything the listener heard, devices included. The page and the button are for members of the devices group, who make devices; the button stays away for everyone else. Note A Shelly with a password of its own refuses EiN; turn the password off on its web page, or set its MQTT there as below. A first-generation Shelly does not use Shelly's cloud while MQTT is on. The same from the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of the devices group automation-found # what can become a device, and is none yet automation-found --all # everything the listener heard automation-found 7c2ebd614055 # one, with all the listener heard of it automation-adopt a8032ab12345 # add the Shelly with this id, as automation-found says it automation-adopt 7c2ebd614055 # add the Cast speaker automation-adopt ec71db0a1b2c --user admin --password 'the password' # add the camera; the leading space keeps it out of your history echo 30 > /dev/kitchen-speaker/volume echo press > /dev/kitchen-speaker/pause automation-ignore d0ad08c5e709 # leave the printer out The listener needs the machine EiN runs on to be on the same network as the devices: mDNS, SSDP and WS-Discovery stay on the network they are sent on. A device on another network, or another VLAN, is not found, and is connected by hand as below. Broker for devices in the Automation settings is the address a device added from the network is given; empty, it is the address the listener says the machine has on the devices' network. With a broker of your own there is no listener: the page says so, and devices are connected by hand. A device is named in EiN as it names itself, in lower case with hyphens, such as hall-sensor , and each of its endpoints by its own name within it, such as hall-sensor/temperature . Commands, routing keys and rules use these names. Edit on a device's page gives it and its endpoints friendlier labels on the pages and leaves the names as they are.

Add an mqtt: block to the device's configuration, with the machine EiN runs on as the broker, and install the configuration on the device as usual: # hall-sensor.yaml, the device's ESPHome configuration esphome: name: hall-sensor mqtt: broker: 192.0 .2 .10 # the machine EiN runs on username: device password: !secret mqtt_password # in secrets.yaml: MQTT_DEVICE_PASSWORD from ~/ein/.env With an mqtt: block ESPHome announces each of its entities the way Home Assistant's MQTT discovery reads them, which is on unless you turn it off. Leave its prefix as it is, homeassistant ( Discovery prefix in the settings). The device is named by its name: , and an endpoint by its entity's own name: a sensor called Temperature on the device above is hall-sensor/temperature . A light is on or off, and has its brightness and its colour beside it when it has them, each to be set: <light>-brightness , 0–100 % whatever scale the light counts in, and <light>-color , as #rrggbb , such as #ff8000 ; 255,128,0 is taken too.
