A light that takes its colour as hue and saturation, or as x and y, as many Zigbee lights do, is read and set in them. # in EiN's terminal, as a member of the devices group echo on > /dev/living-room/ceiling echo 40 > /dev/living-room/ceiling-brightness echo '#ff8000' > /dev/living-room/ceiling-color Other software that announces devices the same way, such as Zigbee2MQTT, is read as far as it keeps to what ESPHome sends; automation-status names what it could not read.

Shelly's Plus, Pro, Gen3 and Gen4 devices are read by the shelly driver. Open the Shelly's own web page, at its address on your network, and go to Settings → MQTT . Turn MQTT on. Set the server to the machine EiN runs on with the port, such as 192.0.2.10:1883 , the user to device , and the password to the device password. Turn on Generic status update over MQTT and RPC status notifications over MQTT . Save. The Shelly restarts and connects. The topic prefix may stay as it is, the Shelly's id, such as shellyplus1pm-a8032ab12345 . It is the device's name in EiN, so a short one of your own, such as hall-plug , makes commands and rules easier to read. Choose it before the Shelly is first heard: a new prefix is a new device. Its endpoints are named after its parts: switch-0 is its first relay, switch-0-power , switch-0-energy , switch-0-voltage and switch-0-current what the relay measures, and input-0 its first input. An input set to button mode gives presses, single , double , triple or long , rather than on and off. A light is light-0 , or rgb-0 , rgbw-0 or cct-0 for a colour or white-tone one such as the Plus RGBW PM, and each can be set: Endpoint What it is light-0 On or off light-0-brightness Its brightness, 0–100 % rgb-0-color Its colour, as #rrggbb , such as #ff8000 ; 255,128,0 is taken too rgbw-0-white Its white channel, 0–255 cct-0-color-temperature Its white's colour temperature, in K A cover, such as a Plus 2PM in cover mode, has cover-0-position (0–100 %, set to move it there), cover-0-state ( open , closed , opening , closing or stopped ), and cover-0-open , cover-0-close and cover-0-stop to press: # in EiN's terminal echo 40 > /dev/desk-lamp/rgbw-0-brightness echo '#ff8000' > /dev/desk-lamp/rgbw-0-color echo 30 > /dev/kitchen-blind/cover-0-position echo press > /dev/kitchen-blind/cover-0-stop

The first generation, such as the Plug S, the 1, the 1PM, the 2.5, the i3, the Dimmer, the Bulb, the Duo and the RGBW2, is read by the shelly-gen1 driver. Open the Shelly's own web page, at its address on your network, and go to Internet & Security → Advanced – Developer Settings . Turn MQTT on. Set the server to the machine EiN runs on with the port, such as 192.0.2.10:1883 , the user to device , and the password to the device password. Leave its custom MQTT prefix off: the driver listens under shellies/ . Save, and restart the Shelly: a first-generation Shelly takes its MQTT settings when it starts. With MQTT on it does not use Shelly's cloud. It is named by its own id, such as shellyplug-s-c8c9a3 , which cannot be changed; give it a label with Rename . Its endpoints are relay-0 for its first relay, relay-0-power and relay-0-energy (the energy since it last started, in Wh) for what the relay measures, temperature for its own, and input-0 for a button's presses: single , double , triple , long , single-long or long-single . A Shelly the bridge has not heard announce itself, because it connected before the bridge started, is asked to. A light is light-0 , and an RGBW2 in white mode has light-0 to light-3 , one for each channel. A light has as many of these as it reports, each of which can be set: light-0-brightness (0–100 %), light-0-color ( #rrggbb ), light-0-white (an RGBW2's white channel, 0–255) and light-0-color-temperature (in K). A light that has both modes, such as a Color Bulb, turns to colour mode when set to a colour, and to white when set to a colour temperature; its brightness is that of the mode it is in. For white light from a Color Bulb, set its colour temperature: it has no white channel to mix with a colour. light-0-power and light-0-energy are what a light that measures it draws, as for a relay. A 2.5 in roller mode has roller-0-state ( open , close or stop , the way it last moved), roller-0-position (0–100 %, empty until the roller is calibrated), and roller-0-open , roller-0-close and roller-0-stop to press.

The http driver asks an address that answers JSON, as often as you say, and keeps the readings you name in its answer: today's weather, the price of electricity this hour, or a device on your network that answers on a web API of its own, and can be switched there. Nothing announces such a device; a member of devices makes it in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create Weather --driver http \ --config 'url=https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=57.7&longitude=11.97&current=temperature_2m,wind_speed_10m' \ --config 'read=temperature=current.temperature_2m °C; wind=current.wind_speed_10m m/s' \ --config interval=15m Config What it is url The address to ask. {date} (2026-11-09), {year} , {month} , {day} and {hour} in it become the day and hour it is asked at, in EiN's time zone. A user and password in it, http://admin:secret@192.0.2.20/status , are sent as the device's sign-in. read The readings, name=path unit , separated by ; . Each becomes an endpoint of that name; the unit may be left out. interval How often it is asked: seconds, or 30s , 15m , 1h . Five minutes unless given, and ten seconds at the least. set The controls, name=address on/off , separated by ; ; see Switching it . May be left out. A path walks the answer from the top: Path Reads current.temperature_2m a field of a field relay:0.power a field whose name has a colon in it energy['total today'] a field whose name has a space in it meters[0].power , items[-1].value the first item of a list, the last [time_start..time_end].SEK_per_kWh the item of a list whose time_start has come and whose time_end has not: this hour's price [from..].price the last item whose from has come, for a list that gives only when each starts . the whole answer, for an address that answers a number or a word as plain text A number written as text, "0.42" , is kept as a number; a list or an object is not kept. A device whose answer has none of its readings, or that does not answer, is offline until it does, and the bridge's log says why once. A reading's unit says what it is: °C is a temperature, W power and kWh energy, so the device's card shows it first. Another: # the price of electricity this hour, in Swedish price area SE3, from elprisetjustnu.se device-create Electricity price --driver http \ --config 'url=https://www.elprisetjustnu.se/api/v1/prices/{year}/{month}-{day}_SE3.json' \ --config 'read=price=[time_start..time_end].SEK_per_kWh SEK/kWh' --config interval=5m A config device-create does not understand is refused with what is wrong, such as a reading is name=path [unit], not 'price' ; the device is made all the same, so change its config, on its Info tab or with device-config , or forget it and make it again: device-config electricity-price 'read=price=[time_start..time_end].SEK_per_kWh SEK/kWh' Switching it A device whose web API also takes commands is switched at an address of its own, which set names for each control: name=address on/off . {value} in the address becomes the value, spelled as the device spells on and off, which is what on/off says: ON/OFF , on/off , 1/0 or true/false . An address without http:// is taken from url 's, sign-in included. A control whose name is also a reading's is a switch that shows that reading as its state, read as on or off however the device spells them; EiN asks the device again a second after it is switched. A control with no {value} and no on/off is a button that asks its address when pressed, such as a restart. Say a garden pump's controller on your network answers {"pump": {"running": true, "power": 420}} at /api/status , runs or stops the pump at /api/pump?run=1 and /api/pump?run=0 , and restarts at /api/restart : device-create Garden pump --driver http --config 'url=http://admin:secret@192.0.2.40/api/status' \ --config 'read=pump=pump.running; power=pump.power W' \ --config 'set=pump=api/pump?run={value} 1/0; restart=api/restart' --config interval=30s pump is then a switch, on while the answer says running is true, and restart a button; both are asked with the sign-in in url . The address, with a password in it, is the device's config, which every member of devices sees. EiN asks it from the machine it runs on, so an address on your home network is asked from there.

The rtsp driver takes a camera on your network that sends its picture over RTSP, as most cameras that work without a cloud do (Reolink, Hikvision, Dahua, Amcrest, Axis, Tapo, …). The camera's manual, or its own web page, names its stream's address; many send a second, smaller stream beside the main one, which costs less to watch and to take a picture of. A member of devices makes the camera in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create 'Front door' --driver rtsp \ --config url=rtsp://192.0.2.30:554/h264Preview_01_main \ --config sub=rtsp://192.0.2.30:554/h264Preview_01_sub \ --config user=viewer --config password= 'the password' # the leading space keeps it out of your history Config What it is url The main stream's address, rtsp://… sub A second, smaller stream's address. May be left out snapshot The address of the camera's still picture, http://… , which a picture is taken from when there is no restreamer. May be left out user The camera's account password That account's password. It is kept in the device's .secret , which the administrator alone reads, and goes only to the sidecar A password or an address that changed is given again on the camera's Info tab, with Change , or in the terminal, and the camera is reached with it at once: device-config front-door password= 'the new password' The camera becomes a device of class camera , with a stream endpoint for each stream: main , and sub with a second one. EiN gives the streams to the sidecar's restreamer , which keeps one connection to the camera however many watch it, and says within a minute how large each picture is and which codec it is sent in. Its page shows a picture of each stream now, taken again every ten seconds while the page is open, and the Live tab plays the picture as it comes: the main stream, or the smaller one, a button away. The Devices page shows a picture of the smaller stream on the camera's card. A picture is a file too, a JPEG of the stream now, taken each time it is read: # in EiN's terminal cat /dev/front-door/main > ~/front-door.jpg With the Archive , the media service also watches each camera's smaller stream for faces: the camera gets a Faces log, which says who each face that came into view was, or unknown , within a second or so, as dev.<camera>.faces for automations, and the faces' pictures are filed under the camera in the archive, where they are named as photos' faces are ( Faces a camera sees ). The media service records the camera's largest stream as well, and a clip of each visit, from a little before the face until a little after, is filed beside them as a video ( A security camera ). The camera is online while it gives a picture, asked every other minute. Who may see the pictures is who may read the stream: the household, as for every device ( Who may do what ). EiN's pages reach the camera only through EiN, signed in, so neither its address nor its password reaches a browser.

Most cameras that work without a cloud also speak ONVIF, a standard for asking a camera what it sends, what it sees and how it turns. Such a camera needs no stream address: EiN asks the camera for it. It is found on the network, where Add on its card asks for the account EiN signs in to it with ( Add a device found on the network ). Many cameras have ONVIF off, or want an account of its own for it, until it is set on their web page, among the advanced network settings: on a Hikvision under Network → Advanced Settings → Integration Protocol . A camera on another network is made in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create 'Back yard' --driver onvif \ --config address=192.0.2.31 \ --config user=admin --config password= 'the password' # the leading space keeps it out of your history Config What it is address The camera's address, 192.0.2.31 or 192.0.2.31:8000 , or its ONVIF service's whole address, http://192.0.2.31/onvif/device_service user The camera's account password That account's password, kept in the device's .secret as rtsp 's is. The camera is sent a digest of it, never the password itself The camera's largest picture becomes its main stream and its smallest its sub , with the codec, size and frame rate the camera says, and everything else about them is as for A camera . EiN asks the camera again every hour, and whenever it is not reached, so a stream the camera moved is followed. One added from the network is asked at the address the listener last heard it at, so it is followed to a new address too. Beside its streams, a camera has what it tells and what it turns: Endpoint What it is motion On while the camera sees motion, off when it stops, as the camera itself detects it person On while the camera sees a person, for a camera that tells people from the rest ptz-preset One of the positions saved on the camera: setting it turns the camera there. For a camera that turns and has positions saved ptz-left , ptz-right , ptz-up , ptz-down , ptz-zoom-in , ptz-zoom-out A button each: a press turns or zooms the camera a short step. For a camera that turns, and zooms motion and person are readings like any other, so an automation takes them: a person in the back yard at night can turn on its light, or turn the camera to the gate. # in EiN's terminal echo Gate > /dev/back-yard/ptz-preset # turn to the position saved as Gate echo press > /dev/back-yard/ptz-left # a step to the left

# in EiN's terminal automation-status What it says What it means 5 devices, 31 endpoints, 18420 messages The bridge is connected: the devices its drivers drive, their endpoints, and the messages it has had since it started. drivers: ha-discovery, shelly, shelly-gen1 The drivers it runs, as Device sources names them. not read: <device>/<endpoint>: <why> An endpoint whose values the bridge cannot read, such as one announced with a template it does not understand. Nothing of it is kept. automations: 4 running, 41 actions The automation engine runs, with how many automations and the actions they took; see Automations . …; no broker set, so only … MQTT broker is empty: the devices EiN asks over the network are read, and none on a broker. Install the broker or give EiN yours for those. cannot reach mqtt://…: <why> The broker does not answer, or refuses EiN's account. The bridge tries again by itself, waiting a second, then twice as long each time, up to a minute. not running The automation-bridge service is stopped: service start automation-bridge , as the administrator. The Status page says the same: its automation bridge check is fine while the bridge is connected, or runs without a broker, a warning while it cannot reach the broker, and failed while its service is stopped ( Health and status ). devices --drivers lists the drivers with their devices while the bridge runs.

Each thing a device announces becomes an endpoint of the device under /dev : The device announces Endpoint Takes A reading: a temperature, power, humidity, a word a log Something on or off it only reads: a door, motion, input a log A button a log of events, its presses A switch, a relay, a light a control, on or off on , off or toggle A number it takes, such as a thermostat's target a control, a number a number within its limits and steps A choice it takes, such as a mode a control, one of its options one of its options Something it does when asked, such as a restart a control, pressed press The device's class comes from the endpoint that says the most of what it is, whichever is heard first: what it switches says the most ( plug for an outlet, light ), then what it senses or a button ( sensor , button ), and a bare relay least ( switch ); its power, energy, voltage or current says nothing. A class the device has is replaced only by one that says more, and one that is none of these, such as heater set by a person, stays. What tells of the device itself, such as its own temperature or its Wi-Fi signal, is marked diagnostic and kept apart on its page. An endpoint the device no longer announces is marked retired, and its history stays. Devices shows how the page draws each.

The toggles on a device's Overview switch it, and so does writing to the control in the terminal: # in EiN's terminal echo on > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 echo toggle > /dev/hall-plug/switch-0 echo 21 > /dev/heater/target The command goes to the device through the broker at once, and the switch shows the new state once the device reports it. When the bridge is not connected, the write is refused with hall-plug/switch-0: not connected to the broker, so nothing was sent , and while its service is stopped with hall-plug's driver shelly is not running : a command is never kept for later, since a lamp switched on an hour after it was asked would surprise. Switch something has the rest.

With the Dashboards module, Automation offers two cards beside the dashboard's own Device and Reading : Camera : a camera's picture filling the card, a new one every 10 seconds ( Seconds between pictures ), with the camera's name and the time the picture is from at its foot. Tap it to watch it live, as on the Live tab, for five minutes; tap again to go back to pictures. Always live plays it live all the time. Stream picks the smaller of its streams, which costs less to send, and Picture whether it fills the card or shows all of it. A camera that cannot be played live (no restreamer, or a codec the browser does not play) shows its pictures, and says why at the top. Button : one large button for a device's control, lit while the control is what the button sets. Without Sets it to , it presses a button, such as a virtual device 's momentary control an automation starts on, and switches something on and off to the other. With it, it sets the control to that value, such as eco for a mode or 21 for a heater, as a scene button does. Ask first makes the first press only ask for a second, for a door or a gate. Icon takes a Tabler icon 's name, such as bell or garage . Who may press a button is who may write its control ( Who may do what ). On a screen opened from a display link , which changes nothing, a button shows its state and does nothing when pressed, and a camera shows its pictures if the screen's account may read the camera.

Every reading, press and change of state is kept in its endpoint and published on the routing key dev.<device>.<endpoint> , and a device coming or going on dev.<device> , where the automation engine reads them and a queue or a log the administrator binds can take them: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator mkqueue -k 'dev.porch-button.#' ~/presses mklog -k 'dev.*.temperature' -r '90 day' ~/temperatures A number is kept and published at most once every 10 seconds for each endpoint ( Seconds between readings ); Readings on the bus shows the messages, and How often a reading is kept the rest.

Who What they may do Members of the devices group See every device, its readings and its history; switch and set devices; share, rename and forget them Someone a device is shared with See that device, and switch it when it is shared to edit Members of the automation group Also make automations , which act with their own rights The administrator Everything: add people to either group, and bind queues and logs to the devices' keys The devices the drivers find belong to the administrator and the devices group, and nobody else reads them, a door or motion sensor included, until a member shares one. Devices and their keys shows how to share a device and keep a switch to some people.

With the Assistant installed, the chat reads the devices: ask "how warm is it in the hall?", "which devices are offline?" or "how much did the heater draw yesterday?", and it answers at once, with a chart of a reading's history when you ask how it went. Asking it to switch something, "turn on the hall lamp", gives a proposal card with the echo line, which you run or decline. Asking for an automation, "turn the hall lamp on when there is motion after dark", gives a proposal card too. The assistant looks up the devices you name and makes the automation from the starting point it fits, with your devices set. One that fits no starting point is proposed as an automation-set line with its YAML. Either line is tried with --dry-run before you see it, and one with something wrong goes back to the assistant to correct, so the card you get is one that can run.

The devices' own commands, devices , device-show , device-history , device-label and device-forget , are EiN's; Devices lists them. The module adds: # in EiN's terminal automation-status # the broker, the drivers, the devices they drive, and the automations automations # the automations, and why one does not run automation-check hall-light # what an automation's nodes would say now Automation commands lists every option.

The module's settings are in the Automation group of Settings → System , and each restarts automation-bridge when saved: Setting On the Settings page Default What it does CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_URL MQTT broker empty; --automation sets it The broker, as mqtt://host:1883 or mqtts://host:8883 . Empty, only the devices EiN asks over the network are read CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_USER MQTT user empty; --automation sets ein The account EiN signs in to the broker with. Empty, it signs in without one CFG_AUTOMATION_MQTT_KEY MQTT password none; --automation sets it That account's password, a key nobody can read back CFG_AUTOMATION_STREAMS_URL Restreamer empty; --automation sets it The restreamer cameras are given to, go2rtc's API as http://host:1984 . Empty, a camera has no live view, and its picture is asked of the camera itself CFG_AUTOMATION_STREAMS_KEY Restreamer password none; --automation sets it The password of the restreamer's account ein , a key nobody can read back CFG_AUTOMATION_STREAMS_RTSP Restreamer for the media service empty; --automation sets it The restreamer's RTSP as the media service reaches it, rtsp://host:8554 . Empty, no camera is watched for faces CFG_AUTOMATION_SOURCES Device sources ha-discovery shelly shelly-gen1 Which drivers the bridge runs, separated by spaces: ha-discovery for ESPHome and whatever announces itself as it does, shelly for Shelly's second generation and later, and shelly-gen1 for the first CFG_AUTOMATION_DISCOVERY_PREFIX Discovery prefix homeassistant The topic ha-discovery devices announce themselves under CFG_AUTOMATION_HISTORY Reading history 365 day How long an endpoint's values are kept: 30 day , 90 day , 365 day or forever . It applies to endpoints found from then on; one found before keeps its own, which attrs on the endpoint changes (below) CFG_AUTOMATION_MIN_INTERVAL Seconds between readings 10 The shortest time between two kept readings of one number, given to endpoints found from then on as their minInterval , which may be changed on each An endpoint found before keeps its retention, and each endpoint can take its own interval, which counts within a minute: # in EiN's terminal, as the administrator attrs -s 'retention=90 day' /dev/hall-sensor/temperature attrs -J minInterval=60 /dev/heater-plug/switch-0-power

Devices : the device pages, switching and history. Devices, endpoints and drivers : endpoints, controls and the routing keys. Automations : nodes wired together that act when something happens. Virtual devices : readings worked out from other devices', and switches with no hardware behind them. Devices and their keys : who may do what with the devices.

An automation makes things happen in the house by itself: a lamp goes on at motion when it is dark and off a while after, a heater keeps a room between two temperatures while someone is home, a button toggles a lamp, a line runs at half past six on weekdays, a scan is filed as it lands in a folder. It is made of nodes wired together : inputs that hear devices, the clock, files coming into a folder and EiN's own events, logic that compares and combines, values worked out from readings, timers, and actions that switch controls, run command lines and raise events for pipelines. Each automation is a YAML file, written by members of the automation group, and runs with the rights of the person whose file it is. This page is for those members. Automation covers connecting the devices, and Devices the devices themselves.

System → Automations in the sidebar, for members of the automation group, opens the automation in the whole of the page below its bar. The list of automations is a drawer over its left edge, each with a dot that says whether it runs (green), is off (grey) or is held back (red, with why under its name); tap or drag the handle on the drawer's edge to slide it away to the left and back. + beside the list's filter makes one, empty or from a starting point. On a phone the drawer covers the page, and closes when you pick one. An automation opens on three tabs, under its name in the bar: Graph : its nodes as cards wired together, which you drag and zoom as a map (the wheel or two fingers, a double tap to zoom in). With no card selected, the panel on the right lists the kinds of node by group, each with what it does, and a filter; click one to add it in the middle of what is in view (on a phone, + in the canvas's corner lists them). Drag a card to move it. Drag from one of a card's outputs on its right edge to another card to wire them (while you drag, the inputs it may go to light up, and the others dim): true is the green output, false the red one, and a switch has one per case. Each kind of node has a colour of its own, on the band behind its card's title. Tap a card to set it up in the panel instead (a drawer on a phone; × goes back to the list): its Name , which is what wires and math name it by and its key in the YAML (renaming it renames it there too), a Label shown on its card instead, and its settings, the required ones starred. A button node has Press , while the automation runs. At the panel's foot, About … nodes says what the kind does, what it sends and what each setting means; fold it away and it stays folded. A card that reads or switches a device has the device to pick, and under it the device's endpoints (its controls, on a card that switches) with their latest values; picking a device picks its first endpoint, and tapping another picks that. Tap a wire and the red bin in the corner, or press Delete, to take it out; the bin at the top right of a node's panel, or Delete on a selected node, asks before the node and its wires go. While the automation runs, each wire is labelled at its middle with the last value that went along it and how long ago, lit for a moment when one just did; a true wire keeps its last true after its node has sent false since. A card says when its timer runs out, and its problems. YAML : the file itself, to read or change as typed. Runs : what it did, as its run log has it, as it happens. The bar also says whether it runs, or how many problems it has: tap 3 problems to read them, and one of them to pick the card it is about. Each card with a problem has a red border and says what it is. There is no Save: every change saves itself a moment after you make it, also when it leaves problems, and an automation with problems is not run until they are gone. The bar says Saving… and then Saved ; YAML typed in the YAML tab is saved once it is YAML again, and until then the bar says Not saved and why: tap it to try again, or the round arrow beside it to read the file again, dropping what was not saved. On turns the automation on and off. A change in the graph writes the YAML anew, so comments in the file are lost; one in the YAML tab keeps it as typed. Opening an automation's file in System → Nodes ( Nodes ) opens it here too. A module's automation is shown but not changed here, with the module's name in the bar, and only the administrator turns it on and off.

p.h: Try one out without switching anything
p.x: The flask among the buttons in the graph's corner simulates the automation: it runs the graph as it is in your browser, on the same engine EiN runs, with nothing real behind it. The bar says Simulating , cards can be moved meanwhile but not wired, set or removed, and the panel on the right (at the foot on a phone) has: A clock of the simulation's own, which keeps pace with the real one, holds still with the pause button, and moves on with +1 min , +10 min , +1 h or Next timer , so a timer of five minutes need not take five minutes. Clocks and between nodes go off as it passes their times. Times are in your browser's time zone, written in your date and time format (Settings → Language). Inputs , one for each node that starts things: a device node takes a reading of on or off , or any value you type, sent as a reading, or as a Press (a button's single or long); an online node is set online or offline; a button node is pressed; a clock node is run on to its next time; a link in is sent a value; a file node is given a file's name, as if it came into its folder; an event in is sent the path of a node, as if its event had come about it. Controls , what each control the automation writes holds in the simulation. Log , newest first: each input you fed, each node that sent something and on which output, each value a node held back and why (a compare or an and that would send what it sent last, a reading a device node does not pass on), and each control it would set, command line it would run and link out it would send to, with what its debug nodes say. What it would do shows only those last. It starts from the devices' latest readings, which it reads but never writes. A control it sets is not switched: the simulated device takes the value, as a real one would report it back, and a toggle flips what it holds. A command line is not run, and sends on an empty value. A link out reaches the automation's own links in, and no other automation. The wires say what went along them, as while it runs. The flask again, or the cross at the top of the panel, ends the simulation; nothing of it is kept.

The hall lamp goes on at motion when it is dark, and off five minutes after the motion ends. On the Automations page, that is + , Motion light , then the devices set to yours on the cards. In the terminal: # in EiN's terminal automation-new hall-light --from motion-light made /etc/automations/hall-light.yaml from motion-light: change its devices to yours The file it makes: description: The hall lamp on at motion when it is dark, off five minutes after the motion ends nodes: motion: { type: device , endpoint: hall-sensor/motion , pos: [ 0 , 0 ], to: [ linger ] } linger: type: timer off-after: 5m pos: [ 240 , 0 ] to: { out: [ dark-and-moving ], false: [ lamp-off ] } lux: { type: device , endpoint: hall-sensor/illuminance , pos: [ 0 , 140 ], to: [ dark ] } dark: { type: compare , below: 30 , pos: [ 240 , 140 ], to: [ dark-and-moving ] } dark-and-moving: { type: and , pos: [ 480 , 60 ], to: { true: [ lamp-on ] } } lamp-on: { type: control , endpoint: hall-lamp/switch-0 , value: on , pos: [ 720 , 0 ] } lamp-off: { type: control , endpoint: hall-lamp/switch-0 , value: off , pos: [ 720 , 140 ] } Read it along its wires ( to ): the motion sensor's readings go to a timer, which says true at once and false five minutes after the motion went false. The light sensor's readings go to a compare, which says true while it is below 30. The and is true while both are, and when it becomes true the lamp is switched on; when the timer says false, it is switched off. Change the devices to yours: edit /etc/automations/hall-light.yaml ( The editor ), then save it with automation-set , which checks it first: # in EiN's terminal automation-set hall-light < /etc/automations/hall-light.yaml An automation that is wrong somewhere is not written, and automation-set says which node and what is wrong with it. --draft writes it anyway, to finish later; it is not run until it is right. Text that is not YAML at all is never written. Check it: # in EiN's terminal automation-check hall-light hall-light has no problems hall-sensor/motion: false hall-sensor/illuminance: 12 hall-lamp/switch-0: "off" motion says false lux says 12 dark says true dark-and-moving says false It runs the latest readings you may read through the automation and says what each node would say now, without switching anything.

p.h: A starting point with your devices
p.x: A starting point's devices and numbers are its slots, and --set gives them yours as it is made, so there is nothing to change afterwards: # in EiN's terminal automation-new hall-light --from motion-light -- set motion=hall-sensor/motion \ -- set lamp=hall-lamp/switch-0 -- set light-level=none --description 'The hall lamp on at motion' made /etc/automations/hall-light.yaml from motion-light none leaves out a device a starting point can do without: this motion light has no light sensor, so it goes on at motion at any light. Set like this, the automation is checked first, as automation-check does, and is not made while something is wrong with it: a slot left unset, or an endpoint you may not read or a control you may not switch. --dry-run makes nothing, and prints the YAML it would write and what is wrong with it. automation-set --dry-run checks YAML of your own the same way, writing nothing. automation-check also names a node left out of the flow: one that sends nowhere though it is no action, or one nothing sends to though it only acts on what comes in. The engine runs such an automation as it is, so the check is where you hear of it. Starting point Slots motion-light motion , lamp , light-level (or none ), dark-below (30), off-after (5m) button-toggle button , lamp , press : single , double or long , or none for every press (single) heater temperature , heater , on-below (19) and off-above (21), one of them none to only switch it off or only on, away : a switch that is on while no one is home, or none morning lamp , at (06:30), days : weekdays , weekends or some of mon,tue,… , or none for every day (weekdays), value written to the lamp (on) dusk-to-dawn lamp , location as <latitude>, <longitude> , from (sunset), until (sunrise) inbox folder watched, match ( *.pdf , or none for every file), to : the folder each file is moved to A device is given as <device>/<endpoint> , as device-show <device> lists them, and a number or a time in parentheses is what the slot holds when it is not set. The automation engine reads the folder again within a second of a change, so the automation works from the moment it is saved. automations lists them all, and automation-status hall-light says what each of its nodes last sent while it runs.

Each automation is a file /etc/automations/<name>.yaml , called by its name: hall-light . automation-new makes one, empty or from a starting point, with its devices set or not ( automation-new --examples lists them), on the database, so it is backed up with everything else. Only members of the automation group see the folder and write in it. The administrator adds someone with group-add-member automation helen , or in Settings → Groups . automation-disable hall-light turns one off without removing it, and automation-enable hall-light on again. To remove one, remove its file. A module can bring automations of its own. They are under /etc/automations.d/<module>/ , called <module>/<name> , run as the administrator, and change only with the module. The administrator turns one off with automation-disable <module>/<name> .

An automation runs as the owner of its file, with that person's rights and nothing more: Helen's automation hears only the endpoints Helen may read, switches only what Helen may switch, hears only of the files Helen may read, and runs its lines as Helen. One whose owner may not read an endpoint it listens to, write a control it switches, or read a folder it watches, is not run, and says which: rights are checked when the file is read and every minute after, so taking a device from someone stops their automations that use it. Copying someone's automation into a file of your own makes it yours. A file that others than its owner may change, by its mode or by an entry on its access list, is not run, since whoever could change it could act as its owner. automation-new makes the file yours alone; after a chmod or a share-set that let others write it, chmod 644 and removing the entry are the way out. What an automation's nodes say, in automation-status <name> and its run log, is for its owner (and whoever may change its file) to see: it holds the readings the owner may read.

Key What it is Needed description A sentence for people, which automations shows No enabled false to keep it from running; automation-disable does the same No nodes The nodes, each under an id of its own Yes Each node has: Key What it is type Its kind, below to The nodes it sends to: a list, such as to: [lamp-on] . A node that says true or false also sends on true and false alone: to: {true: [lamp-on], false: [lamp-off]} ; a list sends both. A switch sends on each of its cases and else , by name label A name for people, beside its id pos Where it is drawn, [x, y] and the settings of its kind. An id is letters, digits, - and _ . A node has one input, and any number of nodes may be wired into it. The wires may not go round in a circle. A device's endpoint is written <device>/<endpoint> , as the device's Info tab and device-show name it: hall-sensor/temperature , hall-plug/switch-0 . A time is a number and s , m , h or d : 30s , 10m , 1.5h , 1d .

What goes along a wire is a value: a reading, a word such as single for a press, on or off , a number. A node that asks whether something is true reads on , true , yes , open , a number other than 0 and any other word as true, and off , false , no , closed , 0 and nothing as false. A node that says true or false ( online , compare , and , or , not , timer , held , between ) sends only when what it says changes, so a stream of readings that keep it true does not switch the lamp again and again. every: true on such a node sends each time. and and or read the latest value of each node wired into them; one that has sent nothing yet counts as false.

Inputs , which nothing is wired into: Type Settings It sends device endpoint ; is Each reading of the endpoint, or each press of a button. With is: single , only that value or kind of press (a Shelly's are single , double , triple and long ) online device True when the device comes online, false when it goes clock at: '07:30' and days , or every ; location The time, once a day at at in the system's time zone (on days : weekdays , weekends or [mon, wed, fri] ), or each time every (a minute or more) has passed on the clock between from , until , days ; location True from from until until , false outside it: from: '22:00' , until: '06:30' goes over midnight button value true , or its value , when it is pressed with automation-trigger <name> <node> link-in name What a link-out of the same name sends, from any automation of the same owner file folder ; match , changes The path of each file that comes into folder ( A file in a folder ) event-in event ; under , with The path of the node each event of that type is about ( EiN's events ) A clock 's at and a between 's from and until may follow the sun: sunrise , sunset , dawn or dusk , with an offset such as sunset-30m or sunrise+1h . Dawn and dusk are when the sun is 6° below the horizon (civil twilight), the light a lamp is first or last needed by. The node then takes location , its latitude and longitude, location: '59.33, 18.07' : each node says where its sun is, so an automation for the summer house reckons with the summer house's. In the node's panel, the button beside Location takes the position of the device you edit on, where the browser gives it (over HTTPS). Where the sun does not set that day, as at midsummer far north, a clock at sunset does not go off and a between from sunset until sunrise stays false; where it does not rise, the other way round. Logic : Type Settings It sends compare is , not , above , below Whether the value meets all that are given: below: 30 , is: on , above: 18 with below: 23 and True while everything wired into it is true or True while anything wired into it is true not True when the value is false switch cases The value, on the first case it meets, else on else : cases: {cold: {below: 18}, warm: {above: 23}} sends on cold , warm or else Values : Type Settings It sends math expression A value worked out from the value and the nodes wired in ( Expressions ) aggregate fn : avg , min , max , sum , count , any , all , last The average, least, most or sum of the latest values of the nodes wired in, how many are true, whether any or all are, or the newest set value Its own value instead of the one that came: a word, a number, or text with ${value} in it, as 'the hall is ${value} °C' Time : Type Settings It sends delay for Each value on, for later timer off-after True at once when a true value comes, false off-after after the value went false, or after the last press. Another true value meanwhile holds it on held for True once the value has been true for for , false as soon as it is not debounce for The last value, once none has come for for throttle for At most one value in for , and the newest at its end Actions : Type Settings It does control endpoint ; value Writes the control, as echo on > /dev/hall-lamp/switch-0 does: its value ( on , off , toggle , a number), or else the value that came, true as on and false as off . A control that already has the value is not written again; toggle always is. Then sends the value on shell run ; timeout Runs the command line as the automation's owner ( Lines ) and sends what it printed on link-out name Sends the value to every link-in of that name in the owner's automations event-out event ; subject Raises an event for pipelines, about the node at subject , or at the value that came ( EiN's events ); the administrator's automations only. Then sends the path on debug Writes the value to the run log

A math node works out a value: value * 1.8 + 32 , round(value, 1) , outdoor - indoor , value > 25 ? 'warm' : 'cool' . value is the value that came, topic where it came from ( hall-sensor/temperature ), and each node wired in is its latest value under its id, with - written _ : a node outdoor-temp is outdoor_temp . The node waits until every one it reads has sent something. Numbers, 'text' , true , false , on , off ; + - * / % ( + also joins text); `== != < <= > = ( == reads on as true, as a compare's is does); and , or , not (or && || ! ); a ? b : c`. round(x) or round(x, digits) , floor , ceil , abs , min , max , avg , sum , and clamp(x, low, high) .

A shell node runs any command line you could type in EiN's terminal, as the automation's owner: todo-add to put something on a list, a script of your own, echo on > /dev/heater-plug/switch-0 . The value that came is $VALUE and where it came from $TOPIC ; it never becomes part of the line itself, so a device can say anything without running anything. What the line prints is the value the node sends on, a number when it prints one. A line that fails or runs longer than its timeout (30 s unless set) sends nothing, and its node and the run log say why. An automation's actions run one after another, each when the one before has ended; another automation's do not wait for them.

Besides its devices, EiN says what happens to the things in it as events ( Changes and pipelines ): a photo's metadata was read ( media.metadata.extracted ), its faces were found ( media.faces.completed ), and a pipeline's run on a file started, ended or failed ( pipeline.instance.started , pipeline.instance.completed , pipeline.instance.failed ). An event-in node hears them; an event-out node raises one of its own, for a pipeline that waits for it. description: Note each photo in the Wrenfield album whose places pipeline failed nodes: failed: type: event-in event: pipeline.instance.failed under: /archive/albums/wrenfield-summer-1987 with: pipeline=place-upkeep to: [ note ] note: { type: shell , run: 'echo "$VALUE" >> ~/failed-places.txt' } event names the event. A word may be * , any one word, or # , any number of words: pipeline.instance.* is a run starting, ending or failing, and media.# every fact about media. under keeps only events about a node in that folder, and with only those whose data says so ( pipeline=place-upkeep ; several pairs separated by spaces); a pipeline's events carry its name as pipeline . It sends the path of the node the event is about, with the event's type as where it came from ( $TOPIC to a line, topic to math). It hears only events about a node the automation's owner may read: someone else's photo is not yours to hear of. Events are many while a large import runs. They wait in a queue of their own, so readings and presses are not held up behind them, and only while an automation listens for them. As with readings, those said more than a minute before the engine starts again move its state and do nothing. An event-out node raises its event (dotted words, such as automation.porch.arrived ) about the node at subject , a path, which may hold ${value} and ${topic} ; without one it is the value that came, which must be a path. A pipeline that waits for it ( on: automation.porch.arrived ) runs on that node, and finds the value that came in $EVENT_VALUE , where it came from in $EVENT_TOPIC and the automation's name in $EVENT_AUTOMATION . Since pipelines run as the administrator, only the administrator raises events: another's automation with an event-out is not run, and says so. An event an automation raises reaches pipelines, never another automation, so two cannot set each other off for ever.

Timers count from when a reading came, not from when the engine heard it, and what an automation waits for is kept when the engine stops. So a lamp whose motion ended four minutes before EiN restarted still goes off a minute after it starts again, and a lamp someone switched on by hand an hour after the motion ended is left on. Readings and presses that come while the engine is stopped wait in its queue. Those said more than a minute before it starts again bring the automations up to date but switch nothing: a press from an hour ago does not toggle a lamp now. A time of day that passed meanwhile is not caught up, and a file that came into a folder meanwhile is not sent.

p.h: A tour of every kind of node
p.x: automation/tour , under System → Automations, is the Automation module's own: eight small flows with every kind of node among them, its YAML commented flow by flow (the YAML tab shows it). Its devices are invented ( example-… ), so it switches nothing real, and it comes off. Simulate it with the flask to see each flow work, or start one of your own from it: + beside the list, starting point Tour of every node , or automation-new <name> --from tour , then set your own devices. A motion light: device, compare, not, and, timer, control. A button: a device's Only when it is , a button node, set, and a control that writes the value that came. Temperature bands: debounce, math, debug, switch. An average indoors, shared: aggregate, throttle, link out. What the link brings: link in, held, or, shell. The clock: clock, delay, between, online. A file: file. EiN's events: event in, event out. Only the administrator raises events, so take the event out from a copy of your own. An and, or, math or aggregate keeps the latest value from each node wired into it, so wire a timer's or a compare's out into it (true and false both), as the motion light does, not its true alone: otherwise it holds the last true for ever.

# automation-new heater --from heater description: The heater keeps the hall between 19 and 21 °C while someone is home nodes: temperature: { type: device , endpoint: hall-sensor/temperature , to: [ cold , warm ] } cold: { type: compare , below: 19 , to: [ cold-a-while ] } cold-a-while: { type: held , for: 10m , to: [ heat ] } away: { type: device , endpoint: indoors/away , to: [ home ] } home: { type: not , to: [ heat ] } heat: { type: and , to: { true: [ heater-on ] } } warm: { type: compare , above: 21 , to: [ warm-a-while ] } warm-a-while: { type: held , for: 5m , to: { true: [ heater-off ] } } heater-on: { type: control , endpoint: heater-plug/switch-0 , value: on } heater-off: { type: control , endpoint: heater-plug/switch-0 , value: off } The heater goes on once the hall has been below 19 °C for ten minutes and nobody is away, and off once it has been above 21 °C for five. indoors/away is a switch of a virtual device , which whoever leaves last turns on.

# automation-new porch --from button-toggle description: A press of the porch button switches the hall lamp on or off nodes: press: { type: device , endpoint: porch-button/input-0 , is: single , to: [ toggle ] } try-it: { type: button , label: Try it , to: [ toggle ] } toggle: { type: control , endpoint: hall-lamp/switch-0 , value: toggle } automation-trigger porch try-it presses the button node, to try the automation without the real button.

# automation-new morning --from morning description: The hall lamp on at half past six on weekdays nodes: morning: { type: clock , at: '06:30' , days: weekdays , to: [ lamp-on , note ] } lamp-on: { type: control , endpoint: hall-lamp/switch-0 , value: on } note: { type: shell , run: 'echo "morning at $VALUE"' , to: [ shown ] } shown: { type: debug } Half past six is in the system's time zone ( TZ in ~/ein/.env , Installing in detail ). Write a time in quotes.

# automation-new inbox --from inbox description: Each PDF scanned into the inbox is moved to the documents folder nodes: scan: { type: file , folder: /home/anna/inbox , match: '*.pdf' , to: [ file-it ] } file-it: { type: shell , run: 'mv "$VALUE" /home/anna/documents/ && echo "filed $VALUE"' , to: [ shown ] } shown: { type: debug } Set your own folders: a scanner that saves to /home/helen/inbox over SFTP , say, and /home/helen/documents . A file node sends the whole path of each file that comes into its folder , made there or moved in, as $VALUE to a line, and the folder as $TOPIC : once the file is written in full, two seconds after the last write to it, so a file written in pieces is sent once. A file that stays empty is not sent, nor one removed or renamed before then; a file written under a name of its own and then renamed, as some scanners do, is sent by its new name. only the files directly in the folder, not those in folders under it. only those whose names match match when it is set: * is any text and ? one character, and upper and lower case are alike, so *.pdf takes Scan.PDF too. with changes: true , also each time a file already there is written again. The automation's owner must be allowed to read the folder, and hears only of the files in it they may read: one the administrator puts there that only the administrator may read is not sent.

# automation-new porch-light --from dusk-to-dawn description: The porch lamp on from sunset until sunrise nodes: dark: { type: between , from: sunset , until: sunrise , location: '59.33, 18.07' , to: { true: [ lamp-on ], false: [ lamp-off ] } } lamp-on: { type: control , endpoint: porch-lamp/switch-0 , value: on } lamp-off: { type: control , endpoint: porch-lamp/switch-0 , value: off } Set location to where the lamp is. from: dusk , until: dawn keeps it off through the twilight.

# in EiN's terminal automations # each, whose it is, whether it runs, and why not automation-status hall-light # what each node last sent, and what it waits for log-read /var/logs/automations/hall-light --since 1d An automation's run log, /var/logs/automations/<name> , keeps 30 days of its actions, the errors of those that failed, what its debug nodes were sent, and its clock firings, one JSON line each: 2026-11-09T06:30:00.512Z {"node":"lamp-on","kind":"action","text":"on > hall-lamp/switch-0","at":"2026-11-09T06:30:00.510Z"} Only its owner and the administrator read it. automation-status sums the engine up in a line, automations: 4 running, 41 actions , with a not run: line under it for each automation the engine holds back, and the automation-engine service's line on the Status page's Services tab says the same.

A virtual device is a device of the Automation module's virtual driver: its readings are worked out from other devices' readings, and its switches and settings hold whatever people and automations set them to. It is a device like any other under /dev , with its page, its history and its readings on the bus, and it is shared the same way. This page is for members of the devices group, who make devices. Use one for: A reading of the house, not of one sensor: the average temperature indoors, the warmest room, whether any window is open, how many lamps are on. A switch or a setting with no hardware behind it: away , a guest mode , the temperature the heating aims for, which automations read and set. Something to share in place of what it is made of: the house's average temperature shared with a guest, who sees no single room's sensor.

# in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices device-create indoors --label Indoors --class sensor --driver virtual \ --config 'read=temperature=avg hall-sensor/temperature kitchen-sensor/temperature; open=any front-door/contact back-door/contact' \ --config 'set=away=bool; setpoint=number 5..30 0.5 °C' This makes /dev/indoors with two readings, temperature (the average of the hall's and the kitchen's) and open (true while either door is), and two controls, away (on or off) and setpoint (5 to 30 in steps of 0.5 °C). New device on the Devices page makes one too: pick the virtual driver and fill in its readings and controls as above.

Each reading is name=<what> <device>/<endpoint> <device>/<endpoint> … , separated by ; or new lines. <what> is one of: What The reading is avg The average of the sources' numbers min The lowest max The highest sum Their sum: the power a whole floor draws count How many sources are on (true, open, a number other than 0) any True while any source is on all True while every source is on last The newest source's reading: whichever of two thermometers spoke latest A reading is worked out again whenever one of its sources changes, from the latest reading of each, and kept when it changes. A source that has not reported yet is left out until it does. An average, a lowest, a highest and a sum take the unit of their sources when they share one.

Each control is name=<kind> : Kind It holds bool On or off; toggle turns it over number [min..max] [step] [unit] A number, such as number 5..30 0.5 °C enum <option> <option> … One of the options, such as enum eco comfort off text Any text momentary Nothing: a press, which automations hear, as a button's Switch one as any control, on the device's page or with echo on > /dev/indoors/away ; it holds the value until it is set again. An automation reads it with a device node and sets it with a control node.

The config is the device's own, so changing it is changing its config attr; the driver sets the device up again, adding the readings and controls that are new and removing those that are gone, with their history: # in EiN's terminal, as a member of devices attrs -J 'config={"read": "temperature=avg hall-sensor/temperature kitchen-sensor/temperature bedroom-sensor/temperature", "set": "away=bool"}' /dev/indoors

A virtual device is the devices group's, as every device is, and is shared on its page or with share-set ( Share a device ). Its readings are worked out with the rights of the devices group and nobody's more. A source the group may not read, such as a motion sensor someone has narrowed to the parents, is refused, so a virtual device never shows anyone what its sources would not. A reading it works out is the group's to read, not to write: nobody adds a reading of their own to it.

What you see What it means What to do device-create says the devices group may not read hall-sensor/motion, or there is no such endpoint The source is misspelt, gone, or narrowed to some people Correct it with device-show , or leave it out its readings go round in a circle: indoors → upstairs → indoors A virtual device reads itself, or two read each other Read the sources themselves the reading temperature takes one of avg, min, … <what> is misspelt or missing Use one from Readings The device is offline The automation-engine service, which runs the driver, is stopped, or its config stopped working service start automation-engine , as the administrator; service logs automation-engine says why A reading stays empty None of its sources has reported since the device was made It fills in at their next reading

Make something found on the network a device: a Shelly is pointed at the broker and restarted, a camera, a printer, a Cast speaker or anything else is added with a driver that asks it itself (for members of the devices group) changes things automation-adopt [--user=<string>] [--password=<string>] <id> Argument What it is <id> what automation-found calls it: its hardware address without colons, or its IP. Option What it does --user=<string> an ONVIF camera's user. --password=<string> an ONVIF camera's password, kept in the device's secret. automation-adopt a8032ab12345 automation-adopt 7c2ebd614055 automation-adopt ec71db0a1b2c --user admin --password s3cret With JSON_OUTPUT=1 : AdoptAnswer: id, label, driver, broker, restarted, device.
